title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now runs the harness and model requests in the same process as your application. Built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

The adapter uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. It no longer needs to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host rather than being forwarded into the sandbox.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: From Single Incident to Standing Inventory: Continuous External Monitoring of SaaS Vendor Edges
description:
From Single Incident to Standing Inventory: Continuous External Monitoring of SaaS Vendor Edges

Incident response ends, and the questions that came up during it get filed away. For the organisations affected by the ConnectWise Cloud Backup suspension, the questions were predictable: which of our tools depend on that vendor, which of our tenants hold its application consent, and what would we watch if this happened again.

The third question is the one that produces lasting value. This article describes a monitoring routine that can be run against a vendor estate on a schedule, using external search for what is published and tenant-side exports for what is granted. Both halves are needed, and neither is sufficient.

The split between observable and internal

External search engines index what is reachable on the internet. A vendor's marketing site, status page, documentation hosts and administration portals appear. The application registration that can authenticate into customer tenants does not. It has no listening service, no certificate and no hostname.

The October incident is a clean demonstration. The abused credential was a client assertion held in the vendor tenant, and the activity was recorded in Microsoft's own sign-in logs. Not one of those facts is discoverable by scanning.

So the routine has two sensors, and they answer different questions.

Sensor one: external estate baseline

Run a fixed query set against the vendor domain on a schedule and store the results with timestamps. For ConnectWise on 28 October 2026, a reference set looked like this.

Query Count Change signal to watch
domain="connectwise.com" 170 Large jumps suggest new exposure or a hostile lookalike
domain="connectwise.com" && country="US" 141 Geographic drift
domain="connectwise.com" && port="443" 76 Unexplained growth in HTTPS listeners
domain="connectwise.com" && port="8443" 28 Administrative surfaces appearing publicly
domain="connectwise.com" && title="login" 11 New authentication pages

Two disciplines make this useful rather than decorative. First, keep the query strings identical across runs so the comparison is like for like; a changed dork produces a changed number for reasons that have nothing to do with the vendor. Second, record zeros and mis-specified fields honestly. app="ConnectWise" returned 0 and domain="connectwise.com" && service="ssl" returned 0, while port 443 within the same domain returned 76. The zeros describe field population, not the absence of TLS.

Sensor two: consent inventory export

The internal half is a periodic export of enterprise applications, their granted Graph scopes, assigned directory roles, and the credentials attached to each. This is the register that answers the question external measurement cannot: what can this vendor's application do inside our tenant right now.

Frequency matters less than comparability. A monthly export taken with the same script produces a diffable record. The diff is where findings appear: a new client secret on a vendor application, a new Global Administrator assignment to a service principal, a consent grant nobody remembers approving.

Joining the two

The value of holding both is that they let an organisation reason about dependency with evidence instead of instinct. When a vendor discloses an incident, three questions can be answered from the register in sequence. Which of our tenants hold the affected application? Which of those depend on it for a function we cannot perform otherwise? Which service principals in those tenants hold elevated roles that would matter if the application were abused?

None of this requires knowing anything about the attacker. It requires knowing what was granted.

A note on watch duration

The ConnectWise incident remains open in one respect: the vendor has not published a restoration timeline, and partners were asked to verify that no configuration changes or persistence remained in their tenants. A monitoring routine should therefore treat post-incident review as a sustained activity rather than a single pass. Configuration changes made during the intrusion window can surface later, and a diff-based register is the instrument that catches them.

Limits

External counts describe exposed services at a point in time and cannot detect compromise. Internal exports describe grants and configuration, not the use of those grants, which lives in sign-in and audit logs. A monitoring programme built only on the first sensor produces reassuring dashboards and little security value; one built only on the second sees changes without knowing whether the vendor's own estate shifted underneath it.

References

  • SecurityWeek, "ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Services in Response to Cyberattack", https://www.securityweek.com/connectwise-suspends-cloud-services-in-response-to-cyberattack/
  • Huntress, "Vendor Credential Enables Unauthorized Access", https://www.huntress.com/blog/vendor-credential-enables-unauthorized-access
  • ConnectWise Cloud Backup technical investigation and remediation guide, https://www.connectwise.com/contentassets/10777cd3364d440c86ed5270a94a5f24/connectwise-cloud-backup-technical-investigation-and-remediation-guide-1.pdf
  • ZoomEye search syntax reference, https://zoomeye.ai/agent.md

title: DocSkill: Skill-Integrated Agentic Reasoning for Multilingual Multi-Hop Document Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.36759v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multilingual multi-hop document question answering (MMHop-DocQA) requires locating and integrating evidence across complex layouts, document pages, and diverse languages. Existing approaches include single-pass processing and adaptive tool use, but learning to coordinate evidence acquisition, cross-page integration, and answer verification remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present DocSkill, an agentic framework with a learned skill-orchestration policy for adaptive evidence acquisition and reasoning. The policy selects, revisits, or skips skills according to the evolving evidence state. To construct supervision for skill orchestration, bounded Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores alternative skill trajectories offline. These trajectories provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further introduce MMHop-DocBench, a multilingual multi-hop document QA dataset with training and test splits, containing 60K QA pairs across 10 languages and eight document domains. Its HopGen pipeline builds hierarchical page-element graphs to derive traceable cross-page evidence paths and generate grounded QA pairs with page- and element-level evidence annotations. Experiments show that DocSkill with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1 on MMHop-DocBench, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points, respectively, and achieving competitive performance on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench.

title: Vision Token Pruning via Query-Vision Interaction Decomposition
description:
arXiv:2610.33215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs), which process both visual inputs and text queries, incur high inference costs due to the large number of visual tokens, making visual token pruning a natural approach for improving efficiency. Recent work has leveraged query information to guide token selection, often through heuristics derived from attention patterns or token dynamics. However, these approaches do not explicitly exploit the underlying structure of query-vision interactions. We address this gap by observing that the query-vision interaction matrix, naturally induced by the query and key projections already present in transformer attention, is effectively low-rank, with a small number of dominant latent interaction modes capturing query-relevant semantics. Motivated by this observation, we propose Query-Vision Decomposition (QViD), a novel training-free query-aware visual token pruning method that exploits this structure. Extensive experiments on both image and video understanding benchmarks show that QViD consistently improves performance under matched token budgets, with the largest gains appearing under aggressive compression regimes.

title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
description:
arXiv:2610.36116v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

title: The 2026 Shift to Sovereign On-Premise AI: Why Mid-Market Enterprises Are Leaving Cloud Wrappers
description:
The 2026 Shift to Sovereign On-Premise AI: Why Mid-Market Enterprises Are Leaving Cloud Wrappers

Across North America and the European Union, enterprise engineering leaders face a mounting crisis: cloud AI lock-in, data sovereignty compliance (EU AI Act, GDPR), and unpredictable API latency.

Relying on public SaaS LLM endpoints for mission-critical workflows introduces severe operational vulnerabilities:

  • Regulatory & Data Sovereignty Exposure: Proprietary data transmitted to multi-tenant cloud APIs violates confidentiality and strict regional residency mandates.
  • Cascading Downtime & Latency Spikes: Upstream cloud outages and rate limits directly halt customer-facing automations.
  • Escalating Token Economics: Uncontrolled inference charges scale linearly with business growth, creating runaway operational expenditures.

To mitigate these risks, mid-market manufacturers, healthcare networks, and technical services are migrating to Sovereign On-Premise AI Infrastructure.

1. What Is Sovereign AI Infrastructure?

Sovereign AI is the deployment of autonomous intelligence on dedicated, private compute—either inside local private clouds or on-premise hardware behind strict zero-trust boundaries:

[ Local Business Operations / CNC / ERP ]
                   |
            (Private Mesh)
                   v
[ Dedicated On-Premise AI Enclave ]
   ├── Local High-Throughput Model Routing (<5ms TTFT)
   ├── Private Knowledge Graphs (Neo4j / GraphRAG)
   └── Sandboxed Task Execution (Zero Public SaaS Leakage)
                   |
            (Verified Output)
                   v
[ Mission-Critical Production Systems ]

Why Mid-Market Teams Are Adopting This Architecture:

  1. Predictable Sub-10ms Latency: Local inference gateways and Redis caching eliminate the 500ms–2000ms latency overhead typical of public cloud APIs.
  2. Fixed-Cost Unit Economics: Replacing variable per-token pricing with dedicated hardware allows unlimited autonomous processing at zero marginal cost.
  3. Absolute Data Enclave: Codebases, customer records, and proprietary schematics never leave the organization's firewall.

2. Bridging Cyber-Physical & Industrial Telemetry

The most lucrative application of sovereign AI is in industrial automation and modern CNC machining facilities.

Legacy manufacturing hubs operating precision CNC equipment (such as FANUC, Siemens, or Heidenhain controllers) generate massive operational telemetry. Bridging these closed-loop controllers to modern real-time WebGL monitoring and predictive anomaly detection unlocks:

  • Real-time spindle load and vibration anomaly detection.
  • Automated G-code validation before physical machine execution.
  • Sub-second factory floor telemetry dispatch without exposing machine networks to the public internet.

3. How to Evaluate Your Organization's Sovereign AI Readiness

Before committing capital to AI infrastructure, evaluate these four baseline criteria:

  1. Data Sensitivity Audit: Do your internal datasets contain regulated IP, client PII, or confidential manufacturing parameters?
  2. Network Perimeter Hardening: Can your existing edge ingress (Caddy/Nginx) enforce Zero-Trust OAuth2 boundaries for model endpoints?
  3. Task Determinism vs. Hallucination: Are your automated agents guarded by deterministic validation gates and E2E acceptance suites?
  4. Local Search & Discovery Indexing: For local B2B service providers, are your localized endpoints structured for instant machine discoverability?

4. Run a Free Technical Diagnostic

title: Frugal Handwritten Text Recognition for Sub-Saharan Civil-Status Registers: A Smartphone-to-Records Pipeline with CPU-Only Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.36540v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Handwritten civil-status registers across Sub-Saharan Africa are being photographed, but rarely transcribed, which leaves their content unsearchable. Local administrations that hold these records typically lack GPUs, reliable connectivity, and the budget for external digitization services. We study whether a frugal pipeline, with consumer-grade capture and CPU-only inference, can make such registers machine-readable. We introduce a corpus of 1,568 smartphone images of handwritten birth, marriage, and death records from a municipal registry in Chad, with line-level transcriptions for 185 records. Our pipeline combines a fully classical preprocessing stage, running at about 2.6 images per second on a laptop CPU, with a Kraken recognizer fine-tuned from a pretrained model in about four hours on a free-tier GPU. On manually corrected line segmentation and a single-registry test set whose writers also appear in training, fine-tuning reduces the character error rate from 14.53% to 0.50% and the word error rate from 56.93% to 3.37%. On a six-core laptop CPU, the recognizer weighs 61 MiB, peaks below 2.6 GiB of RAM, and processes an image in under 6 s on average, excluding line segmentation. Finally, a downstream information-extraction task shows that residual recognition errors cost about 9 F1 points on role resolution, compared with a 36.7-point gap between the fine-tuned and pretrained recognizers. These results are evidence of feasibility within one registry, not of performance on unseen writers or sites; we discuss these limitations in detail.

title: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984)
description:
arXiv:2610.36341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early AI programs were often also theories of how people think, and programs that wrote programs were, in part, theories of how people program. Here we report on the reanimation of two such programs that offer two seemingly different theories of programming and were developed for quite different purposes. The first, Herbert Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961), was an experimental model of programming as problem-solving, applying the means-ends analysis methods of the General Problem Solver to investigate the nature of the programming task. The second, KBEmacs (1984), was a working prototype of an intelligent programming assistant developed by MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project, built on the view that expert programmers recognize and combine familiar patterns, or "cliches." It let a programmer build up programs by combining cliches through a stylized English command language. We approach both through the methodology of Executable Archaeology, the study of historical computational systems by running their original code, a process we call "reanimation." Our reanimation of the Heuristic Compiler reproduces the compiled code appearing in Simon's 1963 paper, and our reanimation of KBEmacs reproduces the SQRT sequence of its December 1984 self-test. Examined side by side, the two theories turn out to have much in common: the Heuristic Compiler also works by adapting existing routines, and Simon later argued that search alone requires a large body of programming knowledge. To highlight the reflexivity of this project, we deliberately used a modern AI-assisted programming tool, Anthropic's Claude Code (Opus 5.5), to carry out much of the detailed reanimation work, building on a significant base of existing software. The explicit, executable theories of programming that both systems embodied are largely absent from today's far more capable AI coding assistants.

title: How Much Fresh Data Should CTR Recalibration Use? A Temporal Evaluation of Post-hoc Calibration
description:
arXiv:2610.33168v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline evaluation of click-through rate (CTR) models still defaults to random splits, although deployed models score future traffic and downstream systems consume calibrated probabilities. On Avazu (40.4M impressions) we train logistic regression (LR), DeepFM, and DCN-v2 under two rolling temporal origins and a random split, three seeds per arm, and recalibrate each test day with Platt scaling and isotonic regression fitted on the preceding hours. At origin 1's nearest test day, random splits report LR's expected calibration error (ECE) at 55-62% of the temporal value in every seed (the deep models' ratio is seed-unstable), and no model's ECE is monotone in temporal distance. With a 6-hour fitting slice, recalibration removes up to 61% of ECE in badly miscalibrated cells but increases it in about a third of applications (14-17 of 48 across seeds). On fixed evaluation sets, a 12-hour slice cuts harm from 13-17 to 3-5 of 36 applications, and 24 hours raises it again. The 12-hour slice subsampled to the 1-hour slice's size (5% of the impressions; 20-25x faster to fit) recovers 88% of the full slice's gain, so impression count alone does not explain it. A slice-ECE gate shows no benefit out-of-origin, and in a simulated auction recalibration moves profit by only about -0.21% to +0.26%. Offline protocols should measure calibration temporally, over multiple origins and seeds; in this data, recalibration fitted on a wide time span beat the freshest few hours, which other logs must confirm.

title: Password Reset Email APIs: 3 Template and Bounce Checks for Marketplaces
description:
TL;DR: Put the email provider at the send boundary. A Node.js marketplace service should own reset tokens, expiry, account policy, and suppression decisions; the provider should own template rendering and delivery attempts. Choose the option that leaves evidence for which recipient was sent, which one bounced, and why the next attempt was blocked.

A password-reset message is small but operationally sharp. A bad link locks out a seller. A retry to a hard-bounced address turns one dirty record into a reputation problem. At 3am, I do not want a green dashboard; I want to know which page fired and whether the audit trail supports the decision.

What should the boundary prove?

The boundary should prove three things: a known template was selected, a send attempt was made, and later bounce or suppression evidence changed recipient state without re-enabling the address accidentally. Keep token generation, single-use enforcement, expiry, and account policy in the application. Send only approved variables to the mail system, and never put the raw reset token in logs.

Templates keep formatting consistent while the service supplies controlled values. Create or update one during deployment, record its revision in configuration, and make the request path select a known revision instead of creating content under load. For compliance evidence, retain the account identifier, protected reset-request reference, template revision, provider request identifier, event status, and suppression decision.

Infrai belongs at this boundary when the team wants a plain REST API. It exposes a public discovery surface without a key, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that is useful when a marketplace has several small services and does not want each one to learn a different client library.

The short version: keep the policy local, make the handoff observable.

Not enough.

Page first.

Which email API supports template-based password reset without hiding the handoff?

SendGrid is a broad email platform with template and event-oriented tooling. Postmark is commonly evaluated for transactional mail, where a focused product-mail workflow is the important boundary. Amazon SES suits teams already operating in AWS and willing to make identity and configuration part of that environment. Mailgun is another API-first option for programmable sending and delivery operations. These are real alternatives; their surrounding assumptions matter more than a generic best-provider label.

An AWS-heavy team may accept SES configuration that would feel like platform work elsewhere. A team separating product mail from campaigns may prefer Postmark. A team wanting a broader communications console may choose SendGrid, while an API-centered operation may evaluate Mailgun. The fair test is whether the option correlates with the application record and whether the team can recover when event evidence arrives late.

Option Integration shape Good fit Boundary to verify
Infrai REST, one key A small service that wants template and send calls over HTTP Pull-based event handling; no hosted email OTP
SendGrid API and platform tooling Teams wanting broad email operations Keep product-mail evidence joined to the application record
Postmark Transactional-mail workflow Teams separating product mail from campaigns Confirm the event records meet the compliance process
Amazon SES AWS-centered service Teams already standardizing identity and configuration in AWS Accept the surrounding AWS operational work
Mailgun API-first mail operations Teams centered on programmable sending Validate correlation and suppression behavior

For this workflow, Infrai fits the template-and-send boundary when a plain REST API is preferable to maintaining another SDK or client-library version. Its documented surface includes /v1/email/template/create for a reusable template and /v1/email/send for delivery, so a Node.js service can make the handoff with ordinary HTTP while keeping token and account policy local. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples across languages reduce client-specific integration knowledge.

Recommendation: try Infrai for a marketplace reset-mail boundary when one HTTP surface and an application-owned suppression decision matter most; choose SES, Postmark, SendGrid, or Mailgun when an existing contract, provider-specific event workflow, or specialist compliance process is the deciding constraint.

The plain API does not solve token security or audit design. It makes the handoff smaller. Infrai is a poor fit if your organization requires a specialist provider contract, webhook-driven orchestration, or a managed email OTP product; choose the provider whose boundary supplies that requirement.

That is a real limitation, not a footnote. The lack of webhook pushes means this choice is worse for a workflow that needs immediate event fan-out; Postmark, SendGrid, SES, or Mailgun may be the better choice when their existing event integration is already part of the compliance evidence.

The operational case is also deliberately narrow. A marketplace may have a long-lived account, several regions, and different retention rules; stuffing all of that into a mail API would make ownership unclear. Keep the durable evidence in the application, poll on a defined schedule, and accept that a REST handoff does not provide real-time orchestration by itself. That boundary is less convenient than a managed workflow, but it is easier to review when a reset request is disputed months later.

The rollback decision should fit on one line.

Here is a minimal Go client for the template-create handoff. The request JSON is supplied by deployment configuration because the exact template fields belong to the capability schema, not to this runbook. It still handles the operational parts that are easy to get wrong: bearer authentication, an explicit method, a stable idempotency key, non-2xx responses, and bounded 429 backoff.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := os.Getenv("INFRAI_TEMPLATE_JSON")
    if key == "" || body == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_TEMPLATE_JSON are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/template/create", bytes.NewBufferString(body))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "marketplace-password-reset-template-v1")

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { panic(readErr) }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("template create failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, data))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(data))
        return
    }
    panic("template create remained rate-limited after retries")
}

How should the reset flow handle a failed send?

  1. Validate and rate-limit the request in the marketplace service.
  2. Generate one reset state and a one-use token.
  3. Select the deployed template revision and approved variables.
  4. Send the message and persist provider and operation identifiers together.
  5. Pull event or status data on a durable schedule.
  6. Transition invalid recipients to suppression idempotently.
  7. Consult suppression state before future reset sends.

Both namespaces use pull-based events rather than webhook pushes, which limits real-time orchestration. A worker needs a durable checkpoint and idempotent processing. A repeated event must not create a second state transition, and a delayed event must not be mistaken for proof that an address is healthy.

There is no hosted email OTP interface here. Build email-code fallback, expiry, attempt limits, and replay protection in the application. SMS OTP is a separate capability, not evidence that email has the same managed flow.

One more boundary is easy to miss: scheduled email has no cancellation route, so do not model a scheduled reset message as freely retractable. For a password reset, immediate send plus application-side expiry is easier to reason about.

Verification and rollback

Test an accepting mailbox, a known bounce in the selected provider's test procedure, and an already-suppressed address. Verify that template revision, provider identifier, and application operation identifier join without exposing the reset token. Replay the same event and confirm that suppression remains one idempotent state.

Watch the question that matters: what page fired? Alert on a growing gap between send attempts and processed event records, repeated retries for one operation, and reset requests rejected by suppression policy. Keep the previous template revision available. If correlation or suppression processing fails, stop new traffic through the new boundary and switch configuration back; do not delete audit records or unsuppress recipients as a shortcut.

SPF is sender authorization, not proof that a reset request was valid or that a bounced address was handled correctly. Domain configuration, event data, application records, suppression transitions, and access controls need to tell one consistent story. If this boundary fits, start with the email API documentation and validate polling and suppression in a non-production mailbox.

References

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • SendGrid Email API: https://docs.sendgrid.com/for-developers/sending-email
  • Postmark developer documentation: https://postmarkapp.com/developer
  • Amazon SES developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • Mailgun API documentation: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/send/mailgun-messages

title: Turn a Repeated Manual Correction into a Testable Requirement
description:
The report is correct because someone fixed it before it left the team.

If you test only the final report, you can miss the repair that made it correct.

Consider a fictional application that exports service records. A reviewer repeatedly corrects one field before the export is used. That is a useful starting point for an engineering investigation, but it does not yet tell you whether the cause is data, code, an integration or an undocumented business rule.

This article proposes a workflow using synthetic examples. It does not report an executed benchmark or a client outcome.

Record the correction before choosing a fix

Capture the original value, corrected value, reason and reference used by the reviewer. Give the example a stable identifier so the input, stored record and output can be compared without relying on memory.

Ask whether the correction is deterministic or requires judgement. A field transformation and an exception that requires approval need different acceptance criteria.

Do not use the reviewer's correction as an unquestioned oracle. Establish the applicable rule and source with the person responsible for the workflow.

Locate where the mismatch enters

Inspect the smallest relevant path through the application. Compare the approved input with the persisted record, screen and exported result.

Observation Question to investigate
Input is already wrong Does the capture step need validation or clarification?
Input is right, stored value differs Is a mapping or write path changing it?
Stored value is right, export differs Does the export apply an obsolete transformation?
Outputs agree, reviewer still changes them Is the business rule missing, disputed or context-dependent?

These are investigation prompts, not diagnoses. Keep enough evidence to distinguish them before editing code.

Write the acceptance condition

Replace “fix the export” with a condition a reviewer can assess. Identify the approved fixture, applicable rule, expected stored value and expected output.

Include the unresolved case. If the source does not establish the correct value, decide whether the application should request clarification, retain an explicit pending state or route the task for review.

Preserve intentional human decisions. Automating a guessed value can conceal uncertainty rather than resolve the original problem.

Check what happens after correction

In the fictional application, a reviewer may fix the preview while the export continues to read an earlier record. Test the save and later output, not only the editable field.

If a correction should update a durable record, verify that record. If it should apply only to a specific output, test that boundary too. The expected behaviour depends on the agreed workflow.

Use isolated test data and controlled destinations. A test should not require sending real customer material to discover whether a correction persisted.

Add AI review evidence when relevant

If an AI step creates the value or draft, record where a reviewer intervenes and why. Distinguish factual repair, formatting preferences and decisions that require human authority.

A count of edits alone can be misleading. One identifier correction may matter more than several stylistic changes. Define the rubric around the task and report the conditions and coverage limits.

Keep deterministic assertions on stored fields separate from evaluations of generated wording where practical. Retain fixture revisions and the relevant configuration so another engineer can investigate a failure.

Verify the change and document the boundary

After implementing a scoped fix, rerun the agreed cases and relevant regressions. Compare the original input, saved state and final output.

Document what changed, what passed, what remains manual and what was not tested. A small verified change can be useful without claiming that the whole workflow has become autonomous.

title: How Aerial Photography Helps Buyers Understand a Neighbourhood Before They Visit
description:
In modern real estate, the initial showing almost always happens online. Before buyers commit time to traveling for a physical walkthrough, they evaluate whether a home aligns with their daily routine, family needs, and long-term lifestyle. While standard listing photos highlight interior finishes, they fail to reveal what it actually feels like to live in the surrounding neighborhood.

Leveraging specialized overhead media solves this information gap. By providing comprehensive spatial context, elevated views empower buyers to evaluate an entire community before stepping foot on the property.

The Challenge: The Blind Spots of Traditional Property Photography

When prospective buyers search for homes online—especially those relocating from interstate or overseas—ground-level photos and static street maps present clear limitations:

Incomplete Community Context: Standard photos rarely show how close a home sits to school zones, busy arterial roads, commercial hubs, or green spaces.

Abstract Map Data: 2D mapping tools show distances as numbers, but fail to show topography, tree canopy, neighborhood density, or visual appeal.

Inefficient Inspection Cycles: Buyers spend hours traveling to physical open homes only to discover the immediate surroundings don't meet their needs.

The Solution: Clear Neighborhood Context from Above

Elevated visual media bridges the gap between home inspections and geographic awareness. High-altitude and drone captures transform how buyers assess location quality by making spatial relationships instantly clear.

Using comprehensive spatial media delivers key advantages for property researchers:

Instant Infrastructure Awareness: Buyers can immediately pinpoint local amenities—such as coastal pathways, parks, transport links, and shopping precincts—in relation to property boundaries.

Topographical and Density Insights: Overhead views reveal neighborhood layout, privacy levels relative to adjoining lots, and streetscape design.

On-Demand Access to Local Archives: Sourcing established libraries of aerial photos of Australia allows property platforms and agencies to provide instant location context for virtually any suburb nationwide.

Delivering Uncompromising Visual Integrity

To make an accurate remote assessment, buyers require images that remain crisp when zoomed in to examine nearby streets and landmarks. Incorporating files with the highest image quality ensures every lot line, road connection, and natural feature is clearly defined.

Real estate agencies and digital portals rely on dedicated providers of aerial photography in Australia to back their digital listings. By embedding high-quality aerial images directly into listing portals, agents simplify the research process for buyers, attract more qualified leads, and reduce wasted open-house visits.

title: Follow the Herd: A Data-Driven Approach for Actionable Recourse
description:
arXiv:2610.36580v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As machine learning systems make increasingly greater decisions about people's lives, it is critical to provide users with actionable recourse about how they can achieve their desired outcomes. This problem is currently tackled by relying on expensive human supervision which involves hand-designing a cost function before searching for low-cost actions that achieve the desired outcome. In this paper, we propose \textit{``Data-Driven Action Recourse"} (DDAR), the first approach for providing action recourse without requiring costly supervision from humans about action costs. We build upon the notion that highly likely trajectories in the historical user data should be associated with lower costs. With this, DDAR first builds a dynamics model of historical user trajectories. Under this model, it then searches for trajectories that achieve the desired outcome. In experiments, we find that this simple approach recommends plausible action recourse without requiring human supervision, achieving lower action costs than the existing approaches.

title: Overlap-Aware Sub-hypergraph Pattern Frequencies for Hypergraph-Level Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.33514v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Classifying whole hypergraphs requires a fixed-length description of inputs whose numbers of vertices and hyperedges vary. Frequent sub-hypergraph patterns provide such a description, but previous work records only whether each pattern is present, which loses two kinds of information: how large the overlap between two hyperedges is, and how much of a hypergraph each pattern makes up. We extend frequent sub-hypergraph mining with overlap labels, the binned intersection size of two pattern hyperedges inherited from the target hypergraph, and represent each hypergraph by the relative frequency of each mined pattern. The vocabulary is mined from training hypergraphs only and then frozen, and validation and test hypergraphs are matched against it. A support rule that depends on pattern size keeps the vocabulary small. On the six hypergraph-classification datasets of DHG-Bench, with a single configuration chosen on validation scores, the method has a higher mean Macro-F1 than the best published mean on five datasets, by 18.67 points on Twitter-Friend and 10.02 points on Steam-Player; on RHG-3 it is 0.21 points lower. Ablations show that on Steam-Player and Twitter-Friend, replacing relative frequencies with presence lowers Macro-F1 by about 18 points, and that removing overlap labels lowers it by 4 to 9 points.

title: A rental yield calculator should show the scenario that loses money
description:
A positive rental yield is easy to demonstrate with a friendly input. The more useful question for a property-data tool is what happens when occupancy falls while fixed costs and loan payments remain due.

We added a browser-based Rental Cashflow Stress Lab to our existing open-source calculator. It compares explicit scenarios instead of replacing uncertain inputs with country presets.

This is a project from NovAsia Estate, where our property research covers Cambodia, Thailand and Bali. All the figures below are synthetic test inputs, not observations about those markets.

Keep capacity rent separate from collected rent

The input we call full-occupancy rent is a capacity assumption:

scenario capacity = full-occupancy annual rent × rent-level multiplier
collected annual rent = scenario capacity × occupancy

For example, 24,000 at 70% occupancy becomes 16,800 of collected annual rent. A downside scenario uses a lower rent level of 85% and occupancy of 35%, giving 7,140.

This simple annual fraction does not model seasonality, cancellation patterns or the difference between asking and achieved rent. Making that limitation explicit is preferable to presenting the result as a forecast.

Fixed costs should survive zero occupancy

Our example has 1,200 of annual common-area charges, 500 of other fixed costs and 6,000 of annual debt service. Management and maintenance-reserve assumptions are 20% and 5% of collected rent.

The core engine calculates operating income and applies the caller's chosen simplified tax base. The stress extension subtracts debt service afterwards. It does not infer tax deductibility of interest, depreciation, a loan balance or an equity-return denominator.

With an illustrative 10% tax on positive operating profit, the three fixture outcomes are:

Scenario Occupancy Rent level Fixed-cost level Net annual cash flow after debt
Base 70% 100% 100% 3,810
Vacancy shock 35% 85% 125% -3,093
Stronger demand 90% 110% 100% 8,508

At zero occupancy, those original fixed costs and debt still produce a loss of 7,700. The tool retains that number. A missing cost is an input error; zero must be entered deliberately.

Break-even needs the same assumptions as the comparison

Let F be fixed operating costs, D annual debt service, k the fraction of collected rent remaining after management and reserve, and t the supplied tax rate.

For a gross-rent tax assumption, the continuous threshold is (F + D) / (k - t) when the retained margin is positive.

For tax on positive operating profit, with k > 0 and t < 1, it is (F + D / (1 - t)) / k.

The example's base case needs about 11,155.56 of collected annual rent, or about 46.48% of its stated capacity. A requirement above 100% occupancy means the entered rent capacity cannot cover the costs. Impossible margins and zero capacity have explicit states rather than a misleading percentage. The exact edge cases, including 100% tax and zero costs, are covered by tests.

These thresholds are approximate continuous results before cent rounding. Breaking even is not the same as earning a positive return.

Keep the experiment reproducible

The extension uses the same engine as the original calculator:

const Stress = require('./docs/stress.js');
const input = require('./examples/stress.json');
const report = Stress.compare(
  input.base,
  input.annualDebtService,
  input.scenarios
);
console.log(report.rows.map(row => [row.name, row.netAfterDebt]));

The source repository contains the fixture and 36 passing contracts, including zero rent, retained losses, both tax bases, impossible break-even states, CSV formula protection and browser/Node consistency. JSON exports retain the assumptions and itemized core results. Browser inputs are calculated locally without upload requests.

For the earlier acquisition stage, our Payment Milestone Studio allocates dated installments with exact integer arithmetic. That is a separate problem: a purchase payment schedule does not establish rental income.

The Stress Lab is a repository and browser extension. The published novasia-sea-yield npm package remains version 2.0.1; we are not describing unshipped npm exports. Contributions that make assumptions clearer are welcome.

title: Neyman Orthogonal Activation Steering
description:
arXiv:2610.33217v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering is a popular approach for shifting LLM output toward a desired behavior, and increasingly for generating realistic synthetic data. The standard recipe estimates a steering direction by contrasting LLM activations on prompts with and without a target concept, such as truthfulness. In this paper, we separate the estimand (the steering direction these methods target) from the estimator used to recover it, two notions the literature often conflates. We frame nearly all existing methods as plug-in estimators of the average gradient of an outcome regression, with the binary contrastive label fixed as the outcome. Using this framing, we can immediately incorporate flexible modeling approaches and extend existing methods to allow for continuous outcomes such as log-probabilities or oracle ratings. Flexible ML models that fit the outcome well, however, might not estimate the gradient well, which motivates estimators that target the gradient directly. Drawing on the debiased machine learning literature, we develop a complementary estimator built on the Stein score, the Riesz representer of the gradient functional. Combining the two routes gives an orthogonalized estimator with classical double-robustness properties. We illustrate the framework on activation steering applied to a number of benchmark datasets.

title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.36545v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.

title: Plenty of Room in the Middle: Revealing Opportunities on a GPU Cluster via Fine-Grained Monitoring
description:
arXiv:2610.36329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GPU clusters have become essential computing resources for AI and scientific research in academia and industry. However, their high cost and growing demand often result in long queueing delays. While previous monitoring efforts have operated at second- or minute-level frequencies, they primarily informed job-level scheduling for clusters and lacked the detail needed to optimize GPU-level utilization.
  This paper presents an in-depth study of a university research GPU cluster, analyzing resource usage at 100 ms intervals. We have developed a lightweight monitoring tool that leverages Nvidia's DCGM library to capture fine-grained "compute utilization" metrics within GPUs. Deployed on a cluster with 89 nodes and 319 GPUs, our tool collected data over several months. This paper focuses on a 10-day period with 7,399 jobs submitted by 150 users from 12 departments. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) the GPU cluster exhibits significant underutilization, with over 70% of jobs using less than 20% of GPU memory and 50% averaging below 5% Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization; (2) 80% of jobs have a drastic mismatch between their requested and actual durations, significantly limiting the scheduler's effectiveness; and (3) the multi-GPU jobs we examined show highly periodic communication patterns. These findings suggest there is plenty of room in the middle: substantial utilization gains are available through better job scheduling and GPU multitasking, independent of hardware or application improvements.
  Our monitoring solution is available as open-source software at https://github.com/als244/gpu_server_monitoring.

title: AI SDK harness layer now supports native subscription authentication
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports authenticating harnesses through their native subscriptions, where the underlying harness supports them. The harness layer runs different coding agents through the same HarnessAgent interface, so you can switch agents without changing your application code.

No code changes or new settings are required. The direct authentication mode uses explicit provider environment credentials when they are present, and otherwise a native subscription found on the host. The default auto mode does the same when no AI Gateway credentials are set. The ai-gateway mode never reads native subscriptions.

Native subscription credentials stay on the host. Just like with API keys, credentials are resolved at the host boundary. OAuth access tokens are refreshed there as needed. Where the sandbox supports it, the harness receives placeholder credentials and the real token is injected into outbound requests on the host.

Native subscriptions work across harness adapters wherever the harness itself supports subscription login. These include Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Pi.

title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.36570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using language agents increasingly modify external systems, yet most runtime safeguards allocate scrutiny by generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics. We introduce CASEL (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer), a model-agnostic runtime allocation policy that combines calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness to choose, for each proposed tool call, among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, approval, and abstention by minimizing a per-mode cost. We formalize direct execution as selective prediction and state and test the validity conditions of a finite-sample threshold and a trajectory risk ledger. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, in which every method has the same intervention menu and the same compute cost, CASEL reduces harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75 percent for an uncertainty-ranked gate to 7.02 percent and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123. A gate ranked by the product of failure probability and consequence reaches similar harm (5.82 percent, 0.120) but sends 45 percent more actions to human approval, and removing reversibility-aware routing raises the rate to 15.53 percent. A trajectory-level risk budget, in contrast, increases harm at equal cost (11.82 percent). Intervention effectiveness is assumed, not measured: the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

Build a Complete SaaS Product with a Shadcn Dashboard

A great SaaS product needs more than a polished landing page. Once users sign up, they'll interact with dashboards, analytics, billing, settings, user management, and other application screens. Pairing your marketing website with a production-ready Shadcn Dashboard helps create a consistent experience from the homepage to the product itself.

Shadcn dashboards are built with reusable UI components, responsive layouts, modern navigation patterns, and application-focused pages that make it easier to build internal tools, SaaS platforms, admin panels, and customer portals. Whether you're building an AI platform, CRM, finance application, project management tool, or analytics product, combining a Shadcn SaaS template with a modern Shadcn Dashboard gives you a complete foundation for launching faster while keeping one design system across your entire product.

For AI-focused SaaS businesses, improving how their content and products appear across AI-driven search experiences can also be important, making AI visibility services a useful consideration as the product grows.

For founders without an in-house design or development team, a web development partner can also help turn a chosen template into a fully customized, production-ready site without slowing down the launch timeline.

How to Choose the Right Shadcn SaaS Template

The best template is the one that matches both your product category and how much you want built in versus customized from scratch. If your existing site only needs a new pricing or feature screen, Shadcn pages offer complete layouts you can adapt without replacing the rest of your site.

  • For the most complete SaaS website: Flow offers production-ready marketing pages with a full marketing experience.
  • For a clean, startup-focused design: Plasma keeps messaging and typography front and center without unnecessary complexity.
  • For a flexible, general-purpose SaaS site: Cosmic adapts to many software categories.
  • For fintech: Zippay fits payment software, digital wallets, and banking products.
  • For a premium minimalist look: Simplistic emphasizes typography and spacing.
  • For animation-rich websites: Magic UI Pro is the pick when polished interactions matter.
  • For heavy customization: Frontier offers a clean, developer-friendly structure.
  • For AI products: AI SaaS Template provides a multi-page structure with room for feature and pricing depth.
  • For developer tools: Meridian includes polished documentation built in.
  • For open-source or community-driven products: Scalar combines docs, blog, and marketing pages.
  • For a full SaaS foundation: Achromatic adds auth, billing, and an admin panel, not just a landing page.
  • For a single-page launch: Foxtrot gets a polished page live quickly.

What to Look for in a SaaS Landing Page Template

Complete Conversion Flow

A good template connects the hero, product benefits, social proof, pricing, objections, and a final call to action. A collection of attractive sections is less useful if the page doesn't tell a coherent story.

Framework and Component Fit

Check whether the template actually uses Shadcn UI or only shares a similar Tailwind look. Adapting a native Shadcn project is usually faster than converting a different component system.

Page Coverage

Decide whether you need a single landing page or a complete website with pricing, docs, blog, and authentication pages. Larger templates can eliminate weeks of repeated layout work.

Responsive Behavior

Test navigation, pricing tables, product screenshots, and animations on small screens. Marketing pages often look impressive on desktop while becoming hard to scan on mobile.

Performance and Animation

Animation-heavy templates feel polished but should still load quickly and stay accessible. Treat motion as an enhancement, not a requirement for understanding the page.

License and Support

Confirm whether the license covers client projects, commercial products, and the number of sites you plan to build before you buy.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Shadcn SaaS template?

A Shadcn SaaS template is a ready-made website or landing page built with Shadcn UI components, usually alongside React and Tailwind CSS. It typically includes reusable sections such as heroes, features, pricing, and calls to action.

What is the best Shadcn SaaS template?

Flow is our best overall pick for a complete, production-ready SaaS website. AI SaaS Template suits AI products, Meridian suits developer tools, and Achromatic is best if you want a full SaaS foundation.

Which template is best for an AI startup?

AI SaaS Template is purpose-built for AI-driven SaaS products, with a multi-page structure and subtle microinteractions.

Are there templates for developer tools?

Yes. Meridian includes Fumadocs-powered documentation with ⌘K search, and Scalar suits open-source and community-driven developer SaaS with docs and a blog.

Can I use these templates with Next.js or Astro?

Several of them can. Meridian, Scalar, and Zippay come in both Next.js and Astro editions, while AI SaaS Template, Foxtrot, and Achromatic are built with Next.js.

Do I need a landing page or a full starter kit?

If you only need a marketing site, a landing page template such as Flow, Plasma, or Cosmic is enough. If you also need authentication, billing, and an admin panel, Achromatic gives you a complete SaaS foundation.

Final Verdict

The Shadcn ecosystem has matured significantly, giving developers and startups high-quality templates that dramatically reduce frontend development time. Flow is our strongest overall pick thanks to its complete marketing experience, production-ready layouts, and flexibility across SaaS categories.

Choose AI SaaS Template for an AI-driven product, Meridian for developer tools with built-in docs, Zippay for fintech, or Foxtrot for a quick single-page launch. If you need more than a landing page, Achromatic gives you auth, billing, and an admin panel already in place.

Once you've settled on a layout, the Shadcn Theme Generator can help you preview colors and styling before applying your brand across the site. Starting with a well-structured template lets you spend less time rebuilding common UI and more time shipping the features that matter.

title: Building a Secure Auth System in Go: JWT, 2FA, OAuth, Sessions, and Rate Limiting
description:
Authentication seems simple at first glance. Then you add "remember me", OAuth, 2FA, and proper session revocation, and it gets complicated fast.

Wapi is a live streaming app tailored for African content, with a backend written in Go using Gin. Its auth system covers many production concerns, from token rotation to two-factor login. In this post I'll walk through the pieces, why each one matters, and the mistakes that are easy to make along the way.

The Token Strategy: Access and Refresh Tokens

Wapi uses the classic dual-token approach. Short-lived access tokens authenticate API requests, and longer-lived refresh tokens obtain new access tokens without forcing the user to log in again.

The login endpoint returns both tokens along with the user profile. When the access token expires, the client calls the refresh endpoint, which issues a new access token and a new refresh token.

That second part is the important one: refresh token rotation. Every time a refresh token is used, it is invalidated and replaced. This limits the damage if a refresh token is stolen, because the thief and the real user can't both keep using the same token.

Rotation also gives you theft detection. If someone presents a refresh token that has already been rotated, one of two things happened: a client retried badly, or a token was copied. Either way, the safe response is to revoke the entire session the token belonged to and force a fresh login.

JWTs Done Right

JSON Web Tokens are convenient and easy to misuse. A few rules go a long way:

  • Keep access tokens short-lived. Minutes, not hours. The shorter the lifetime, the smaller the window an attacker has with a stolen token.
  • Sign properly. Use a strong secret (HMAC) or an asymmetric key pair (RSA or ECDSA). Pin the expected signing algorithm when parsing, so a token can't claim a weaker one.
  • Never put sensitive data in the payload. A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Anyone holding the token can read its claims.
  • Validate everything. Check the signature, the expiry (exp), and the issuer and audience where they apply.
  • Store minimal claims. Usually just the user ID, a token ID (jti), and the expiry. Don't bloat the token, since it travels with every request.

In a Gin application this lives in middleware. It extracts the Bearer token from the Authorization header, validates it, and attaches the user ID to the request context so downstream handlers never have to parse tokens themselves.

There is one trade-off to be honest about. A pure JWT is stateless, so the server can't "un-issue" it before it expires. That is why access tokens must be short-lived, and why real revocation happens at the refresh token and session level. If you need instant revocation of access tokens, for example after a ban, you can check the token's session ID against a store on each request. That reintroduces state, so it's a deliberate trade of some of JWT's simplicity for control.

Session Management

Tokens alone aren't enough. Users and the system both need to be able to see and end sessions. Wapi exposes endpoints to list active sessions, revoke a specific session, and revoke all sessions at once.

This matters for several scenarios:

  • "Sign out of all devices" after a lost phone or a password change
  • Killing suspicious sessions once a login looks wrong
  • Meeting security expectations that users increasingly take for granted

To support it, you track each refresh token (or session ID) in the database along with metadata: device or user agent, IP address, creation time, and last-used time. Validating a refresh token then means checking that it exists and hasn't been revoked, and logging out means revoking it. The metadata is what turns a bare list of tokens into something a user can understand, such as "Chrome on Windows, last active two hours ago".

Store a hash of the refresh token rather than the token itself, the same way you would treat a password. If the database leaks, the stored values shouldn't be usable.

Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

Adding 2FA is one of the biggest security upgrades you can make. Wapi implements TOTP (Time-based One-Time Passwords), which works with Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, and similar apps.

The flow has four stages:

  1. Setup. An authenticated user requests 2FA setup. The server generates a secret and returns an otpauth:// URI, which the client renders as a QR code. The secret is stored (encrypted) against the user but not yet active.
  2. Verification. The user scans the QR code and enters the code their app displays. The server checks it against the stored secret, and only then switches 2FA on. This confirms the user's app is configured correctly before they can lock themselves out.
  3. Login with 2FA. When 2FA is enabled, a correct email and password no longer produce tokens. The server returns a short-lived challenge instead, and the user completes login by submitting a TOTP code. Only then are access and refresh tokens issued.
  4. Disabling. Turning 2FA off requires re-authentication, so someone with a briefly unattended session can't quietly weaken the account.

Two details deserve attention. First, the login challenge should be a single-purpose credential: short expiry, usable only to complete 2FA, and never accepted as an access token. Second, 2FA verification needs its own strict rate limit. A six-digit code has only a million possibilities, and brute-forcing that is realistic if attempts are unthrottled.

Finally, plan for account recovery. Users lose phones, so you'll want backup codes, generated at setup, stored hashed, and single-use.

OAuth 2.0 (Google and Facebook)

Social login is convenient for users and has its own pitfalls. Wapi uses the standard authorization code flow:

  1. The client hits the server's login endpoint for a provider, which redirects to the provider's authorization page.
  2. The user authenticates with the provider and consents.
  3. The provider redirects back to the server's callback endpoint with an authorization code.
  4. The server exchanges the code for tokens with the provider and fetches the user's profile.
  5. The server finds or creates a local account linked to that provider identity.
  6. The server issues its own access and refresh tokens.

Step 6 is where Wapi does something smart. Instead of putting tokens in the redirect URL, it redirects the browser back to the frontend with a short-lived one-time code, and the frontend exchanges that code for tokens through a separate endpoint. URLs end up in browser history, server logs, and Referer headers, so tokens don't belong there. A code that is single-use and expires in seconds is a much safer thing to leak.

A few OAuth details are easy to miss:

  • Validate the state parameter to protect against cross-site request forgery on the callback.
  • Use PKCE where the provider supports it.
  • Be careful when linking accounts by email. Only auto-link to an existing local account if the provider confirms the email is verified. Otherwise an attacker can register at a provider with someone else's address and take over their account.

Rate Limiting for Abuse Prevention

Auth endpoints are prime targets for credential stuffing and brute-force attacks. Wapi applies different limits depending on the endpoint:

Endpoint type Limit Keyed by
Signup, login, password reset 10 per minute IP
OAuth initiation 5 per minute IP
2FA verification (suggested) Stricter than login, for example 5 attempts per 15 minutes IP and user or session

The limiter is built on golang.org/x/time/rate, with buckets stored per key. When a limit is hit, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests with a clear error code so clients can back off gracefully.

An in-memory limiter is fine for a single instance, but note what happens when you scale out. Each instance counts separately, so your effective limit is multiplied by the number of instances. When you run more than one, move the counters to Redis, using a sliding window or token bucket, so every instance shares the same view. Also remember that IP-based limits are blunt: users behind a shared NAT share a bucket, and attackers rotate IPs. That matters even more for a mobile-heavy audience, where carrier-grade NAT can put many real users behind one IP. That is why the 2FA limit also keys on the user or session.

Security Best Practices to Keep in Mind

  • Password hashing. Never store plaintext passwords. Use bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt with a sensible cost factor, and raise it over time as hardware improves.
  • Email verification. Verify addresses before allowing sensitive actions.
  • Password reset. Use time-limited, single-use tokens delivered by email, and invalidate existing sessions when a reset completes.
  • Account enumeration. Return the same response whether or not an email exists, for login errors and for password reset requests.
  • CORS. Lock allowed origins down to the ones you actually use.
  • Secure headers. Add standard security headers in production.
  • Token storage on the client. HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies protect tokens from theft via XSS in a way localStorage can't. The trade-off is that cookie-based auth needs CSRF protection, which SameSite helps with. If you send tokens in an Authorization header instead, keep them in memory and accept the refresh-on-reload cost.

Putting It All Together

A robust auth system isn't about implementing every feature at once. It's about layering defenses. Start with solid password authentication and short-lived JWTs. Add refresh token rotation and session management so users can end sessions remotely. Layer on 2FA for accounts that matter, add OAuth for convenience, and wrap everything in rate limiting.

What stands out in Wapi's implementation is that these pieces are wired up and work together rather than existing as isolated features. The routes are organized logically, the middleware is reusable, and each flow closes the gaps the previous layer leaves open. It's a solid reference for anyone building auth in Go.
