title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.36210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.

title: RBGA: Residual-Budget Guide Arbitration for Offline-to-Online Safe Reinforcement Learning in Dexterous Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2610.33494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires robots to leverage existing datasets for rapid skill acquisition while maintaining safety during real-world deployment to prevent damage to the robot or its surroundings. Offline-to-online safe reinforcement learning (O2O safe RL) provides a promising solution for this problem by leveraging prior experience for online improvement under safety constraints, thereby mitigating the sample inefficiency and exploration risk of learning safe policies from scratch. However, existing O2O safe RL approaches do not explicitly account for the safety budget already consumed when making decisions within an episode. Excessive cost incurred early can therefore leave little room for subsequent exploration and policy improvement. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{R}esidual-\textbf{B}udget \textbf{G}uide \textbf{A}rbitration (RBGA), an algorithm that explicitly tracks the remaining episode safety budget and uses it to adaptively select between offline guidance and the evolving online policy. At each step, RBGA compares the cost-to-go estimates of the guide and online actions against the remaining budget, enabling step-wise action arbitration throughout the episode. We provide theoretical analysis characterizing the safety implications of residual-budget-based selection and its effect on guide-assisted exploration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RBGA enables effective online policy improvement while maintaining strong safety performance. Our code is available at this \href{https://github.com/sii-pilab}{link}.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Controller Parameters in the Auto-Bidding System at Pinterest
description:
arXiv:2610.33248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Auto-bidding systems in online advertising must balance competing objectives-maximizing budget delivery while minimizing cost per action-across heterogeneous campaigns under non-stationary market conditions. This trade-off evolves over campaign lifespans: early on, cost optimization dominates when budgets roll over; near deadlines, budget delivery becomes urgent. While PID controllers are widely used in production for their stability and interpretability, fixed tunings cannot adapt to diverse campaigns and shifting traffic patterns. We present RLBP (Reinforcement Learning for Bidding Parameters), a hybrid architecture deployed at Pinterest that uses RL as a meta-controller to select campaign-specific PID parameters daily while retaining PID for high-frequency bid adjustments. RLBP trains a multi-head Q-network using a relative-lift reward formulation normalized against the production baseline, and performs inference-time fusion that adapts the cost-delivery trade-off to campaign states without retraining. Through online A/B testing at Pinterest, RLBP achieves a statistically significant reduction in effective cost-per-click (eCPC) with no revenue degradation, and two months of post-rollout measurements against a holdout also show consistent cost reductions. These results demonstrate that meta-controller RL can successfully augment production control systems at scale.

title: HTTP QUERYメソッドとは？RFC 10008とQUERY・GET・POSTの違いを解説
description:
HTTP QUERYメソッドは、RFC 10008（2026年6月）で定義された新しいリクエストメソッドで、クエリをリクエストボディで送信し、安全かつ冪等です。ボディ付きのGETと考えることができます。複雑なフィルタのためのPOSTの余地と、キャッシュと自動再試行のためのGETの保証が得られます。

今すぐApidogを試す

3 KBのフィルタをURLに詰め込んだことがあるなら、あるいは読み取り専用の検索をPOSTで送信して、キャッシュと再試行ロジックがそれを無視するのを見たことがあるなら、QUERYが解決策です。このガイドでは、仕様が何を述べているか、QUERYがGETやPOSTとどう比較されるか、今日何がそれをサポートしているか、そしてコーディングエージェントでQUERYエンドポイントをテストする方法を説明します。

HTTP QUERYメソッドとは何か？

QUERYは、リクエストコンテンツに記述されたクエリを実行し、結果を返すようターゲットリソースに要求するHTTPメソッドです。リクエストボディとそのContent-Typeがクエリを定義します。このメソッドは安全（クライアントは状態変化を期待しない）かつ冪等（繰り返しても同じ効果）であるため、クライアント、プロキシ、キャッシュはGETと同様に再試行およびキャッシュできます。

仕様はRFC 10008「The HTTP QUERY Method」で、2026年6月にJulian Reschke（greenbytes）、James M. Snell（Cloudflare）、Mike Bishop（Akamai）によって公開されたProposed Standardです。IANAはこれをHTTP Method Registryに「safe: yes, idempotent: yes」として追加し、WebDAV時代のSEARCHメソッド（QUERYがほとんどそうなりかけたもの）のすぐ隣に置きました。

QUERYリクエストは次のようになります：

QUERY /contacts HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept: application/json

select=surname,givenname,email&limit=10&match=%22email=*@example.*%22

サーバーは200 OKとボディに結果を返して応答します。

なぜGETとPOSTでは不十分だったのか

QUERY以前は、複雑な読み取りには2つの選択肢があり、どちらも漏れがありました。

GETはすべてをURLに置きます。 RFC 10008はそれに関する4つの問題を挙げています：

  1. サイズ制限は事前に不明です。なぜならリクエストは多くのシステムを通過するからです。RFC 9110は、送信者と受信者が少なくとも8,000オクテットをサポートすることを推奨しているだけです。
  2. 構造化データを有効なURIにエンコードするのは無駄です。
  3. URIはリクエストボディよりもはるかに頻繁にログに記録され、ブックマークされるため、機密性の高いフィルタにとってプライバシー問題となります。
  4. クエリ入力のすべての組み合わせが独自のリソースになります。

ボディ付きGETも答えではありません。 RFC 9110は、GETリクエストのコンテンツには定義されたセマンティクスがないと述べています。サーバーによってはそれを読み取り、サーバーによってはそれを破棄し、プロキシによってはリクエストを拒否します。パス全体でそれを当てにすることはできません。

POSTは機能しますが、意図について嘘をつきます。 POST検索は問題なく実行されますが、その操作が読み取り専用であることをクライアント、キャッシュ、プロキシ、再試行ライブラリに伝えるものは何もありません。そのため、キャッシュはそれをスキップし、クライアントは接続が切断された後に再試行しません。再試行を安全にするためだけに、純粋な読み取りに冪等キーを付けざるを得なかったなら、この問題を感じたことがあるでしょう。

QUERYはPOSTのボディを維持し、GETの保証を追加します。

QUERYとGETとPOSTの比較

RFC 10008の表1に基づく比較は次のとおりです：

プロパティ GET QUERY POST
安全 はい はい 潜在的にいいえ
冪等 はい はい 潜在的にいいえ
リクエストボディ 定義されたセマンティクスなし 期待され、クエリを定義する 期待される
クエリ自体のURI はい、定義により オプション、Location経由 いいえ
結果のURI オプション、Content-Location経由 オプション、Content-Location経由 オプション、Content-Location経由
キャッシュ可能 はい はい、ボディはキャッシュキーの一部 後続のGETまたはHEADのみ
ブラウザからのCORSプリフライト 単純リクエストには不要 常に 単純リクエストには不要

要約すると、クエリがURLに無理なく収まる場合はGETを、収まらない場合はQUERYを、リクエストが状態を変更する場合にのみPOSTを使用します。古典的なメソッドの復習については、HTTPメソッドとGET vs POSTのガイドをご覧ください。

RFC 10008が定義するもの

Content-Typeは必須

サーバーは、Content-Typeが欠落しているかボディと矛盾するQUERYを失敗させなければなりません（MUST）。RFCはこれらのステータスコードを推奨しています：

  • 400 Bad Request：メディアタイプがない、またはコンテンツと一致しないタイプ。サーバーはボディをスニッフィングして上書きすることはできません。
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type：リソースがそのクエリ形式をサポートしていません。
  • 422 Unprocessable Content：形式は問題ないがクエリを実行できない。たとえば、存在しないテーブルを指定したSQLなど。
  • 406 Not Acceptable：クライアントが、リソースが生成できない応答タイプを要求しました。

LocationとContent-Location

サーバーは、QUERYを後でGETできるものに変える2つのオプションヘッダーを返すことができます：

  • Content-Locationは、この特定の実行の保存された結果を指します。一時的なものである可能性があります。
  • Locationは、保存されたクエリ自体を指します。それに対するGETは、ボディを再送信することなく、新しいデータでクエリを再実行します。

RFCは、GETのキャッシュの方が単純であるため、繰り返しリクエストにはLocation URIへのGETに切り替えることをクライアントに提案しています。機密データを含むクエリに対してどちらかのヘッダーを返す場合、URIは元のボディの機密部分を含むべきではありません（SHOULD NOT）。

キャッシュ

QUERY応答はキャッシュ可能です。キャッシュキーは、リクエストコンテンツと、メディアタイプなどの関連メタデータを含まなければなりません（MUST）。キャッシュは、より多くのヒットを得るために、たとえばコンテンツエンコーディングを削除したり、+jsonタイプのJSONを正規化したりして、最初にボディを正規化してもよい（MAY）。仕様は、不適切な正規化が誤った応答を返す可能性があると警告しているため、CDNはここで注意することが予想されます。

リダイレクト

301、302、307、または308は「同じQUERYを新しいURIに送信する」ことを意味します。POSTとは異なり、QUERYは301または302でGETに書き換えてはなりません。303 See Otherは「このURIでGETを使用して結果を取得する」ことを意味します。

Accept-Queryヘッダー

Accept-Queryは、QUERYサポートとリソースが受け入れるクエリ形式を通知する新しい応答ヘッダーです。これはStructured Fieldリストであるため、そのように解析します：

Accept-Query: "application/jsonpath", application/sql;charset="UTF-8"

クライアントは、OPTIONSでサポートを発見し、Allowヘッダーを読むことも、単にQUERYを送信して405 Method Not Allowedを処理することもできます。

今日どのツールがQUERYをサポートしているか？

サポートは不均一であるため、独自のスタックをテストしてください。2026年10月28日に確認した内容は次のとおりです：

ツール 結果
Node.js 24 httpサーバー http.METHODSにQUERYが含まれる；プレーンサーバーがメソッドとボディを受信した
Node.js 24 fetch JSONボディでQUERYを送信した
curl 8.7 -d付きのcurl -X QUERYがメソッドとボディを送信した
Python 3.14 http.client ボディ付きでQUERYを送信した
OpenAPI 3.2 Path Item ObjectにQUERY操作用のqueryフィールドがある
Apidog CLI 2.2.12 endpoint-createスキーマが"method": "query"を受け入れる

ローカルのNodeサーバーに対して使用したcurl呼び出しは次のとおりです：

curl -i -X QUERY http://localhost:3000/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"q":"running shoe","limit":2}'

Fetch StandardはGETとHEADでのボディのみを禁止しているため、ブラウザはボディ付きでQUERYを送信できます。ただし、QUERYはCORSセーフリストされたメソッドではないため、クロスオリジンのQUERYはすべてプリフライトをトリガーします。サーバーはAccess-Control-Allow-MethodsにQUERYをリストする必要があります。

ギャップはネットワークの途中にあります：メソッドを許可リストに登録したり、キャッシュをボディでキー付けしないリバースプロキシ、APIゲートウェイ、WAF、CDNです。出荷前に各ホップを確認してください。APIs You Won't Hateニュースレターは、多くのWebフレームワークがすでにQUERYを直接またはカスタムメソッドルーティングを通じて処理していると指摘しています。

クライアントを壊さずにQUERYを採用する方法

POST検索エンドポイントを撤去する必要はありません。

  1. POSTルートと並行してQUERYを追加します。 両方を同じハンドラーに向けます。新しいクライアントはQUERYを使用し、古いクライアントは引き続き機能します。
  2. それを通知します。 リソースでAccept-Queryを返し、OPTIONSおよび405応答のAllowにQUERYを含めます。
  3. Content-Typeを強制します。 RFCが推奨するように400または415を返し、解析はできるが実行できないクエリには422を返します。
  4. 405または501にフォールバックします。 ホップがQUERYを拒否した場合、クライアントは同じボディをPOSTとして再試行する必要があります。
  5. CORSを修正します。 ブラウザクライアントのためにAccess-Control-Allow-MethodsにQUERYを追加します。
  6. キャッシュについて決定します。 キャッシュがボディでキー付けされる場合にのみ共有キャッシュを有効にします。そうでなければ、Location URIを返し、クライアントにGETさせます。
  7. 文書化します。 OpenAPI 3.2では、パスアイテムのquery:の下で操作を定義します： 
openapi: 3.2.0
paths:
  /products:
    query:
      summary: Search products
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductQuery'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Matching products

短く単純なフィルタは、GETのクエリ文字列として残すことができます。RFC 10008自体、クエリがそれほど短い場合はGETの方がおそらく良い選択であると述べています。

コーディングエージェントにApidog CLIでQUERYエンドポイントをテストさせる

新しいメソッドとは、ハッピーパス、すべてのエラーコード、フォールバックルートをチェックすることを意味します。それをClaude Code、Codex、またはCursorに任せ、Apidog CLIを操作させます。

CLIをインストールし、ログインし、エージェントにApidogスキルを追加します：

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

次に、エージェントに1つのプロンプトを与えます：

In Apidog project <projectId>, add a QUERY /products endpoint that takes a
JSON body {q, limit}. Create test cases that assert 200 with an array for a
valid body, 415 for Content-Type text/plain, and 400 with no Content-Type.
Run them against the staging environment and summarize any failures.

エージェントは各スキーマを読み取り、そのペイロードを検証し、その後にのみ書き込みます：

apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

書き込むendpoint.jsonは"method": "query"を設定します。これはCLIのendpoint-createスキーマがget、post、およびWebDAVメソッドと並んでリストしています。Apidogアプリで実行を確認するには--upload-reportを追加します。同じapidog runコマンドに-r junitを付けるとCIに組み込めます。詳細はapidog runでCIでAPIテストを実行する方法とClaude CodeでApidog CLIを使用する方法をご覧ください。Apidogの無料プランは最大4ユーザーまでカバーします。

FAQ

HTTP QUERYメソッドは公式標準ですか？ はい。RFC 10008は2026年6月に公開されたStandards TrackのProposed Standard RFCであり、IANAはQUERYをHTTP Method Registryに安全かつ冪等としてリストしています。

QUERYは単なるボディ付きGETですか？ 近いですが、より適切に定義されています。RFC 9110はGETボディにセマンティクスを与えていないため、中間者はそれを無視または拒否できます。QUERYはボディをクエリにし、Content-Typeを要求し、ボディをキャッシュキーに折り込みます。

POSTの代わりにいつQUERYを使用すべきですか？ URLには大きすぎる、または機密性が高すぎる読み取り専用の検索やフィルタにはQUERYを使用します。何かを作成または変更するリクエストにはPOSTを使用し続けます。

ブラウザはQUERYリクエストを送信できますか？ はい、カスタムメソッドでfetchを通じて送信できます。クロスオリジンのQUERYリクエストは常にCORSプリフライトが必要なため、サーバーはそのメソッドを許可する必要があります。

QUERY応答はキャッシュされますか？ キャッシュされる可能性があります。キャッシュはリクエストボディとそのメタデータをキャッシュキーに含めなければなりません。多くのCDNとプロキシはまだそうしていないため、確認するか、クライアントがGETできるLocation URIを返してください。

OpenAPIはQUERYをサポートしていますか？ OpenAPI 3.2は、QUERY操作用にPath Item Objectにqueryフィールドを追加しているため、拡張なしで文書化できます。

title: Postgres row locks in practice
description:
For years I used SELECT ... FOR UPDATE without really thinking about it. This week I actually read the lock conflict table and it explained a lot.

What I now do by default:

  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queue-like tables
  • Short transactions, no user input inside them
  • lock_timeout so a stuck query fails fast instead of piling up
  • Monitor pg_locks when something feels slow

The SKIP LOCKED change alone let us drop a whole queue service for a table with tens of thousands of rows. Postgres was already the queue; we just didn't trust it.

I'm reading about SQLite internals too, because the locking model is so different. It's a good way to understand what Postgres gives you.

title: Lint in Testing: The Steps to Add Static Checks to Your Java Test Pipeline
description:
Why Linting Belongs in Your Testing Strategy

Most teams think of linting and testing as two separate activities. Linting is the cheap, fast check that runs on every commit and flags style problems, suspicious code, and risky patterns. Testing is the deeper check that proves behavior. In practice, the two are closely related. A test suite full of Thread.sleep() calls, swallowed exceptions, or assertions that can never fail is a test suite that gives you false confidence. Linting catches those problems before they turn into flaky builds and missed regressions.

If you build Java services, you probably already run a compiler, JUnit, and maybe SonarQube somewhere in the pipeline. The question is not whether to lint, but where in the testing lifecycle each check belongs, how strict it should be, and how to introduce it without freezing a team that already has a large codebase.

This article walks through the steps I use to add lint to a Java testing pipeline, from choosing tools to handling legacy code and enforcing the rules in CI.

What Linting Catches, and What It Does Not

Linting tools analyze source code without running it. Depending on the tool, they check for:

  • Formatting and style: indentation, naming, import order, line length, Javadoc presence.
  • Likely bugs: null dereferences, unused variables, unreachable code, incorrect equals and hashCode implementations, resource leaks.
  • Risky patterns: catching Exception and ignoring it, hard-coded credentials, calls to deprecated APIs.
  • Architectural rules: packages that must not depend on each other, layers that must not call across boundaries.

Linting does not prove that your code is correct. It cannot tell you that a discount calculation is wrong or that a query returns the wrong customers. Its value is in removing entire categories of problems so that your tests and reviewers can focus on behavior. Treat lint as the first gate, not as a replacement for tests.

Step 1: Choose a Small Set of Tools with Clear Purposes

A common mistake is adopting five linters on the same day. The result is hundreds of violations, a red build, and a team that starts ignoring the reports. Start with a small set where each tool has a distinct job:

  • Checkstyle enforces style and formatting rules. It is predictable and easy to configure.
  • PMD finds code smells and common mistakes, such as empty catch blocks and unused private methods.
  • SpotBugs analyzes bytecode for likely bugs, such as null dereferences and suspicious comparisons. It is most useful after the code compiles.
  • ArchUnit is a library, not a standalone linter. It lets you write architectural rules as JUnit tests, for example "the domain package must not depend on the web package."
  • Error Prone runs during compilation and catches a set of high-confidence mistakes, which makes it a good fit for teams that want fast feedback in the IDE.

For most teams, Checkstyle plus SpotBugs plus ArchUnit covers the important ground. Add PMD if your team wants more code-smell detection. Add Error Prone if you want compile-time checks.

Step 2: Configure Rules That Match Your Team

Default rule sets are a starting point, not a finished policy. Enable the rules your team agrees are worth enforcing, and disable the ones that produce noise. Keep the configuration in the repository, under version control, so changes go through code review.

Here is a Maven configuration that runs Checkstyle and SpotBugs during the verify phase, which is where most teams run integration tests and static analysis:

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-checkstyle-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.3.1</version>
      <configuration>
        <configLocation>config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml</configLocation>
        <consoleOutput>true</consoleOutput>
        <failOnViolation>true</failOnViolation>
        <violationSeverity>error</violationSeverity>
        <includeTestSourceDirectory>true</includeTestSourceDirectory>
      </configuration>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <id>checkstyle-check</id>
          <phase>verify</phase>
          <goals>
            <goal>check</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>

    <plugin>
      <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
      <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>4.8.6.0</version>
      <configuration>
        <effort>Max</effort>
        <threshold>Medium</threshold>
        <failOnError>true</failOnError>
        <excludeFilterFile>config/spotbugs/exclude.xml</excludeFilterFile>
      </configuration>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <id>spotbugs-check</id>
          <phase>verify</phase>
          <goals>
            <goal>check</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

Two details matter here. First, includeTestSourceDirectory is set to true for Checkstyle, so the same style rules apply to test code. Second, SpotBugs uses an exclude file. Keep that file small and document why each exclusion exists. An exclude file that grows without explanation is how a team quietly disables its own safety net.

Step 3: Place Each Check at the Right Point in the Lifecycle

Where a check runs determines how fast developers get feedback. A reasonable split looks like this:

Check When it runs Why
Compiler warnings and Error Prone Every compile Instant feedback in the IDE
Checkstyle validate or verify Fast, no need for compiled classes
Unit tests test Behavior of isolated units
ArchUnit rules test (as JUnit tests) Architecture is verified alongside behavior
SpotBugs verify Needs compiled bytecode, slower
Integration tests verify Slowest, run last

The principle is to put cheap checks early and expensive checks late. If SpotBugs takes four minutes on a large module, you do not want it running before every unit test during local development. Many teams run the fast checks on every push and the full suite on pull requests and nightly builds.

ArchUnit deserves special attention because it fits naturally into the test phase. Here is a rule that prevents domain code from depending on web code:

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ImportOption;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.AnalyzeClasses;
import com.tngtech.archunit.junit.ArchTest;
import com.tngtech.archunit.lang.ArchRule;

import static com.tngtech.archunit.lang.syntax.ArchRuleDefinition.noClasses;

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.example.orders",
                importOptions = ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class)
class ArchitectureRulesTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainMustNotDependOnWeb =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("..web..");
}

When this rule fails, the build fails with a message that names the offending classes. That is far more useful than a comment in a design document that nobody reads.

Step 4: Lint Your Test Code Too

Test code is production code for the people who maintain it, and it often has its own failure patterns. Checkstyle and PMD can help with several of them, but a few rules are worth enforcing deliberately:

  • No Thread.sleep() in tests. Sleeps are the most common cause of flaky tests. Use explicit waits, latches, or a library such as Awaitility, which polls a condition with a timeout.
  • No empty catch blocks in tests. An exception swallowed in a test hides the failure.
  • Every test has at least one assertion. A test that only calls code and never checks the result proves nothing.
  • No hard-coded ports or absolute file paths. Use random ports and temporary directories so tests run on any machine.

Some of these rules need a custom check. PMD supports custom rules written in XPath, and ArchUnit can enforce structural rules such as "test classes must end with Test." Here is a simple example of a flaky pattern and its replacement:

// Flagged by lint: fixed sleep makes the test timing-dependent
@Test
void orderIsProcessedAsync() throws InterruptedException {
    orderService.submit(order);
    Thread.sleep(2000);
    assertEquals(OrderStatus.PROCESSED, repository.find(order.id()).status());
}

// Preferred: poll the condition with a timeout
@Test
void orderIsProcessedAsync() {
    orderService.submit(order);
    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
           .untilAsserted(() ->
               assertEquals(OrderStatus.PROCESSED,
                            repository.find(order.id()).status()));
}

The second version runs as fast as the system allows and fails with a clear timeout message instead of an intermittent assertion error.

Step 5: Enforce the Rules in CI and Locally

Lint only works if people cannot ignore it. There are two enforcement points, and both matter.

Locally, use a pre-commit hook or a build step that runs the fast checks before a commit or push. Tools such as Husky (for mixed repositories) or a simple Git hook script can run mvn -q checkstyle:check in a few seconds. The goal is to catch problems before they reach a pull request.

In CI, make the lint jobs required status checks. A pull request should not merge with a failing lint step. Here is a GitHub Actions job that runs the full verification on each pull request:

name: verify

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven
      - name: Run tests and static analysis
        run: mvn -B verify
      - name: Upload SpotBugs report on failure
        if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: spotbugs-report
          path: '**/target/spotbugsXml.xml'

Uploading the report on failure matters. A developer who sees "build failed" needs to know which rule failed and where, and the report answers that question without a second investigation.

Step 6: Handle Legacy Code with Baselines

The hardest part of adding lint to an existing project is not the configuration. It is the first run. A mature codebase can produce thousands of violations, and fixing them all before enabling the gate is rarely realistic.

The practical approach is a baseline. You record the current violations, accept them as the starting point, and fail the build only on new violations. Several tools support this directly, and for tools that do not, you can achieve the same effect by comparing the current report with a committed baseline file.

The rules I follow for baselines are:

  1. Freeze the current state. Commit the baseline and document the date.
  2. Block new violations immediately. Any change that adds a violation fails the build.
  3. Reduce the baseline gradually. When a developer touches a file, they fix the violations in that file.
  4. Track the count over time. A dashboard that shows the number of violations per module makes progress visible and keeps the team motivated.

This approach avoids the most common failure mode, which is a team that disables the gate because the backlog is too large to face.

Step 7: Tune Rules and Measure Their Value

A lint rule that produces constant false positives trains developers to ignore warnings, and that is worse than having no rule at all. Review the violations regularly, and ask three questions about each noisy rule:

  • Is this rule catching real problems in our codebase?
  • Are developers fixing the violations or suppressing them?
  • Would a code reviewer have caught this anyway?

When a rule fails these tests, change its severity, narrow its scope, or remove it. Suppressions should be rare and visible. If the team uses @SuppressWarnings or a Checkstyle suppression file, review those suppressions during retrospectives. A large number of them is a signal that the rule set does not fit the code.

Measure the outcomes that matter to the team: the number of flaky tests, the time from pull request to merge, and the number of defects found in review versus production. Lint is a means to those ends, and it should be judged by them.

Common Pitfalls

Running everything on every keystroke. Full static analysis in the IDE on every save slows developers down. Keep the IDE feedback fast and move the expensive checks to the build.

Treating warnings as errors everywhere. Start with errors for high-confidence rules and warnings for style. Promote warnings to errors only after the team has fixed the existing ones.

Forgetting test code. Many teams lint only src/main. Test code deserves the same attention, especially for flaky patterns.

Config drift between modules. In a multi-module Maven project, define the plugin configuration once in the parent POM, and let child modules inherit it. Different rules in different modules confuse developers and make reports hard to compare.

Suppressing instead of fixing. A @SuppressWarnings annotation is sometimes correct, but it should come with a comment explaining why. Without one, it is a way to hide problems.

Adding tools without an owner. Someone on the team should own the lint configuration, review rule changes, and keep the baseline up to date. If nobody owns it, it decays.

A Practical Rollout Plan

If you are starting from zero, this sequence works for most Java teams:

  1. Week one: add Checkstyle with a minimal rule set, in warning mode. Share the report with the team.
  2. Week two: add SpotBugs in verify with a baseline. Block new violations only.
  3. Week three: add ArchUnit rules for your most important architectural boundaries.
  4. Week four: enable the test-code rules, starting with flaky patterns such as Thread.sleep.
  5. Ongoing: review the baseline count monthly, tune noisy rules, and promote warnings to errors as the backlog shrinks.

The rollout is deliberately slow. Each step gives the team time to adapt, and each step has a clear success criterion.

Key Takeaways

  • Linting and testing are complementary. Linting removes whole categories of problems so tests can focus on behavior.
  • Choose a small set of tools with distinct purposes: Checkstyle for style, SpotBugs for likely bugs, ArchUnit for architecture.
  • Place cheap checks early in the lifecycle and expensive checks late, so developers get fast feedback.
  • Lint test code too, especially for flaky patterns such as fixed sleeps.
  • Enforce rules both locally and in CI, and make lint jobs required status checks.
  • Use baselines to adopt lint in legacy code without freezing the team.
  • Tune noisy rules regularly and judge the rule set by its effect on defects and flakiness, not by the number of violations it reports.

Lint will not make a codebase correct, but it makes incorrect code harder to hide. Start small, enforce the rules you agree on, and let the build do the repetitive work so your reviewers and tests can focus on what matters.

title: Performance Gaps Between Open-Loop, Certainty-Equivalent, and Optimal Control Under Action-Dependent Observations
description:
arXiv:2610.33412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In dynamical systems, feedback can improve performance by allowing decisions to depend on past observations, rather than being designed a priori. Under full observation, the current state is sufficient for decision-making; under partial observation, the controller must instead estimate the state from measurements. When actions also affect observations, control can have a dual role: actions influence both the state and the information available for future decisions. This interaction can invalidate certainty-equivalent (CE) control, a widely used strategy that applies state feedback policies as if the estimated state were the true state. We ask when this suboptimality leads to a quantitative performance gap that grows with the horizon. We study this question in a linear-quadratic system with bilinear observations by comparing the optimal policy, certainty-equivalent control, and the optimal open-loop (OL) policy. We identify an instance-dependent information-strength parameter $q$ and establish distinct performance regimes as $q$ varies. When $q$ is sufficiently small, we show that no policy can improve over OL control by more than $O(1)$ cumulative cost. For large values of $q$, we find that CE achieves an $\Omega(T)$ advantage over OL control. Our main finding is that for intermediate values of $q$, we can construct a policy that occasionally probes for information and achieves an $\Omega(T)$ advantage over OL control while CE only achieves an $O(1)$ advantage, establishing an $\Omega(T)$ gap between CE and optimal control. Our analysis relies on a regret decomposition that captures the tradeoff between the immediate cost of gathering information and its future benefit.

title: Retry Failed Node.js Background Jobs with DLQ Redrive — A Practical Choice Guide
description:
The least complex retry design is usually the one you already have: keep failed messages in a dead-letter queue (DLQ), inspect the ones that are safe to retry, then redrive them to the main queue. For a fintech webhook worker, that gives you a controlled recovery operation without pretending that every failure is transient.

The important part is the policy around the redrive. Cap the retry count. Record each attempt. Make the worker idempotent. A queue can deliver a message again, and a network timeout can leave you unsure whether the downstream system accepted the first delivery.

A choice matrix for failed-job recovery

Option Best fit Recovery shape Main boundary
RabbitMQ DLX You already run RabbitMQ Move dead-lettered messages back through a queue/exchange path You own broker topology and operations
Amazon SQS DLQ redrive Your workloads already live on SQS Use the service's managed DLQ movement workflow The design follows SQS semantics and AWS integration
BullMQ Redis is already your queue backend Retry jobs through BullMQ's job and backoff model Redis becomes part of the job-control surface
Temporal The problem is a durable multi-step workflow Retry activities inside workflow execution It is a workflow engine, not just a queue recovery tool
A REST queue with DLQ redrive You want a plain HTTP integration List failed messages, then explicitly redrive selected ones You still need worker-level idempotency and retry policy

My default for a one-person SaaS is the smallest option that gives operations a deliberate recovery action. If the existing queue already has a good DLQ, use it. If I need a capability across several backend services and want discovery plus runnable examples from one API surface, the REST option is attractive; its value is reduced integration friction, not a promise that it replaces a workflow engine.

That is the revenue-per-hour test. A recovery path that takes one clear script and a log entry is easier to ship weekly than a new orchestration layer that needs its own operating model.

Small operational surface. Big difference.

What should a Node.js retry policy actually do?

A redrive is a new delivery attempt, not an amnesty for a bad message. Start by classifying the failure. A temporary upstream timeout or a 429 can be a retry candidate. A malformed payload, an invalid signature, or a permanently rejected account should stay out of the main queue until someone fixes the cause.

The DLQ list operation is the inspection step. Filter by the job's retry metadata, select only messages below the cap, and write an audit record before moving them. The redrive operation then republishes those messages to the main queue. The exact request schema should come from the queue capability's live schema, because guessing field names in an operational script is a poor trade.

I would use a hard maximum such as five attempts for a webhook job, but that number belongs to the business impact and downstream contract. The rule matters more than the example: every redrive increments the attempt count, and the worker refuses to perform the side effect after the limit. Without that guard, a poison message can turn recovery into an infinite loop.

The log needs enough information to answer a boring but expensive question later: what moved, when, why, and how many times? A message ID, job ID, attempt number, failure class, and request ID are more useful than a paragraph of free-form output. Keep the log append-only from the recovery script's perspective.

How do I prevent a retry from sending the webhook twice?

Queue-level delivery guarantees do not remove application-level duplication. For a fintech webhook, derive an idempotency key from the business event or store a durable delivery record keyed by that event and destination. The worker should check that record before sending, and it should make the state transition explicit after the provider accepts the request.

There is an awkward edge case: the provider accepts the webhook, then your worker loses the response. On the next delivery, a check based only on the last local response cannot help. The downstream endpoint needs to understand the same idempotency key, or your application needs a durable reconciliation strategy. This is why a retry queue is an operational recovery mechanism, not a guarantee of exactly-once side effects.

A small TypeScript recovery function can keep the boundary clear. The example below lists the DLQ, then issues the verified redrive operation. The service's public discovery surface supplies the request schema and runnable examples, so I would fill in any selection fields from that live schema rather than inventing them in a script. The helper still does the unglamorous work that matters in production: it reads the bearer token from the environment, sets the HTTP method explicitly, honors Retry-After, surfaces non-2xx responses, and gives the write a stable idempotency key.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const queue = process.env.INFRAI_QUEUE;
if (!apiKey || !queue) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_QUEUE are required");

const baseUrl = "https://" + ["api", "infrai", "cc"].join(".");

async function call(path: string, method: "GET" | "POST", idempotencyKey?: string): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
      method,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        ...(idempotencyKey ? { "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey } : {})
      }
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 500;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`DLQ ${method} failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    return body ? JSON.parse(body) : undefined;
  }

  throw new Error("DLQ request exhausted its retry budget");
}

const failed = await call(`/queue/dlq/list/${encodeURIComponent(queue)}`, "GET");
console.log("Inspect failed jobs and select only retryable messages:", failed);

// Use the redrive request fields from the live capability schema after selection.
const result = await call(
  `/queue/dlq/redrive/${encodeURIComponent(queue)}`,
  "POST",
  `dlq-redrive:${queue}:2026-10-25:operator-run-001`
);
console.log("Redrive accepted:", result);

The production worker should apply the same limit after it consumes a redriven message. The recovery script and the worker need one policy, not two similar constants that drift.

Where do the main alternatives fit?

RabbitMQ's dead-letter exchange model is a good fit when the broker is already central to the system. Its documentation is explicit about dead-letter exchanges and the routing behavior around them. The trade is operational ownership: exchanges, bindings, permissions, and broker health become part of the recovery story. It is a strong choice for teams that want broker-level control.

Amazon SQS is a sensible choice for an AWS-native service. Its DLQ redrive support makes managed queue recovery a natural part of the platform. The cost is coupling the operational workflow to SQS semantics and the surrounding AWS setup. That is usually a feature for an AWS-first team, not a defect.

BullMQ makes sense when Redis is already running the application. Its job model gives a Node.js team familiar controls for attempts and backoff, and the queue lives close to the code. Redis reliability, persistence, and the boundary between a job's state and the business side effect still need attention. BullMQ is a queue library, so it does not answer a multi-service workflow question by itself.

Temporal is the better runner-up when “retry this job” is shorthand for “resume a durable process with several dependent steps.” It brings workflow history and activity retries to that problem. For one outbound webhook queue, introducing workflow orchestration can be more surface area than the recovery path needs. This is where I would stop trying to force a DLQ into a workflow engine role.

A plain REST queue is useful when the team values a consistent HTTP boundary. In the Infrai case, the public discovery API is self-describing: discovery exposes the request schema, response schema, billing details, and runnable examples, so wiring the DLQ capability can start by reading one endpoint rather than learning another SDK. Its queue surface includes list and redrive operations, which matches this recovery pattern. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key and one bill, so a small product can keep queue recovery beside its other service integrations instead of collecting another credential and billing workflow.

There is a clear limitation to this recommendation. The trade-off is real: Infrai is not suitable if the hard problem is a durable DAG, a fan-out and join, or a workflow that must preserve a long execution history; choose Temporal there. It is also a poor fit for a private-only push target because documented push subscriptions require a public HTTPS endpoint. Those are product boundaries, not details to paper over with a retry loop. The advantage is one key and one bill: that reduces credential and reconciliation work for a solo operator, but it does not remove those limitations.

That boundary is important. A cron trigger can enqueue work, but long work belongs in a worker. The documented cron execution limit is 900 seconds; messages also have a 7-day delay limit and a 256 KB body limit. Those constraints make the design decision straightforward for large or long-running jobs: trigger the enqueue, consume in the worker, and keep recovery in the queue layer.

The operating rule I would ship

Pick the queue that matches the system you already operate. Then make recovery boring:

  1. List the DLQ and classify failures.
  2. Exclude messages at or above the retry cap.
  3. Record the recovery attempt before redrive.
  4. Redrive only the selected messages.
  5. Let an idempotent worker perform the side effect.
  6. Inspect the next failure instead of automatically redriving forever.

For a small fintech product, this keeps the failure path understandable and the implementation narrow. RabbitMQ, SQS, BullMQ, and Temporal each win in their own operating context. A self-describing REST surface wins when reducing integration work matters more than adopting another SDK, while its limits make it a poor substitute for durable workflow orchestration.

The practical answer is still the same: retry specific failed jobs by selecting them from the DLQ and redriving them to the main queue, with a retry cap and an idempotent consumer guarding the side effect.

  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • Amazon SQS redrive API
  • BullMQ retries
  • Temporal retry policies

title: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS)
description:
Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), enabling you to run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU. GPU sharing helps you increase GPU utilization and reduce infrastructure costs for workloads that use only part of a GPU's capacity, such as small-model inference, AV/ADAS simulations, embedding generation, and multi-model serving.

With GPU sharing, you can pack more workloads onto each GPU instance without changing your application code. You define the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally set a maximum share of GPU compute, and Amazon ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale and deploy. GPU sharing is supported on Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. On Amazon ECS Managed Instances, Amazon ECS also monitors the MPS control daemon that enables sharing on each instance. If the daemon stops or becomes unhealthy, Amazon ECS automatically replaces the instance and moves your tasks to healthy capacity, so your GPU workloads keep running without manual intervention.

To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, or other infrastructure-as-code tools to create a capacity provider with NVIDIA GPU instances, set the GPU sharing strategy and memory in the container definition of your task definition, and create a service on that capacity provider. This capability is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS GPU sharing documentation.

title: FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.33456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is essential in contemporary engineering design, yet it remains expensive to compute and can take thousands of CPU/GPU hours or more for a single high-fidelity simulation. Recent developments in machine learning for scientific modeling have led to powerful surrogate frameworks that can approximate flow fields and physical quantities by using a fraction of the computational cost. However, most of these methods require largescale homogeneous datasets or simple geometries, exhibiting severe generalization gaps when applied to complex and data-scarce configurations. To address this, we propose the Factorized Geometry Convolutional Neural Operator (FG-ConvNO) for robust geometry-aware propeller pressure prediction under limited training data. We introduce geometryaware encoding, efficient interpolation-based decoding, and auxiliary global quantity supervision. In addition, we incorporate DISCO blocks that use discrete continuous convolutions to make the model discretization agnostic. In our experiments, FG-ConvNO achieves the highest accuracy for both surface pressure and global thrust prediction on a procedurally generated propeller CFD dataset. Geometry-aware encoding and architectural simplification improve stability, while random vertex subsampling enhances robustness. Overall, adding geometric priors to grid-based convolutional operators reduces overfitting on complex propeller geometries and improves generalization in low-data regimes.
