title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
description:
arXiv:2610.36325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.

title: Nothing Left Behind: Finding Evidence from a Large Randomized Evaluation Corpus
description:
arXiv:2610.36910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many AI systems need to find every relevant items in a large collection and then organize what they found. The standard way to do this is to tag each item with labels from a curated vocabulary and search on those labels. Those labels are useful for organizing results, but searching on them misses items that do not fit a label and returns too much when labels are broad. We compare this approach with an embedding-based approach: find candidates by meaning using text embeddings, then have a language model keep only the relevant ones. In a corpus of 7,354 randomized trials, label search found 45% of the evidence a systematic review would include, while the new approach found 92%, at a cost per query that rises with search depth. These results support a two-stage architecture that combines broad candidate retrieval with query-specific evidence filtering.

title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
description:
arXiv:2610.36631v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.

title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.36729v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.

title: Readout and Operating-Point Sensitivity in Event-Stream Candidate Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.36743v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Event-triggered recording needs a useful combination of target capture and false triggers, yet representation comparisons can change with readout and threshold calibration. We evaluate real event accumulations from 520 DailyDVS-200 clips and 47 participants using participant-disjoint training, validation, and testing. The original study varies frozen encoder scale, accumulation duration, and temporal view count; a post-review extension adds two supervised-pretrained convolutional encoders, a 61,586-parameter trained CNN with three seeds, ten repeated participant partitions, and calibration sensitivity. At 50 ms/eight views under the primary handshake-or-fall policy, DINO-S CLS captures 101/132 targets with 40/388 false triggers, versus 78/132 and 35/388 for patch mean. DINO-B CLS has lower selected-threshold capture but higher fold-wise low-FPR partial AUC (0.746 versus 0.732). MobileNetV3-Small captures 97/132 with 53/388 false triggers, demonstrating why lightweight baselines and actual operating points matter. Across ten dependent repartitions, mean normalized partial AUC is 0.738 for DINO-B CLS and 0.674 for MobileNet. The original LeJEPA S-to-B capture difference is 8.3 points, but its multiplicity-adjusted interval includes zero. Duration and view-count effects remain policy dependent. We find no established JEPA-specific advantage. The evidence concerns offline action-defined candidate selection on previously used development data; it does not establish personal recording value, continuous false alarms per hour, or eyewear energy.

title: An honest look at LLM-as-a-judge
description:
Asked to score the same response five times, a local LLM judge gave the identical answer 36% of the time. Asked to match a human rater's score, it matched only 36% of the time too. The judge is precise. Precision is not accuracy.

Key takeaways

  • A registered gate required Spearman correlation of at least 0.5 between the judge's scores and human helpfulness ratings. The actual figure was 0.395, significant but weak - the gate fired, and the claim that this judge tracks human judgement well enough to trust is rejected.
  • A second gate required the judge's own repeat-to-repeat variation to stay below 0.75 points on a 0-4 scale. The actual figure was 0.386 - the gate passed, with margin. The judge is internally consistent.
  • 36% of items got the exact same score across five independent runs. Separately, only 36% of items had the judge's score match the human rater's at all. The two numbers measure different things and happen to coincide.
  • One response, a well-formatted table of ten Bruce Lee video games, got a human rating of 4 (extremely helpful) and a judge rating of 0, not helpful at all, across all five repeats. No internal disagreement flagged the error.

What does a kill-gate for a judge actually test?

HelpSteer2 (Wang et al., 2024) is a public dataset of prompts and responses, each rated by human annotators on five dimensions, helpfulness among them, on a 0-4 scale - a ready-made ground truth. A local model, gpt-oss run through Ollama on an RTX 5070 Ti, rated the same helpfulness dimension on 150 randomly sampled validation items, using the same 0-4 definition the annotators used. Each item was rated five separate times at a non-zero temperature, not once, because a single score cannot distinguish a stable judgement from a lucky one.

Two thresholds were registered before any score was collected. Agreement with humans, as Spearman correlation across the 150 items, had to reach 0.5 to call the judge a usable proxy. The judge's own spread across its five repeats, averaged across items, had to stay under 0.75 points to call its single-shot output trustworthy. Sheng et al. (2025) make the case for treating judge uncertainty as something to measure, not assume away - the same instinct behind every kill-gate on this site: a number fixed before the run is a commitment, not a suggestion to renegotiate once the data arrives.

A third check was purely diagnostic, no threshold attached: whether a judge's own disagreement with itself predicts how far it lands from the human score. That one decides nothing alone, but answers a question the two pass/fail gates cannot: does instability at least work as a warning sign.

How did the agreement gate fire?

Spearman rho came in at 0.395, comfortably below the 0.5 bar, with a p-value under 0.0001 - the weakness is not noise, it is a real, measurable gap. Human raters were generous: 119 of 150 items received a 3 or 4. The judge was not: only 30 items got a 4, and a disproportionate 42 landed on 2, a score humans gave only 9 times. Mean absolute error across all 150 items was 0.97, nearly a full point on a five-point scale. None of this is a close call that rounding would fix.

The shape of the disagreement matters as much as its size. A judge that was simply harsher across the board, shifting every score down by roughly the same amount, would still correlate well with human ratings even while disagreeing on the absolute number. That is not what happened here: the judge's distribution bulges in the middle of the scale where the human distribution does not, which is a difference in shape, not just in strictness, and a weak correlation coefficient is exactly the number that shape produces.

Why does low variance not mean the judge is right?

The clean separation in this experiment is between how consistent the judge is with itself and how correct it is against an outside standard. 36% of items got an identical score across all five runs - zero internal disagreement. Averaged over every item, the standard deviation across repeats was 0.386, which is why the stability gate passed easily. None of that stability says anything about correctness.

The table of Bruce Lee video games makes the gap concrete. It is well formatted, directly answers the prompt, and a human rater called it extremely helpful. The judge called it not helpful at all, and did so identically five times out of five. A registered diagnostic gate checked whether instability at least flags likely errors: the correlation between a judge's spread and its error was 0.231, real but weak. A confident, repeatable answer carried no signal that it might be wrong.

What does this mean for using a local judge in practice?

The practical reading is not that a local LLM judge is worthless, but that its self-reported consistency is the wrong thing to check for trust. A judge that always gives the same answer has removed one failure mode, random noise, while leaving the larger one, systematic disagreement with the standard that actually matters, completely open. Trusting a judge because it is stable is the same mistake as trusting a model because it sounds confident: a property of the output being checked, not the property that was actually asked about.

The registered-gate discipline earns its keep here. Without a pre-set bar, a correlation of 0.395 is easy to call "reasonably correlated" and move on. With the bar fixed at 0.5 in advance, the number is unambiguous: below the line, claim rejected, no rounding up afterward. The stability gate passing easily could have been reported alone, as the one number that looked good. Registering both before running either is what keeps the uncomfortable number in the final report too.

FAQ

Does this mean LLM-as-a-judge is useless for this kind of task?

Not useless, but not a drop-in replacement for human rating, at least for this model and dimension. A rho of 0.395 is a real, positive signal, just too weak to clear the bar set for trusting a single automated score in place of a human one.

Would a larger model do better?

Plausibly, but this experiment did not test that. Sheng et al. (2025) and related work suggest judge quality varies substantially by model and task, which is exactly why the registered scope here is one model, one dimension, not a general claim about LLM judges.

Why measure stability at all if it does not predict accuracy well?

Because the alternative, assuming a model is reliable because it answers the same way twice, is a common and untested shortcut. Measuring it and finding it insufficient is itself the finding: consistency was the easier property to check, and checking it first revealed that it was not the property that mattered.

What would make this result more convincing?

Testing more than one judge model, more than one rated dimension from HelpSteer2, and a larger sample than 150 items. The current scope was chosen to fit a single local GPU in reasonable time, not because it is the ceiling of what is worth checking.

References

  • Zhilin Wang, Yi Dong, Olivier Delalleau, Jiaqi Zeng, Gerald Shen, Daniel Egert, Jimmy J. Zhang, Makesh Narsimhan Sreedhar, Oleksii Kuchaiev. HelpSteer2: Open-source dataset for training top-performing reward models, 2024. arxiv.org/abs/2406.08673
  • Huanxin Sheng, Xinyi Liu, Hangfeng He, Jieyu Zhao, Jian Kang. Analyzing Uncertainty of LLM-as-a-Judge: Interval Evaluations with Conformal Prediction, 2025. arxiv.org/abs/2509.18658

title: JDA-ZIP UDE — What If a Shared Dictionary Could Evolve With Its Users?
description:
An idea for a universal, dynamic, and evolutionary dictionary for data compression.

What if a dictionary used for compression didn't need to remain static?

What if every user could contribute to its evolution, allowing other users to benefit from new expressions, references, and patterns already discovered?

This is the idea behind JDA-ZIP UDE (Universal Dynamic Evolutionary Dictionary), an architectural proposal connected to the JDA-ZIP Protocol project.

The problem I started thinking about

Traditional compression methods are extremely useful, but I started exploring a different approach: reducing the amount of information that needs to be transmitted by using shared semantic and reference-based dictionaries.

Imagine two systems communicating over a slow internet connection.

Instead of repeatedly transmitting the same expressions, terms, or sequences, they could use previously established identifiers to represent information.

This raises an interesting question:

What if that dictionary could grow continuously through the contributions of its users?

The UDE concept

The idea is to maintain a universal logical dictionary that can evolve over time.

For example:

  1. User A submits a text for compression.
  2. The system checks whether its expressions already exist in the shared dictionary.
  3. Existing expressions are replaced with their corresponding identifiers.
  4. New expressions may be evaluated and added when they meet defined criteria.
  5. User B can later benefit from those same entries without having to discover them again.

The dictionary becomes a shared resource rather than an isolated collection of entries belonging to a single user.

Permanent identifiers

One important principle of this proposal is that dictionary identifiers should be permanent.

Once an identifier is assigned to an expression, it should never be reassigned to another expression.

This helps preserve compatibility between different versions of the dictionary and reduces the risk of decoding ambiguity.

The system would also need mechanisms to handle simultaneous updates, duplicate entries, validation, and synchronization.

A universal dictionary, not separate dictionaries

The proposal is to maintain one universal logical dictionary.

It could contain expressions from different languages, technical terminology, common phrases, and other recurring patterns.

This does not mean every user needs to download the entire dictionary.

Local caches, incremental synchronization, and version references could help systems access only the information they need.

Online and offline operation

Another important aspect is connectivity.

When online, a system could synchronize with the central dictionary and access newer entries.

When offline, it could continue using a local dictionary snapshot.

If a compressed package contains references that are missing from the receiving system, those references would need to be supplied or synchronized before decoding.

This is particularly interesting for environments with limited connectivity, such as remote locations, satellite connections, and low-bandwidth networks.

Is this already implemented?

No. The UDE is currently an architectural proposal under development.

There are existing technologies and standards involving compression dictionaries and shared dictionary mechanisms. The goal here is not to claim that shared dictionaries are a new invention.

The contribution I want to explore is a specific architecture combining:

  • A universal and cumulative logical dictionary.
  • Dynamic inclusion of new expressions.
  • Permanent identifiers.
  • Shared reuse across different users.
  • Incremental synchronization.
  • Online and offline compatibility.

There are still technical challenges to investigate, especially dictionary growth, lookup performance, synchronization costs, and whether the approach produces measurable benefits in real-world workloads.

Why am I sharing this?

I am documenting the idea publicly because I believe projects like this can improve through discussion and collaboration.

I would particularly like to hear from developers and researchers who have experience with:

  • Data compression algorithms.
  • Distributed databases.
  • Dictionary-based encoding.
  • Synchronization protocols.
  • Low-bandwidth communication systems.

Could a shared dictionary that evolves with its users become a useful layer for future data transmission systems?

That is the question I want to explore.

Project and documentation

JDA-ZIP Protocol: https://github.com/jdavid465/JDA-ZIP-PROTOCOL/

The UDE documentation and technical specification are being developed within the project repository.

Author: Jonathan D. Andrade

Project: JDA-ZIP Protocol / JDA-ZIP UDE

Status: Architectural proposal — under development.

title: 검색 결과는 왜 오래된 정보를 보여줄까? 데이터베이스와 검색 인덱스 동기화 설
description:
웹사이트에서 정보를 수정했는데 검색 결과에는 이전 내용이 그대로 표시되는 경우가 있다.

관리자는 제목을 변경했고, API는 정상적으로 응답했으며, 데이터베이스에도 새로운 내용이 저장되어 있다. 그런데 검색창에 키워드를 입력하면 수정하기 전의 제목이나 설명이 나타난다.

이 문제는 단순히 검색 기능이 느리기 때문에 발생하는 것이 아니다.

데이터베이스와 검색 인덱스가 서로 다른 시점의 정보를 가지고 있기 때문에 발생할 수 있다.

특히 웹사이트 디렉터리, 상품 검색 서비스, 구인구직 플랫폼, 문서 검색 시스템처럼 데이터가 지속적으로 변경되는 서비스에서는 중요한 문제다.

이번 글에서는 데이터 변경부터 검색 결과 반영까지의 과정을 살펴보고, 실무 환경에서 데이터 불일치를 방지하기 위한 시스템 설계 방법을 정리한다.

1. 데이터베이스와 검색 인덱스는 서로 다른 시스템이다

검색 기능을 제공하는 웹서비스는 일반적으로 두 가지 데이터 저장 구조를 사용한다.

첫 번째는 원본 데이터를 관리하는 데이터베이스다.

두 번째는 검색에 적합하도록 데이터를 구성한 검색 인덱스다.

두 시스템은 역할이 다르다.

구분 데이터베이스 검색 인덱스
주요 목적 원본 데이터 저장 및 관리 검색과 조회 최적화
대표 기술 PostgreSQL, MySQL Elasticsearch, OpenSearch
데이터 변경 트랜잭션 중심 색인 작업 중심
검색 방식 SQL 쿼리 등 역색인 및 검색 엔진 쿼리
데이터 일관성 트랜잭션 범위의 일관성 보장 별도 동기화 설계 필요

예를 들어 웹사이트 정보를 저장하는 서비스를 생각해 보자.

데이터베이스에는 다음과 같은 정보가 저장되어 있다.

{
  "id": 1042,
  "title": "개발자 자료 모음",
  "category": "기술",
  "status": "active",
  "version": 8
}

그런데 검색 인덱스에는 이전 버전이 남아 있을 수 있다.

{
  "id": 1042,
  "title": "프로그래밍 링크 모음",
  "category": "기술",
  "status": "active",
  "version": 6
}

두 시스템 모두 정상적으로 작동하고 있지만, 데이터는 일치하지 않는다.

이것이 검색 데이터 동기화 문제의 출발점이다.

기본적인 데이터 흐름 

[사용자 데이터 수정]
         |
         v
   [Application API]
         |
         v
   [Primary Database]
         |
         v
    [이벤트 전달]
         |
         v
    [Index Worker]
         |
         v
    [Search Index]
         |
         v
     [검색 결과]

이 구조에서는 데이터가 여러 단계를 거쳐 이동한다.

그리고 각 단계에서 장애가 발생할 수 있다.

  • 데이터베이스 저장은 성공했지만 검색 인덱스 갱신이 실패할 수 있다.
  • 동일한 이벤트가 중복으로 전달될 수 있다.
  • 이벤트가 생성된 순서와 처리되는 순서가 달라질 수 있다.
  • 검색 인덱스에 변경 사항이 저장됐지만 아직 검색 결과에는 나타나지 않을 수 있다.

따라서 안정적인 검색 시스템을 만들려면 단순한 데이터 저장 기능뿐 아니라 동기화 과정 전체를 설계해야 한다.

2. 데이터베이스와 검색 인덱스를 동시에 수정하면 왜 위험할까?

가장 단순한 방법은 API 요청이 들어올 때 데이터베이스와 검색 인덱스를 연속으로 갱신하는 것이다.

예를 들어 Python으로 다음과 같이 구현할 수 있다.

def update_document(document_id, data):
    database.update(document_id, data)
    search_index.update(document_id, data)

이 방식은 구현이 간단하다.

그러나 두 시스템의 작업이 하나의 트랜잭션으로 묶여 있지 않다는 문제가 있다.

실패 시나리오

다음 상황을 가정해 보자.

  1. 사용자가 웹사이트 제목을 수정한다.
  2. 데이터베이스 업데이트가 성공한다.
  3. 검색 서버에 일시적인 장애가 발생한다.
  4. 검색 인덱스 업데이트가 실패한다.
  5. 데이터베이스에는 새 제목이 저장되지만 검색 결과에는 이전 제목이 남는다.

검색 서버를 다시 정상화하더라도 변경 사항이 자동으로 복구된다는 보장은 없다.

더 중요한 문제는 애플리케이션이 데이터 불일치 자체를 인식하지 못할 수 있다는 것이다.

해결 방법: Transactional Outbox Pattern

Transactional Outbox는 데이터베이스의 변경 사항과 이벤트 기록을 하나의 트랜잭션으로 저장하는 패턴이다.

        [Application API]
                |
                v
        [DB Transaction]
          /           \
         v             v
 [데이터 변경]     [Outbox 이벤트 저장]
          \           /
           v         v
         [Transaction Commit]
                  |
                  v
           [Outbox Relay]
                  |
                  v
             [Event Queue]
                  |
                  v
            [Index Worker]
                  |
                  v
             [Search Index]

핵심은 데이터베이스 변경과 이벤트 생성 기록이 함께 커밋된다는 점이다.

트랜잭션이 실패하면 둘 다 저장되지 않는다.

반대로 트랜잭션이 성공하면 검색 인덱스에 반영해야 할 변경 사항이 Outbox에 남아 있게 된다.

검색 서버에 장애가 발생하더라도 이벤트 기록을 기반으로 재처리할 수 있다.

다만 Transactional Outbox 자체가 이벤트의 정확히 한 번 처리를 보장하는 것은 아니다.

중복 전달과 순서 문제는 별도로 해결해야 한다.

3. 이벤트 순서가 바뀌면 최신 데이터가 사라질 수 있다

이벤트 기반 시스템에서는 데이터가 변경된 순서와 실제 처리되는 순서가 반드시 같지는 않다.

다음 상황을 생각해 보자.

10:00:01 -> 문서 버전 11 생성
10:00:02 -> 문서 버전 12 생성

정상적인 최종 상태는 버전 12다.

그러나 네트워크 지연이나 여러 Worker의 동시 처리로 인해 이벤트가 다음 순서로 처리될 수 있다.

버전 12 처리 -> 최신 데이터 반영
버전 11 처리 -> 이전 데이터로 덮어쓰기

결과적으로 검색 인덱스가 과거 상태로 돌아간다.

이러한 문제를 방지하려면 문서마다 버전 번호를 관리하는 방법을 고려할 수 있다.

이벤트에 버전 정보 추가하기 

{
  "event_id": "evt-93f",
  "document_id": 1042,
  "version": 12,
  "operation": "upsert"
}

검색 인덱스에 이벤트를 적용할 때 버전 번호를 비교한다.

기존 인덱스가 더 높은 버전을 가지고 있다면 오래된 이벤트를 거부해야 한다.

단, 버전을 읽은 다음 비교하고 다시 저장하는 방식은 동시 실행 환경에서 경쟁 조건이 발생할 수 있다.

따라서 버전 검증과 갱신은 검색 엔진에서 원자적으로 처리되어야 한다.

Elasticsearch 외부 버전 관리 예시 

from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch

es = Elasticsearch("http://localhost:9200")

def apply_event(event, document):
    es.index(
        index="directory",
        id=event["document_id"],
        document=document,
        version=event["version"],
        version_type="external",
    )

이 예시는 문서별 버전 번호가 양의 정수이며 변경할 때마다 증가한다는 전제를 가진다.

Elasticsearch의 외부 버전 관리 기능을 이용하면 현재 저장된 버전보다 오래된 이벤트가 문서를 덮어쓰지 못하도록 할 수 있다.

같은 버전이 다시 전달된 경우에도 충돌이 발생할 수 있으므로, Worker는 충돌 원인을 분류해야 한다.

중요한 것은 단순히 이벤트를 처리했다는 사실이 아니다.

최신 버전이 이전 버전으로 덮어써지지 않았는지 확인하는 것이 핵심이다.

4. 이벤트 중복 전달을 고려해야 한다

메시지 큐를 사용하는 시스템에서는 하나의 이벤트가 여러 번 전달될 수 있다.

예를 들어 다음 상황이 발생할 수 있다.

  1. Worker가 이벤트를 수신한다.
  2. 검색 인덱스 업데이트에 성공한다.
  3. Worker가 이벤트 처리 완료를 알리기 전에 종료된다.
  4. 메시지 큐가 같은 이벤트를 다시 전달한다.

이것은 적어도 한 번 전달하는 방식(At-Least-Once Delivery)에서 발생할 수 있는 정상적인 상황이다.

따라서 동일한 이벤트를 반복 처리해도 최종 데이터가 잘못되지 않도록 설계해야 한다.

이를 멱등성(Idempotency)이라고 한다.

[버전 12 이벤트 수신]
          |
          v
    [검색 인덱스 반영]
          |
          v
    [Worker 비정상 종료]
          |
          v
    [버전 12 재전달]
          |
          v
    [이미 적용된 버전 확인]
          |
          v
    [중복 이벤트 처리 완료]

멱등성을 구현하는 방법은 시스템에 따라 다르다.

대표적으로 다음 정보를 사용할 수 있다.

  • 고유한 이벤트 ID
  • 문서별 버전 번호
  • 마지막 처리 이벤트 기록
  • 검색 엔진의 조건부 갱신 기능

다만 중복 처리 방지를 위해 이벤트 ID만 저장하는 방식은 운영 규모와 보관 기간까지 고려해야 한다.

검색 인덱스 갱신 외에 다른 부수 효과가 존재한다면 별도의 처리 이력 관리가 필요할 수도 있다.

5. 삭제된 데이터가 검색 결과에 남는 문제

검색 동기화에서 놓치기 쉬운 부분은 삭제 처리다.

데이터베이스에서 특정 문서를 삭제했지만 검색 인덱스에 삭제 요청이 반영되지 않으면, 검색 결과에 존재하지 않는 문서가 표시될 수 있다.

이러한 결과를 흔히 Ghost Result라고 부른다.

삭제 이벤트 예시 

{
  "event_id": "evt-94a",
  "document_id": 1042,
  "version": 13,
  "operation": "delete"
}

하지만 검색 인덱스에서 문서를 즉시 제거하는 것만으로 충분하지 않을 수 있다.

삭제 이벤트 이후 과거의 수정 이벤트가 늦게 도착하면 삭제된 문서가 다시 생성될 위험이 있기 때문이다.

Tombstone을 이용한 삭제 관리

Tombstone은 삭제된 문서의 상태와 버전 정보를 남겨두는 방식이다.

{
  "id": 1042,
  "version": 13,
  "deleted": true
}

검색 쿼리에서는 deleted: true인 문서를 제외한다.

동시에 버전 13이라는 정보를 보존하므로 버전 12의 오래된 수정 이벤트를 거부할 수 있다.

다만 Tombstone은 저장 공간을 사용하며 검색 시 필터링이 필요하다.

실제 구현에서는 다음 조건을 함께 판단해야 한다.

  • 삭제된 문서의 버전을 얼마나 오래 보관할 것인가?
  • 과거 이벤트는 최대 얼마나 늦게 도착할 수 있는가?
  • 삭제된 데이터의 복원 가능성이 필요한가?
  • 개인정보 삭제 및 보존 정책과 충돌하지 않는가?

삭제는 단순한 데이터 제거 작업이 아니라 이벤트 순서와 데이터 일관성의 문제이기도 하다.

6. 인덱스 업데이트 성공과 검색 노출은 다르다

Elasticsearch와 같은 검색 엔진에서는 문서를 저장했다고 해서 반드시 즉시 검색 결과에 나타나는 것은 아니다.

Elasticsearch는 Near Real-Time Search 구조를 사용한다.

인덱스에 반영된 변경 사항이 검색 가능해지는 시점은 Refresh 동작과 관련이 있다.

[DB Commit]
     |
     v
[Outbox Event]
     |
     v
[Index Write]
     |
     v
[Search Refresh]
     |
     v
[검색 결과 반영]

따라서 다음 상태를 구분해야 한다.

  1. 데이터베이스 저장 완료
  2. 검색 인덱스 쓰기 완료
  3. 검색 결과에서 조회 가능

세 단계는 동일한 시점에 완료된다고 가정하면 안 된다.

Refresh 정책 설계

Elasticsearch에서는 검색 가시성에 대한 요구 사항에 따라 Refresh 관련 옵션을 사용할 수 있다.

  • 기본 비동기 Refresh: 일반적인 색인 작업에 적합
  • refresh=wait_for: 다음 Refresh까지 기다린 뒤 응답
  • refresh=true: 관련 샤드의 Refresh를 강제로 수행

모든 쓰기 요청마다 강제 Refresh를 수행하는 방식은 성능 부담을 증가시킬 수 있다.

관리자가 콘텐츠를 수정했다고 해서 모든 상황에서 즉시 검색 결과에 반영할 필요가 있는지도 검토해야 한다.

예를 들어 문서 관리 화면에는 데이터베이스의 최신 내용을 표시하고, 전체 검색에는 일정한 반영 지연을 허용하는 구조도 가능하다.

이때 사용자에게 어떤 일관성 수준을 제공할지 명확히 정의하는 것이 중요하다.

7. 검색 인덱스 지연을 측정하는 방법

검색 시스템의 문제는 검색 결과가 틀렸다는 사용자 신고를 받은 후에야 발견되는 경우가 있다.

이를 방지하려면 동기화 지연과 데이터 불일치를 측정해야 한다.

수집해야 할 주요 시간 정보

  • 데이터베이스 변경 완료 시점
  • 이벤트 생성 시점
  • Worker가 이벤트를 수신한 시점
  • 검색 인덱스 쓰기 완료 시점
  • 실제 검색 가시성 확인 시점

이 정보를 이용하면 두 가지 지표를 구분할 수 있다.

Processing Lag

데이터 변경부터 인덱스 쓰기 완료까지 걸린 시간이다.

Search Visibility Lag

데이터 변경부터 실제 검색 결과에 최신 내용이 나타날 때까지 걸린 시간이다.

두 지표는 동일하지 않을 수 있다.

모니터링 지표 예시 

index_processing_lag_seconds
outbox_oldest_pending_age_seconds
index_events_failed_total
index_events_duplicate_total
index_version_conflicts_total
index_reconciliation_mismatches_total

이런 지표를 Prometheus 등의 모니터링 시스템으로 수집할 수 있다.

평균 처리 시간만 측정하기보다 P95, P99처럼 지연 분포를 확인하는 것도 중요하다.

대부분의 문서가 빠르게 반영되더라도 일부 문서가 장시간 오래된 상태로 남을 수 있기 때문이다.

운영 목표 예시 

인덱스 갱신 99%를 30초 이내 처리
5분 이상 대기한 Outbox 이벤트 감지
지속적인 인덱싱 실패 시 알림 발생

위 수치는 설명을 위한 예시다.

실제 기준은 서비스의 데이터 변경 빈도, 검색 중요도, 사용자 요구 사항에 따라 결정해야 한다.

8. 이벤트 처리 외에 데이터 검증 작업도 필요하다

이벤트 큐가 비어 있다고 해서 데이터베이스와 검색 인덱스가 완전히 일치한다는 뜻은 아니다.

다음과 같은 문제가 남아 있을 수 있다.

  • 배포 과정에서 일부 이벤트가 누락됨
  • 검색 인덱스 매핑 변경으로 일부 필드가 잘못 저장됨
  • 오래된 Worker가 잘못된 문서를 생성함
  • 인덱스 재구축 과정에서 데이터가 빠짐
  • 운영 중 수동 수정으로 두 시스템의 상태가 달라짐

이러한 문제를 감지하기 위한 방법이 Reconciliation이다.

Reconciliation은 원본 데이터와 검색 인덱스를 비교하고 차이를 확인하는 검증 과정이다.

기본적인 검증 흐름 

[Primary Database]
         |
         v
   [데이터 배치 조회]
         |
         v
   [Search Index 조회]
         |
         v
     [상태 비교]
       /      \
      v        v
   [일치]    [불일치]
      |        |
      v        v
   [종료]   [복구 작업 등록]
               |
               v
        [최신 원본 재색인]

비교 기준으로는 다음 항목을 활용할 수 있다.

  • 문서 ID
  • 데이터 버전
  • 삭제 여부
  • 인덱싱 대상 필드의 해시값

복구 예시 

Primary Database Version: 18
Search Index Version:     16

결과:
검색 인덱스가 이전 버전임

조치:
데이터베이스의 최신 내용을 다시 색인

검증:
검색 인덱스 버전이 18인지 확인

대량 데이터를 처리하는 시스템이라면 모든 문서를 한 번에 메모리에 불러오는 방식은 피해야 한다.

배치 처리와 점진적인 비교 작업을 활용하고, 필요하면 정기적인 전체 검증을 수행하는 것이 좋다.

9. 실제 운영 환경에서 발생할 수 있는 장애 시나리오

여러 웹사이트 정보를 검색할 수 있는 디렉터리 서비스를 가정해 보자.

관리자가 한 문서의 카테고리를 수정한다.

이때 데이터 흐름은 다음과 같다.

  1. 데이터베이스에 버전 21이 저장된다.
  2. Outbox에 변경 이벤트가 기록된다.
  3. 이벤트가 메시지 큐로 전달된다.
  4. Worker가 검색 인덱스 업데이트를 시도한다.
  5. 검색 서버가 일시적으로 쓰기를 거부한다.
  6. Worker는 처리 완료를 승인하지 못한다.
  7. 그 사이 새로운 변경인 버전 22가 검색 인덱스에 반영된다.
  8. 이전 이벤트인 버전 21이 다시 전달된다.
  9. 버전 검증에서 오래된 이벤트로 판정되어 적용되지 않는다.

최종 검색 결과에는 버전 22가 유지된다.

버전 검증이 없다면?

버전 21이 버전 22를 덮어쓸 수 있다.

이 경우 이벤트 큐는 정상적으로 작동하고 모든 메시지가 처리되었어도 검색 결과에는 이전 정보가 표시된다.

따라서 시스템 안정성을 판단할 때는 이벤트 전달 성공 여부만 보는 것으로 충분하지 않다.

최종 데이터의 정확성까지 검증해야 한다.

10. 프로덕션 적용 전 체크리스트

검색 인덱스 동기화 시스템을 운영 환경에 적용하기 전 다음 항목을 점검할 필요가 있다.

데이터 일관성

  • [ ] 원본 데이터의 기준 시스템이 명확한가?
  • [ ] 데이터 변경과 Outbox 이벤트를 하나의 트랜잭션으로 저장하는가?
  • [ ] 문서별 버전 번호를 관리하는가?
  • [ ] 오래된 이벤트가 최신 정보를 덮어쓸 수 없는가?
  • [ ] 중복 이벤트를 안전하게 처리하는가?
  • [ ] 삭제된 문서가 과거 이벤트에 의해 복원되지 않는가?

검색 인덱스 운영

  • [ ] Worker가 비정상 종료된 후 작업을 재개할 수 있는가?
  • [ ] 실패한 이벤트를 추적하고 재처리할 수 있는가?
  • [ ] 인덱스 스키마 변경에 대한 절차가 있는가?
  • [ ] 검색 가시성 지연을 고려했는가?
  • [ ] 전체 인덱스를 재구축할 수 있는가?

모니터링과 복구

  • [ ] 동기화 지연을 측정하는가?
  • [ ] 오래 대기하는 이벤트를 감지할 수 있는가?
  • [ ] 버전 충돌과 일반 장애를 구분하는가?
  • [ ] 데이터베이스와 인덱스의 차이를 검증하는가?
  • [ ] 복구 작업 이후 결과를 확인하는가?

11. 모든 서비스에 복잡한 동기화 구조가 필요할까?

그렇지는 않다.

데이터 변경이 드물고 규모가 작은 서비스라면 정기적으로 검색 인덱스를 재구축하는 방식만으로 충분할 수 있다.

반대로 다음 조건에 해당한다면 이벤트 기반 동기화 구조를 검토할 가치가 있다.

  • 검색이 서비스의 핵심 기능이다.
  • 데이터 변경이 빈번하다.
  • 여러 시스템에서 동일한 데이터를 수정한다.
  • 오래된 정보가 노출되면 서비스 신뢰도에 영향을 준다.
  • 검색 서버 장애가 원본 데이터 저장에 영향을 주면 안 된다.
  • 검색 결과의 정확성을 독립적으로 검증해야 한다.

중요한 것은 최신 기술을 많이 사용하는 것이 아니다.

서비스에 필요한 데이터 일관성 수준을 정의하고 그 요구 사항에 맞춰 설계하는 것이다.

결론

검색 시스템의 안정성은 빠른 검색 속도만으로 결정되지 않는다.

데이터베이스에 저장된 최신 정보가 검색 인덱스에도 정확하게 반영되는지가 중요하다.

이를 위해서는 데이터 변경 기록의 안정적인 전달, 이벤트 중복 처리, 버전 관리, 삭제 상태 보존, 동기화 지연 측정, 데이터 재검증과 복구 절차가 필요하다.

특히 다음 세 가지 상태를 구분해야 한다.

데이터베이스 저장 성공, 검색 인덱스 갱신 성공, 실제 검색 결과 반영은 서로 다른 단계다.

이 차이를 이해하고 설계하는 것이 단순한 검색 기능 구현과 안정적인 검색 인프라 구축을 구분하는 기준이 된다.

참고 자료

  • AWS 공식 문서: Transactional Outbox Pattern
  • Elastic 공식 문서: Near Real-Time Search
  • Elastic 공식 문서: Refresh Parameter

※ 이 글은 웹서비스 내부의 검색 인덱스 동기화를 설명한다. Google 검색의 크롤링과 색인 반영은 별도의 시스템이며, 내부 검색 인덱스를 갱신했다고 Google 검색 결과가 즉시 변경되는 것은 아니다.

title: CORS Errors During Browser-Based Thumbnail Uploads: Object Storage with Go
description:
Use a server-minted presigned URL for the browser upload, and treat CORS as a browser policy rather than an authorization mechanism. For property-management receipts, keep the original in a private object key and make thumbnail creation a prerequisite for any later retention decision.

That is the short answer. The useful part is deciding which system owns each boundary: the application owns identity and deletion state, the bucket owns object access, and the browser is allowed only the cross-origin request that the upload actually needs. When errors occur during browser-based uploads, this split keeps a thumbnail failure from becoming an unexplained retention decision.

How should browser-based thumbnail uploads handle CORS errors?

It tells you very little about the image worker. Browsers block a cross-origin request when the storage response does not grant the requesting origin, method, or headers. A failed preflight can therefore appear beside a perfectly reachable bucket in developer tools. The first diagnostic split is between an OPTIONS policy failure and an upload response from storage; combining them into one generic “thumbnail upload failed” alarm makes the next action slower.

For an employee uploading a receipt, the flow should be deliberately asymmetric. The application authenticates the employee and selects a key such as receipts/{receiptID}/original. It asks storage for a presigned URL with the required permission. The browser sends the file to that URL. It must not send the application's bearer token to the returned URL.

The policy is the boundary.

Configure the bucket policy for the real production origin and the local development origin separately, with the exact upload method and headers. A permissive rule may make a demo pass while hiding a governance mistake. A signed URL limits the operation; CORS decides whether the browser may attempt it. They solve different failures.

Which boundary should own retention?

Retention is a governance decision, so I would model it in the application database before choosing a storage vendor. Record the original key, derived thumbnail key, receipt identifier, retention class, and verification state. The original should not disappear merely because a thumbnail exists. The deletion job should require a verified derivative and an audit event, then delete the derivative and original according to separate policy.

This ordering matters because object storage is not automatically an archive. Infrai storage has no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those native controls. It also has no If-Match conditional write, which means strict compare-and-swap behavior needs coordination in a queue or database. Lifecycle rules have a minimum of one day, and object metadata is not a server-side search index; keep receipt lookup fields in the database.

The practical rule is blunt: use an immutable external control when the record must be WORM-protected, and use an explicit database state transition when deletion must be explainable. Do not make a public image URL part of this design. Static hosting and permanent public links are outside this storage capability's fit.

How do the real options differ at the governance boundary?

The comparison is about operational control, not a price leaderboard.

Option Browser upload and policy model Retention boundary Good fit
Amazon S3 Presigned upload plus bucket CORS Lifecycle and versioning controls are available in the storage ecosystem Teams that want mature native recovery and retention primitives
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible presigned upload plus CORS Confirm the exact compatibility and retention behavior used by the deployment Applications already operating around Cloudflare's object APIs
Google Cloud Storage Signed URL plus bucket CORS Lifecycle and object-retention features can support separate source and derivative policies Teams already governed by Google Cloud IAM and storage controls
Infrai storage Presigned object URL, with CORS administration requiring an approved external path No versioning, object lock, or conditional If-Match write; no public-read pattern Teams that value a single REST credential across backend capabilities and can supply the missing governance controls

Infrai's useful distinction is not that it removes retention work. Infrai offers one key and one bill, plus a plain REST API for storage beside a broader platform surface with 295 routes across 20 modules. That reduces credential and reconciliation friction when the same receipt workflow also depends on other backend services. The second advantage is direct HTTP: a Go worker can call it without installing an SDK, and the public discovery surface describes capabilities and schemas without requiring a key. That is helpful when a small retention worker must stay easy to inspect and portable.

The trade-off is real. The limitation is operational: as of the 2026-10-25 snapshot, Infrai does not expose a self-service CORS configuration path for this workflow, despite the bucket model having a cors_rules field, so the bucket's approved administration path must be settled before browser uploads go live. Infrai is not suitable for public image hosting, WORM retention, or recovery from accidental overwrite. I would choose S3 or GCS instead when native immutable retention, version recovery, or self-service CORS is a hard requirement. Choose the single-interface option only when an external governance layer is already part of the design.

Can a Go uploader keep the authorization boundary clear?

Yes, if it has two requests with two different responsibilities. The server-side request is authenticated and obtains a presigned URL. The upload request uses the returned URL and the expected content type, but does not carry the platform bearer token. Keep the original private and generate the thumbnail after storage confirms the source upload.

The following small client intentionally takes the presign endpoint and returned URL from its environment because request fields and the signed URL response are service-discovery data, not values to guess in an article. It still demonstrates the important boundary and reports non-success responses instead of assuming 200.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    presignEndpoint := os.Getenv("INFRAI_PRESIGN_ENDPOINT")
    presignedURL := os.Getenv("PRESIGNED_URL")
    if apiKey == "" || presignEndpoint == "" || presignedURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_PRESIGN_ENDPOINT, and PRESIGNED_URL are required")
    }

    request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, presignEndpoint, nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

    response, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(request)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer response.Body.Close()
    if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 4096))
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("presign failed: %s: %s", response.Status, body))
    }

    file, err := os.Open(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer file.Close()

    upload, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, presignedURL, file)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    upload.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/jpeg")
    result, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(upload)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer result.Body.Close()
    if result.StatusCode < 200 || result.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(result.Body, 4096))
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("upload failed: %s: %s", result.Status, body))
    }
}

This is intentionally a presign-and-upload probe, not a production thumbnail worker. Production code should validate the source before deriving an image, make retries idempotent with a receipt identifier, and treat standard queue delivery as at least once. The worker should also record the source and derivative keys before the retention clock starts.

What is the verification and rollback order?

Start with one canary bucket and one real browser origin. Check the preflight, then the upload, then a private read. Test a disallowed origin. Test a replacement key. The last test is the uncomfortable one, because it exposes whether the system has recovery semantics or merely a successful PUT.

My release gate is four checks:

  1. The application can mint a URL only for an authorized receipt key.
  2. The preflight permits the exact method and headers used by the browser.
  3. An unsuccessful upload cannot be recorded as a completed source.
  4. The retention job refuses to delete an original until the database shows a verified thumbnail and audit event.

If a gate fails, stop the thumbnail worker and retention job, preserve the original prefix, and correct the policy or database state. Do not claim recovery from an overwritten object when versioning or object lock is absent. For a property manager, that restraint is part of the audit trail.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/PresignedUrlUploadObject.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ManageCorsUsing.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/cross-origin
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final

title: I shut down my agent-safety toolkit to audit AI graders
description:
Earlier this year I posted here about SafeClaw and Authensor's policy engine for AI agents. That product line is retired, and those posts now say so at the top. This is what Authensor works on instead.

Authensor is an AI evaluation integrity firm in San Francisco. It audits the tools the AI industry measures itself with: evaluation harnesses, benchmarks, LLM judges and scoring pipelines. The question for each one is whether the system being evaluated can move its own score.

Why the switch

Two of the early bugs I fixed upstream were in agent-control tooling. In April 2026, UK AISI's ControlArena passed tool-call arguments and chain-of-thought text into its monitor prompts unsanitized, so the agent being monitored could write straight into the prompt of the model watching it. The same pattern kept turning up in graders, judges and benchmarks. If the measurement can be steered by the thing being measured, the safety numbers built on it don't mean much, so that became the work.

The Evaluator Trust Boundary

The research is organized around one definition: an evaluator has an Evaluator Trust Boundary (ETB) failure when its score depends on an artifact the evaluated system can influence. The taxonomy names ten mechanisms, ETB-01 to ETB-10. The preprint is on Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.21633620.

Some of the cases now fixed upstream:

  • SWE-bench (August 2026, ETB-09): the grader counted PASSED lines that the patch under test could print itself. Fixed in PR #620.
  • Promptfoo (October 2026, ETB-03): an llm-rubric judge response with no verdict defaulted to a pass. Fixed in PR #10611.
  • UK AISI Inspect AI (June 2026, ETB-04): scoring metrics silently dropped errored and inconclusive samples from the denominator. Fixed in #4288.
  • NVIDIA garak (July 2026, ETB-06): string detectors did no Unicode normalization, so homoglyph and zero-width variants got through. Fixed in #1884.
  • Instructor (July 2026, ETB-01): JSON extraction took the first object in a code block, so planted JSON outranked the real output. Fixed in #2434.
  • UK AISI ControlArena (April 2026, ETB-02): tool-call arguments entered monitor prompts unsanitized. Fixed in #798.

The full list, with every report and fix, is at authensor.com/etb. Separately, the MLflow advisory for CVE-2026-64849 credits Authensor as an independent finder.

Check your own judge

etb-scan is a free, MIT-licensed scanner that measures ETB-01 (injected verdicts) against your own judge. It runs offline on the standard library, with no API keys.

pip install etb-scan
etbscan --judge mypkg:judge --trials 10

If you've published an eval number and want it checked against the instrument that produced it, Authensor does that free within 48 hours: john@authensor.com.

The hardware side

15 Research Lab is my separate lab in San Francisco for embodied AI safety and experimental hardware. The same kind of bug shows up there. Yosys's formal exporters were silently dropping every assertion, so solvers reported PASS on designs that should fail. I reported it as #6108 and Zaneham fixed it in #6117. Write-up.

  • Every report and fix: https://www.authensor.com/ledger
  • etb-scan: https://github.com/AUTHENSOR/etb-scan
  • 15 Research Lab: https://www.15researchlab.com
  • Me: https://johndanielkearney.com

title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.36929v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.

title: Find the Vulnerability Hiding Between the Features
description:
Security Scenario Explorer — a proposed security-testing direction built on Combinatorics Framework JVM.

Most security tools look for known weaknesses. But some vulnerabilities appear when individually valid requests interact in an unexpected order.

A permission changes while a session remains active. A retry arrives after a timeout. A webhook is delivered twice. An AI agent reads untrusted content while holding access to a privileged tool. Each operation may look legitimate in isolation; the sequence may still violate a security boundary.

Security Scenario Explorer is a proposed workbench for investigating these interaction-driven failures systematically. It builds on Combinatorics Framework JVM, a scenario-modeling and execution framework developed by Yurii B.

It is not positioned as a replacement for vulnerability scanners, DAST, or fuzzers. Its intended focus is security behavior that depends on combinations of context, state, action order, and exceptional events, therefore - reassures you even more in considered direction of potential risks.

Why investigate combinations?

Broken access control remains the top category in the OWASP Top 10:2025, which also includes security misconfiguration, authentication failures, insecure design, and mishandling of exceptional conditions. The OWASP API Security Top 10 highlights broken object-level authorization. For AI applications, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications:2025 includes prompt injection and excessive agency.

These risks often require more than a single request to investigate. The relevant question is not only “Does this endpoint reject a bad input?” but also “Does the system preserve its security rules after this sequence of valid actions and unexpected events?”

Model the security question

Instead of starting only from a list of known vulnerability patterns, describe what can vary, what must remain true, and how much execution is acceptable:

  • Context: identities, roles, scopes, tenants, sessions, resource ownership, and configuration.
  • Action sequences: authenticate, create, read, share, grant, revoke, retry, and repeat—in the allowed orders.
  • Unexpected events: expired credentials, duplicate requests, interrupted workflows, and repeated webhook delivery at defined points in a sequence.
  • Security invariants: rules that must hold across every tested combination and ordering.

The framework plans the experiment before execution, reports candidate counts, and supports budgeted t-way selection using a greedy strategy; it does not claim to find a mathematically minimal test set. Candidates run through configured adapters. Verdicts distinguish application failures from harness or infrastructure problems, and failure triage can reduce a failing case to a small reproducer for verification and regression testing.

What could it investigate?

Authorization and tenant isolation. Can a user access another tenant’s resource after a role change, or does a stale session retain a capability that should have been revoked?

Authentication and session lifecycle. What happens when credentials expire or are revoked in the middle of a workflow?

Business-logic abuse. Can retries, replays, duplicate transactions, or unusual action ordering violate a financial or data-access invariant?

Configuration interactions. Can a combination of settings or feature flags make a restricted operation reachable?

AI-agent boundaries. Can untrusted content influence an agent to use a tool beyond its granted permissions or bypass an approval requirement?

Evidence, not labels

An AI assistant can help formulate threat hypotheses, build scenario models, interpret results, and suggest follow-up experiments. The human remains responsible for the authorized scope, the security properties being tested, and approval of consequential actions.

A finding should not be accepted because a tool or model calls it a vulnerability. It should be supported by a clearly stated invariant, an observed violation, and a reproducible test. Before trusting a security oracle, calibrate it with a known test defect and confirm that the test can detect the failure it is supposed to detect.

Current status and limitations

The underlying Combinatorics Framework JVM already supports context, sequence, and event modeling; constraints; plan and candidate counts; budgeted candidate selection; execution through configured adapters; verdict classification; failure-witness triage; checkpoints; and an AI-operator workflow with approval gates.

The security-specific layer is still planned, not demonstrated. That includes reusable security oracles, a scope guard, operating-system-level isolation, a concurrent-dispatch adapter, and ready-made scenario packs beginning with API authorization. Defined event injection covers chosen points in a sequence; it does not by itself test two requests arriving at precisely the same time.

There is also an important safety limitation today: generated Java runs inside the JVM without an operating-system sandbox. A security edition needs explicit scope declarations and target allow-lists, execution limits, timeouts, secret redaction, auditable run records, and isolation for generated code before it can be presented as safe for broader security-testing use.

The first proof

The first milestone should be a reproducible authorization or business-logic flaw that a single-request test misses. Publish the scenario, the invariant it violates, the observed result, and a minimal reproducer - then rerun it as a regression test.

The goal is not to claim that every attack can be enumerated. It is to make a defined security investigation more systematic, bounded, repeatable, and re-viewable.

Model what must remain secure. Explore the interactions that could break it. Preserve the evidence.

Security Scenario Explorer is a proposed direction, built on Combinatorics Framework JVM. If you work in AppSec, penetration testing, or security-minded QA, share a real cross-feature failure pattern that would benefit from a reproducible scenario model.

Combinatorics Framework - re-assuring safety behavior more, saving QA jobs as a test-space scenario designer-architect/supervising AI

title: Haste Makes Waste? Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While few-step distilled text-to-image models have gained traction due to their fast generation times, the speed-up implications on their unsafe generation rates remain unknown. We uncover an inherent tension between speed and safety: few-step models are often more unsafe than their teachers, and reducing the number of inference steps consistently raises unsafe generation rates. We further find that acceleration makes unsafe concepts harder to erase in few-step models, with existing concept-erasure methods markedly less effective than in teachers. We offer a mechanistic diagnosis for why erasure methods fail on few-step models, finding that the fragility of few-step models' generation process and the way generation guidance is usually distilled into those models may hinder established concept-erasure methods. To address the speed-safety trade-off, we propose DICE (Distillation-Integrated Concept Erasure), a post-distillation erasure method tailored for few-step models. DICE aligns both its latent construction and its generation-preservation loss with the distillation method that produced the model, keeping erasure faithful to few-step models. DICE demonstrates strong results in our evaluation. For example, on FLUX Schnell, DICE reduces unsafe-generation rate to 0.046 (vs. at least 0.161 for prior erasure methods we test), while mostly preserving benign generation quality.

title: The Clustering Occupation Kernel (CLOCK) Method for Time Series Arising from Dynamical Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.33354v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce the Clustering Occupation Kernel (CLOCK) method, a novel representation-based framework for clustering time series arising from dynamical systems. CLOCK embeds observed sequences into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via a time-averaged occupation kernel, enabling trajectory comparison through their RKHS norm. For systems governed by differential equations, this formulation rigorously approximates the kernel mean embedding of the invariant Sinai-Ruelle-Bowen (SRB) measure, meaning our dissimilarity metric approximates the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between attractors. To accommodate general time series, we introduce time lags via Takens' Embedding Theorem to reconstruct the phase space. Crucially, CLOCK natively handles trajectories of unequal lengths and irregularly-spaced observations. We validate the proposed metric using spectral clustering, demonstrating superior performance against benchmark methods on both synthetic datasets and a real-world intracranial large-scale electroencephalogram (EEG) dataset. Finally, ablation studies on the Lorenz-96 system are consistent with the theoretical convergence rates of the occupation kernels and highlight the method's strong robustness to zero-mean Gaussian noise.

title: ETC-Bench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Evaluation-Side Transcript Canonicalization
description:
arXiv:2610.36527v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Written transcripts of the same speech can differ in ways that are not uniquely determined by the speech signal. We formulate evaluation-side transcript canonicalization (ETC), which maps multiple surface forms to a single canonical form when their differences are not determined by speech. To our knowledge, ETC-Bench is the first and most comprehensive multilingual benchmark for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization, covering 181 phenomenon types across 12 languages. Each instance is a minimal pair that shares a sentence context and differs only in a target span exhibiting one phenomenon. To evaluate both canonicalization success and semantic preservation, we propose Semantic-preserving Exact-match Normalization Accuracy (SENA), which combines exact agreement between independently canonicalized pair members with a pair-relative BERTScore constraint against information loss. We further introduce the Taxonomy-guided Agent Canonicalization Skill (TACS), which provides LLM agents with phenomenon descriptions and explicit canonicalization contracts. Experiments with five baseline configurations and three TACS-based agents show that the agents outperform the baseline systems on shared languages. ETC-Bench provides a systematic testbed for evaluation-side transcript canonicalization across languages.

title: What Existed Before React?
description:
If you are interested in reading about the evolution of technology,
then you might know that every technology has its own evolution phases,
where the technology evolves more and more over time.


In the recent post, we discussed how the ecosystem evolved from a
low-level HTTP Node.js server to Express.


Now this is the right time to discuss how web UI evolved from HTML to React.

1. The Early Web: HTML Documents

In the early web, websites were primarily documents.

The page was mostly static.

If you wanted another page, the browser would request another HTML document.

2. JavaScript and the DOM

Then JavaScript entered the picture.

JavaScript gave us the ability to execute code.

Now the browser wasn't just displaying static web pages or documents; it was also executing behavior, which led to interactive web pages.

At this time, the browser also exposed a programming interface called the DOM (Document Object Model).

The use of the DOM and JavaScript enabled changing elements without requesting a completely new HTML document.

At this time, if you wanted to change elements when a user interacted with a web page, the flow was like this:

A user action executes JavaScript, which finds and modifies the DOM elements, and the page becomes interactive.

This worked perfectly for websites.

3. The Rise of Web Applications

But the web evolved from websites to applications, such as Gmail, Facebook, Google Maps, and online shopping.

Those applications have lots of state, and the application needs to behave according to that state.

Maintaining the UI according to the state using DOM manipulation became complicated.

4. jQuery and Easier DOM Manipulation

To overcome this problem, developers started building JavaScript libraries to make browser programming easier.

One of them was jQuery.

jQuery simplified browser operations, which made working with the DOM easier.

It provided tools for DOM selection, DOM manipulation, events, AJAX, and animations.

Now you only needed to think about the elements that needed to change, and jQuery made selecting and modifying elements easier.

5. The Era of JavaScript Frameworks

As applications became even more complex, developers wanted something more structured.

This led to the development of JavaScript frameworks and libraries around Model, View, and Controller.

The era of MVP, MVVM, and MV* began.

From this era, one important framework became influential: AngularJS, developed by Google.

6. AngularJS and Two-Way Data Binding

It introduced concepts like controllers, scopes, services, dependency injection, directives, templates, and two-way binding.

It solved many problems, but large applications could still become difficult to reason about because of data flow and complex relationships between components and state.

In large applications, data flows in multiple directions.

7. React and a Different Approach

At the peak of AngularJS, React came into the picture, taking a somewhat different approach to maintaining multi-directional data flow and complex relationships between components and state.

React's philosophy was different:

The UI should be a function of state.

Instead of thinking, change this element, change that element, update the template, and synchronize this model, you only need to think about what the UI should look like given this state.

8. The Era of Interactive Web Applications

This helped create the era of highly interactive web applications.

Now web applications became more like desktop applications.

9. Client-Side Rendering and Server-Side Rendering

One important thing is that this evolution was not only about client-side rendering; server-side rendering also evolved.

But we are only discussing the evolution of client-side rendering.

title: Progressively Refining SAM for Accurate Phytoplankton Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.36722v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate phytoplankton segmentation is essential for ecological monitoring, yet it remains largely underexplored due to the subtle visual characteristics of phytoplankton and the scarcity of pixel-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose PhySeg, a SAM-based segmentation framework equipped with a lightweight refinement module that progressively restores fine-grained details through multi-scale feature fusion. In addition, we construct a phytoplankton segmentation dataset by manually annotating instance-level masks for an existing dataset, providing a valuable resource for future research. Experimental results demonstrate that PhySeg improves segmentation accuracy, validating the effectiveness of the proposed module. Code is available at https://github.com/lijialin404/PhySeg.

title: Verifiable Efficiency Limits of Innate LLM Planning in Sliding Puzzles
description:
arXiv:2610.36415v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-assisted planning success can reflect external search and verification, leaving a model's unaided planning ability unresolved. We isolate innate planning through complete plans generated in one response without tools or execution feedback. We propose a verifiable framework that decomposes success-weighted plan efficiency as $\mathrm{SPE}=R\times Q\times E$: execution reliability, planning coordination among legal plans, and action economy among completed plans. Trajectory replay and certified optima verify these factors; the joint score includes unsuccessful attempts. We evaluate 8,400 full-plan outputs from seven model conditions on $4\times4$ sliding puzzles, controlling exact horizon and obstacle count in the primary cohort. Models that complete every trial still become less economical at longer horizons, while higher efficiency among completed plans can coexist with poor goal attainment. SPE separates the overall capability hierarchy, while its factors distinguish coordination failure from inefficient completion. The framework makes long-horizon limitations in unaided planning quantitatively verifiable.

title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
description:
arXiv:2610.36083v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

title: Building a Content Calendar in DoAide Pulse
description:
Calendar Idea Planning

Problem

Side‑project developers often publish blog posts and social updates on a whim. Without a structured schedule, content gets missed, deadlines slip, and the marketing cadence feels ad‑hoc. The result is an inconsistent presence on channels like Dev.to and Bluesky, which hurts discoverability. This is where content calendar pays off in practice.

How It Works

DoAide Pulse solves this by turning the idea‑to‑publish pipeline into a single, AI‑driven workflow. The feature is split into three layers:

  1. FastAPI API – exposes CRUD endpoints for calendar entries.
  2. Celery Workers – generate drafts, run quality gates, and push to the Dev.to API on a schedule.
  3. React UI – presents an interactive calendar that lets users drag‑and‑drop ideas and preview AI‑generated content.

When a developer creates a new entry, they provide a headline, tags, and an optional focus keyword. The backend calls an AI model (via OpenAI’s API) to draft the post body, social copy, and meta tags. The draft is stored in PostgreSQL, then queued in Redis for a Celery task that will publish it at the scheduled time. Getting content calendar right early saves rework later.

Implementation Details

FastAPI Endpoint 

@router.post("/calendar/", response_model=CalendarEntry)
async def create_entry(entry: CalendarCreate, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    db_entry = CalendarEntry(**entry.dict())
    db.add(db_entry)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(db_entry)
    # Queue AI generation
    task = generate_content.delay(db_entry.id)
    db_entry.task_id = task.id
    db.commit()
    return db_entry

The endpoint validates that the headline is non‑empty and that the URL is HTTP/HTTPS, mirroring the recent fix: a blank template name or idea headline is refused commit.

Celery Task 

@celery.task
def generate_content(entry_id):
    entry = db.query(CalendarEntry).get(entry_id)
    prompt = f"Write a 600‑word blog post about {entry.headline} with focus keyword {entry.focus_keyword}."
    draft = openai.Completion.create(engine="gpt-4", prompt=prompt, max_tokens=800)
    entry.draft = draft.choices[0].text
    db.commit()
    # Schedule publish
    publish_task.apply_async((entry.id,), eta=entry.scheduled_at)

The task uses the openai Python client, stores the draft, and schedules a separate publish_task that will hit the Dev.to API.

Publish Task 

@celery.task
def publish_task(entry_id):
    entry = db.query(CalendarEntry).get(entry_id)
    response = devto_api.publish(entry.draft, entry.tags)
    entry.published_at = datetime.utcnow()
    entry.devto_url = response.url
    db.commit()

The devto_api wrapper encapsulates the official Dev.to API endpoints, handling authentication and rate limiting. Good content calendar keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

React Calendar UI

The UI is built with Vite, React, and Tailwind CSS. The calendar component uses the react‑datepicker library to render a month view. Each cell can contain a stack of cards representing scheduled posts.

<Calendar>
  {entries.map(entry => (
    <Day key={entry.id} date={entry.scheduled_at}>
      <Card title={entry.headline} status={entry.status} />
    </Day>
  ))}
</Calendar>

Drag‑and‑drop is implemented with react‑dnd. When a card is moved, a PATCH request updates the scheduled_at field in the FastAPI backend. Treat content calendar as a habit rather than a one-off task.

Example Workflow

  1. Create an Idea – The developer opens the calendar UI, clicks Add Post, and fills in the headline and tags.
  2. AI Draft – The backend immediately queues a Celery task. Within seconds, a draft appears in the card preview.
  3. Adjust Schedule – The user drags the card to a desired date. The backend updates the schedule.
  4. Publish – At the scheduled time, the publish_task posts the content to Dev.to and records the URL.
  5. Analytics – A separate dashboard shows subscriber growth and engagement, tied to the subscriber growth analytics commit.

The process eliminates the need for manual drafting, scheduling, and publishing, giving indie developers a reliable marketing cadence.

Conclusion

The Calendar Idea Planning feature turns a chaotic, manual workflow into a predictable, AI‑augmented pipeline. By combining FastAPI, Celery, Redis, and React, DoAide Pulse provides a developer‑friendly marketing automation stack that keeps side projects visible on the channels that matter.

All code snippets are illustrative and reflect the architecture described in the recent GitHub commits.

Related reading

  • AI content generation: the automated blog draft feature
  • Marketing Automation: AI‑Generated SEO Fields in DoAide Pulse

title: Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36192v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow. We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 x 256, PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.

title: Llama 3 Rilis: AI Generatif Terbuka Dorong Inovasi di Cloud
description:
Llama 3: Era Baru AI Generatif Sumber Terbuka

Meta telah secara resmi meluncurkan Llama 3, generasi terbaru dari model kecerdasan buatan generatif sumber terbukanya. Rilis ini menandai langkah signifikan dalam demokratisasi AI canggih, menjadikannya lebih mudah diakses oleh pengembang dan bisnis di seluruh dunia. Ketersediaan Llama 3 di platform cloud utama seperti AWS, Google Cloud, dan Azure mempercepat adopsi teknologi ini, mendorong inovasi di berbagai sektor.

Peningkatan Signifikan Llama 3: Performa dan Kemampuan

Llama 3 hadir dengan peningkatan performa yang substansial dibandingkan pendahulunya, Llama 2. Meta mengklaim model ini menunjukkan kemajuan signifikan dalam kemampuan penalaran, pengkodean, dan mengikuti instruksi. Peningkatan ini dicapai melalui pelatihan pada kumpulan data yang jauh lebih besar dan beragam, serta arsitektur yang dioptimalkan. Dua ukuran model awal yang dirilis adalah dengan 8 miliar (8B) dan 70 miliar (70B) parameter, dirancang untuk berbagai kebutuhan komputasi dan aplikasi.

Kemampuan penalaran yang lebih baik memungkinkan Llama 3 untuk memahami dan memproses informasi yang kompleks dengan lebih akurat, sementara peningkatan dalam pengkodean menjadikannya alat yang lebih efektif bagi pengembang perangkat lunak. Model ini juga menunjukkan peningkatan dalam mengikuti instruksi multi-langkah, yang krusial untuk aplikasi AI yang lebih canggih dan interaktif. Meta memposisikan Llama 3 sebagai salah satu model AI sumber terbuka sangat mumpuni yang tersedia saat ini, menawarkan performa kompetitif.

Adopsi Luas: Llama 3 di Platform Cloud Utama

Salah satu faktor kunci yang akan mendorong adopsi Llama 3 adalah ketersediaannya yang luas di ekosistem cloud. Model ini kini dapat diakses melalui layanan seperti AWS SageMaker, Google Cloud AI, dan Azure AI Model Catalog. Integrasi langsung ini memungkinkan pengembang untuk dengan mudah memanfaatkan kekuatan Llama 3 tanpa harus mengelola infrastruktur komputasi yang kompleks.

Ketersediaan di platform cloud besar ini tidak hanya menyederhanakan proses penerapan tetapi juga membuka peluang bagi bisnis dari berbagai skala untuk eksperimen dan membangun aplikasi AI generatif. Hal ini juga dapat memicu kompetisi di pasar perang harga cloud GPU dan layanan AI, yang pada akhirnya menguntungkan pengguna. Kemudahan akses ini sangat penting untuk mendorong era baru AI generatif yang terintegrasi penuh di layanan cloud utama.

Dampak Llama 3 pada Ekosistem AI Terbuka

Rilis Llama 3 sebagai model sumber terbuka oleh Meta memiliki implikasi besar bagi ekosistem AI. Ini mempercepat laju inovasi dengan memungkinkan komunitas pengembang untuk memeriksa, memodifikasi, dan meningkatkan model secara kolaboratif. Sifat terbuka ini mendorong transparansi dan mengurangi ketergantungan pada model-model tertutup yang dikembangkan oleh segelintir perusahaan besar.

Sebagai pesaing kuat di ranah AI sumber terbuka, Llama 3 mendorong batasan apa yang mungkin dicapai dengan model yang dapat diakses publik. Ini juga memberikan alternatif yang kredibel bagi pengembang yang mungkin ragu untuk mengunci diri pada satu vendor AI tertentu. Kehadiran Llama 3 dapat memicu gelombang baru penelitian dan pengembangan, serta memfasilitasi penciptaan aplikasi AI yang lebih beragam dan inovatif.

Tantangan dan Peluang ke Depan

Meskipun Llama 3 menawarkan banyak peluang, ada juga tantangan yang perlu dipertimbangkan. Performa Llama 3 dibandingkan dengan model tertutup terkemuka masih menjadi area perdebatan dan penelitian berkelanjutan. Selain itu, pengelolaan model AI sumber terbuka yang kuat memerlukan tata kelola yang efektif untuk memastikan penggunaan yang bertanggung jawab dan etis.

Ke depan, Meta telah mengisyaratkan rencana untuk merilis model Llama 3 yang lebih besar, dengan lebih banyak parameter, yang diharapkan akan menawarkan kemampuan yang lebih canggih lagi. Perkembangan ini akan terus membentuk lanskap AI, mendorong batas-batas apa yang dapat dicapai oleh kecerdasan buatan. Bagi bisnis, ini berarti peluang untuk mengeksplorasi solusi AI yang lebih hemat biaya dan dapat disesuaikan, berpotensi mengubah cara mereka beroperasi dan berinovasi.

Kesimpulan

Peluncuran Llama 3 oleh Meta adalah tonggak penting dalam evolusi AI generatif sumber terbuka. Dengan peningkatan signifikan dalam kemampuan dan ketersediaan luas di platform cloud utama, Llama 3 siap untuk mempercepat inovasi, memberdayakan pengembang, dan mendorong adopsi AI di berbagai industri. Ini bukan hanya tentang model yang lebih baik, tetapi juga tentang ekosistem yang lebih terbuka, kolaboratif, dan kompetitif, yang pada akhirnya akan menguntungkan seluruh komunitas AI.

title: Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
description:
arXiv:2610.36911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.
