title: Learning Where to Trust: Reliability-Guided Expert Routing and Velocity Gating for 3D Deformable Registration
description:
arXiv:2610.36672v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deformable image registration relies on accurate anatomical correspondences. However, explicitly coupling local matching reliability with spatial context selection and deformation update strength remains insufficiently explored in learning-based registration. This challenge is particularly pronounced in homogeneous, weakly textured, and severely deformed regions, where ambiguous matches may induce erroneous deformation updates. We propose ReliMorph, a reliability-routed symmetric framework for 3D deformable registration that couples correspondence assessment with spatial context selection and update strength.Local correlation distributions characterize correspondence ambiguity using shared anatomical features with modality-specific adaptation. These reliability cues guide spatial expert fusion and gate residual velocities during coarse-to-fine refinement. Updated inverse-inconsistency feedback guides routing and gating at finer pyramid levels. To our knowledge, ReliMorph is the first 3D deformable registration framework to jointly condition spatial expert routing and residual velocity gating on correspondence reliability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReliMorph consistently outperforms competing methods in anatomical overlap, highlighting its effectiveness across unimodal and multimodal registration tasks.

title: Giải thích phương thức HTTP QUERY: RFC 10008, QUERY vs GET vs POST
description:
Phương thức HTTP QUERY là một phương thức request mới, được định nghĩa trong RFC 10008 (tháng 6 năm 2026), gửi một truy vấn trong phần thân request và vừa safe vừa idempotent. Hãy hình dung nó như GET có body: bạn có được không gian của POST cho các bộ lọc phức tạp và sự đảm bảo của GET về caching và tự động retry.

Dùng thử Apidog ngay hôm nay

Nếu bạn từng nhét một bộ lọc 3 KB vào URL, hoặc gửi một tìm kiếm chỉ đọc dưới dạng POST và thấy cache cùng logic retry của mình phớt lờ nó, thì QUERY chính là giải pháp. Hướng dẫn này trình bày những gì spec quy định, QUERY so với GET và POST như thế nào, những gì hỗ trợ nó hiện nay, và cách kiểm thử một endpoint QUERY với coding agent của bạn.

Phương thức HTTP QUERY là gì?

QUERY là một phương thức HTTP yêu cầu resource đích thực thi truy vấn được mô tả trong nội dung request và trả về kết quả. Phần thân request và Content-Type của nó định nghĩa truy vấn. Phương thức này là safe (client không mong đợi thay đổi trạng thái) và idempotent (lặp lại nó có cùng hiệu ứng), nên client, proxy và cache có thể retry và cache nó giống như GET.

Spec là RFC 10008, "The HTTP QUERY Method", một Proposed Standard được xuất bản vào tháng 6 năm 2026 bởi Julian Reschke (greenbytes), James M. Snell (Cloudflare) và Mike Bishop (Akamai). IANA đã thêm nó vào HTTP Method Registry với "safe: yes, idempotent: yes", ngay cạnh phương thức SEARCH thời WebDAV mà nó suýt trở thành.

Một request QUERY trông như sau:

QUERY /contacts HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept: application/json

select=surname,givenname,email&limit=10&match=%22email=*@example.*%22

Server trả lời bằng 200 OK và kết quả nằm trong body.

Vì sao GET và POST chưa đủ

Trước QUERY, bạn có hai lựa chọn cho một truy vấn đọc phức tạp, và cả hai đều rò rỉ.

GET đặt mọi thứ vào URL. RFC 10008 liệt kê bốn vấn đề với cách này:

  1. Giới hạn kích thước không thể biết trước, vì một request đi qua nhiều hệ thống. RFC 9110 chỉ khuyến nghị rằng bên gửi và bên nhận hỗ trợ ít nhất 8.000 octet.
  2. Mã hóa dữ liệu có cấu trúc thành một URI hợp lệ là lãng phí.
  3. URI bị ghi log và đánh dấu trang thường xuyên hơn nhiều so với phần thân request, đây là vấn đề riêng tư đối với các bộ lọc nhạy cảm.
  4. Mỗi tổ hợp đầu vào truy vấn trở thành một resource riêng.

GET kèm body cũng không phải là câu trả lời. RFC 9110 nói rằng nội dung trong một request GET không có ngữ nghĩa được định nghĩa. Một số server đọc nó, một số bỏ qua, và một số proxy từ chối request. Bạn không thể trông cậy vào nó trên toàn bộ đường đi.

POST hoạt động, nhưng nó nói dối về ý định. Một tìm kiếm bằng POST chạy tốt, nhưng không có gì cho client, cache, proxy hay thư viện retry biết rằng thao tác này chỉ đọc. Vì vậy cache bỏ qua nó và client sẽ không retry nó sau khi kết nối bị ngắt. Nếu bạn từng phải gắn thêm một idempotency key vào một truy vấn chỉ đọc chỉ để retry an toàn, bạn đã cảm nhận được điều này.

QUERY giữ body của POST và thêm các đảm bảo của GET.

QUERY vs GET vs POST

Đây là bảng so sánh, dựa trên Bảng 1 của RFC 10008:

Property GET QUERY POST
Safe Yes Yes Potentially no
Idempotent Yes Yes Potentially no
Request body Không có ngữ nghĩa được định nghĩa Được mong đợi, định nghĩa truy vấn Được mong đợi
URI cho chính truy vấn Có, theo định nghĩa Tùy chọn, qua Location Không
URI cho kết quả Tùy chọn, qua Content-Location Tùy chọn, qua Content-Location Tùy chọn, qua Content-Location
Cacheable Có Có, body là một phần của cache key Chỉ cho GET hoặc HEAD sau đó
CORS preflight từ trình duyệt Không với các request đơn giản Luôn luôn Không với các request đơn giản

Tóm tắt ngắn: dùng GET khi truy vấn vừa vặn thoải mái trong URL, dùng QUERY khi không, và chỉ dùng POST khi request thay đổi trạng thái. Để ôn lại các phương thức cổ điển, xem hướng dẫn của chúng tôi về HTTP methods và GET vs POST.

RFC 10008 định nghĩa những gì

Content-Type là bắt buộc

Server BẮT BUỘC phải làm thất bại một QUERY có Content-Type bị thiếu hoặc không nhất quán với body. RFC khuyến nghị các mã trạng thái sau:

  • 400 Bad Request: không có media type, hoặc một type không khớp với nội dung. Server không thể sniff body và ghi đè nó.
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type: resource không hỗ trợ định dạng truy vấn đó.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: định dạng ổn nhưng truy vấn không thể chạy, ví dụ SQL gọi tên một bảng không tồn tại.
  • 406 Not Acceptable: client yêu cầu một loại response mà resource không thể tạo ra.

Location và Content-Location

Server có thể trả về hai header tùy chọn biến một QUERY thành thứ bạn có thể GET sau này:

  • Content-Location trỏ đến kết quả đã được lưu của lần chạy cụ thể này. Nó có thể là tạm thời.
  • Location trỏ đến chính truy vấn đã được lưu. Một GET trên đó sẽ chạy lại truy vấn với dữ liệu mới, mà không cần gửi lại body.

RFC gợi ý client chuyển sang GET trên URI Location cho các request lặp lại, vì caching GET đơn giản hơn. Nếu bạn trả về một trong hai header cho một truy vấn có dữ liệu nhạy cảm, URI KHÔNG NÊN chứa các phần nhạy cảm của body gốc.

Caching

Các response QUERY có thể cache được. Cache key BẮT BUỘC phải bao gồm nội dung request và metadata liên quan như media type. Cache CÓ THỂ chuẩn hóa body trước, ví dụ bằng cách loại bỏ content encoding hoặc chuẩn hóa JSON cho type +json, để có thêm hit. Spec cảnh báo rằng chuẩn hóa sai có thể trả về response sai, nên hãy mong đợi các CDN phải cẩn trọng ở điểm này.

Chuyển hướng

Một 301, 302, 307 hoặc 308 nghĩa là "gửi cùng QUERY đến URI mới". Khác với POST, một QUERY không được viết lại thành GET trên 301 hoặc 302. Một 303 See Other nghĩa là "lấy kết quả bằng một GET trên URI này".

Header Accept-Query

Accept-Query là một response header mới quảng bá hỗ trợ QUERY và các định dạng truy vấn mà một resource chấp nhận. Nó là một danh sách Structured Field, nên hãy parse nó như vậy:

Accept-Query: "application/jsonpath", application/sql;charset="UTF-8"

Client cũng có thể khám phá hỗ trợ bằng OPTIONS và đọc header Allow, hoặc chỉ cần gửi QUERY và xử lý 405 Method Not Allowed.

Những công cụ nào hỗ trợ QUERY hiện nay?

Mức hỗ trợ không đồng đều, nên hãy kiểm thử stack của chính bạn. Đây là những gì chúng tôi đã xác nhận vào ngày 28 tháng 10 năm 2026:

Công cụ Kết quả
Node.js 24 http server http.METHODS bao gồm QUERY; một server thông thường đã nhận được phương thức và body
Node.js 24 fetch Đã gửi một QUERY kèm body JSON
curl 8.7 curl -X QUERY với -d đã gửi phương thức và body
Python 3.14 http.client Đã gửi một QUERY kèm body
OpenAPI 3.2 Path Item Object có trường query cho các thao tác QUERY
Apidog CLI 2.2.12 Schema endpoint-create chấp nhận "method": "query"

Đây là lệnh curl chúng tôi dùng với một server Node cục bộ:

curl -i -X QUERY http://localhost:3000/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"q":"running shoe","limit":2}'

Fetch Standard chỉ cấm body trên GET và HEAD, nên trình duyệt có thể gửi QUERY kèm body. Tuy nhiên, QUERY không phải là phương thức nằm trong danh sách an toàn CORS, nên mọi QUERY cross-origin đều kích hoạt preflight. Server của bạn phải liệt kê QUERY trong Access-Control-Allow-Methods.

Các lỗ hổng nằm ở giữa mạng: reverse proxy, API gateway, WAF và CDN — những thứ allowlist phương thức hoặc không key cache theo body. Hãy kiểm tra từng chặng trước khi phát hành. Bản tin APIs You Won't Hate lưu ý rằng nhiều web framework đã xử lý QUERY trực tiếp hoặc thông qua định tuyến phương thức tùy chỉnh.

Cách áp dụng QUERY mà không làm hỏng client

Bạn không cần phải loại bỏ các endpoint tìm kiếm POST của mình.

  1. Thêm QUERY song song với route POST. Trỏ cả hai vào cùng một handler. Client mới dùng QUERY; client cũ vẫn tiếp tục hoạt động.
  2. Quảng bá nó. Trả về Accept-Query trên resource và thêm QUERY vào Allow trong các response OPTIONS và 405.
  3. Thực thi Content-Type. Trả về 400 hoặc 415 như RFC khuyến nghị, và 422 cho các truy vấn parse được nhưng không chạy được.
  4. Dự phòng bằng 405 hoặc 501. Client nên thử lại cùng body dưới dạng POST khi một chặng từ chối QUERY.
  5. Sửa CORS. Thêm QUERY vào Access-Control-Allow-Methods cho client trình duyệt.
  6. Quyết định về caching. Chỉ bật shared caching ở nơi cache của bạn key theo body. Nếu không, hãy trả về URI Location và để client GET nó.
  7. Ghi tài liệu cho nó. Trong OpenAPI 3.2, định nghĩa thao tác dưới query: trên path item: 
openapi: 3.2.0
paths:
  /products:
    query:
      summary: Search products
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductQuery'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Matching products

Các bộ lọc ngắn, đơn giản có thể vẫn là query string trên GET. Chính RFC 10008 nói rằng nếu truy vấn của bạn ngắn như vậy, GET có lẽ là lựa chọn tốt hơn.

Để coding agent của bạn kiểm thử một endpoint QUERY với Apidog CLI

Một phương thức mới đồng nghĩa với việc phải kiểm tra luồng thành công, mọi mã lỗi và route dự phòng. Hãy giao việc đó cho Claude Code, Codex hoặc Cursor và để nó điều khiển Apidog CLI.

Cài đặt CLI, đăng nhập, và thêm skill Apidog vào agent của bạn:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Sau đó đưa cho agent của bạn một [REDACTED PROMPT]
In Apidog project , add a QUERY /products endpoint that takes a
JSON body {q, limit}. Create test cases that assert 200 with an array for a
valid body, 415 for Content-Type text/plain, and 400 with no Content-Type.
Run them against the staging environment and summarize any failures.


Agent đọc từng schema, xác thực payload của nó và chỉ sau đó mới ghi:


bash
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project --file case.json
apidog run --test-case --project -e -r cli,json




`endpoint.json` mà nó ghi sẽ đặt `"method": "query"`, mà schema `endpoint-create` của CLI liệt kê cùng với `get`, `post` và các phương thức WebDAV. Thêm `--upload-report` để xem lần chạy trong ứng dụng Apidog. Cùng lệnh `apidog run` với `-r junit` có thể đưa vào CI; xem [cách chạy kiểm thử API trong CI với apidog run](https://apidog.com/vi/blog/apidog-run-command-reference?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) và [cách dùng Apidog CLI trong Claude Code](https://apidog.com/vi/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation). Gói Free của Apidog hỗ trợ tối đa 4 người dùng.

## FAQ

**Phương thức HTTP QUERY có phải là tiêu chuẩn chính thức không?** Có. RFC 10008 là một RFC thuộc Standards Track, Proposed Standard, được xuất bản vào tháng 6 năm 2026, và IANA liệt kê QUERY trong HTTP Method Registry là safe và idempotent.

**QUERY có phải chỉ là GET kèm body không?** Gần đúng, nhưng nó được định nghĩa rõ ràng hơn. RFC 9110 không gán ngữ nghĩa nào cho body của GET, nên các intermediary có thể bỏ qua hoặc từ chối nó. QUERY biến body thành truy vấn, yêu cầu một `Content-Type`, và đưa body vào cache key.

**Khi nào tôi nên dùng QUERY thay vì POST?** Dùng QUERY cho bất kỳ tìm kiếm hay bộ lọc chỉ đọc nào quá lớn hoặc quá nhạy cảm để đặt trong URL. Giữ POST cho các request tạo mới hoặc thay đổi thứ gì đó.

**Trình duyệt có thể gửi request QUERY không?** Có, thông qua `fetch` với một phương thức tùy chỉnh. Các request QUERY cross-origin luôn cần CORS preflight, nên server của bạn phải cho phép phương thức này.

**Các response QUERY có được cache không?** Có thể. Cache phải bao gồm phần thân request và metadata của nó trong cache key. Nhiều CDN và proxy chưa làm điều đó, nên hãy kiểm tra của bạn hoặc trả về URI `Location` mà client có thể GET.

**OpenAPI có hỗ trợ QUERY không?** OpenAPI 3.2 thêm trường `query` vào Path Item Object cho các thao tác QUERY, nên bạn có thể ghi tài liệu cho chúng mà không cần extension.

title: FORESEE-MS: Toward Prospective Spatial Forecasting of Future Multiple Sclerosis Lesions from Baseline FLAIR MRI
description:
arXiv:2610.36428v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Traditional multiple sclerosis (MS) image analysis has primarily focused on retrospectively detecting and segmenting lesions. This study investigates whether baseline FLAIR MRI can identify regions at risk for future lesion formation beyond population-level spatial patterns. We introduce FORESEE-MS, an evaluation protocol that uses a fold-specific population-prior atlas as a baseline and assesses predictions using pooled voxel-level discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC) and within-patient lesion localization (Recall@Top-K%), with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We evaluated five deep learning models (3D U-Net, Attn+ResBlock+VAE, ViT, and two SwinUNETR variants) using 5-fold cross-validation on 39 subjects from the MSSEG-2 dataset. The atlas achieved the highest pooled voxel-level AUROC and AUPRC, with no deep learning model reliably outperforming it on either metric. However, the 3D U-Net and Attn+ResBlock+VAE achieved higher mean voxel-level within-patient Recall@Top-K% than the atlas at all evaluated thresholds, although most paired confidence intervals for the differences included zero. These findings suggest that baseline FLAIR may contain patient-specific predictive information, but in this small cohort, it remains uncertain whether this information improves lesion forecasting beyond a population-prior atlas.

title: Protect production deployments for free on every plan
description:
Vercel Authentication can now protect all deployments in a project, including production, at no additional cost on every plan. Previously, protecting production domains required the $150-per-month Advanced Deployment Protection add-on.

When enabled, visitors must sign in with a Vercel account that has access to the project. This makes it useful for internal tools, private dashboards, and sites that aren’t yet ready to launch.

From your project, open Security in the sidebar, select Deployment Protection, then choose All Deployments from the dropdown.

You can also make this the team default, so every new project starts with Vercel Authentication enabled for all deployments.

With this change:

  • Deployment Protection Exceptions are now free on every plan. Use an exception to make a specific preview domain public while keeping the rest of the project protected.

  • Pro teams can now enable Password Protection for individual projects instead of purchasing it for the entire team.

Learn more in the Deployment Protection documentation.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

title: Agentic Data Sampling Framework for Multilingual ASR via Linguistic-Aware Error-Driven Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.36538v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved rapid progress with large-scale pretrained models and multilingual speech corpora. Previous studies have proved the pivotal role of data sampling in multilingual ASR performance. However, existing sampling strategies largely rely on time-consuming manual, heuristic-based designs. To address this, we propose a linguistic-aware agentic data sampling framework that introduces a data sampling LLM agent into the multilingual ASR training loop. The agent is driven by a linguistically grounded rubric that analyzes ASR errors from phonological, morphological, and syntactic perspectives, and uses the resulting feedback together with training statistics, budget constraints, and algorithm profiles to select domain-level, sample-level, and token-level sampling strategies. This design turns evaluation results into adaptive data-selection decisions rather than treating WER/CER as final endpoints only. We conduct experiments on twelve Common Voice languages using Whisper-medium as the ASR backbone. The results show that our method achieves performance better than full-data training while using less training data and lower computational resources, and substantially accelerates training convergence compared to conventional sampling strategies.

title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression
description:
arXiv:2610.36411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.

title: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni: Elastic Self-Refining Unified Diffusion LLM with Cross-Paradigm On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.36466v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni (NLD-Uni), a unified discrete diffusion large language model (DLLM) for visual understanding and generation tasks. Compared with prior unified diffusion models, NLD-Uni introduces two major innovations. First, we propose a unified cross-paradigm on-policy distillation (OPD) framework that successfully transfers the visual understanding ability of autoregressive VLMs and visual generation ability of continuous flow models, to a unified DLLM. Second, NLD-Uni incorporates a novel progressive self-refining diffusion process that gradually corrupts each token across multiple steps during training, as opposed to adopting the conventional masked diffusion formulation that directly corrupts a clean image token to an uninformative mask token. At inference, this design allows NLD-Uni to make intermediate commit to a token, enabling progressive self-refinement for better visual quality. Through extensive experiments, we show that NLD-Uni achieves state-of-the-art performance among unified DLLMs on diverse tasks including visual question-answering, multi-modal reasoning, object grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing.

title: Variational Atlas Autoencoders and Self-Supervised Chart Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.33577v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex, high-dimensional data lie on manifolds that a single global latent coordinate system cannot represent without distortion. We introduce Variational Atlas Autoencoders, a mixture-of-charts framework that learns an atlas of local latent representations, each responsible for one region of the data manifold. The central difficulty in learning an atlas is deciding which chart should be responsible for which data point without labels. We show that this decision need not be a heuristic. By treating the chart index as a latent variable, the evidence lower bound yields the training objective and casts chart assignment as posterior inference, valid for any routing distribution. Within this framework, we propose latent-evidence routing, which assigns a point to a chart in proportion to the evidence of its encoding under that chart's latent prior. This has a simple interpretation: the closer a point lands to the center of a chart's latent space, and the more confidently it is placed there, the more likely it is to belong to that chart. Chart assignment thus emerges as posterior inference, depends on the encoder alone, and is fully self-supervised, so the charts discover structure in the data on their own, separating classes and subclasses such as distinct types of shoes or faces without access to labels. We further recover an atlas from the trained charts by identifying their overlaps and transition maps, enabling continuous interpolation within and across charts that stays close to the data manifold rather than traversing unsupported regions of latent space. Compared to capacity-matched baselines, Variational Atlas Autoencoders yields better-structured latent spaces and higher sample quality on image datasets including CelebA, while sampling requires evaluating only a single chart's decoder.

title: Training-Free Inference Acceleration for Video Large Language Models: Methods, Trade-offs, and Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.36327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.

title: No Tokenizer, Still a Gap: Cross-Lingual Fairness of Homoglyph and Invisible-Character Watermarking
description:
arXiv:2610.36432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Homoglyph and invisible-character watermarks are edit-based watermarks. Instead of changing how a model generates text, they hide a signal in the text after it is written. They swap some characters for homoglyphs, which look the same, or very similar, but have different Unicode code points, or they insert characters that do not display, all without access to the model that wrote the text. Generation-time watermarks work less well for lower-resourced languages due to how tokenizers split their text. Because they work on individual characters, these watermarks never touch a tokenizer, so we ask whether they escape this gap. Across 40 language varieties in 24 scripts, we measure capacity (the hidden bits each character can carry), how much of it survives routine handling and targeted removal, and how much text a keyed detector needs. Capacity varies 3.3-fold and script accounts for 96\% of that variation. Within Latin script, resource level makes no detectable difference ($\rho=+0.095$, $p=0.78$), but across scripts capacity rises with it ($\rho=+0.54$, 95\% CI $[+0.14,+0.83]$), because lower-resourced languages tend to use scripts with few homoglyphs. Ordinary copy-paste, which strips invisible characters, widens the gap: a detector then needs about 2 code points of English or Persian but 93 of Lao. Removing the tokenizer does not remove the inequity, but instead only changes its source.

title: How to find verified Alibaba suppliers with a low MOQ in bulk (and what a first order really costs)
description:
I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify ($1.50 per 1,000 products) with a free trial credit.

If you have ever sourced on Alibaba, you know the loop: search "yoga mat", open 40 tabs, check each one for the Verified badge, scroll to find the MOQ, squint at "US $7.50-$14.00", then try to remember which supplier was 3 years old and which was 18. Alibaba's own filters help, but they only show you one page at a time and you can't sort by "how much cash do I need to place a first order".

This post shows how to get that whole table at once: every listing for a keyword with its MOQ, price ladder, Verified / Trade Assurance status, supplier age, rating and the inspection company behind the badge. First the no-code way (a form and a CSV), then a short Python script. All numbers below come from a real run of Alibaba Scraper on 24 Sep 2026: 75 listings each for "bluetooth earbuds", "yoga mat", "custom tote bags" and "led strip lights".

What "verified" actually means on Alibaba

Three different badges get mixed up:

  • Verified supplier: the company was inspected on site by a third party. The scraper returns who did it in supplierVerifiedBy. In our run that was always one of SGS, TÜV Rheinland or Intertek.
  • Trade Assurance: Alibaba's payment protection on the order. Almost everyone has it (73 of 75 earbud listings, 75 of 75 yoga mats), so it doesn't separate anyone.
  • Gold supplier: a paid membership. All 300 listings in our run had it, so it says nothing either.

The badge that filters is Verified: 32 of 75 earbud listings, 60 of 75 yoga mats, 61 of 75 tote bags, 62 of 75 LED strips. Combine it with supplier age and rating and the list shrinks fast:

Keyword Listings Unique suppliers Verified Verified + MOQ ≤ 50 ...and 5+ years, rating 4.5+
bluetooth earbuds 75 71 32 24 19
yoga mat 75 29 60 43 10
custom tote bags 75 48 61 13 3
led strip lights 75 56 62 46 29

Two things stand out. Yoga mat results come from only 29 suppliers for 75 listings, so the same factories repeat a lot (dedupe by supplier before you contact anyone). And custom tote bags are a high-MOQ category: the median MOQ was 100 pieces, so only 3 suppliers pass a strict low-MOQ filter.

The number Alibaba doesn't show: cash for a first order

A listing's MOQ times the unit price at that quantity is the smallest order you can place. For yoga mats, the median listing needs $377 for a first order (median MOQ 50 at the first price tier). For earbuds it's $99, for LED strips $115. That's the column I sort a shortlist by when testing a product.

Here are the cheapest first orders among verified, 5+ year, 4.5+ rated yoga mat suppliers in that run (one row per supplier):

Product (shortened) MOQ Unit price at MOQ First order Supplier Years Rating Verified by
Eco Friendly Custom Logo Pilates Mat 2 pieces $2.99 $5.98 Ningbo Boga Sports Goods 5 4.7 TÜV Rheinland
Arch Oval Curve Shaped Mat 1 piece $14.00 $14.00 Nantong Vigor Sport Goods 8 4.9 TÜV Rheinland
LEECORK Organic Cork TPE Yoga Mat 12 pieces $8.51 $102.12 Xi'an Leecork 18 4.9 SGS
Micogo Anti Slip Custom Logo Mat 12 pieces $13.80 $165.60 Ningbo Winz Sports Goods 8 4.7 TÜV Rheinland
Natural Rubber PU Leather Mat 50 pieces $10.00 $500.00 Dongguan Tongtianxia Rubber 19 4.8 SGS

That is five inspected, established factories you can order samples from for under $500 total, found in one run instead of an afternoon of tabs.

Option 1: no code (form in, spreadsheet out)

  1. Open the actor page and click Try for free (new Apify accounts get a monthly free credit, which covers a few thousand products).
  2. In Search terms, add your keywords, one per line: yoga mat, cork yoga mat, tpe yoga mat. Narrow variants matter because Alibaba serves about 960 products per keyword.
  3. Under Filters, tick Verified suppliers only, set Max MOQ (for example 50) and optionally a Supplier country (CN, IN, VN, TR...).
  4. Set Max results per search to 200 and click Start. 1,000 products take about 20 seconds.
  5. In the Output tab, download CSV or Excel and open it in Google Sheets or Excel.

In the sheet, keep these columns and sort by minOrderValue (the first-order cash, computed for you in the current version): title, moq, moqUnit, priceAtMoq, minOrderValue, supplierName, supplierYears, supplierRating, supplierVerifiedBy, responseRate, contactSupplierUrl. The last one opens Alibaba's own contact form for that product, so outreach stays on Alibaba with Trade Assurance.

Option 2: Python, 25 lines 

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import csv

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("rel8ble/alibaba-product-search-scraper").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": ["yoga mat", "cork yoga mat", "tpe yoga mat"],
    "maxResultsPerSearch": 200,
    "verifiedSuppliersOnly": True,
    "maxMoq": 50,
    "includeAds": False,
})

best = {}  # one row per supplier: their cheapest first order
for p in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    tiers = p.get("priceTiers") or []
    unit = tiers[0]["price"] if tiers else p.get("priceMax")
    if not unit or not p.get("moq"):
        continue
    if (p.get("supplierYears") or 0) < 5 or (p.get("supplierRating") or 0) < 4.5:
        continue
    cash = round(p["moq"] * unit, 2)
    name = p["supplierName"]
    if name not in best or cash < best[name]["cash"]:
        best[name] = {"cash": cash, "moq": p["moqText"], "unit": unit, "years": p["supplierYears"],
                      "rating": p["supplierRating"], "verifiedBy": p.get("supplierVerifiedBy"),
                      "title": p["title"][:70], "url": p["url"]}

rows = sorted(best.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]["cash"])
with open("alibaba_shortlist.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["supplier", "first_order_usd", "moq", "unit_price", "years", "rating", "verified_by", "title", "url"])
    for name, r in rows:
        w.writerow([name, r["cash"], r["moq"], r["unit"], r["years"], r["rating"], r["verifiedBy"], r["title"], r["url"]])
print(f"{len(rows)} suppliers -> alibaba_shortlist.csv")

The filters (verifiedSuppliersOnly, maxMoq) run on Alibaba's side, so you only pay for products that already pass them. The years and rating cut runs locally because Alibaba has no filter for it.

Things that tripped me up

  • MOQ units differ. LED strips are sold by the meter in 42 of 75 listings, yoga mats sometimes by the dozen. Filter moqUnit before comparing prices across listings.
  • Sponsored listings repeat. 37 of 75 LED strip results were ads. Set includeAds: false for a clean comparison, or keep them and filter isAd later.
  • New suppliers aren't bad, just unproven. The cheapest verified earbud listing came from a 1-year-old supplier. I keep them in a separate tab and ask for samples first.
  • Prices are list prices. Shipping, customization and payment fees come on top. The quantity ladder in priceTiers shows how much the price drops at 500 or 1,000 units.

Run it on a schedule

Add a weekly schedule in Apify and join runs on productId to see price changes and new suppliers in your category. It also works from Make, n8n or Zapier (each has an Apify module that runs an actor and returns the dataset), or from an AI agent through the Apify MCP server.

Store page: https://apify.com/rel8ble/alibaba-product-search-scraper
Python examples (MIT): https://github.com/Rel8ble/alibaba-product-scraper-python

This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks
description:
arXiv:2610.36298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. SNNs communicate through sparse, discrete spikes, and their outputs depend on membrane potentials that evolve over time rather than on a static mapping from input to output. This temporal mode of computation suggests that the decision behavior of an SNN may be harder to reconstruct from its responses. This work tests that possibility by benchmarking four representative MSAs, namely the Papernot, Tram\`er, T-RND, and color perturbation attacks, against SNNs and their ANN counterparts on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Across every attack and dataset, SNNs prove consistently more difficult to steal. Surrogates of SNNs achieve 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target model and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs. We attribute this resistance to the way SNNs compute, as their spike-based and time-dependent dynamics yield decision boundaries that ANN-based surrogates struggle to approximate, even under large query budgets. These findings extend the known resilience of SNNs beyond attacks on training data to the replication of model functionality, strengthening the case for neuromorphic architectures in security-sensitive applications.

title: Language Models Keep Abandoned Analyses: Residue and Adaptation after Garden-Path Sentences
description:
arXiv:2610.36797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reading "While the man hunted the deer ran into the woods" requires giving up the analysis in which "the deer" is the object of "hunted". People who have just read such a sentence still produce more transitive structures, so the abandoned analysis primes later language. We ask whether language models keep using an analysis they have abandoned, and what in the model carries it. In 24 open models from 124M to 70B parameters, a garden-path sentence leaves two traces in the context. A residue of the abandoned analysis raises later object attachment, by about three quarters of the effect of a sentence in which the noun phrase really is an object, and it appears in sampled text, on held-out and human-normed items and for a second type of garden path. An adaptation toward the resolved structure scales with the sentence's disambiguation error and acts mainly on comprehension-like measures. Activation patching separates the two. Later text reads the residue from the role information in the noun phrase's states, which were computed under the object analysis before the disambiguation, and replacing these states removes almost all of the residue in the 32B and 70B models. The adaptation is read from the states that processed the disambiguation. Overridden statements show the same persistence (a corrected value keeps pulling later predictions in 8 of 9 models), and in most models the pull is carried by the positions after the statement. Finally, the human paradigm transfers only with controls for punctuation, because the models also write garden-path sentences themselves, which reverses the paradigm's raw statistic.

title: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern language models are trained on far more language than children experience, but we know much less about learning from small, naturalistic datasets. We train small GPT-2 models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (BabyView) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (TinyDialogues), varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data. Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. Much of this specialization is lexical and distributional: a simple 5-gram model reproduces the cross-child pattern (r=.91). Training on data from multiple children clearly improves prediction of pooled held-out language relative to training on a single child's input without a similarly clear improvement on grammatical benchmarks. Across data sizes, naturalistic and synthetic training inputs also produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, with important differences between grammatical phenomena. Together, these results show that small-data language learning depends not only on how much language a model sees, but on which environments it comes from and how well that input matches what the model is asked to predict.

title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
description:
Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop.

Today, Vercel Shop, our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify, is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them.

Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK. The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available.

Give agents the information and tools they need

Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content, including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products.

Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site.

Customize the experience for all customers

Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve. The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers.

Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences.

Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel

Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout.

Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform, it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime.

title: Building a Music Theory API (and learning JavaScript along the way)
description:
Building a Music Theory API (and learning JavaScript along the way)

Back when I was a grad student, I’ve always wanted a tool that could quickly spell out complex chords. In advanced music theory courses, verifying a chord spelling meant physically stacking thirds and writing them out on paper — a process that gets tedious fast when you’re working with augmented major sevenths in Ab harmonic minor at 11pm.

So I built one.

The API

The Music Theory Explorer is a REST API built with Python and Flask that encodes core music theory concepts as retrievable endpoints:

  1. Scale spellings across major, natural minor, and harmonic minor
  2. Interval identification and inversion
  3. Triad and seventh chord spellings with inversions
  4. Diatonic chord sets with Roman numerals

The data reflects the modern equal temperament tradition and what’s generally known as the common practice period.

The backend felt natural as I had built apps in Python/Flask before. Python’s readable syntax maps pretty well onto music theory logic; e.g. a scale is just a dictionary lookup, a chord is a list of notes derived from that scale.

The problem

When the API was complete, I realised something: music majors with no programming background can’t explore a REST API. Showing a fellow musician a JSON response and expecting them to find it useful is like handing someone a car engine and asking them to go for a drive.

I needed a frontend.

Learning JavaScript reactively

Here’s the honest part: I didn’t know JavaScript until now. I’d worked with Python and had a plan for the UI, but the actual JS was new territory.

Rather than sitting through tutorials, I wrote the frontend code with Claude and then walked through every change myself — one bug at a time. The approach was simple: make a change, understand why, move on. No change went in without me knowing what it did.

Some things that clicked quickly:

const is just a named box

js
const API = '/api';

A constant is a label for a value that won’t change.

Template literals are Python f-strings

js
const url =${API}/scales/${tonic}/${mode};

The backticks and ${} syntax does exactly what Python’s f-strings do; paste a value into a string. Once I saw that parallel it made sense.

data.field is dictionary lookup

js
const notes = data.scale;

When your API returns JSON, JavaScript reads it as an object. data.scale is the same idea as data["scale"] in Python.

The bug that taught me the most

The most instructive moment was a note conversion bug. My Flask API internally uses German notation (H for B natural, B for Bb -- see my first Blog Post for why!) but converts everything to English before responding. My JavaScript was then running those already-converted notes through a second German→English conversion — turning B into Bb, since Claude had given the initial template without looking at my existing code.

C major was showing as: C D E F G A Bb

The fix was luckily just one word: removing the conversion function call, and displaying the note directly.

What it looks like now

The finished frontend has four sections: Scales, Intervals, Chords, and Diatonic Chords. Each call the relevant API endpoint and display the results in a musician-friendly way. No JSON visible anywhere. Roman numerals, note spellings, interval names all presented cleanly for a non-technical musician.

The API URL is shown at the bottom of each result, though, for technically curious users who want to peek under the hood.

What’s next

  1. Deploying to a platform like Render, so musicians can use it without cloning a repo
  2. A chord progression analyser (/key/{tonic}/{mode}/analyze) that returns Roman numeral analysis
  3. Historical tuning system support in a future version

title: Ghost in the Machine: git-spectre — Local AI Digital Séances for Your Haunted Git History
description:
DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 4: "Ghost in the Machine" 🎃👻
A submission for the Overall category and Best Use of Gemma.

Repo: https://github.com/kingmin8768/git-spectre · License: MIT · Language: Python · AI: Google Gemma (open-weight, via Ollama) with a zero-dependency Standalone Haunted Engine fallback

👻 The Motivation: Your Commit History Is a Diary. Why Are You Pasting It Into a Chatbot?

Before we get to the ghosts, let's talk about the actual monster under the bed.

Every developer's git history is an intimate document. It contains your real name, your email, the hour you actually go to bed, the functions you were ashamed of, the wip confessions you never cleaned up, and the anatomy of proprietary code your company would rather not see pasted into a hosted LLM's training pipeline "anonymized or otherwise."

And what does the AI-hype era tell us to do with that history? Paste it into a cloud chatbot for "AI-powered commit insights." That's not a feature; that's a data-leak dressed up in a Halloween costume.

git-spectre takes the opposite deal. It summons the ghosts of your repository using a local, open-weight model — Google's Gemma, served on-device through Ollama — and, when no model is installed, a built-in Standalone Haunted Engine that needs nothing but Python. The consequence is the whole point:

  • 🔒 Codebase privacy: commit messages, authors, diffs, and blame never leave the machine. Not once, not anonymized, not "just the metadata."
  • 🌐 Zero-leakage by architecture: there is no API call to make, no endpoint to misconfigure, no vendor to trust. Privacy here is not a policy — it is physics.
  • ✈️ Offline dev: airplane, bunker, cabin in the woods — the séance works anywhere git works.
  • 💸 No keys, no costs, no rate limits: no API token in your CI, no meter running on every haunting.

Open-weight models like Gemma are what make this trade possible: you get the ghost, the wit, and the personality — and the blame stays on your disk, where the ghosts belong.

🪦 What I Built

git-spectre — "the haunted git history & digital séance CLI" — treats every repository as what it truly is: a graveyard. Commits are graves, branches are crypts, TODO comments are voices still whispering under the floorboards. Four rites let you interact with the dead:

1. git-spectre haunt — the ghosts review their own code

It reads recent commits (or one you point at), profiles the crime behind each one, and summons the departed developer's spirit to comment on it. Ghost personas are chosen from measurable sins:

Persona Summons when
🕒 The 3 AM Poltergeist commits made between 00:00 and 05:00
👹 The Colossus a single commit of 500+ changed lines
🩹 The Bearer of 'WIP' messages like wip, fix, tmp, asdf
📅 The Weekend Wraith Friday-and-later commits
👻 The Forgotten Contributor everything else

Real output from the demo repository:

╭───── 834f3bf · Bob Cursed · 31 Oct 2024 03:14 · "wip" 1 file(s), +6/-0 ──────╮
│ The 3 AM Poltergeist 🕒                                                      │
│    ✦ This was written at 03:14 AM-ish. The dead keep those hours. So,        │
│ apparently, did Bob Cursed.                                                  │
│    ✦ The commit message reads 'wip'. Archaeologists of the future will weep. │
│    ✦ This grave dates to 31 Oct 2024. Whatever problem it solved, the        │
│ problem has since been reborn twice.                                         │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

2. git-spectre seance <file|commit> — the digital séance

Light a candle, close the circle, and interrogate the spirit of whoever wrote a file. On a file, git-spectre runs git blame, identifies the dominant spirit, and puts the questions to them — with the blame summary entered into evidence. This is the feature that hits hardest in code review culture: before you refactor someone's function, hear them explain themselves.

🕯️ Candle lit. Summoning the spirit of Bob Cursed…

╭───────────────── SÉANCE — Bob Cursed (departed 31 Oct 2024) ─────────────────╮
│ summoned via commit 834f3bf: "wip"                                           │
│                                                                              │
│   Q: Why did you write this?                                                 │
│   A: It was 03:14. I thought I was brilliant. I was merely awake.            │
│   Q: What were you thinking at the time?                                     │
│   A: The build was broken. The coffee was gone. The code wrote itself and I  │
│ signed it.                                                                   │
│   Q: Do you repent?                                                          │
│   A: I repent of nothing at 03:14. Repentance requires consciousness.        │
│   Q: Who else touched what you touched?                                      │
│   A: Top spirit: Bob Cursed holds 6 lines of 'cursed.py'. Their fingerprints │
│ are everywhere. So are mine.                                                 │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The candle is out. The spirit returns to the blame.

3. git-spectre graveyard — Día de los Muertos for your dead code

For the Day of the Dead side of the challenge window, graveyard excavates four kinds of remains — TODO ghosts 🕯️, commented-out corpses 🥀, deprecated tombstones 🪦, and zombie branches 🧟 (unmerged, 90+ days cold, found via merge-base --is-ancestor) — and raises an actual ofrenda: a markdown altar, OFRENDA.md, with ASCII tombstones, marigolds, pan de código, and Rites of Resurrection that tell you how each kind of dead can either cross over or be laid to rest.

Exhumation complete: 6 soul(s) found in 'demo-spectre'.

┃ 🕯️ todo           │ cursed.py:1 │ # TODO: fix this before the demo
┃ 🥀 commented_code │ cursed.py:2 │ # def old_summoning():
┃ 🪦 deprecated     │ cursed.py:4 │ @deprecated
┃ 🧟 zombie_branch  │ doomed      │ doomed

The altar has been raised: OFRENDA.md
Haunt Index: 34/100 — Actively Haunted 😱 — cold spots in the blame

And in the generated OFRENDA.md:

        ╔═══════════════════════╗
        ║         R. I. P.      ║
        ║                       ║
        ║      TODO: fix th     ║
        ║                       ║
        ║   cursed.py:1         ║
        ╚═══════════════════════╝

> *"TODO: fix this before the demo"*

4. git-spectre diagnose — the Haunt Index

One number for how haunted your repository is, from 🕯️ Pristinely Poltergeist-Free to 💀 Fully Possessed. It weighs witching-hour commits, cursed brief messages, colossal commits, all four kinds of dead code, and sole-author graveyards (a repository haunted by exactly one restless soul is its own kind of sad).

🧠 Tech Stack & Architecture

Python 3.9+ · Typer · Rich · the git binary · Google Gemma (open-weight) via Ollama · a hash-seedable Standalone engine · pytest

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      cli.py (typer + rich)                 │
│        haunt · seance · graveyard · diagnose · epitaph     │
└───────────────┬────────────────────────────┬───────────────┘
                │                            │
┌───────────────▼──────────────┐  ┌──────────▼─────────────────────┐
│      git_scanner.py          │  │       ghost_engine.py          │
│  (read-only exhumation)      │  │  dual-mode voices of the dead  │
│  · commit log + numstat      │  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  · line-porcelain blame      │  │  │ OllamaGemmaEngine        │  │
│  · branch merge-base check   │  │  │  (Gemma via ollama run)  │  │
│  · dead-code excavator       │  │  ├──────────────────────────┤  │
│    TODO / FIXME / HACK / XXX │  │  │ StandaloneHauntedEngine  │  │
│    commented-out code        │  │  │  (hash-seeded personas,  │  │
│    @deprecated tombstones    │  │  │   zero dependencies)     │  │
│    zombie branches (90d)     │  │  └──────────────────────────┘  │
└───────────────┬──────────────┘  └──────────┬─────────────────────┘
                │                            │
┌───────────────▼────────────────────────────▼───────────────┐
│                     graveyard.py                           │
│   Día de los Muertos renderer → OFRENDA.md + terminal wake │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The dual-mode engine is the technical heart. ghost_engine.py exposes one interface with two implementations:

  • OllamaGemmaEngine — detects any pulled Gemma-family model with ollama list (no network), builds a character prompt from commit metadata (author, hour, size, message) and lets Gemma improvise the ghost. When it narrates, the panel is stamped via gemma2:2b so you always know whose voice you're hearing.
  • StandaloneHauntedEngine — a deterministic, hash-seeded template engine. Each persona is selected from measurable properties of the commit (hour band, size band, message laziness, weekday), and the flavor lines are chosen with a RNG seeded by the commit sha — so the same ghost always says the same thing, which makes output reproducible for docs, demos, and CI.

The fallback is seamless and automatic: if Ollama exists but has no Gemma, or fails mid-séance, the standalone engine finishes the haunting and nobody notices the curtain move.

The scanner is strictly read-only. git-spectre never commits, never rewrites history, never touches a ref. The only file it creates is the altar.

Testing: 38 pytest tests build real temporary git repositories — a 3 AM wip commit, a cursed file, a zombie branch abandoned in 2020 — and run every command end-to-end against them, scanner to altar. All 38 pass.

🎬 Demo 

pip install git-spectre    # or: pip install . from a clone
ollama pull gemma2:2b      # optional — the standalone engine works without it

cd your-most-haunted-repo

git-spectre haunt          # the dead review their own diffs
git-spectre seance src/    # interrogate the spirit of a file's author
git-spectre graveyard      # raise the OFRENDA.md altar for Día de los Muertos
git-spectre diagnose       # how haunted is this repository, really?

Full captured terminal sessions, including a complete OFRENDA.md altar, are in the repository under demo/. The README carries an extended, copy-pasteable transcript of every rite.

🎃 How It Connects to the Theme

Ghost in the Machine asks what it means for the past to keep living inside our tools. Here's the thing: it already does.

The person who wrote a function at 3 AM in 2021 is still in every line they touched. They answer for it every single time someone runs git blame. Their habits, their shortcuts, their one terrible Friday — all of it persists in the machine, silent, until summoned.

Halloween gives those ghosts a voice: haunt and seance let the departed explain, deflect, and complain about your refactoring plans. Día de los Muertos gives them an altar: graveyard treats dead code not as garbage to delete in shame but as familiares worth honoring before you let them cross over — with marigolds, candles, and rites of resurrection instead of rm -rf.

And the AI twist that makes it all work: the ghost in the machine is running in the machine. A local Gemma model channels your repository's actual dead without a single byte of them leaving the séance room. The ghost was never a metaphor. It was the blame.

  • License: MIT

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: Meet Maltrail: Your Open-Source Digital Detective for Network Security!
description:
Quick Summary: 📝

Maltrail is a network traffic detection system that identifies malicious infrastructure communication and network anomalies by matching observed network data against a set of indicators called 'trails'. It consists of a Rust-based sensor for traffic capture and detection, and a Python server for reporting, event intake, and API access.

Key Takeaways: 💡

  • ✅ Maltrail is an open-source network traffic detection system that identifies communication with known malicious infrastructure.

  • ✅ It uses a high-performance Rust sensor for real-time traffic analysis and a Python server for event reporting and API access.

  • ✅ Maltrail leverages a vast, constantly updated database of 'trails' (indicators) and heuristic detections.

  • ✅ It offers easy configuration with plain-text custom trails and whitelists, facilitating version control and auditing.

  • ✅ The project integrates seamlessly with existing security operations via syslog (CEF) and Logstash JSON output, providing proactive threat detection.

Project Statistics: 📊

  • ⭐ Stars: 8643
  • 🍴 Forks: 1266
  • ❗ Open Issues: 37

Tech Stack: 💻

  • ✅ Python

Ever worry about hidden threats lurking in your network? Malicious actors constantly try to sneak in, and spotting their communication can feel like finding a needle in a haystack. What if there was a smart, open-source tool that could act as your network's personal detective, constantly scanning for suspicious activity and alerting you to potential dangers? Well, get ready to meet Maltrail! Maltrail is an incredible network traffic detection system designed to unmask communication with known malicious infrastructure. Think of it like this: it has a massive database of 'trails' – indicators like bad domains, suspicious IP addresses, or dodgy User-Agents. When traffic on your network matches any of these trails, Maltrail flags it immediately.The project is cleverly split into two main parts: the Sensor and the Server. The Sensor, built with fast and efficient Rust using libpcap, is the vigilant eye. It sits on your network, capturing and analyzing traffic in real-time. It's constantly comparing what it sees against those millions of known 'trails' and even uses smart heuristics to spot unusual patterns like scanning attempts or suspicious downloads. Then there's the Server, powered by Python. This is where all the detections from the Sensor come together. It provides a super handy reporting interface, allowing you to see all the suspicious events in one place. It also offers an API, so you can integrate Maltrail's insights into your existing security tools. This modular design means you can run them on the same machine or spread them across your infrastructure for better scalability and coverage.Why should you care? Maltrail offers some serious advantages for developers and sysadmins alike. First, it gives you peace of mind by actively monitoring for known threats. You're not just waiting for something bad to happen; you're proactively detecting it. The extensive trail database, constantly updated from over 3,000 curated files and 39 public feeds, means you're getting top-tier intelligence right out of the box. Its simple, plain-text custom trails and whitelists are a game-changer. You can easily review and version-control your security configurations, making collaboration and auditing a breeze. Need to integrate with your SIEM or Logstash? No problem! Maltrail supports various logging formats, including CEF over syslog and Logstash JSON output, making it a perfect fit for existing security operations centers. For those who value performance, the Rust-based sensor is incredibly efficient, ensuring minimal overhead while providing robust detection capabilities. Whether you're securing a small office network or a larger enterprise, Maltrail's ability to quickly identify communication with malware, botnets, and other threats can save you countless hours of manual investigation and potentially prevent major incidents. It's like having a dedicated security analyst watching your network 24/7, but without the salary! So, if you're looking to bolster your network's defenses with an open-source, powerful, and easy-to-manage solution, Maltrail is an absolute must-check-out. Dive into its GitHub repo, explore its features, and give your network the guardian it deserves!

title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36449v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

title: d-engine Dev Notes (Part 1): The Hard Parts of Software Development
description:
Want

To explain where d-engine really came from, I have to go back four or five years — to before d-engine itself existed.

The first time I came across Kafka — especially Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect — I got hooked on event streaming platforms: pulling data in different formats together and aggregating it solved a lot of real business problems. An event is an abstraction of the real world: something that has already happened, a plain fact. That idea of "event" goes back, in my memory, to reading how Martin Fowler talks about event-driven architecture. But actually standing up and running a real Kafka cluster eats up a lot of hardware and a lot of your ops team's time — and using Confluent, the commercial version, is expensive for SMEs (small and medium-sized businesses). My impression at the time was that it was billed by the hour.

What I really wanted, even back then, was to make distributed streaming cheap and simple enough for any developer to run on their own — not something only a large team with a dedicated ops org could afford. That's the same vision that later became d-engine's: distributed coordination should be cheap to run and simple to use.

My own background has always been tied to messaging — I built an XMPP-based “online presence” component in Erlang early on, and later worked on a push notification platform — the same kind of system behind things like Google's push notification services (GCM). So I spent a year and a half building my own Kafka-style distributed event streaming platform in Go, starting with my own stream core. I got stuck at the consumer group part — it was just too slow, and looking back, some of that was probably just my own inexperience at the time. For the underlying distributed storage layer, I used embedded etcd rather than a standalone etcd cluster — I really liked that design. There were a lot of detours and research along the way.

Before deciding to implement Raft myself, I looked at alternatives — TiKV, for example — but they all assumed a standalone cluster, and standing one up was just as expensive. That wasn't what I wanted. So after a while, I decided to start by implementing the Raft protocol myself. The hardest part wasn’t writing the code — it was proving the implementation actually matched the Raft paper, that it was correct, not just that it ran. So I spent a few months learning TLA+. TLA+ isn’t a programming language at all — it’s a formal specification language: you use math to abstract Raft's components and how they behave, then use a model checker to explore the reachable states of that model, verifying that things like leader election still hold up under concurrent events — within the bounded state space you define, not an exhaustive proof over every possible case. It's a white-box method, and later on I paired it with Jepsen, which tests the same kind of thing from the outside, as a black box.

I respected Leslie Lamport, the author of Paxos. He hosts The TLA+ Video Course. What drew me in was how he taught — every lecture filmed in a different natural setting, and he kept changing his outfit. Small things, but they gave a dry subject some warmth and wonder, and I found myself looking forward to the next lecture every time. A few months later I had a model-checked design for d-engine’s Raft core, and only then did I start actually coding.

I guess what I’m trying to say is: wanting to do something always has a cost. And paying that cost is exactly how you find out how real your interest actually was.

Follow Nature

If I had to point at one idea that quietly shapes most of d-engine's architecture, it's this: in nature, the things that go with the flow — that work with nature's own rules instead of fighting them — take the least energy. I've felt this pattern again and again, and it's the same principle d-engine's architecture tries to follow.

A good example is how d-engine drains its inbound event channel. I was stuck on a performance problem, and the moment I saw this pattern in the open-source world, I knew it was the answer — because I already carried an old story with me: Li Bing and the Dujiangyan irrigation project. He didn't try to tame the flood by damming it; he worked with the flow instead, channeling it. Draining the channel follows the same idea: instead of pulling one event at a time, or blocking until a batch is "full," just drain whatever is sitting in the channel right now, up to a cap:

/// Drain all pending inbound events (up to max_batch_size).
async fn drain_inbound_events(&mut self) -> Result<()> {
    let max = self.ctx.node_config.raft.batching.max_batch_size;
    let mut count = 0;
    while count < max {
        match self.event_rx.try_recv() {
            Ok(inbound_event) => {
                if self.buffered_inbound_event.is_empty() {
                    self.inbound_event_oldest_pending_since = Some(std::time::Instant::now());
                }
                self.buffered_inbound_event.push_back(inbound_event);
                count += 1;
            }
            Err(_) => break,
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

try_recv never blocks — it just grabs what's already there. So when traffic is quiet, this loop exits almost instantly with a small batch. When traffic spikes, it keeps pulling, up to max_batch_size, and the batch naturally grows. Nothing is throttled; the batch is simply capped at max_batch_size, growing and shrinking with the flood.

See

Seeing the problem is hard too, especially in a distributed, async system. Inside a single millisecond, a huge number of things are happening at once — across machines, code paths, and the network. Concurrency has to preserve ordering and consistency, on top of coordinating Raft's own network layer. There's just too much going on at once. Making all of that complexity something you can actually see, simply — that's the core of how I deal with architecture debugging.

AI is being used more and more these days, and I've tested this myself: hand a pile of performance metrics to a model, and it's quick to catch small bugs — but in the face of this many variables moving at once, it tends to miss the one thing that actually matters most, the real design flaw. Spotting that still takes an experienced human eye; AI isn't there yet. So rather than wait for a model that can "see" for me, I built a few side tools that make all that complexity something I can see for myself — repeatably, almost boring in a good way.

A diagnostic screenshot: 3 nodes and the load generator on one 8-core machine, data on a RAM disk. It shows where one write spends its time, not a benchmark result.

This kind of work pays off many times over — just stare at this chart for a while, let your mind drift, and ideas start popping into your head on their own. This is the view that grounds me; it’s how I actually figure out what to fix next.

Closing Thoughts

The hardest things in this world are often the simplest ones — and that's exactly why they're so hard to write about. A post like this can't really capture something simple; you only get there by practicing it, by living inside it for a while.

I’ve been writing d-engine’s code for three or four years now, as a solo developer. It's been my way of putting how I understand the world into practice, one commit at a time. I hope it can give something back to the open-source community, even in a small way. Thanks for reading, and for the support.

title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?
description:
arXiv:2610.36589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
