title: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface
description:
TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most TypeScript engineers reach for interfaces when they need structured data. That reflex breaks when an API returns coordinates, a useState hook returns [value, setter], or middleware needs to compose through a chain of handlers. Arrays do not enforce length or per-index types. Interfaces force named property access when destructuring is cleaner.

The type system accepts [string, number] as valid but offers no hints at the call site. Engineers write result[0] with no indication whether zero holds a user ID or an error message. The compiler stays silent when position assumptions drift.

Labeled tuple elements fix this. The syntax [id: string, count: number] preserves position semantics while surfacing parameter names in autocomplete and signature help. Variadic tuple types compose middleware signatures. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The mechanics have been in TypeScript since 4.0 (August 2020) with variadic tuples and 4.2 (February 2021) with leading/trailing rest elements, per the TypeScript 4.0 release notes and 4.2 release notes. By 2026 the patterns are stable. What remains is knowing when a tuple wins over an interface and when adding a fourth element means you picked the wrong tool.

Key Takeaways

  • Labeled tuple elements [id: string, count: number] surface parameter names in IDE autocomplete and signature help with zero runtime cost.
  • Variadic tuple types enable type-safe function composition and middleware pipelines by spreading rest parameters into tuple positions.
  • Tuples beat interfaces when destructuring order matters, when position carries semantic meaning, or when returning small fixed-length collections from functions.
  • Readonly tuples and as const assertions prevent runtime mutations and lock down literal types at compile time.
  • Long tuples (more than 4 elements) sacrifice readability; switch to an interface when named properties clarify intent better than position.

What Makes TypeScript Tuples Different From Arrays in 2026

A tuple enforces fixed length and per-index types; an array enforces element homogeneity across unknown length.

An array of numbers number[] accepts zero elements or a million. The type system cannot tell you what lives at index three. A tuple [string, number, boolean] must hold exactly three elements with those exact types at those exact positions.

// Array: homogeneous, variable length
const scores: number[] = [42, 97, 88];
scores.push(103); // valid
const first = scores[0]; // type: number | undefined

// Tuple: heterogeneous, fixed length
const user: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
user.push(true); // error: Argument of type 'boolean' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string | number'
const name = user[0]; // type: string (exact)

The array allows mutation and length changes. The tuple enforces structure. When an API returns a latitude/longitude pair, [number, number] guarantees two elements. number[] leaves the consumer guessing whether the array holds two values or twenty.

Tuples compose with union types. A function returning [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] models a result type with discriminated positions. The caller destructures and checks the second element to know whether the first element is valid.

function fetchUser(id: string): [data: User, error: null] | [data: null, error: Error] {
  // implementation
}

const [data, error] = fetchUser("123");
if (error) {
  console.error(error.message);
} else {
  console.log(data.name); // TypeScript knows data is User here
}

Arrays do not support this pattern. The type system cannot track which index holds the discriminant and which holds the payload. Tuples give you that precision.

TypeScript tuple type checking in IDE

Labeled Tuple Elements: Self-Documenting Types That Show Up in Your IDE

Labeled elements annotate each position with a parameter name, surfacing that name in IDE tooltips and autocomplete without changing the runtime shape.

The syntax [x: number, y: number] looks like a function signature. That is deliberate. When you destructure const [x, y] = getCoordinates(), the IDE shows those labels in the autocomplete list. The compiler still enforces position, not property access.

// Without labels
type Unlabeled = [number, number];
const point: Unlabeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const point: [number, number]

// With labels
type Labeled = [x: number, y: number];
const labeledPoint: Labeled = [10, 20];
// IDE shows: const labeledPoint: [x: number, y: number]
// Destructuring autocomplete suggests 'x' and 'y'

Labels do not change destructuring semantics. You can still write const [a, b] = labeledPoint and a will hold the first element. Labels serve documentation, not enforcement. The compiler does not reject const [latitude, longitude] = labeledPoint even though the labels say x and y.

The real payoff comes in function signatures. A handler accepting (event: [type: string, payload: unknown]) => void shows those labels when you hover over the parameter. Compare that to (event: [string, unknown]) => void, which forces the reader to guess what the second element represents.

Labeled tuples pair well with utility types. A tuple [id: string, count: number] passed to Readonly<[id: string, count: number]> preserves labels while preventing mutation. The labels survive through type transformations.

Per the TypeScript 4.0 handbook on labeled tuple elements, labels must appear on all elements or none. Mixing labeled and unlabeled positions within the same tuple triggers a compiler error. Consistency keeps the intent clear.

Variadic Tuple Types: Composing Function Signatures and Middleware Pipelines

Variadic tuples spread rest parameters into fixed positions, enabling type-safe function composition and middleware stacks without manual overload declarations.

Before variadic tuples, composing two functions meant writing overloads for every arity. A pipe utility accepting (a: A) => B and (b: B) => C could not infer types for a third function without another overload. Variadic tuples solve this with spreads.

// A compose function that preserves types
type Fn<T extends unknown[], R> = (...args: T) => R;

function compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(
  f: Fn<A, B>,
  g: Fn<[B], C>
): Fn<A, C> {
  return (...args: A) => g(f(...args));
}

const addOne = (x: number) => x + 1;
const toString = (n: number) => n.toString();

const addThenStringify = compose(addOne, toString);
const result = addThenStringify(5); // type: string, value: "6"

The A extends unknown[] parameter captures the first function's argument tuple. The return type Fn<A, C> spreads that same tuple into the composed function's signature. TypeScript infers A as [number] when you pass addOne, then enforces that the composed function accepts number.

Middleware pipelines benefit more. An HTTP handler chain starts with [req: Request, res: Response] and each middleware adds context. Variadic tuples let you compose handlers that append parameters without losing type safety.

type Handler<T extends unknown[]> = (...args: T) => void | Promise<void>;

function withAuth<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    // auth logic
    return next(...args);
  };
}

function withLogging<T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]]>(
  next: Handler<T>
): Handler<T> {
  return async (...args: T) => {
    const [req] = args;
    console.log(req.url);
    return next(...args);
  };
}

const baseHandler: Handler<[Request, Response]> = (req, res) => {
  res.send("OK");
};

const protected = withAuth(withLogging(baseHandler));
// Type inferred: Handler<[Request, Response]>

The T extends [Request, Response, ...unknown[]] constraint preserves the leading two elements and allows trailing additions. Each middleware wraps the next without breaking the type chain. The final handler still accepts [Request, Response].

Variadic tuples also model Promise.all correctly. The built-in Promise.all<T extends readonly unknown[]>(values: T): Promise<{ [K in keyof T]: Awaited<T[K]> }> uses variadic spreads to map each promise to its resolved type. You get Promise<[string, number]> from Promise.all([Promise.resolve("a"), Promise.resolve(1)]) instead of Promise<(string | number)[]>.

When a Tuple Beats an Interface: Position, Destructuring, and Performance

Tuples win when position carries meaning, destructuring is idiomatic, or the structure is small and temporary.

An interface forces named property access. A tuple lets you destructure in the parameter list or assignment. When a hook returns [state, setState], destructuring is idiomatic. Forcing { state, setState } adds noise.

// Tuple: destructure at call site
function useCounter(): [count: number, increment: () => void] {
  // implementation
}
const [count, increment] = useCounter();

// Interface: named access
interface CounterResult {
  count: number;
  increment: () => void;
}
function useCounterObj(): CounterResult {
  // implementation
}
const { count, increment } = useCounterObj();

Both work. The tuple version mirrors React's useState convention. The interface version clarifies when return values exceed two or three fields. Pick based on idiom and size.

Criterion Tuple Interface
Element count 2-4 elements 4+ fields
Destructuring const [a, b] = fn() const { a, b } = fn()
Property renaming Position-based, rename freely Must match property names or use alias
Documentation Labels in IDE, position implicit Property names explicit
Type overhead No keys, direct access Property lookup, structural check
Extension Cannot add optional trailing elements Can extend with optional properties

Tuples avoid property name collisions. When merging two results, destructuring with different names is trivial: const [user, setUser] = useUser(); const [post, setPost] = usePost();. Interfaces require renaming: const { data: userData } = fetchUser(); const { data: postData } = fetchPost();.

Performance differences are negligible. Both compile to arrays or objects. Tuples carry less metadata at runtime (no property keys), but modern engines optimize both paths. Choose based on semantics, not speed.

Tuples also model discriminated unions compactly. A result type [ok: true, data: T] | [ok: false, error: Error] discriminates on the first element. Interfaces would need a separate status field and duplicate the discriminant check.

Readonly Tuples and as const: Preventing Mutations at Compile Time

Readonly tuples block push, pop, and index assignment; as const assertions lock down literal types and infer readonly tuples automatically.

A bare tuple [string, number] allows mutation. The compiler accepts tuple[0] = "new value" and tuple.push(42) (though push violates the fixed length, the runtime allows it). Wrapping in Readonly<...> or using readonly [string, number] prevents both.

// Mutable tuple
const mutable: [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
mutable[0] = "Bob"; // allowed
mutable.push(100); // runtime error, but TypeScript allows it

// Readonly tuple
const immutable: readonly [string, number] = ["Alice", 29];
immutable[0] = "Bob"; // error: Index signature in type 'readonly [string, number]' only permits reading
immutable.push(100); // error: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly [string, number]'

The readonly modifier removes push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, and index assignment. The tuple becomes a pure value. Functions accepting readonly [string, number] signal they will not mutate the input.

The as const assertion infers readonly tuples and narrows literals to their exact values. Without it, TypeScript widens ["Alice", 29] to (string | number)[]. With it, the type becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with literal types.

// Without as const
const widened = ["Alice", 29]; // type: (string | number)[]

// With as const
const narrowed = ["Alice", 29] as const; // type: readonly ["Alice", 29]
const name = narrowed[0]; // type: "Alice" (literal)
const age = narrowed[1]; // type: 29 (literal)

This pairs well with exhaustive checks. A tuple ["success", "error", "pending"] as const gives you a union "success" | "error" | "pending" when spread. The compiler ensures switch statements cover all three cases.

const statuses = ["success", "error", "pending"] as const;
type Status = typeof statuses[number]; // "success" | "error" | "pending"

function handleStatus(status: Status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "success":
      return "OK";
    case "error":
      return "Failed";
    case "pending":
      return "Loading";
    default:
      const _exhaustive: never = status; // compiler error if a case is missing
      return _exhaustive;
  }
}

Readonly tuples prevent a class of bugs where shared state mutates unexpectedly. When a function returns readonly [User, Metadata], callers cannot accidentally modify the cached result. The type system enforces immutability without defensive copying.

Per the TypeScript handbook on const assertions, as const applies recursively. A nested tuple [["a", 1], ["b", 2]] as const becomes readonly [readonly ["a", 1], readonly ["b", 2]]. All layers lock down.

TypeScript readonly tuple preventing mutations

Real-World Patterns: API Returns, Event Handlers, and Multi-Value State

Tuples model API results with error/data pairs, event payloads with type and data, and stateful hooks returning value and setter.

A common pattern wraps API calls in a result tuple. The first element holds data on success, null on error. The second element holds the error or null. Destructuring gives immediate access to both.

async function fetchUserSafe(id: string): Promise<[data: User | null, error: Error | null]> {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    const user = await response.json();
    return [user, null];
  } catch (err) {
    return [null, err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(String(err))];
  }
}

const [user, error] = await fetchUserSafe("123");
if (error) {
  console.error("Failed to fetch user:", error.message);
} else {
  console.log("User:", user.name);
}

The caller checks the error element first. If null, the data element is safe to use. If present, the data element is null. The type system enforces this through union narrowing. No try/catch block needed at the call site.

Event handlers in frameworks like Svelte or custom event systems use tuples to pair event type with payload. A handler signature (event: [type: "click", target: HTMLElement]) => void documents both fields.

type ClickEvent = [type: "click", target: HTMLElement];
type KeyEvent = [type: "keydown", key: string];
type AppEvent = ClickEvent | KeyEvent;

function handleEvent(event: AppEvent) {
  const [type, payload] = event;
  if (type === "click") {
    console.log("Clicked:", payload.tagName);
  } else {
    console.log("Key pressed:", payload);
  }
}

The discriminant lives in the first position. TypeScript narrows payload based on type. A union of labeled tuples models tagged unions compactly.

Stateful hooks return tuples to mirror React conventions. A custom useToggle hook returns [value: boolean, toggle: () => void]. The caller destructures with meaningful names: const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle(false).

function useToggle(initial: boolean): [value: boolean, toggle: () => void] {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = () => setValue(v => !v);
  return [value, toggle];
}

Tuples keep the return compact. An interface would force { value, toggle }, which adds boilerplate. The tuple version reads cleaner when composing multiple hooks in a component.

For more on validating complex structures, see our guide on TypeScript form validators and custom validation logic, which covers zod and yup integration.

Common Pitfalls: Long Tuples, Type Inference Traps, and When to Use Objects Instead

Tuples lose clarity beyond four elements, inference fails when types are too similar, and objects win when order is arbitrary.

A tuple with six elements becomes unreadable. [string, number, boolean, string, Date, null] forces the reader to count positions. Named properties clarify intent faster than position.

// Bad: long tuple
type UserData = [id: string, name: string, age: number, email: string, createdAt: Date, deletedAt: Date | null];

// Better: interface
interface UserData {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  age: number;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
}

The interface version documents each field. The tuple version hides meaning behind indices. When you need more than four elements, switch to an object.

Type inference struggles when adjacent elements share types. A function returning [string, string] gives no hint which string holds the user ID and which holds the display name. Labels help, but the compiler cannot enforce destructuring order.

function getUser(): [id: string, name: string] {
  return ["u123", "Alice"];
}

const [name, id] = getUser(); // swapped, but compiler allows it

The destructured variables have the right types (both string), but the semantics are wrong. The compiler cannot catch this. When adjacent elements share types, consider an interface or an object with distinct keys.

Optional trailing elements create inference ambiguity. A tuple [string, number?] can hold one or two elements. Destructuring const [a, b] = tuple gives a: string and b: number | undefined, but you cannot tell from the type whether the tuple had one element or two.

type OptionalTuple = [name: string, age?: number];

const single: OptionalTuple = ["Alice"];
const double: OptionalTuple = ["Bob", 30];

const [name1, age1] = single; // age1: number | undefined
const [name2, age2] = double; // age2: number | undefined

The type system cannot distinguish at the call site. If the presence of the second element matters, model it as a discriminated union: [name: string] | [name: string, age: number].

Tuples also fail when order is arbitrary. A coordinate pair [x: number, y: number] has semantic order (horizontal, vertical). A user record with [email: string, phone: string] does not. Which comes first is a convention, not a constraint. Use an interface when order is arbitrary.

For a deeper dive into advanced type constraints, see our post on TypeScript generic constraints with extends and keyof.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use a labeled tuple instead of an interface?

Use a labeled tuple when the structure has 2-4 elements with semantic position order and the consumer will destructure it. Examples include coordinate pairs [x: number, y: number], React hook returns [state: T, setState: (val: T) => void], or result tuples [data: T | null, error: Error | null]. Use an interface when the structure exceeds four fields, when property names clarify intent better than position, or when order is arbitrary.

How do variadic tuple types improve function composition?

Variadic tuple types spread rest parameters into fixed positions, letting you compose functions without manual overloads. A compose utility can preserve the first function's argument tuple through type inference: compose<A extends unknown[], B, C>(f: (...args: A) => B, g: (b: B) => C): (...args: A) => C. The type system infers A from the first function and applies it to the composed result, maintaining type safety across the chain.

What happens when you use as const on a tuple literal?

The as const assertion infers a readonly tuple with literal types for each element. ["Alice", 29] as const becomes readonly ["Alice", 29] with types "Alice" and 29 instead of string and number. The readonly modifier prevents mutation, and the literal types enable exhaustive checking in discriminated unions. The assertion applies recursively to nested structures.

Can you extend a tuple type with additional elements?

TypeScript supports optional trailing elements with ? syntax: [required: string, optional?: number]. You cannot extend a named tuple type with inheritance the way you extend interfaces. Variadic tuple types allow composition: type Extended<T extends unknown[]> = [...T, extra: boolean] appends an element to the end. For dynamic extension, use rest elements: [first: string, ...rest: number[]].

When does a tuple perform better than an interface?

Tuples and interfaces both compile to runtime arrays or objects, and modern JavaScript engines optimize both paths aggressively. Tuples carry slightly less metadata (no property keys), but the performance difference is negligible in practice. Choose tuples for semantic reasons (position matters, destructuring is idiomatic) rather than performance. Microbenchmarks may show tiny differences, but they vanish under real workload variance.

Tuples in 2026: What You Should Reach For and When to Walk Away

Tuples deliver position-based type safety when destructuring is idiomatic and structure is small. Labeled elements clarify intent without runtime cost. Variadic spreads compose function signatures cleanly. Readonly tuples prevent mutation.

The pattern breaks at five elements. When property names clarify better than position, an interface wins. When adjacent elements share types, the compiler cannot catch swapped destructuring. When order is arbitrary, forcing a tuple sacrifices clarity for no gain.

Reach for tuples when returning small fixed-length collections from functions, modeling discriminated unions compactly, or composing middleware pipelines. Walk away when the structure grows past four fields, when naming beats numbering, or when the caller does not destructure. The type system gives you both tools. Use the one that documents intent.

For further refinement of type utilities, explore our coverage of Partial, Required, and DeepPartial patterns in TypeScript.

title: Beyond Affine Reconstruction: Multi-Resolution Transformer DeepONets for the Radiative Transfer Equation
description:
arXiv:2610.33668v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radiative heat transfer plays a dominant role in fire simulations, where solving the radiative transfer equation (RTE) is a computational bottleneck. Neural operators can accelerate these computations by learning solution operators from offline simulation data. However, conventional DeepONet surrogates rely on fixed-grid inputs and affine reconstruction, limiting their flexibility across resolutions and their approximation accuracy at a fixed latent dimension. In this paper, we develop a transformer-based DeepONet for multi-resolution RTE surrogate modelling. The proposed approach combines a Perceiver encoder, which maps temperature and absorption coefficient fields at different spatial resolutions into a fixed-size latent representation, with a cross-attention decoder that enables non-affine reconstruction of the radiative intensity. This architecture allows a single model to process inputs at varying resolutions without resampling them onto a common grid. We formulate a computable empirical version of a previously derived theoretical lower bound for affine reconstruction, enabling direct comparison with model errors on the same dataset. Experiments on a two-dimensional pool-fire dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms autoencoder-based DeepONets in predicting both radiative intensity and incident radiation, with fewer trainable parameters. Power spectral density analysis shows improved preservation of small-scale structures. Both affine baselines remain above the corresponding lower bound at all evaluated ranks, whereas the proposed model achieves a training error below it at one matched latent dimension, demonstrating the potential of non-affine reconstruction to overcome this representational limitation. Experiments on a dataset combining three spatial resolutions confirm the accuracy advantage of the approach at each input resolution.

title: The Cost of an Unknown Horizon for the Last Iterate of Clipped SGD under Heavy-Tailed Noise
description:
arXiv:2610.33381v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training is often stopped at a data-dependent time, so guarantees for the last iterate must hold at all times simultaneously. We determine the optimal time-uniform rate for the last iterate of clipped SGD on smooth convex objectives under heavy-tailed noise with a bounded central $p$th moment, $1

\beta_p$, even with adaptive step sizes and thresholds. This rate lies between the optimal rate $O(T^{-\alpha_p})$ for a known horizon $T$, $\alpha_p=(p-1)/p$, and the previous time-uniform rate $\tilde O(t^{-2(p-1)/(3p)})$ (Chezhegov et al., ICLR 2026); under finite variance, the exponents are $1/2$, $2/5$, and $1/3$. Their conjecture that a better schedule reaches the optimal rate thus holds with a known horizon (Liu; Jiang et al.) but fails without one. Querying gradients at the running average attains $\tilde O(t^{-\alpha_p})$ at all times, whereas heavy-ball momentum with geometric forgetting and polynomially bounded steps cannot improve on $\beta_p$.

title: An Empirical Study of Reinforcement Learning Scaling Laws
description:
arXiv:2610.33420v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The discovery of scaling laws enables prediction of the performance, the optimal resource allocation strategy, and the best hyperparameter configuration of a large-scale training job based on inexpensive experiments at smaller scales. Guided by these empirical scaling laws, the deep learning community has achieved great success in training large (self-)supervised models on Internet-scale datasets. In contrast, despite its potential and wide application, reinforcement learning (RL) has yet to find a guiding principle for predictable scaling. In this work, we conduct an empirical study of RL scaling laws of an actor-critic algorithm in two procedurally generated environments, Starpilot and Craftax. We discover empirical scaling laws with strong predictive performance in both environments. The discovered scaling laws accurately predict the aforementioned three quantities for larger-scale training jobs up to two orders of magnitude in total training compute. In particular, we employ a variant of Elo scores for the single-agent RL paradigm as an alternative performance metric than the commonly used mean episode return. Our results show that the Elo score is a much more predictable metric than the mean episode return, making it a better choice for fitting scaling laws. By applying our discovered scaling laws to increase training compute, we establish a new state of the art in the challenging Craftax environment. Beneath the surface of the global scaling trend, we also observe a non-monotonic scaling pattern of the compute-optimal model size in Craftax. We connect this observation to a pathology known as Ray interference.

title: What I Fix in My Android Build Before Starting a 14-Day Google Play Closed Test
description:
The 14-day clock in Google Play closed testing doesn't care whether your build is ready. It starts when testers opt in, and every bug they hit after that costs you goodwill you'll need on day 9.

So I treat the day before the closed test like a release day. Not a full mobile app testing cycle, just a short preflight that catches the things testers would otherwise find for me. This is that list, in the order I do it.

Quick version of the rule first: if your personal developer account was created after November 13, 2023, you need at least 12 testers opted in to a closed test for 14 continuous days before you can apply for production access. Meeting it lets you apply. Google still decides.

1. Push the exact build to internal testing first

Internal testing is the cheapest place to find out your AAB is broken. Builds there reach testers fast, and I'm the only tester that matters at this stage.

What I check on my own phone, installed from the Play Store link and not from Android Studio:

  • The app installs from Play, not just via adb install. Signing and Play App Signing problems show up here.
  • The version name on the About screen matches what I uploaded. With more than one build flavor it's easy to upload the wrong one, and this is the only check that catches it.
  • R8/ProGuard didn't strip something the release build needs. Debug builds hide this completely.

One warning: internal testers don't count toward the 12, and anyone opted in to your internal test isn't eligible for the closed test until they leave it. Keep the internal list to yourself and maybe one teammate.

2. Read the pre-launch report before anyone gets a link

When you publish to a testing track, Play Console can run a pre-launch report. Google installs your build on a set of real devices in its test lab, crawls it for a few minutes and lists crashes, ANRs, accessibility warnings and screenshots per device.

I don't treat every warning as a blocker. I do treat these as blockers:

  • Any crash on launch.
  • A crawler stuck on the login screen. That usually means I forgot to give it credentials in the pre-launch report settings, so it tested one screen and called it a day.
  • Screenshots showing a broken layout on a small or very tall screen.

If the crawler can't get past your sign-in, neither will a tester who skims your instructions.

3. Make the first launch boringly crash-free

First launch is where testers decide whether to open your app again tomorrow. A crash on day 1 is how you end up with someone who opted in but never comes back.

I run these on a fresh install, with app data cleared:

  • Cold start with no network. Airplane mode, open the app. It should show something useful, not a blank screen or a crash.
  • Every permission denied. Notifications, location, camera, whatever you ask for. Tap Don't allow on all of them and keep using the app.
  • Onboarding skipped or backed out of. Testers press Back in places you never expected.
  • An older Android version. If your minSdk is 24, I want at least one run on something old, even an emulator.


My seven preflight checks, grouped by what breaks if I skip them.

4. Give testers a way in without a support ticket

If your app needs an account, decide how a stranger gets one before the test starts.

My options, in order of preference:

  1. Let people sign up normally, and test that flow from a brand-new Google account.
  2. If sign-up is invite-only or paid, create a shared test account and put the login in the tester message.
  3. If parts of the app are behind sign-in, fill in App access under App content in Play Console, so reviewers can get in too.

What I avoid: email verification links that land in spam, SMS codes that don't reach some countries, and "contact us for access". Each one costs testers, and testers are the whole point of this exercise.

5. Store listing and countries set on the closed track

Testers land on your Play listing from the opt-in page. A placeholder icon and a one-line description make the app look abandoned before it's installed.

My minimum: a real icon, a short description that says what the app does, two or three phone screenshots, and a privacy policy URL that actually loads.

Then the setting people forget: the closed track has its own Countries / regions list. If a tester's Play country isn't selected, they can opt in and still not be able to install. I select every country my testers might be in, not just my launch market.

6. One feedback channel, set before day 0

On the Testers tab there's a feedback URL or email field. Whatever you put there shows on the opt-in page. Leave it blank and feedback goes nowhere.

I pick one channel and stick to it. A shared email works. A simple form works. Five channels mean I miss things, and missed feedback makes Google's production-access questions harder to answer later.

7. A version plan for the 14 days

This is the one most developers skip, and it's the one I'd keep if I could only do one.

Testers stay opted in when you publish updates to the closed track. Their copy just updates. That's good, but it means a bad update reaches everyone at once, and every release goes through review, so a hotfix isn't instant.

My plan looks like this:

  • Day 0: the build that passed steps 1 to 6.
  • Around days 4 to 6: one planned update with fixes from the first feedback.
  • Around days 9 to 11: a second update only if feedback justifies it.
  • Last few days: freeze. No new features, nothing that touches login.

Every release bumps versionCode, gets a short "what's new" note, and goes to internal first for a quick sanity check. I also keep the previous build's AAB handy in case I need to ship it again with a higher version code.


Two planned update windows and a freeze. Testers stay opted in through updates, so a bad build hits everyone at once.

What I don't fix before day 0

Being honest about scope keeps the preflight short:

  • Minor UI polish and copy tweaks.
  • Features that aren't on the main path testers will use.
  • Performance work, unless it's an ANR.

All of that can go in the day 4 to 6 update, and the feedback usually tells me which polish matters.

If you don't have 12 people ready

The preflight gets your build ready. It doesn't give you Android app testers. If you're still working out how to get 12 testers for 14 days, TestMyApps runs 14 testers on real Android phones for 16 days, from $15, with testers joining within 6 hours. Their how-it-works page lists the same prep I'd want from anyone: a live closed release, the right opt-in link, working login details and a stable build. There's a free retest, and a refund if that still isn't approved. Details are on the 12 testers for 14 days page.


Live testmyapps.app/how-it-works page (captured 28 Oct 2026). The prep list lines up with steps 1, 4 and 7 above.

The night-before check

Before I send the opt-in link, I answer five questions:

  1. Does the Play-installed build launch offline with every permission denied?
  2. Did the pre-launch report get past my login screen?
  3. Can a stranger sign in with only the tester message?
  4. Are all my testers' countries selected on the closed track?
  5. Do I know what goes in the day 4 to 6 update, and what doesn't?

If any answer is no, I wait a day. Starting the clock a day late is cheap. A test where half the testers quit after one crash costs a lot more.

title: Multiple Importance Sampling for Guided Speculative Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.33368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study an extension of the Guided Speculative Inference (GSI) algorithm for test-time-scaling of large language models (LLMs) to a novel setting where an ensemble of smaller LLMs proposes draft reasoning steps which are later verified by a larger base model and a process reward model. Using the established framework of multiple importance sampling (MIS), we introduce weighting schemes to aggregate samples from a diverse collection of proposal distributions. We provide new bounds on the KL divergence from the optimal reward-tilted target distribution and the expected reward degradation, then demonstrate that the well-known balance heuristic is optimal. Compared to GSI with a single well-tuned drafter, combining several diverse LLMs while retaining the same total number of samples maintains competitive pass-at-$N$ downstream performance while being mathematically robust to situations where the support of a single draft model does not cover that of the target, where GSI may fail.

title: A Unified Analysis of Importance-Corrected Momentum Actor-Critic over a Markovian Trajectory
description:
arXiv:2610.33477v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a generic actor-critic method that combines a ridge-regularized pathwise least-squares temporal-difference (LSTD) critic with importance-corrected momentum (ICM) actors. The critic solves a ridge-regularized system per frame by Newton-Schulz inversion and needs no stepsize, no knowledge of the mixing time, and no rank condition. Averaging stochastic policy gradients over frames of $T$ consecutive transitions, the ICM actors incur a frame-dependent gradient bias of order $\frac{1}{T}$. To our knowledge, we establish the first finite-time bounds for ICM actor-critic methods with normalized and unnormalized steps along a single Markovian trajectory. Up to a stationary-to-discounted distribution mismatch, the averaged gradient norm over $K$ updates is bounded by ${\cal O}(K^{-1/3}+\frac{1}{T})$ for normalized steps and by ${\cal O}(K^{-1/4}+\frac{1}{T})$ for unnormalized steps. We specialize these bounds to Muon, normalized stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum, SGD with momentum, and AdaNorm, and compare them in the nuclear norm. With a dimension-free stepsize, Muon confines the factor $\min\{m,n\}^{1/2}$ associated with an $m\times n$ actor parameter matrix to the noise and correction terms. The comparison also characterizes when orthogonalization guarantees a larger noiseless ascent than normalization: exactly when the gradient's nuclear rank exceeds the spectral-to-Frobenius curvature ratio.

title: The JavaScript We Never Questioned
description:
We often reach for JavaScript because that's how we've learned to solve frontend problems. Need to calculate a layout value? Write a function. Need to coordinate styles across components? Add some logic. Need to handle a visual behavior? Start with an event listener.

Sometimes that's the right call. But sometimes we're writing JavaScript to work around a limitation that no longer exists.

CSS has evolved far beyond styling colors, spacing, and typography. Features like container queries, :has(), and modern layout capabilities have changed how we can approach problems that once required extra code.

The interesting part isn't that CSS can replace JavaScript. It can't, and it shouldn't try to. The real question is whether we're adding complexity because the problem demands it, or because we're still using an old solution out of habit.

In this article, I'll look at a few common frontend patterns, how modern CSS changes the equation, and where JavaScript still makes more sense.

The goal isn't to write less JavaScript just for the sake of it. It's to stop writing code that the platform can already handle.

title: 5 Common GBase Database Cluster Installation Errors and How to Troubleshoot Them
description:
GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster installation errors can look unrelated, but many can be traced to five layers: SSH login, configuration parameters, node roles, operating system compatibility, and recovery procedures.

The fastest way to troubleshoot is to identify the failing stage, verify its prerequisites, and change one variable at a time. Repeatedly replacing packages or reinstalling the entire cluster can waste time and make the original problem harder to diagnose.

This guide covers five common GBase Database cluster installation problems, what to check first, and how to approach each one safely.

1. SSH Login Failure: Permission denied

Layer: Login and authentication

A message such as Fail to login ... Permission denied usually indicates that the installer cannot authenticate to a target host. Before changing the cluster configuration, verify the SSH port, account, authentication method, and network connectivity.

Common causes include:

  • The actual SSH port differs from the value configured in demo.options.
  • The dbaUser account cannot authenticate to the target node.
  • SSH keys or their directory permissions are incorrect.
  • Passwords containing special characters are handled incorrectly by the shell or installation script.
  • SSH access was configured for root, but the installer connects as gbase.

Test connectivity using the same account and port that the installer will use:

ssh -p 22 gbase@192.168.146.20

Check the SSH server configuration on the target host, where permitted:

grep -E '^[[:space:]]*(Port|PermitRootLogin)' \
  /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Remember that the effective SSH configuration may also depend on included configuration files and other authentication settings.

Recommended fix: Make sure sshPort, dbaUser, and the actual authentication configuration agree. Test every target host from the initiating node before rerunning the installation.

2. Parameter Parsing Failure: invalid literal for int()

Layer: Configuration parameters

An error such as invalid literal for int() indicates that a value expected to be numeric could not be parsed as an integer. The cause is not necessarily a password: it could also be a malformed port, NodeID, or another parameter.

Start by identifying the exact parameter mentioned in the traceback or installation log.

Check for:

  • Unexpected characters in numeric fields.
  • Missing or extra delimiters in demo.options.
  • Incorrect quotation marks or whitespace.
  • Passwords containing shell-sensitive characters that may have been interpreted incorrectly.
  • Hidden control characters introduced while editing or copying the file.

Inspect the relevant configuration lines and compare them with the template supplied with your installed GBase Database version.

Recommended fix: Correct the specific malformed value and validate the configuration before retrying. Do not weaken a production password to work around a parsing error. Use the documented escaping or credential-handling procedure for the installer.

3. GCware Registration Failure: fail to add new datanodes to gcware

Layer: Node roles and cluster configuration

This error can occur when the installation process reaches GCware registration but cannot complete the expected node operation.

One area to investigate is the relationship between the three host lists in demo.options:

  • coordinateHost
  • dataHost
  • gcwareHost

Check that each host is assigned the intended role, that the IP addresses or hostnames resolve correctly, and that NodeIDs match the expected configuration.

Also verify that the affected node can communicate with the relevant cluster services and that GCware is operating as expected.

Recommended fix: Compare the configured host lists against the actual deployment plan. Then check the affected node's installation logs, network connectivity, and GCware status. Avoid editing multiple role assignments simultaneously, because that can make the original cause harder to identify.

4. Operating System Validation Failure

Layer: Platform compatibility

A message such as operating system is 'xxx', must be centos7 indicates that an installation prerequisite check rejected the detected operating system.

Do not assume this is merely a naming mismatch. First establish whether the target platform is actually supported by the selected package.

Check the kernel information:

uname -r

Also inspect the operating system release information:

cat /etc/os-release

Compare the results with the compatibility requirements for your GBase Database release and installation package.

Some installer versions provide options to bypass particular validation checks. However, bypassing a check does not make an unsupported operating system compatible.

Recommended fix: If the platform is supported but the installer misidentifies it, follow the documented workaround for that exact release. If the operating system or kernel is unsupported, use a compatible package or supported environment rather than forcing installation.

Only use an option such as -i when the version-specific documentation confirms its meaning and the reason for bypassing the check has been validated.

5. Reinstalling the Entire Cluster After One Node Fails

Layer: Recovery and change management

A failed node does not automatically mean the entire GBase Database cluster must be rebuilt.

First determine how far installation progressed, which nodes completed successfully, and whether the existing cluster remains in a supported operational state. Preserve the installation logs before attempting recovery.

For an established cluster, a documented node-addition procedure may use gcChangeInfo.xml and gcadmin addnodes. However, this is appropriate only when the cluster state, node condition, and release-specific procedure support adding the node.

A partially completed initial installation may require a different recovery process.

Recommended fix: Identify the failed stage, inspect the current cluster state, and follow the documented recovery or cleanup procedure. Avoid rebuilding healthy nodes unnecessarily, but do not assume that adding a node is always safe after a failed installation.

A Practical Troubleshooting Order

When GBase Database cluster installation fails, work through the layers in order:

  1. Login: Verify SSH connectivity, authentication, account, and port.
  2. Parameters: Inspect the exact configuration value associated with the error.
  3. Roles: Validate host lists, NodeIDs, and GCware registration prerequisites.
  4. System: Confirm operating system, kernel, architecture, and package compatibility.
  5. Recovery: Decide whether to retry, repair, add a node, or perform a controlled cleanup.

These categories can overlap. For example, an SSH problem can prevent a node from completing GCware registration. Fix the earliest confirmed failure before changing later-stage configuration.

After resolving the issue, record the original error, its root cause, the corrective action, and the verification result in the deployment handover notes.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster installation problems become easier to diagnose when the failing stage is isolated before changes are made.

Start with SSH access, validate the parameters, confirm node-role consistency, check platform compatibility, and choose a recovery procedure based on the actual cluster state.

The goal is not simply to get the installer running again. It is to identify the failed prerequisite and restore a deployment process that can be repeated reliably.

For parameter syntax, supported platforms, installer options, and node-recovery procedures, always consult the documentation for your specific GBase Database release.

title: ATEMPO: Amortized Transfer Entropy Model Per-lag Over-Time
description:
arXiv:2610.36536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When one time series informs another, the delay at which that information arrives determines if models can utilize this relationship effectively. A source may be strongly predictive at one delay but uninformative at neighboring lags. Therefore, fixed input windows may obscure this structure by bundling informative and irrelevant history together. Transfer entropy (TE) can recover these delays by measuring how much a source's past tells us about a target beyond the target's own history. However, existing TE estimators require separate fits across source and conditioning depths, with further estimation on local windows to track delays over time. We introduce ATEMPO, a diffusion-based transfer entropy estimator amortized over lags and time. ATEMPO samples source and conditioning depths during training and conditions explicitly on temporal position, allowing a single score network to estimate the full TE surface without refitting. Differencing this surface recovers when information arrives. Across synthetic datasets with ground-truth TE, ATEMPO achieves the lowest mean relative error among baselines, and on datasets with known lags, ATEMPO achieves $0.98\pm0.04$ lag-detection accuracy. ATEMPO requires a single fit across source depths $K=6$ and target depths $L=3$, whereas existing estimators require 18 separate fits to evaluate the same $K \times L$ grid. On three systems with time-varying lag, ATEMPO is the only estimator to maintain perfect lag-detection accuracy across all evaluated window lengths. These recovered delays improve downstream forecasting: ATEMPO-selected inputs reduce MSE on WEATHER-5K by 7.25%, while 120 selected inputs outperform the benchmark's 240-feature default by 4.6%. Across three brain-computer interface tasks, using ATEMPO-selected lags achieves the highest or equal-best $R^2$, improving mean $R^2$ by 4.1% relative to the strongest competing baseline.

title: The State and Fate of Multilingual, Contextual Evaluation in the NLP World
description:
arXiv:2610.36990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multilingual evaluation benchmarks are the primary instrument for assessing whether large language models generalize beyond English, yet the adequacy of these benchmarks has received little systematic scrutiny. We present a data-driven audit of 51 recent multilingual benchmarks spanning 242 datasets and 219 languages, organized around three pillars: coverage, representativeness, and rigor. Our analysis reveals that coverage is wide but thin with 36% of evaluated languages appearing in only a single benchmark, entire regions (Oceania, the Americas, Central Asia) are near-zero, and a stark task equity gap leaves low-resource languages evaluated on only 1-3 task categories versus 14 for high-resource languages. Representativeness is structurally compromised: translation from English remains the dominant construction strategy where 56% of all dataset-language instances are translated introducing artifacts and English-centric framing, while culturally grounded content is concentrated in a handful of community-driven benchmarks with narrow language scope. The ecosystem thus forces a trade-off between breadth and validity. Rigor is undermined by benchmark contamination, including translated benchmark leakage and parallel corpus overlap that evade surface-form detection. We synthesize these findings into concrete recommendations for building evaluation frameworks that are natively constructed, culturally grounded, contamination-aware, and designed to serve the communities whose languages they claim to evaluate. The dashboard with all the metadata collected can be found at https://aka.ms/multilingual-evals.

title: How Tailscale built a customer-facing model router on AI Gateway
description:
Tailscale on Vercel

  • Hundreds of AI models shipped to customers in-product

  • Model access granted and revoked by tailnet network identity

  • Went from model routing prototype to paying customers in months

Tailscale connects a company's laptops, servers, cloud instances, and personal devices into one private network called a tailnet. Remy Guercio, who leads product for Aperture by Tailscale, describes it simply: "It's basically like a VPC that can span any cloud, on-prem, your house, and your phone."

Aperture takes that same idea and applies it to AI. Instead of giving every employee, agent, or tool a separate provider API key, Aperture lets companies control model access through the tailnet itself. Add someone to the network, and they can immediately use approved models. Remove them, and access disappears.

Under the hood, Aperture is built on Vercel AI Gateway and Vercel Sandbox. AI Gateway gives Tailscale one API for hundreds of models. Sandbox gives agents a safe place to run. Together, they let Tailscale offer model access and agent execution inside a customer's private network, without their team building every piece of AI infrastructure from scratch.

Model routing is harder than it looks

Tailscale is an infrastructure company, so building the routing and execution layers in-house was the obvious first option. But once they took a deeper look into the engineering effort required, they chose not to.

The provider layer looked deceptively simple from the outside. "You would think all of the endpoints are the same," Remy says. "They are not."

David Carney, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, has the receipts, because Tailscale still maintains that plumbing for a few customers who haven't migrated to Aperture yet. "There are a lot of things the big providers don't do that blow my mind that the gateway does, like simply putting the cost in the response," he says. "We initially built those systems for customers ourselves, and the complexity is insane."

Agents raised the stakes further. An agent that can read private data, act on the text it reads, and reach the public internet is a security problem now called the "lethal trifecta." The right mitigation is an isolated sandbox with identity and access controls baked in. "I think we wouldn't have been able to deliver the product if we were also trying to build a sandbox ourselves," David says. "But we were able to go from prototype to paying customers in months on Vercel."

Building a custom model router on AI Gateway

Tailscale shopped the routing layer first. "We did talk to a lot of other folks, including providers themselves, and Vercel just made it very easy," Remy says. AI Gateway gives Aperture one API across hundreds of models, and returns cost and usage on every request, so Aperture can surface spend to customers without Tailscale maintaining price tables for each provider.

Tailscale's customers care about protecting their data, and Zero data retention (ZDR) was table stakes for Aperture. Tailscale chose AI Gateway because:

  • The AI Gateway itself retains no data.

  • They can set ZDR globally or use the per-request zeroDataRetention flag, which automatically restricts routing to ZDR-compliant providers.

"All this ZDR stuff is a moving target, like, which models have zero data retention versus not," David says, "but we don't have to write any of that logic, because it's all handled for us."

Zero cost markup for Tailscale and their customers

AI Gateway doesn't mark up token costs on any provider or model, including when Tailscale's customers bring their own keys. Aperture's customers pay the same rate they would going direct, across every model in the catalog.

Time to first token, from signup

Ask David what Vercel is worth to Aperture, and his answer is simple: time to first token. But that means something different to David than it does to Remy, and both are right.

"[David] Carney likes to overload the term time to first token," Remy says. "In the AI infrastructure world it has a very specific meaning, which is how long it takes to load the cache, generate the response, and deliver it back to the user." Remy explains David's definition: "It's the time from user signup to their first model call, which is the real value Aperture provides to our customers."

And Aperture's success is measured by that time-to-value. "I constantly push the team to remove the most barriers possible to get someone to that wow moment as fast as we can," David says. "After months of testing different products, Vercel was the answer to the infrastructure side, because AI Gateway has such low latency."

Running agents on the tailnet in Vercel Sandbox

Once Aperture had model access in place, the team focused on making it safe to run agents inside a tailnet. This is the workflow:

  • A sandbox spins up and connects to Aperture.

  • Aperture connects to AI Gateway.

  • Tailscale validates the identity.

  • The agent does its work.

  • The sandbox shuts down.

No key is ever issued to the agent.

Tailscale shopped the sandbox layer too, and even had a working implementation on a different provider before deciding to switch. "We wanted to focus on network identity, not sandbox security boundaries, and Vercel's sandboxes are bulletproof," says Remy.

Migrating Tailscale's internal AI layer to AI Gateway

Tailscale's own AI usage had grown the way most companies' has: a mix of direct provider accounts and cloud endpoints, accumulated one team at a time. Internally, those requests went through Aperture, but behind the proxy, it was still calling separate providers directly. After implementing AI Gateway for their customers, they knew they wanted to make the migration themselves.

Tailscale's engineering team built a switch in Aperture that pointed requests to AI Gateway instead of the individual provider APIs, so now they have one integration rather than separate ones for each provider. Nothing changed for employees. Aperture was still the endpoint they called, and every model they were already using was in the AI Gateway catalog, so the cutover happened with zero interruption. Tailscale now uses their own migration as the playbook for enterprise customers juggling dozens of provider accounts and keys.

What's next

Aperture started as a raw gateway for engineers to point a coding agent at. It now has a chat UI, MCP connectors, and sandboxes launchable as ephemeral nodes, all running on tailnet identity.

Aperture's new goal is time to first app. David wants users to sign up, run a prompt, build an app, and share it, all in ten minutes or less.

"We don't exactly know what that's going to look like, but we know we're going to have to iterate quickly," Remy says. "Having partners you can work with hand in hand on that is incredibly important."

David's advice to other companies is to focus on the product they deliver to customers, not the infrastructure required to run it. "A lot of people want to build their own router. And look at us, we tried to do it too," he says. "But you don't need to build another router."

About Tailscale: Tailscale is a secure connectivity platform that connects a company’s users, devices, servers, cloud infrastructure, and services through an identity-based private network. Their model router, Aperture by Tailscale, extends that network to AI models and agents.

title: LabWorld: Learning Interactive 4D Worlds for Scientific Experimentation
description:
arXiv:2610.36592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.

title: Reading Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby job boards from their public JSON endpoints
description:
AI disclosure: this post was written with AI assistance (drafting and editing). I ran every request and code sample below myself on October 28, 2026 and checked the output. Select "AI-Assisted" in the DEV editor before publishing.

If you want a list of open jobs at a set of companies, you usually do not need a headless browser. Most tech companies host their career page on an applicant tracking system (ATS), and three of the most common ones, Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby, expose the same postings their career pages render as plain JSON. No API key, no login.

This post covers the three endpoints, the fields worth keeping, and a small reader that turns all three into one shape.

1. Find the board name

The board name is in the career page URL:

ATS Career page looks like Board name
Greenhouse boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb or job-boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb airbnb
Lever jobs.lever.co/spotify spotify
Ashby jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp ramp

If a company uses its own domain, view the page source and search for greenhouse, lever.co or ashbyhq. The embed script or the apply links usually give it away.

2. The endpoints

Greenhouse (Job Board API, docs):

GET https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs?content=true

Returns {"jobs": [...], "meta": {"total": N}}. Each job has id, title, location.name, absolute_url, updated_at, first_published and, with content=true, an HTML-escaped description in content. Drop content=true if you only need titles; the response gets much smaller.

Lever (Postings API, docs):

GET https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{site}?mode=json

Returns a bare JSON array. Useful fields: id, text (the title), categories.location, categories.team, categories.commitment, workplaceType, hostedUrl, createdAt (epoch milliseconds). Companies on Lever's EU instance use api.eu.lever.co instead. An unknown site returns {"ok": false, "error": "Document not found"} with a 404, so check for a list before iterating.

Ashby (public job posting API, docs):

GET https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}?includeCompensation=true

Returns {"jobs": [...]}. Fields: id, title, department, team, location, secondaryLocations, isRemote, workplaceType, employmentType, publishedAt, jobUrl, applyUrl. With includeCompensation=true, many jobs carry compensation.compensationTierSummary, a ready-to-display string such as $211.4K – $290.6K • Offers Equity. Salary data is the main reason I reach for Ashby boards first.

3. One reader for all three

Standard library only:

import json
import urllib.request

UA = {"User-Agent": "job-board-reader/1.0 (+you@example.com)"}


def get_json(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA)
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        return json.load(r)


def greenhouse(board):
    data = get_json(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs?content=true")
    for j in data["jobs"]:
        yield {
            "source": "greenhouse", "id": str(j["id"]), "title": j["title"],
            "location": (j.get("location") or {}).get("name"),
            "posted": j.get("first_published") or j.get("updated_at"),
            "url": j["absolute_url"],
        }


def lever(site):
    for j in get_json(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{site}?mode=json"):
        cats = j.get("categories") or {}
        yield {
            "source": "lever", "id": j["id"], "title": j["text"],
            "location": cats.get("location"),
            "posted": j.get("createdAt"),  # epoch milliseconds
            "url": j["hostedUrl"],
        }


def ashby(board):
    data = get_json(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}?includeCompensation=true")
    for j in data["jobs"]:
        yield {
            "source": "ashby", "id": j["id"], "title": j["title"],
            "location": j.get("location"),
            "posted": j.get("publishedAt"),
            "url": j["jobUrl"],
        }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    jobs = [*greenhouse("airbnb"), *lever("spotify"), *ashby("ramp")]
    print(len(jobs), "jobs")

When I ran it, it printed 456 jobs (195 Greenhouse, 89 Lever, 172 Ashby), in under a second end to end.

4. Things that bite

  • Dates come in three formats. Greenhouse uses ISO 8601 with a local offset, Ashby uses ISO 8601 in UTC, and Lever uses epoch milliseconds. Normalize before you sort or filter by "posted in the last N days".
  • Greenhouse updated_at is not the posting date. It changes when a recruiter edits the job. Prefer first_published when it is present.
  • Locations are free text. "Remote - USA", "United States" and "New York, NY (HQ)" all appear. Ashby's isRemote and Lever's workplaceType are more reliable than parsing strings.
  • IDs are only unique per ATS. Prefix them (ashby:<id>) before you dedupe across sources.
  • Descriptions are HTML. Greenhouse's is HTML-escaped HTML, so unescape first, then strip tags.
  • Detecting new jobs is just a set difference: store the prefixed IDs you have seen, and on the next run keep only IDs you have not seen.

5. Be a polite client

These endpoints exist so career pages can render, and that is the reason they are open. Treat them that way:

  • Send a descriptive User-Agent with a contact address.
  • Check robots.txt. On the day I wrote this, api.lever.co/robots.txt allowed everything with Crawl-delay: 1, and boards-api.greenhouse.io/robots.txt disallowed only /embed/.
  • One request per board is enough. Each endpoint returns the whole board, so polling once or twice a day covers almost every use case.
  • Only collect what the company has already published. Do not try to reach application data or anything behind a login.

Workday career sites are the big platform missing from this list. They also serve JSON, but through a per-tenant POST endpoint with pagination and facets, which deserves a post of its own.

This article was created with the help of AI. The endpoints, numbers and code were tested by me before publishing.

title: SAGE: Semantic-Augmented Geometric Experts for Point Cloud Registration
description:
arXiv:2610.36658v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Point cloud registration is an essential task for scene reconstruction, requiring the alignment of partially overlapping point clouds. Under low-overlap conditions, this task remains challenging because existing geometry-only methods cannot distinguish geometrically similar but semantically distinct structures (e.g., TV corners vs. desk corners and chair legs vs. table legs), resulting in incorrect correspondences. To address this geometric ambiguity, we present Semantic-Augmented Geometric Experts (SAGE), which integrates frozen pre-trained point cloud semantic representations into the registration pipeline without requiring additional sensors or fine-tuning the semantic encoder. To effectively leverage these semantic distinctions, SAGE employs a Semantic-Guided Mixture of Experts (SG-MoE) architecture. Through semantic-aware routing, SG-MoE enables each expert to specialize in distinct semantic-geometric patterns, reducing mismatches that confound geometry-only methods. With a structure-aware estimator, SAGE achieves the highest registration recall on 3DLoMatch while remaining competitive on 3DMatch. When evaluated with the same number of refinement iterations, SAGE further achieves the highest inlier ratio and registration recall on both benchmarks. These results indicate that frozen semantic representations provide effective cues for resolving geometric ambiguity in low-overlap registration.

title: Building E-commerce Product Pages That Convert: A Developer's Checklist
description:
As developers, we tend to judge a product page by how it looks. Shoppers judge it by how fast it answers their questions. This is the build checklist I use for e-commerce product pages: image strategy and compression, benefit-led copy structure, trust-signal placement, mobile-first layout, checkout friction, and Product structured data — the same QA pass we run before any store goes live, from real-device testing to a pre-launch checklist.

A beautiful online store can still struggle to sell. The homepage looks polished, the ads bring visitors in, and then the sale quietly slips away — on the product page.

That page is where the buying decision actually happens. Yet most product pages are built like a catalogue entry: one photo, a price, and a short description. A catalogue tells a shopper that an item exists. A selling page tells them why it is worth buying, answers their doubts, and makes the next step obvious.

If your visitors browse but rarely add to cart, the problem is usually not traffic. It is the product page.

YOUR PRODUCT PAGE IS NOT A CATALOGUE

Think of a cotton kurta listed on a small Pakistani clothing store. A catalogue entry says: "Cotton kurta, price, sizes S–XL." A selling page says what the fabric feels like, how it fits, whether it needs special care, what sizes are actually in stock, how long delivery takes, and what happens if the size is wrong.

The shopper cannot touch the fabric, try the fit, or ask a salesperson a question. Your product page has to do all of that work. Every missing answer is a reason to leave the page open — and eventually close it.

aimEncoders builds e-commerce websites for small businesses, and this is one of the first things we check in a store review: does each product page answer the questions a careful buyer would ask before paying? Most do not, and the fixes are usually smaller than owners expect.

WHY VISITORS BROWSE BUT DO NOT BUY

Shoppers rarely leave because they dislike the product. They leave because something on the page made them hesitate.

Unclear benefits and thin descriptions: "High quality" and "best design" say nothing. A shopper wants to know what the product does for them: is this skincare product for dry or oily skin? Does this phone cover fit their exact model? Is this dinner set dishwasher-safe?

Poor photos and missing details: One blurry photo, no close-up, no sense of scale, and no photo of the product in use. For clothing, there is no size chart. For electronics, no specifications. For furniture, no dimensions.

Hidden costs and weak trust signals: Delivery charges that only appear at the final checkout step, no delivery estimate, no return policy, and no reviews. In Pakistan, where cash on delivery is common, shoppers also want to know whether COD is available and what the return conditions are.

WHAT MAKES A PRODUCT PAGE CONVERT

  1. Photos that show the real product: Use several sharp photos — multiple angles, close-ups, scale, and one lifestyle photo of the product in use. Keep images consistent, allow zoom, write descriptive alt text, and compress images properly, since heavy photos slow the page and lose shoppers. This is part of the same discipline as our Core Web Vitals checks.
  2. Copy that leads with benefits, then proves them: Start with what the product does for the buyer, then support it with materials, dimensions, compatibility, care instructions, and what is included in the box. Use short paragraphs and scannable bullets, put the most important information first, and write a unique description for each product.
  3. Trust signals placed where hesitation happens: Genuine reviews and ratings near the price and buy button, plus delivery charges, delivery estimates, return and refund conditions, accepted payment methods, and an easy way to contact support.
  4. A mobile page that is actually usable: Test on a real phone — can a shopper read the price, pick a size, and tap Add to Cart without pinching, zooming, or hunting for the button? Are size, colour, and quantity selectors simple and clearly labelled?
  5. A checkout with as little friction as possible: Keep the path from product page to order short. Show delivery charges and conditions early, minimise checkout fields, offer guest checkout where possible, and make Add to Cart prominent near the price. See also our earlier guide on "e-commerce checkout mistakes that kill conversions".

PRODUCT PAGE SEO: HELP CUSTOMERS FIND WHAT YOU SELL

Write unique, descriptive product titles and descriptions using the words shoppers actually search for, naturally. Optimise images with descriptive file names and alt text. Link related products and categories. Where supported, use accurate Product structured data for price, availability, and reviews — it helps search engines understand the page, though enhanced display is never guaranteed. Write for the shopper first, and the rankings usually follow.

A SIMPLE PRODUCT PAGE CHECKLIST FOR SMALL BUSINESSES

  • Clear title and visible price, with any discount shown honestly
  • Several high-quality photos, including close-ups and scale
  • A benefit-led, original description with specs and options
  • Size chart, dimensions, or compatibility details where relevant
  • Visible stock status and delivery information
  • Genuine reviews and a clear returns policy
  • A prominent Add to Cart button near the price
  • A fast, mobile-friendly layout tested on a real phone
  • A simple checkout with transparent costs shown early
  • Analytics tracking: page views, add-to-cart rate, and completed purchases

Measure before and after you change a page. If add-to-cart rate rises but checkout completion does not, the problem is in checkout, not the product page. If views are high but add-to-cart is low, the page itself needs work.

START WITH YOUR BEST-SELLERS

You do not need a full redesign to improve sales. Start with your highest-traffic product pages, find where shoppers hesitate — missing photos, vague descriptions, hidden delivery costs, a slow mobile layout — fix those first, measure the change, then roll the same standard out across the store. That is how aimEncoders approaches e-commerce work: practical improvements to the pages that already get traffic, tested before launch with the same QA process we run on every website — real devices, real checkout flows, and a pre-launch checklist.

A product page that sells is not louder than a catalogue page. It is simply more helpful: clearer photos, honest copy, visible trust signals, and a short path to checkout.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

What should a good e-commerce product page include? Clear photos, a descriptive title and visible price, a benefit-led description, accurate options and availability, genuine reviews, delivery and returns information, and a prominent purchase button.

How can I increase conversions on my product pages? Improve imagery, write clearer benefit-led copy, add trust signals, show costs transparently, and simplify checkout — then measure add-to-cart and checkout completion rates against your previous numbers.

Does product page design affect e-commerce SEO? Yes. Descriptive content, optimised images, internal links, mobile performance, and structured data all help search engines understand and rank the page.

How do I improve product pages on a small budget? Start with your best-sellers: better photos and descriptions, clear delivery and returns information, genuine reviews, and fixes for the biggest mobile issues — before investing in advanced features.

AUTHOR BIO

Muhammad Asad Ullah is the founder of aimEncoders, a web development agency building custom websites, web applications, and e-commerce stores for small businesses — every site QA-tested before launch.

title: Detect Before You Disambiguate: Perturbation-Based Input Ambiguity Detection in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36353v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often answer ambiguous inputs as if they had a single intended meaning. This is problematic because input ambiguity is an upstream source of uncertainty: when a prompt admits multiple valid interpretations, the key question is whether the model should answer directly at all. Existing input uncertainty methods often rely on LLM-generated statements or clarifications, but such transformations may already disambiguate the input before the ambiguity is measured. We propose a label-preserving perturbation framework for input ambiguity detection in which perturbations remain close to the original input while preserving its label. We instantiate this principle with two detectors: a black-box rule-based perturbation library and a white-box importance-guided method using model-internal signals. Experiments across four datasets in open-domain, conversational, and visual QA show that our methods outperform output-side uncertainty baselines and LLM-paraphrase-based perturbation baselines. Our results highlight the importance of detecting ambiguity before attempting to disambiguate it. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/Xiao0o0o/input-ambiguity-detection}{\textcolor{purple}{here}}.

title: Words or Deeds? How LLMs Predict Users' Decisions in Human-Agent Dialogue
description:
arXiv:2610.36813v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web systems increasingly predict users' decisions from what users say, yet when interests partly conflict, users may promise to cooperate to win the other side's cooperation and then not do so. Sales or service agents that rely on such promises may grant concessions to users who then do not keep their promises, at a cost to the party they represent. We test how LLMs combine users' statements with decision records to predict users' decisions, using 1,260 rounds in which 42 users played a repeated prisoner's dilemma-style game with five agents, each prompted to express a dominant Big Five trait, and could talk with the agent before every decision. Across eight open-weight LLMs, predictions from decision records separated cooperation from defection well (AUC = .80), and adding dialogue brought no detectable gain. With dialogue, predictions agreed with users' statements more often, and errors concentrated on rounds in which users broke their statements: accuracy on rounds with a statement barely changed (.73 to .74), while it rose on kept statements (.76 to .95) and fell sharply on broken ones (.65 to .17). Predictions weighted statements more heavily than users' behavior warranted: when users stated a decision they had not yet made in that game, the predicted probability of keeping it rose from .13 to .69, whereas users kept .40 of such statements. Users' decisions also varied with the agent they faced, but predictions hardly reflected this: users cooperated more with the Agreeableness agent than with the Extraversion agent (70.6% vs. 54.5%), whereas predicted cooperation was nearly identical (64.5% vs. 63.1%). Users also cooperated more with an agent when they themselves scored higher on that agent's trait, whereas predicted cooperation barely changed with these scores. Dialogue-based predictions should therefore weigh users' statements by their earlier decisions and the agent they face.
