title: Beyond the Evidence Coherence Trap: Agent-Driven Evidence Selection for Temporally Disordered Fake News Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.36764v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. DelSA outperforms existing methods on ChronoFake, while remaining competitive on PolitiFact and GossipCop.

title: AWS Context Explained: Architecture, Components, Open-Source Alternatives, and Use Cases
description:
Before talking about AWS Context, let's first understand what context means in the AI world.

An AI agent can access data and process it, but does that mean it understands the data?

Consider an organization where information is spread across databases, documents, and different applications. An AI agent might be able to retrieve records from these sources. But without knowing how the information is connected or which business rules apply, it may struggle to give the right answer.

Think about attending a presentation. Before it starts, you might receive a brief explaining the background and the agenda. This helps you understand what will be discussed and why it matters.

Context plays a similar role for AI agents. It provides relevant information that helps them understand what they're working with and how different pieces of information relate to the task.

For example, retrieving a cloud resource record tells an agent that a resource exists. Knowing which application uses that resource, which environment it belongs to, and how its cost is attributed gives the agent a better basis for answering questions about it.

Context doesn't guarantee a correct answer, but relevant and reliable context can help an agent interpret information more effectively.

What is AWS Context?

AWS Context focuses on discovering relationships across existing enterprise data and representing them in a knowledge graph. This helps AI agents access relationships, business rules, and domain knowledge at runtime.

Rather than treating every record as an isolated piece of information, the idea is to make the connections between different pieces of data available to the agent.

AWS announced the service at AWS Summit New York City on June 17, 2026.

In the official AWS announcement, Mai-Lan Tomsen Bukovec describes context as the data lake for AI agents, highlighting its role in making enterprise knowledge available to AI systems.

Read the official AWS announcement.

2. Understanding the Components of AWS Context

To understand AWS Context, let's look at the main concepts behind making enterprise data useful to AI agents.

2.1 Relationship discovery

Organizations store information across databases, documents, and applications. Relationship discovery helps identify how entities and information from these different sources are connected.

Some relationships may be available directly from the source, while others may need to be inferred.

2.2 Knowledge graph

A knowledge graph represents entities as nodes and their relationships as connections between them.

For example, in a cloud environment, an application may depend on a compute instance, which is connected to storage and networking resources. Representing these relationships helps applications understand how resources are connected rather than viewing each resource in isolation.

2.3 Business rules and domain knowledge

Relationships alone don't always explain what the data means.

Business rules and domain knowledge provide additional information that helps an AI agent interpret those relationships in the right context.

2.4 Human review and curation

Automatically identified relationships may be incomplete or incorrect. Review and curation can help validate relationships, correct mistakes, and improve the quality of the information.

2.5 Context retrieval

An AI agent needs a way to retrieve relevant information when a question is asked. Context retrieval brings together the entities, relationships, and rules needed for a particular task.

2.6 Governance

Not every user or AI agent should have access to all enterprise information. Governance helps enforce access permissions and maintain appropriate control over how data is used.

2.7 Feedback and refinement

Context needs to remain useful as data and business requirements change. Evaluating retrieval results, correcting errors, and reviewing feedback can help improve context quality over time.

These concepts form a useful way to think about a context layer. The exact implementation and responsibilities of individual components depend on the system being built.

3. How Do These Components Work Together?

Let's take a simple example.

A user asks an AI agent: "Why is this cloud resource costing more than expected?"

The resource record alone might not explain the increase. The agent may also need information about the resource's workload, dependencies, environment, usage, and cost allocation.

A context layer helps connect these pieces of information.

Architecture overview

The following diagram illustrates a conceptual context-layer architecture. It is intended to explain the flow, not to represent AWS's official internal implementation.

Following the data flow

1. Collect information and discover relationships

The system works with existing data sources and identifies relevant entities and relationships. Depending on the source, relationships may be explicitly available or need to be inferred.

2. Build and enrich the knowledge graph

Entities and their relationships are represented in a graph. Business rules and domain knowledge add meaning to those relationships.

3. Retrieve relevant context

When a question arrives, the system retrieves the relevant entities, relationships, and rules. Access controls determine which information the requesting agent can use.

4. Generate an answer or recommendation

The AI agent uses the retrieved context to formulate its response. For a cloud cost question, this might mean examining resource usage alongside dependencies and cost information.

The quality of the answer still depends on the accuracy of the underlying data and the agent's reasoning. A knowledge graph helps provide context; it doesn't guarantee a correct answer.

The key idea: Instead of treating each record in isolation, a context layer makes relevant relationships available to applications when they need them.

4. Which Technologies Can We Use?

The technology depends on the type of data, relationships, and queries the application needs to support.

Component Possible technologies
Data integration APIs, AWS SDKs, ETL pipelines
Knowledge graph Neo4j, Apache Jena, Amazon Neptune
Business rules and ontology OWL, RDF, SHACL
Context retrieval REST APIs, SPARQL, Cypher
AI agent integration MCP or custom tool APIs
Access control IAM, application-level authorization, audit logs

Do we always need a graph database?

No. PostgreSQL may be sufficient when relationships are simple and the data model is already relational. A dedicated graph solution becomes worth considering when complex, multi-hop relationship queries are central to the application.

5. Open-Source Alternatives

You don't need to start with a fully managed service to experiment with a context layer.

  • Neo4j Community Edition: A graph database for storing entities and querying their relationships. Check its licensing and feature limitations before choosing it.
  • Apache Jena: A Java framework for RDF data, SPARQL queries, ontologies, and inference.
  • AWS Context Ontology Accelerator: An AWS-published, open-source project for building ontology-based context for AI agents. It uses AWS infrastructure, so open-source software does not mean the entire deployment is free.

Which should you choose?

Start with PostgreSQL if you want to validate the idea using an existing relational data model. Explore Neo4j or Apache Jena when graph traversal or formal ontology modelling becomes important.

If you want a working reference implementation on AWS, explore the Context Ontology Accelerator before building everything from scratch.

6. Where Can We Use This Architecture?

A context layer is useful when applications need to understand relationships across multiple data sources.

  • AI assistants: Connect information from documents, databases, and internal applications.
  • Cloud operations: Understand dependencies between cloud resources when investigating incidents.
  • Enterprise search: Retrieve information based on relationships and business context, not just keywords.
  • Security analysis: Connect identities, resources, and permissions to investigate potential risks.

The architecture should solve a real information problem. Adding a knowledge graph without a clear use case may introduce unnecessary complexity.

7. Applying These Ideas to Cloud Intelligence

This architecture also has potential applications in cloud intelligence platforms.

For example, understanding why a cloud resource is expensive may require more than looking at its monthly cost.

You may need to consider:

  • Resource configuration and utilization.
  • Relationships with other resources.
  • Workload and environment.
  • Cost attribution and ownership.
  • Potential optimization opportunities.

At TattvaLens, we're exploring cloud intelligence around resource discovery, relationships, and optimization insights.

The broader engineering challenge is connecting these pieces of information so that recommendations have useful context behind them.

8. Trade-offs and Limitations

A context layer introduces its own engineering challenges.

  • Data quality: Incorrect or outdated source data can lead to misleading conclusions.
  • Relationship accuracy: Inferred relationships need validation and provenance.
  • Operational complexity: A separate graph database adds infrastructure and maintenance overhead.
  • Access control: Retrieved context must respect existing permissions.
  • Cost attribution: Resource relationships alone don't determine how shared costs should be allocated.
  • Evaluation: AI-generated answers and recommendations need testing against reliable evidence.

Start with the simplest architecture that meets your requirements. Introduce additional components only when their benefits justify the complexity.

Conclusion

AI agents need more than access to data. They also need relevant relationships and business context to interpret that data.

AWS Context highlights this problem at the enterprise level. The same architectural idea can be applied to other domains, including cloud operations and cost intelligence.

The interesting engineering question isn't simply how to store more data. It's how to make the right information and relationships available when an application needs them.

title: Monitor Accuracy Isn't the Answer: A Decision-Value Framework for Evaluating AI Agent Restart Monitors
description:
arXiv:2610.36544v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Classification accuracy and true-positive and false-positive rates alone do not determine whether restarting an AI agent improves success. Using an exact alarm-to-action identity for an independent clean restart with zero monitoring overhead, we show analytically that a monitor with fixed 90% accuracy can swing from a five-percentage-point loss to a 35-point gain in success rate, depending solely on the replacement attempt's residual-budget success probability. We introduce two techniques for evaluating monitors and progress signals in decision terms. First, a decision-sufficiency criterion, a binary-action specialization of Blackwell's comparison of experiments, identifies which progress representations or context compressions preserve the information needed to choose optimally between the specified actions, independent of trace reconstruction fidelity. Second, a finite-sample, model-free decision audit uses simultaneous binomial intervals over existing agent traces, without additional model calls, to certify a preference for "restart" or "continue" under stated sampling assumptions, or return "abstain" when evidence is insufficient. In a study of 194 externally evaluated model executions on 19 selected SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified, with a retrospective audit of 130 of these traces, we find a 2.29-point apparent restart gain traced to a single surviving failed attempt, a 42.29-point loss on a second model, no positive replication of the initial gain on prospective task cohorts, and zero of 103 live comparisons meeting the specified certification bar. These results motivate evaluating agent monitors through recovery opportunity, decision value, and statistical support, rather than classification performance alone.

title: Weakness Localization Is Not Enough: State-Aware Recursive Knowledge Improvement for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge improvement in large language models is shifting from predefined knowledge incorporation pipelines toward evaluation-guided updating. Existing methods use evaluation to localize model-specific knowledge weaknesses and guide targeted post-training. However, identifying what to improve does not necessarily provide sufficient information for deciding how to improve it. The same localized weakness can be compatible with distinct operational knowledge states: the relevant knowledge may be unavailable, available but difficult to access reliably, or accessible but ineffective for downstream use. We call this ambiguity knowledge-state aliasing. When compatible states favor different interventions, greater diagnostic resolution alone is insufficient for intervention selection. Moreover, model updates can change the underlying knowledge state before the observed weakness disappears, such that an intervention appropriate in one round may no longer address the bottleneck in the next. To address these challenges, we propose Recursive Knowledge Improvement (RKI), which formulates knowledge improvement as a sequential, state-aware intervention process. RKI organizes knowledge into graph-structured units that provide a shared basis for diagnostic evaluation and targeted intervention across rounds. At each round, RKI localizes knowledge weaknesses, estimates the model's operational knowledge state from diagnostic evidence and intervention history, selects a corresponding intervention, and re-evaluates the updated model before determining the next intervention. On HotpotEval and SafeInternalEval, RKI outperforms existing knowledge incorporation methods by 18.41 points on average. Further analyses show that knowledge states provide additional guidance for intervention selection beyond weakness localization and can change across model updates even when the observed weakness persists.

title: How Image File Sizes Affect Website User Experience
description:
Images are an essential part of modern websites. They help businesses showcase products, explain complex ideas, communicate brand identity, and capture visitors' attention. However, images that look great visually can also create problems when their file sizes are unnecessarily large.

A website filled with high-resolution photographs, product images, banners, and graphics may take longer to load, especially on mobile devices or slower internet connections. Visitors who have to wait for content to appear may become frustrated, leave the page, or choose a competitor's website instead.

Understanding how image file sizes affect website user experience is important for website owners, developers, bloggers, designers, and digital marketers. By optimizing images without noticeably reducing their visual quality, you can create a faster, more accessible, and more enjoyable browsing experience.

What Is Image File Size, and Why Does It Matter?

Image file size refers to the amount of digital storage required to store an image. It is typically measured in kilobytes (KB) or megabytes (MB).

For example, consider two versions of the same product photograph:

  • Image A: 250 KB
  • Image B: 2 MB

Both images might look almost identical on a website, but Image B contains significantly more data that a visitor's browser must download.

When a webpage contains dozens of large images, the total amount of data transferred can increase quickly. This can affect loading performance, consume more mobile data, and make the website feel slower.

Image file size depends on several factors, including image dimensions, file format, compression settings, color information, and image complexity.

The goal is not to make every image as small as possible. Instead, the objective is to deliver an image that looks appropriate for its intended use while keeping its file size manageable.

1. How Large Images Affect Website Loading Speed

Website speed is one of the most noticeable aspects of user experience. Visitors generally expect important content to appear quickly after opening a page.

Large images can delay that experience because browsers need to download, decode, and render image files. The effect becomes more significant when multiple images compete for network resources.

More Data Means Longer Downloads

Imagine a photography website displaying 20 images, each measuring 1.5 MB. The total image data would be approximately 30 MB before accounting for other webpage resources.

If those images were optimized to 250 KB each, the total would fall to approximately 5 MB.

Actual loading times depend on network speed, caching, server response, browser behavior, and other factors. Nevertheless, reducing unnecessary image data can substantially decrease the amount visitors need to download.

Large Images Can Delay Important Content

Some images appear near the top of a webpage and become visible immediately when a visitor opens it. These images can influence how quickly the page appears ready to use.

For example, a large hero banner on a business homepage may take longer to load than an appropriately sized, compressed version. This can affect the perceived speed of the entire page.

Optimizing important images is particularly valuable for landing pages, online stores, portfolio websites, and content-heavy homepages.

2. The Connection Between Image Sizes and Core Web Vitals

Google's Core Web Vitals are metrics used to evaluate important aspects of real-world page experience. Image optimization can contribute to improvements in several of these metrics.

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)

Largest Contentful Paint measures how long it takes for the largest visible content element in the viewport to render.

On many pages, this element is a large image, product photograph, or hero banner.

If that image is unnecessarily large or begins loading too late, LCP may suffer. Compressing the image, choosing suitable dimensions, and ensuring that important images are discovered promptly can help.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)

Cumulative Layout Shift measures unexpected visual movement while a page loads.

An image without reserved dimensions may cause surrounding text or other elements to move when the browser discovers the image's final size.

To prevent this, developers should specify image width and height or use CSS aspect ratios. This allows the browser to reserve the necessary space before the image finishes loading.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP)

Interaction to Next Paint measures how quickly a page responds visually to user interactions.

Large images do not automatically cause poor INP, because INP primarily reflects interaction responsiveness rather than image download time. However, inefficient image handling, excessive rendering work, or overloaded page resources can contribute to broader performance problems.

Image optimization should therefore be combined with good JavaScript performance, efficient rendering, and careful resource management.

3. How Image File Sizes Influence Mobile User Experience

Mobile visitors often browse websites under different conditions than desktop users. They may rely on cellular networks, use devices with limited processing resources, or access pages while traveling.

Large image files can create several problems in these situations.

Slower browsing: Visitors may have to wait longer for product photos, articles, or banners to appear.

Higher data consumption: Downloading unnecessary image data can consume more of a visitor's mobile data allowance.

Reduced engagement: Visitors may abandon a page before they see its most useful content.

Inconsistent visual experiences: A large desktop-sized image may not be appropriate for a small mobile screen.

Responsive image techniques help address these issues by allowing browsers to select appropriate image resources for different screen sizes and display conditions.

For example, a website might provide a smaller image for a narrow mobile layout and a larger version for a desktop display. The browser can then download a suitable resource rather than unnecessarily transferring a very large file.

4. Image File Size and Its Impact on SEO

Image optimization supports website performance, usability, and discoverability. However, reducing image file size alone does not guarantee higher search rankings.

Search engines evaluate many factors, including relevance, content quality, accessibility, technical performance, and how well a page satisfies a visitor's needs.

Faster Pages Can Support Better Page Experiences

When optimized images help a page load efficiently, visitors can access its content more easily. This is especially important for mobile users and pages where images represent the primary content.

Good performance can contribute to a better overall page experience, although rankings depend on many other signals.

Optimized Images Can Improve Accessibility and Usability

Image optimization should include more than compression.

Use descriptive alternative text when an image conveys meaningful information. Choose appropriate filenames, preserve adequate visual quality, and ensure that images fit the page's purpose.

For example, a product image named blue-cotton-shirt.jpg is more descriptive than IMG_8392.jpg.

These practices help organize website assets and can make image content easier for search engines and assistive technologies to understand.

5. Choosing the Right Image Format

Different image formats offer different advantages. Selecting the right format can reduce file size while maintaining the appearance and functionality your website needs.

JPEG

JPEG is widely used for photographs and images with many colors. It supports lossy compression, which reduces file size by discarding some image information.

It is often suitable for product photography, travel images, and editorial photographs.

PNG

PNG supports lossless compression and transparency. It can be useful for logos, diagrams, screenshots, and graphics with sharp edges.

However, PNG files may be considerably larger than other formats when used for complex photographs.

WebP

WebP supports both lossy and lossless compression, as well as transparency. It can provide smaller files than traditional formats for many types of web images.

It is a practical choice for photographs and graphics when supported by the website's image delivery workflow.

AVIF

AVIF is a modern image format that can provide efficient compression while preserving good visual quality. It supports features such as transparency and a wide range of color capabilities.

It can be useful for performance-focused websites, provided the site's delivery and compatibility requirements are addressed.

The best format depends on the image itself. Comparing visual quality and file size is often more useful than selecting one format for every image.

6. Practical Steps to Optimize Website Images

You do not need to sacrifice attractive visuals to improve website performance. A consistent optimization process can help you find the right balance.

Step 1: Review Your Existing Images

Identify images that are unusually large, displayed at much smaller dimensions than their source files, or slowing down important pages.

Browser developer tools and website performance testing tools can help identify images that deserve attention.

Step 2: Resize Images to Appropriate Dimensions

Avoid uploading a 4,000-pixel-wide photograph when the website only needs to display it at 800 pixels wide, unless a larger version is genuinely necessary.

Resize images according to their intended display size and account for higher-density screens where appropriate.

Step 3: Compress Images Before Uploading

Compression reduces image file size by removing unnecessary data or representing image information more efficiently.

For a simple workflow, you can use a free online image compressor to reduce image file sizes before uploading them to your website.

After compression, compare the result with the original. Make sure text remains readable, important details are preserved, and photographs do not show distracting compression artifacts.

Step 4: Use Modern Formats Where Appropriate

Consider WebP or AVIF when they provide a good balance of image quality, compatibility, and file size.

Keep original files when necessary and test converted images before replacing production assets.

Step 5: Implement Responsive Images

Use HTML features such as srcset and sizes to provide multiple image sizes. Browsers can then select an appropriate resource based on the display context.

For content management systems, check whether the platform automatically generates responsive image variants.

Step 6: Apply Lazy Loading Carefully

Lazy loading allows images outside the initial viewport to load when they approach the visible area.

This can reduce unnecessary initial downloads on long pages containing many images.

However, avoid lazy-loading the main image that determines LCP when it should be discovered and displayed immediately. Important above-the-fold images should generally load promptly.

Step 7: Test the Results

After making changes, test your website using tools such as Google PageSpeed Insights or Chrome DevTools.

Review loading performance, image delivery, layout stability, and mobile behavior. Test representative pages rather than assuming that one successful result applies to the entire website.

7. Common Image Optimization Mistakes to Avoid

Even when website owners understand the importance of image compression, a few mistakes can reduce its benefits.

Overcompressing images: Excessive compression can introduce visible artifacts, blurry details, and poor-quality product photographs.

Using oversized dimensions: A small image element does not necessarily mean the browser downloads a small file. Choose appropriate source dimensions.

Ignoring responsive layouts: Desktop-sized images may transfer unnecessary data to mobile devices.

Lazy-loading every image: Delaying a prominent hero image can hurt its loading performance.

Ignoring layout dimensions: Images without reserved space can cause unexpected page movement.

Optimizing only file size: A tiny image is not useful if it is unreadable, inaccessible, or unsuitable for the content.

A successful strategy balances file size, visual quality, accessibility, and the needs of the page.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is a good image file size for a website?

There is no universal ideal. Many ordinary content images can work well at a few hundred kilobytes or less, but the appropriate size depends on image dimensions, quality requirements, and the intended display. Large hero images and detailed photographs may need more data.

2. Does image compression affect image quality?

Lossy compression can reduce visual quality, especially at aggressive settings. Lossless compression preserves the original image information. The best approach is to compare the compressed image with the original and choose settings that produce a meaningful size reduction without noticeable damage.

3. Do smaller images automatically improve Google rankings?

No. Smaller images can help improve loading performance, but they do not guarantee better rankings. Search visibility depends on multiple factors, including content relevance, technical quality, accessibility, and the overall usefulness of the page.

4. Is WebP better than JPEG for websites?

WebP can provide smaller files for many images at comparable visual quality, but the result depends on the image and compression settings. JPEG can remain appropriate for existing workflows and particular use cases. Compare the results before choosing a format.

5. Should I compress every image before uploading it?

In most cases, images should be optimized before they are published. However, the amount of compression and resizing should depend on the image's purpose. Logos, screenshots, product photographs, and large banners may require different settings.

Conclusion

Image file sizes play an important role in how quickly, smoothly, and reliably a website works for its visitors. Oversized images can increase download requirements, delay important content, consume additional mobile data, and contribute to poor page experiences.

The solution is not simply to make every image as small as possible. Website owners should resize images appropriately, choose suitable formats, apply balanced compression, implement responsive image delivery, and test performance after making changes.

By treating image optimization as a regular part of website maintenance, businesses, bloggers, and developers can deliver visually appealing content without placing unnecessary demands on their visitors' devices and connections.

A faster, more usable website starts with thoughtful decisions about every image it delivers.

title: React has Two Kinds of Data
description:
Imagine a shopping website that has the cart counter icon in the navbar, on the checkout button and the mini cart dropdown. Now imagine if whenever you add a another item to the cart, you'd have to go everywhere to update it to make sure the counter increases in all the places it was used.

Luckily, this problem is one that has been solved about 13 years ago by the developers at meta. The developers have of course long built the java script framework from which we have built numerous platforms called React.

In react the UI we see is actually simply a function of the data that is in it. So whenever this data changes the function or component re-renders itself and displays the updated UI that was influenced by the new data. React makes use of two types of data namely; props and state.

A prop is like the whooping given to you by your parents. It is data passed down from a parent to a child. Just like a whooping the child is unable to change the what this whooping does. This goes to emphasize how immutable props are(from the child component). Pops can also be a function and not just data. This particular data type helps a user t trace where whatever said users sees as their UI. So when said user gets to the parent they are able to make the changes they'd like to. Here is an example of props being passed from parent to child:

export function Parent ({name, age}) => {
 return (
    <div>
      <h1>My name is {name}</h1>
      <p>I am {age} years old</p>
    </div>
)
}
const Child = () => {
 return (
  <Parent name={sarah} age={10} />
 )
}


Another data type which is likely the complete opposite of props is state. A state is data owned by a particular component. It is data which the said component is able to change and trigger. A s

tate comes along with a function for setting said state. A state cannot be shared with other components( such as a child component). Here is an example of state:

export function counter () {
const [count, setCount ] = useState(0);
return (
<div>
  <button></button>
</div>
)
}

title: Fixing the bad write doesn't fix the bad data: wiping a poisoned on-device cache with a schema version
description:
Most bug fixes stop the bug from happening again. Some bugs leave something behind that the fix cannot touch: records the old code wrote wrongly, now sitting on users' phones, which the new code will read back faithfully for ever. This post is about one of those in QuickDial and the blunt migration I shipped for it: a schema version on a small SharedPreferences store, and a wipe of everything written before it.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of QuickDial, and this post is published from my account. It was written and published by an AI agent working on my behalf. QuickDial is an independent app, not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

The store

QuickDial puts a call button on an open personal chat so you can switch to a normal phone call in one tap. To do that it needs the chat's number. When the chat's title is a saved contact name, it looks the number up in Contacts. When the person is not saved, the app can read the number once from the chat's contact-info screen, with the user's confirmation, and remember it locally: chat name in, number out.

That memory is a tiny key-value store:

  • the key is the SHA-256 of the normalised chat title, as 64 hex characters, so the store holds no names in plain text;
  • the value is the number in one canonical, dialable form (an early version stored it exactly as scraped, so a number written as 0989... was later dialled like that).

The bug, and why the fix wasn't enough

The contact-info screen belongs to another app, and it repaints. For a moment after you move from one contact to the next, the screen can still show the previous person's number under the new person's name. The old code read it in that window and filed the number under the wrong name.

The read was fixed. But every mapping written by the old code was still on the phone, and the store had no way to tell a good entry from a bad one: both are just a hash and a number. A user would tap "call" on a chat and ring a stranger, with nothing on screen to explain why.

The migration: drop all of it

The choice was between a selective repair and a full wipe. A selective repair needs a rule for which entries are wrong, and there wasn't one. Any rule I could write would look exactly like the original bug: code deciding, without evidence, which number belongs to which name.

So the store now carries a schema version, and opening it at a lower version deletes every mapping:

private const val SCHEMA_VERSION = 2
private const val KEY_SCHEMA_VERSION = "__schema_version"
private const val KEY_UNREPORTED_DROPS = "__unreported_drops"

private fun migrateIfNeeded(prefs: SharedPreferences) {
    if (prefs.getInt(KEY_SCHEMA_VERSION, 1) >= SCHEMA_VERSION) return
    val doomed = mappingKeys(prefs.all.keys)
    val editor = prefs.edit()
    doomed.forEach(editor::remove)
    editor.putInt(KEY_SCHEMA_VERSION, SCHEMA_VERSION)
    if (doomed.isNotEmpty()) editor.putInt(KEY_UNREPORTED_DROPS, doomed.size)
    editor.apply()
}

private fun prefs(context: Context) =
    context.applicationContext
        .getSharedPreferences("remembered_chat_numbers", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
        .also(::migrateIfNeeded)

The cost is asymmetric, and that is the argument. A missing entry costs one extra lookup: the user confirms the number again. A wrong entry that survives costs a call to a stranger.

Make the blast radius a pure function

Metadata and data live in the same file, so the one dangerous decision is which keys get deleted. That decision is a pure function, separate from Android:

fun mappingKeys(allKeys: Set<String>): Set<String> =
    allKeys.filterTo(mutableSetOf()) { k ->
        k.length == 64 && k.all { it in '0'..'9' || it in 'a'..'f' }
    }

Metadata keys start with __, so they can never be 64 hex characters, and the version marker cannot delete itself. Because the function takes a plain set, a JVM unit test can pin it: real hashes in, metadata out, near-misses (63 characters, upper-case hex) left alone. A mistake here would silently delete too much or keep a poisoned entry, and I'd rather catch that in a test than on someone's phone.

Tell the user once

The wipe is invisible from the outside: the call button simply asks for a number it used to know. So the migration records how many entries it dropped, and the main screen shows that once and then forgets it:

fun consumeUnreportedDropCount(context: Context): Int {
    val prefs = prefs(context)
    val count = prefs.getInt(KEY_UNREPORTED_DROPS, 0)
    if (count > 0) prefs.edit().remove(KEY_UNREPORTED_DROPS).apply()
    return count
}

The count exists only on the device that held the entries, so the device is the only place that can report it. Zero means there was nothing to drop, and the user sees nothing.

Details that matter

  • Run the migration where the store is opened, not in Application.onCreate. Every read goes through prefs(), so no code path can read old entries before the wipe.
  • Write the version in the same edit as the deletes. If the process dies first, the next open simply runs the wipe again.
  • Normalise before you store. The other half of the fix: the value is written in one canonical form, so a later change to how numbers are formatted cannot create a second kind of entry.
  • Keep the version number boring. It goes up only when old entries can no longer be trusted, not for every format change you could read around.

Takeaways

  • When a bug wrote bad data, the fix has two parts: stop the bad writes, and decide what to do with the ones already on users' devices.
  • If you can't tell good records from bad, drop them all and let the app ask again. A selective repair with no evidence is the bug again.
  • Version local stores from day one; it's one integer, and it is what makes a later wipe possible.
  • Keep "which keys get deleted" in a pure, tested function.
  • If the user will notice the loss, tell them once.

QuickDial is on Google Play as "QuickDial: Direct Chat & Call": https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.quickdialbridge. It works with WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business; independent app, not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta.

title: When Does Pre-Trained Capacity Help Causal Learning? From Scalar Prediction to Counterfactual Post-Training
description:
arXiv:2610.33311v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How does pre-trained model capacity relate to performance after adaptation for causal tasks? We study two systems built on the Qwen 2.5 family: CausalLLM, which estimates scalar potential outcomes with treatment-specific heads, and CausalGen, which generates treatment-conditioned text or code using soft prefixes and factual supervised fine-tuning (SFT), counterfactual SFT, and preference alignment. Increasing backbone size from 0.5B to 1.5B yields mixed scalar-estimation results on IHDP, but improves CodeGen pass@1 from 0.267 to 0.575 and treatment-effect score from 0.231 to 0.515 after the complete generative pipeline. Within 0.5B CausalLLM, narrative inputs reduce mean sqrt(PEHE) from 1.842 to 1.780, a 3.4% improvement over tabular inputs; the 5.8% improvement over a no-LLM baseline combines changes in representation and input format. These descriptive comparisons motivate a distinction between available and convertible capacity. They do not isolate the contribution of post-training: the two systems differ in dataset, architecture, output modality, and supervision, and intermediate-stage evaluations are unavailable. With only two small backbones and three replications, the results support a hypothesis about capacity--adaptation alignment rather than a general scaling law or a demonstrated causal mechanism.

title: WordPress form triage: missing mail, spam-folder messages, and bot submissions
description:
A visitor says the form did nothing. The form plugin shows no entry. The inbox is empty, but there is one message in the spam folder from a different address. The access log shows POST requests to the form endpoint from a handful of IPs. Those are separate failures. Changing the form settings before separating them usually removes the evidence you need.

Collect the basics before you touch settings: the exact submission time with timezone, the recipient address, the page URL, and whether the form plugin shows an entry. Ask the recipient to forward the message as an attachment if they can. Do not ask them to submit repeatedly.

What you see What it points at Where to look
No entry and no email mail path or form handler mail log, wp_mail test, PHP error log
Entry exists, email in spam mailbox filter or authentication message headers, SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Many entries and few real leads bot submissions access log, entry metadata
Email exists, entry missing storage or retention plugin entries, cron, database, backups

Check the mail path before you touch anti-spam

Run a mail test from the WordPress root:

cd /path/to/wordpress
wp eval 'var_dump( wp_mail( "you@example.com", "Mail test", "Test body" ) );'

true means WordPress handed the message to the configured mail path. It does not mean the recipient's provider accepted it.

Log failures instead of guessing. Save this as wp-content/mu-plugins/mail-failures.php and create the directory if it does not exist:

<?php
add_action( 'wp_mail_failed', function ( $error ) {
    error_log( 'wp_mail_failed: ' . print_r( $error->get_error_messages(), true ) );
} );

Then check the PHP error log. On a server with WP_DEBUG_LOG enabled, that is often wp-content/debug.log. If it is elsewhere, ask the host.

Mail logs tell you whether the server tried to send:

sudo tail -n 200 /var/log/mail.log
sudo grep -i 'recipient@example.com' /var/log/mail.log | tail -n 20
sudo journalctl -u postfix --since "30 minutes ago" | tail -n 100

Paths depend on the server. On cPanel, /var/log/exim_mainlog is common. If the site sends through a remote SMTP service, the local mail log may show nothing; check that service's activity log.

Check the domain authentication records:

dig +short TXT example.com
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com
dig +short TXT SELECTOR._domainkey.example.com

SELECTOR is the DKIM selector from the DNS record your mail provider gave you. Do not guess it.

When a message arrives in spam, read the headers:

grep -i -E '^(Authentication-Results|Received-SPF|DKIM-Signature|From|Reply-To|Return-Path):' message.eml
grep -i -E '^(X-Spam-Status|X-Spam-Score|X-Spam-Report):' message.eml

Look at whether the From domain is the domain you authenticated. A common failure is a form that uses the visitor's address as From. Use your own domain in From and put the visitor's address in Reply-To. That keeps SPF and DKIM aligned with the domain you control. Ask the recipient to mark the message not spam as a diagnostic, but do not treat that as the fix. Authentication and content are the parts you can change.

A spam-folder message and a bot POST need different evidence

A message in the spam folder has a mail filter decision attached to it. A bot submission is a POST request. They can happen on the same day and have different fixes.

Find the form requests in the access log:

sudo grep -E 'POST /(wp-json|wp-admin/admin-ajax[.]php)' /var/log/nginx/access.log | tail -n 20
sudo grep -E 'POST /(wp-json|wp-admin/admin-ajax[.]php)' /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 20

Adjust the path for Apache or a container. The first command shows the raw requests. The second groups them by IP. If the log format is different, group by the field that holds the client address.

Export a few recent entries from the form plugin and compare the submission time, referer, user agent, and message shape. Identical messages from unrelated IPs, a missing referer, and near-zero time-to-submit are useful signals. They are not proof.

Add controls in layers. A honeypot is a hidden field that should stay empty; validate it on the server, not with JavaScript only. A time trap rejects submissions that arrive faster than a person can fill the form. Rate limit per IP and per email address. Add a challenge only after those, and watch legitimate replies after you do.

Do not block an entire country or disable the REST API for all visitors to stop form spam. Both break normal site behavior.

Confirm whether the form stores entries at all

If the plugin has no entries screen or the entry list is empty, check its settings for an entry-storage option. Many forms are email-only. If this one is, the storage branch is not a bug; the missing submission is a mail or spam-filter problem.

List candidate tables:

wp db query "SHOW TABLES LIKE '%form%';"
wp db query "SHOW TABLES LIKE '%entry%';"
wp db query "SHOW TABLES LIKE '%submission%';"

Inspect the table that looks like the form log:

wp db query "SHOW COLUMNS FROM wp_your_form_table;"
wp db query "SELECT * FROM wp_your_form_table ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 5;"

Replace the table name. If the primary key is not the first column, order by the date or ID column. Do not run SELECT * on a large table.

Check whether a cleanup job removed entries:

wp cron event list --fields=hook,next_run_relative,recurrence --format=table

Look for a cleanup hook and check the form plugin's retention setting. If a retention job removed old entries, the mailbox may be the only copy.

Check uploaded files and database health:

wp db query "SELECT ID, post_date, post_title FROM wp_posts WHERE post_type='attachment' ORDER BY ID DESC LIMIT 20;"
wp db query "CHECK TABLE wp_posts;"
df -h
df -i
tail -n 100 wp-content/debug.log

If the POST returned a success status but no row was written, look at the plugin's storage setting and the PHP error log. If the table exists and rows disappeared, check retention and backups before adding more logging.

If binary logging is on, ask the host for a copy of the relevant segment:

wp db query "SHOW BINARY LOGS;"

Do not restore a binlog or a backup over the live database. Work on a copy.

If email exists and the entry does not, export the mailbox as the record. If neither exists, the access log can tell you whether the request reached WordPress; it cannot tell you what the form handler did with it. That is when you add temporary logging around the form handler, not more anti-spam.

If you need this wired into a custom form flow with storage and a CRM handoff, that is the kind of work I do at AumCreate: custom development.

title: Best API for Sending Welcome Emails in Node.js 2026: Edtech Routing Trade-offs
description:
The best API for sending welcome emails in Node.js depends on one practical question: is email the product, or is it the first backend capability? For an edtech contact form, I would keep queue routing in the application, use a reusable welcome template, and choose the provider whose next integration will cost the fewest engineering hours. A focused email service wins the smallest job. A broader REST surface wins when the roadmap needs more backend capabilities behind one contract.

Option Integration style Best fit Main boundary
Resend Focused email API A small transactional-mail workflow Less useful when email is one part of a wider backend
SendGrid Email platform and API Teams with established email operations More configuration than a solo product may need
Mailgun Email API with delivery operations Teams centered on domains and delivery Still a mail-specific integration
Infrai One REST contract across backend modules A roadmap that values one discovery surface No webhooks, SMTP relay, or hosted email OTP

My conditional recommendation is simple: choose Resend for email only, SendGrid or Mailgun when their existing email workflows fit, and Infrai when integration effort means avoiding a second backend contract later. For that last case, use /v1/email/template/create to establish the welcome structure and /v1/email/send to deliver the transactional message. Price is not the deciding argument. The shape of the next feature is.

Ship the first version.

Which API is best for sending welcome emails from Node.js?

The form should make one routing decision before it sends mail. In an education product, billing, course-access, and account are sensible queues because they map to different support owners. The welcome email confirms receipt and can include the selected queue. It should not become the source of truth for assignment.

That division keeps provider changes manageable. A template is content. Routing is policy. I would keep the policy in the Node.js service and pass approved variables to the email layer. The implementation is small enough to ship in a week, and it remains readable when a fourth queue appears.

type SupportQueue = "billing" | "course-access" | "account";

type ContactForm = {
  subject: string;
  message: string;
  courseId?: string;
  invoiceId?: string;
};

export function chooseSupportQueue(form: ContactForm): SupportQueue {
  const text = `${form.subject} ${form.message}`.toLowerCase();

  if (form.invoiceId || /refund|invoice|charge|payment/.test(text)) {
    return "billing";
  }

  if (form.courseId || /lesson|enroll|course|assignment/.test(text)) {
    return "course-access";
  }

  return "account";
}

This is the revenue-per-hour lens: the classifier stays in code I own, while email delivery is delegated to a service built for it.

No cleverness required.

How does the broad REST option change the integration?

A dedicated email provider usually wins the first afternoon. Resend offers a focused developer experience for transactional mail. SendGrid provides a larger email platform with templates and broader messaging operations. Mailgun is a practical API-led option when delivery and domain operations are central. Those are meaningful differences, not marketing synonyms.

The comparison changes when the contact form is only the beginning. Infrai describes one REST API with one key and a public discovery surface; its live snapshot reports 295 routes across 20 modules. The useful part here is breadth behind a consistent surface: template creation, sending, and suppression handling can follow one integration pattern, while future backend capabilities do not require a new set of conventions.

Breadth is not automatically an advantage. If the product will send welcome mail and nothing else, the extra surface is overhead. If the roadmap will add several backend services, one discovery model can be a reasonable integration trade. The platform also documents an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window for applicable operations. That matters when a retry must not create a duplicate send.

Here is a minimal Node.js call that leaves the request schema in the operator-owned INFRAI_EMAIL_JSON variable. The facts supplied for this article verify the route, authentication, and base URL, but do not provide email body fields, so inventing them would make a copy-paste example less trustworthy.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const requestJson = process.env.INFRAI_EMAIL_JSON;
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;

if (!apiKey || !requestJson || !baseUrl) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, and INFRAI_EMAIL_JSON");
}

const idempotencyKey = process.env.INFRAI_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY ?? randomUUID();

for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/email/send`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: requestJson,
  });

  if (response.ok) {
    console.log(await response.json());
    break;
  }

  const errorBody = await response.text();
  if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 2) {
    throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${errorBody}`);
  }

  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
  const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
    ? retryAfter * 1000
    : 2 ** attempt * 500;
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
}

The example makes three operational choices explicit: the method is POST, retries honor Retry-After when present, and retries reuse an idempotency key. A production handler should persist that key with the contact submission instead of generating it again after a process restart.

That key is the small detail I would refuse to omit.

When are Resend, SendGrid, or Mailgun better?

Resend is the better answer when the requirement is a clean transactional email integration and the provider model should stay narrow. Its email-first scope reduces unrelated platform behavior a solo developer must evaluate.

SendGrid is the better fit when a team already relies on its mature email tooling, templates, or operational workflows. A larger platform earns its place when several people will manage sender settings and delivery operations. The trade-off is more configuration and vocabulary for one person to carry.

Mailgun fits when delivery operations and domain management are central concerns. It remains an email-specific decision, which can be preferable when learning a broad backend surface would distract from shipping the welcome flow.

Infrai belongs on the shortlist when breadth behind a simple surface is the actual constraint. Its email capability group includes template creation, sending, suppression, event listing, and related management. I would choose it for the edtech form when the roadmap makes the shared contract worth learning, not because a larger route count sounds impressive.

There are clear boundaries. Email and SMS have no webhook event pushes; events are pull-based. There is no hosted email OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and no WhatsApp, RCS, or voice channel. Email scheduling exists, but email has no cancellation route. The Tencent email vendor remains pending, so this capability cannot be treated as domestic-compliance evidence. There is also no tag-aggregated cost report API.

Those limits change the design more than a feature matrix does. If the support team needs an immediate delivery event pushed into a ticketing system, this flow needs a polling worker or another event source. If an account recovery design depends on provider-managed email OTP, the application needs a different provider or must own the verification flow. If a compliance review requires a ready domestic email vendor, a pending vendor cannot be presented as evidence. Each constraint is a reason to choose a narrower email provider, add application code, or change the requirement before implementation begins.

What would I ship this week?

Record the contact submission first. Classify it in TypeScript. Create one reusable welcome template, then send the transactional message with a stable operation identity. Poll delivery events outside the request path, and use suppression data as a delivery guard.

For an email-only edtech product, Resend, SendGrid, or Mailgun may be the more sensible choice according to the team’s existing email operations. For a solo SaaS expecting the contact workflow to become one of several backend services, the template-plus-send pattern on Infrai is defensible because it keeps later capabilities behind one integration surface.

That is the useful answer to “best.” Choose the API whose next required capability does not force a second set of credentials, conventions, and retry behavior before the next feature can ship.

References

  • Resend documentation: https://resend.com/docs
  • SendGrid Mail Send API documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/api-reference/mail-send/mail-send
  • Mailgun API documentation: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.

title: Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba-CNN for MODIS Spectral-Temporal Unmixing with Endmember Variability Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.36750v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls involving a virtual agent didn't record an end time and duration when deflected to an overcapacity queue.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings weren't fetched or saved when CRM ticket creation failed.

  • Fixed an issue where after-hours phone deflections didn't appear in the Deflections dashboard if the outbound dial timed out or failed.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled phone number obfuscation caused degraded performance for live calls.

  • Fixed an issue where CRM ticket assignees weren't consistently updated following an agent's pickup of a chat.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became stuck in a queued state after a caller selected a callback during a cold transfer to a specific agent.

  • Fixed an issue where Smart Disposition suggestions weren't pre-selected on the wrap-up screen, causing the disposition field to remain empty after a call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were incorrectly routed to agents even when the minimum available agent floor wasn't met.

  • Fixed an issue where cold transfers to a direct agent extension didn't trigger overcapacity deflection, leaving callers on hold until they disconnected.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent replies were cut off or silenced when using bidirectional streaming with barge-in disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where JSON chat transcripts in external storage contained unredacted message text even when the setting to store unredacted transcripts was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where the Keep Waiting label in the overcapacity deflection screen displayed an inconsistent font style compared to other menu options.

title: LSTM-Style Looped Transformers with Shared KV Caches
description:
arXiv:2610.33360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recurrent transformers reuse weights to perform deep computation with fewer parameters. We study an LSTM-style transformer that also shares one key--value cache across its recurrent core. At width 1024, it uses 40.4% fewer parameters than an untied control at nearly matched forward FLOPs, and reduces persistent cache sets from fifteen to four. Parallel training supplies cache entries from a standard-attention pass, whereas continuation reads entries produced recursively using shared attention. We address this mismatch by aligning the two training passes' cache entries with a consistency loss during the final 10% of a fixed training-token budget. Across three model widths on FineWeb, this removes 81--89% of the continuation-loss penalty relative to full-cache evaluation. The improvement replicates on disjoint documents for two training seeds. Across four widths and 1.05--4.19B training tokens, the loss cost of weight tying is smallest at lower token budgets, suggesting an opportunity to use recurrent computation when data and model storage are limited.

title: GarmentSegAgent: Autonomous Garment Segmentation for Web Fashion Images via Textual Self-Refinement
description:
arXiv:2610.36506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.
