title: Satellite-derived bathymetry of Arabian Gulf ports under leakage-free validation: a multi-site benchmark of empirical, machine-learning and deep-learning models against 285,000 multibeam soundings, with an outlook for UAE waters
description:
arXiv:2610.33609v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) is often proposed as a low-cost complement to multibeam surveys of ports, but its accuracy is seldom measured on an area the model has never seen. We test SDB in the turbid, shallow and tidal waters of the Abu Dhabi coast against 285,619 multibeam soundings from twelve surveys at six port areas, reduced to Lowest Astronomical Tide. The Stumpf ratio, the Lyzenga transform, a monotonic gradient-boosted tree model (LightGBM) and a U-Net ensemble were trained on 72 Sentinel-2 images and tested in transfer to an unseen site and with local control (about 20% of a site's soundings, spatial blocks beyond a 225 m buffer). The validation design changed the result more than the model: the same LightGBM model gave 0.57 m RMSE under a random pixel split, 1.30 m under spatial blocks and 1.66 m at an unseen site. In transfer the Stumpf ratio (1.45 m) was not beaten by LightGBM, the U-Net or Lyzenga. With local control a hybrid of the tree output and the band ratio reached 1.11 m over 0-11 m, 67% of pixels within the IHO S-44 Order 2 tolerance and a conformal 95% interval with 95% observed coverage; in clear water it reached 0.29-0.53 m. The seabed could not be read beyond 11 m, and summer images were five to six times more turbid than winter ones. ICESat-2 ATL24 agreed with the surveys to 0.25 m after a depth-dependent offset was removed. A 60 m reconnaissance mosaic of 17,200 km2 of the UAE coast, calibrated cell by cell on ICESat-2 without any vessel survey, reached 1.42 m RMSE on held-out blocks over half of the product. Sentinel-2 SDB with about a hundred control depths per image is a usable reconnaissance and change-monitoring tool in these waters to about 10 m; it does not meet S-44 Order 1 without local control, and accuracies from random splits should not be taken as operational accuracy.

title: Faithful Federated Tabular Data Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.33403v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthetic data is an important data source in the AI era. This paper studies the generation of mixed-type tabular synthetic data in federated settings, where two key challenges arise: ensuring distributional fidelity and effectively handling mixed-type data. We propose Federated Integrative Two-Step Synthesis (FITS), a framework for mixed-type tabular data synthesis. At its core is a two-step federated algorithm for estimating conditional cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) using local linear regression. Building on this algorithm, we develop a federated synthesis procedure based on the probability chain rule to ensure distributional fidelity. To handle mixed-type data, FITS introduces a continualization method that lifts discrete variables into a continuous space and recovers their discrete distributions without loss at both the density-function and CDF levels. This transformation provides a unified continuous representation of mixed-type variables, facilitating the application of local linear regression and synthetic data generation. Our theoretical analysis characterizes the conditional density and cumulative distribution functions of the continualized mixed-type variables and establishes the uniform convergence of the resulting federated conditional CDF estimators. Experiments demonstrate that FITS-generated synthetic data improves downstream task performance for all clients, with the benefits depending on how the synthetic data is used.

title: ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.36509v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.

title: Meet LEANN: An Open-Source Vector Index that Shrinks a 60M-Chunk RAG Index from 201 GB to 6 GB
description:
UC Berkeley’s LEANN vector index stores a pruned graph and recomputes embeddings at query time. It matches HNSW accuracy at 90% recall using 4 GB instead of 188 GB, at the cost of seconds-level search.

title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization
description:
arXiv:2610.36456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.

title: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.36437v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, a task's primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward: on a failing response, an auxiliary cannot exceed the primary. However, group-relative advantage estimators treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, so it can reverse the primary's order, and at the primary's ceiling only auxiliaries order responses. Keeping gated auxiliaries hurts some tasks, while dropping them hurts others. We propose CONCUR, an advantage estimator that replaces the standardized scores of each gated auxiliary with the closest scores that satisfy two conditions: responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores, and responses at the primary's ceiling receive equal scores. CONCUR-T applies both conditions throughout training, and CONCUR-A lifts the second for an auxiliary that agrees with the primary's order more often than it reverses it among passing responses. On three models from two families and across math, code, instruction following, and writing, both variants score higher on average than all baselines and than when all the gated auxiliaries are dropped.

title: RadonBench: A Benchmark of Classical and Learning-Guided Search Techniques for Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
description:
arXiv:2610.33259v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Classical optimization and learning-guided search offer complementary approaches to open problems in discrete mathematics, but their outputs are difficult to compare when search spaces, validity checks, and stopping rules differ. We present \emph{RadonBench}, a benchmark for constructing maximum-cardinality Radon-free lattice configurations: finite subsets of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ admitting no integral Radon partition. It remains open whether Radon-free configurations with $11$ points in $\mathbb{Z}^3$ or $21$ points in $\mathbb{Z}^4$ are possible. If they exist, they would improve the corresponding lower bounds on the integer Radon numbers. We compare exhaustive extension, greedy local search, PatternBoost, AlphaZero, and AlphaEvolve. All outputs use one success predicate: a convex target-sized configuration succeeds exactly when its number of integral Radon points is zero. PatternBoost and AlphaZero construct verified Radon-free configurations of sizes $10$ and $20$, one point short of the respective targets; AlphaZero's best convex target terminals have two integral Radon points in both dimensions. Exhaustive extension over fixed seeds and declared finite search boxes likewise reaches a minimum of two integral Radon points. Greedy local search and AlphaEvolve each produce target-sized near misses with one integral Radon point. No audited run reaches zero. These results establish reproducible near-miss baselines over explicitly scoped search domains.

title: Physics Informed Neural Networks for Solving the Drift-Diffusion Equations
description:
arXiv:2610.33133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The drift-diffusion equations are the fundamental building block for the modeling, design, and optimization of modern semiconductor devices. Solutions of the drift-diffusion equations rarely give way to analytical forms, and exhibit strong nonlinearity, with the solutions ranging over several orders of magnitude. These attributes have led to research into numerical solvers, and while many commercial Technology Computer Aided Design (TCAD) packages now exist, they may require long simulation times, exhibit sensitivity to initial guesses, and rely on mesh generation. Further, these solvers are not well suited for inverse problems where the design parameters of a device are retrieved from its desired functional characteristics. To address all these challenges, this work demonstrates the usage of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for the solution of the drift-diffusion equations with errors comparable to traditional simulation software using advanced training techniques to solve problems beyond the well-behaved equilibrium regime. For this study, we specifically choose an abrupt PN-junction in both one and two dimensions that features extreme gradients of the carrier concentrations at the Ohmic contacts and an abrupt discontinuity in the doping profile. Using the proposed PINN architecture, we are able to retrieve accurate results for all observables under all bias conditions. Additionally, we apply the PINN solver towards the inverse problem of retrieving doping profiles directly from desired electric field distributions or electrostatic potentials under non-zero applied biases. Our work establishes a powerful PINNs-based approach for semiconductor device modeling with the ability to solve inverse problems under non-equilibrium conditions for microelectronics research and discovery.

title: Error-Subspace Calibration for Multi-Task Model Merging
description:
arXiv:2610.33483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model merging combines task-specific expert models into a single model without joint training on their original datasets, but often incurs a performance gap relative to the individual experts. Post-merging calibration can reduce this gap through task-specific representation alignment, but the alignment objective alone does not specify which feature directions to correct. We propose Error-Subspace Calibration (ESCal), a post-merging calibration framework that identifies low-dimensional error subspaces from weight differences between expert and merged models. At each intermediate block boundary, a bridge module projects the merged representation onto the next block's input-projection error subspace and maps these coordinates to an additive correction in the current block's output-projection error subspace. The subspace bases remain fixed, so calibration learns only these linear maps, yielding a parameter-efficient mechanism for feature correction. We find that ESCal brings the merged model closer to the experts in both representations and predictions, indicating more faithful recovery of task-specific behavior. Experiments on vision and natural language understanding benchmarks show that ESCal improves merged-model performance across diverse architectures and merging methods using a small calibration set for each task.

ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

title: SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model
description:
arXiv:2610.36419v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Scalable Pixel-anchored End-to-end Diffusion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie's formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140x and 61x faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256x256 generation. With a more efficient 32x compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512x512 generation.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36767v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.

title: Do AI Scientists Know What's New?
description:
arXiv:2610.36511v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A major challenge facing AI scientific discovery pipelines is how to determine when a generated idea is meaningfully novel. Ideally, novelty checks in these pipelines must be able to reject non-novel ideas while not rejecting too many novel ideas, and they should also be able to distinguish which parts of a proposal are non-novel, as opposed to opaquely discarding entire proposals. We design an analytical framework for evaluation of novelty checks with temporal ground truth at both the proposal- and claim-level, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals built from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas matching ones the field went on to publish. Auditing existing novelty checks with this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are later realized by human researchers, and observe that checks built to evaluate proposals as a whole can point to claim-level prior art only by rejecting the whole proposal. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module. ClaimNov catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate, and its claim-level novelty profile cuts the LLM judge's false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%. Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, ClaimNov also keeps proposals that build on established contributions, rejecting only 3% of ICLR-accepted proposals with a reviewer-disputed contribution and keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced prior contribution, against 76 for the strongest existing check. Code and data are available at https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov.

title: Scenario Analysis: A 409A Valuation Tool for Startups
description:
The Problem

When a startup is preparing for equity rounds, founders and CFOs need to understand how the fair‑market value (FMV) of their shares could shift under different market conditions. A single static valuation can leave teams uncertain about the true cost of equity compensation and expose them to compliance risk under IRC 409A. This is where 409a valuation pays off in practice.

Traditionally, teams would pull data into spreadsheets, run multiple scenarios manually, and then generate a report. That process is slow, error‑prone, and hard to audit. Moreover, if a valuation is incorrect, it can trigger a costly audit defense.

How Scenario Analysis Works

N409’s scenario analysis feature addresses this by allowing users to define four distinct valuation states:

  1. Bull – optimistic market growth.
  2. Base – current market conditions.
  3. Bear – pessimistic outlook.
  4. Custom – user‑defined parameters.

Using the platform’s AI‑driven engine (built on OpenRouter AI and Python), the system automatically recalculates the valuation for each scenario. The underlying logic is the same 13 valuation methodologies that N409 supports, but the inputs are adjusted according to the chosen scenario. For example, revenue growth rates, discount rates, and market multiples are tweaked to reflect the bullish or bearish outlook. Getting 409a valuation right early saves rework later.

A recent commit (fix(grants): blank what-if FMV terms are absent, not $0 scenarios) ensures that when a user leaves a scenario field empty, the system correctly treats it as “no change” rather than defaulting to zero, keeping scenario outputs accurate.

User Experience

From the client portal, a founder selects the Scenario Analysis tab. A clean form lists the four scenarios, each with sliders and numeric fields for key variables like revenue growth, discount rate, and market multiple. When a change is made, the AI engine runs in real time, and the portal displays:

  • A side‑by‑side comparison of FMV per share for each scenario.
  • A visual chart that highlights the spread between bull and bear values.
  • A plain‑English summary that explains the impact of each variable on the final valuation.

The portal also offers real‑time progress tracking. As the AI processes each scenario, a progress bar shows the status, and once complete, the user can export a CSV or PDF report that includes the scenario breakdown. These exports respect the new export logic (fix(export): an empty id selection exports nothing, not the whole scope), ensuring that only the intended data is shared. Good 409a valuation keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

Under the Hood

The scenario engine is a microservice written in Python, orchestrated by NestJS and TypeScript on the backend. PostgreSQL stores the base valuation data, while Redis caches intermediate calculations for speed. The AI component, powered by OpenRouter, applies natural‑language prompts to refine assumptions and verify that scenario parameters stay within realistic bounds.

Security and compliance are baked in: each request carries a unique ID (fix(errors): every response carries its request id), and logs are enriched with that ID for audit trails (fix(observability): route code logs with the request id). These features make the scenario outputs ready for audit defense.

Why It Matters

Scenario analysis turns a static valuation into a dynamic decision tool. Founders can now: Treat 409a valuation as a habit rather than a one-off task.

  • Quickly see how a 10% change in revenue growth affects FMV.
  • Communicate clearly with investors by showing a range of outcomes.
  • Meet 409A compliance requirements with documented, AI‑verified assumptions.

By automating the calculation of multiple scenarios, N409 reduces manual effort, lowers the risk of human error, and provides a transparent audit trail—all critical for startups managing equity compensation.

Live Demo

Try the feature yourself at https://n409.aiknol.com. The open‑source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/r2st/N409.

1. Decoupling the Monolith: Edge-Rendered Micro-Frontends

Traditional monolith web applications bundle routing, data fetching, state management, and heavy styling runtimes into massive JavaScript bundles that delay the browser's critical rendering path.

title: Nowcasting aerosol particle size distributions from PM2.5 with physics-regularized flow matching
description:
arXiv:2610.33557v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The mass concentration of particles smaller than 2.5um (PM2.5) is cheap to measure and widely monitored, whereas the particle number size distribution (PSD) requires costly instruments and is measured at only a few research stations. Yet many aerosol effects, such as vapor uptake, cloud droplet formation and deposition in the human respiratory tract, depend on the PSD rather than on mass. We explore whether recent generative deep learning models can nowcast the PSD: from the PM2.5 record and eight meteorological parameters over a 24h window, a model generates an ensemble of plausible hourly size distributions for the same window, reflecting that one mass can arise from many size distributions. Rather than proposing a single best model, we use two contrasting Finnish stations, the boreal forest site Hyyti\"al\"a and the urban site Kumpula, as a controlled testbed. On it, we benchmark six generative models against deterministic and climatological baselines, locally and after transfer between sites, and test physical constraints for neural network training. Flow matching performs best overall; its guided variant has the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at both sites. A constraint based on a reduced aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE) lowers the CRPS by 5.5-11.5% at the training site and reduces errors after transfer between sites. Transfer remains harder than local estimation, identifying training on large multi-station data sets as the next step towards PSD estimates at unmonitored locations. This benchmark establishes physics-informed generative models as a promising route from routine air-quality monitoring to size-resolved aerosol information.

title: The 10 Best New CSS Features in 2026 Already Supported in All Major Browsers
description:
CSS has evolved far beyond styling colors, spacing, and layouts. Modern CSS can respond to a component's available space, react to elements inside a selector, generate more consistent color palettes, improve typography, and handle UI behavior that once required JavaScript.

But there is an important distinction: a feature being available in 2026 does not mean it was invented in 2026, or that every browser version supports it.

In this updated guide, we'll look at ten practical groups of CSS features worth knowing in 2026, including several from my 2025 CSS roundup. We'll also explore three newer capabilities that deserve attention but should be introduced progressively.

The support notes use Web Platform Baseline and current MDN documentation. Baseline is a useful starting point for cross-browser decisions, but it doesn't guarantee compatibility with older browsers, embedded webviews, or every detail of a feature.

Let's get into it.

1. Container Queries: Make Components Responsive to Their Own Space

Traditional media queries respond to the viewport. That's useful for page layouts, but it can become awkward when the same component appears in different places.

Imagine a product card used in a full-width grid, a narrow sidebar, and a mobile layout. A viewport media query tells the card how wide the screen is, not how much room the card actually has.

Container queries solve this problem by letting a component respond to its container's size.

.product-card {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.product-card__content {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
}

@container (min-width: 34rem) {
  .product-card__content {
    grid-template-columns: 9rem 1fr;
    align-items: center;
  }
}

The card's content switches to a two-column layout when the container becomes wide enough. The same component can now work in different layouts without relying on viewport-specific breakpoints.

This is especially useful for reusable components in design systems, dashboards, product grids, and component-driven React applications.

Why it matters: You can make components more independent of the page layout in which they are used.

Browser support: Container size queries are widely available in modern browsers. See MDN's container queries guide.

2. Container Style Queries: Let Components React to Their Context

Size queries ask, "How much space does my container have?"

Style queries ask a different question: "What styling context does my container provide?"

For example, a component might need a different appearance when its parent declares a dark theme or a compact layout. Container style queries can check a custom property on the container and apply styles to its descendants.

.theme-context {
  --theme: dark;
}

@container style(--theme: dark) {
  .card {
    background: #111827;
    color: #f9fafb;
    border-color: #374151;
  }
}

Here, the .card can react to the value of --theme on an ancestor container rather than requiring JavaScript to attach another class to every card.

You can use the same principle for design-system variants, compact components, and other context-dependent styling decisions.

One important detail: style queries can use custom properties, but their support and syntax should still be checked against the browser versions your application targets.

Why it matters: CSS can express more component-level styling rules without making every variation a JavaScript-managed state.

Browser support: Container style queries became Baseline Newly Available in 2026. That makes them worth learning, but older browser versions may not support them. See MDN.

3. The :has() Selector: CSS Can React to Descendants

For a long time, styling an element based on what it contained often meant adding a class with JavaScript.

The :has() pseudo-class gives CSS a way to select an element based on matching descendants or related elements.

For example, you can highlight an entire form group when one of its inputs is invalid:

.form-group:has(input:invalid) {
  border: 1px solid crimson;
  background: #fff5f5;
}

.card:has(img) {
  padding: 0;
  overflow: hidden;
}

The first selector reacts to the state of an input inside the form group. The second changes a card's layout when it contains an image.

You can also combine :has() with other selectors to build more expressive UI rules:

.form-group:has(input:focus-visible) label {
  color: #6d28d9;
}

This is useful for forms, navigation, selected cards, and UI states that can be described through the DOM.

There is one limitation worth remembering: :has() doesn't replace all JavaScript state management. Use JavaScript when the behavior involves application logic, asynchronous data, or state that cannot be inferred reliably from the document.

Why it matters: It reduces the need for extra classes and DOM-manipulation code when the desired style depends on element relationships.

Browser support: :has() is widely available in modern browsers. It was also one of the most-used features in the State of CSS 2026 survey.

4. CSS Nesting, Cascade Layers, and :where(): Keep Large Stylesheets Manageable

CSS projects become difficult to maintain when component rules are scattered throughout a stylesheet, specificity keeps increasing, and third-party styles conflict with application styles.

Three established features can help: native CSS nesting, cascade layers, and the :where() selector.

Native CSS nesting

You can group related selectors inside a parent rule:

.card {
  border: 1px solid #e5e7eb;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
  overflow: hidden;

  .card__title {
    font-size: 1.25rem;
    font-weight: 700;
  }

  &:hover {
    box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / 10%);
  }
}

The card's title and hover styles now live beside the styles they belong to. This is built into CSS, so a preprocessor such as Sass is not required just to nest selectors.

Cascade layers

Use @layer to define a deliberate order for your stylesheet:

@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer base {
  :where(h1, h2, h3) {
    line-height: 1.15;
  }
}

@layer components {
  .button {
    padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
    border-radius: 0.5rem;
  }
}

@layer utilities {
  .text-red {
    color: crimson;
  }
}

For normal declarations, later named layers take precedence over earlier layers, regardless of selector specificity. There is an important caveat: normal declarations outside named layers take precedence over normal layered declarations. For predictable results, plan how your project uses layered and unlayered styles.

Reduce specificity with :where()

The :where() pseudo-class has zero specificity:

:where(.button, .link) {
  border-radius: 0.5rem;
  text-decoration: none;
}

This makes it useful for resets, default styles, and shared design-system rules that should be easy to override.

Why it matters: These features help make CSS easier to read, organize, and maintain as a project grows.

Browser support: CSS nesting, cascade layers, and :where() are widely available in modern browsers. See MDN's CSS nesting documentation and cascade layers guide.

5. Better Typography: text-wrap, font-size-adjust, and Ruby Layout

Good typography is more than choosing a font. Line breaks, fallback fonts, and annotations can all affect readability.

Balance headings with text-wrap: balance

A heading can look awkward when a single word is left on its own line. text-wrap: balance asks the browser to distribute text across lines more evenly.

h1,
h2,
h3 {
  text-wrap: balance;
}

It's especially useful for titles, hero headings, and short text blocks. Avoid applying it indiscriminately to every long paragraph: balancing text has a computational cost, and browsers limit how many lines they balance.

Improve paragraph wrapping with text-wrap: pretty

For longer text, text-wrap: pretty asks the browser to favor more pleasing line breaks, including reducing awkward short final lines.

.article-content {
  text-wrap: pretty;
}

It's a useful enhancement for blogs, documentation, and editorial websites. However, support for this value varies more than support for text-wrap: balance, so test the browsers your readers use.

Keep fallback fonts more consistent with font-size-adjust

When a preferred font is unavailable or hasn't loaded, the fallback may have very different lowercase letter proportions.

body {
  font-family: "MyWebFont", Arial, sans-serif;
  font-size-adjust: 0.52;
}

The value is only an example; choose one appropriate to your intended font metrics. This property adjusts font sizing to help preserve visual proportions when different fonts are rendered.

Use Ruby layout for annotated text

For languages and learning materials that use ruby annotations, such as Japanese furigana, the ruby-align and ruby-position properties can provide more control.

ruby {
  ruby-align: center;
  ruby-position: over;
}

This is a specialized feature rather than a universal requirement, but it is valuable for multilingual education and reference content.

Why it matters: These properties make it possible to improve readability and text layout with less manual adjustment.

Browser support: text-wrap is broadly available, but individual values can differ in support. font-size-adjust and Ruby layout properties are also available in current browsers; check their precise compatibility before relying on a particular value. Useful references: text-wrap, font-size-adjust, and ruby-position.

6. More Stable Layouts and Faster Long Pages: aspect-ratio and content-visibility

Two features can make visual content more predictable and reduce unnecessary rendering work.

Reserve the right shape with aspect-ratio

When an image container has a known aspect ratio, the browser can reserve the correct space before the image is displayed.

.thumbnail {
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.thumbnail img {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
}

This is handy for video thumbnails, product images, article cards, and galleries. Consistent dimensions help keep surrounding content from jumping around.

Skip unnecessary rendering work with content-visibility

Long pages often contain large sections that are far outside the visible area. content-visibility: auto allows the browser to skip much of the rendering work for off-screen content until it becomes relevant.

.article-section {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 42rem;
}

The intrinsic size provides a placeholder estimate so the browser can account for the section's space while its contents are not being rendered normally.

This can help with long articles, large repeated lists, and other pages with expensive off-screen content. It's not a substitute for measuring performance, though: choose a sensible placeholder size and test scrolling, anchor links, and layout stability with realistic content.

Why it matters: aspect-ratio helps create predictable layouts, while content-visibility can reduce work on pages with a lot of content.

Browser support: Both features are widely available in modern browsers. References: aspect-ratio and content-visibility.

7. Modern Color: oklch(), color-mix(), light-dark(), and Relative Colors

Color management is another area where CSS has become considerably more capable.

Use oklch() for more controlled color palettes

oklch() represents a color using perceptual lightness, chroma, and hue. This can make it easier to generate coherent variants of a brand color than manually guessing a collection of unrelated hex values.

:root {
  --brand: oklch(62% 0.2 255);
}

Changing the lightness while keeping chroma and hue stable can produce more consistent visual variations, although the resulting color should still be checked for gamut and contrast.

Mix colors with color-mix() 

.button {
  background: var(--brand);
}

.button:hover {
  background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand) 85%, white);
}

This lets you generate color variations in CSS rather than maintaining a separate hard-coded value for every state.

Support light and dark themes with light-dark() 

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;

  --surface: light-dark(#ffffff, #171717);
  --text: light-dark(#171717, #f5f5f5);
}

body {
  background: var(--surface);
  color: var(--text);
}

The color-scheme declaration tells the browser that the page supports both schemes. light-dark() then chooses a value based on the active color scheme.

Derive colors from an existing color

Relative color syntax lets you create a new color from an existing one:

:root {
  --brand: oklch(62% 0.2 255);
  --brand-light: oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l + 0.12) c h);
}

Here, the lightness is increased while chroma and hue are retained. The exact result still depends on the source color and the target color space.

Why it matters: These features help build consistent themes and interactive color states with fewer duplicated values.

Browser support: oklch(), color-mix(), and light-dark() are available in current mainstream browsers. Relative color syntax should be checked for the browser versions you support. Always test color contrast rather than assuming that a perceptually uniform color space guarantees accessibility. References: OKLCH and color functions, light-dark(), and relative colors.

8. Better Forms with field-sizing and accent-color

Form controls are essential to most applications, but custom styling can become complicated when developers rebuild native inputs from scratch.

Two properties offer simpler alternatives.

Let fields size themselves around their content 

.comment-box {
  field-sizing: content;
  min-height: 3rem;
  max-height: 14rem;
  width: 100%;
}

On a supported browser, a textarea can grow or shrink with its content instead of remaining at a fixed preferred size. Minimum and maximum constraints help keep it usable.

<textarea
  class="comment-box"
  rows="2"
  placeholder="Write a comment..."
></textarea>

This can reduce the need for JavaScript that measures text and updates the field's height.

Match native controls to your theme 

input[type="checkbox"],
input[type="radio"],
input[type="range"] {
  accent-color: #7c3aed;
}

This changes the accent color of supported native controls while preserving their standard behavior. For many forms, that's a better starting point than hiding native inputs and recreating their appearance and interactions manually.

Why it matters: Native form controls can look more consistent with your design while retaining familiar behavior and accessibility features.

Browser support: accent-color is widely supported. field-sizing became Baseline Newly Available in 2026, so it may not work on older browser versions. Keep the default field behavior usable as a fallback. References: field-sizing and accent-color.

9. More Declarative UI with :open, Exclusive Accordions, and Popovers

HTML already provides useful building blocks for interactive interfaces. Modern CSS and browser features make it easier to style these controls without implementing every state from scratch.

Style open elements with :open 

details:open > summary {
  color: #7c3aed;
  font-weight: 700;
}

The :open pseudo-class can select elements in an open state, including relevant details and dialog elements.

For a straightforward disclosure widget, the traditional attribute selector is also a useful fallback:

details[open] > summary {
  color: #7c3aed;
}

Create exclusive accordions with native HTML

When only one item in an accordion group should stay open, the name attribute on <details> can provide that behavior without a custom JavaScript controller.

<details name="faq">
  <summary>What is container querying?</summary>
  <p>It lets a component respond to its container's size.</p>
</details>

<details name="faq">
  <summary>What is CSS nesting?</summary>
  <p>It lets related selectors be written inside a parent rule.</p>
</details>

Give the related <details> elements the same name value to place them in the same exclusive group.

Use the Popover API for simple overlays 

<button popovertarget="help-panel">
  Open help
</button>

<div id="help-panel" popover>
  <p>Helpful information goes here.</p>
</div>

The browser handles showing and hiding the popover through the built-in HTML behavior. An automatically dismissed popover can close when the user clicks outside it or presses Escape, depending on its configuration.

The Popover API is not a replacement for a modal dialog in every situation. A modal has different focus and interaction requirements; use <dialog> and its appropriate behavior when a truly modal interaction is needed.

Why it matters: Native HTML behavior can replace fragile custom interaction code, while CSS handles the appearance of each state.

Browser support: :open became Baseline Newly Available in 2026. The Popover API is available in current major browsers, but version support differs. For older targets, use the appropriate fallback or keep the essential interaction independent of the newer selector. References: :open, HTML <details>, and Popover API.

10. Small Improvements That Make Interfaces Feel More Polished

Not every useful CSS feature transforms an entire architecture. Sometimes, a tiny improvement solves a persistent UX problem.

Prevent scrollbar-related layout shifts 

.scroll-panel {
  overflow: auto;
  scrollbar-gutter: stable;
}

On systems that use classic scrollbars, reserving the gutter can help prevent content from shifting when a scrollbar appears. Overlay scrollbars behave differently, so the visible result depends on the platform.

Style the scrollbar 

.scroll-panel {
  scrollbar-color: #64748b #e2e8f0;
}

This sets the thumb and track colors in browsers that support scrollbar-color. Keep adequate contrast and avoid making the scrollbar difficult to see or operate.

Highlight text reached through a text fragment 

::target-text {
  background: #fef08a;
  color: #111827;
}

When a supported text-fragment link navigates to a specific part of a page, ::target-text lets you style the matched text. This can be helpful for documentation and long articles.

Keep ruby annotations readable

For text that uses ruby annotations, ruby-align and ruby-position provide finer control over alignment and placement. These are especially useful for Japanese learning materials and similar content, rather than a requirement for most websites.

Why it matters: These improvements refine usability, navigation, and content presentation without requiring a larger JavaScript framework.

Browser support: scrollbar-gutter and font-size-adjust are Baseline 2024 features, while scrollbar-color and ::target-text became Baseline Newly Available in later cycles. Ruby properties also have broad support in current browsers, but individual values can vary. See scrollbar-gutter, scrollbar-color, and ::target-text.

Three More Capabilities to Adopt Progressively

The ten groups above cover many practical improvements. Three additional capabilities are worth experimenting with, but they deserve more care when supporting a broad range of browsers.

11. CSS Anchor Positioning: Position UI Relative to Another Element

Tooltips, menus, and small popovers often need to stay attached to a trigger button. Traditionally, developers used JavaScript to measure element positions and update them during scrolling or resizing.

CSS Anchor Positioning lets a positioned element refer to another element through an anchor relationship.

.trigger {
  anchor-name: --help-trigger;
}

.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --help-trigger;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  margin-top: 0.5rem;
}

This is a simplified example of the relationship; real interfaces may also need fallbacks for collisions with the viewport or other layout constraints.

Some anchor-positioning capabilities reached Baseline Newly Available during 2026, but support for the wider set of positioning and fallback behaviors is not identical across all browsers. Don't assume that one supported declaration guarantees all the advanced behavior you want.

For production use, provide a sensible fallback and feature-detect the functionality you rely on:

.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  top: 100%;
  left: 0;
}

@supports (position-anchor: --help-trigger) {
  .tooltip {
    position-anchor: --help-trigger;
    top: anchor(bottom);
    left: anchor(left);
  }
}

Best use cases: Tooltips, dropdown menus, contextual labels, and other UI elements positioned relative to a trigger.

Support note: Check the precise feature and browser versions using MDN's anchor-positioning documentation before replacing a mature positioning library.

12. Scroll-Driven Animations: Let Scrolling Control the Animation

Traditional CSS animations progress with time. Scroll-driven animations can tie an animation's progress to scrolling or to an element entering the viewport.

For example, you can enhance a content-reveal effect without making it a requirement for the page to work:

.reveal {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: none;
}

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  .reveal {
    animation: reveal linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 40%;
  }

  @keyframes reveal {
    from {
      opacity: 0;
      transform: translateY(1rem);
    }

    to {
      opacity: 1;
      transform: translateY(0);
    }
  }
}

The normal state remains visible when the browser doesn't support scroll-driven animation timelines. Supported browsers receive the additional effect.

Use motion thoughtfully. Animations should help users understand changes rather than distract them, and you should consider reduced-motion preferences.

Best use cases: Reading-progress indicators, subtle content reveals, scroll-linked visual effects, and other experiences that benefit from a scroll-based timeline.

Support note: Scroll-driven animations remain a feature to adopt progressively. Check MDN's documentation and use feature detection.

13. transition-behavior: allow-discrete: Transition Properties Such as display

Not every CSS property can interpolate smoothly between two values. Properties with discrete values, such as display, normally switch from one value to another rather than gradually changing.

The transition-behavior property adds an allow-discrete option for certain discrete transitions:

.panel {
  transition:
    opacity 200ms,
    display 200ms allow-discrete;
}

.panel.is-hidden {
  opacity: 0;
  display: none;
}

This can be useful when combining visibility changes with opacity transitions. Entry animations from display: none often need additional setup, such as @starting-style; consult the relevant documentation rather than assuming the simple example covers every case.

Best use cases: Small UI transitions where content appears or disappears, including some popover and panel effects.

Support note: transition-behavior is not yet Baseline across all major browsers. Keep the basic show/hide functionality working without it. See MDN's transition-behavior reference.

A Related Platform Feature: The Navigation API

The 2026 research also covers the Navigation API. It is worth knowing about, but it is a JavaScript web API, not a CSS feature, so it shouldn't be presented as another CSS property.

The Navigation API provides browser navigation events and methods that can simplify certain client-side routing implementations. Whether it's a good fit depends on your routing architecture, browser targets, and framework.

For a broader look, see MDN's Navigation API documentation.

How to Use These Features in Production

Learning a new property is only half the job. The other half is deciding when to use it and how to handle browsers that don't support it.

1. Start with the support status

Web Platform Baseline distinguishes widely available features, newly available features, and features with limited availability.

  • Widely available: A good starting point for most new projects, while still considering your actual browser targets.
  • Newly available: Supported in recent Baseline browsers, but older browser releases may lack support.
  • Limited availability: Use feature detection or a fallback when the feature matters to your design.

Baseline is a compatibility signal, not a guarantee that every user will see identical results. Older devices, embedded webviews, assistive technology, and specific feature details may require additional testing.

Read the official Baseline overview.

2. Prefer progressive enhancement

Start with a working interface. Add the advanced behavior only when the browser supports it.

For CSS, @supports is often enough:

.card {
  padding: 1rem;
}

@supports (container-type: inline-size) {
  .card {
    container-type: inline-size;
  }
}

The fallback should preserve essential readability and functionality. A visual enhancement shouldn't make the entire component unusable when it's unavailable.

3. Measure performance instead of assuming

A feature can reduce code without automatically improving performance in every situation. content-visibility, for example, is most helpful when it avoids work on substantial off-screen content. Adding it everywhere without measuring can lead to disappointing results.

Test actual workloads using browser developer tools and realistic content. Pay attention to rendering, scrolling, input responsiveness, and layout shifts.

4. Avoid JavaScript when CSS or native HTML already solves the problem

You don't need JavaScript for every visual state. Container queries can handle component sizing, :has() can respond to DOM relationships, and native controls can provide useful behavior without custom event handlers.

But CSS isn't a replacement for application logic. Keep state, validation rules, data fetching, and other complex interactions in the parts of your application that are designed to manage them.

title: One Meta App, Many Businesses: Routing WhatsApp Webhooks in a Multi-Tenant SaaS
description:
If you build a WhatsApp product for other businesses, every customer's events arrive at the same place: one Meta app has one webhook callback URL and one app secret, so all of your tenants share an endpoint. Multi-tenancy is something you add on your side. Resolve the tenant from the IDs Meta sends, metadata.phone_number_id first and the WABA ID in entry[].id when that's all there is. Park anything you can't match instead of guessing, process each change on its own, and scope every query by tenant from then on. This post covers the routing, plus the onboarding and offboarding events that keep your tenant table true.

The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases shown.

One endpoint, everyone's events

When a business connects through your app, its WhatsApp Business Account (WABA) is subscribed to your app, and from then on its events are sent to your app's callback URL. A webhook looks like this:

{
  "object": "whatsapp_business_account",
  "entry": [
    {
      "id": "<WABA_ID>",
      "changes": [
        {
          "field": "messages",
          "value": {
            "messaging_product": "whatsapp",
            "metadata": { "display_phone_number": "15550100001", "phone_number_id": "<PHONE_NUMBER_ID>" },
            "messages": [{ "id": "wamid...", "from": "15550123456", "type": "text", "text": { "body": "Hi" } }]
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Three facts shape everything else:

  • entry and changes are arrays. Meta's webhook endpoint guide says requests are "aggregated and sent in a batch with a maximum of 1000 updates", and also that "batching cannot be guaranteed". Loop over both, every time.
  • The signature isn't per tenant. The same guide says the X-Hub-Signature-256 hash is calculated with "your app secret as the secret key". You verify every tenant's webhooks with one secret, before you know whose they are. (We covered verification in handling webhooks in Node.js.)
  • Retries repeat events. Failed deliveries are "retried immediately, then a few more times with decreasing frequency over the next 7 days", and Meta's webhooks overview warns that "These retries can result in duplicate webhook notifications".

Resolve the tenant from Meta's IDs, and nothing else

Every change has to become a tenant ID before any business logic runs. The order matters:

  1. metadata.phone_number_id, when the change has one. Messages, statuses and calls carry it, and it identifies exactly one business number.
  2. The WABA ID, for account-level changes that have no phone number ID. That's usually entry[].id, but Meta's docs only state it for some events, and account_update names the account in value.waba_info.waba_id, with a different ID in entry.id. Log a few live payloads and check yours.
  3. Nothing else. Not the customer's phone number, not a display name, and never a tenant ID from a query string you added to the callback URL.

Account-level changes are the awkward part. The phone number quality update (phone_number_quality_update), which also reports messaging-limit changes, carries the WABA ID and a display_phone_number directly on value, but no metadata and no phone_number_id. If a WABA holds more than one of your numbers, narrow by that display number. If it still isn't one tenant, stop:

// Map one webhook change to the tenant that owns it, using only IDs Meta sent.
export type NumberRecord = { tenantId: string; wabaId: string; phoneNumberId: string; displayPhone: string; active: boolean };

export type Resolution = { tenantId: string; phoneNumberId: string | null } | { unknown: string };

const digits = (value: string) => value.replace(/\D/g, "");

export const resolveTenant = (
  numbers: NumberRecord[],
  wabaId: string,
  metadata?: { phone_number_id?: string; display_phone_number?: string },
): Resolution => {
  const live = numbers.filter((n) => n.active);

  // Most changes carry the business number: the most specific key there is.
  if (metadata?.phone_number_id) {
    const match = live.find((n) => n.phoneNumberId === metadata.phone_number_id);
    return match ? { tenantId: match.tenantId, phoneNumberId: match.phoneNumberId } : { unknown: `number ${metadata.phone_number_id}` };
  }

  // Account-level changes only name the WABA.
  const inWaba = live.filter((n) => n.wabaId === wabaId);
  if (inWaba.length === 0) return { unknown: `WABA ${wabaId}` };
  if (inWaba.length === 1) return { tenantId: inWaba[0].tenantId, phoneNumberId: inWaba[0].phoneNumberId };

  // Several numbers in one WABA: narrow by the formatted display number, if sent.
  const wanted = digits(metadata?.display_phone_number ?? "");
  const byDisplay = wanted ? inWaba.filter((n) => digits(n.displayPhone) === wanted) : [];
  if (byDisplay.length === 1) return { tenantId: byDisplay[0].tenantId, phoneNumberId: byDisplay[0].phoneNumberId };

  const tenants = new Set(inWaba.map((n) => n.tenantId));
  return tenants.size === 1 ? { tenantId: inWaba[0].tenantId, phoneNumberId: null } : { unknown: `ambiguous WABA ${wabaId}` };
};

Two cases from the tests are worth calling out:

  • A reconnected number. A business deletes its account with you, then connects the same number under a new account. Both tenant records hold the same phone_number_id, so only active records may match, or the new owner's messages land in the old owner's inbox.
  • An unknown number isn't guessed from its WABA. If the phone number ID isn't in your table, don't fall back to "whoever owns this WABA". That's how one tenant's number ends up feeding another tenant's inbox.

Park unknown events; don't create tenants from them

It's tempting to auto-create an account when a webhook arrives for a number you've never seen, so messages "just work" before setup finishes. In a multi-tenant system, that creates a tenant nobody owns, holding real customers' messages, with no user who can see them and nothing tying it to a signup. Park the event instead: store it with the reason, alert on it, and replay it once the connection is complete. Unknown events are normal in a few situations, such as the seconds between a subscription and your own database write, or a tenant who has just left.

Process each change on its own

One POST can carry events for several tenants. If a bug in one tenant's handler throws and you answer the whole request with a 500, Meta retries the whole batch, and every other tenant gets their events again. So acknowledge after the signature check, then process each change separately, with a deduplication claim in front:

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { resolveTenant, type NumberRecord } from "./resolve-tenant.ts";

type Change = { field: string; value: Record<string, any> & { metadata?: { phone_number_id?: string; display_phone_number?: string } } };
type Payload = { object: string; entry: { id: string; changes: Change[] }[] };

export type Deps = {
  numbers: () => Promise<NumberRecord[]>;
  claim: (key: string) => Promise<boolean>;
  handle: (tenantId: string, phoneNumberId: string | null, change: Change) => Promise<void>;
  park: (reason: string, wabaId: string, change: Change) => Promise<void>;
};

// Duplicate deliveries hash to the same key, so a retried change is skipped.
const changeKey = (wabaId: string, change: Change) =>
  createHash("sha256").update(JSON.stringify([wabaId, change.field, change.value])).digest("hex");

// account_update names the WABA in waba_info; entry.id can be a different ID there.
const wabaIdOf = (entryId: string, change: Change): string => change.value.waba_info?.waba_id ?? entryId;

// Called after the signature check and the 200. Never throws: one tenant's
// failure must not fail, or replay, another tenant's events.
export const processBatch = async (body: Payload, deps: Deps) => {
  const result = { handled: 0, duplicates: 0, parked: 0, failed: 0 };
  if (body.object !== "whatsapp_business_account") return result;
  const numbers = await deps.numbers();

  for (const entry of body.entry) {
    for (const change of entry.changes) {
      try {
        if (!(await deps.claim(changeKey(entry.id, change)))) {
          result.duplicates++;
          continue;
        }
        const owner = resolveTenant(numbers, wabaIdOf(entry.id, change), {
          phone_number_id: change.value.metadata?.phone_number_id,
          // Account-level changes put the display number on `value` itself.
          display_phone_number: change.value.metadata?.display_phone_number ?? change.value.display_phone_number,
        });
        if ("unknown" in owner) {
          await deps.park(owner.unknown, entry.id, change);
          result.parked++;
          continue;
        }
        await deps.handle(owner.tenantId, owner.phoneNumberId, change);
        result.handled++;
      } catch {
        result.failed++;
      }
    }
  }
  return result;
};

Note wabaIdOf: for account_update, the WABA ID comes from waba_info. The claim key is a hash of the change, which catches whole-batch redeliveries. In production, also dedupe on the IDs inside the change, such as message IDs, and record failures somewhere you can replay them from, because once you've answered 200, Meta won't send that change again.

Scope every query by tenant

After routing, the tenant ID has to follow the event into every read and write. Tenancy enforced only in application code fails the first time someone writes Contact.findOne({ where: { phone } }) without it. Make the unscoped query the hard one to write: give handlers a data handle that's already bound to a tenant.

// Every read and write goes through a handle bound to one tenant.
type Row = { tenantId: string; [key: string]: unknown };

export const forTenant = <T extends Row>(table: T[], tenantId: string) => ({
  find: (where: Partial<T> = {}) =>
    table.filter((row) => row.tenantId === tenantId && Object.entries(where).every(([k, v]) => row[k] === v)),
  insert: (row: Omit<T, "tenantId">) => {
    const stored = { ...row, tenantId } as T;
    table.push(stored);
    return stored;
  },
});

In a real database this is a repository or query helper that adds WHERE tenant_id = ? to every query, or row-level security in Postgres. The test that matters is the negative one: a handle for one tenant must return nothing, and write nothing, for another.

Onboarding: subscribe each account, and check it worked

With Embedded Signup, the browser gets a code that Meta's implementation guide says "has a time-to-live of 30 seconds", so exchange it on your server straight away for a business integration system user access token. Store that token per tenant, encrypted. The Tech Provider onboarding guide then has you subscribe your app to the customer's account and register their phone number.

The subscription is per account. Meta's webhook management guide says you "must individually subscribe to every Messaging account":

curl -X POST "https://graph.facebook.com/<VERSION>/<WABA_ID>/subscribed_apps" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BUSINESS_TOKEN"

# Confirm your app is listed
curl "https://graph.facebook.com/<VERSION>/<WABA_ID>/subscribed_apps" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BUSINESS_TOKEN"

Treat a failed subscription as a failed connection. If you log it and carry on, the tenant sees a connected number that can send but never receives a reply, which looks like a WhatsApp outage, not a setup error.

Offboarding: listen for account_update

Tenants leave from Meta's side too: they uninstall your app or unshare their account in Business Manager. Make sure account_update is among the webhook fields you receive, and react to these events, as listed in Meta's account_update reference:

  • PARTNER_APP_UNINSTALLED: "a business customer deauthenticated or uninstalled the app".
  • PARTNER_REMOVED: the account "has been unshared with a Solution Partner".
  • ACCOUNT_DELETED: "the Messaging account was deleted". 
// What an account_update event means for the tenant's connection.
export type ConnectionChange = "disconnected" | "deleted" | "connected" | "no-change";

const EFFECT: Record<string, ConnectionChange> = {
  PARTNER_APP_UNINSTALLED: "disconnected",
  PARTNER_REMOVED: "disconnected",
  ACCOUNT_DELETED: "deleted",
  PARTNER_APP_INSTALLED: "connected",
  PARTNER_ADDED: "connected",
};

export const connectionChange = (value: { event?: string }): ConnectionChange =>
  EFFECT[value.event ?? ""] ?? "no-change";

On a disconnect, mark the tenant's numbers inactive, stop its scheduled sends, and tell its admins in the app. Without this, a departed tenant's campaigns keep failing with permission errors until someone notices.

Account-level webhooks such as account_update always go to your app's main callback URL; Meta's override guide doesn't allow them to be redirected. Per-account and per-number overrides are useful for pointing one test tenant at staging, as in testing webhooks outside production, but your production endpoint still has to handle these events.

Keep one tenant from slowing the rest

Meta's limits are set per customer, not per app: throughput is per phone number ("up to 80 messages per second (mps) by default", per the throughput guide), and messaging limits are "calculated and set at the business portfolio level". Your workers are shared. One tenant's 50,000-message campaign, and the status webhooks it generates, can sit in front of another tenant's single inbound message on a shared queue. Give inbound handling its own queue, separate from bulk sending, and partition bulk sends per tenant or per number so a big campaign can only slow itself down.

Checklist

  • Loop over every entry and every change; never assume one.
  • Verify the signature with the app secret before routing.
  • Route by phone_number_id, then by WABA ID (from waba_info on account_update), and only to active records.
  • Park unknown or ambiguous events; never create a tenant from a webhook.
  • Acknowledge, then process each change independently with a dedupe claim.
  • Bind every query to a tenant, and test that cross-tenant reads return nothing.
  • Exchange the Embedded Signup code at once, store the business token per tenant, and fail the connection if the subscription fails.
  • Subscribe to account_update and deactivate tenants that leave.
  • Keep inbound processing off the queue that carries bulk sends.

title: SageMaker MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16
description:
Amazon SageMaker AI MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16, bringing a redesigned tracing experience and faster experiment tracking to your generative AI and machine learning workflows.

MLflow 3.16 improves debugging and analysis of generative AI applications and agents.
