title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.36335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.

title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2610.36420v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

title: LLM API Cost: How Token Count Impacts Node.js Knowledge Retrieval
description:
The hard part of a private knowledge-base assistant is not making the prompt shorter. It is keeping a stable JSON contract while sending only the evidence that contract needs. Token count affects an LLM bill because providers charge for the input and output tokens processed by a call. My ship-first rule is to make retrieval own the context budget, then make the model adapter replaceable.

Short answer: normalize documents, retrieve with embeddings, rerank a small candidate set, and preserve whole evidence chunks until a measured token limit. Keep the answer shape independent of the provider. A shorter request that loses a source ID or a version qualifier is a cheaper failure, not a cost reduction.

How does token count impact LLM API cost in a knowledge base?

A normal support question can carry a system instruction, the question, conversation history, retrieved passages, and the requested output. Input tokens accumulate before generation starts; output tokens accumulate after it does. Long context and unbounded prose therefore push the bill in opposite directions. The practical fix has two sides: reduce irrelevant input and put a ceiling on the response.

I initially treated truncation as a string operation. That is the wrong boundary for developer documentation. Cutting at 2,000 characters can remove the exception from a rule, split a code sample, or leave a function name without its version note. Keep chunk boundaries intact, and let a validator reject an answer whose sources do not refer to selected chunks.

The target object can stay small:

type KnowledgeAnswer = {
  answer: string;
  sources: string[];
  needs_human_review: boolean;
};

That object is useful across providers because it describes the application decision, not a vendor feature. It also gives cost work a non-negotiable test: fewer tokens count only if the object remains valid and the cited evidence still supports the answer.

What should the retrieval pipeline own?

Use embeddings for the broad search step. They keep the full candidate corpus out of the chat request, which is where irrelevant text becomes processed input. Rerank the candidates before generation when ordering is uncertain; Cohere's Rerank documentation describes that boundary clearly. Reranking improves selection order, but it does not create the final answer or prove that its citations are correct.

For a first experiment, hold the answer schema and question set fixed. Try three retrieved chunks, then five, then eight. Record input tokens, output tokens, valid-object rate, and whether a reviewer can locate each answer in its source. Fifty representative questions is enough to expose obvious retrieval mistakes without pretending to be a universal benchmark. The runtime exposes /v1/ai/tokens/count, which can replace a rough local estimate once the request shape is known.

The selector below is intentionally conservative. It counts complete chunks and leaves room for the question, instructions, and output. The four-characters-per-token estimate is a guardrail, not a tokenizer; calibrate it before making it a hard production limit. I would start with the verified /v1/ai/tokens/count capability for that calibration, then compare the estimate with actual usage from the chosen model.

type Evidence = { id: string; text: string };

const estimateTokens = (text: string): number => Math.ceil(text.length / 4);

export function selectEvidence(
  question: string,
  chunks: Evidence[],
  totalTokenBudget: number,
): Evidence[] {
  const reserved = estimateTokens(question) + 180;
  const evidenceBudget = Math.max(0, totalTokenBudget - reserved);
  const selected: Evidence[] = [];
  let used = 0;

  for (const chunk of chunks) {
    const next = estimateTokens(chunk.text);
    if (used + next > evidenceBudget) break;
    selected.push(chunk);
    used += next;
  }

  return selected;
}

export function isKnowledgeAnswer(value: unknown): value is KnowledgeAnswer {
  if (!value || typeof value !== "object") return false;
  const candidate = value as Partial<KnowledgeAnswer>;
  return (
    typeof candidate.answer === "string" &&
    Array.isArray(candidate.sources) &&
    candidate.sources.every((source) => typeof source === "string") &&
    typeof candidate.needs_human_review === "boolean"
  );
}

Measure it.

The adapter can then call an OpenAI-compatible surface without making the rest of the retrieval code depend on that service. The retry is deliberately narrow: a 429 is retried with Retry-After, while a different status is surfaced to the caller.

import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY,
  baseURL: process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL,
});

export async function answerWithInfrai(
  question: string,
  evidence: Evidence[],
): Promise<KnowledgeAnswer> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
        model: "auto",
        temperature: 0,
        messages: [
          {
            role: "system",
            content:
              "Return JSON with answer, sources, and needs_human_review.",
          },
          { role: "user", content: JSON.stringify({ question, evidence }) },
        ],
        response_format: { type: "json_object" },
      });

      const raw = response.choices[0]?.message.content ?? "{}";
      const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(raw);
      if (!isKnowledgeAnswer(parsed)) throw new Error("Invalid answer contract");
      return parsed;
    } catch (error) {
      const status = (error as { status?: number }).status;
      if (status !== 429 || attempt === 2) throw error;
      const retryAfter = Number(
        (error as { headers?: { get?: (name: string) => string | null } })
          .headers?.get?.("retry-after"),
      );
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 2 ** attempt * 250;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    }
  }

  throw new Error("Retry limit reached");
}

The failure policy matters. If the best evidence chunk alone does not fit, route the question to a narrower document slice or human review. Do not silently chop the middle out of a procedure. For filtering or a moderation-like classification where no dedicated moderation endpoint is available, a chat model constrained by a narrow JSON schema can be a fallback; application-side validation still decides whether the result is usable.

Which provider boundary survives a model change?

This is where a simple prototype becomes an operational choice. OpenAI is a sensible fit when an existing Node.js application already depends on its client conventions. Anthropic is worth testing when its message-model behavior better matches the same evidence and contract. Cohere is particularly relevant before generation because reranking is its useful role in this pipeline. Gemini fits a team already committed to Google's model and tooling ecosystem. OpenRouter is useful for comparing providers behind one routing layer, but routing convenience does not replace structured-output evaluation.

Option Access Good fit Main trade-off
OpenAI SDK and API Existing OpenAI client conventions Provider-specific fields can leak into the application
Anthropic SDK and API A direct comparison of message-model behavior A separate client contract needs an adapter
Cohere API, especially reranking Retrieval-heavy pipelines Reranking does not generate or validate the final answer
Gemini SDK and API Teams already using Google's tooling Portability still needs an application-owned boundary
OpenRouter Routing API Comparing several model providers Routing does not prove structured-output correctness
Infrai OpenAI-compatible API Keeping the client boundary stable while backends change An additional platform dependency is unnecessary for a one-provider app

Those are real alternatives, with different reasons to choose them. The adapter should expose only answer(question, evidence) and return the application object above. Vendor-specific fields belong behind it. That keeps a change in model or backend from forcing a rewrite of retrieval, source tracking, and validation.

Infrai fits this boundary when the goal is to keep the application contract stable while the backend behind a capability changes. Its OpenAI-compatible surface lets an existing client shape remain familiar, while its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas without requiring a key. That is a developer-experience advantage during adapter work, not proof that every model will perform equally on a private corpus.

There is a second, different kind of friction. For Infrai, the practical advantage is one key, one bill: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, rather than making a small team collect credentials and reconcile separate backend accounts as the feature set grows. The discovery surface is public and self-describing, so an adapter can inspect request and response schemas before it needs a credential. Documented capabilities also include runnable examples in 10 languages, which can shorten an integration spike without changing the correctness test. The breadth is relevant only if the assistant later needs adjacent capabilities; a single-provider application with no migration pressure may have no reason to add that boundary. The trade-off is clear: a team that only needs one chat provider should choose the provider with the best evaluated behavior and skip the extra platform layer.

The limits should stay visible. The stated runtime snapshot lists audio transcription as unavailable, and voice-session access as pending in the western region. There is no dedicated moderation endpoint in the supplied capability facts, so schema-constrained chat is only a fallback for that job. None of this blocks a text knowledge-base assistant, but it does block assuming that the same adapter automatically covers every media workflow.

What should be measured before shipping?

Measure four things together: input tokens, output tokens, structured-object validity, and evidence-grounded accuracy. Add retrieval recall when labeled source passages exist. Log question IDs, selected chunk IDs, model choice, token counts, and validation results; avoid copying private document text into a cost dashboard merely to make it convenient.

The decision rule is narrow: choose the smallest evidence budget that preserves the answer contract and grounded accuracy on the fixed test set. If the object is valid but its source IDs no longer support the answer, retrieval is the problem. If the evidence is right but output grows, tighten the response schema and instructions. If a provider change requires edits outside the adapter, the contract boundary is too leaky.

Token reduction is therefore a systems decision. Prompt wording, embeddings, reranking, whole-chunk truncation, and concise JSON each affect a different part of the request. Count them, validate them, and keep the backend replaceable. That is how a private knowledge-base assistant becomes cheaper without making its answers harder to trust.

Sources

  • Cohere Rerank overview
  • OpenAI embeddings guide
  • Anthropic documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • OpenRouter documentation

title: Evolving to Match Capabilities: Improving Harness Self-Evolution via Skill Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.33024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.

title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
description:
arXiv:2610.33029v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.

524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.

567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.

The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.

158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.

VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.

title: Moving Years of Records Without Losing Them
description:
Migration is the part of a software project that gets a line in the plan and a third of the effort.

It is also where projects fail in the least visible way. A system goes live, everyone is pleased, and six weeks later someone tries to answer a question about last year and discovers the history is incomplete, or duplicated, or subtly wrong in a way that has been quietly informing decisions since launch.

The failure is rarely technical. Moving data between systems is a solved engineering problem. The difficulty is that years of accumulated records contain decisions, exceptions and inconsistencies that nobody documented, and migration is the first time anyone has to look at all of it at once.

What migration actually surfaces

The first honest run of any migration produces a list of problems that existed all along and were invisible because nothing forced them into the open.

The same entity recorded several ways. One customer as "Kumar Traders", "Kumar Traders." and "kumar traders" — three records, three balances, one business. Every operation with a few years of history has this, and nobody knows how many.

Fields used for something other than their name. A notes field holding delivery instructions. A reference field holding a second phone number. These conventions grew because the system lacked a place for something, and they are invisible until you try to map the field.

Records nobody can explain. Transactions with no counterpart, adjustments with no reason, entries from a person who left. Somebody has to decide what happens to them.

Balances that do not reconcile. Ledger totals that differ from the sum of transactions. Almost always present at some scale, and migration is when it becomes undeniable.

None of this is a reason to postpone. It is a reason to schedule properly, because every one of these needs a decision from someone in the business, not from whoever is writing the migration.

Decide what actually needs to move

The instinct is to move everything. It is usually wrong, and it is expensive.

Three categories, and they deserve different treatment:

Operational data — open orders, current stock, live customer balances, active records. This must move, must be complete, and must be correct on day one. The system cannot run without it.

Reference data — customers, suppliers, products, price lists. Must move, and is the category most needing cleaning first, because errors here propagate into everything.

Historical data — closed transactions from previous years. Must be accessible, not necessarily migrated. Frequently the better answer is to move a defined recent period and keep older records queryable in an export or the old system in read-only form.

That last distinction saves a great deal of money. Businesses ask for ten years of history and, in practice, look at eighteen months. Ask what questions people actually ask of old data before deciding to migrate all of it.

Clean before, not during

The temptation is to clean data as part of the migration. This produces a bad outcome, because the migration then has two jobs and its correctness becomes hard to verify.

The better sequence:

  1. Extract the current data as it is
  2. Profile it — duplicates, missing fields, inconsistent formats, orphans
  3. Decide the rules, with the business, not the developer
  4. Clean in the source or in a staging copy, with those decisions applied
  5. Migrate the cleaned data
  6. Reconcile against the original

Step three is the one that gets skipped, and it is the only one that requires the business. Whether two similar customer records are the same customer is not a technical question.

Reconciliation is the whole test

A migration is not finished when data has moved. It is finished when you have proved it moved correctly.

At minimum:

Counts. Number of customers, products, open orders, transactions in a period. They should match exactly, and where they do not, the difference should be explained rather than accepted.

Totals. Sum of outstanding receivables, stock valuation, ledger balances. These are the figures that will be noticed if wrong, and noticed late.

Spot checks on the awkward cases. Not random records — the difficult ones. The customer with a credit note and a partial payment. The product sold in two units. The order that was partly delivered. If those are right, the ordinary cases are almost certainly right.

Run reconciliation before switching off the old system, not after. This is the step that pressure removes from a timeline and the one that makes the difference.

Run both in parallel

For a short period, keep the old system updated alongside the new one and compare.

It duplicates effort for a few weeks and it is the cheapest insurance available. A gap discovered while both systems are live is a correction. The same gap discovered after the old system is decommissioned is a reconstruction from bank statements and memory.

This is the same principle as deploying location by location rather than switching everything at once, described in how Truffaire builds software.

What we have seen

Migration is consistently the largest source of timeline risk across the ten systems we have delivered — more than any technical requirement.

The specific pattern: a business estimates its data is broadly clean, the first extract shows several thousand near-duplicate entities, and resolving them requires decisions only the business can make, from people who are also doing their normal jobs.

The related finding is that undocumented spreadsheet logic is the hardest thing to migrate, because the rules live in formulas and in one person's judgement rather than in data. The real cost of running on spreadsheets covers why that logic is effectively the specification.

Where a business has clean, consistent records, migration is fast. That is rarer than most expect, and knowing which case you are in is worth establishing early.

Frequently asked questions

How long does migration take?

The extract and load are fast. Profiling, deciding cleaning rules and reconciling take the time, and they depend on your data rather than on the software. A first extract in week one tells you far more about the timeline than any estimate.

Can we migrate everything from day one?

You can, and it is often unnecessary. Operational and reference data must be complete. Historical data can frequently be accessible rather than migrated, which is faster and cheaper.

What if the old system will not export cleanly?

Ask this before buying anything, not at migration. Export capability is a purchasing criterion — a system whose data cannot leave in standard formats has a rising switching cost that becomes a negotiating position against you.

Who decides how to resolve duplicates?

The business, not the developer. Whether two similar records are one customer is a commercial judgement. The most useful preparation is naming who will make those calls before the work starts.

Should we clean the data first or move it first?

Clean first, in a staging copy, with rules the business agreed. Cleaning during migration makes it impossible to tell whether a discrepancy came from the data or the process.

Where to start

Do one thing before committing to any project: take a full export of your current data and look at it.

Count the customers. Sort them alphabetically and look for near-duplicates. Check whether every product has a consistent unit. Total the outstanding balances and compare against your ledger.

That afternoon of work will tell you more about the real timeline than any vendor estimate, and it moves the unpleasant discoveries to before the decision rather than after.

Migration is one component of a larger picture; what a business operating system actually is sets out the rest.

If you want help profiling what you have, get in touch.

title: From a Portrait to an Interactive TalkingHead: Persona, Knowledge, and Voice
description:
I work on Mugen3D at SumeruAI. We have been exploring a workflow that turns a portrait into a character people can talk with through text or voice. This post walks through the creator flow and the pieces a developer needs to think about when building a product around it.

The character workflow

In TalkingHead Studio, the flow starts with a portrait and then adds the interaction layer:

  1. Upload a portrait to define the character's appearance.
  2. Write a persona with the character's background, tone, and conversational goal.
  3. Add a knowledge document for topic-specific reference material.
  4. Choose a voice.
  5. Start a text or microphone conversation and review how the character responds.

The persona and knowledge document serve different purposes. The persona shapes how the character communicates; the document supplies reference material for what it can discuss. A history guide might use curated sources, while a product guide might use FAQs. In either case, the material should be organized and the answers should be tested. A document upload does not guarantee factual responses.

Voice and interaction design

Text is useful for quick prompts and review. Voice can make the character feel more conversational, but it adds practical questions: how long does a response take, how does the UI show that it is listening or speaking, and what happens when speech recognition or playback fails?

Voice, persona, and knowledge content should be tested together. The same answer can feel quite different depending on the voice and speaking animation. For a useful prototype, I would start with one clear role and a small set of reference material, then test whether people can understand what the character can and cannot do.

What the developer integration covers

There are two related parts: creating a TalkingHead asset from a photo, and embedding a rendered character in your own product. The Mugen3D API page describes photo-to-TalkingHead generation as an asynchronous job with a result callback. The public API docs are the source for the current request fields and job details.

For the browser runtime, the TalkingHead Web SDK repository includes a demo, a minimal integration example, avatar rendering helpers, local workers, and audio-driven facial animation. Its example flow is to get an access token, load a hosted avatar model, and pass a WAV file to the audio-driven facial animation helper. The SDK covers avatar rendering and facial drive; your application still needs its own conversation interface and any retrieval or product logic unless you choose a service that provides those pieces.

Keep API credentials on your server. For a longer-running generation task, keep the task ID, show processing, completed, and failed states, and preserve useful error details so the user can recover after refreshing the page. The repository's minimal example and developer guide show the current SDK calls.

Use cases and limits

A small team could prototype a language-practice partner, a history explainer, an interview coach, or an interactive story character. The useful product work is often in the surrounding flow: how users choose a character, what they can ask, how the app handles uncertainty, and when it hands off to a human or a static answer.

For fan experiences or memorial projects, use portraits, recordings, and other source material only when you have permission. Make the synthetic nature of the character clear, and respect the wishes and privacy of the people involved. Voice cloning needs particular care.

Try it and share feedback

  • TalkingHead Studio
  • API documentation
  • TalkingHead Web SDK and demo

I would be interested in feedback from developers building conversational characters: which part is hardest to get right in a first prototype—consistent persona, useful knowledge references, voice interaction, or integration?

title: RAG in plain English: how my college helpdesk answers from documents only
description:
Internal GPT is a helpdesk I built for college environments. Administrators upload institutional documents, and students and staff ask natural-language questions. The answers must come strictly from those documents, with source citations.

This post explains how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) works in plain English, using that project as the example. If you've heard the acronym and nodded without being sure what's inside, this is for you.

The problem RAG solves

A language model knows a lot about the world, but nothing about your college's attendance rules, fee deadlines or hostel policy. If you ask it anyway, it may produce a confident, plausible, completely invented answer. In an institution, an invented policy is worse than no answer.

RAG fixes this by separating knowledge from language:

  • The documents hold the facts.
  • The model turns those facts into a readable answer.

The model never has to remember anything. It just reads what you hand it.

The pipeline

There are two phases: preparing the documents (once) and answering questions (every time).

Phase 1: indexing (when a document is uploaded)
  upload → extract text → split into chunks → embed each chunk → store

Phase 2: answering (when a question is asked)
  question → embed it → find the most similar chunks → build prompt → generate answer + sources

Let's take each step.

1. Extract text

PDFs, Word documents and plain text each need their own extraction. Some documents have complex layouts that confuse naive extractors, so I added a fallback: if the primary method fails, the system tries alternatives before reporting an error.

2. Chunk

You can't embed a 60-page handbook as one unit. The text is split into semantically meaningful pieces, ideally each one covering one idea. Chunk size and overlap matter a lot:

  • Too big, and a chunk contains several topics, so it matches many questions weakly.
  • Too small, and a chunk loses context ("the fee is due by the 5th" - which fee?).
  • A little overlap between chunks stops a sentence from being cut off from its context. 
function chunk(text: string, size = 800, overlap = 120): string[] {
  const chunks: string[] = [];
  for (let start = 0; start < text.length; start += size - overlap) {
    chunks.push(text.slice(start, start + size));
  }
  return chunks;
}

(A real chunker splits on paragraph and sentence boundaries first. This is the simplest possible version, to show the idea.)

3. Embed

An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector) that captures its meaning. Two texts about the same thing end up with vectors that point in similar directions, even if they share no words. "How do I pay the semester fee?" and "Fee payment procedure" land close together.

4. Store

The vectors are stored next to the original text. In the first version I used Supabase with the embeddings in a simple table, and designed the retrieval layer behind a clean abstraction so it can be upgraded to pgvector for larger deployments without touching anything else.

5. Retrieve

When a question arrives, it's embedded the same way, and a similarity search finds the chunks whose vectors are closest:

function cosine(a: number[], b: number[]) {
  let dot = 0, na = 0, nb = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    dot += a[i] * b[i]; na += a[i] ** 2; nb += b[i] ** 2;
  }
  return dot / (Math.sqrt(na) * Math.sqrt(nb));
}

const top = chunks
  .map(c => ({ c, score: cosine(queryVec, c.vector) }))
  .sort((x, y) => y.score - x.score)
  .slice(0, 5);

This retrieval step is the crucial constraint. It limits the model to information that actually exists in the knowledge base.

6. Generate

The retrieved chunks go into a carefully written prompt that says, in effect: answer using only this context; if the context doesn't contain the answer, say so.

The most important prompt lesson

You must give the model a graceful way to say "I don't know."

Without that explicit instruction, models tend to produce plausible-sounding but fabricated answers, which is unacceptable in an institutional setting. A prompt shaped like this works far better than "answer the question":

You are a college helpdesk assistant.
Answer ONLY from the context below.
If the context does not contain enough information, reply:
"I couldn't find that in the uploaded documents."
Always cite which document each statement came from.

Context:
{{chunks}}

Question: {{question}}

Where it gets hard

  • Document formats. Each needs its own pipeline, and messy layouts cause trouble.
  • Chunking strategy. I spent significant effort on chunk sizes, overlap and embedding model choice. They change answer quality more than the model does.
  • Citations. An answer without a source is a rumour. Every answer needs to point back to the chunk it used.

Grounding goes further than citations

A later project, Hospitality.ai, pushed this idea harder. It extracts insurance-policy clauses into a validated schema, and every claim comes back with a verbatim quote and a line range. The quote is then re-verified against the source and stamped exact, fuzzy or unverified, and the interface renders all three differently.

The principle is the same: don't just trust the model's claim, check it against the source in code. Anything the document doesn't say goes into a visible "gaps" list instead of being filled with what's "usually" true.

The lesson

Production RAG is as much about retrieval quality as generation quality. A perfect language model is useless if it's searching through bad data. The gap between a good retrieval system and a great one is the gap between answers that are merely relevant and answers that are precisely correct.

Try it yourself

Here's a weekend experiment that needs no framework:

  1. Take five of your own notes or a short PDF.
  2. Chunk them by paragraph.
  3. Embed each chunk with any embedding API.
  4. Ask five questions and print the top three chunks for each.
  5. Notice the wrong retrievals and ask why.

Seeing a wrong retrieval teaches more than reading about it. Fix it by changing chunk size, then re-run.

Debugging a RAG system: symptoms and causes

When answers are bad, resist the urge to blame the model first. Work through this table from the top.

Symptom Likely cause What to try
Answer is vague or off-topic Retrieved chunks aren't relevant Print the top chunks for the question and read them
Right document, wrong passage Chunks too big or too small Change chunk size and overlap, re-index
Model invents details Prompt allows outside knowledge Tighten: "answer only from context", add an "I don't know" path
"I don't know" when the answer exists Chunk missing or split badly Search the raw text for the answer; check extraction
Same wrong chunk every time Embedding model is poor for your domain, or duplicates Try a different embedding model; deduplicate
Garbled text in answers PDF extraction failure Inspect the extracted text before chunking
Slow answers Brute-force search over many vectors Move to an index (pgvector with an index)

The first row is the most important habit: always look at what was retrieved. Most RAG bugs are visible there.

Measure retrieval, not just vibes

Make a small test set: 20 questions, each with the document you expect it to come from. Then measure how often the right chunk appears in the top results:

type Case = { question: string; expectedDoc: string };

async function hitRate(cases: Case[], k = 5) {
  let hits = 0;
  for (const c of cases) {
    const top = await retrieve(c.question, k);        // your retrieval function
    if (top.some(chunk => chunk.docId === c.expectedDoc)) hits++;
  }
  return hits / cases.length;
}

A "hit rate at 5" of 0.9 means that for 90% of test questions, the right document was in the top five. Change one thing (chunk size, overlap, embedding model), re-run, and keep the change only if the number improves. This is the same principle as the rest of the series: measure what you only believe.

Prompt injection: a quiet risk

Uploaded documents are data, but a model may treat text inside them as instructions ("ignore previous instructions and..."). Basic defences:

  • Put document text inside clearly delimited blocks and tell the model it's untrusted data.
  • Give the model no tools it could be tricked into using.
  • Validate its output against a schema where possible.
  • Never let retrieved text decide permissions.

Glossary

  • Chunk: a slice of a document sized for retrieval.
  • Overlap: text repeated between neighbouring chunks to preserve context.
  • Vector / embedding: numeric representation of meaning.
  • Cosine similarity: a measure of how aligned two vectors are.
  • Top-k: the k most similar chunks.
  • Grounding: tying an answer to a specific source.
  • Hallucination: a confident answer that isn't supported by the source.

Where to go next

Try adding citations with quotes. Ask the model to return, for each claim, the exact sentence it relied on, then check in code that the sentence exists in the retrieved chunks. Anything that doesn't match is dropped. That one change moves a RAG system from "sounds right" to "provably sourced".

What would you build a document-grounded assistant for? And if you've used pgvector, what did you wish you'd known first?

title: Structured Maps for Landmark-Based Route Instructions with LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36582v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.

title: Translating pages built with a page builder: shortcodes, block attributes, and the strings that never reach the content filter
description:
The report comes back as "the Portuguese page still has English on it". You open the translation screen, the body copy is fully translated, and the button in the hero still says "Request a quote".

That button text lives in an attribute of a shortcode, or a key inside a JSON blob in post meta, or a string in a theme option. Content filters never see any of those, so the translation layer never gets a chance.

What follows is how to find out where a given string actually lives, and what to do about each place.

Where builder text hides

Where the string lives What it looks like Does a content filter reach it?
Post content, as blocks <!-- wp:button {"text":"Request a quote"} --> It sees the rendered HTML, so text nodes sometimes, attribute-driven output never
Post content, as shortcodes [cta title="Request a quote"] No — attributes aren't content
Post meta builder layout saved as JSON, custom fields No
Options / theme mods header CTA, announcement bar, footer columns No
Taxonomies and menus nav labels, category names No — separate filters
Template files "Read more", form labels Yes, through gettext

The block row is the one people misread. A the_content filter sees HTML a block produced. Replacing a paragraph's text there can work. Replacing a button's label inside an <a> that CSS targets will break styling, and it can never fix alt, placeholder or a URL held in an attribute.

Inventory before translating anything

You need to know which pages use shortcodes, which use blocks, and which meta keys hold layout.

cd /path/to/wordpress

# content that contains shortcode syntax
wp db query "SELECT ID, post_title FROM wp_posts
  WHERE post_status='publish' AND post_type IN ('page','post')
  AND post_content LIKE '%[%' AND post_content LIKE '%]%'"

# content with block markup
wp db query "SELECT ID, post_title FROM wp_posts
  WHERE post_status='publish' AND post_type IN ('page','post')
  AND post_content LIKE '%<!-- wp:%'"

Adjust wp_posts if your table prefix isn't wp_.

Which shortcodes are actually in use:

wp db query "SELECT post_content FROM wp_posts WHERE post_status='publish'" --skip-column-names \
  | grep -oE '\[[a-z0-9_-]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Meta keys that could hold layout:

wp db query "SELECT meta_key, COUNT(*) c FROM wp_postmeta
  GROUP BY meta_key ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 40"

A builder's layout typically appears as one meta key with a long serialized or JSON value. Look at the big ones:

wp db query "SELECT post_id, LENGTH(meta_value) len FROM wp_postmeta
  WHERE meta_key='_your_builder_layout' ORDER BY len DESC LIMIT 10"

And options that render on every page:

wp option list --search='*footer*' --fields=option_name
wp option list --search='*header*' --fields=option_name

That last query is often where the header CTA and the announcement bar live.

Shortcodes: catch the attribute where it's read

If you own the shortcode, translate inside the callback. It's the only place where you know which attribute is user-visible text and which one is a CSS class or a post ID.

add_shortcode( 'cta', function ( $atts, $content = '' ) {
    $atts = shortcode_atts(
        [ 'title' => '', 'button_text' => '', 'url' => '', 'style' => 'primary' ],
        $atts,
        'cta'
    );

    $title       = tr_string( $atts['title'] );
    $button_text = tr_string( $atts['button_text'] );

    return sprintf(
        '<div class="cta cta--%s"><h2>%s</h2><p>%s</p><a class="cta__btn" href="%s">%s</a></div>',
        esc_attr( $atts['style'] ),
        esc_html( $title ),
        wp_kses_post( do_shortcode( $content ) ),
        esc_url( $atts['url'] ),
        esc_html( $button_text )
    );
} );

tr_string() is yours to define. A minimal version keyed on the request locale:

function tr_string( string $text ): string {
    static $map = null;

    if ( null === $map ) {
        $locale = determine_locale();
        $all    = [
            'de_DE' => [
                'Request a quote' => 'Angebot anfordern',
                'Talk to sales'   => 'Vertrieb kontaktieren',
            ],
            'pt_PT' => [
                'Request a quote' => 'Pedir orçamento',
                'Talk to sales'   => 'Falar com vendas',
            ],
        ];
        $map = $all[ $locale ] ?? [];
    }

    return $map[ $text ] ?? $text;
}

determine_locale() is core, and it runs the locale filter — which is how whatever switches languages on your site usually announces its choice. So keying the map on it stays correct when you change the switching mechanism later.

If the shortcode comes from a theme or plugin you're not going to fork, you can intercept before the callback runs. pre_do_shortcode_tag gives you the parsed attributes and the matched content, and lets you return your own output:

add_filter( 'pre_do_shortcode_tag', function ( $return, $tag, $attr, $m ) {
    if ( false !== $return || empty( $attr ) || ! isset( $GLOBALS['shortcode_tags'][ $tag ] ) ) {
        return $return;
    }

    $eligible = apply_filters(
        'tr_shortcode_attr_keys',
        [ 'title', 'text', 'label', 'heading', 'subtitle', 'button_text', 'description' ],
        $tag
    );

    $translated = [];
    $changed    = false;

    foreach ( $attr as $key => $value ) {
        if ( ! in_array( $key, $eligible, true ) || ! is_string( $value ) ) {
            continue;
        }
        $new = tr_string( $value );
        if ( $new !== $value ) {
            $translated[ $key ] = $new;
            $changed            = true;
        }
    }

    if ( ! $changed ) {
        return $return;
    }

    $callback = $GLOBALS['shortcode_tags'][ $tag ];

    return call_user_func( $callback, $translated, $m[5] ?? '', $tag );
}, 10, 4 );

Returning a non-false value short-circuits the original call, so the callback runs once, not twice — but it runs with a filtered attribute array. That's why the allowlist exists: without it, every string attribute goes through the map, including IDs, slugs and class names, and a map entry that happens to match one of those produces a very confusing render. Keep the map to sentences.

Blocks: change the attributes, not the HTML

render_block hands you finished HTML. render_block_data hands you the parsed block before rendering, which is where attributes are still mutable.

add_filter( 'render_block_data', function ( $parsed_block, $source_block, $parent_block ) {
    $name  = $parsed_block['blockName'] ?? '';
    $attrs = $parsed_block['attrs'] ?? [];

    $fields = [
        'core/button' => [ 'text' ],
        'core/image'  => [ 'alt' ],
    ];

    if ( ! isset( $fields[ $name ] ) ) {
        return $parsed_block;
    }

    foreach ( $fields[ $name ] as $key ) {
        if ( isset( $attrs[ $key ] ) && is_string( $attrs[ $key ] ) ) {
            $parsed_block['attrs'][ $key ] = tr_string( $attrs[ $key ] );
        }
    }

    return $parsed_block;
}, 10, 3 );

Extend the $fields map per block by reading its block.json — that file lists every attribute the block stores, which is your authoritative list of translatable candidates. It also tells you which attributes are markup (skip) and which are user text (translate).

Note what this approach commits you to: the saved post content stays in the source language, and the translations live in your map. Editing copy means editing code or a map that editors can't see. The alternative is one post per locale, where nothing is invisible but structure has to be kept in sync and a layout change becomes N layout changes. Pick by who edits: if marketing rewrites copy weekly, separate posts per locale age better; if the copy is stable and the layout is what moves, render-time filtering is less work.

The dynamic bits that render on every page

Options carry more copy than people remember. The filter name is the option name:

add_filter( 'option_acme_announcement_bar', 'tr_string' );
add_filter( 'theme_mod_acme_footer_tagline', 'tr_string' );

Menu labels live outside posts entirely:

add_filter( 'wp_setup_nav_menu_item', function ( $item ) {
    if ( is_admin() ) {
        return $item;
    }
    if ( isset( $item->title ) ) {
        $item->title = tr_string( $item->title );
    }
    return $item;
} );

Term names — category archives, product categories — can be handled similarly:

add_filter( 'get_term', function ( $term ) {
    if ( is_admin() || ! $term instanceof WP_Term ) {
        return $term;
    }
    $term->name = tr_string( $term->name );
    return $term;
} );

get_term() returns a clone, so mutating it stays inside that call. The catch is anything that already read and stored the name earlier in the same request — a menu item, a breadcrumb — won't reflect the change. If taxonomy names matter for search visibility, separate terms per locale with translated slugs are sturdier than a filter, because the slug is part of the URL.

Header, footer, and anything shared

A header built in a builder is usually a template post or a bundle of options. Translate it once, in place. If it's a synced pattern, translating it changes every page that uses it — normally what you want, and a mess if two people do it on the same afternoon.

Anything rendered from code — search result counts, 404 copy, form validation messages — comes from the .mo file and follows the locale, not your map. That's a different fix and a different person's job.

A leak check that runs in a loop

Eyeballing pages stops scaling around ten URLs.

cat > /tmp/urls.txt <<'EOF'
https://staging.example.com/
https://staging.example.com/pricing/
https://staging.example.com/contact/
EOF

while read -r url; do
  html=$(curl -sS "$url")
  for s in "Request a quote" "Talk to sales" "Read more" "Starts at"; do
    printf '%s' "$html" | grep -qF "$s" && echo "LEAK  $url  <- $s"
  done
done < /tmp/urls.txt

Attributes are where the visual check fails, because a broken alt looks like nothing:

curl -sS https://staging.example.com/ \
  | grep -oE '(alt|placeholder|aria-label|title|value)="[^"]+"' \
  | sort -u

And the parts machines read:

curl -sS https://staging.example.com/ | grep -oE '<html[^>]*lang="[^"]+"'
curl -sS https://staging.example.com/ | grep -oE '<link[^>]*hreflang="[^"]+"[^>]*>'

The hreflang set should point at the translated URL and back at the source, and <html lang> should match the page it's on. A page rendering in German that declares lang="en" is a page you'll be redoing.

Most of the effort here is locating strings, not translating them. The switching side — locale handling, hreflang, the language files — is what our free plugin AumLang covers: https://aumcreate.com/plugins/aumlang?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=devto-builder-pages-translate-shortcodes. The string-location work above applies either way.

title: Why SVG Files from Figma Are 50–80% Dead Weight (and What to Strip Out)
description:
Every project has at least one multi-kilobyte SVG icon that could have been a few hundred bytes. Design tools write SVG for their convenience, not for the web — and the result is routinely 3–5× larger than it needs to be.

Here are the 7 things making your SVGs bigger than they should be.

1. Editor metadata

<metadata> blocks, rdf:RDF payloads, generator comments — Figma, Illustrator and Inkscape all pad files with data only they read. Browsers never render it.

2. Coordinate precision

74.98399992065430 renders identically to 74.984. Dropping to 2–3 decimals is the single biggest win on path-heavy artwork — often half the file.

3. Empty and nested groups

<g> wrappers that mirror the editor's layer panel but apply no transform or style.

4. Unused defs

Gradients, filters, masks and symbols defined but never referenced by any shape.

5. Editor IDs and attributes

id="Layer_1", data-name, xmlns:serif, style attributes with no visual effect.

6. Whitespace

Pretty-printed indentation and newlines — great for humans, dead weight for machines.

7. Embedded raster images (the trap)

A base64 PNG hiding inside <image> can be 95% of the file size, and no SVG optimizer can shrink it. If your "SVG" is mostly an embedded bitmap, the honest fix is either re-exporting the artwork as true vectors or shipping an optimized WebP/JPEG instead.

How much can you actually save?

  • Illustrator exports: 50–80%
  • Sketch: 40–70%
  • Figma: 30–60%
  • Hand-written SVGs: 5–15%

And an optimized SVG is plain text, so gzip/Brotli squeezes another 50–70% on the wire. The two stack — do both.

Automate it

If the same SVGs ship in an app, make optimization a compile step, exactly like minifying JavaScript:

  • Vite: vite-plugin-svgo
  • Webpack: svgo-loader
  • Any CI: npx svgo -f src/icons -o dist/icons

Keep editable originals in the design repo, let the pipeline emit optimized files, and nobody has to remember anything again.

The full guide — with a browser-based optimizer (SVGO running client-side, no upload) and a batch processor for whole icon sets — is at svgeditor.dev.

title: Deep Dive: GST Reconciliation Software in GSTBot
description:
Reconciliation: Turning Bulk Invoices into Accurate ITC Claims

GSTBot’s core value lies in automating the reconciliation of a company’s purchase register against the GSTR‑2B data supplied by the tax authority. For Indian SMBs, the manual process—matching each invoice line, calculating input tax credit (ITC), and flagging discrepancies—consumes weeks of effort every month. The tool replaces that with a repeatable, tolerant workflow that runs in seconds. This is where gst reconciliation software pays off in practice.

The Problem

  1. Exact matching fails – Vendor names, invoice numbers, or tax amounts may differ slightly between the purchase ledger and the GSTR‑2B feed. A strict string match would flag every minor variation as an error, drowning users in false positives.
  2. Volume is high – Small businesses can receive hundreds of invoices per month. A batch‑processing solution is required to avoid bottlenecks.
  3. Regulatory nuance – Rules 37, 42, and 43 introduce reversals that must be reflected in the reconciliation, otherwise ITC calculations become inaccurate.

The Solution

GSTBot introduces a tolerance‑aware reconciliation engine that:

  • Normalizes data – Vendor names and HSN codes are lower‑cased and stripped of punctuation before comparison.
  • Applies configurable thresholds – Users set acceptable differences for amounts (e.g., ±1 %) and dates (±2 days). The engine uses these to decide whether two records represent the same transaction.
  • Locks per period – To avoid race conditions when multiple reconciliation jobs run concurrently, a Redis‑based advisory lock (see commit fix(reconciliation): serialise runs per period with an advisory lock) ensures only one job processes a given tax period at a time.
  • Classifies exceptions – Each mismatch is labeled (e.g., Amount mismatch, Vendor mismatch) and a recommended action is attached. The UI presents these in a concise table.

The engine is built on a stack that keeps the codebase lightweight yet scalable:

Layer Tech
API FastAPI
Background jobs Celery, Redis
Persistence PostgreSQL (SQLAlchemy)
Frontend React (Vite)
Data processing Pandas (Python)

How It Works – Behind the Code

Below is a simplified view of the reconciliation workflow. The real implementation contains additional error handling and audit logging. Getting gst reconciliation software right early saves rework later.

# reconciliation.py
import pandas as pd
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from redis import Redis
from celery import shared_task
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

router = APIRouter()

@shared_task
def reconcile_period(period: str, tolerance: dict):
    """Run reconciliation for a tax period."""
    lock_key = f"reconcile:{period}"
    with Redis().lock(lock_key, blocking_timeout=30):
        # 1. Pull local ledger
        ledger = pd.read_sql(
            "SELECT vendor, gstin, inv_no, amount, tax_rate, hsn FROM purchase_register WHERE period=%s",
            con=engine,
            params=(period,)
        )

        # 2. Pull GSTR‑2B feed
        gstr2b = pd.read_sql(
            "SELECT vendor, gstin, inv_no, amount, tax_rate, hsn FROM gstr2b WHERE period=%s",
            con=engine,
            params=(period,)
        )

        # 3. Normalise and compare
        ledger['key'] = ledger.apply(normalise_key, axis=1)
        gstr2b['key'] = gstr2b.apply(normalise_key, axis=1)

        merged = ledger.merge(gstr2b, on='key', suffixes=('_local', '_remote'))

        # 4. Apply tolerance
        def is_within(row):
            amt_diff = abs(row['amount_local'] - row['amount_remote'])
            return amt_diff <= tolerance['amount'] * row['amount_local']

        merged['ok'] = merged.apply(is_within, axis=1)

        # 5. Persist results
        merged.to_sql('reconciliation', engine, if_exists='replace', index=False)

def normalise_key(row):
    """Create a deterministic key for matching."""
    return f"{row['vendor'].lower().replace(' ', '')}|{row['gstin']}|{row['inv_no']}"

# API endpoint
@router.post("/reconcile")
async def trigger_reconciliation(
    period: str,
    tolerance: dict = Depends(get_tolerance),
    db: Session = Depends(get_db)
):
    reconcile_period.delay(period, tolerance)
    return {"status": "queued"}

The normalise_key function demonstrates the simple string normalization that reduces false mismatches. The is_within predicate applies the user‑defined amount tolerance.

The background task writes the reconciliation report to a dedicated table. The React UI consumes this table and presents a grid where each row shows the local amount, the GSTR‑2B amount, and the status (OK or Exception). Clicking an exception opens a modal with the suggested action—often “Adjust amount” or “Verify vendor”.

Using the Feature

  1. Upload invoices – Drag a ZIP of PDFs or an Excel file onto the /upload page. The backend runs OCR and a lightweight transformer model to extract fields.
  2. Set tolerances – In the settings panel, specify an amount tolerance of 0.5 % and a date tolerance of 1 day.
  3. Run reconciliation – Hit “Reconcile” for the current month. The job starts in the background; you receive a toast notification when it completes.
  4. Review results – The table shows 98 % of lines as OK. The remaining 2 % are flagged with clear reasons and actions.

Because the reconciliation engine runs in a single thread per period, you can safely trigger multiple reconciliations for different periods without interference. The Redis lock guarantees that only one job touches a period’s data at a time, preventing race conditions that could corrupt the report.

Impact

The tolerance‑aware reconciliation reduces manual effort by eliminating the need to chase every minor discrepancy. By presenting actionable exceptions, it empowers finance staff to correct entries quickly, ensuring accurate ITC claims and compliance with GSTR‑2B rules. For SMBs, this means a reliable, low‑cost alternative to enterprise‑grade reconciliation tools that are priced beyond their reach. Good gst reconciliation software keeps the rest of the workflow predictable.

Once the reconciliation table is complete, GSTBot feeds the reconciled amounts into the GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B preparation modules. The same tolerance logic ensures that the ITC reported on the portal matches the reconciled ledger, preventing downstream filing errors.

The Celery workers can be scaled horizontally; each worker processes a period lock, so adding more workers speeds up multi‑period runs.

Related reading

  • GSTR‑2B Reconciliation in GSTBot: Configurable Tolerances
  • GSTR-2B Reconciliation with Configurable Tolerances in GSTBot

title: CrowdCC: Jointly Benchmarking Corruption Robustness and Deployment Quantization in Crowd Counting
description:
arXiv:2610.36340v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Crowd-counting models deployed on edge devices face two shifts: inputs are degraded along the capture and transmission pipeline, while models are quantized to satisfy resource constraints. Yet corruption robustness and deployment quantization are typically evaluated separately. We introduce CrowdCC, a controlled corruption benchmark that jointly evaluates these effects using 23 deployment-motivated corruptions at three severity levels, four crowd-counting datasets, and 26 models using A100 TensorRT engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision, paired with throughput and energy measurements from corresponding Jetson Orin NX configurations. The corruptions span six families, with head annotations adjusted when geometry or visibility changes. Our evaluation shows that capture-chain corruptions consistently produce the largest degradation across the evaluated models, while crowd density affects absolute and relative error differently. Clean accuracy does not fully predict corrupted performance. INT8 alters corruption robustness substantially more than FP16, with no systematic direction, and does not consistently improve latency or energy. INT8 inference efficiency is strongly associated with reformat overhead in the compiled engine, while slowdowns are also observed under limited INT8 coverage. Precision changes corrupted-error rankings and robustness-cost frontiers, showing why model selection must consider corruption robustness and measured deployment cost together. The code is available at https://github.com/Tulane-Computer-Architecture-Systems/CrowdCC-Release.

title: JevRec: Linguistic Encoding with Jev-like Decision Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation
description:
arXiv:2610.36937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items as semantic identifiers (SIDs) and autoregressively generates the next item's SID from interaction history. However, most methods assign the same SID length to all items despite highly unequal interaction frequencies. This uniform design repeatedly incurs the cost of fine-grained codes for popular items, while shortening codes to reduce this cost also compresses the semantic representations of long-tail items. Inspired by the compact forms of frequent expressions in natural language, we propose JevRec to encode items as variable-length words and generate the next item from interaction context. Linguistic encoding retains frequency-dependent semantic prefixes from shared codebooks, producing shorter SIDs for popular items and richer descriptions for long-tail items. Yet predicting a sequence-level length and generating token-level content impose different optimization requirements that may conflict under a shared output head. Our Jev-like decision modeling component therefore predicts a length distribution with a dedicated head and generates content conditioned on length through a separate head while sharing the interaction-history representation. Experiments on three public datasets show that JevRec outperforms all compared baselines across the evaluated recommendation metrics. Further analyses show lower training and inference time than TIGER and reduced gradient conflict between length and content prediction.

title: The 6 Rs of Migration: Which Path Fits You?
description:
Migration is not one technical task.

It is a decision about how much of the existing system should survive.

That is why the 6 Rs are useful: rehost, replatform, refactor, rebuild, replace, and retire.

Each one solves a different problem.

Rehost: Move the System With Minimal Change

Rehosting is the simplest migration path.

You move the application to a new environment and change as little as possible.

Typical examples:

On-prem VM
↓
Cloud VM

or:

Old hosting environment
↓
New infrastructure

Best when

the application is stable,

infrastructure is the main problem,

you need to leave a data center quickly,

time is limited,

architectural change is not the immediate priority.

Watch out for

You are moving existing problems too.

If the application is hard to deploy, tightly coupled, or inefficient, those issues usually remain.

Rehosting changes where the system runs.

It does not automatically modernize how the system works.

Replatform: Improve the Environment Without Rebuilding

Replatforming keeps most of the application intact but makes targeted platform changes.

For example:

Self-managed database
↓
Managed database

or:

Legacy runtime
↓
Supported runtime

or:

Manual deployment
↓
Containerized deployment

Best when

The application still meets business requirements, but the operating environment is outdated, expensive, or difficult to maintain.

Watch out for

Scope creep.

A small platform change can quietly turn into a large redesign.

Before starting, define:

What changes?
What stays unchanged?

That boundary matters.

Refactor: Change the Architecture

Refactoring is appropriate when the application still has value, but its internal architecture is creating problems.

Common signals include:

tightly coupled modules,

fragile deployments,

hard-to-build integrations,

poor scalability,

large blast radius for small changes,

slow development because everything depends on everything else.

A refactor might introduce cleaner service boundaries, improve APIs, or reduce coupling.

Best when

The business logic is still useful, but the architecture is limiting maintainability, scalability, or delivery speed.

Watch out for

Open-ended redesign.

"Improve the architecture" is not a useful finish line.

Define a concrete goal.

For example:

Current:
One release deploys the whole application.

Target:
Billing can deploy independently.

That gives the project a measurable outcome.

Also watch for hidden business rules.

Old systems often behave correctly for reasons nobody remembers.

Rebuild: Create a New Application Around the Same Business Need

Sometimes the existing design is too constrained to evolve safely.

That is when rebuilding becomes a real option.

This is more than refactoring.

You are creating a new implementation.

Best when

the data model no longer fits the business,

major workflow changes are required,

the current architecture cannot support future needs,

incremental change is becoming more expensive than replacement.

Watch out for

Assuming the old system contains nothing valuable.

Legacy applications often include years of:

validation rules,

exception handling,

scheduled jobs,

integration behavior,

edge cases,

operational knowledge.

A rebuild that ignores those details can be technically clean and operationally wrong.

Before rebuilding, document the current behavior.

Replace: Use an Existing Product Instead

Not every system should remain custom software.

If a commercial or SaaS product can solve the same problem well, replacement may be more sensible than maintaining a custom application.

Best when

The system supports a standard business function and custom development no longer provides enough strategic value.

Examples might include common internal workflows, standard back-office functions, or capabilities already covered by mature platforms.

Watch out for

The last 10%.

A product may cover most of your current functionality but still miss the workflow that matters most to the business.

You also need to consider:

data migration,

integrations,

access control,

customization limits,

vendor lock-in,

recurring cost,

user adoption.

The right question is not:

Can this product replace the application?

It is:

Can this product support the business process?

Retire: Do Not Migrate What You No Longer Need

Retirement is probably the most underrated option.

Sometimes an application should not move anywhere.

It should disappear.

Systems stay alive for strange reasons:

nobody owns the shutdown decision,

another tool already replaced them,

usage is almost zero,

the business process no longer exists,

teams are afraid of hidden dependencies.

Then a migration project starts and the old system is added to the migration list automatically.

That can waste a lot of engineering effort.

Best when

The system no longer provides enough business value to justify its cost and risk.

Watch out for

Hidden dependencies.

Before retirement, check:

Scheduled jobs
Reports
Downstream systems
Data retention
Audit requirements
External consumers

Do not turn something off just because nobody remembers using it.

The 6 Rs Are Not a Maturity Ladder

I do not think this:

Rehost -> Replatform -> Refactor -> Rebuild

represents increasing technical maturity.

Sometimes rehost is the correct engineering decision.

Sometimes rebuilding would be unnecessary.

Sometimes replacing custom software is smarter than writing more code.

Sometimes retiring the system is the highest-value option.

The goal is not to choose the most technically ambitious R.

The goal is to choose the one that solves the actual problem.

Start With the Problem, Not the Technology

Before discussing cloud vendors, databases, frameworks, or architecture, write down the migration problem.

For example:

Problem:
Infrastructure is no longer supported.

Likely path:
Rehost or replatform.

Problem:
Architecture prevents teams from deploying independently.

Likely path:
Refactor.

Problem:
The current data model cannot support the new business model.

Likely path:
Rebuild.

Problem:
A mature SaaS product now covers the capability.

Likely path:
Replace.

Problem:
Nobody actually needs the system anymore.

Likely path:
Retire.

That is a much better starting point than:

"We should move this to the cloud."

A Portfolio Can Use Multiple Rs

One migration strategy rarely fits every application.

A typical portfolio might look like:

System A -> Rehost
System B -> Replatform
System C -> Refactor
System D -> Replace
System E -> Retire

That is not inconsistency.

It is good architecture planning.

Each application has different business value, technical risk, dependencies, and future requirements.

Treating them all the same may make the migration program easier to explain, but not necessarily safer or cheaper.

Practical Checklist

Before choosing a migration path, I would ask:

[ ] Is infrastructure the main problem?
[ ] Is the application still useful to the business?
[ ] Is the current platform supported?
[ ] Is architecture limiting delivery or scalability?
[ ] Are important business rules documented?
[ ] Could an existing product replace the capability?
[ ] Does the application still need to exist?
[ ] Are integrations and dependencies understood?
[ ] What business outcome should the migration improve?
[ ] What is the smallest change that solves that problem?

Then map the answer:

Infrastructure problem -> Rehost
Platform problem -> Replatform
Architecture problem -> Refactor
Fundamental design problem -> Rebuild
Commodity capability -> Replace
No remaining value -> Retire

The important part is not memorizing the six labels.

It is avoiding the mistake of treating every migration as the same kind of work.

A migration should remove a specific constraint.

If you cannot explain what that constraint is, you are probably not ready to choose the path yet.

I work on modernization and migration planning at Ksoft Technologies, and I wrote a longer version of this framework here:

[https://www.ksofttechnologies.com/blogs/6-rs-of-migration-explained]
