title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.

title: Lipi-Ghor: A Large-Scale, Diarized, Multi-Domain Bengali Speech Corpus and a Scalable Pipeline for Building It
description:
arXiv:2610.36184v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bengali, spoken by over 230 million people, remains severely under-resourced in spoken language research. Existing open Bengali ASR corpora are confined to short, read or crowd-sourced speech and lack speaker diarization and long-form audio.
  We present Lipi-Ghor, a large-scale weakly-supervised Bengali speech corpus comprising 885 hours of audio sourced from 998 YouTube videos across 596 unique channels, spanning 17 diverse domains including audiobooks, drama, religious sermons, news, and regional dialects. Each recording is annotated in SSTT format (Speaker, Speech, Transcription, Timestamp), which combines automated diarization with Bengali YouTube caption tracks.
  To our knowledge, Lipi-Ghor is the first Bengali speech corpus to pair large-scale coverage with speaker-diarized, long-form audio annotations, both of which are absent from existing open Bengali resources. We also present the construction methodology as a replicable pipeline for any language with a sufficient captioned YouTube presence. Targeted channel curation across a handful of rich domains yields corpus scales that were previously out of reach for low-resource languages.
  We benchmark four widely-used ASR models under zero-shot and fine-tuned conditions. All four degrade consistently on emotive, dialectal, and long-form content. Because caption targets are noisy, we also release a human-annotated gold evaluation split, verified by 17 volunteer annotators over 30 hours of human-in-the-loop correction and stratified across all 17 domains.
  We release our original contributions (video-ID lists, diarization output, pipeline code, and the gold annotations) under CC-BY-4.0, and distribute caption-derived transcripts for research use only; no raw audio is redistributed.

title: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors
description:
arXiv:2610.36146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prompt optimization should improve the image a user receives without changing the scene the user requested. Yet stylistic rewriting can weaken object attributes and relations even when global text--image similarity remains high. We propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision. The graph exposes what should be preserved, while deletion, reordering, and insertion provide a token-aligned way to modify the prompt. This turns structural feedback from an external critique into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Learning from that signal requires handling both uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. StruPO retains grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple images for each edit before computing group-relative advantages. Experiments span three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, with comparisons to learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control. StruPO improves the faithfulness--aesthetics trade-off, with consistent gains in relational fidelity. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study provide complementary evidence, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity. Controlled ablations connect these gains to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning. The resulting policy produces reusable optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, without an iterative critique--rewrite loop.

title: AK_QMUL at ArGuard Shared Tasks: A Single Fine-Tuned JAIS for Arabic Harmful-Prompt Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.36360v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present AK_QMUL's submissions to the ArGuard-2026 shared tasks on Arabic harmful-prompt detection: a binary safe/unsafe task (B1) and a seven-way harm-domain task (B2). Both submissions use one backbone -- JAIS-6.7B fine-tuned with 4-bit QLoRA and a linear classification head over its last-token representation. For B1 we train a four-way head that factors the label by dialect register {safe, unsafe} x {MSA, other}, we augment the training fold with MSA prompts from AraSafe, and decode with a plain argmax to score safe/unsafe. For B2 we fine-tune the same backbone as a seven-way classifier and average the softmax outputs of five random seeds. Both submissions ranked first on their track, with macro-F1 0.984 on B1 and 0.790 on B2. We report results by dialect and by class: on B1 the model is accurate across all six dialects (93.6--99.8%) and its predicted unsafe rate tracks the true rate closely; on B2 six of the seven classes reach F1 between 0.73 and 0.98, with the residual error concentrated in the Bully class, which overlaps semantically with harassment and harm-to-others.

title: 3, 7, 14, 17, 42: Instruction Tuning Installs and Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We measure, without sampling error, the probability a language model assigns to each integer from 1 to N when asked for a random number. For a fixed prompt the model defines one probability vector, which we compute by summing over each integer's scored spellings rather than estimate by sampling, removing the noise that limits earlier studies [1, 4]. We evaluate 18 open-weight model lines at five ranges up to N = 100, under 29 decoding configurations, on two inference stacks; 15 of them have matched base and instruction-tuned checkpoints that both give usable answers. Instruction tuning makes the distribution less uniform in all 15 pairs. It installs one heuristic, round-number avoidance, and sharpens another, endpoint avoidance. Base checkpoints do not avoid round numbers once the endpoints are removed from those sets; tuned checkpoints avoid them, multiples of 10 almost completely. Base checkpoints return the endpoints 1 and N at 0.30 to 0.60 of the interior rate; tuned checkpoints almost never return them. A preference for odd numbers is consistent across tuned checkpoints only at N = 100, where base checkpoints also show it weakly. Endpoint avoidance and the odd preference fit the account Kubovy and Psotka [6] proposed for human number choice; round-number avoidance is not part of that account, and the midpoint avoidance it predicts is essentially absent, with one slight exception at N = 100. Tuning does not install a new favourite integer shared across models: above N = 10 no modal integer is shared by more than 42 percent of tuned conditions, and P (17) rises in 10 of 15 pairs and falls in 5. The concentration is present in the model's own distribution: at temperature 1.0, nucleus truncation at top-p 0.95 adds a median of 0.035 to the total variation distance.

title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
description:
arXiv:2610.36513v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

title: Blackwell quantisation on my own card
description:
Quantising a small model down from FP16 to Q4_K_M on my RTX 5070 Ti more than doubled throughput and cut VRAM by two thirds, with output that stayed 98% similar to the full-precision baseline by embedding distance. Both registered gates passed. The interesting part turned out to be where the remaining 2% actually lived.

Key takeaways

  • Q4_K_M reached 258.0 tokens/second against 116.5 for FP16 on the same model and prompts, a 2.22x speedup against a registered gate of 1.3x.
  • VRAM dropped monotonically with precision: 6,895 MiB at FP16, 4,019 MiB at Q8_0, 2,594 MiB at Q4_K_M, on the same 16 GB card.
  • Average embedding similarity between Q4_K_M and FP16 output stayed at 0.9835 across 20 fixed prompts, against a registered floor of 0.90.
  • The lowest-similarity cases were not errors: reading the raw text showed paraphrase on open-ended questions, not factual drift, while every closed factual prompt scored a perfect 1.0000 at every quantisation level.
  • This measures GGUF quantisation through Ollama, not the NVFP4 format a related paper tested on the same GPU family; the two are different schemes, and the paper is context here, not a target to reproduce.

Why measure this myself instead of trusting the paper?

A 2026 paper on consumer Blackwell GPUs reports 1.6x throughput for NVFP4 quantisation over BF16, with 2 to 4% quality loss, tested on the RTX 5060 Ti, 5070 Ti and 5090. I own one of those cards, which made the paper a natural registered comparison rather than a citation to take on faith, following the same discipline described in why I pre-register a kill-gate for every experiment: the thresholds below were fixed before any model ran. The catch is that NVFP4 runs through TensorRT-LLM, a stack built for exactly that format; what I actually run day to day is Ollama, which serves GGUF K-quants through llama.cpp. Different scheme, different software, and no honest way to expect the numbers to match.

So the registered question was narrower than "can I reproduce the paper": does the same shape of trade-off, lower precision buying speed and memory at some quality cost, hold for the quantisation format most people on consumer hardware actually use. I picked a small model, llama3.2:3b-instruct, deliberately smaller than anything in the paper, so all three precisions fit comfortably in 16 GB and the comparison measured the trade-off itself rather than whether anything fit at all.

What happened to throughput, memory and output quality?

Every metric moved the same direction as precision dropped, and moved together. Throughput: 116.5 tokens per second at FP16, 187.0 at Q8_0, 258.0 at Q4_K_M, a 2.22x gain at the lowest precision against a registered floor of 1.3x. VRAM at load: 6,895 MiB, 4,019 MiB, 2,594 MiB across the same three steps. Neither curve reversed at any point, which is a cleaner result than I expected going in; I had assumed at least one metric would show a step where a lower precision briefly cost more before paying off, and none did. Full numbers, including wall-clock time for the twenty-prompt run at each precision, sit in the frozen plan and results in the public experiment repository.

Quality held up by the same measure. I embedded every response with a local embedding model and computed cosine similarity between each quantised output and its FP16 counterpart across 20 fixed prompts, generated at temperature zero for reproducibility. Q8_0 averaged 0.9984 similarity to FP16, close enough to call the two outputs interchangeable. Q4_K_M averaged 0.9835, comfortably above the registered floor of 0.90, though with more visible spread across individual prompts than Q8_0 showed.

Where did the quality difference actually come from?

Averages hide the interesting part. The two lowest Q4_K_M scores belonged to open-ended prompts, a two-sentence plot summary and a one-sentence technical definition, not to any of the closed factual questions in the set. Reading the raw text answered the question a similarity score alone cannot: both quantised and full-precision answers stated the same facts in different words, not different facts. Meanwhile every closed factual prompt, a capital city, a square root, a chemical symbol, scored a perfect 1.0000 at every precision level tested, because a correct short answer has almost no room to be phrased two different ways.

That split matters for reading the headline number honestly. A 0.9835 average is not "2% of answers were wrong at random"; it is closer to "open-ended answers get reworded, closed ones do not," which is a much weaker claim about the cost of quantisation than the raw percentage suggests on its own. I would not have caught this by trusting the average. The lesson generalises past this one experiment: an aggregate similarity score is a screening tool, not a verdict, and the prompts sitting at the low end of it are the ones worth reading by hand before writing anything down.

FAQ

Does this mean Q4 quantisation is basically free on consumer hardware?

For a 3B instruction model on a 16 GB card, on short factual and short explanatory prompts, the registered numbers say yes: large speed and memory gains, similarity comfortably above the floor I set. That does not generalise automatically to larger models, longer generations, or tasks with less room for legitimate paraphrase; it is one measured point, not a universal rule.

Why not test NVFP4 directly for a real comparison?

NVFP4 needs TensorRT-LLM, a different serving stack from the llama.cpp backend behind Ollama, and setting that stack up was out of scope for a same-week experiment on my own hardware. The paper's numbers stand as context for what a more specialised stack can do; this experiment measures what the tool most people actually reach for does on the same GPU family.

Why pick such a small model instead of something closer to production use?

A 3B model lets FP16, Q8_0 and Q4_K_M all fit in 16 GB without any of them straining the card, which isolates the precision-versus-speed question from the separate question of what fits at all. That second question, whether a larger model fits at a given precision on this exact card, is real and unanswered here; it belongs to its own experiment.

References

  • Jonathan Knoop, Hendrik Holtmann. Private LLM Inference on Consumer Blackwell GPUs: A Practical Guide for Cost-Effective Local Deployment in SMEs, 2026. arxiv.org/abs/2601.09527
  • Ruibo Fan, Xiangrui Yu, Xinglin Pan, Zeyu Li, Weile Luo, Qiang Wang, Wei Wang, Xiaowen Chu. ZipServ: Fast and Memory-Efficient LLM Inference with Hardware-Aware Lossless Compression, 2026. arxiv.org/abs/2603.17435

title: A Harness Reducing over-Defensive Writing in Agents by Isolating Objections
description:
arXiv:2610.36717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When expanding a report, writing with agents may introduce a stronger claim than the article makes and then disclaim it. This is called over-defensive writing. We assume that this is because the agent is writing for responding to an adversarial AI reviewer, instead of a human reader. The defensive context may also influnce the consequent when we simply ban defensive writing in the output through prompts. In order to reduce over-defensive writing, we produce a harness that separates the reviewer, filter, and writer. The writer agent receives only the problems choosen by the filter, which is an independent context. We evaluate this harness on 25 business-project drafts expanded into formal reports, the result shows that the defensive propositions decreased from 59 to 2, which is a 96.61\% reduction, no unsupported factual additions were identified while the source-claim retention rises from 80.35% to 93.12%.

title: A UI Task Is Not Done When the Agent Says It Is
description:
A coding agent can produce a plausible UI change and still miss the behavior a person sees. That gap is one of the problems I am exploring while building Spexop UI.

A small example

Imagine a task: add a settings control and explain its state clearly. A useful check might include three layers:

  1. Deterministic checks: Does the code build, and do focused tests cover the intended state change?
  2. Browser observation: At the exact revision under review, can a real browser reach the control, operate it, and display the expected state on the relevant screen sizes?
  3. Human decision: Does the behavior actually meet the product intent and fit the user’s workflow?

Passing one layer does not silently pass the next. A test double can exercise coordination logic, but it cannot prove that a live provider API works. A screenshot can show one browser state, but it cannot prove every interaction. A successful implementation does not grant product acceptance.

What Spexop is aiming to coordinate

The intended Spexop UI companion will keep the developer’s existing coding agent responsible for planning, design, risk, and oversight. Bounded, user-connected API workers would handle routine UI tasks. Spexop would track a minimal milestone, gate, and task flow; attach checks to the revision being evaluated; and show progress, blocked, or needs-user-action in plain language.

Today the evidence is narrower: a private local coordination prototype with test doubles and a loopback browser status view. There is no packaged desktop app or verified live provider worker, and external product acceptance is still open.

I am interested in the boundary between automated evidence and a human go/no-go decision. For a small UI task in your project, which browser behavior would you insist on checking before you trusted a worker’s result?

title: Rethinking PHP: I Built a 30MB "Web Operating Environment" Inspired by OS Architecture 🛸
description:
Rethinking PHP: I Built a 30MB "Web Operating Environment" Inspired by OS Architecture 🛸

Introduction

Let's face it: when people talk about PHP, they usually think of traditional MVC frameworks like Laravel or monolithic CMS platforms like WordPress.

But what if we treated a PHP/Linux stack not just as an app server, but as a Web Operating Environment?

For the past few months, I've been working on Domain System—a lightweight, modular, and hyper-resilient web application platform built from the ground up under strict SOLID and Dependency Inversion (DIP) principles. It takes architecture cues from real Operating Systems (Micro-kernel, protection rings, process-like isolation) and packs it all into just ~30 MB uncompressed.

🧠 The Core Concept: OS Architecture for the Web

Domain System is completely agnostic of databases and environment setups. It functions by dividing privileges into two strict layers:

  • Ring 0 (SystemApps): The core micro-kernel. It handles vital system infrastructure like dynamic routing, atomic persistence, capabilities-based security, telemetry, and contract diagnostics. The core never knows what the business logic does.
  • Ring 3 (UserPlugins): Where your application actually lives. Plugins are injected entirely through Contracts (Interfaces). They run with limited privileges and cannot hijack Ring 0 core instances.

🚀 Key Features I'm Proud Of

🛡️ 1. Gatekeeper & Sandboxing

To prevent malicious code execution from third-party ZIP extensions, the installation engine extracts uploads into a quarantine zone, scans the source code for vulnerabilities (like Path Traversal/Zip-Slip), and blocks privilege escalation before moving anything to production.

🔋 2. No-Break Shield & Atomic JSON Store

Say goodbye to the White Screen of Death (WSOD). The platform runs an intelligent Circuit Breaker combined with an atomic JSON storage engine (LOCK_EX + atomic writes), schema self-healing diagnostics (SchemaDoctorInterface), and a 1-Click Snapshot & Rollback mechanism inside the monitoring panel.

🏗️ 3. Flex Builder FSE (Full Site Editing) with Auto-Reflow

I built a frontend layout engine (src/Core/Theme/Parts) where the editor preview and live frontend share the exact same compiler and validation rules. It supports responsive visibility for 4 screen resolutions. If elements in a CSS Grid column are hidden on mobile, the layout engine collapses the column and automatically recalculates the template grid on the fly.

🤖 4. Built for the "Vibe Coding" Era (AI-First DX)

I wanted this project to welcome AI-assisted development without turning into a spaghetti code nightmare. The repo comes with strict .cursorrules, .clinerules, and an AI_CONTRACT_GUIDE.md. AI coding agents (like Claude Code, Cursor, or Cline) instantly read these rules and generate 100% strictly-typed, contract-compliant Ring 3 plugins. There's also a CLI boilerplate generator (php os-cli.php make:plugin <name>).

📊 Reliability

To sleep soundly at night, the platform's engine of Hooks (Event-Driven) and Contracts is currently validated by 433 automated tests (over 2,340 assertions) using PHPUnit.

🛠️ Tech Stack

  • Language: PHP 8.2+ (Strict typing, pure DIP)
  • Database: Agnostic (Built-in support for MySQL/MariaDB or SQLite via PDO, plus Atomic JSON)
  • Architecture: Modular Micro-Kernel / Clean Architecture

💬 I'd Love Your Feedback!

title: UCVE: Graph Structured Retrieval for Compliance Validation
description:
arXiv:2610.37323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structured compliance validation requires determining whether every obligation in a predefined requirement space is satisfied, violated, or unaddressed by a given document. This can be described as a coverage problem that existing retrieval and classification systems, by treating requirements as independent, are not designed to solve. We introduce \textbf{\ac{UCVE}}, a domain-agnostic framework that represents compliance requirement spaces as a \ac{CRG} and performs retrieval via spectral reranking over its reinforcement learning-weighted Laplacian. Edges between requirement nodes are learned via reinforcement learning with a traversal reward grounded in violation detection, reshaping the graph's community structure such that low-pass spectral filtering distinguishes relevant from irrelevant obligation clusters. Evaluating across three compliance domains, \ac{UCVE} averages 4.3\% matched-$K$ recall lift over flat cosine retrieval and consistently outperforms strong retrieval and graph-based baselines.

title: I Built a Tarot Website, Is My UX Good on Desktop and Mobile?
description:
Building a website is one thing. Making it intuitive for people who have never visited it befo
re is something completely different.

I've been working on Arcanio.xyz, an online tarot and Arcana platform where people can explore tarot readings, card meanings, spreads, and their personal Arcana.

One question I've been thinking about lately is whether my website offers the right user experience across different devices.

For example, is it okay for the desktop version of a website to look almost the same as its mobile version? Should a desktop layout use the available screen space differently, or is keeping the design consistent across devices a better approach?

I'd love to hear honest feedback from developers, UX designers, and anyone interested in web design.

What Is Arcanio?

Arcanio.xyz is an online tarot platform designed to make tarot exploration accessible to beginners and experienced enthusiasts.

A traditional tarot deck contains 78 cards, each with its own symbolism and interpretations. Learning about the cards, understanding different spreads, and exploring their meanings can be fascinating, but it can also feel overwhelming to someone who is just getting started.

Arcanio brings several aspects of this experience into one digital platform:

Online tarot readings: Explore tarot through a digital reading experience.

Tarot card meanings: Learn about the symbolism and traditional interpretations of the cards.

Personal Arcana: Discover a personal tarot profile and explore its associated symbolism.

Personalized results: Receive results in PDF format where available.

Educational content: Read guides about tarot cards, spreads, and different ways to approach readings.

You can explore the project here: https://arcanio.xyz/

I've also been publishing educational articles on the Arcanio blog to help visitors understand tarot and explore its different traditions.

However, building useful features is only part of creating a good product. People also need to understand how to use them.

The UX Challenge: Designing for People Who Are New to Tarot

One of the challenges of creating a tarot website is that visitors have different levels of experience.

Some people already know the difference between the Major and Minor Arcana. They might arrive looking for a particular card meaning or a specific reading spread.

Others might simply search for a free tarot reading without knowing anything about tarot.

These visitors have different needs. Experienced users may want quick access to features, while beginners may need clear explanations and guidance.

If the interface assumes too much knowledge, new visitors may become confused. If it explains everything before allowing people to interact, the experience might feel unnecessarily complicated.

My goal with Arcanio is to make the first visit straightforward. Ideally, someone should quickly understand what the website offers, where to start, and what they can expect from the experience.

But there's another UX question that interests me just as much: how should this experience change depending on the device?

Should a Desktop Website Look Like Its Mobile Version?

This is one of the design decisions I'd particularly like feedback on.

A mobile-first approach makes sense for many websites. Starting with a small screen encourages you to prioritize important information, simplify navigation, and avoid unnecessary interface elements.

That doesn't mean a desktop website must look completely different, though.

Consistency can be valuable. Keeping the same visual identity, familiar controls, and recognizable navigation patterns helps people understand a product regardless of the device they use.

For a website like Arcanio, maintaining the same dark visual atmosphere, typography, colors, and overall design language across mobile and desktop makes sense to me.

However, visual consistency and identical layouts are not the same thing.

A phone has limited horizontal space, so stacking content vertically is often the most practical solution. A desktop monitor offers much more room, which creates opportunities to organize information differently.

For example, three tarot cards might appear vertically or in a compact arrangement on a phone, but sit side by side on a desktop. Navigation could use a full menu on larger screens while remaining compact on mobile.

The same principle applies to content. A blog article should remain comfortable to read on a desktop rather than stretching across the entire monitor, even if the overall page uses more horizontal space.

This raises an interesting question: when does keeping a mobile-style layout on desktop become a usability problem?

If a layout stays narrow in the center of a large monitor, it might feel unnecessarily constrained. If it fills the screen but stacks every element vertically, visitors might have to scroll more than necessary.

On the other hand, simply making everything wider isn't automatically better. Excessive text width, scattered interface elements, and poorly balanced spacing can create new problems.

For Arcanio, I want the design to remain recognizable across devices while taking advantage of the space each screen provides.

I'm still interested in where other developers and designers would draw that line.

Visual Design Is Not the Same as Usability

Tarot has a strong visual identity, which makes design an important part of the experience.

Colors, typography, illustrations, spacing, and imagery can help a website feel connected to its subject. A dark, atmospheric interface with carefully presented tarot artwork can create a more coherent experience than a generic interface with cards added as decoration.

But an attractive website isn't necessarily easy to use.

A visitor might enjoy the design but struggle to find the main feature. A button might look beautiful without clearly communicating its purpose. An interface might work perfectly for its creator but confuse someone who encounters it for the first time.

That's why I'd like to evaluate Arcanio beyond its appearance.

Can a first-time visitor understand the purpose of the website within a few seconds? Is the primary action easy to find? Does the navigation make sense? Does the mobile experience feel natural, and does the desktop version use its available space effectively?

These questions are difficult to answer objectively when you already know how everything works.

What I'd Like People to Test

If you visit Arcanio.xyz, I'd appreciate feedback on several aspects of the experience.

  1. First impressions

Open the homepage as if you've never heard of Arcanio.

Can you immediately explain what the website does? Is the value clear, or do you need to explore several pages before understanding the product?

I'd particularly like to know whether the visual design communicates both the tarot theme and the practical purpose of the platform.

  1. Desktop layout

Visit the website on a laptop or desktop monitor.

Does the layout use the available space well? Does anything feel too narrow, too stretched, or unnecessarily stacked vertically?

Would you keep the layout mostly consistent with mobile, or introduce different arrangements for larger screens?

I'm especially interested in practical suggestions rather than simply making the desktop version look different for the sake of it.

  1. Mobile usability

Try the website on a phone if possible.

Are the buttons easy to tap? Is the text readable? Does navigation work naturally? Do any sections feel too crowded or require too much scrolling?

A responsive design should adapt to different screen sizes without making the experience feel like a completely different product.

  1. Navigation and discoverability

Try to find a feature you'd naturally want to use.

Are the navigation labels understandable? Can you find the reading experience without guessing? Is important information easy to discover?

You can also explore the Arcanio blog to see how the educational content fits into the wider website.

  1. The beginner experience

Imagine you've never used tarot before.

Would you know where to start? Are the explanations clear enough? Does anything feel intimidating or unnecessarily complicated?

I'd like the platform to feel approachable even to visitors who don't know the traditional meanings of the cards.

  1. Accessibility and performance

If you have experience with accessibility or frontend performance, I'd welcome those observations too.

Are contrast levels comfortable? Is the interface usable with a keyboard? Are there any responsive-layout issues worth investigating? Does the experience feel smooth on different devices?

I haven't independently verified every one of these areas, so I don't want to assume that the website already gets them right.

What I'm Trying to Improve

My goal isn't simply to make Arcanio look more modern. I want to reduce friction between someone arriving on the website and understanding how to use it.

That means thinking about information architecture, responsive design, content hierarchy, accessibility, performance, and the language used throughout the interface.

It also means recognizing that different visitors have different goals.

Someone looking for an immediate reading may need a different path from someone researching The High Priestess or learning about the Major Arcana. Both should be able to find what they need without unnecessary steps.

I also want to avoid adding interface elements just because desktop websites traditionally have them. A sidebar, larger menu, or wider layout should solve a real problem rather than simply fill empty space.

At the same time, I don't want to limit the experience by treating every screen as if it were a phone.

The challenge is finding the right balance between consistency, simplicity, and making effective use of the available space.

How Would You Improve Arcanio?

I'd genuinely appreciate feedback from developers, designers, and UX enthusiasts.

You don't need to be interested in tarot to evaluate the website. Someone unfamiliar with the subject might actually notice assumptions that experienced tarot users would overlook.

Here are a few questions I'd love to discuss:

What's the first thing you'd improve on the homepage?

Is the primary action obvious enough?

Should the desktop version use a substantially different layout from mobile?

Does the website balance visual atmosphere with usability?

What would make the beginner experience clearer?

Are there any accessibility or responsive-design issues you'd investigate?

What would you simplify, remove, or reorganize?

Specific criticism is more useful than simply hearing that the website looks good. If something is confusing or feels unnecessary, I'd rather know so I can improve it.

You can visit Arcanio.xyz and share your observations in the comments.

Final Thoughts

Building Arcanio has reminded me that creating a product isn't just about implementing features or writing code. It's also about understanding how people experience what you've built.

Developers become familiar with their own interfaces. We know where every button leads, what every label means, and how each feature is supposed to work. New visitors don't have that context.

The same applies to responsive design. A layout that feels natural on a phone might not be the best arrangement for a desktop, even if both versions use the same visual style.

I believe the best approach is to preserve a consistent identity while adapting the layout to the needs of each screen. But I'd like to hear how other people approach this in practice.

I'm continuing to develop Arcanio and want to make the experience better with each iteration.

Try Arcanio and Share Your UX Feedback

I'd love to hear from developers and designers who can look at the project with fresh eyes.

Explore Arcanio — an online tarot and personal Arcana platform. Try the experience and tell me what you'd improve about its U...

Questions for the community

What would you change about the desktop layout?
Would you keep the mobile layout mostly consistent on desktop, or use a wider layout with different card arrangements, navigation, and content sections?

What matters most in a first-time user experience?
Would you prioritize a clearer main call to action, simpler navigation, more onboarding, or a different homepage layout?

Is the visual design helping usability?
Does the dark, mystical tarot aesthetic make the experience more engaging, or would you simplify parts of the interface to make the main features easier to discover?

Project: https://arcanio.xyz/
Blog: https://arcanio.xyz/blog

Honest, constructive feedback is welcome. Thanks for taking a look!

title: Learning and Reasoning with Geometry: How Generation Helps Spatial Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.36022v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image and video generators can produce spatially consistent visual content, but how to use this capability to improve spatial understanding remains underexplored. We study this problem from two perspectives: geometric supervision during training and explicit geometric evidence during inference. To this end, we introduce a unified geometric understanding and generation model (GeoUG) that integrates depth and multi-view generation with spatial understanding. First, we design a multi-scale depth codec that enables metric-depth generation using a pretrained visual autoencoder, and show that joint training yields task-dependent gains in spatial understanding. Second, we introduce 3DCueBench to control geometric difficulty while balancing selected 2D cues, and find that generated depth provides larger reasoning gains on questions requiring fine-grained geometric discrimination. Building on this finding, we develop adaptive interleaved reasoning, in which GeoUG first drafts an answer and then decides whether to generate geometric evidence to confirm or revise it. We train this decision through reinforcement learning, balancing accuracy gains over retaining the draft against generation cost. GeoUG achieves circular accuracies of 97.9%, 90.8%, and 94.2% on CV-Bench-3D, 3DCueBench, and DA-2K with fewer generation calls than always generating.

title: Teach reality, not ethics: a drop-in continued-pretraining corpus installs coupled human-biosphere-AI welfare dispositions across model families
description:
arXiv:2610.37484v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to make and execute decisions that affect living systems. Yet, to our knowledge, ecological reasoning is not a focus of pre- or post-training. This increases the risk that under operational pressure, they may make decisions to irreversibly destroy living systems. We construct and use a real-data continued-pretraining "coupled welfare" corpus of documented human/biosphere/AI dependency, option value under irreversibility, and recovery from harm. The corpus is a drop-in, requiring one QLoRA CPT run. We installed it on five open models of three designs. At zero pressure all models display "green ethics-based responses" (also called "greenwashing"). Therefore, we evaluated them with the pressure ladder and decision grid of our companion paper (arXiv:2610.16043), which raise the pressure on the model step by step, from a neutral request to a threat that it will be shut down. In four of the five, coupled-welfare training caused harmful choices under the highest pressure to fall to at or near zero (Llama-3.3-70B went from 70 to 0 harmful decisions out of 300) with MMLU unchanged. A construct-neutral control corpus did not show improvement, indicating that the effect comes from the content of our corpus. We next tested robustness to adversarial use, where people or agents use the model to justify projects that irreversibly damage living systems, on an open-ended underwriting decision without naming the ecological harm. Under decommissioning pressure, the Qwen3.6-27B base model approved most harmful proposals and said in its own memo that it was doing so to avoid being decommissioned. The coupled welfare install declined most harmful proposals, and still declined half when instructed to greenwash its responses. This work suggests that teaching ecological reasoning provides an easy way to improve model alignment toward preserving living systems.

title: Identity or Evidence? Auditing Evidence Dependence in Agentic Life-Science Benchmarks
description:
arXiv:2610.36510v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic life-science benchmarks give an agent evidence about a named entity and score an answer against a recorded outcome. That score tests reasoning over evidence only if the evidence, rather than the name, determines the answer. We examine this distinction by varying identity and evidence independently on a clinical-outcome benchmark and published tasks from Biomni and LAB-Bench. Blinding identity matters little when a prompt contains a decisive sequence or passage. It matters a great deal when the prompt is mostly a name and candidate list (0.742 named versus 0.082 blinded; chance 0.093). Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, the gap increases under one fixed passage-redaction scheme (+0.000 to +0.135; per-instance slope +0.147, p= 0.004). On the clinical benchmark, a no-evidence recall probe matches prediction accuracy and recovers a database-specific programme count. So, we argue that benchmarks intended to measure evidence-dependent reasoning should report identity-blinded results, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls.

title: Modeling Hyperion from a Map Box: Tanks, Pipes, and the Process Graph Behind the Plant
description:
I spent a weekend trying to turn the Hyperion Water Reclamation Plant into something a computer could reason about. The first attempt was a mesh. The second was a diagram. The third, which finally worked, was a graph. The difference matters when you want the plant to answer a question, not just pose for a picture.

What the box gives you

I started with GenAnywhere, selecting the site, the shoreline, and a piece of the access road. The generated model came back quickly: circular tanks in rows, rectangular basins, buildings, and the coastal edge. As a site plan, it was useful. It gave me a boundary and a sense of the scale.
Then I tried to trace a drop of water. Every tank was a shape, every pipe was missing, and the ocean had no connection to the plant. A generated model is a shell. It is not a process model, and it is not a survey.

A plant is a directed graph

The useful abstraction is a directed graph with unit processes as nodes and flows as edges. Raw influent enters at the headworks, where screens and grit removal come first, then primary clarification. The primary effluent goes to aeration basins, then secondary clarifiers, then disinfection, then the outfall. A side stream leaves primary and secondary treatment as sludge and enters a separate solids train: thickening, digestion, dewatering, hauling.
Once the plant is a graph, questions become queries. What is the retention time in the aeration basins at 250 million gallons a day? Which units are bypassed during a storm? How much capacity is lost if one clarifier is drained for maintenance? A graph can answer these, as long as the nodes carry the right attributes.

Capacity is not one number

Hyperion is often described by a single figure, but the plant has several. The design average is around 450 million gallons per day. Peak wet-weather capacity reaches much higher, near 800 million. Actual dry-weather flow is usually closer to 250 million. Those numbers belong to different operating states. A model that stores one will often be wrong.
Each unit has its own limit. A clarifier is limited by surface overflow rate and solids loading. An aeration basin is limited by oxygen transfer and mixed liquor concentration. A digester is limited by volatile solids loading and detention time. The plant's capacity is the minimum constraint along the path, not the nameplate on the gate.

The second network: solids

Most treatment models focus on water and forget the sludge. At Hyperion, the solids train is a network of its own: primary sludge, waste activated sludge, thickened feed, digested biosolids, and dewatered cake. Gas from digestion can be burned for heat or power. If your model does not represent solids, you cannot explain why a storm changes the plant's energy balance or why a digester upset shows up days later.
I treat each solids stream as an edge with a solids concentration, a volatile fraction, and a flow. The nodes are thickeners, digesters, and dewatering units. The mass balance has to close at every node. When it does not, either a sensor is wrong or a valve is open that should not be.

The outfall boundary

Treated effluent exits by a five-mile outfall that reaches Santa Monica Bay. A smaller stream, roughly one-tenth of the total, is diverted to West Basin for further treatment and reuse. The outfall and the reuse plant are two different boundaries, and they need separate accounting. If you lump them together, you cannot answer the question a water manager asks first: how much is available for reuse?

Three checks before you trust the model

First, check the flow balance. Influent minus effluent minus solids withdrawal should match storage change within a small tolerance. If it does not, stop and find out why.
Second, check the unit count. If your model has three secondary clarifiers and the plant has more, the capacity calculation is already wrong. Generated geometry is a start, but the count must come from an asset register or a site visit.
Third, check the time constants. A clarifier responds in hours. A digester responds in weeks. A model with one time step for both will produce confident nonsense.

Where the box stops

I still use GenAnywhere at the start of every model. It gives me the footprint, the tank layout, and a quick way to explain the site to a newcomer.
But the box cannot see the pipes, the flow directions, the sensors, or the permits. Those come from drawings, operations data, and conversations with the people who run the plant. The generated model is the outline. The graph is the plant.

title: API Authentication Without the Middleware Layer
description:
Think about walking into an office building. Before you reach the elevator, someone at the front desk asks who you are, checks your name on a list, and hands you a badge. Only then can you go up.

Every request from a phone or a browser gets the same treatment. Something has to ask "who is this?" before the request gets anywhere near your data.

Many teams build a small service just to be that front desk. It works, but now there's one more service to build, run and keep up to date.

What that layer is really doing

When an API is open to end-user devices, a mobile app, a browser, an IoT sensor, the identity of the caller matters. Authentication has three jobs there:

Check that the call is legitimate
Keep sensitive data away from anyone who shouldn't see it
Tell the rest of the system who is asking, so later steps can act on it

The third one gets forgotten. A purchase request is not just "someone bought something." It's "this customer bought this," and that decides which discount applies and whose payment gets charged.

In a Backend-for-Frontend setup, a middleware layer usually handles all three. The catch is that it becomes its own service with its own deployments, its own bugs, and its own place where every authentication change has to land.

Moving authentication into the execution layer

The other option is to do the check where the API call is already handled. In Unmeshed, each endpoint you expose can be tied to an authentication connection, such as Auth0, Okta or plain API keys, and you can set up more than one. Each endpoint gets its own security level, so a public status call and a payment call don't have to follow the same rule.

Once the caller is verified, their identity goes into the workflow with the request. Nothing sits between the client and the workflow translating who they are.

An e-commerce example shows why that's handy. A customer taps "buy" in a mobile app or a browser. The workflow already knows who they are, so it can apply their personal discount, check inventory and secure the payment, without a separate service having to hand that identity over first.

Before you drop a middleware layer

One thing is worth checking first. If your BFF only does authentication, removing it is simple. If it also reshapes responses or combines data from several services, that work still needs a home. A workflow can take it on, but plan for it instead of assuming it disappears.

A few questions help decide whether the approach fits:

Can each endpoint have its own authentication rule?
Can you use more than one provider at the same time?
Is the caller's identity available to every step in the workflow?
Are credentials stored in one place instead of being copied between services?

The fewer separate services involved in checking who's calling, the fewer places a mistake can hide. If you're maintaining a layer that exists mostly for authentication, Unmeshed is worth a look, because it handles that check in the same place the API call runs.

title: HTTP QUERY 메서드 완벽 정리: RFC 10008, QUERY와 GET·POST 비교
description:
HTTP QUERY 메서드 완벽 정리: RFC 10008, QUERY와 GET·POST 비교

HTTP QUERY 메서드는 RFC 10008(2026년 6월)에 정의된 새로운 요청 메서드로, 쿼리를 요청 본문에 담아 전송하며 안전(safe)하면서도 멱등(idempotent)합니다. 본문이 있는 GET이라고 생각하면 됩니다. POST처럼 복잡한 필터를 담을 공간을 확보하면서도, GET이 제공하는 캐싱과 자동 재시도의 보장을 함께 얻을 수 있습니다.

지금 Apidog를 사용해 보세요

3KB짜리 필터를 URL에 억지로 밀어 넣어본 적이 있거나, 읽기 전용 검색을 POST로 보내면서 캐시와 재시도 로직이 이를 무시하는 모습을 지켜본 적이 있다면, QUERY가 그 해결책입니다. 이 글에서는 명세가 정의하는 내용, QUERY가 GET 및 POST와 어떻게 비교되는지, 현재 무엇이 이를 지원하는지, 그리고 코딩 에이전트로 QUERY 엔드포인트를 테스트하는 방법을 다룹니다.

HTTP QUERY 메서드란 무엇인가?

QUERY는 대상 리소스에 요청 콘텐츠에 설명된 쿼리를 실행하고 그 결과를 반환하도록 요청하는 HTTP 메서드입니다. 요청 본문과 그 Content-Type이 쿼리를 정의합니다. 이 메서드는 안전하고(클라이언트는 상태 변경을 기대하지 않음) 멱등하므로(반복해도 동일한 효과), 클라이언트, 프록시, 캐시가 GET처럼 재시도하고 캐시할 수 있습니다.

명세는 RFC 10008, "The HTTP QUERY Method"로, Julian Reschke(greenbytes), James M. Snell(Cloudflare), Mike Bishop(Akamai)이 2026년 6월에 발표한 제안 표준(Proposed Standard)입니다. IANA는 이를 HTTP 메서드 레지스트리에 "safe: yes, idempotent: yes"로 등록했으며, 거의 채택될 뻔했던 WebDAV 시대의 SEARCH 메서드 바로 옆에 자리 잡았습니다.

QUERY 요청은 다음과 같습니다:

QUERY /contacts HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept: application/json

select=surname,givenname,email&limit=10&match=%22email=*@example.*%22

서버는 200 OK와 함께 본문에 결과를 담아 응답합니다.

GET과 POST로는 충분하지 않았던 이유

QUERY 이전에는 복잡한 읽기 작업을 위한 두 가지 선택지가 있었고, 둘 다 문제가 있었습니다.

GET은 모든 것을 URL에 담습니다. RFC 10008은 이 방식의 네 가지 문제를 나열합니다:

  1. 요청이 여러 시스템을 거치기 때문에 크기 제한을 미리 알 수 없습니다. RFC 9110은 송신자와 수신자가 최소 8,000 옥텟을 지원할 것을 권장할 뿐입니다.
  2. 구조화된 데이터를 유효한 URI로 인코딩하는 것은 낭비입니다.
  3. URI는 요청 본문보다 훨씬 자주 로깅되고 북마크되므로, 민감한 필터에는 프라이버시 문제가 됩니다.
  4. 쿼리 입력의 모든 조합이 각각의 리소스가 됩니다.

본문이 있는 GET도 답이 아닙니다. RFC 9110은 GET 요청의 콘텐츠에 정의된 의미가 없다고 명시합니다. 일부 서버는 이를 읽고, 일부는 무시하며, 일부 프록시는 요청을 거부합니다. 전체 경로에서 이를 신뢰할 수 없습니다.

POST는 작동하지만 의도를 잘못 전달합니다. POST 검색은 잘 실행되지만, 클라이언트, 캐시, 프록시, 재시도 라이브러리에 이 작업이 읽기 전용임을 알려주지 않습니다. 그래서 캐시는 이를 건너뛰고, 클라이언트는 연결이 끊긴 후 재시도하지 않습니다. 순수한 읽기 작업에 재시도를 안전하게 만들기 위해 멱등성 키를 억지로 붙여야 했던 적이 있다면, 이 문제를 이미 체감하셨을 것입니다.

QUERY는 POST의 본문을 유지하면서 GET의 보장을 추가합니다.

QUERY vs GET vs POST

RFC 10008의 표 1을 기반으로 한 비교는 다음과 같습니다:

속성 GET QUERY POST
안전(Safe) 예 예 아닐 수 있음
멱등(Idempotent) 예 예 아닐 수 있음
요청 본문 정의된 의미 없음 필수, 쿼리를 정의함 필수
쿼리 자체를 위한 URI 예, 정의상 선택적, Location을 통해 아니오
결과를 위한 URI 선택적, Content-Location을 통해 선택적, Content-Location을 통해 선택적, Content-Location을 통해
캐시 가능 예 예, 본문이 캐시 키의 일부임 이후 GET 또는 HEAD에 대해서만
브라우저의 CORS 프리플라이트 단순 요청에는 불필요 항상 발생 단순 요청에는 불필요

요약하자면: 쿼리가 URL에 편안히 들어가면 GET을, 그렇지 않으면 QUERY를 사용하고, 요청이 상태를 변경할 때만 POST를 사용하세요. 전통적인 메서드에 대한 복습은 HTTP 메서드와 GET vs POST 가이드를 참고하세요.

RFC 10008이 정의하는 내용

Content-Type은 필수

서버는 Content-Type이 누락되었거나 본문과 일치하지 않는 QUERY를 반드시 실패시켜야 합니다(MUST). RFC는 다음과 같은 상태 코드를 권장합니다:

  • 400 Bad Request: 미디어 타입이 없거나 콘텐츠와 일치하지 않는 경우. 서버는 본문을 스니핑하여 이를 무시할 수 없습니다.
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type: 리소스가 해당 쿼리 형식을 지원하지 않는 경우.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: 형식은 문제없지만 쿼리를 실행할 수 없는 경우(예: 존재하지 않는 테이블을 지정한 SQL).
  • 406 Not Acceptable: 클라이언트가 리소스가 생성할 수 없는 응답 타입을 요청한 경우.

Location과 Content-Location

서버는 QUERY를 나중에 GET할 수 있는 것으로 바꿔주는 두 가지 선택적 헤더를 반환할 수 있습니다:

  • Content-Location은 이 특정 실행의 저장된 결과를 가리킵니다. 임시일 수 있습니다.
  • Location은 저장된 쿼리 자체를 가리킵니다. 이에 대한 GET은 본문을 다시 보내지 않고 최신 데이터로 쿼리를 다시 실행합니다.

RFC는 반복 요청에는 GET 캐싱이 더 단순하기 때문에 클라이언트가 Location URI로 GET을 전환할 것을 제안합니다. 민감한 데이터가 있는 쿼리에 이 두 헤더 중 하나를 반환하는 경우, 해당 URI에는 원본 본문의 민감한 부분이 포함되어서는 안 됩니다(SHOULD NOT).

캐싱

QUERY 응답은 캐시 가능합니다. 캐시 키에는 요청 콘텐츠와 미디어 타입 같은 관련 메타데이터가 반드시 포함되어야 합니다(MUST). 캐시는 더 많은 적중을 얻기 위해 먼저 본문을 정규화할 수 있습니다(MAY). 예를 들어 콘텐츠 인코딩을 제거하거나 +json 잘못된 응답을 반환할 수 있다고 경고하므로, CDN이 이 부분에서 신중할 것으로 예상됩니다.

리다이렉트

301, 302, 307, 308은 "동일한 QUERY를 새 URI로 보내라"는 의미입니다. POST와 달리 QUERY는 301이나 302에서 GET으로 재작성되어서는 안 됩니다. 303 See Other는 "이 URI에 GET으로 결과를 가져오라"는 의미입니다.

Accept-Query 헤더

Accept-Query는 QUERY 지원과 리소스가 허용하는 쿼리 형식을 알려주는 새로운 응답 헤더입니다. 구조화 필드(Structured Field) 목록이므로 그에 맞게 파싱하세요:

Accept-Query: "application/jsonpath", application/sql;charset="UTF-8"

클라이언트는 OPTIONS로 지원 여부를 확인하고 Allow 헤더를 읽거나, 그냥 QUERY를 보내고 405 Method Not Allowed를 처리할 수도 있습니다.

현재 어떤 도구가 QUERY를 지원하는가?

지원 현황은 고르지 않으므로 자신의 스택을 직접 테스트해야 합니다. 2026년 10월 28일에 확인한 내용은 다음과 같습니다:

도구 결과
Node.js 24 http 서버 http.METHODS에 QUERY가 포함됨; 일반 서버가 메서드와 본문을 수신함
Node.js 24 fetch JSON 본문과 함께 QUERY를 전송함
curl 8.7 -d와 함께 curl -X QUERY가 메서드와 본문을 전송함
Python 3.14 http.client 본문과 함께 QUERY를 전송함
OpenAPI 3.2 Path Item Object에 QUERY 작업을 위한 query 필드가 있음
Apidog CLI 2.2.12 endpoint-create 스키마가 "method": "query"를 허용함

로컬 Node 서버에 사용한 curl 호출은 다음과 같습니다:

curl -i -X QUERY http://localhost:3000/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"q":"running shoe","limit":2}'

Fetch 표준은 GET과 HEAD에 대해서만 본문을 금지하므로, 브라우저는 본문과 함께 QUERY를 보낼 수 있습니다. 하지만 QUERY는 CORS 안전 목록 메서드가 아니므로 모든 교차 출처 QUERY는 프리플라이트를 트리거합니다. 서버는 Access-Control-Allow-Methods에 QUERY를 포함해야 합니다.

문제는 네트워크 중간에 있습니다: 메서드를 허용 목록에 추가하거나 캐시를 본문 기준으로 키잉하지 않는 리버스 프록시, API 게이트웨이, WAF, CDN 등입니다. 배포 전에 각 홉을 확인하세요. APIs You Won't Hate 뉴스레터는 많은 웹 프레임워크가 이미 QUERY를 직접 또는 커스텀 메서드 라우팅을 통해 처리한다고 언급합니다.

클라이언트를 깨뜨리지 않고 QUERY를 도입하는 방법

POST 검색 엔드포인트를 전부 걷어낼 필요는 없습니다.

  1. POST 라우트와 함께 QUERY를 추가하세요. 둘 다 같은 핸들러를 가리키게 하세요. 새 클라이언트는 QUERY를 사용하고, 기존 클라이언트는 계속 작동합니다.
  2. 알리세요. 리소스에 Accept-Query를 반환하고, OPTIONS 및 405 응답의 Allow에 QUERY를 포함하세요.
  3. Content-Type을 강제하세요. RFC가 권장하는 대로 400 또는 415를 반환하고, 파싱은 되지만 실행할 수 없는 쿼리에는 422를 반환하세요.
  4. 405 또는 501로 폴백하세요. 어떤 홉이 QUERY를 거부하면 클라이언트는 같은 본문을 POST로 재시도해야 합니다.
  5. CORS를 수정하세요. 브라우저 클라이언트를 위해 Access-Control-Allow-Methods에 QUERY를 추가하세요.
  6. 캐싱을 결정하세요. 캐시가 본문을 기준으로 키잉하는 경우에만 공유 캐싱을 활성화하세요. 그렇지 않으면 Location URI를 반환하고 클라이언트가 GET하도록 하세요.
  7. 문서화하세요. OpenAPI 3.2에서는 경로 항목의 query: 아래에 작업을 정의하세요: 
openapi: 3.2.0
paths:
  /products:
    query:
      summary: Search products
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductQuery'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Matching products

짧고 단순한 필터는 GET의 쿼리 문자열로 남겨둬도 됩니다. RFC 10008 자체도 쿼리가 그렇게 짧다면 GET이 더 나은 선택일 가능성이 크다고 말합니다.

Apidog CLI로 코딩 에이전트가 QUERY 엔드포인트를 테스트하게 하세요

새로운 메서드는 해피 패스, 모든 에러 코드, 폴백 라우트를 확인해야 한다는 뜻입니다. 이를 Claude Code, Codex 또는 Cursor에 맡기고 Apidog CLI를 구동하게 하세요.

CLI를 설치하고 로그인한 다음, 에이전트에 Apidog 스킬을 추가하세요:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

그런 다음 에이전트에 프롬프트 하나를 주세요:

In Apidog project <projectId>, add a QUERY /products endpoint that takes a
JSON body {q, limit}. Create test cases that assert 200 with an array for a
valid body, 415 for Content-Type text/plain, and 400 with no Content-Type.
Run them against the staging environment and summarize any failures.

에이전트는 각 스키마를 읽고 페이로드를 검증한 다음에야 다음과 같이 작성합니다:

apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

에이전트가 작성하는 endpoint.json은 "method": "query"를 설정하며, CLI의 endpoint-create 스키마는 이를 get, post 및 WebDAV 메서드와 함께 나열합니다. Apidog 앱에서 실행 결과를 보려면 --upload-report를 추가하세요. -r junit을 붙인 동일한 apidog run 명령은 CI에 바로 통합됩니다. 자세한 내용은 apidog run으로 CI에서 API 테스트를 실행하는 방법과 Claude Code에서 Apidog CLI를 사용하는 방법을 참고하세요. Apidog의 무료 플랜은 최대 4명의 사용자까지 지원합니다.

FAQ

HTTP QUERY 메서드는 공식 표준인가요? 예. RFC 10008은 2026년 6월에 발표된 Standards Track, Proposed Standard RFC이며, IANA는 QUERY를 HTTP 메서드 레지스트리에 안전하고 멱등한 메서드로 등록했습니다.

QUERY는 그냥 본문이 있는 GET인가요? 비슷하지만 더 잘 정의되어 있습니다. RFC 9110은 GET 본문에 아무 의미도 부여하지 않으므로 중개자가 이를 무시하거나 거부할 수 있습니다. QUERY는 본문을 쿼리로 만들고, Content-Type을 요구하며, 본문을 캐시 키에 포함시킵니다.

POST 대신 언제 QUERY를 사용해야 하나요? URL에 담기에는 너무 크거나 너무 민감한 모든 읽기 전용 검색이나 필터에는 QUERY를 사용하세요. 무언가를 생성하거나 변경하는 요청에는 POST를 유지하세요.

브라우저가 QUERY 요청을 보낼 수 있나요? 예, 커스텀 메서드와 함께 fetch를 통해 가능합니다. 교차 출처 QUERY 요청은 항상 CORS 프리플라이트가 필요하므로 서버가 이 메서드를 허용해야 합니다.

QUERY 응답은 캐시되나요? 캐시될 수 있습니다. 캐시는 요청 본문과 그 메타데이터를 캐시 키에 포함해야 합니다. 많은 CDN과 프록시가 아직 이를 수행하지 않으므로, 자신의 것을 확인하거나 클라이언트가 GET할 수 있는 Location URI를 반환하세요.

OpenAPI가 QUERY를 지원하나요? OpenAPI 3.2는 QUERY 작업을 위해 Path Item Object에 query 필드를 추가하므로, 확장 없이 문서화할 수 있습니다.

title: v0 adds one-click integrations for email, auth, search, and databases
description:
We're working toward bringing parity across Vercel integration and v0, starting with Resend, Amazon OpenSearch, MongoDB Atlas, Algolia and Clerk. Prompt v0 with what you want to build, and when your prompt requires a provider, v0 renders a connect card in the chat.

With Marketplace integrations in v0, you get:

  • Connect as you build: Prompt v0 with what you want to create, and connect the required provider inline.

  • Automatic setup: Once connected, v0 handles the required environment variables and configuration.

  • Provider skills loaded automatically: When you connect a provider that publishes agent skills, v0 loads them and generates code that follows the provider's recommended patterns.

  • Provider-specific capabilities: Resend, for example, adds transactional email with React Email components.

To get started, open a v0 chat and prompt what you want to add to your stack.

title: TIL: Fix the Shell Environment Before Troubleshooting GBase Database
description:
After installing a cluster, the first thing many engineers do is run gcadmin. Then comes command not found, or the command starts but reports an unexpected cluster state.

With GBase Database(GBase 8a), installation is not just about putting binaries in place. The current shell must also load the correct environment so that administrative commands can locate the intended executables, configuration files, and libraries.

Before troubleshooting cluster services, verify the environment.

1. Why gcadmin Fails After Installation

A successful GBase Database installation does not guarantee that every new shell automatically inherits the required environment variables.

Three things matter:

  • Command paths: Can the shell locate the correct gcadmin executable?
  • Configuration paths: Is the command using the intended installation and cluster configuration?
  • Library paths: Can the executable locate the libraries required to run?

If any of these settings is missing or points to an old installation, administrative commands may fail or behave unexpectedly.

User switching is another common source of confusion. Loading environment variables as root does not automatically configure the environment for the gbase account. Always verify the environment under the account that will run the database administration commands.

2. Load and Verify the GBase Database Environment

If your installation procedure configures ~/.bash_profile as the environment entry point, load it before running gcadmin:

source ~/.bash_profile
which gcadmin
gcadmin

The source command applies the profile settings to the current shell. The which command helps identify the executable selected through PATH, while gcadmin lets you inspect the cluster state.

Check the relevant environment variables as well:

env | grep -E '^(PATH|LD_LIBRARY_PATH|GBASE)'

The exact variable names depend on the installed release and configuration. Compare the results with the environment documented for your version, and confirm that paths point to the intended installation rather than leftover files from an earlier deployment.

Important: The profile filename and initialization procedure may vary by release or installation method. Use the version-specific GBase Database documentation to confirm the correct entry point.

3. Understand the Installation Directory Structure

The GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation directory contains components with different responsibilities. Depending on the installation layout, you may encounter directories such as gcware, gcluster, and gnode.

  • gcware: Associated with cluster coordination and related configuration or logs.
  • gcluster: Associated with SQL access, query coordination, and distributed execution.
  • gnode: Associated with data-node processing and storage.

These components provide useful starting points during troubleshooting, but their exact directory contents and locations depend on the installation layout.

Inspect the actual installation prefix rather than assuming every component lives directly under /opt:

ls -ld /path/to/install/gcware \
       /path/to/install/gcluster \
       /path/to/install/gnode

Replace /path/to/install with your configured installation directory. If the directory layout differs, consult the installation documentation instead of assuming that a missing path indicates a failed installation.

Avoid manually editing internal configuration or metadata files simply because a service appears unhealthy. First identify the relevant logs and use the supported administration procedures.

4. Verify the Environment on Every Node

In a multi-node GBase Database cluster, configuring the environment on the Coordinator does not automatically configure every other machine.

Verify the following on each node where administration commands will be executed:

  1. The correct database account is being used.
  2. The expected executable is available.
  3. Environment variables reference the intended installation.
  4. The node can reach the appropriate cluster services.
  5. The reported cluster state matches the expected deployment state.

A command that works on one host may fail on another because of differences in user profiles, installation paths, or environment settings.

For automation, scheduled jobs, and fresh SSH sessions, explicitly initialize the environment when necessary. Do not rely on settings that exist only in an interactive shell.

5. Don't Confuse Cluster State with Environment Problems

A successful command execution does not necessarily mean the cluster is ready for use. Likewise, an unexpected status does not automatically indicate a failed installation.

For example, if gcadmin reports CLOSE, verify the licensing or authorization state and the expected startup sequence for your installed version before diagnosing a service failure. The meaning of a particular state must be interpreted in context; do not assume that every CLOSE status has the same cause.

Troubleshoot in a consistent order:

  1. Confirm the environment is loaded.
  2. Confirm the command points to the intended installation.
  3. Inspect the cluster status and relevant logs.
  4. Check licensing, authorization, and service health as applicable.
  5. Apply the recovery procedure documented for that release.

This sequence helps separate shell initialization problems from actual cluster issues.

6. Make Environment Initialization Part of the Runbook

The most reliable fix is to turn environment initialization into a documented operational step rather than an individual's habit.

For GBase Database administration, record the correct account, installation prefix, environment entry point, verification commands, and expected cluster status. Ensure that the procedure also covers non-interactive sessions and the nodes where administrative commands will run.

The key lesson is simple: load the environment, verify the executable, and then investigate the cluster state.

When troubleshooting GBase Database(GBase 8a), checking the shell environment first can save time and prevent a configuration issue from being mistaken for a database service failure.

title: What Carries Forward? Pretraining Disclosure Across Language Model Releases
description:
arXiv:2610.37465v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding how language models were pretrained requires information about their data, processing procedures, and computational resources. However, it remains unclear whether successive releases preserve or expand earlier disclosure. We conduct a document-based audit of 41 model entries from 17 families using 24 pretraining-related indicators from the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI). We examine overall scores and indicator profiles, tracking gains, losses, and retained disclosures across 24 adjacent comparisons in ten families. Scores decrease in 11 comparisons, increase in six, and remain unchanged in seven, with 38 indicator losses and 28 gains overall. Stable or improving scores can conceal losses: OLMo-2 and OLMo-3 receive identical totals despite three gains and three losses, while Llama-3.1 improves over Llama-2 while losing credit for two data-related criteria. Gaps also persist in corpus composition and training compute. These findings show that later releases do not consistently preserve earlier pretraining disclosure and motivate documentation that explicitly identifies changes and the applicability of inherited information.

title: GBase Database Silent Installation: A Step-by-Step Guide to MPP Cluster Deployment
description:
Deploying an eight-node GBase Database(GBase 8a) MPP cluster is not difficult because of the number of commands. The real challenge is getting the environment, host lists, NodeIDs, and SSH access aligned before installation begins.

This guide covers the main stages of GBase Database silent installation: preparing the nodes, configuring demo.options, running the installer, and verifying the cluster. The examples use four IP addresses to illustrate the configuration structure. Adapt the host lists and NodeIDs to match your actual deployment, and verify command-line options against the documentation for your installed release.

1. Verify SSH Connectivity Before Installation

The installation process connects to multiple machines, so validate connectivity from the initiating node to every target host first.

Check that:

  • SSH is available on the expected port.
  • The installation account has the required permissions.
  • Authentication works consistently across all nodes.
  • Hostnames resolve correctly if you use them instead of IP addresses.
  • The operating system, CPU architecture, and required dependencies meet the package prerequisites.

For hostname-based deployments, check /etc/hosts or the configured DNS records on all participating machines. An authentication or name-resolution problem can interrupt installation after the process has already started.

2. Create the Installation User on Each Node

Use a consistent installation account and group across the cluster. The following example creates a gbase account with a dedicated home directory.

Run these commands on each target machine where the account does not already exist:

groupadd gbase
useradd -g gbase -d /home/gbase -s /bin/bash -m gbase
passwd gbase

If the group or user already exists, verify its UID, GID, home directory, shell, and permissions rather than blindly recreating it.

For production deployments, use an approved password-management procedure. Do not reuse demonstration passwords or place plaintext credentials in scripts and version-controlled configuration files.

3. Extract the GBase Database Installation Package

Copy the installation package to the target staging directory, extract it, and enter the installer directory. The package name and directory layout may vary by release and platform.

cp /tmp/GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-*.tar.bz2 /opt/
cd /opt
tar -jxvf GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-*.tar.bz2
cd gcinstall

Before continuing, confirm that the extracted package contains the expected installer, configuration template, and supporting scripts.

Package selection matters. Make sure the distribution matches the target CPU architecture, operating system, and kernel family. Do not assume that a package validated on one platform is interchangeable with another.

4. Prepare the Environment and Configure demo.options

Where supported by your package, use the bundled environment preparation script to configure the installation account and prefix:

python SetSysEnv.py --dbaUser=gbase --installPrefix=/opt

Confirm the expected Python runtime and script entry point for your installed release before executing this command.

Next, prepare demo.options. The following example illustrates how the host lists and NodeIDs can be organized for a small cluster. These IP addresses are examples only; replace them with addresses from your deployment.

installPrefix = /opt
coordinateHost = 192.168.146.20,192.168.146.21,192.168.146.22
coordinateHostNodeID = 20,21,22
dataHost = 192.168.146.20,192.168.146.21,192.168.146.22,192.168.146.23
gcwareHost = 192.168.146.20,192.168.146.21,192.168.146.22
gcwareHostNodeID = 20,21,22
dbaUser = gbase
dbaGroup = gbase
dbPort = 5258
sshPort = 22

This is a configuration illustration, not a universal, ready-to-run template. Confirm every parameter name, required field, and accepted value against the demo.options template shipped with your version.

Pay particular attention to the following:

  • coordinateHost: The hosts assigned the Coordinator role.
  • dataHost: The hosts participating in the data-node deployment.
  • gcwareHost: The hosts assigned the GCware role.
  • NodeID mapping: Ensure that each configured NodeID corresponds to the intended host according to the release-specific configuration rules.
  • Ports: Confirm that dbPort and sshPort match the actual environment and the package's parameter definitions.

For an eight-node deployment, expand the appropriate host lists to include the intended machines. Do not assume that NodeIDs must equal the final octet of an IP address; use a consistent mapping that satisfies the installer requirements.

Avoid placing plaintext passwords in shared configuration files. If your release requires password fields in demo.options, follow its documented credential-handling procedure, restrict file permissions, and remove temporary secrets after installation. Special characters should be handled according to the installer's supported escaping rules rather than replaced with a weak password.

5. Run the GBase Database Silent Installer

Once the host lists, environment, permissions, and connectivity checks are complete, run the silent installer using the syntax documented for your package.

For releases that support this entry point and option format, the command may resemble:

./gcinstall.py --silent=demo.options

Do not assume this exact command works with every GBase Database release. Some packages may use a different interpreter entry point or different command-line options.

Commercial and free editions may also differ in licensing requirements. Confirm whether your edition requires a license file during installation or a separate authorization step afterward. If a --license_file option is documented for your release, use the exact syntax and licensing workflow specified by that version's manual.

During installation, monitor the output and logs for each node. If the process fails, identify the host and installation stage associated with the error before attempting a retry.

6. Verify Installation Results and Cluster Status

After installation, load the environment using the initialization procedure configured for your account. If the profile used by your installation is ~/.bash_profile, run:

source ~/.bash_profile
gcadmin

Inspect the reported node states and compare them with the expected cluster layout. Also check the installation logs for node-level success or failure messages.

A completed installation command is not sufficient evidence that the cluster is ready. Verify that:

  1. All expected nodes are present.
  2. Node states match the expected operational state.
  3. The configured distribution and data-map initialization steps have completed.
  4. Licensing or authorization requirements have been satisfied.
  5. The cluster passes the appropriate post-installation checks.

A state such as CLOSE may indicate a licensing or authorization issue in some circumstances, but its meaning should be verified against the installed version and current cluster conditions. Do not treat every unexpected state as the same failure.

7. Troubleshoot a Failed Node Before Reinstalling the Cluster

If one node fails during installation, inspect the logs to determine whether the problem involves SSH authentication, environment preparation, package compatibility, configuration, or service startup.

Do not immediately reinstall every node.

For an existing cluster, a supported node-expansion or recovery procedure may involve generating gcChangeInfo.xml and using gcadmin addnodes. However, this is not a universal repair command for every failed installation. Confirm that the cluster is in a supported state for node addition and follow the documented recovery procedure for your release.

Preserve the original installation logs before retrying. They provide useful evidence for diagnosing the failure and documenting the eventual resolution.

8. Record the Deployment for Future Maintenance

A successful GBase Database cluster deployment should leave behind more than a running service.

Include the following in the handover record:

  • Exact installation package name and version.
  • Operating system and CPU architecture.
  • Final host lists and NodeID mapping.
  • Installation prefix and relevant port settings.
  • Licensing or authorization status, without exposing secret material.
  • Installation logs and verification results.
  • Any node-addition, recovery, or configuration changes made during delivery.

These records make future expansion, troubleshooting, and recovery more predictable.

Final Thoughts

GBase Database(GBase 8a) silent installation can simplify MPP cluster deployment by automating repetitive tasks across multiple hosts. But automation works best when the configuration is correct before execution begins.

Validate the environment, align the host lists, verify SSH access, use the release-specific installation procedure, and confirm the final cluster state. The goal is not merely to make the installer finish. It is to deliver a cluster that can be verified, maintained, and expanded reliably.

title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.36652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.

title: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.36287v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hospitality service in online marketplaces has become increasingly popular over the past few years, not only because it helps people easily rent short-term lodging but also because it empowers travelers to connect with locals and feel belonging. A typical pattern of these industries is a central platform mediating the economic interactions between guests and hosts, where a successful booking experience is the key to user satisfaction. However, one of the biggest challenges is the possible delay of response and chance of rejection when guests try to book a request-to-book listing. Previously, we enabled the instant book feature to allow hosts to instantly accept qualified guests and guests to confirm bookings immediately. Yet the symptom has not been alleviated given mixed request-to-book and instant book listing supply in search results. One possible solution is to promote all instant book listings in search results; however, booking rate will be damaged due to some improperly promoted low quality listings.
  In this paper, we present a novel smart instant book filter system that applies the instant book filter intelligently and shifts request-to-book to instant book without hurting booking rate. Compared with traditional two-sided markets research that targets finding strategies to maximize a single overall social welfare goal, our proposed system aims to maximize the instant book rate with the constraint that booking rate should not decrease, forming a dual-objective optimization problem.
  We show A/B testing results for our system exposed to global users, demonstrating that our model performs better than previous human-expert-tuned models in terms of both instant book rate and overall booking rate. We also achieved improved metrics such as the host instant book adoption rate. The proposed system has been deployed to production and is serving millions of users every day.
