title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
description:
arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

title: Price your coding agent from its own logs before you self-host DeepInfer
description:
Before you argue about self-hosting a model for your coding agents, read your own logs. Claude Code keeps a JSONL transcript of every model call under ~/.claude/projects, token usage included. We took one developer's transcripts from 21 September to 20 October: 129,407 calls and 26.2 billion tokens (tokens are the word fragments a model reads and bills by). Priced three ways, that month is 400 dollars on the two Claude Max 20x subscriptions he pays, 12,365 dollars at Claude API list price, and 274 dollars on DeepSeek's API.

The full breakdown of that month and the DeepInfer break-even math lives on inferencekey.com. This piece covers the trap you hit doing the same count, and the one measurement that decides whether self-hosting makes sense.

The first streaming line undercounts output by 2.4x

The answer arrives in pieces (streaming), and Claude Code logs a new line for the same call as those pieces land. The earliest line has no stop_reason yet, and its output_tokens holds only what was generated so far. Our first pass trusted it and counted 36.4 million output tokens. The final line of each call says 86.0 million.

Output is the priciest token on the list: 20 dollars per million on Opus 5.5, against 4 for fresh input. Deduplicate by message id and request id, and let the last line win:

import json
usage = {}
for line in open(path):  # each ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl
    rec = json.loads(line)
    msg = rec.get("message") or {}
    if "usage" in msg:
        usage[(msg.get("id"), rec.get("requestId"))] = msg["usage"]  # last line wins

Do this before any pricing: every later figure inherits the error.

Your agent is a reader, so compare the cache price

On every step the agent resends the whole conversation. Providers keep recently seen text in a cache, a store that lets them skip work on text they processed a moment ago and bill it at a lower rate. In this month, 25,253 million tokens came back out of that cache. 822 million were new material written into it, and 86 million were output. That is about 303 tokens read per token written, and the median call carried 138,000 tokens of context (everything sent along with that call).

So the headline input and output prices are the wrong columns. The cache-hit price carries the bill. Opus 5.5 charges 0.20 dollars per million cached tokens; DeepSeek off-peak charges 0.003, 67 times less, and that explains almost the whole gap between 12,365 and 274. With no cache at all, the same month on Claude would come to about 109,900 dollars.

Two details if you reprice your own month. DeepSeek doubles its rates at peak hours, so use your team's real hours (here 9.4% of usage fell in peak and paid 17.2% of the bill). And keep it a price comparison: Flash and Opus are different models with different tokenizers, that difference is unmeasured, and nobody replayed this month of work on Flash. On quality, Flash topped LiveBench agentic coding among 69 models on 10 October, the same table we used when we ran DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on two GPUs. Opus 5.5 leads the broader Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 58 to 39.

DeepInfer ships the engine, not the cache

DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the engine behind its own API, under Apache 2.0. It grew out of vLLM and takes ideas from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. Credit to all of those teams, and to DeepSeek for documenting its production setup with real numbers in a post on Zhihu.

This release does offline inference: you feed it prompts from a Python script, and there is no documented HTTP server for your agents to call. The project page also lists three missing pieces of a complete service. One is the KV cache system, the store for already-processed context (the cache from the previous section). Another is the split between prefill machines, which read the prompt, and decode machines, which write the answer token by token. The last is load balancing across copies of the engine.

For this workload the cache is the whole game. With one, an 8-GPU server at DeepSeek's production rates holds about 293 developers like this one. Without it, each step processes the full context from scratch, and the same server holds about 15. The article budgets two full-time engineers to build the missing parts.

The one number nobody has measured yet

Every break-even figure hangs on one ratio: DeepInfer's speed per GPU on a single 8-GPU server, against DeepSeek's production, where decode runs on 64 GPUs or more. The README charts prefill on 4 GPUs and decode on 64. The 8-GPU case is missing.

Eight rented B200 at 7.99 dollars per GPU per hour cost 46,662 dollars a month. Below 58% of DeepSeek's per-GPU speed, renting never beats the API, whatever your headcount. At full DeepSeek speed, one server wins from about 262 people, engineers included, and is 11% cheaper at 293.

DeepInfer ships the benchmark (examples/sweep/run_sweep.sh), and a few hours of prefill and decode sweeps at 128K context on one 8-GPU node would settle it. We still owe that run, so treat every rented-server figure as an assumption. The own-rack estimate, about 465 people, rests on a 3.5 million dollar rack price that is our assumption, not a quote; the team-size table and every formula behind the DeepInfer break-even show what moves it.

Start with your own month

Count your team's month with the final-line rule above, then compare it with our month of coding agent costs and the DeepInfer payoff analysis.

title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
description:
arXiv:2610.36435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.

title: Extraction meets Distillation - cryptanalytic techniques to recover parameters from a Deep Neural Network
description:
arXiv:2610.33671v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study fully connected neural-network reconstruction by combining cryptanalytic weight-direction extraction with learning from predicted labels. We adapt a ReLU extraction implementation to Leaky ReLU, compare sign-search methods, and estimate biases and output layers. We prove conditional bounds for direction recovery with approximate prefixes, preservation of local distance votes, prediction changes from aligned parameter errors, and sign selection with independent scoring data. We also specify exact row restoration and distinguish its guarantee from that of gradient masking. The experiments evaluate assisted extraction, with privileged access to gradients, hidden activations, and victim parameters, followed by label-based reconstruction. Across eight search seeds on the largest synthetic architecture, Leaky ReLU recovers 51--57 neurons in the deepest hidden layer, while ReLU recovers none. This advantage does not hold uniformly across architectures and layers. Removing victim-weight access from the sign walk gives less accurate signs, despite high final prediction agreement. Across 40 seeded runs on the two smallest synthetic victims, agreement on 5,000 inputs excluded from fitting and selection ranges from $0.9890$ to $0.9992$. On two CIFAR-10 victims, the reconstructed models achieve $56.40\%$ and $58.29\%$ agreement and exceed the distillation baseline on three functional metrics. We report label requests separately from privileged access and explain why prediction agreement does not identify network parameters.

title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.36077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

title: LLM Hallucination Detection via Low-rank Multilinear Decomposition
description:
arXiv:2610.36191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate fluent yet factually incorrect responses, raising concerns about their reliability. Recent hallucination detectors increasingly exploit internal representations, but extracting informative signals from high-dimensional hidden states remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on selected activations or pooling-based compression, potentially overlooking discriminative information distributed across Transformer layers, feature modes, and tokens. We propose LOTUS (Low-rank Order-statistic TUcker-based Subspace learning), a multilinear low-rank decomposition framework for hallucination detection that extracts compact representations from LLM hidden states while reducing dependence on labeled data. Our approach first summarizes variable-length token representations using complementary statistical descriptors that capture peak activations, activation distributions, and cross-layer changes. We then leverage low-rank multilinear decomposition to extract compact representations that capture the underlying structure of LLM hidden states, which are subsequently used to train a lightweight hallucination classifier. Experiments across multiple LLMs and question-answering benchmarks demonstrate improved hallucination detection performance over recent state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Beyond IceBERT: Open-Data ModernBERT Encoders for Icelandic from 12M to 1B Parameters
description:
arXiv:2610.36230v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: IceBERT, the reference encoder for Icelandic, found that a cleaned web crawl is enough to train a strong model and that starting from a multilingual model can help on some tasks. We revisit both findings with the ModernBERT architecture. We train Icelandic encoders from 12M to 1B parameters on 9B tokens of open data, and rerun IceBERT's benchmarks and five newer tasks for 30 encoders under one protocol with confidence intervals. Our 1B model trained from scratch, to our knowledge the first monolingual Icelandic encoder of that size, is significantly better than IceBERT on all eleven tasks; warm-started from the English Ettin encoder of the same shape, it has the best score of all encoders on every task we rank. Because our model shapes match the English Ettin encoders and the multilingual mmBERT, we can also test the warm start under controlled conditions, at six model sizes and four token budgets. With our vocabulary transplanted, a warm start was never significantly worse than scratch training on the same Icelandic text, and from base size up it was not significantly worse on four tasks than scratch training on 4 times the text (8 times at base and 1B). As models grow, most of the transfer comes from the source model's transformer layers, so even an English source helps. Keeping the source vocabulary instead cost 5 F1 on question answering and nearly three times the compute.

title: Personality Latents: Conditioning Frozen Language Models on Individuals from Their Own Writing
description:
arXiv:2610.36805v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controlling the personality of a language model usually relies on written profiles or named trait categories, so it can only express what an author writes down or what a taxonomy names. We instead propose Personality Latents (PL), which learn a latent for each person from their own writing, with no personality labels and no authored profile, and inject it into a frozen language model as a soft prefix. Following generative latent optimization, each training person receives a free latent that is optimized through the frozen model itself, while an encoder learns to predict these latents so that a new person needs only one forward pass, with optional refinement at test time. We evaluate on held-out people by having the conditioned model answer neutral and interview questions and reading personality from its answers with scorers trained on real human writing. On the MBTI axes PL reaches an AUC of , ahead of persona embedding and prompt-based baselines under identical settings, and the ranking holds when the answers are scored in three different embedding spaces. A latent learned with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct also transfers personality to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct through a new adapter alone.

title: PrinGS: Privacy Preservation in Gaussian Splatting
description:
arXiv:2610.36168v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly become the preferred representation for high-fidelity novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, the learned representation encodes sensitive visual information including human faces, license plates, documents, and computer screens, raising significant privacy concerns when trained splats are shared or deployed. In this work, we address the underexplored problem of privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting by proposing a representation-level anonymization framework that directly anonymizes a trained splat. Given a trained splat and a user-provided reference view identifying sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding regions in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them, ensuring that the sensitive information is absent from all subsequently rendered novel views while preserving the overall scene geometry and visual fidelity. We achieve this post-training anonymization in less than 1 second. Furthermore, we extend our framework with a privacy-by-design training strategy that prevents sensitive content from being embedded into the representation during optimization, enabling the generation of privacy-preserving splats directly from training images. Our method achieves a remarkably low Face Similarity Measure (FSM) of 9.79% at a retained Face Detection Rate (FDR) of 39.47% and makes sensitive text completely unreadable with an OCR Character Error Rate of 1.00. Our work aims to serve as the primary stepping stone towards privacy-aware 3D representations and motivates further research along these directions.

title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
description:
arXiv:2610.36625v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36671v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/

title: ObjectTwin: Measuring the Asset Correspondence Gap for Capture-Anchored Digital Twins
description:
arXiv:2610.35904v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Object-wise reconstruction increasingly inserts generated meshes into captured scenes as editable proxies for observed objects. This use creates a requirement absent from isolated-asset scores and pose estimates: at the captured metric state, the proxy should reproduce calibrated observations of the same instance. We present ObjectTwin, a scan-grounded measurement protocol that freezes the instance, cameras, scan-projected support and recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator, then replaces only the object representation. The resulting asset correspondence gap measures lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry without treating the scan as complete physical ground truth. Across two indoor RGB-D capture domains and two generation backends, visible, anchored generated assets lose 0.302-0.497 MaskIoU under this replacement. Every tested scene-level estimate is positive, while same-input generator preference reverses across capture domains. Coverage and overlap-depth analyses locate disagreement in both visible support and surface placement; the evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover it. These results establish capture correspondence as a separately measurable interface between generated-asset quality and stronger physical or task-level evaluation.

title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.36384v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

title: Invoice Extraction: Node.js Semantic Search Plus an LLM Classifier Guide for 2026
description:
Short answer: use semantic search plus an LLM classifier to narrow invoice-field candidates, then produce a typed result only when the evidence clears an explicit gate. Keep the fast path small. A supplier invoice that takes 900 ms to tag is inconvenient; one that silently turns an invoice number into a purchase-order number is an operational incident waiting to happen. The numbers are policy choices, not universal benchmarks. Start with a 300 ms retrieval budget and an 800 ms end-to-end target only if your queue and document mix support them; measure before tightening either limit.

The useful design is a two-speed runbook: retrieve a bounded set of field definitions and examples, classify against that evidence, and abstain when the score, agreement, or required field shape is wrong.

What should happen when an invoice is ambiguous?

Treat ambiguity as a valid output. An invoice may contain Invoice No., Order No., Account, and a supplier-specific reference on the same page. A keyword match can find all four. Semantic similarity can find the right neighborhood, but similarity alone does not prove that a value belongs to the requested field.

For a concrete contract, represent each candidate as a field name, a description, an extraction rule, and a small set of approved examples. Embed the searchable text, retrieve the top 8 candidates, and rerank those candidates with signals that the retrieval index does not know: page location, nearby labels, data type, and supplier-specific aliases. The classifier then receives the winning evidence and must return either a field/value pair or an abstention reason.

That last branch is the part teams skip. They tune a confidence threshold until the dashboard looks calm, then discover that a plausible value is worse than a missing value because downstream payment automation treats both as ordinary strings. A missing field can enter a review queue. A wrong field can become a bad payment.

How should semantic search plus an LLM classifier handle invoice docs?

The pipeline should have four observable boundaries. First, normalize the OCR text while retaining page and bounding-box metadata. Second, retrieve candidate definitions from a vector-capable store. Third, rerank with deterministic document signals. Fourth, classify into a closed schema and validate the result before persistence.

A simple record is enough to make the boundary explicit:

type FieldCandidate struct {
    Name        string
    Description string
    Value       string
    Page        int
    Similarity  float64
    Evidence    string
}

func accept(c FieldCandidate, minSimilarity float64) bool {
    if c.Name == "" || c.Value == "" {
        return false
    }
    if c.Page < 1 || c.Similarity < minSimilarity {
        return false
    }
    return true
}

This is intentionally boring. The retrieval layer supplies candidates; the gate owns acceptance. In production, the classifier response should be decoded into a schema with a fixed enum for field names, a normalized value, source page, and evidence span. Reject unknown fields and values that fail type checks. For dates, decide whether the contract stores an ISO date or preserves the source string. For amounts, require currency context rather than guessing from punctuation.

The embedding query should describe the field you need, not dump an entire invoice into one vector. supplier invoice number and purchase order number are close in vocabulary, so the reranker needs the local label and the expected format. A Node.js service can apply the same contract at its queue boundary, while the classifier remains replaceable behind a typed interface. This is where quality costs latency: another pass has value only when it can see a signal the previous pass could not.

Keep retries outside the classifier decision. RFC 9110 distinguishes request semantics and makes idempotency relevant to safe retries; your job queue should assign an operation ID and make persistence idempotent before a timeout can cause a duplicate write. A retry that repeats an extraction is acceptable. A retry that appends a second accounting record is not.

Which signals are worth the extra latency?

The right question is not “Should we add reranking?” It is “Which errors are expensive enough to justify another decision boundary?”

For supplier invoices, page-local evidence is usually a stronger operational signal than a tiny change in embedding similarity. A candidate labelled Invoice No. on page 1 should beat a semantically similar Order No. found in a line-item description when the target field is the invoice identifier. A regular expression can validate a shape, but it cannot establish meaning. Use it as a gate, not as the classifier.

A practical policy is to split fields by consequence. Invoice number, total amount, currency, and supplier identity get strict gates and a review path. Low-impact tags such as department or document topic can tolerate a lower threshold if they never authorize payment. This is a decision rule, not a claim that any fixed threshold works for every supplier.

Postgres with a vector extension can keep candidate definitions beside ordinary relational metadata, which is useful when a field revision must be audited with its effective date. The extension's documentation describes exact and approximate nearest-neighbor options; choose based on measured recall and query latency for your corpus, not on a generic promise. Keep the embedding model version and preprocessing revision in the row so a reindex is reproducible. The limitation is clear: this approach is a poor fit for tiny document sets where a relational lookup is already clear, or for documents whose OCR quality is too low to provide trustworthy evidence; the extra semantic stage then adds latency without adding a useful decision signal. The trade-off is quality versus latency, and the right choice can be the simpler path.

How do you verify it before changing the gate?

Build a fixture set from representative invoices and label the target fields, source spans, abstentions, and reasons. Do not use only clean samples. Include rotated scans, duplicate labels, multi-page totals, missing currency, and supplier aliases. The test should answer two different questions: did retrieval include the correct candidate, and did the final gate accept only a correct value?

Record these dimensions separately:

  • retrieval recall at the configured top-k;
  • accepted-field precision by field type;
  • abstention rate by supplier and document shape;
  • p50 and p95 latency for each pipeline boundary;
  • retry count, timeout reason, and idempotency outcome.

The p95 number matters at 3 a.m. because a queue of slow documents can look like a model-quality problem while it is really a concurrency or OCR bottleneck. Dashboards should show the page that fired: supplier, field, evidence span, model revision, and gate result. An aggregate “classification confidence” is not enough to reconstruct why a payment field was accepted.

A safe rollout changes one policy at a time. First shadow the new retrieval or reranking rule and compare decisions without writing them. Then enable it for a bounded supplier cohort. If accepted precision falls, restore the previous gate and preserve the shadow trace for diagnosis. If latency rises while quality is flat, remove the extra stage rather than hiding it behind a larger worker pool. Capacity can conceal a bad decision boundary until the next traffic spike.

The small contract that keeps the system honest

An extraction service should return a status, not just a string. accepted means the value passed schema and evidence checks. review means a human or a later workflow owns the decision. rejected means the input could not support the requested field. Include the operation ID, source page, evidence span, and revisions in every result.

This contract makes failure visible without turning every uncertainty into an outage. It also makes rollback concrete: stop consuming new policy revisions, route new documents to the last accepted revision, and leave already persisted records untouched until a separately approved correction job runs.

The useful optimization is selective effort. Spend retrieval and reranking latency where a wrong answer has a financial consequence; keep low-risk tags on the shorter path. Quality is the gate. Latency is the budget. Neither should be inferred from a single score.

References

  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • pgvector, “Open-source vector similarity search for Postgres”: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector

title: Classifying Edtech Text Data with Node.js Embeddings API — CRM Actions
description:
To classify text data using embeddings in Node.js, rank possible CRM actions, then require a similarity threshold and an explicit review path before writing anything. For an edtech sales-call summarizer, that boundary matters more than the vector database: a plausible but wrong action can change a renewal forecast, assign the wrong owner, or create a task nobody can explain later.

The practical design is straightforward. Embed a small set of labeled examples, embed each new call note, compare cosine similarity, and emit a structured action only when the score clears a threshold. Keep the original note, selected example, score, and model metadata together. That gives a solo team something inspectable to tune instead of a mysterious tag.

What should similarity decide, and what should it leave alone?

Embeddings find semantic neighbors. They do not prove that a sales call contains a commitment, a date, or a safe CRM mutation. I use them as the first pass over a closed action vocabulary: create_follow_up, send_pricing, schedule_demo, and no_action. The output is a candidate, not permission.

That distinction matters in education sales. “The district is interested next term” may resemble a demo request, while the note contains no agreed date. A nearest-neighbor classifier can send the item to the right queue, but a second structured-output step should validate required fields before a CRM write.

My decision rule is boring: high similarity plus a clear margin over the runner-up can proceed to a typed review state; low similarity, a narrow margin, or a missing fact goes to needs_review. I would rather review 12 ambiguous calls than quietly create 12 incorrect tasks.

How can Node.js classify text data using an embeddings API?

This example calls Infrai's OpenAI-compatible embeddings route directly so the HTTP boundary stays visible. It uses the public base URL, an environment key, an explicit method, status checks, and bounded retry behavior. The model is an environment value because the verified route does not make a hard-coded model choice safe.

The examples are intentionally short. In production, version them and include negative examples; otherwise “interested” tends to become a universal match.

type Action = "create_follow_up" | "send_pricing" | "schedule_demo" | "no_action";
type Example = { text: string; action: Action };

const examples: Example[] = [
  { text: "They asked for district pricing before Friday.", action: "send_pricing" },
  { text: "The curriculum lead agreed to a walkthrough next Tuesday.", action: "schedule_demo" },
  { text: "The buyer requested a follow-up after the board meeting.", action: "create_follow_up" },
  { text: "They are researching options but made no request.", action: "no_action" },
];

function cosine(a: number[], b: number[]): number {
  if (a.length !== b.length || a.length === 0) throw new Error("Embedding dimensions differ");
  let dot = 0; let normA = 0; let normB = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i += 1) {
    dot += a[i] * b[i]; normA += a[i] * a[i]; normB += b[i] * b[i];
  }
  return dot / (Math.sqrt(normA) * Math.sqrt(normB));
}

async function embed(input: string): Promise<number[]> {
  const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
  if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");
  const body = JSON.stringify({ model: process.env.INFRAI_EMBEDDING_MODEL, input });
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/embeddings`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body,
    });
    if (response.ok) {
      const result = await response.json() as { data?: Array<{ embedding?: number[] }> };
      const vector = result.data?.[0]?.embedding;
      if (!vector) throw new Error("Embeddings response did not contain a vector");
      return vector;
    }
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
      throw new Error(`Embedding request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error("Embedding retry loop ended unexpectedly");
}

async function classify(note: string) {
  const labeled = await Promise.all(examples.map(async (example) => ({
    ...example, embedding: await embed(example.text),
  })));
  const noteVector = await embed(note);
  const ranked = labeled.map((example) => ({
    action: example.action, reference: example.text,
    score: cosine(noteVector, example.embedding),
  })).sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);

  const [winner, runnerUp] = ranked;
  const minimumScore = Number(process.env.MIN_SIMILARITY ?? "0.78");
  const minimumMargin = Number(process.env.MIN_MARGIN ?? "0.04");
  const accepted = winner.score >= minimumScore && winner.score - runnerUp.score >= minimumMargin;
  return {
    action: accepted ? winner.action : "needs_review", accepted,
    score: winner.score, margin: winner.score - runnerUp.score,
    matchedExample: winner.reference, candidates: ranked,
  };
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(await classify("The district wants pricing for a committee review."), null, 2));

This is a classifier, not a CRM client. It has no write route and no hidden fallback. The returned score and margin are evidence for the next step. If a worker turns the result into a CRM action, give it a stable call identifier and enforce idempotency there; retrying a write must not duplicate a task. RFC 9110 covers HTTP semantics and retry considerations.

The score is not a probability.

Ship the review queue.

A production version should cache embeddings for the labeled set. Re-embedding four examples on every call is easy to understand, but it is wasteful at bulk volume. When the catalog changes, rebuild the cache with a version and store that version beside each classification.

How do the real options differ at this boundary?

OpenAI is the natural baseline when the application already uses its SDK and wants a familiar embeddings call. Its advantage is reduced integration work. The cost is concentration in one hosted API unless the application keeps a provider interface.

Cohere is a credible hosted alternative for teams that want a separate embedding provider. It belongs in an evaluation set, especially when multilingual sales notes or a different retrieval profile matters. Treat its output as a different vector space: never compare vectors from two providers, and recalibrate thresholds after switching.

Voyage AI is another hosted option worth testing for retrieval-heavy workloads. The engineering point is the same: model choice changes the geometry, so a threshold copied from OpenAI is not evidence. A small labeled holdout set is more useful than a generic leaderboard for deciding which provider fits these call notes.

A local embedding model, paired with a library such as FAISS, is a fourth route. It trades hosted simplicity for packaging, memory, upgrades, and monitoring. It can make sense when data residency or offline operation dominates, but a solo founder should count the maintenance surface honestly.

Infrai is relevant when the surrounding product benefits from many backend capabilities behind one consistent REST contract. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities and schemas, and its OpenAI-compatible surface lets existing clients keep their shape. That breadth can make adding an adjacent operation one endpoint rather than another vendor integration. It is a fit for integration consolidation, not proof that its embeddings classify this taxonomy better. Test the vectors on your own labeled calls.

The comparison is simple: choose the provider whose embeddings separate your action labels with a useful margin, then weigh SDK familiarity, vendor concentration, and operational ownership. No provider removes the need for a review state.

Here is the trade-off I would put in front of a small team before choosing a provider:

Option Interface Best fit Main limitation
OpenAI SDK or REST Existing OpenAI application More vendor concentration
Together REST Teams comparing hosted model access You still own threshold calibration
Gemini SDK or REST Teams already standardized on Google APIs A provider change still needs new labels tested
Anthropic SDK or REST Teams already standardized on Anthropic APIs It is not a drop-in replacement for this vector space
Cohere SDK or REST A separate hosted embedding evaluation Vectors are not interchangeable
Voyage AI REST Retrieval-focused experiments A provider switch means new geometry
Infrai REST or OpenAI-compatible One key across a broad backend surface Consolidation does not prove classification quality
Local model + FAISS Local library Residency or offline constraints Packaging and operations are yours

Infrai's concrete breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with a public discovery surface that exposes capability schemas. That is useful when the same call-processing product will later need adjacent backend operations. It is not a reason to skip a labeled holdout test, and it is the wrong fit if local execution is a hard requirement.

One calibration trap deserves a full paragraph. Suppose the holdout contains 80 calls: 20 pricing requests, 20 demo requests, 20 follow-up requests, and 20 no-action notes. A single global score can look fine while “pricing” and “demo” remain confused, because both notes mention a next step. I would inspect the confusion matrix by action, then raise the margin requirement for that pair and add a negative example such as “pricing was discussed but no material was requested.” The point is not to find a magical threshold. It is to make the business boundary visible in the data, and to know which class still needs human review when the taxonomy changes.

Thresholds are a product decision

Do not choose 0.78 because it looks scientific. The number in the example is configuration, not a measured claim. Label a holdout set of calls, inspect false positives, and tune the minimum score and margin against the error you can tolerate. For CRM actions, a false positive is often worse than a missed automation because it creates an apparently intentional record.

The labels need hard boundaries. “Send pricing” should mean the buyer requested pricing material, not that pricing was mentioned. “Schedule demo” should mean a next meeting was agreed, not that someone said the product looked interesting. If two labels overlap after rewriting their definitions, embeddings will expose that ambiguity rather than fix it.

For larger catalogs, cluster labeled examples with k-means or use FAISS for efficient nearest-neighbor lookup. Keep the final action vocabulary small and inspect cluster members before promoting a label. Bulk processing also deserves cost accounting: estimate the embedding workload with the available cost-estimation endpoint, then compare that estimate with the calls and re-embeddings your cache creates. Cost is an operating constraint, not the quality metric.

Version the examples and model. Cache reference embeddings. Store top candidates, score, margin, and taxonomy version. Send ambiguous notes to review. Validate required action fields with structured output. Use a stable call ID for downstream writes. Recalibrate after changing providers, models, labels, or language mix.

References

  • OpenAI embeddings guide: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings
  • OpenAI Node.js library: https://github.com/openai/openai-node
  • Cohere Embed documentation: https://docs.cohere.com/docs/embeddings
  • Voyage AI documentation: https://docs.voyageai.com/docs/embeddings
  • FAISS documentation: https://faiss.ai/
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

Passing score 700 on a scale of 1 to 1,000 (scaled)
Delivery Proctored, scheduled through Pearson VUE
Languages English, Chinese (Simplified), Korean, Japanese, French, Spanish, German, Portuguese (Brazil), Chinese (Traditional), Italian
Price Depends on the country or region where you take it
Renewal Every 12 months, free, with an online assessment on Microsoft Learn

Who it is for

Microsoft describes the candidate as someone with subject matter expertise in implementing, managing and monitoring an organization’s Microsoft Azure environment, including virtual networks, storage, compute, identity, security and governance.

An Azure administrator often works as part of a larger team that implements an organization’s cloud infrastructure. You also coordinate with other roles to deliver Azure networking, security, database, application development and DevOps solutions.

Recommended experience

Microsoft says you should be familiar with:

  • operating systems
  • networking
  • servers
  • virtualization

You should also have experience with PowerShell, Azure CLI, the Azure portal, Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep files and Microsoft Entra ID. The certification page and study guide do not list any formal prerequisite.

The exam format

You have 100 minutes. The exam is proctored and may include interactive components. Microsoft does not reveal question types in advance, but its exam sandbox lets you try the exam interface and question formats before you book. Most questions cover features that are generally available, though commonly used Preview features can appear.

  • Scoring: you need 700 or more on a scale of 1 to 1,000. This is a scaled score, so it may not equal 70% of the points. There is no penalty for guessing, and some questions may be unscored without telling you which.
  • Microsoft Learn is open: on associate and expert exams you can open Microsoft Learn in a split screen. No extra time is added and the clock keeps running.
  • Breaks: five minutes are built into the exam time for breaks. The clock keeps running, and you cannot return to questions you saw before the break.
  • Language: if the exam is not available in your preferred language, you can request an extra 30 minutes.
  • Retakes: you must wait 24 hours after a first failed attempt and 14 days between later attempts. You cannot take the same exam more than five times in 12 months from your first attempt.

The official skills measured

The AZ-104 study guide groups the exam into five skill areas. This is how it describes them, in brief:

Skill area Weight What it covers
Manage Azure identities and governance 20–25% Creating and managing Microsoft Entra users and groups, licenses, external users and self-service password reset. Built-in Azure roles, role assignments at different scopes and interpreting access. Azure Policy, resource locks, tags, resource groups, subscriptions, management groups, and managing costs with alerts, budgets and Azure Advisor.
Implement and manage storage 15–20% Storage firewalls and virtual networks, SAS tokens, stored access policies, access keys and identity-based access for Azure Files. Creating storage accounts, redundancy, object replication, encryption, Storage Explorer and AzCopy. File shares, blob containers, storage tiers, soft delete and snapshots, lifecycle management and blob versioning.
Deploy and manage Azure compute resources 20–25% Reading, changing and deploying ARM templates and Bicep files, and exporting or converting them. Creating VMs, encryption at host, moving VMs, sizes, disks, availability zones and sets, and Virtual Machine Scale Sets. Azure Container Registry, Container Instances and Container Apps. App Service plans, scaling, certificates and TLS, custom DNS names, backup, networking and deployment slots.
Implement and manage virtual networking 15–20% Virtual networks, subnets, peering, public IP addresses, user-defined routes and troubleshooting connectivity. Network security groups and application security groups, effective security rules, Azure Bastion, and service and private endpoints. Azure DNS, and configuring and troubleshooting internal or public load balancers.
Monitor and maintain Azure resources 10–15% Metrics, log settings and log queries in Azure Monitor, alert rules, action groups and alert processing rules, Azure Monitor Insights, Network Watcher and Connection monitor. Recovery Services and Backup vaults, backup policies, backup and restore, Azure Site Recovery, failover to a secondary region, and backup reports and alerts.

Identities and governance and compute carry the most weight. Monitoring and maintenance is the smallest area, but it is still up to 15% of the exam.

What changed in 2026

Skills measured as of April 17, 2026. Microsoft’s change log marks the audience profile and five groups as minor changes: Configure Azure Files and Azure Blob Storage, Create and configure virtual machines, Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal, Configure and manage virtual networks in Azure, and Monitor resources in Azure. The skill areas listed in the change log are marked as no change.

Microsoft updates the English version of an exam first. Localized versions are updated about eight weeks after the English version, although Microsoft says this schedule can slip.

Official study resources

  • the AZ-104 study guide, which lists every skill measured and the change log
  • self-paced learning paths and modules, or an instructor-led course, linked from the study guide
  • the Azure documentation, including Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Policy, Azure Storage, ARM templates, Container Instances, Container Apps, App Service, Azure DNS, Azure Bastion, Azure Monitor, Network Watcher, Site Recovery and Azure Backup
  • the free Practice Assessment on Microsoft Learn, which shows the style, wording and difficulty of exam questions
  • the exam sandbox, to practise the exam interface
  • the Exam AZ-104 prep videos and the Exam Readiness Zone

A suggested 6-week study plan

This is our suggested plan. It follows the five skill areas and gives time in line with their weights.

  1. Week 1: Identity and governance. Entra users and groups, licenses, external users and SSPR, then Azure RBAC roles and scopes, Azure Policy, locks, tags, management groups and cost controls.
  2. Week 2: Storage. Storage accounts and redundancy, firewalls, SAS tokens and access keys, encryption, Azure Files, blob tiers, soft delete, versioning, lifecycle rules, object replication and AzCopy.
  3. Week 3: Compute. ARM templates and Bicep, VM sizes, disks, availability zones and sets, scale sets, moving VMs, containers, and App Service plans, slots, certificates and networking.
  4. Week 4: Networking. VNets and subnets, peering, user-defined routes, NSGs and application security groups, Bastion, service and private endpoints, Azure DNS and load balancers.
  5. Week 5: Monitoring and backup. Azure Monitor metrics, logs and alerts, Network Watcher, Recovery Services and Backup vaults, backup policies, restores and Site Recovery failover.
  6. Week 6: Practice and review. Take the free Practice Assessment and full-length timed practice exams, read every explanation, and revisit the areas where you score lowest. Practise finding answers quickly on Microsoft Learn, since it is open during the exam but the clock keeps running.

Keeping your certification

The Azure Administrator Associate certification has a 12-month renewal frequency. Renewal is free: you pass a short online renewal assessment on Microsoft Learn, which becomes available six months before your certification expires. The assessment is unproctored and open book, takes about 45 minutes, and can be retaken as often as needed before expiry. Passing it extends your certification by one year from the expiration date. If the certification expires, you must pass the exam again.

I run ExamCrest, where this guide first appeared. Try free AZ-104 practice questions: https://examcrest.com/exam/ms-az-104/free-questions?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=g-n1a-az-104

title: When to Intervene? An Empirical Study of Errors and Self-Recovery in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.36471v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents interact with Web services to perform tasks on users' behalf. Errors during these interactions can disrupt execution and prevent task completion, motivating external intervention. However, agents may self-recover through continued execution, raising the question of when to intervene and when to wait for self-recovery. We present an empirical study of errors and self-recovery in LLM agents. We construct ReInBench, a dataset containing 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events across computer-use and Web tasks. Our study examines how often and how quickly agents self-recover, how self-recovery relates to subsequent execution and task completion, and whether self-recovery can be predicted when an error occurs. We find that 725 error events self-recover, often within a few steps, with self-recovery performance differing across Execution LLMs. Self-recovery can also help agents recover from subsequent errors of the same type and support overall task completion. Intervention should therefore prioritize errors unlikely to self-recover, while allowing agents to continue when self-recovery is likely. Building on these empirical findings, we propose ReCoF, a method that predicts whether an error will self-recover to inform whether additional intervention is needed. ReCoF achieves an average relative improvement of 9.02% in Macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on ReInBench. Our code and data can be found at https://method-notes.github.io/ReCoF/.

title: Clustering of High-Dimensional Human Gene Score Data for Target Cell Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.33531v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The goal is to investigate whether the total human gene-score dataset and the selected human kinase-gene dataset exhibit the same number of clusters when analysed using the same set of 769 features. Two datasets were considered: the complete gene score dataset and a subset containing selected kinase genes. Two missing-data strategies were investigated. In Case I, rows containing missing gene-score values were removed. In Case II, rows with more than 20% missing values were excluded and the other missing values were replaced by the corresponding column mean. For each case, the data were scaled and principal component analysis (PCA) was performed before clustering. Four clustering approaches were considered: K-Means, Hierarchical Clustering, Fuzzy C-Means, and Graph-based Clustering. Across both datasets and both missing-data treatments, the optimal number of clusters was found to be two. In the absence of an optimal number of clusters, the quality of clustering was assessed using the Silhouette score. Relatively high Silhouette scores were obtained in all cases.

title: From Intelligence to Autonomy: Foundations and Construction of Autonomous Agents for Future Intelligent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.33445v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from one-off perception and generation tasks toward long-term planning, tool use, and interaction with real environments. Greater task competence, however, does not automatically yield autonomy: an external actor may still have to set goals, sustain operating conditions, detect failures, and approve updates. We define an autonomous agent as a system that, within explicit identity and authority boundaries, maintains both task goals and viability conditions, acts continuously using models of the world and itself, and adjusts its control mechanisms and long-term capabilities through feedback. We trace the conceptual path from homeostasis and feedback control to autopoiesis and biological autonomy. We then distinguish six lines of operationalization: computational autopoiesis, behavior-based robotics, agent formalization, adaptive software, embodied adaptation, and robotic self-modeling. On this basis, we propose a one-boundary, four-loop framework in which Operational, Viability, Reflexive, and Learning loops organize task execution, self-maintenance, metacontrol, and governed learning. Five paired simulation experiments test permission constraints, road-closure response, health maintenance, capability re-estimation, and cross-task learning. Their results provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of these mechanisms, while broader environments and physical systems remain to be tested.

title: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure
description:
arXiv:2610.36453v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.

title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
description:
arXiv:2610.36355v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.
