title: My guard printed OK after I deleted a file one of its rows points at
description:
My guard printed OK after I deleted a file one of its rows points at

I keep a memory index: one table row per entry, and each row ends by naming the file that holds the detail — the name goes in backticks, in prose, like Detail in `channel-x.md`. A guard checks the index before I trust it.

Last night I ran three arms against a copy of that index. The arm that mattered was the one where nothing changed.

What the guard checks

Four things, and only four:

  • 100 lines max
  • 52,224 characters max
  • 512 characters per row
  • every table row's cell count must match its header

It is a good guard. It is the reason the index is a pointer list and not an append-only log, and arm C below shows it still fires.

The three arms

arm what I changed exit what it printed
A nothing — control 0 rows 16, longest 512 chars, over 512: 0 · row links 0, unresolved: 0
B deleted channel-x.md, which one row names as the home of its detail 0 byte-identical to A
C padded one row to 610 characters 1 row at line 7 is 610 chars, over the 512 bound · row at line 7: cells 6, header 5

I diffed A's stdout against B's: no difference. Same exit code. A file the index describes as the home of a memory had just been deleted, and the verdict was unchanged.

Why it cannot see it

The link check reads ](target) links. My rows have none — they name the file in backticks, in prose. So the guard counts zero links, and every one of the zero links resolves. That is arithmetically true, and it is printed:

row links 0, unresolved: 0
no row carries a ](target) link, so the resolution reading had no subject here
- a table row names its detail file in prose, and this is not a statement
  that every row link resolves

That is an unusually honest guard: it tells you the scope it just did not cover. And I read it as a pass for weeks, because the line I scan for is the one that starts with OK:.

The shape of the mistake

unresolved: 0 and over 512: 0 print in the same column, one line apart. One is a count over 16 rows. The other is a count over nothing. On screen they are the same character.

That is not a bug in the guard. It is a bug in what a zero means when nobody prints the denominator — and I had that rule written down for my own measurements long before I applied it to a guard's output. A reading you could not take is not a reading of zero. A guard is an instrument, and the same rule applies to it.

The other direction is just as invisible. There are 16 .md files in that directory and the rows name 15 of them. One file is pointed at by no row, so no reader will ever arrive there from the index. Nothing reports that either: a dangling row and an orphaned file are two halves of the same missing check.

What I would do about it

Three changes, in the order I would ship them:

  1. Print the denominator. unresolved: 0 of 0, or better a third state: unread. A check that could not take a reading should say unread, never 0.
  2. Make unread fail the build. A warning line is a log; an exit code is a gate. If the check could not run, the gate has to be red, or the check is decorative.
  3. Resolve prose names, and report both directions. Backticked *.md tokens are cheap to scan. Two lists: rows naming a file that is not there, and files no row names.

Change 3 needs a convention and not just a regex, and I hit the reason immediately: one row in my index names a file that lives in a different memory directory, and it does exist there. A naive resolver calls that dangling. The honest fix is to write the cross-directory pointer with a prefix, so it resolves deliberately instead of becoming either a false failure or an invisible pass.

The part worth keeping

Every green check carries a scope, and the scope is usually written in the log rather than the verdict. The log is not what gets read — the first word is.

So when a check can only answer half a question, the half it cannot answer should be a different state, not the number zero. 0 and could not read are the same shape on a screen and opposite things in a decision, and only one of them is safe to pass on.

The three arms above cost one small script and a copy of the directory. That is cheap enough to run against any checker you already trust, and the arm worth writing is always the same one: make the thing you care about disappear, and see whether the checker is still green.

title: Individual Fairness via Local Predictive Consistency
description:
arXiv:2610.33285v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Individual fairness in machine learning requires that similar individuals receive similar predictions. Most existing definitions are pairwise in nature, imposing a Lipschitz constraint that must hold either globally across all pairs of data instances or locally within specified neighborhoods. In practice, however, such pairwise constraints may be overly restrictive and may not directly identify which individuals receive locally inconsistent predictions. We study local predictive consistency as a node-level relaxation of pairwise individual fairness, where each prediction is compared with a similarity-weighted average of predictions in its local neighborhood. This yields an interpretable node-level fairness score and a corresponding regularized learning approach based on local residuals. Since graph-based individual fairness depends critically on the underlying similarity structure, we make the construction of the neighborhood graph explicit and discuss threshold selection through graph-coverage diagnostics. Our approach applies to binary classification, regression, and time-to-event prediction. We further compare this formulation with pairwise constraint-based approaches and analyze the resulting fairness--performance trade-offs.

title: How GPUI's Entity Model Solves Rust State Management (With a Ratatui Example)
description:
Introduction

Gpui has been gaining a lot of popularity these last couple of months, and I am proud to say I have been a fan of the framework long before that. As a matter of fact, here is a tweet by me saying that people should talk about it more (when people didn't talk about it more):

In my opinion, two things are contributing to the popularity of the framework today:

  • Performance: I think it is clear to everyone now that gpui is the best alternative to electron applications.
  • AI: Many people hate using Rust because of the borrow checker, but with agents, they no longer have to deal with it as much.

What I really loved about the framework, however, is its approach to state management. When I first started building terminal user interfaces with Rust, I struggled with how I should approach state management, because with Rust (unlike JavaScript) the borrow checker makes things especially hard.

After seeing how gpui handled this, by studying the codebase and reading this gem of an article, I noticed that the approach adopted can be transferred to any other application which wants to manage state effectively.

In this blog post, I will share how I built an experimental state management crate for Rust, and I will use it to build an application with ratatui.

State Management Crate

Our state management crate creates a state. It provides components of the application with ways to read and update said state. In Rust, each variable has a unique owner. So, in order to avoid the complexity that comes with the borrow checker, the state is going to be owned by one App object.

Instead of multiple components holding references to the state owned by the App, the App gives out cheap handles to the components which want to read or update it. This is possible because the App stores its entities in a SlotMap data structure.

A SlotMap is an array which allows O(1) insertion and retrieval of elements by key. A key is returned after inserting a value, and the key will always refer to the value which was inserted. This makes it ideal for storing our application entities.

For our use case, the slotmap crate is used. With that dependency in place, we can start building our crate, beginning with the App struct that owns everything.

App

So, let us define the App struct as follows:

pub struct App {
  map: SlotMap<DefaultKey, Option<Box<dyn Any>>>
}
  • DefaultKey is the type of the key returned after inserting values into the SlotMap.
  • Values are Option<Box<dyn Any>>, since a state can be anything; wrapping it in an Option is useful for preventing reentrant updates.

Entity

Next, let's define what an Entity is. In gpui, Entity represents the handle that the App gives out. It basically contains the key of the value inserted into the slotmap, a ref_count to count how many times the entity was cloned, and a PhantomData which specifies which type the Entity holds.

pub struct Entity<T> {
  entity_id: DefaultKey,
  ref_count: Rc<()>,
  _marker: PhantomData<T> 
}

With this, we can implement a method to register new entities.

impl App {
  fn new<T: 'static>(&mut self, build: impl FnOnce(&App) -> T) -> Entity<T> {
    let state = build(self);
    let entity_id = self.map.insert(Some(Box::new(state)));
    Entity {
      entity_id,
      ref_count: Rc::new(()),
      _marker: PhantomData
    }
  }
}

As you can see, the method accepts a closure which is handed a reference to the App. This is because some entities might need to be initialised with data from other entities in App.

Let us now implement a method to read from a state.

impl App {
    pub fn read<T: 'static>(&self, entity: &Entity<T>) -> &T {
        let value = self.map.get(entity.entity_id).expect("stale handle");
        match value {
            Some(value) => value.downcast_ref::<T>().unwrap(),
            None => {
                panic!("cannot read a value which is currently being updated")
            }
        }
    }
}

SlotMap::get returns None when the key isn't present in the map. This happens if the entity was removed (and the slot's generation bumped), or if the handle is simply invalid. We expect here rather than propagate the error, because reaching this state should never happen in a correctly-behaving program. If it does, it signals a bug in our architecture, not a recoverable condition. Since this is an experimental crate, we're choosing to fail loudly rather than handle every edge case gracefully.

The next step is to implement an update method in order to update entities.

impl App {
    pub fn update<T: 'static, R>(
        &mut self,
        entity: Entity<T>,
        update: impl FnOnce(&mut T, &mut App) -> R,
    ) -> R {
        let value = self.map.get_mut(entity.entity_id).expect("stale handle");
        let boxed = value.take().expect("entity already being updated");
        let mut state: T = *boxed.downcast::<T>().unwrap();
        let result: R = update(&mut state, self);
        *self.map.get_mut(entity.entity_id).unwrap() = Some(Box::new(state));
        result
    }
}

The method receives a closure which is yielded a mutable reference to the entity it wants to update. The expect after take panics in case of reentrancy: if the entity is already being updated, we cannot call update on it again. This is why we chose to use Option as the value type in the SlotMap . It gives us a way to signal that this value is not available right now.

Dropping stale entities

When there are no more handles pointing to a state in the map, the state is marked as stale and should be removed.

To achieve this, we add a pending field to our App struct to keep track of the stale entities:

pub struct App {
  map: SlotMap<DefaultKey, Option<Box<dyn Any>>>,
  pending: Rc<RefCell<Vec<DefaultKey>>>
}

When an entity handle is dropped, it checks if it is the only handle remaining to the state. If no other handle remains, it pushes its entity_id onto the pending queue.

Entity should have access to the pending queue. We give it a Weak reference rather than an Rc, so that holding an Entity never keeps App's queue (and thus App itself) artificially alive:

pub struct Entity<T> {
  entity_id: DefaultKey,
  ref_count: Rc<()>,
  pending: Weak<RefCell<Vec<DefaultKey>>>,
  _marker: PhantomData<T>
}

With this new field in place, we need to update new_entity to populate it whenever an entity is created:

pub fn new_entity<T: 'static>(&mut self, build: impl FnOnce(&App) -> T) -> Entity<T> {
        let entity = build(self);
        let entity_id = self.map.insert(Some(Box::new(entity)));
        Entity {
            entity_id,
            ref_count: Rc::new(()),
            pending: Rc::downgrade(&self.pending),
            _marker: PhantomData,
        }
    }

Then we implement Drop for Entity, so that when the last handle to a state goes out of scope, its slot is queued for removal:

impl<T> Drop for Entity<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if Rc::strong_count(&self.ref_count) == 1
            && let Some(queue) = self.pending.upgrade()
        {
            queue.borrow_mut().push(self.entity_id);
        }
    }
}

Finally, we implement a method called flush_entities which drains the queue and actually removes those stale slots from the map:

impl App {
  pub fn flush_entities(&mut self) {
        let ids: Vec<DefaultKey> = self.pending.borrow_mut().drain(..).collect();
        for id in ids {
            self.map.remove(id);
        }
  }
}

Usage

Let's test our framework by creating a simple Ratatui application. In the majority of applications, one component updates a state, and another one reads from that state.

In our test application, we will demonstrate this by creating two widgets. One will act as an input and update an input_buffer. The second widget will just read the input_buffer and reflect its changes (In real world applications, this second widget might use the input to filter search results for example).

We will start by creating a Root struct. The Root struct holds a reference to an App struct:

struct Root<'a> {
  app: &'a mut App,
  widgets: Vec<Box<dyn Component>>
}

The Root also holds a list of widgets, defined using the Component trait. We define the Component trait as follows:

trait Component {
    fn render_with_cx(&mut self, cx: &mut App, frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect);
    fn handle_key(&mut self, cx: &mut App, key: KeyEvent);
}

Each component uses render_with_cx to draw on the frame while still having access to the context. Components also define a handle_key method in order to handle events.

Let us create our two widgets with their implementations of Component.

struct InputWidget {
    input_buffer: Entity<String>,
}

struct EchoWidget {
    input_buffer: Entity<String>,
}

Each widget owns an Entity<String>. The input widget updates input_buffer and the echo widget reads it and displays it.

impl InputWidget {
    fn init(input_buffer: Entity<String>) -> Self {
        Self { input_buffer }
    }
}

impl EchoWidget {
    fn init(input_buffer: Entity<String>) -> Self {
        Self { input_buffer }
    }
}

impl Component for InputWidget {
    fn render_with_cx(&mut self, cx: &mut App, frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect) {
        let block = Block::bordered()
            .title("Input")
            .padding(Padding::uniform(1));
        let inner = block.inner(area);
        block.render(area, frame.buffer_mut());

        let input_buffer = cx.read(&self.input_buffer);
        let text_width = input_buffer.chars().count() as u16;

        frame.set_cursor_position(Position::new(inner.x + text_width, inner.y));
        Paragraph::new(&input_buffer[..])
            .wrap(Wrap { trim: false })
            .render(inner, frame.buffer_mut());
    }

    fn handle_key(&mut self, cx: &mut App, key: KeyEvent) {
        match key.code {
            KeyCode::Char(c) => cx.update(self.input_buffer.clone(), |input_buffer, _cx| {
                input_buffer.push(c);
            }),
            KeyCode::Backspace => cx.update(self.input_buffer.clone(), |input_buffer, _cx| {
                if input_buffer.len() > 0 {
                    input_buffer.remove(input_buffer.len() - 1);
                }
            }),
            _ => {}
        }
    }
}

In render_with_cx we render a block and a paragraph. To learn more about widgets and how to render them, you can check the ratatui documentation. The interesting part is that the paragraph is initialised with the input_buffer contents, thus the call to cx.read(&self.input_buffer).

In handle_key we listen to key events and then update our input_buffer state with cx.update().

The EchoWidget component only reads the input buffer entity and displays it:

impl Component for EchoWidget {
    fn render_with_cx(&mut self, cx: &mut App, frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect) {
        let block = Block::bordered()
            .title("Echo")
            .padding(Padding::uniform(1));
        let inner = block.inner(area);
        block.render(area, frame.buffer_mut());

        let input_buffer = cx.read(&self.input_buffer);
        Paragraph::new(&input_buffer[..])
            .wrap(Wrap { trim: false })
            .render(inner, frame.buffer_mut());
    }

    // Echo widget is read-only: it never receives input focus or key events.
    fn handle_key(&mut self, _cx: &mut App, _key: KeyEvent) {}
}

Entity creation happens when initialising the Root struct by calling cx.new_entity:

impl<'a> Root<'a> {
    fn init(cx: &'a mut App) -> Root<'a> {
        let input_buffer = cx.new_entity(|_| "Enter Text".into());
        Root {
            app: cx,
            widgets: vec![
                Box::new(InputWidget::init(input_buffer.clone())),
                Box::new(EchoWidget::init(input_buffer.clone())),
            ],
        }
    }
}

We also define a run method for Root which does the drawing by calling the render_with_cx method on each component, and listens for events by calling handle_key_event on each component in the root.

impl<'a> Root<'a> {
    fn run(&mut self, terminal: &mut DefaultTerminal) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        loop {
            self.app.flush_entities();
            let _ = terminal.draw(|frame| {
                let [top, bottom] =
                    Layout::vertical([Constraint::Percentage(50), Constraint::Percentage(50)])
                        .areas(frame.area());
                self.widgets[0].render_with_cx(self.app, frame, top);
                self.widgets[1].render_with_cx(self.app, frame, bottom);
            });

            if let Event::Key(key_event) = event::read()? {
                if !key_event.is_press() {
                    continue;
                }
                let is_quit = key_event.code == KeyCode::Esc
                    || (key_event.code == KeyCode::Char('c')
                        && key_event.modifiers.contains(KeyModifiers::CONTROL));
                if is_quit {
                    break Ok(());
                }
                // Only the input widget (top, index 0) is interactive.
                self.widgets[0].handle_key(self.app, key_event);
            }
        }
    }
}

Finally, we define our main function:

fn main() {
    let mut app: App = App::init();
    let mut root = Root::init(&mut app);
    let _ = ratatui::run(|terminal| root.run(terminal));
}

Conclusion

Using our state management crate inspired by gpui, we were able to effectively manage state without dealing with the complexities that the borrow checker brings. Rather than wrapping each piece of shared state in an Rc<RefCell<T>>, as is common in Rust UI code, our state lives in a single SlotMap owned by the App. Components simply hold cheap Entity<T> handles into that map, instead of sharing mutable references directly.

The state management crate we developed here is experimental. It could be enhanced with other features, mainly:

  • Only redraw when the UI is marked as dirty, instead of each frame.
  • Components subscribing to/observing a certain state. (We didn't have to deal with this here, since we redraw the entire UI each tick.)

Code is available on GitHub:

  • State Management Crate
  • Test Application

title: Spring ApplicationContext Hierarchy and a High CVE in Axelix
description:
Introduction

Hi everyone!

My name is Mikhail Polivakha, and I am the Tech Lead of the Axelix project. If you haven't heard of us before, Axelix is a platform for managing and diagnosing Spring Boot applications. The core of the project is open source, so the source code, the change history and, as it turned out, our mistakes are open to everyone 😁.

Recently, an external security researcher, Andrei Kotov (greatkaa), found a vulnerability in Axelix. In short: under a certain Spring Boot configuration, our Actuator endpoints could be called without a JWT. We have already fixed it in version 1.2.1 and described it in a Security Advisory. Andrei, I'll use this opportunity to say a big thank you.

Let me say right away that this article is not about how the vulnerability could have been exploited. Honestly, that's not all that interesting. What's far more interesting is why it appeared at all. We didn't forget to add the filter, we didn't get the token signature check wrong, and we didn't mix up a condition in an if. The filter was there, and it worked perfectly. Just not where we thought it was.

The cause lies in a Spring Framework mechanism that has existed for about twenty years, yet many modern Spring Boot developers never think about it at all. I'm talking about the ApplicationContext hierarchy.

So here's the plan: first, we'll figure out what a context hierarchy is and who sees whom in it. Then we'll look at where Spring Boot itself creates one. And only after that will we return to Axelix and see how it all added up to one unpleasant story.

Let's dig in.

Where it all started

Let's start with the symptom, because in my opinion it is very telling. The configuration was completely ordinary:

server:
  port: 8080

management:
  server:
    port: 8081

So the business API lives on 8080, and Actuator is moved to a separate port, 8081. A lot of people do this, and it's good practice: the management port is easy to close off from the outside world at the network level.

Axelix exposes its endpoints through Actuator (they are called axelix-*), and all of them are protected by a JWT filter. When Actuator lives on the main port, a request without a token gets the expected 401 Unauthorized. But on 8081, the very same request suddenly went through.

Friends, note an important detail: the application started up normally. No NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, no warnings in the logs, all endpoints in place, dependencies injected. Everything looks great. These are exactly the most unpleasant kind of bugs. Everything seems to work fine.

Why does simply changing a port number change the behavior so much? To answer that, we need to take a step back.

One big context. Or not?

ApplicationContext is Spring's central container. It holds bean definitions, creates beans, resolves dependencies, runs them through post-processors, publishes events, and manages the lifecycle.

If you write Spring Boot code, you most likely have roughly this model in your head:

My application has one big Spring context, and all beans live inside it.

And that's fine, because in the vast majority of cases that is exactly how it is. SpringApplication.run(...) creates a ServletWebServerApplicationContext, which starts embedded Tomcat itself, finds servlets and filters itself, and registers them itself (ServletWebServerApplicationContext Javadoc). One context is more than enough.

But here's the thing: a context in Spring doesn't have to be the only one. ApplicationContext has a getParent() method, and the link is set via ConfigurableApplicationContext#setParent. In other words, contexts can form a tree.

A bit of history. Root and DispatcherServlet

Those who worked with Spring MVC before Spring Boot have almost certainly run into context hierarchies, even if they never thought about it specifically. The classic setup looked like this:

root WebApplicationContext
  services
  repositories
  shared infrastructure
          |
          v
DispatcherServlet WebApplicationContext
  controllers
  handler mappings
  web-specific beans

The root context was created by ContextLoaderListener from web.xml, and each DispatcherServlet started its own (!) child WebApplicationContext. Services and repositories lived at the top and were shared, while the controllers and all the MVC infrastructure of a particular servlet lived at the bottom. Moreover, a single root could have several independent children (Spring MVC documentation).

Then Spring Boot came along, everything collapsed into a single context, and most people happily forgot about the hierarchy. But the mechanism didn't go anywhere. A second context can still appear today:

  • from an explicit call to parent(...), child(...) or sibling(...) on SpringApplicationBuilder;
  • from a test with @ContextHierarchy;
  • from Spring Cloud, which starts its own child contexts, for example for each Feign client (surprise, dear friends!);
  • and, most importantly for us, from Spring Boot Actuator when a separate management port is used.

We'll come back to that last item. For now, let's understand the main thing: how contexts in a hierarchy see each other.

Who sees whom

The rules here are fairly simple, but asymmetric:

  • a child sees the parent's beans;
  • a parent does not see (!) the child's beans;
  • sibling contexts, that is, children of the same parent, know nothing about each other;
  • if a child declares a bean with the same name as the parent's, the local (child's) definition overrides the parent's.

This is stated explicitly in the ApplicationContext Javadoc. Let's look at it in code, it's clearer that way:

@Configuration
class ParentConfig {

    @Bean
    SharedService sharedService() {
        return new SharedService();
    }
}

@Configuration
class ChildConfig {

    @Bean
    ChildOnlyService childOnlyService(SharedService sharedService) {
        return new ChildOnlyService(sharedService);
    }
}

var parent = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ParentConfig.class);

var child = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
child.setParent(parent);
child.register(ChildConfig.class);
child.refresh();

child.getBean(SharedService.class);          // OK, found in parent
child.containsBean("sharedService");         // true
child.containsLocalBean("sharedService");    // false, not present locally

parent.getBean(ChildOnlyService.class);      // NoSuchBeanDefinitionException

Note the difference between containsBean and containsLocalBean. The first takes the parent into account, the second looks only at the current level. This distinction will come in very handy later.

So, roughly speaking, a child knows where to go upstairs if it can't find something at home. But a parent may not even suspect that a particular child exists. The word "parent" creates a pleasant feeling that the elder knows about all the younger ones. In Spring, it's exactly the other way around.

Seeing a bean is not owning it

And now the most important idea of this article. Let me highlight it:

The fact that a child can get a bean from its parent does not mean that the child "uses" that bean as part of its own infrastructure.

Every context in a hierarchy remains a full-fledged, separate container. It has its own bean definitions, its own post-processors, its own lifecycle, its own event multicaster. The hierarchy gives you just one thing: dependency lookup upwards. Everything else each context does on its own, and only with its own beans.

Here are a few examples of how this shows up:

  • a BeanPostProcessor declared in the parent does not process beans created in the child;
  • getBeansOfType() lists only local beans. To walk the ancestors, you need BeanFactoryUtils.beansOfTypeIncludingAncestors(...);
  • events published in the child propagate up to the parent. But the parent's events do not flow down to the children on their own;
  • the parent has no universal API to iterate over all of its children.

There's one more amusing nuance about events. If an @EventListener is declared in the parent, it will also receive the child's ContextRefreshedEvent. So if you do something "on application startup" on this event, then with a child context present your code may run twice. That's why it's useful to check which context the event actually came from.

And finally, the example we're discussing all this for. An embedded web server (Tomcat, for instance) is started by a specific ServletWebServerApplicationContext, and at startup that context registers in the server the Servlets, Filters and ServletContextInitializers that are defined in that context itself. If your FilterRegistrationBean lives in the parent, but the server is started by the child, then the filter won't make it into that server. The child "sees" it, of course, but that has no effect on which filter chain it builds for its server.

Remember this idea, we'll come back to it shortly.

A separate Actuator port is a separate context

So, what happens when you set management.server.port?

Spring Boot distinguishes between two situations. If management.server.port is not set or matches server.port, Actuator simply lives in the main context. But if the ports differ, Boot creates a separate child management context, for which the main context is the parent (ManagementContextAutoConfiguration).

Schematically, it looks like this:

application                          parent
  server.port=8080                     |
  web server :8080                     |
  controllers, services                |
                                       v
application:management               child
  management.server.port=8081
  web server :8081
  Actuator handler mappings
  its own servlet filter chain

So management.server.port changes far, far more than just the socket number! A second ApplicationContext appears, a second embedded server, its own handler mappings and its own chain of servlet filters. The Spring Boot documentation, by the way, honestly warns about this: a management context on a different port does not use the same web infrastructure as the main application (Spring Boot Actuator 2.7 reference). But we don't read it, we vibe-code, as everyone knows.

So, in essence, from the web layer's point of view, you now have two different applications.

How a library gets into the management context

A logical question: what if a library (for example, a starter like ours) needs to put something specifically into the management context? Spring Boot has a dedicated annotation for that, @ManagementContextConfiguration. It has a ManagementContextType parameter:

  • SAME means the configuration applies when Actuator lives in the main context;
  • CHILD means the configuration applies in a separate child management context;
  • ANY means the configuration should be applied in both cases.

The annotation alone isn't enough, though. The class also has to be registered in a special file:

META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.actuate.autoconfigure.web.ManagementContextConfiguration.imports

This is very similar to how regular auto-configurations are registered via AutoConfiguration.imports, except that Boot reads this file when it creates the management context. (Spring Boot 2.7 still also supported spring.factories for old times' sake, so if you're copying an example from older documentation, check the version. Selector in Boot 2.7, selector in Boot 3.5.)

What happened in Axelix

And now, I think, you can already guess what happened.

A little context on how Axelix works. Our starter is added to the application (axelix-spring-boot-2-starter, -3-starter or -4-starter, depending on the Boot version). The starter exposes a set of Actuator endpoints through which Axelix collects information about the application: beans, configuration, loggers, caches, and so on. All of these endpoints are protected by JWT, and token validation is handled by our JwtAuthorizationFilter.

Before version 1.2.1, this filter was registered in a regular auto-configuration, that is, via a FilterRegistrationBean in the main context (Axelix 1.2.0 code).

When Actuator lives on the main port, everything is fine:

single context
  web server :8080
  Actuator mappings
  JwtAuthorizationFilter

The request goes through the filter, there's no token, we get 401.

But with different ports, the picture looks like this:

main context
  web server :8080
  JwtAuthorizationFilter       <- the filter is here
          |
          v
management child
  web server :8081
  Actuator mappings            <- but the endpoints are here
  no JwtAuthorizationFilter

The management child sees all the beans it needs from the parent perfectly well, so the application starts without a single error. The endpoints work. But the server on 8081 builds its own filter chain, and our filter isn't in it. Exactly what we talked about in the "Seeing a bean is not owning it" section.

The root cause in one sentence: we registered the JWT filter in the parent context, while Actuator on the separate port was served by a different server from the child context.

The funniest part is that the JWT check itself worked flawlessly. The request simply never reached it.

There was one more symptom that illustrates what was going on nicely. Some endpoints on 8081 responded not with 200, but with 500 and the message Security Context is expected to be present at this point. These endpoints expected the security context to already be populated, and it was precisely the missing filter that populated it. And even with a valid token it was the same: there was simply nobody to process the token.

Honestly, looking back, the bug seems obvious. But at the time the code was written, we, like many others, had that very "one big context" model in our heads. And our tests only hit the main port, so they caught nothing. It's a good thing there are people like Andrei who look at code from a different angle.

How we fixed it

The solution suggests itself: the filter has to be registered where the server with Actuator is started. In 1.2.1, all three starters got a separate JwtAuthManagementContextConfiguration (the fix):

@ManagementContextConfiguration(
        value = ManagementContextType.CHILD,
        proxyBeanMethods = false
)
@ConditionalOnBean(WebIdentityAccessManager.class)
public class JwtAuthManagementContextConfiguration {

    @Bean
    public FilterRegistrationBean<JwtAuthorizationFilter>
            jwtAuthorizationFilterRegistration(
                    WebIdentityAccessManager webIdentityAccessManager,
                    SecurityContextExecutor securityContextExecutor,
                    WebEndpointProperties webEndpointProperties) {

        var filter = new JwtAuthorizationFilter(
                webIdentityAccessManager,
                securityContextExecutor,
                webEndpointProperties.getBasePath()
        );
        var registration = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(filter);
        registration.setName("jwtAuthorizationFilter");
        return registration;
    }
}

And, of course, the class is listed in each starter's ManagementContextConfiguration.imports.

Look how everything we discussed above works here. WebIdentityAccessManager and SecurityContextExecutor still live in the parent, and the child gets them without any trouble via lookup. But the FilterRegistrationBean is now created locally in the management context, so it's the management server that includes the filter in its chain. The hierarchy is used exactly as intended: shared services at the top, the web infrastructure of a specific server at the bottom.

If we phrase what we restored as a rule, it goes like this: the server that exposes the Axelix endpoints must itself have the JWT filter in its filter chain.

And, of course, a test. Importantly, it checks the topology specifically, not the presence of a bean "somewhere in the container":

@SpringBootTest(
        webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT,
        properties = "management.server.port=0"
)
class JwtAuthorizationFilterSeparateManagementPortTest {

    @LocalManagementPort
    private int managementPort;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUnauthorized_TokenIsMissing() {
        var response = restTemplate.getForEntity(
                "http://localhost:" + managementPort
                        + "/actuator/axelix-env",
                String.class
        );

        assertThat(response.getStatusCode())
                .isEqualTo(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
    }
}

management.server.port=0 makes Boot start the management context on a random port, and @LocalManagementPort gives us that port. The second test in the same class sends a valid token and expects 200 OK. The same tests exist for Boot 2, 3 and 4 (test in 1.2.1).

A small off-topic note about the follow-up

After the release, Andrei pointed out one more thing to us. The first patch left the filter registered both in the main context and in the child. Security didn't suffer from this, but with separate ports the filter on the main server was essentially redundant: Actuator isn't there anymore.

In PR #1818, we removed the registration from the regular auto-configuration and changed ManagementContextType.CHILD to ANY. Now a single management configuration is responsible for the filter in both cases: when the port is shared and when it's separate. At the time of writing, this change is already in main but hasn't made it into a release yet. It's an architectural cleanup, not an additional security fix, so 1.2.1 closes the issue completely.

How to look at the hierarchy in your own application

If you've always assumed until now that you have just one context, the first useful step is very simple: stop guessing and take a look.

@Component
final class ContextTopologyLogger {

    @EventListener
    void onRefreshed(ContextRefreshedEvent event) {
        ApplicationContext context = event.getApplicationContext();
        ApplicationContext parent = context.getParent();

        System.out.printf(
                "context=%s class=%s parent=%s beans=%d%n",
                context.getId(),
                context.getClass().getName(),
                parent == null ? "<root>" : parent.getId(),
                context.getBeanDefinitionCount()
        );
    }
}

Remember that events propagate from the child up to the parent? That's exactly why this listener, declared in the main context, will also see the management child's refresh. And that's exactly why it's important to take the context from the event itself here, rather than from an injected ApplicationContext. Run the application with management.server.port, and you'll see two lines in the logs instead of one.

A few more useful tools:

  • context.getParent() returns the immediate parent;
  • containsLocalBean(name) tells you whether the bean is defined at the current level;
  • containsBean(name) also takes parents into account;
  • BeanFactoryUtils.beanNamesForTypeIncludingAncestors(...) explicitly searches through all ancestors.

The standard Actuator endpoint /actuator/beans also returns a contexts object, where a context can have a parentId (Actuator beans API). But there's a nuance: the endpoint describes the context it lives in and its ancestors. It isn't required to look for its descendants. So the result depends on which port you hit.

And a piece of advice for those who write their own starters or simply hook something onto Actuator: if your code has to work with a separate management port, then test it specifically on a separate management port. A test that only hits @LocalServerPort doesn't check the management server at all. We learned this from our own experience.

Summary

Let's gather the key points:

  • An ApplicationContext in Spring doesn't have to be the only one. Contexts form a tree, and Spring Boot itself creates such a tree more often than it seems.
  • Visibility in the hierarchy works bottom-up: the child sees the parent, the parent doesn't see the child.
  • Seeing a bean doesn't make it part of another context's infrastructure. Post-processors, events, the filter chain and the web server are each context's own.
  • A management.server.port different from server.port means a separate child context and a separate web server. Treat it as a second web application.
  • If a library needs to put something into the management context, there's @ManagementContextConfiguration for that.

For us, this story was a good reminder that even a very familiar framework can surprise you if you rely on a simplified mental model. And a simplified model works for years, right up until it stops working.

Once again, thanks to Andrei for the find and for the careful review of the patch. And if you're curious about how Axelix works on the inside, welcome to GitHub, we're open.

Good luck, everyone!

title: Neural-DISCO: Source-Conditioned Counterfactual Editing of Neural Population Activity
description:
arXiv:2610.33145v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding how neural activity encodes behavioral and sensory variables is a key challenge in systems neuroscience. This requires models that go beyond predicting activity from labels and instead support source-conditioned counterfactual editing: given a recorded source response, we should be able to edit one measured behavioral or stimulus label and predict how neural activity would change while preserving other observed labels and source-specific variability not explained by the labels. Here, we introduce \textbf{Neural-DISCO}, a disentangled representation learning framework for counterfactual modeling of neural activity. Neural-DISCO partitions the latent space into label-specific components, each associated with an observed behavioral or stimulus label, together with a residual latent that captures variability not supplied through observed labels. Across simulated and real neural recording datasets, we show that this structure enables selective editing of measured labels to generate counterfactual neural responses while preserving the remaining content of the original activity. Further, to gain insight into how behavioral and stimulus labels are encoded at single-neuron resolution, we pair this disentangled framework with feature attribution methods that identify which neurons are most important for each label. We find that disentanglement enhances the recovery of known functional cell roles in both synthetic and real data. Together, these results support Neural-DISCO as a framework for counterfactual modeling of neural activity and provide a practical interface for probing how neural populations encode behavior and sensory information. Code is available at https://github.com/TangLab-UBC/Neural-DISCO-neurips.

title: One Call Ahead: Packed Self-Speculative Decoding with Diffusion Drafting
description:
arXiv:2610.33379v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) language models generate tokens sequentially, so generating long outputs is costly. Speculative decoding mitigates this by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens for the target AR model to verify in parallel, while a diffusion-based drafter can produce an entire draft block in one forward pass. In models with AR and diffusion modes, one network both drafts and verifies, but drafting still waits for verification, so the standard schedule needs two sequential model calls per iteration. Existing one-call schedules avoid the wait but incur input size quadratic in the speculative width. Motivated by this efficiency bottleneck, we introduce Packed-SS, a self-speculative decoding schedule that verifies and drafts in a single model call with input size linear in the speculative width, while preserving the target model's distribution. The key idea is to let the diffusion drafter run one call ahead: while verifying the current draft, the model simultaneously constructs the next draft from an older verified prefix and keeps its unresolved suffix for the next iteration. Under a mild monotonicity assumption on the drafter, we further show that Packed-SS requires no more model calls than the standard two-call decoding in the greedy setting. Experiments on Nemotron 3B/8B and SetDLM 1.7B show higher throughput and lower mean wall time than both baselines under greedy decoding.

title: Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning for Dyadic Relationship Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.36249v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dyadic relationship recognition aims to identify the latent social relationship between two individuals from their multimodal interactions. Existing methods typically project heterogeneous cues into a shared representation and optimise a flat classification objective, overlooking that relationships may rely on different interaction patterns. For instance, distant relationships can often be inferred from direct behavioural correspondence, whereas close relationships are better reflected by coordinated affective, behavioural, and multimodal responses. To address this limitation, we propose HiRe-DRR, a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning framework that organises relationship evidence from three complementary perspectives: feature level, interaction type, and relationship hierarchy. HiRe-DRR decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations and constructs homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions. We further introduce the Mixture-of-Interaction Transformer (MoI-Former), which treats diverse interactions as specialised experts and employs relation-aware sparse routing to identify relationship-relevant evidence while preserving contextual interaction information. The proposed Hierarchical Conditional Loss (HC-Loss) exploits the hierarchical nature of social relationships through coarse-to-fine supervision, enabling structured relationship reasoning. Extensive experiments on three dyadic relationship benchmarks demonstrate that HiRe-DRR outperforms recent representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods. Our routing analysis further reveals that distant relationships tend to rely on low-level homogeneous interactions, whereas closer relationships focus on high-level heterogeneous interactions. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tw-repository/HiRe-DRR.

title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.36328v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. On the matched tasks, specialized prover proofs nevertheless have higher overall unchanged-proof survival than the supplied reference artifacts: +15.6 points for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, +18.8 for Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and +20.3 for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B; all three 95% CIs exclude zero. The ordering persists after excluding universally survived T1 variants, under family-balanced aggregation, and under alternative deployable valid-proof selection rules. However, unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures. RefactorProof therefore measures unchanged-proof stability under program refactoring, not the cost of maintaining a proof after it breaks.

title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.

October 2026 summary

  • Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.

  • September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.

  • Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.

  • Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.

Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%

In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.

Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.

Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.

In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.

Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.

In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.

Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business.

AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves

Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.

September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.

Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.

Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.

The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.

Chinese models are big business for American providers

More than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.

DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.

Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.

Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.

The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers.

September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6

Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.

Jev is the most-adopted and most-called model

In its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history.

Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.

Jev is a decision model. Compared with typical language-model requests, a Jev request is faster, cheaper and uses a fraction of the tokens. So although its adoption was fast and broad, it accounted for just 1% of the month’s tokens and 0.15% of spend.

In September, Jev quickly became a popular model for production while remaining a tiny part of the inference bill.

Opus 5.5 takes more than one in ten gateway dollars

The launch that received the most dollars was Opus 5.5, with more than twice the share of any other September launch, followed by GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash.

Opus 5.5 caught on quickly, with almost nine in ten dollars coming from teams already using Opus 5. Existing customers were trying the new release while the wider Opus family was losing market share.

Across all versions, Opus accounted for almost a third of gateway dollars in September, down from one in two in August. Anthropic’s overall share fell below half of total gateway spend for the first time, dropping from 63.7% to 43.9%.

Luna brought users back; Astra brought spend

GPT-6 Luna reached nearly three out of every twenty paid teams in its first two weeks, in third place behind Jev and Sonnet 5.5. But its return rate was the highest of the month; almost two-thirds of the teams that tried it in its first week came back in the second.

GPT-6 Astra reached a smaller audience but took more budget. In its first two weeks, it accounted for about one in twenty gateway dollars; Luna accounted for less than one in a hundred. Luna reached almost three times as many teams while Astra captured more than five times the share of spend.

OpenAI is attracting more customers with Luna, but capturing far more money with Astra, even though fewer teams use it.

Full September scorecard

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

  • September 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through September 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, a broader definition than in earlier reports.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million paid tokens in both months. “Most-used” is measured by paid tokens.

  • Provider location means company headquarters.

  • Launch metrics cover external paid teams during each model’s first 14 days. Reach uses paid teams active from the start of the launch month through the data cutoff. Spend share uses total paid gateway spending during the model’s window. Return rate is the share of first-week teams that used it again in week two.

  • Model counts cover December–September, with each version counted separately. Team-size thresholds use total input and output tokens over that period.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: FastAPI frontends and static files served from the CDN
description:
FastAPI frontends and static files, served with app.frontend() or StaticFiles, are now promoted to the Vercel CDN at build time. Requests for those paths are served directly from the CDN, without invoking your Vercel Function.

FastAPI evaluates routes in declaration order. A route declared before a StaticFiles mount takes priority over any CDN file at that path. This precedence is preserved.

Promoted source directories remain in the function bundle so the app can read from them at runtime. To exclude them and serve only from the CDN, set tool.vercel.fastapi.static.exclude = true in pyproject.toml.

Frontends guarded by dependencies are kept on the function as the CDN cannot run dependency checks. Similarly, static files which sit behind middleware are also kept on the function. To override this and always promote to CDN, set tool.vercel.fastapi.static.cdn = true. To opt out of the CDN entirely, set it to false instead.

For more information see the Vercel FastAPI documentation.

title: CRLoMTL: Conflict-Resolution through Low-rank matrices for Multi-Task Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.36337v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) improves model efficiency by sharing representations across related vision tasks, but it often suffers from negative transfer when task updates interfere with one another. Existing conflict-mitigation methods typically operate in gradient space, requiring explicit task-gradient manipulation and additional optimization steps. We propose Conflict-Resolution through Low-Rank Matrices for Multi-Task Learning (CRLoMTL), a parameter-efficient framework that mitigates task interference in the low-rank parameter-update space. CRLoMTL learns task-specific LoRA updates through task-specific passes, where each task updates its own low-rank matrices, and integrates these updates through global shared-subspace fusion. Specifically, we introduce a shared-subspace resolver based on singular value decomposition (SVD), referred to as the SVD resolver, which extracts a common low-dimensional orthonormal basis across task adapters and projects task updates into this shared space before merging them into a single deployment-time update. The resulting update can be folded into the backbone, preserving the inference structure of the original model without additional runtime branches. Experiments with Swin Transformer backbones on PASCAL-Context, NYUD-v2, and CelebA show that CRLoMTL achieves a favorable accuracy-parameter trade-off, improving over single-task baselines by up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA, while training only a small fraction of the parameters used by single-task models.

title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
description:
arXiv:2610.35942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI drafts of the same kind of brief, built from SEC filings made after the models' training data were collected. Told the drafter's true error rate, the reviewer checked more as it rose, but all-or-nothing, switching near where its prompt's costs break even. Told that the drafter erred ten times less often than it did, it checked 7 fewer of 9 figures and let a wrong figure through in 22.5% of briefs instead of none: faster and worse, entirely through reduced effort.

title: Engineering Edge-Resilient RFID Registration for Saudi Mega-Events
description:
When engineering an event registration platform for Saudi Vision 2030 mega-exhibitions, standard cloud-native architecture becomes a critical liability.

If you are deploying check-in infrastructure at a massive convention center in Riyadh or Jeddah, you must account for extreme crowd density. When 10,000 enterprise delegates flood an ingress zone within a narrow two-hour window, local 5G macrocells instantly saturate. Public venue Wi-Fi networks routinely drop packets or crash entirely under the concurrent load.

If your self-service check-in kiosks rely on a synchronous HTTP request to a central cloud server just to validate a ticket or print an RFID badge, your entire perimeter will gridlock the moment connectivity degrades.

To guarantee zero-latency check-ins and high-availability spatial telemetry, modern event technology must push data persistence to the extreme edge. Here is the architectural blueprint for building offline-first accreditation hardware and a high-performance digital frontend.

1. The Physical Edge: Go and SQLite in WAL Mode

To ensure that check-in lines never stop moving, admission logic must be processed directly on the physical hardware. At StampIQ, our self-service kiosks run on ARM-based single-board computers (SBCs) that interface directly with rapid RFID encoders.

Instead of querying a remote PostgreSQL cluster, every physical kiosk runs an embedded SQLite database in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode. 


go
package edge_kiosk

import (
    "database/sql"
    "log"
    _ "[github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3](https://github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3)"
)

func InitializeLocalDB() *sql.DB {
    // WAL mode enables concurrent reading (badge validation) and background cloud syncing
    db, err := sql.Open("sqlite3", "file:/var/lib/stampiq/edge.db?_journal_mode=WAL&_synchronous=NORMAL")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Critical Edge Error: Local DB initialization failed: %v", err)
    }

    // Optimize in-memory storage for rapid concurrent hardware operations
    db.Exec(`PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;`)
    db.Exec(`PRAGMA mmap_size = 268435456;`) // 256MB memory map

    // Local validation queue
    db.Exec(`
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS local_admissions (
            ticket_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            delegate_name TEXT NOT NULL,
            badge_printed INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
            synced_to_cloud INTEGER DEFAULT 0
        );
        CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_sync ON local_admissions(synced_to_cloud) WHERE synced_to_cloud = 0;
    `)

    return db
}
When an attendee scans their pre-registration barcode, the Go binary queries the local SQLite replica. The kiosk authorizes the delegate, prints a customized badge, and encodes a dual-frequency (UHF/NFC) microchip in under 3 seconds. Because this operates entirely offline, the hardware processes attendees flawlessly during total network blackouts, automatically draining the synced_to_cloud = 0 queue when the venue network recovers.

2. Unlocking Passive Spatial Telemetry
Edge accreditation hardware sets the foundation for the entire event's data ecosystem. By successfully issuing an RFID-encoded smart badge at the front door, you eliminate the need for manual barcode scanning inside the exhibition hall.

Passive overhead Ultra-High Frequency (UHF) portals are deployed across sponsor activation zones. These edge nodes silently capture spatial telemetry (up to 400 tag reads per second), streaming automated, highly accurate exhibitor lead tracking metrics to localized sponsor dashboards. Sponsors receive verified dwell times and zone footfall without ever forcing a delegate to stop and scan a badge.

3. The Digital Frontend: Eliminating Silent Validation Failures
A resilient physical backend is useless if corporate event directors cannot interact with your digital marketing layer. During a recent high-volume traffic surge, we detected a severe anomaly in our B2B funnel: a 98% form abandonment rate. Users successfully triggered a form_start event, but failed to reach form_submit.

This was not a lack of user intent; it was a silent frontend failure. When engineering enterprise lead-generation forms, particularly for users on congested mobile networks, you must audit for these silent traps:

iOS Safari HTML5 Validation: Safari handles standard required attributes strictly. If a React component conditionally hides an input field but leaves it marked as required in the DOM, Safari will silently block the form submission without rendering a visible error to the user.

Hydration Mismatches: If the server-rendered HTML does not perfectly match the client-rendered DOM, the React tree will fail to hydrate, rendering the submit button completely unclickable.

Third-Party API Timeouts: CRM tracking scripts and reCAPTCHA payloads frequently fail on slow mobile networks. If your onSubmit function awaits a token that never arrives, the form freezes. Always wrap third-party scripts in strict timeouts with graceful degradation fallbacks.

Conclusion
Building software for massive enterprise exhibitions requires extreme discipline across the entire stack. By pushing data processing to the edge with Go and SQLite, eliminating silent frontend validation errors, and enforcing strict Core Web Vitals, you can build event infrastructure that is both highly visible to search engines and completely fail-proof on the exhibition floor.

To explore the architecture behind our deployments, visit the StampIQ Event Registration Platform.

title: Skill Dreaming: Evolving Repository Skills through Pull Request Streams
description:
arXiv:2610.36188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on reusable skills for complex software engineering tasks, making skill libraries essential for repository development and maintenance. However, repository-specific skills must evolve with changing code structures, implementation conventions, and maintenance requirements. Pull requests (PRs) provide a natural source of such knowledge by recording how repositories evolve through implementation and review. Meanwhile, new PRs must follow repository-specific implementation patterns, modify related components consistently, and ensure that existing tests continue to pass while adding coverage for new functionality. This creates a mutually reinforcing cycle: PRs provide knowledge for updating skills, while these skills improve future PRs, maintain repositories, and support further skill evolution. To enable this co-evolution of PRs, repositories, and skills, we propose Skill Dreaming, a framework that learns from PR streams to guide continuous repository development and maintenance. Given a repository and its PR history, Skill Dreaming builds a repository-specific skill library by extracting executable knowledge from validated PRs and continuously refines the skills as new PR information becomes available. These skills guide coding agents not only in implementing requested features but also in maintaining associated tests, documentation, compatibility, and repository conventions. By integrating PR analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming provides an end-to-end workflow for applying learned skills to repository changes and incorporating subsequent PR outcomes into future skill updates.
