title: TrawMem: Reframing Agent Memory as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces
description:
arXiv:2610.36918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on memory systems to leverage long-term interactions, yet existing systems typically retrieve memories based on their relevance to the current query and use them as contextual evidence. However, relevance alone does not characterize how a memory contributes to task solving: the same memory may serve different roles across tasks, such as directly supporting the answer or linking to complementary memories with weaker semantic relevance but necessary information. We therefore reframe agent memory systems as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces, where memories are selected and organized by their task-oriented roles and relations. Based on this view, we propose TrawMem, which organizes interaction histories into local threads and constructs task-oriented workspaces by assigning roles and jointly selecting complementary memories. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemGallery with four open- and closed-source backbones show consistent improvements over representative memory systems, with macro-F1 gains of 2.23-3.14 points. On LoCoMo, TrawMem improves the LLM-Judge score over SimpleMem by 4.07 and 4.31 percentage points on Qwen3.5-9B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively, while requiring approximately 12.8% and 5.1% fewer context tokens, respectively.

title: MCP Token Cost: I Cut My MCP Server From 15 Tools to 4
description:
MCP Token Cost: I Cut My MCP Server From 15 Tools to 4

Every tool you expose in an MCP server ships its name, description, and JSON Schema to the model on every request. That metadata is paid for in tokens—every turn, for every agent that connects. I had 15 tools in a file-management MCP server. My system prompt was 4,800 tokens before the user said a word. After trimming to 4 tools and lazy-loading the rest, the baseline dropped to ~1,100 tokens, and my agent got measurably faster and cheaper. Here is the problem, the solution, and the code.

The Problem: Tool Metadata Is a Fixed Tax

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers advertise capabilities via tools/list. Clients typically inject that list into the model context so the LLM can decide which tool to call. The cost isn't the tool call—it's the advertisement. A typical tool looks like this:

{
  "name": "read_file_chunked_with_encoding",
  "description": "Read a file in chunks, optionally specifying encoding, offset, and length. Supports UTF-8, UTF-16, latin-1...",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string", "description": "Absolute path to the file"},
      "encoding": {"type": "string", "enum": ["utf-8", "utf-16", "latin-1"]},
      "offset": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
      "length": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1}
    },
    "required": ["path"]
  }
}

That's roughly 120–180 tokens. Fifteen of those plus the server instructions put me near 3,000 tokens of schema alone. Worse, the model has to reason over 15 options, which increases latency and mis-selection.

I measured with a simple tokenizer count on the serialized tools/list response—no magic, just len(encoding.encode(json.dumps(tools))) using tiktoken.

The Solution: Fewer, Coarser Tools + a Discovery Tool

The insight: most of my 15 tools were variations (read_file, read_file_chunked, read_file_with_encoding, list_dir, list_dir_recursive, stat_file, ...). Models don't need 15 verbs; they need 4 primitives and a way to discover the long tail.

My final surface:

  1. fs_read – read a file (path, optional offset/limit)
  2. fs_write – write or append to a file
  3. fs_list – list a directory (non-recursive; recursion via repeated calls)
  4. fs_search – search file contents with a regex

Plus one meta-tool, fs_help, that returns detailed docs for advanced operations on demand. The meta-tool is not in the default list—it's invoked only when the model is stuck, so its schema cost is paid rarely.

This is MCP-style tool design: I'm still speaking the protocol, just with a smaller surface.

Implementation

1. A minimal MCP-style server (stdio JSON-RPC)

Below is a compact, runnable server that implements the initialize, tools/list, and tools/call methods. It is not a full MCP SDK implementation—it is a protocol-shaped example so you can see the token math. For production, use the official mcp Python SDK.

import json, sys, re, os
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path(os.environ.get("MCP_ROOT", ".")).resolve()

def safe_path(p: str) -> Path:
    target = (BASE / p).resolve()
    if not str(target).startswith(str(BASE)):
        raise ValueError("path escapes root")
    return target

TOOLS = [
    {
        "name": "fs_read",
        "description": "Read a UTF-8 text file. Optional offset/limit are line numbers.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "path": {"type": "string"},
                "offset": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
                "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
            },
            "required": ["path"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "fs_write",
        "description": "Write text to a file. Set append=true to append.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "path": {"type": "string"},
                "content": {"type": "string"},
                "append": {"type": "boolean", "default": False},
            },
            "required": ["path", "content"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "fs_list",
        "description": "List entries in a directory (non-recursive).",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"path": {"type": "string", "default": "."}},
            "required": [],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "fs_search",
        "description": "Search file contents under a directory using a Python regex.",
        "inputSchema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "path": {"type": "string", "default": "."},
                "pattern": {"type": "string"},
                "max_results": {"type": "integer", "default": 50},
            },
            "required": ["pattern"],
        },
    },
]

def call_tool(name: str, args: dict) -> str:
    if name == "fs_read":
        p = safe_path(args["path"])
        lines = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
        off = args.get("offset", 0)
        lim = args.get("limit", len(lines))
        return "\n".join(lines[off:off + lim])
    if name == "fs_write":
        p = safe_path(args["path"])
        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        mode = "a" if args.get("append") else "w"
        with p.open(mode, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(args["content"])
        return f"wrote {len(args['content'])} chars to {p}"
    if name == "fs_list":
        p = safe_path(args.get("path", "."))
        return "\n".join(sorted(x.name for x in p.iterdir()))
    if name == "fs_search":
        p = safe_path(args.get("path", "."))
        rx = re.compile(args["pattern"])
        hits, cap = [], args.get("max_results", 50)
        for f in p.rglob("*"):
            if not f.is_file():
                continue
            try:
                for i, line in enumerate(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), 1):
                    if rx.search(line):
                        hits.append(f"{f.relative_to(BASE)}:{i}: {line}")
                        if len(hits) >= cap:
                            return "\n".join(hits)
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):
                continue
        return "\n".join(hits)
    raise ValueError(f"unknown tool: {name}")

def handle(req: dict) -> dict:
    method = req.get("method")
    if method == "initialize":
        return {"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05", "capabilities": {"tools": {}},
                "serverInfo": {"name": "mini-fs", "version": "0.1.0"}}
    if method == "tools/list":
        return {"tools": TOOLS}
    if method == "tools/call":
        params = req.get("params", {})
        result = call_tool(params["name"], params.get("arguments", {}))
        return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": result}]}
    return {"error": {"code": -32601, "message": "method not found"}}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for line in sys.stdin:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        try:
            resp = handle(json.loads(line))
        except Exception as e:
            resp = {"error": {"code": -32603, "message": str(e)}}
        print(json.dumps(resp), flush=True)

Security warning: safe_path is a basic containment check, not a substitute for OS-level sandboxing. fs_write and fs_search operate on the real filesystem. Run this server in a container or a dedicated user account, and never point MCP_ROOT at a sensitive directory. The regex in fs_search is user-supplied; catastrophic backtracking can hang the process—consider a timeout or a linear-time engine.

2. Measuring the savings 

import json, tiktoken
from pathlib import Path

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

def schema_tokens(tools_path: str) -> int:
    tools = json.loads(Path(tools_path).read_text())
    return len(enc.encode(json.dumps(tools)))

print("before:", schema_tokens("old_tools.json"))
print("after :", schema_tokens("new_tools.json"))

In my run: before: 2,914, after: 612. Add server instructions and the system prompt lands around 1,100 tokens. That's a ~60% reduction in fixed overhead per request.

3. An agent loop with explicit termination

If you wire these tools into an agent, define when it stops. Here is a minimal loop with three hard stops: max iterations, an explicit finish sentinel, and a token budget.

MAX_ITERS = 8
TOKEN_BUDGET = 20_000

def run_agent(user_msg, call_model, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
    used = 0
    for _ in range(MAX_ITERS):
        reply = call_model(messages, tools)  # returns {"tool": ..., "args": ...} or {"text": ...}
        used += reply.get("tokens", 0)
        if used > TOKEN_BUDGET:
            return "stopped: token budget exceeded"
        if "text" in reply:
            return reply["text"]
        result = call_tool(reply["tool"], reply["args"])
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "name": reply["tool"], "content": result})
    return "stopped: max iterations reached"

Note: call_model is your transport to the LLM—I'm not calling eval or executing model output as code. Tool arguments are validated by the schema and dispatched through the if/elif in call_tool; unknown names raise. If you extend this, keep that allowlist.

Key Takeaways

  • Tool schemas are a per-request tax. Count them with tiktoken before and after any refactor.
  • Collapse variations into parameters. Three read_file* tools become one fs_read with offset/limit.
  • Use a discovery meta-tool for the long tail. Keep the frequently used 4 in tools/list; document the rest behind fs_help.
  • Shorter descriptions are real savings. Drop marketing prose; keep types and constraints.
  • Measure, don't guess. A 15→4 cut moved my baseline from ~4,800 to ~1,100 tokens.
  • Sandbox file tools. Path containment is necessary but not sufficient; use OS isolation and input limits.

The protocol didn't change—the surface did. Smaller surfaces are cheaper, faster, and easier for models to use correctly.

title: Information-Theoretic Scaling Laws for Generative Diffusion Training
description:
arXiv:2610.33337v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models trained on increasingly large datasets sampled from the same data distribution will converge to the same learned distribution. However, in practice, a model trained on finite data depends on the particular training dataset; this dependence is reflected in properties of the model's outputs, such as memorization and sample quality. To understand this dependence through an information-theoretic lens, we study \textit{model information}, a computationally tractable measure of how much samples from the trained model depend on the particular training dataset. We explore its scaling behavior as model size and training dataset size vary. Specifically, we uncover two qualitatively distinct scaling regimes: (1) a nonlinear model information regime marking the transition from pure memorization to imperfect generalization, and (2) a generalization regime characterized by linear scaling of the model information and progressively improved generalization and sample quality. We then posit an information-theoretically principled scaling law to quantify these two regimes, and show that this law yields induced scaling laws for memorization and sample quality. We finally demonstrate that these induced scaling laws extrapolate well outside the fit's domain. Our results demonstrate information-theoretic principles for memorization and sample quality scaling laws in diffusion models. Our code is publicly available on \href{https://github.com/DruvPai/diffusion_info_theory_scaling_law}{GitHub}.

title: A Quantitative Approach to Asch Conformity in Frontier Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36668v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Asch conformity experiment has recently gained considerable attention as a way of measuring conformity in large language models (LLMs). While previous studies have focused on demonstrating conformity in LLMs, our work adds a further quantitative layer to this approach. Instead of sampling a frontier LLM on a suite of questions, our approach samples a single question repeatedly, leveraging the probabilistic nature of LLMs to produce a distribution of answers. In doing so, we can compare the distributions of answers before and after the model is presented with the manufactured consensus. Our experiments confirm that frontier LLMs do conform, reinforcing prior literature, and, through our distribution-to-distribution comparisons, provide additional quantitative data on the conditions that lead to conformity and the degree to which it occurs.

title: Causal Localization of Evidence Effects in Transformers
description:
arXiv:2610.36524v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can controlled symbolic inputs reveal attention heads that influence a language model's decisions from natural language evidence? We introduce controlled evidence aggregation (CEA), which varies the counts and order of two symbols in otherwise fixed prompts and measures changes in a frozen Transformer's preference between two answer tokens. The preference is measured by their logit difference; the prompts prescribe no correct answer. Balanced utility causal selection (BUC) identifies compact head sets by jointly evaluating how much ablating their outputs removes the count effect and how closely patching mean outputs between count conditions recovers the effect in both directions. We derive conditional bounds linking head attribution to intervention effects and specifying when the attribution shortlist can be recovered from finite samples. In Pythia-410M, ablating sets of 1-12 heads selected separately for four ordering regimes removes 65.5-91.6% of the count effect. The sets retain their influence on count comparisons not used for selection. To test relevance beyond symbolic inputs, we evaluate a natural language task asking which state is supported by more reports. Ablating eight heads selected only on symbolic yes/no prompts lowers mean accuracy by 8.2 percentage points, versus 0.8 for random sets matched by size and layer. Our results demonstrate that controlled symbolic probes can identify compact attention head sets whose causal influence extends to natural language decisions.

title: Give Your Desktop App a Useful Title Bar and Real Tools
description:
A document editor needs room for the document. Giving an entire row to a title, then adding another row for Save and Search, spends that room quickly.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

You can now put Codename One components into the title area of native macOS, Windows and Linux apps. It's a niche capability until you're building an editor. Then the details of window dragging and button hit testing become part of your product.

This weekly follow-up also covers two less visible desktop capabilities: launching external tools and reading or writing ZIP streams. Together they make it easier to build an application that fits into the user's existing workflow.

Our native macOS editor prototype, cropped to its title area and ribbon. Save, Undo, document status and command search use the top row; the document begins below the ribbon.

Put Save where the user is already looking

Use desktop.titleBar=custom, then supply a title component through the ordinary toolbar API. This is the guide's editor example:

public static Form createEditor(Command save, Command search) {
    Display.getInstance().setProperty("desktop.titleBar", "custom");
    Toolbar.setGlobalToolbar(true);
    Form editor = new Form("Quarterly report", new BorderLayout());
    Container title = new Container(new BorderLayout());
    title.add(BorderLayout.WEST, new Button(save));
    title.add(BorderLayout.CENTER, new Label("Quarterly report"));
    title.add(BorderLayout.EAST, new Button(search));
    editor.getToolbar().setTitleComponent(title);
    return editor;
}

Call it from the application's normal lifecycle, after framework initialization and before constructing other forms that need this mode. The Command arguments are your actions. You can also select the mode with codename1.arg.desktop.titleBar=custom in the build settings.

Don't add fixed padding for macOS traffic lights or Windows caption buttons. The framework reserves space for the real OS controls, accounting for changes such as window DPI. Your components stay in the Java component tree while the port handles window gestures.

Native desktop Who owns the window behavior?
macOS AppKit keeps the traffic lights, resizing and system menu. Empty title space follows native dragging and the user's double-click preference.
Windows The Desktop Window Manager keeps caption controls. Native hit testing handles empty title space and resize edges.
Linux A GTK header bar places rendered application content beside real window controls and follows desktop decoration settings.

Buttons, editable fields and other interactive descendants keep their input. Disabled buttons are excluded from dragging too. Plain labels and passive container backgrounds can move the window. For a custom painted background, Toolbar.setTitleBarDragRegion(component, true) opts it into dragging while preserving interactive children.

There are platform differences. Windows custom mode omits the separate Win32 menu row; provide visible access through your toolbar, side menu or ribbon. Linux keeps its menu row below the header, and macOS keeps the system menu bar. This applies to the main form in native desktop builds. Separate dialogs retain their decorations, and browser pages don't gain control of browser chrome.

The desktop integration guide has the full contract, introduced in PR #6019. The useful feature is the complete interaction, including the parts that keep a click on Search from moving the window.

Call the tool your user already has

We originally wanted a Process API for backend work. It made sense for desktop applications too: an editor can invoke a converter, inspect a tool's version or run an existing command-line utility.

The shared classes are com.codename1.io.ProcessBuilder and com.codename1.io.Process. Check support before offering the action:

boolean canRunTools = com.codename1.io.ProcessBuilder.isSupported();

The API works in JavaSE desktop builds, the native Windows/macOS/Linux ports, the JVM backend and the packaged Linux ParparVM backend. Android, iOS and the browser don't support process launching through this API.

Here is the launch portion of a worker task, assuming toolPath names an installed executable:

try (com.codename1.io.Process child =
        new com.codename1.io.ProcessBuilder(toolPath, "--version")
                .redirectErrorStream(true)
                .start()) {
    child.getOutputStream().close(); // This command needs no stdin.
    // Start a reader for child.getInputStream() before waiting.
    // Apply a timeout, inspect the exit code, and handle the output.
}

This is a launch excerpt, not a complete runner. The complete guide example drains output on a separate thread and uses a timed wait. Waiting first can deadlock if the child fills its output pipe. Keep both process I/O and waits off the UI event thread.

Arguments are passed literally; the API doesn't insert a shell. Working directories are native path strings. File redirection, pipelines and ProcessHandle aren't part of this subset. Closing the process requests termination and closes its streams, but doesn't kill descendants or wait for exit. PR #6010 contains the implementation.

Give users an archive they can use

ParparVM now implements the streaming subset of java.util.zip. That includes ZIP entry streams, GZIP, deflate/inflate and checksums. JVM and Android builds use their platform implementations; ParparVM uses the existing Java compression engine.

Writing a small UTF-8 entry looks familiar. Here destination is the output stream your caller supplies; closing the ZIP also closes it:

try (java.util.zip.ZipOutputStream zip =
        new java.util.zip.ZipOutputStream(destination)) {
    zip.putNextEntry(new java.util.zip.ZipEntry("report.txt"));
    zip.write("Completed rides\n".getBytes("UTF-8"));
    zip.closeEntry();
}

A project export has an extra requirement: its launcher should still be executable after extraction. ZipArchiveOutputStream adds a permission argument to the familiar entry operation:

ZipEntry launcher = new ZipEntry("project/run.sh");
launcher.setTime(0);
zip.putNextEntry(launcher, 0755);
// Copy the launcher bytes to zip, then call closeEntry().

Here zip is a com.codename1.io.zip.ZipArchiveOutputStream. The server download example streams directly to an HTTP response and includes the full copy loop. This avoids building an entire archive in memory, although entry metadata still takes space.

This isn't every Java SE archive feature. ParparVM's subset excludes random-access ZipFile, ZIP64 and encrypted archives. Reading to the end of an entry verifies its CRC and size; closing an archive early doesn't verify unread entries. An importer still needs to validate paths and bound extracted data. PR #6006 introduced the streaming support.

A useful title area, an external tool and an export users can open are modest features individually. They are also the things that decide whether a desktop app can become part of someone's daily work.

Discussion

What would you put in your app's title area if the window controls were already handled?

title: Shipping websites for UK clients? A WCAG 2.2 AA checklist for what the Equality Act expects
description:
If you build websites for UK businesses, sooner or later a client asks: "Do we legally have to make the site accessible?" The short answer: the Equality Act 2010 applies to anyone providing services to the public in England, Scotland and Wales, of any size. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) names websites and internet services as one of the areas where providers must avoid discrimination and make reasonable adjustments.

The Act doesn't name a technical standard. In practice the benchmark everyone works to is WCAG 2.2 Level AA, the level the UK public sector has to meet. This post turns that into things you can check in code and in a browser. (It's general information, not legal advice.)

The legal bit, in developer terms

Three points matter for the work you ship:

  1. The duty is anticipatory. A business can't wait for a disabled customer to complain. It has to think ahead about what people with a range of impairments might need. For you, that means accessibility goes into the acceptance criteria, not a post-launch ticket.
  2. "Reasonable" depends on size and resources. A two-person shop and a national retailer aren't held to identical expectations. But the EHRC notes that many adjustments aren't particularly expensive, especially when they're built in from the start.
  3. Public sector sites have stricter rules. The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 require WCAG 2.2 AA and a published accessibility statement. If your client is a council, NHS body or some charities, those rules apply on top.

The WCAG 2.2 criteria that older UK sites usually fail

WCAG 2.2 added criteria that sites built against 2.0 or 2.1 often miss. Check these first.

Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.4.11

Sticky headers and cookie banners (very common on UK sites because of PECR consent) often cover the focused element when someone tabs through the page.

/* Keep focused elements clear of a 72px sticky header */
html {
  scroll-padding-top: 80px;
}

/* Never remove the focus ring without replacing it */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1d4ed8;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Test it by tabbing through every page with the cookie banner still open.

Target Size (Minimum), 2.5.8

Pointer targets need to be at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing around them (there are exceptions, such as links inside a sentence). Icon-only buttons in headers and carousels are the usual offenders.

.icon-button {
  min-width: 24px;
  min-height: 24px;
  /* 44px is a more comfortable target on touch screens */
}

Accessible Authentication (Minimum), 3.3.8

Logging in shouldn't require a cognitive test. In practice that means:

<!-- Let password managers and paste work -->
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="username">
<input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">

Don't block paste on password fields, and don't use a puzzle CAPTCHA without an accessible alternative.

Dragging Movements, 2.5.7

Sliders, sortable lists and map pins need a single-pointer alternative, such as buttons or an input.

The checklist I run on every UK client site

These catch most of the common problems before a proper audit:

  • Keyboard only: every link, menu, form, modal and checkout step works with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and Esc, in a logical order, with a visible focus indicator.
  • Contrast: normal text is at least 4.5:1, large text at least 3:1. Colour is never the only signal, for example red borders on form errors need text too.
  • Images: meaningful images have short, accurate alt; decorative ones get alt="".
  • Forms: a visible <label> for every field (placeholder text is not a label), required fields marked in text, and errors that say what went wrong and how to fix it, tied to the field with aria-describedby.
  • Structure: a unique <title> per page, one <h1>, a logical heading order, and link text that makes sense out of context ("Read the delivery policy", not "click here").
  • Zoom and reflow: at 400% zoom (or a 320px-wide viewport) content reflows without sideways scrolling.
  • Media: captions on pre-recorded video, transcripts for audio.
  • Motion: carousels can be paused, nothing flashes, and prefers-reduced-motion is respected.
  • PDFs: important documents are accessible, or the same content exists as an HTML page.

Testing: automated tools are only the start

The W3C is clear that no tool alone can tell you whether a site meets accessibility standards. A realistic test plan:

  1. Automated scan (axe DevTools, Lighthouse, WAVE) on key templates to catch missing labels, contrast and ARIA errors quickly. Add @axe-core/playwright or similar to CI so regressions fail the build.
  2. Keyboard pass through the main journeys: find a product or service, submit the contact form, book or check out.
  3. Screen reader pass with NVDA on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS/iOS.
  4. Zoom and mobile pass at 200% and 400%, and on a real phone.
  5. Feedback from disabled users where the budget allows. The W3C recommends involving them throughout a project.

Re-test after redesigns, new features and plugin or theme updates. Accessibility breaks quietly.

Give the client an accessibility statement

Private businesses aren't legally required to publish one, but it's good practice and easy to ship. The W3C suggests at minimum:

  • a commitment to accessibility;
  • the standard you work to (WCAG 2.2 AA);
  • contact details for people who hit a problem or need content in another format.

Add known limitations, what was tested and with which assistive technologies, and the review date. Keep it honest: describe what you tested, not "this site is fully accessible".

FAQ

Does the Equality Act apply to small business websites?
The EHRC says it applies to service providers whatever their size. What counts as a reasonable adjustment depends on the organisation's size, nature and resources.

Is WCAG 2.2 AA a legal requirement for UK private businesses?
The Act doesn't name a standard. WCAG 2.2 AA is the public sector requirement and the usual benchmark for showing a site was built and tested with accessibility in mind.

Can an accessibility overlay make a site compliant?
An overlay doesn't fix the underlying markup, and the W3C's position is that no automated tool alone can determine conformance. Fix the code.

What about Northern Ireland?
Northern Ireland has its own disability discrimination law, and the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland is the regulator there.

If you need a second pair of eyes on a client site before launch, my team at Dzimark runs a website accessibility audit against WCAG 2.2 AA with manual keyboard and screen reader testing.

title: The View from Nowhere: Population-Centered Agent Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.36660v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents.
  These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness.
  Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. In our evaluation, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. These results suggest that treating the population as evidence--not merely as candidates for selection--provides a complementary principle for agent evolution.

title: Decoupling Consistency and Conflict across MLLM Layers for Fake News Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.36569v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The trustworthiness of Web content faces a growing threat from multimodal fake news. Real news usually shows aligned image-text semantics, while fake news often contains a few conflicts at varying levels, such as mismatches in objects, scenes, events, and claims. However, existing methods usually treat consistency and conflict in a coarse and static way, limiting their ability to capture sparse conflicts and adapt to varying conflict levels. Inspired by the distinct knowledge encoded across layers in large language models, we propose Multi-Level Consistency and Conflict Decoupling (MLCCD), which captures conflicts at different levels from different layers of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first use the MLLM's final decision representation to select visual and textual tokens relevant to the task, preventing irrelevant content from diluting sparse conflicts. Then, we preserve tokens whose representations change sharply between adjacent layers, capturing the knowledge each layer adds. Finally, we decouple this knowledge into consistency and conflict evidence and aggregate each across layers with its own router, adapting to varying conflict levels. Experiments on three benchmarks show that MLCCD outperforms existing methods.

title: Is Token Confidence Just Chain Length? A Signal-Processing Audit of Reasoning Traces
description:
arXiv:2610.36709v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning language models answer math problems by writing long chains of thought, and sampling many chains per problem and taking a majority vote raises accuracy at a large cost in generated text. A popular way to cut that cost scores each chain by the model's confidence in each token it writes, where a token is a word or part of a word. The method averages this confidence over a sliding window of 2048 tokens and keeps or stops chains based on the lowest average. We treat the confidence, recorded token by token, as a signal in the sense of audio or radio, and examine the method with standard signal-processing tools such as spectral analysis and statistical tests for detecting a sudden change. We sampled 16 chains for each of 500 problems from two math benchmarks with a small open reasoning model. The windowed-minimum score turns out to measure mostly how long a chain is. Ranking chains by length alone does as well as or better than the confidence score, and once length is accounted for the score carries no information about correctness. Signal processing explains why: the minimum of a longer stretch of a slowly drifting signal is lower by chance alone, and the confidence signal drifts slowly enough that this effect dominates. The spectrum does hold a small signal that length does not explain, since incorrect chains carry more rapid token-to-token fluctuation, but it is too weak to improve the vote. For stopping chains early, neither the sliding average nor a classical change detector beats the simpler choice of sampling fewer chains.

title: Reflection AI's Beam now available on AI Gateway for free
description:
Beam from Reflection AI, previously available in stealth as stealth/cat-jam, is now available on AI Gateway. Beam is free to use for a limited time during the launch period when serviced by Reflection AI.

Beam is an low latency US open-weight reasoning model for coding and agentic tasks, with weights released under Apache 2.0. Then select reflection/beam or reflection/beam-free in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

title: The cloud is moving to orbit. Here is what is real so far.
description:
On 1 October, Google put four of its AI chips into orbit on a satellite about the size of a refrigerator. Two weeks later, Nvidia's CEO said his engineers are designing a new kind of server with SpaceX, meant to run in space. For software developers, the cloud they deploy to may one day include machines that are not on the ground at all. This post looks at what is real today, who gains from it, and what the next step looks like.

What is real comes first. In November 2025, a startup called Starcloud launched Starcloud-1, a satellite of about 60 kilograms carrying one Nvidia H100 GPU. It was the first data center class GPU to run in orbit, and the team used it to train a small language model in space [1][2]. On 1 October 2026, Google's Project Suncatcher prototype followed with four TPUs. Because of heat limits, those chips run Google's open Gemma model for 15 minutes at a time, and the mission is planned to operate for a year [3].

That is two satellites and five data center chips.

Then there is what has been proposed. In February, the FCC accepted SpaceX's application for up to one million orbital data center satellites [4]. Starcloud filed for up to 88,000 on 3 February [2], and a young startup called Orbital filed for up to 100,000, with 10 gigawatts of computing power [5]. Together, those three filings ask for about 1.19 million satellites, by my own count.

Between the two sit the designs. In June, SpaceX showed AI1, its first data center satellite design, at about 150 kW peak and 120 kW sustained, with a 70 metre wingspan [5]. A Google research paper published in October says each data center satellite may need 50 to 100 kW, roughly what one rack draws on Earth [6]. On 15 October, Jensen Huang said Nvidia and SpaceX engineers are designing a new server together, one that could run in space and on Earth [7].

So the honest picture is this. A few chips are flying, the designs are serious, and the filings are requests for permission, not proof that anything works at scale. The companies say so themselves. SpaceX's IPO prospectus calls orbital AI compute a very hard technical problem [8], and the lead of Project Suncatcher does not expect space compute to beat ground data centers on cost within five years [9].

Every new place to run software creates new work. The people closest to the hardest constraint usually gain first, and in orbit that constraint is power.

Developers who write lean software come first. In orbit, every watt has to be collected by a solar panel and every bit of waste heat has to leave through a radiator. Code that does the same work with less compute is worth more there than anywhere else. The model running on Google's prototype is Gemma, a small open model [3]. Engineers who know how to make models smaller and faster gain a place where that skill is the whole job.

Electronics, thermal and power engineers gain too. Orbital is hiring engineers for thermal, power, mechanical and electrical work [10]. Starcloud's next satellite is planned to carry the largest commercial deployable radiator flown so far [11]. Hardware that survives radiation and sheds heat without air is becoming its own product category.

For infrastructure and reliability engineers, the job changes shape. A technician cannot walk up to a server in orbit and replace a part [3]. Systems that report clearly, recover on their own and move work away from a failing node become the core of the job. Teams that already run large fleets through automation start with an advantage.

In large scale engineering, the cost of every compute cycle is visible. In my own work on systems at that scale, I saw decisions that were perfectly acceptable on a small system become a clear no once scale came in. Precomputing a new data point for every customer, back through all their history, is fine when the data is a few gigabytes. When the data runs to exabytes, the better move is to first ask which customers actually need it.

Teams whose data is born in space gain in a very direct way. Earth observation satellites can produce hundreds of terabytes of raw data a day, more than the links to the ground can easily carry [12]. Processing that data in orbit means sending down answers instead of raw images. Starcloud planned to use its first satellite to analyse radar data from Capella Space for exactly this reason [13]. Farmers, shipping companies and city planners who rely on satellite data stand to get their answers sooner.

Satellite operators gain as well. Starlink satellites perform a collision avoidance maneuver about every two minutes on average, and most of the processing behind them still happens on the ground [12]. More compute on board lets those decisions happen where the satellite is.

Founders and small teams have room here too. Starcloud designed, built and launched its first satellite in 21 months on 3 million dollars of pre-seed money, and in August it raised again at a 2.3 billion dollar valuation [14]. Big companies will build the satellites. Small teams can build the layer around them: scheduling, monitoring and testing for compute that nobody can touch.

If I had to name who gains most, it is two groups: people whose data already lives in orbit, and developers who treat compute as something scarce.

In 2018, Microsoft sealed 864 servers inside a steel tube and lowered it to the seafloor off the Orkney Islands. When the tube came back up in July 2020, those servers had failed at one eighth the rate of a matching group on land [15]. Microsoft did not go on to build undersea data centers, but it kept the lessons for its research on reliability [16].

I am not trying to predict what orbital data centers will become. What I take from Project Natick is simpler. Putting compute somewhere new teaches engineers things they could not learn at home, even when the place itself does not become the new normal.

The next step is not a million satellites. It is small and specific. Google plans to launch two satellites in 2027 to test whether they can share work over laser links between them [17]. Starcloud plans a second satellite with its large radiator and paying customers on board [11]. These are plans, not achievements, and plans in space often move.

There are real hurdles. Heat has to leave through radiators, launch still costs a great deal, and nobody can drive over to fix a broken server. People have cleared hurdles like these before, one experiment at a time. That is the question this series keeps asking: what changes for engineers when orbit becomes an ordinary place to run software? The answer starts with satellites like the one Google launched four weeks ago.

For now, running compute in orbit costs far more than running it on the ground. One analyst's rough model puts the cost of launching and running a GPU in space for a year at ten times or more the cost on Earth [12]. The clearest early customers are the jobs that need compute next to the sensor: processing Earth observation data in orbit and helping satellites avoid each other. For a small team, the opening is the software that makes remote, power-limited compute easy to use.

Companies are looking at orbit because compute on Earth is scarce and power hungry. The same scarcity shows up on every developer's bill as tokens and GPU hours. An AI coding tool that reads the whole repository for every question, or retries a failing call without limits, spends compute nobody planned for. The tools that last will treat every call as having a cost and will show that cost before they spend it.

The picture changes again once humans live and work beyond Earth. Communication between planets already depends on relays. On Mars, the rovers send most of their science data up to orbiters, which pass it on to Earth, because each rover loses its line of sight to Earth for about 12 hours a day. A one-way signal between the two planets takes between 3 and about 22 minutes [18]. In September, NASA chose Blue Origin, under a contract worth up to 700 million dollars, to build a dedicated Mars telecommunications orbiter, due for delivery by the end of 2028 and planned to operate at Mars by 2030 [19]. Around the Moon, ESA's Moonlight programme plans five satellites for communication and navigation, with first services in late 2028 [20].

A relay that can also compute is a natural next step from there. With minutes of delay on every message, a question asked on Mars cannot wait for an answer from Earth. A data center sitting in orbit next to the relay could process data where it arrives, answer local questions on the spot, and send only the results across the long link home. Seen that way, the cost question also looks different. On Earth, an orbital data center competes with a cheaper building on the ground. For a crew on Mars or a base on the Moon, the comparison is with having no nearby compute and no fast link at all. When communication becomes something a community depends on, the price of building that infrastructure is weighed against the value of staying connected.

Sources

The 1.19 million total and the five chip count are my own sums of the figures below.

  3. NPR via GPB: Google launches Project Suncatcher, 1 October 2026

  5. SpaceNews: Orbital files plans for 100,000 orbital data centers and SpaceNews: Orbital raises 5 million dollars, with SpaceX AI1 figures
  6. CNN: Google is launching its first test of an orbital AI data center
  7. Benzinga: SpaceX and Nvidia team up on AI data centers in space, 16 October 2026
  8. Kiplinger: Orbital data centers are about to be put to the test, 21 October 2026
  9. WUNC: Google launches Project Suncatcher
  10. DCD: Orbital joins the space data center race
  11. TechCrunch: Starcloud raises 170 million dollars
  12. IEEE Spectrum: Why orbital data centers are harder than Silicon Valley thinks
  13. GeekWire: Starcloud plans its next moves

title: Learning Human Sports Motion Feasibility via Quantile Regression on Tracking Data
description:
arXiv:2610.36183v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study time-to-arrival (TTA) in sports: the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach an arbitrary location on the pitch given their current kinematic state, estimated as the lower envelope of observed locomotion times. Rather than modeling space ownership through position density estimation or closed-form physics-based models, we cast TTA as a conditional quantile regression problem, estimating the lower quantile of locomotion time so the model learns a player's lower-envelope arrival time. We train the model on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the PFF FC FIFA World Cup 2022 dataset, and evaluate a lightweight multilayer perceptron against six player-motion models from the literature, re-expressed as TTA predictors, and a learned reachable- hull baseline. Across our evaluation metrics, the MLP consistently outperforms every physics-based baseline. To probe the generality of the learned locomotion model, we further evaluate it on basketball tracking data and a single-game NFL tracking dataset, analyzing the transferability of player motion dynamics across sports. Our project is available at https://github.com/mguti97/TTA-Quantile.

title: Collective Collaboration of Recursive Autonomous Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.33515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Smart factories must translate order-level objectives into production tasks at multiple scales and combine the capabilities of individual units into an overall delivery capability. To address repeated adaptation of organizational mechanisms across equipment, workshops, and factories, as well as coordination across levels under changing production conditions, this paper develops a framework for the collective collaboration of recursive autonomous agents (RAAs). A common task and capability interface supports the recursive decomposition of production objectives from the top down and the aggregation of conditional capabilities through peer collaboration from the bottom up. Composite units can therefore participate in higher-level organizations as agents of the same kind. We formulate organizational models for leaf and composite units, specify interface closure under composition and conditions for finite task expansion, and develop operational mechanisms linking task decomposition, resource commitments, result aggregation, and coordination within the scope affected by change. A production network integrating machining, inspection, and logistics across multiple workshops illustrates how a common organizational kernel is instantiated at the equipment-service, workshop, and factory scales. The framework connects recursive organization with explicit task responsibilities, capability conditions, and execution interfaces for manufacturing systems.

title: PwnEscape (CVE-2026-99999): The VM Escape That Was Never in the Hypervisor
description:
Every cloud tenant lives behind one promise: your virtual machine cannot touch the host, and the host cannot be reached by the tenant next door. CVE-2026-99999, nicknamed PwnEscape, breaks that promise, and the break is not where anyone was looking. The flaw is not in KVM. It is in the host kernel's IPv4 networking code, in a checksum optimization that trusted metadata supplied by the guest.

TL;DR

  • What: A Linux kernel flaw in IPv4 checksum offload handling. A guest VM sends packets with crafted checksum metadata; the host kernel's skb_checksum_help() then writes out of bounds and rewrites an IPv4 header it had already validated (CWE-787).
  • Impact: Host memory disclosure, host crash, and, demonstrated in the researcher's lab, controlled host-kernel writes and root-level code execution on the host. A guest-to-host escape primitive.
  • Severity: 9.3 Critical on the CVE.org record; Red Hat scores it 8.8. The disagreement is one CVSS metric (privileges required).
  • Affected: KVM hosts on unpatched kernels 4.4 through 6.18 that pass guest traffic through virtio-net/TAP. AWS says its managed services (EC2, Lambda, Fargate) are not affected; self-managed KVM is the exposure.
  • Exploitation status: No public exploit and no reported in-the-wild use as of publication. Red Hat says it is tracking the flaw as an active-exploit case; it is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (catalog of 2026-10-21, checked 2026-10-22). Those are different statements, and the difference matters.

How a checksum rewrites a header

Checksum offloading exists to save CPU: instead of checksumming a packet immediately, the kernel defers the work and records where the calculation should start and where the result belongs. That metadata travels in the packet buffer (sk_buff) as csum_start and csum_offset.

In a virtualized setup, the metadata arrives from the guest. The host kernel trusted it without checking it against the packet it described.

The sequence is the bug:

  1. A packet arrives from a guest over virtio-net/TAP. The host parses its IPv4 header normally: version 4, header length 20 bytes (0x45). Routing and fragmentation decisions are made on those values.
  2. Later, fragmentation calls skb_checksum_help() to complete the deferred checksum. Working from the guest-supplied csum_start, it writes into memory that overlaps the already-parsed IPv4 header.
  3. In the researcher's demonstration, the first header byte changes from 0x45 to 0x4f. The version nibble is unchanged, so the packet is still IPv4, but the header-length field now reads 15 instead of 5: a 20-byte header is suddenly interpreted as 60 bytes. Fragmentation then treats bytes beyond the real header, bytes the attacker controls, as IPv4 options.

From that primitive, the researchers demonstrated repeated 32-byte disclosures of host memory, a two-packet host crash, controlled writes into host kernel memory, and a chain to root code execution on the host across four cold boots in their own lab. Against Vercel's production sandboxes, the memory-disclosure stage is what was confirmed. Nobody is claiming a production cloud was rooted, and neither are we.

It is a time-of-check/time-of-use shape: state that was validated early is altered later by data that crossed a trust boundary in between. The vulnerable pattern is old; some coverage puts it at roughly 18 years in the tree.

Timeline

  • August 2026: Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai finds the flaw during Vercel's $1 million Sandbox security challenge; the initial memory-disclosure report goes to Vercel on August 20.
  • September 4, 2026: Root cause privately reported to the Linux kernel maintainers.
  • October 8, 2026: Fix lands in net.git, commit 6785011f8b16 ("ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum").
  • October 14–15, 2026: Fix reaches mainline; the kernel CVE team announces CVE-2026-99999 publicly on October 15.

The score disagreement, briefly

The CVE.org record scores PwnEscape 9.3 (AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H). Red Hat scores it 8.8, differing only on privileges required (Low vs None). Both agree on what matters operationally: the attack is local to a guest, needs no host credentials, and changes scope, meaning the vulnerable component and the impacted component are different machines. On any multi-tenant host, "the attacker must already run code in a guest" describes every tenant you have.

What our index can and cannot tell you

We run cl0q, an independent search engine that maps the public web: 48,321,576 domains and 35,364,497 pages in our current index snapshot (generated 2026-10-26 01:35 UTC, sample-based, approximate).

We cannot see kernel versions from the web, and we will not pretend otherwise. No banner grab tells you whether a host has applied commit 6785011f8b16. Anyone selling you a per-domain "PwnEscape vulnerable: yes/no" list built from web crawling is inventing it.

What the index does show is how concentrated the exposure decision is. Web hosting runs on a small number of networks, and most of them are virtualization-heavy:

Hosting network Domains in the index
Cloudflare (AS13335) 7,611,200
Amazon (AS16509 + AS14618) 3,472,400
OVH (AS16276) 1,095,550
Google (AS15169) 1,013,150
Squarespace (AS53831) 997,250

The five largest networks alone account for roughly 29% of all domains we index. For most of the web, the question "is my host patched?" is really "has my provider's kernel program shipped the fix?", and it is answered by a handful of operators. If you run your own KVM hosts, on rented bare metal or your own racks, that answer is yours to produce, and the fix is a kernel update, not a config change.

You can look up any domain's dossier on cl0q to see the hosting network it sits on: cl0q.com/site/example.com. That tells you whose patch status your exposure rides on. For bulk work across a portfolio, the same data is in our datasets and API.

What to do

  1. Patch KVM hosts first, guests second. The vulnerable code runs on the host. Update hosts to a kernel carrying commit 6785011f8b16 or your distribution's backport. Amazon Linux has published fixed packages (for example kernel-5.10.269-270.1108.amzn2 and kernel-6.1.188-233.385.amzn2023); Red Hat's fixes were still in progress at disclosure.
  2. Prioritize multi-tenant and sandbox hosts. A single-tenant host you fully control is a different risk from a host running untrusted workloads. Sandboxes, CI runners, and shared hosting are the front of the queue.
  3. Do not wait for a KEV listing. The catalog lags confirmed exploitation routinely; Red Hat is already tracking this as an active-exploit case. Patch on the disclosure, not on the listing.
  4. Know where your sites actually live. Inventory your domains' hosting networks (the dossiers above do this one by one) so a provider's patch advisory maps to your properties immediately.

The lesson worth keeping

Isolation boundaries are not just the hypervisor. They are every optimization that moves data across the boundary on trust: checksum offload today, another offload tomorrow. PwnEscape sat in one of the most-read code paths in computing, packet forwarding, for years, because the metadata about the packet was never treated as hostile. Anything a guest can influence is input. Validate it like input.

cl0q is a free, independent web search engine with its own crawler and index: cl0q.com. Sources for this article, including the Red Hat and AWS advisories, the SOC Prime analysis, and our CISA KEV check, are listed in the research notes we keep with this draft.

title: I built a leaderless service-discovery system in Go. Here's what broke along the way
description:
For the past few weeks I've been building Atlas, a distributed service-discovery system in Go. It answers one question every microservice setup eventually asks:

Where is the payments service right now, and which copies of it are actually alive?

Most tools answer that with a central database or a leader node (Consul's servers, etcd, ZooKeeper). I wanted to see how far I could get without any leader at all.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/manziosee/atlas
🟢 Live demo (read-only): open the dashboard

How it works

Every node runs the same ~14 MB binary. Nodes find each other with SWIM gossip, the same family of protocols behind HashiCorp's memberlist:

  1. Each node pings a random peer every second.
  2. No answer? It asks up to three other nodes to try (ping-req).
  3. Still nothing? The peer is marked suspect, and the rumour spreads by gossip.
  4. If the peer is actually alive, it refutes by bumping its incarnation number. Otherwise it's declared dead within seconds.

On top of that sits a service registry. Every node stores registrations in SQLite and replicates them to every other node over the same gossip. So any node can answer "where is payments?" from its own memory, with no network hop to a central store.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://atlas-edge.fly.dev/v1/lookup/payments?tag=primary"

Three bugs that taught me the most

1. The cluster that never healed.
My chaos test cut a node off the network, waited for the others to declare it dead, then plugged it back in. It stayed dead. Forever. Each side had marked the other dead, gossip only goes to live members, and nodes only contacted their seeds at startup. Nothing ever crossed the healed link. The fix was small (keep pulling state from a random seed every 30 seconds), but finding it meant really understanding the protocol.

2. Health checks that flapped.
One slow response marked a service unhealthy; the next one marked it healthy again. Now a service needs 3 consecutive failures to go down and 2 passes to come back, and checks can be HTTP, TCP or gRPC-health.

3. "Only the owner can update this."
A registration belongs to the node that accepted it. That's simple and consistent, but clients behind a load balancer kept hitting the wrong node and getting 409. Now every node gossips its API address and quietly forwards the write to the owner, using the caller's own credential.

What's in it today

  • Membership with failure detection, suspicion, refutation and partition recovery
  • Replicated registry with TTL heartbeats, idempotent registration, If-Match updates and draining for zero-downtime deploys
  • Routing that prefers healthy instances in your region, with consistent hashing
  • HTTP + typed gRPC APIs, DNS (A/AAAA/SRV), and a live event stream you can resume
  • Client-side load balancing in Go: http://payments.atlas/... and grpc.NewClient("atlas:///payments") just work
  • Go and Python clients, a CLI, and an embedded dashboard
  • Encrypted gossip (AES-256-GCM), scoped and expiring tokens, signed releases, CI with race tests, chaos tests and a 1,000-node simulation 
transport := atlas.NewTransport(client, nil, atlas.InstanceOptions{Region: "eu"})
httpClient := &http.Client{Transport: transport}
resp, err := httpClient.Get("http://payments.atlas/v1/charges") // round-robin across live instances

Honest positioning

Atlas isn't trying to replace Consul. Consul, Netflix's Eureka and Fly.io's Corrosion inspired a lot of it. The goal was to build these ideas from first principles and make the result small, secure by default and easy to run on an edge platform. Building it taught me more about distributed systems than anything I've read.

Want to help?

It's open source (Apache 2.0), and there's real work for any level:

  • 🟢 Good first issues: runnable examples, docs, a Node.js/TypeScript client
  • 🟡 Medium: a cluster map with live latency in the dashboard, TLS rotation tests
  • 🔴 Deep end: chaos tests with packet loss, a multi-region demo, per-node cryptographic identity

👉 https://github.com/manziosee/atlas/issues

Feedback on the design is just as welcome as code. If something looks wrong to you, it probably is, and I'd love to know.

I'm also open to backend / infrastructure / platform engineering roles (remote or relocation). If your team works on problems like this, reach me at manziosee@gmail.com or here on DEV.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

title: Efficient Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval via Interaction-Free Recall and Text-Guided Reranking
description:
arXiv:2610.36756v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote sensing (RS) image-text retrieval plays a critical role in understanding massive RS imagery. However, the dense multi-object distribution and complex backgrounds in RS imagery make it difficult to simultaneously achieve fine-grained cross-modal alignment and efficient retrieval. Existing methods either rely on complex cross-modal interactions that lead to low retrieval efficiency, or depend on large-scale vision-language adaptation, which requires massive data and computational resources. To address these issues, we develop a fast-then-fine (FTF) retrieval framework centered on interaction-free multi-granular recall and parameter-free text-guided cross-modal reranking with the Balanced Text-guided Interaction Block (BTIB). Specifically, interaction-free multi-granular recall pre-computes gallery embeddings and matches them with the corresponding query embedding without full-gallery token-level text-image interaction, while text-guided cross-modal reranking with BTIB refines local semantic correspondence within the top-K candidate set. Furthermore, an inter- and intra-modal loss is designed to jointly optimize cross-modal alignment across multi-granular representations. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that the FTF achieves competitive retrieval accuracy while significantly improving retrieval efficiency compared with existing methods.

title: Lower expected Fisher rank implies better PAC generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.33208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep learning architectures tend to generalize well to unseen data, but explaining this capability is still an open area of research. Under the assumption of i.i.d. data, PAC-Bayes provides a bound on generalization error, and its tightness relies on a parameter distribution that covers a large volume of low-loss solutions. The Fisher information metric endows the parameter space with a geometry for which distances reflect functional changes, and whose zero-component captures functional invariances. We define and study a Fisher-aligned parameter distribution for which we can simultaneously guarantee (1) a low-loss, thanks to the exploration constrained on the functional invariances and (2) a large log-volume of parameters, proportional to the number of zero eigenvalues. This distribution results in a high-probability generalization error bound, which scales with the expected rank of the Fisher information matrix, shedding light on the relevance of this quantity.

title: How Featured's users make 100K media pitches per month on Vercel
description:
Featured on Vercel

  • 3 engineers supporting 3 brands and 100,000+ users on Vercel

  • Migrated 374 Sanity sites from AWS Elastic Beanstalk to Vercel

  • AI SDK and AI Gateway power Featured's chat bot across 17 models

  • Workflow SDK replaced custom long-running job infrastructure

Featured is a co-pilot for public relations (PR) that subject matter experts and PR teams use to find media opportunities. Tell Featured's agents what you know, and it surfaces opportunities across journalist requests, podcasts, awards, and GEO, with no PR background required.

Founder Brett Farmiloe knows from experience how hard and time consuming getting press is. He spent 10 years running Markitors, a digital marketing agency with 500 small business clients. Every client, from an eyelash extension supplier to an equipment financing company, had real expertise to share, but no way to get it in front of journalists. PR, as Farmiloe puts it, "has always been about who has access to what." He founded Featured to change the question from who has access to who has knowledge.

Featured connects one of their users with a journalist or publisher every 6 seconds. Their agents deliver more than 100,000 media pitches per month, and have sent over 100 million Help A Reporter Out (HARO) emails in the past year.

Behind it all is an engineering team of just three people. With a team that lean, there's no time to manage servers or piece together custom integrations. Every hour spent on infrastructure is an hour taken away from building features what will help their customers land more media placements.

The cost of managing infrastructure by hand

Before Vercel, Featured’s infrastructure work pulled the team away from product development. Hosting lived on AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AI features depended on custom provider integrations, and long-running, multi-step jobs ran on separate orchestration infrastructure. Each layer worked, but each one added operational overhead for a three-person team supporting multiple brands.

One platform for compute, AI primitives, and model access

The migration to Vercel started with a forcing function: Featured needed to launch 374 Sanity sites at once, and every Elastic Beanstalk deploy had to be manually spun up, migrated, and then torn down.

When you multiply that process by almost four hundred, the math doesn't work, even when you divide it across a team of three. Vercel collapsed each site launch into to a single-click deploy.

Once the sites were live, the team evaluated Vercel for background jobs and AI tooling, eventually migrating their entire app and the agents that run in it.

Compute without the clusters

Deploys that once meant standing up a new EB instance, migrating the URL, and terminating the old one became a single click. On Vercel, all 374 sites shipped from one platform, and rollouts across all three brands now happen centrally, instead of one cluster at a time. "In hindsight, doing each one of those by hand was kind of crazy," Farmiloe admits.

AI SDK and AI Gateway: one abstraction for every model

AI SDK and AI Gateway handle all of Featured's model traffic through a single abstraction, so their team doesn't have to manage custom rate-limit or API integrations from multiple providers.

Featured routes across 17 models at any given time. Calling a model is one standardized function with a schema, and swapping providers is a configuration change instead of a rewrite. When a new model ships, the team can test it against Featured's use cases right away.

Workflow SDK for long-running backend jobs

After migrating their AI stack, Featured moved long-running jobs from a separate orchestration system onto Workflow SDK. These are the processes that can't live in a request cycle: monitoring the media around the clock, qualifying opportunities, and combining all of those signals to deliver more than 100,000 pitches a month.

Chat became the product

As users kept choosing conversation over navigation, the team made chat Featured's primary interface, and they deliver it through eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework.

eve's useEveAgent hook made the new interface easy to implement. Instead of wiring up an agent by hand, the team got durable sessions, streaming, tool calls, and approval prompts out of the box, with model calls routed through AI Gateway so they can pick the right model per task without managing provider keys.

What would have been a months-long rebuild was a week-long replace and refactor. Now, instead of a dashboard with dozens of buttons, users ask Featured questions, and the team adapts the product to their needs, not the other way around.

What's next

Featured is building toward being the AI layer for public relations, the same way dedicated agent platforms have emerged for legal and finance. The goal is to make it faster and easier for anyone with expertise to share their knowledge and get featured in the media.

The team's advice to other founders building in the agentic era:

  • Know that your data is your moat. For us, access to good information is what lets Featured connect people with the sources that want to publish them.

  • Lean on tested abstractions like Vercel instead of reinventing security and infrastructure by hand.

About Featured: Featured is a co-pilot for public relations that helps people find media opportunities, submit pitches, and get featured in the press. Featured also owns and operates Help A Reporter Out (HARO) and Connectively, journalist request platforms connecting sources with publishers.
