title: Rollback Capability Makes pg_walex a Truth Regret Pill
description:
Rollback Capability Makes pg_walex a Truth Regret Pill

The smallest, most powerful, fastest, and easiest-to-use PostgreSQL WAL log parsing tool—smooth as Dove chocolate

pg_walex 1.1.0 turns PostgreSQL WAL from a "read-only black box" into a "reversible time machine."

Version Update Preview

  • Output now includes operation type type, lsn, and timestamp
  • --rollback + GET/POST /api/v1/rollback: each forward statement is immediately followed by its inverse operation, enabling replay-based undo
  • Enhanced rollback capability for truncate and drop
  • Fixed the strncopy warning issue when compiling with older C compilers
  • Replaced strncopy with memcopy
  • Real-time monitoring + GET /api/v1/item

1. Main New Features

  • --rollback supports data rollback capability
  • RESTful API rollback capability, integrable with multiple platforms

2. Source Code Download

Source code is available from github, gitee, and gitcode:

git clone https://github.com/shaohuasong-fang/pg_walex.git
git clone https://gitee.com/developerhonor/pg_walex.git
git clone https://gitcode.com/sungsasong/pg_walex.git

3. Compilation and Installation

3.1 Build 

# make -j$(nproc)
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_util.o src/pwe_util.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_version.o src/pwe_version.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_wal.o src/pwe_wal.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_tuple.o src/pwe_tuple.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_catalog.o src/pwe_catalog.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_recon.o src/pwe_recon.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_output.o src/pwe_output.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_main.o src/pwe_main.c
cc -O2 -g -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-parameter -pthread -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L -D_DEFAULT_SOURCE -Iinclude -Isrc -c -o src/pwe_http.o src/pwe_http.c
cc  -o pg_walex src/pwe_util.o src/pwe_version.o src/pwe_wal.o src/pwe_tuple.o src/pwe_catalog.o src/pwe_recon.o src/pwe_output.o src/pwe_main.o src/pwe_http.o -pthread

3.2 Install 

# make install PREFIX=/usr/local
install -d /usr/local/bin
install -m 0755 pg_walex /usr/local/bin/pg_walex

3.3 Check Version 

# pg_walex --version
pg_walex 1.1.0

4. Verify Basic DML Rollback Capability

4.1 Create Database 

# psql -U postgres -d postgres -p6432
psql (18.4)
Type "help" for help.

postgres=# create database db_rollback;
CREATE DATABASE

4.2 Ensure wal_level = logical 

db_rollback=# show wal_level ;
 wal_level 
-----------
 logical
(1 row)

4.3 View LSN and Corresponding File 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB47AF10
(1 row)

4.4 Create Sample Table 

db_rollback=# CREATE TABLE tab_rollback(id int primary key,name varchar(20));
CREATE TABLE
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_rollback VALUES(1,'Verifying rollback');
INSERT 0 1

4.5 View LSN and Corresponding File Again 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB47DAC8
(1 row)

4.6 Simulate Accidental Data Deletion 

db_rollback=# DELETE FROM tab_rollback WHERE id = 1;
DELETE 1

4.7 View Log LSN and Corresponding File 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB47DB38
(1 row)

4.8 Find the Accidentally Deleted Data

Here, search within the interval between start LSN 5/BB47DAC8 and end LSN 5/BB47DB38:

[root@PGServer ~]# pg_walex -f /data/tmp/data/pg_wal/0000000100000005000000BB --rollback -s 5/BB47DAC8 -e 5/BB47DB38
\connect db_rollback
-- pg_walex: type=delete,xid=1233,lsn=5/BB47DAC8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:02:10.117709+00
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM public.tab_rollback WHERE id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 1;
-- pg_walex: rollback,xid=1233,lsn=5/BB47DAC8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:02:10.117709+00
INSERT INTO public.tab_rollback (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Verifying rollback');
COMMIT;

5. Verify Rollback Capability for DROP and TRUNCATE

Note: The recovery of delete operations and TRUNCATE is limited by cache size. If data is accidentally deleted, stop writing to the database as soon as possible.

5.1 Verify DROP Rollback Capability

5.1.1 View LSN and File Location 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB47DC78
(1 row)

5.1.2 Create Table and Insert 5 Rows 

db_rollback=# CREATE TABLE tab_drop(id int primary key,name varchar(20));
CREATE TABLE
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_drop VALUES(1,'first');
INSERT 0 1
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_drop VALUES(2,'second');
INSERT 0 1
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_drop VALUES(3,'third');
INSERT 0 1
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_drop VALUES(4,'forth');
INSERT 0 1
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_drop VALUES(5,'fifth');
INSERT 0 1

5.1.3 Execute DROP TABLE 

-- LSN before deletion, used as the start LSN for the DROP operation
db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB4A89A0
(1 row)

db_rollback=# DROP TABLE tab_drop ;
DROP TABLE

5.1.4 View LSN and File Location 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB4ACB68
(1 row)

5.1.5 WAL Rollback Capability for DROP 

[root@PGServer ~]# pg_walex -f /data/tmp/data/pg_wal/0000000100000005000000BB --rollback -s 5/BB4A89A0 -e 5/BB4ACB68
\connect db_rollback
-- pg_walex: type=drop,xid=1240,lsn=5/BB4ABB08,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:11:09.278194+00
BEGIN;
DROP TABLE public.tab_drop;
-- pg_walex: rollback,xid=1240,lsn=5/BB4AC640,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:11:09.278194+00
CREATE TABLE public.tab_drop (
  id int4 NOT NULL,
  name varchar(20),
  PRIMARY KEY (id)
);
INSERT INTO public.tab_drop (id, name) VALUES (3, 'third');
INSERT INTO public.tab_drop (id, name) VALUES (2, 'second');
INSERT INTO public.tab_drop (id, name) VALUES (1, 'first');
INSERT INTO public.tab_drop (id, name) VALUES (5, 'fifth');
INSERT INTO public.tab_drop (id, name) VALUES (4, 'forth');
COMMIT;

5.2 Verify TRUNCATE Rollback Capability

5.2.1 Simulate Data 

db_rollback=# CREATE TABLE tab_truncate(id int primary key,name varchar(20));
CREATE TABLE
db_rollback=# INSERT INTO tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES
    (1, 'Alice'),
    (2, 'Bob'),
    (3, 'Charlie'),
    (4, 'Diana'),
    (5, 'Eve');
INSERT 0 5

5.2.2 View LSN and File Location 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB4D55D0
(1 row)

5.2.3 Clear Data 

db_rollback=# truncate table tab_truncate ;
TRUNCATE TABLE

5.2.4 View LSN and File Location 

db_rollback=# SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()),pg_current_wal_lsn();
     pg_walfile_name      | pg_current_wal_lsn 
--------------------------+--------------------
 0000000100000005000000BB | 5/BB4D9E30
(1 row)

5.2.5 Verify TRUNCATE Rollback Capability 

[root@PGServer ~]# pg_walex -f /data/tmp/data/pg_wal/0000000100000005000000BB --rollback -s 5/BB4D55D0 -e 5/BB4D9E30
\connect db_rollback
-- pg_walex: type=truncate,xid=1243,lsn=5/BB4D9AA8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:18:03.800537+00
BEGIN;
TRUNCATE TABLE public.tab_truncate;
-- pg_walex: rollback,xid=1243,lsn=5/BB4D9CF8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:18:03.800537+00
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (3, 'Charlie');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (2, 'Bob');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Alice');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (5, 'Eve');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (4, 'Diana');
COMMIT;

In summary: For tables affected by DROP and TRUNCATE, the data can also be recovered through WAL logs.

6. RESTful API Support

6.1 Start 

[root@PGServer ~]# pg_walex --serve --monitor --listen 0.0.0.0 --port 8900 \
  --token my-secret-token --dir  /data/tmp/data/pg_wal
pg_walex 1.1.0 REST API listening on http://0.0.0.0:8900/api/v1
pg_walex: default WAL directory: /data/tmp/data/pg_wal
pg_walex: monitoring /data/tmp/data/pg_wal; latest statement at /api/v1/item

6.2 Verify Monitoring Starting from a Specified LSN 

[root@PGServer ~]# curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer my-secret-token"   'http://127.0.0.1:8900/api/v1/sql?dir=/data/tmp/data/pg_wal&start_lsn=5/BB4D55D0'
\connect db_rollback
-- pg_walex: type=truncate,xid=1243,lsn=5/BB4D9AA8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:18:03.800537+00
BEGIN;
TRUNCATE TABLE public.tab_truncate;
COMMIT;

6.3 Verify Rollback API Capability 

[root@PGServer ~]# curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer my-secret-token" \
  'http://127.0.0.1:8900/api/v1/rollback?dir=/data/tmp/data/pg_wal&start_lsn=5/BB4D55D0'
\connect db_rollback
-- pg_walex: type=truncate,xid=1243,lsn=5/BB4D9AA8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:18:03.800537+00
BEGIN;
TRUNCATE TABLE public.tab_truncate;
-- pg_walex: rollback,xid=1243,lsn=5/BB4D9CF8,timestamp=2026-10-27 08:18:03.800537+00
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (3, 'Charlie');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (2, 'Bob');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Alice');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (5, 'Eve');
INSERT INTO public.tab_truncate (id, name) VALUES (4, 'Diana');
COMMIT;

Conclusion

pg_walex lets you: read, restore, regret, and monitor in real time.
Make DROP no longer the end, and TRUNCATE no longer a matter of prayer—if the WAL is still there, there is still a way to recover.

title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
description:
arXiv:2610.36006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.

title: 4D Reconstruction with Events & RGB
description:
arXiv:2610.36610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution, offering a complementary signal that is largely immune to these artifacts, but whether this modality can be incorporated into existing RGB based 4D reconstruction pipelines without a full architectural redesign remains an open question. In this preliminary study, we investigate a minimal extension: we augment Monst3R, an existing RGB-only 4D reconstruction model, with an additional event-camera input branch, leaving the rest of the architecture unchanged. Across 3 benchmark datasets, this simple RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average relative to the RGB-only Monst3R baseline, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the improvement grows with the magnitude of camera and object motion, with the largest gains observed under high object motion conditions where RGB-only reconstruction degrades most. These early results suggest that even a lightweight, non-invasive fusion of event data can meaningfully improve 4D reconstruction robustness, motivating a more thorough architectural investigation in future work.

title: How to keep a RAG knowledge base fresh without re-embedding everything
description:
Most RAG pipelines I look at are refreshed by brute force: re-crawl the docs site every night, re-chunk everything, re-embed everything, overwrite the index. It works, eventually, but it's wasteful and it hides three bugs a nightly rebuild never fixes.

Below is what actually goes stale, what a full rebuild really costs (less than you'd think in embeddings, more elsewhere), a do-it-yourself content-hash pattern you can drop into any scraper, and how we handle it in MeshArc, the crawler I'm building. The first half needs no sign-up for anything.

What goes wrong when a knowledge base ages

A stale chunk does not announce itself. It still sits close to the query in vector space, so retrieval still ranks it highly and the model still quotes it with confidence. Three failure modes are worth separating:

  1. Stale chunks. The page changed; the index holds the old wording. The assistant recommends a deprecated flag or an old price.
  2. Zombie chunks. The page was deleted, but its vectors were not. Nightly upserts never remove anything, so deleted pages live on indefinitely unless something deletes them on purpose.
  3. Flicker re-embeds. A cookie banner, a "last updated 3 minutes ago" line or a rotating testimonial makes every page look modified on every run, so a "changed pages only" pipeline quietly turns back into a full rebuild.

There is a fourth, nastier one: the blocked crawl that deletes your index. If the site rate-limits you halfway through a run and your pipeline treats "not seen this run" as "removed", you wipe half the knowledge base. Any deletion logic needs a guard against partial runs.

What a full nightly rebuild costs

Here is the arithmetic for a mid-sized documentation site. The assumptions are ours and stated so you can swap in your own:

  • 2,000 pages, averaging 1,200 words each.
  • Chunks of about 350 words with a 40-word overlap, which gives roughly 4 chunks per page and 8,000 chunks in all.
  • About 1.3 tokens per English word.
  • OpenAI text-embedding-3-small at $0.02 per million input tokens (OpenAI's model page, checked on 23 October 2026).

That is roughly 2.8 million embedded words, or 3.7 million tokens, per full rebuild: about $0.07. Thirty nights is about $2.20 a month.

So, to be fair to the brute-force approach: with a small embedding model, the embedding bill is not what hurts. A larger model, a bigger corpus or a hosted embedding service with per-request pricing changes that, but the real costs of rebuilding everything are usually elsewhere:

  • Fetching. 2,000 pages × 30 nights is 60,000 page reads a month, every one of which can be blocked, rate-limited or billed.
  • Index writes. 8,000 chunk upserts a night, most of them writing identical vectors over identical vectors. Managed vector databases tend to price writes, and self-hosted ones still pay for them in compaction and I/O.
  • Correctness. A rebuild that overwrites by ID still leaves zombies behind, and a rebuild that drops and recreates the index has a window in which the assistant answers from nothing.

The fix for all of these is the same: find out what changed, and touch only that.

The do-it-yourself version: hash, compare, delete deliberately

You do not need any particular vendor for this. The pattern is:

  1. Normalise each page's text (strip boilerplate, collapse whitespace) and hash it.
  2. Compare against the hash you stored last time.
  3. Re-chunk and re-embed only pages whose hash moved; give every chunk an ID that starts with the page URL.
  4. Before adding a changed page's new chunks, delete all of its old ones. The chunk count can shrink, so overwriting by ID is not enough.
  5. Delete pages that have disappeared, but only if the run reached most of the site. 
import hashlib, json, re
from pathlib import Path

STATE = Path("hashes.json")

def normalise(text: str) -> str:
    text = re.sub(r"Last updated[^\n]*", "", text)   # add your own volatile lines
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

def plan_refresh(pages: dict[str, str], expected_urls: int):
    """pages: {url: markdown} from this run. Returns what to embed and delete."""
    old = json.loads(STATE.read_text()) if STATE.exists() else {}
    new = {u: hashlib.sha256(normalise(t).encode()).hexdigest() for u, t in pages.items()}

    changed = [u for u, h in new.items() if old.get(u) != h]
    removed = [u for u in old if u not in new]

    # Guard: a run that saw under 90% of the site must not delete anything.
    if len(pages) < 0.9 * expected_urls:
        removed = []
        new = {**old, **new}          # keep unseen pages' hashes for next time

    STATE.write_text(json.dumps(new))
    return changed, removed

# changed -> delete chunks with IDs starting f"{url}#", then embed and add new chunks
# removed -> delete chunks with IDs starting f"{url}#"

Two honest caveats. First, this still fetches every page every night to compute the hashes; it saves embedding and index writes, not crawling. Second, the normalise function is where the work lives. Every site has its own flicker, and you will be adding regexes for months.

If you are already on LangChain, its indexing API (a record manager plus index() with incremental cleanup) does the hash-and-skip part for documents you hand it. It does not fetch pages or know whether a crawl was partial, so the first and last steps above remain yours.

Skipping the fetch as well: sitemap lastmod

Many sites publish a lastmod date per URL in their sitemap. If it is trustworthy, you can skip fetching pages that have not changed at all. "If" is doing real work there: plenty of sitemaps stamp every URL with today's date, and some never update it. A sensible incremental crawler checks how many entries carry lastmod, falls back to a full crawl when coverage is poor, and runs a full pass periodically anyway to catch pages whose dates lie.

How MeshArc does it

This is the part where we describe our own product, so weigh it accordingly. Everything below is from our docs and pricing page.

A project is a site plus its settings, run on a schedule (hourly, daily, weekly or manual). Every run is diffed against the previous one, page by page: added, modified, removed, same, withheld. Boilerplate such as cookie banners, newsletter prompts and share bars is stripped by default, and a modified page with fewer than notify_min_words changed words (default 5) does not count as changed.

With sitemap_incremental on, a scheduled run fetches only pages the sitemap shows as new or with a newer lastmod, and carries the rest forward from the last full run. A full run is forced every sitemap_full_every runs (default 10), whenever fewer than 90% of entries carry lastmod, or when a carried page is over 30 days old. Carried-forward pages cost 0 credits. So do refused pages, 404s and 410s.

Removals are only reported when a run reached at least 90% of the site. Below that, missing pages are withheld, not removed, so a blocked crawl cannot empty your index.

pip install mesharc langchain-mesharc

from mesharc import MeshArc

arc = MeshArc()  # reads MESHARC_API_KEY

project = arc.projects.create(
    "https://docs.example.com",
    name="Docs KB",
    schedule="daily",
    config={"include_paths": ["/docs/*"], "sitemap_incremental": True},
)

run = arc.runs.start(project["id"], wait=True)   # first run is the baseline
record = arc.changes(project["id"])
print(record["change"]["counts"])

Then, after each scheduled run (from the run.finished webhook or a cron of your own), load only what changed and apply it to any LangChain vector store:

from langchain_mesharc import MeshArcLoader

def refresh(store, project_id: str) -> None:
    docs = MeshArcLoader(mode="changes", project_id=project_id,
                         include_removed=True).load()
    gone = [d.metadata["url"] for d in docs if d.metadata["change"] == "removed"]
    fresh = [d for d in docs if d.metadata["change"] != "removed"]
    if gone:
        store.delete(ids=gone)
    if fresh:
        store.add_documents(fresh, ids=[d.metadata["url"] for d in fresh])

That keys one document per URL. If you split pages into chunks before embedding, use chunk IDs that start with the URL and delete a page's old chunks first, exactly as in the DIY version. The LangChain integration docs have the details.

If you would rather not run that code at all, MeshArc can write straight into Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate or pgvector as a destination. It splits Markdown into paragraph-aligned chunks of about 350 words with a 40-word overlap, embeds them with your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint and key (we add no markup on embeddings), and by default writes only pages classed as added, modified or removed. Destinations are included on every plan.

The same docs site, priced

Back to the 2,000-page site, read daily on our Growth plan ($99 for 500,000 credits, so about $0.20 per 1,000 plain fetches). Assume the pages fetch plainly at 1 credit each, and that around 2% change on a typical day — your site's real churn will differ, which is the point of measuring it.

Approach Page reads a month Credits Cost on Growth
Full re-crawl every night 60,000 60,000 ~$11.88
sitemap_incremental, ~40 changed pages a night, plus 3 forced full runs ~1,080 + 6,000 ~7,080 (plus sitemap reads at 1 credit per file) ~$1.40

Embeddings follow the same shape: only the ~40 changed pages a day are re-embedded, instead of all 2,000. Pages that need a real browser cost 4 credits rather than 1, so multiply accordingly; our Firecrawl pricing breakdown works through the per-rung maths in more detail.

Where this does not fit

  • One-off corpora. If you index a site once for a demo, none of this matters. Any scraper will do.
  • Sites without a usable sitemap. Incremental fetching needs lastmod. Without it, MeshArc still diffs and still writes only changed pages to your store, but it has to fetch every page to know.
  • Logged-in content. Pages behind your own SSO are better pulled from the source system (Confluence, Notion, a CMS export) than scraped.
  • Self-hosting. MeshArc is not open source. If you need the crawler on your own hardware, the DIY approach above with an open-source crawler is the honest answer; our comparison page lists the trade-offs by vendor.

Try it on your own docs

The quickest test is to point a project at a site you already index, let it run twice, and look at the change counts: that number, not the page count, is what your pipeline should be embedding each night. The RAG pipeline use case has the overview; if your assistant reads whole sites at once, the llms.txt generator is a free alternative to embeddings altogether.

Try a page in the playground · Start free — 1,000 credits, no card

I drafted this post with AI assistance and reviewed and edited it myself; the code and numbers come from our own docs and pricing.

Originally published on mesharc.dev.

title: Full Collapse Is Suboptimal: Controlled Partial Neural Collapse for Long-Tailed Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.36460v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent long-tailed recognition (LTR) methods incorporate neural collapse (NC) and align features to a fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) as a uniform target for all classes. However, forcing tail classes to fully collapse over-contracts their samples and weakens generalization. To address this, we propose a controlled partial neural collapse, realized through two coordinated controls on a backbone: the Class-Adaptive Sparse Activation (CASA) classifier and the ETF-constrained adaptive margin (ETF-AM) loss. Rather than forcing a uniform full collapse, this regime allows head classes to collapse along the ETF while tail classes retain within-class diversity. This prevents the tail from being forced into full collapse, which is suboptimal under imbalance. To set the dimensionality of collapse, CASA induces class-related node specialization through feature-conditioned gating so that tail classes occupy their own feature directions. For the clearance axis, ETF-AM applies a frequency-adaptive margin, with smaller margins for head classes and larger for tail classes. On CIFAR100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and iNaturalist-2018, our method achieves the best overall accuracy over prior methods. In the empirical analysis, within-class spread increases monotonically from head to tail classes, consistent with tail classes retaining variability rather than fully collapsing.

title: Exact Unlearning After Data Curation
description:
arXiv:2610.33426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training pipelines often remove similar examples before fitting a model. Deleting a raw record can change that selection and admit an example that was excluded before. What must a service retain to reproduce training after such requests? We answer this question for a fixed rule in which earlier similar records block later ones. A limit on the total number of future deletions identifies exactly which records can still enter training. We use this boundary to build a summary of training statistics that can be repaired exactly after repeated deletions. The repaired summary is the same as rebuilding it on the surviving data with the remaining budget. We also construct finite-precision features for ridge regression, a linear learner with a penalty on coefficient size. With exact rational outputs, allowing one more deletion changes the required private information. It rises from zero to every private feature sign in the excluded candidates. An encoding attains this conditional private-information minimum on the constructed family throughout a sequence of requests. On 1,001 AskUbuntu development records, deleting an initially excluded record admits another record at 13 of 51 fixed similarity cutoffs. Exact membership repair passes 13,056 deletion-step checks. Two model-based semantic calibrations fail their fixed criteria, so the downstream task study is not run. The central result is a retention contract: the future deletions a service promises to support determine which excluded data can still be needed.

title: CCAR-F in a Job Interview: Turning Exam Prep Into Answers
description:
A credential gets your resume a second look. The interview is where you show what it stands for. For the Claude Certified Architect Foundations exam (CCAR-F), that is good news: Section 1 of the exam guide (CCAR-F) says the exam validates that you can make informed decisions about tradeoffs when implementing real-world solutions with Claude. That is close to what a technical interview for a role building with Claude sets out to test. The preparation you did for one can carry you through the other, if you turn it into answers you can say out loud.

Know where the line is first

Before you talk about the exam at all, know what you can share. Section 14 of the guide (CCAR-F) is a confidentiality agreement: everything on the exam, including questions, answer options and scenarios, is confidential, and you agree not to disclose any of it. Section 13 adds that disclosing exam content can lead to revocation of your credential.

What you can discuss freely is everything the guide publishes: the five domains and their weights, the task statements in Section 6, and the format. That is plenty. Our guide to listing the credential covers what to say when an interviewer asks what was on the exam, and the short version is to talk about the kind of decisions it tested, then move straight to one you made in your own work.

Expect judgment questions, not trivia

An interviewer can look up any configuration flag. What they cannot look up is how you choose between two reasonable designs. That is also how the exam is built: Section 1 describes questions grounded in realistic scenarios that require practical judgment about architecture, configuration and tradeoffs in production deployments. In a realistic hiring pipeline, the technical screen and the system design round are where that judgment gets tested.

So prepare answers that follow one shape: the situation, the options you weighed, the one you chose, and what you gave up. A choice with no alternative named sounds like a guess. A choice with a cost named sounds like experience.

Turn each domain into one story

Section 4 of the guide (CCAR-F) splits the exam into five weighted domains. Prepare one story for each, drawn from something you have built. Here is a prompt to practice against for each domain, and what a strong answer shows.

Agentic Architecture and Orchestration (27%)

Practice prompt: "Walk me through an agent you built. What did the model decide, and what did your code enforce?"

A strong answer separates the two clearly. Section 6 lists the distinction between programmatic enforcement, such as hooks and prerequisite gates, and prompt-based guidance, and it notes that prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate. If you can explain why one rule in your system had to be a hard check while another could live in the prompt, you are showing exactly the judgment this domain tests. Our breakdown of the guarantee or accuracy question type gives you a clean way to frame that choice.

Tool Design and MCP Integration (18%)

Practice prompt: "How do you design a tool so an agent uses it correctly?"

Talk about descriptions and errors. Section 6 treats tool descriptions as the primary mechanism a model uses to choose between tools, and it lists structured error responses that tell the agent whether a failure is worth retrying. An answer that covers both, with an example of a description you rewrote or an error you made machine-readable, stands out. The case for tool errors written for the model makes a good talking point.

Claude Code Configuration and Workflows (20%)

Practice prompt: "How would you set up Claude Code for a team of ten developers?"

The strong answer is about scope: what belongs in shared, version-controlled configuration, what stays personal, and how conventions reach the right files. Section 6 covers the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, path-specific rules, project-scoped commands and skills, and when to use plan mode instead of direct execution. Mention one problem you solved with that structure, such as a convention that was not reaching a teammate, and you have a story.

Prompt Engineering and Structured Output (20%)

Practice prompt: "An automated review is flagging too many false positives. What do you change?"

Interviewers want to hear that you would replace vague instructions with explicit criteria, not ask the model to be more careful. Section 6 says general instructions like "be conservative" fail to improve precision compared with specific categorical criteria, and it adds few-shot examples and schema-validated output through tool use. If you have ever tightened a prompt and measured the result, lead with the measurement.

Context Management and Reliability (15%)

Practice prompt: "How do you keep a long-running agent from losing important details?"

A strong answer names a concrete technique. Section 6 lists keeping transactional facts in a persistent block outside summarized history, trimming verbose tool output before it fills the context, and using scratchpad files across long sessions. Pair one of those with the failure it prevented in your own work.

Practice the system design round out loud

Section 5 of the guide (CCAR-F) publishes six production contexts the exam draws on, including a customer support agent, a multi-agent research system, Claude Code in a CI/CD pipeline and a structured data extraction system. Those published descriptions make good practice prompts for a design interview, as long as you work from the guide's own summaries and nothing you saw on exam day.

Pick one, set a timer for 30 minutes, and design it out loud: the components, where the model makes decisions, where code enforces rules, how errors flow, and when a person gets involved. Record yourself once. Most people discover they skip the "what I gave up" part, and that is the part interviewers remember.

Bring the evidence

Every story above lands harder with something to show. Section 2 of the guide (CCAR-F) describes the typical candidate as having 6+ months of practical experience building with the Claude APIs, Agent SDK, Claude Code and MCP, and an interviewer will want to see that experience. A small, finished repository you can open on screen does more than any description. If you have one, follow the steps for turning your prep into a portfolio project so it is ready to walk through. If you are coming from a developer background, it helps to know what your existing experience already covers so you can connect old work to new skills.

If you have not passed yet

You can still bring it up. Say that you are preparing for the CCAR-F and when your exam is scheduled. Never say "certified" before you are. Then use the domain stories above anyway: an interviewer cares more about how you think than about the badge.

Sharpen your answers with timed practice

The exam gives you 120 minutes for 60 items, two minutes each, which forces you to commit to an answer with a reason. That is the same habit an interview rewards. Start with the free diagnostic, which breaks your results down by domain, and build your first story around your weakest one. Then, before your interview loop, take a full 60-question mock exam under the 120-minute limit. After each wrong answer, say out loud why the right option beats the one you picked. That is interview practice in disguise.

title: What Survives Distillation? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of GPT-2 and DistilGPT-2
description:
arXiv:2610.37157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large language models into compact students that preserve aggregate metrics, yet the mechanistic consequences of depth-reduction distillation remain largely uncharacterized. This work applies linear CKA, logit lens analysis, attention pattern decomposition, sparse autoencoder feature statistics, and activation patching to compare GPT-2 and its six-layer student DistilGPT-2 across two canonical circuits: the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit and the Greater-Than (GT) circuit. The results reveal a compression-collapse dichotomy: the IOI circuit suffers complete mechanistic collapse (DistilGPT-2: 35.2% accuracy vs. 94.8%, zero name-mover preservation), while the GT circuit survives with 87.7% task performance recovery through active remapping of the teacher's layer-9 comparison head into student layer~4 (mean Pearson r = 0.945). These findings demonstrate that circuit compressibility governs mechanistic survival under distillation, and that aggregate metrics are insufficient diagnostics for circuit integrity.

title: We thought exact match was enough for LLM evals. It wasn't.
description:
We run a service that reads research manuscripts and answers questions editors actually act on.

  • Is there an ethical approval statement?
  • Does the paper mention a clinical trial registration?
  • Are figure references consistent?
  • Is the self-citation rate too high?

Each question is a separate check, and an LLM does most of the reading. Because the system is already in production, mistakes matter in a very practical way: a false missing signal wastes someone’s time, and a false pass lets a real issue move further down the line.

At first, evaluating these checks looked simple. Most of them felt like yes/no questions, so exact match seemed like the obvious metric.

That worked for about two checks.

As soon as we started asking for supporting citations and structured extractions, exact match stopped measuring correctness and started measuring formatting noise.
A curly quote, a dash changed by PDF extraction, or one extra sentence around the right passage was enough to mark a correct answer as wrong.

This post is about what broke, what we changed, and why we ended up with a much simpler eval setup than we expected.

Why evals matter once the system is in production

Once a system is live, evals stop being a one-time validation exercise and become part of day-to-day engineering. Every new requirement, bug fix, or prompt update has to answer two questions: did it solve the target problem, and did it reduce accuracy anywhere else?

That second question matters more than it first appears. In LLM systems, small changes in prompts can have wide effects. A prompt tweak that helps one check may subtly change behavior on another set of manuscripts that was previously working. Without a repeatable eval set, those regressions are easy to miss until users hit them.

Our way of handling that is simple: for each check, we maintain a set of test documents in SharePoint and use them as a stable evaluation baseline. When something changes, we rerun the check on that same set and compare the outputs with the expected results. That gives us a practical way to protect existing behavior while still improving the system.

TL;DR

We started with exact match because most checks looked strict enough for it.

That fell apart as soon as checks started returning cited passages and extracted metadata. The model was often right, but exact match still said it was wrong.

We moved to a mix of exact match,F1 and fuzzy matching, with different thresholds depending on the field type.

The checks do not all fail in the same way

One of the first useful lessons was that “LLM checks” is too broad a category.

The checks we run fall into a few different shapes:

- Presence: is a required statement or section there at all?
- Position: is it where it should be in the paper?
- Extraction: pull out structured metadata such as authors, affiliations, or funding.
- Reference checks: do figures and tables cited in the text actually exist, and are they cited correctly?
- Inference: does the answer depend on combining evidence from several parts of the manuscript?

Most of the checks return structured JSON. That made the first version of the eval almost embarrassingly easy to build.

We started with exact match

The first setup was straightforward.

For every check, we keep a folder of expected outputs: one JSON file per test manuscript. We run the same prompt the service uses, save the output, and compare it against the expected JSON.
Same value, score 1. Different value, score 0.

For yes/no style checks, this worked surprisingly well. “Does the paper contain a consent statement?” has a concrete answer, and the model either gets it or it does not. We could change a prompt, rerun the suite, and see within minutes whether anything moved.

The harness itself is plain Python. One script runs every manuscript through the model and writes the outputs to a .jsonl file.

Each check has its own evaluator, which reads the actual outputs, compares them with the expected JSON, and writes a score. A small report script then combines those scores so runs can be compared over time.

It was simple, cheap, and easy to reason about.

Then we needed citations.

Then citations broke the metric

A lot of the useful checks do not just answer yes or no. They also point to the text that supports the answer: the sentence where the ethical approval is mentioned, the paragraph referencing Figure 3, the row of a table.

That is where exact match started lying to us.

The model would return the right passage, but with a curly quote where the expected file had a straight one. Or a hyphen had turned into a different dash. Or a Greek symbol, superscript, or special character had changed slightly during PDF conversion. Sometimes the model returned the relevant sentence plus one adjacent sentence, while the expected output contained only the shorter span chosen by the human annotator.

By any reasonable reading, those are correct answers.

By exact match, they are failures.

The clearest example was metadata extraction. In one run, that check scored 0.50 on exact match and 0.97 on F1. Looking at the failures made it obvious what was happening: the model was mostly correct, but the scoring method was punishing superficial differences.

That created a second problem. If the metric keeps reporting cosmetic failures, people stop trusting the report. Once that happens, a real regression can sit in the same output looking no different from all the false alarms.

We stopped scoring every field the same way

The fix was not to find one better universal metric.

The fix was to admit that different fields need different scoring rules.

We ended up with a simple split:

  • Booleans and enumerations stay strict. A yes is not a maybe. These use a threshold of 1.0.
  • Metadata fields get a high but not perfect threshold, around 0.95, because names and affiliations often vary in small ways without changing the answer.
  • Reference text gets a looser threshold, around 0.85, because what matters is whether the model found the right passage, not whether it reproduced every character exactly.

For text fields, we normalize first. That includes lowercasing, collapsing whitespace, and stripping harmless punctuation differences and brackets. After that, we compare using fuzzy matching from rapidfuzz, taking the best score across token sort, token set, and partial ratio.

We also added a containment rule. If the model returns a meaningful chunk of the expected text, or if the expected text sits inside the returned text, that should count as a strong match. We scale that score by how much of the longer text is covered.

Stripped down, the logic looks like this:

def fuzzy_match_score(expected: str, actual: str, threshold: float = 0.85):
    if expected == actual:
        return {"exact_match": True, "fuzzy_score": 100.0, "passes_threshold": True}

    a, b = normalize_text(expected), normalize_text(actual)

    shorter, longer = sorted([a, b], key=len)
    if len(shorter) > 20 and shorter in longer:
        ratio = len(shorter) / len(longer)
        if ratio > 0.3:
            score = 85 + ratio * 15
            return {
                "exact_match": False,
                "fuzzy_score": score,
                "passes_threshold": score >= threshold * 100,
            }

    score = max(
        fuzz.token_sort_ratio(a, b),
        fuzz.token_set_ratio(a, b),
        fuzz.partial_ratio(a, b),
    )
    return {
        "exact_match": False,
        "fuzzy_score": score,
        "passes_threshold": score >= threshold * 100,
    }

The report now shows exact match, F1, and fuzzy match side by side.

Reading those together matters more than any single score. If exact match is low but fuzzy is high, the problem is usually formatting noise. If all three are low, something is actually broken.

For list-like outputs, such as figure references, we match greedily by item rather than by position. If the model finds the same five references in a different order, that should not count as five mistakes.

Why we kept the eval boring on purpose

We considered more sophisticated approaches.

LLM as a judge was the obvious one. Ask another model whether the output is correct. It is flexible, and it reduces the need for exact expected text. But it also adds a second non-deterministic component. When a score changes, you then have to work out whether the system under test moved or the judge moved. For checks with a clear right answer, that felt like adding noise to fix noise.

We also looked at evaluation frameworks such as promptfoo, DeepEval, and Ragas. They are useful tools, especially if you are starting from scratch. In our case, the checks return structured, domain-specific JSON with per-field scoring rules, so we would still have ended up writing most of the custom logic ourselves.

Embedding similarity was another option. It is attractive for free text, but it can be too forgiving. A sentence that mentions approval from the wrong committee can still look semantically very close to the correct answer. For our use case, “close in meaning” is sometimes still wrong in a way that matters.

And of course there is human review of every run, which is the most accurate option and also the least scalable.

What we ended up trusting most was much less exciting: ground-truth files, deterministic scoring, and simple string and set comparisons.

It is not fancy. But it is cheap, transparent, and fast. More importantly, when a score drops, we can open the actual and expected JSON files and see exactly why.

That turned out to matter more than any advanced metric.

Where the ground truth comes from

Our QE team prepared the expected outputs.

The manuscripts are a mix of real production papers and curated edge cases. Some were selected because they reflect the kinds of papers the service sees every day. Others were chosen or created specifically to stress the checks: unusual structure, buried statements, missing sections, or text that looks like the thing we want but is not actually the thing.

That mix is deliberate.

Real data tells you how the checks behave on typical manuscripts. Curated cases tell you how they behave on the papers that cause trouble. If you only use real data, the eval can look flatteringly easy. If you only use adversarial cases, it can look unrealistically harsh.

The dataset is small: roughly eight papers per check.

That is enough to catch obvious regressions after a prompt or pipeline change. It is not enough to claim a precise accuracy number, and we try not to pretend otherwise.

What I would tell someone starting out

Start with exact match. It is a good way to discover which fields are genuinely strict and which ones only look strict at first.

Choose metrics per field type, not per project. A boolean answer and a quoted passage should not share the same definition of correctness.

When a score drops, read the diffs before touching the prompt. More than once, the thing that was broken was the eval, not the model.

Keep a few ugly cases in the dataset on purpose. Production data is representative, which usually means it is mostly easy.

If part of a check is deterministic code, evaluate that part together with the model. The user experiences the whole pipeline, not just the prompt.

And version your prompts next to your eval results. Otherwise, a few weeks later, you will not remember which change moved which number.

title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets
description:
arXiv:2610.36386v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.

title: CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36734v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.

title: Building Single-File HTML Templates: Clean Code Without the Framework Overhead
description:
When building websites, it is easy to get caught up in modern framework stacks, build steps, and endless dependencies. However, for many business and landing pages, keeping everything clean, fast, and self-contained in a single file is hard to beat.

Here is why keeping HTML, CSS, and JavaScript inline within a single document works so well for template efficiency:

The Advantages of Inline Single-File Builds

  1. Zero Build Steps: No need for compilers, bundlers, or package managers. Just open the file and code.
  2. Instant Deployment: Uploading a single clean file via SFTP takes seconds and eliminates missing asset paths.
  3. Streamlined Performance: Less network overhead means lightning-fast load times and consistent 90+ PageSpeed Insights scores.
  4. Complete Code Portability: Anyone can easily inspect, understand, and customize the site without needing complex environments.

By stripping away unnecessary framework bloat, you deliver pure performance directly to the browser.

Do you prefer keeping small project setups completely self-contained, or do you still reach for build tools by default?

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: OmniBrain-0: A Unified Agentic Model for Embodied Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.36013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. Specialist policies alone do not ensure task-level reliability, while powerful multimodal agents rely on costly reasoning and external experience that compact models struggle to reproduce. We introduce OmniBrain-0, a lightweight unified embodied agent that coordinates manipulation and navigation through a shared high-level decision model, integrating task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery. Our progressive training framework combines embodied pretraining, domain-specialized agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). It distills powerful teachers' interaction experience into manipulation and navigation experts, then consolidates their decision capabilities into OmniBrain-0. Unification therefore occurs within the learned decision model rather than only at the tool interface. We further introduce Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), a data flywheel in which a Meta-Agent turns execution evidence into refined rubrics, step-level reminders, and verified trajectories for domain-expert updates before their reconsolidation into OmniBrain-0 through MOPD. We evaluate OmniBrain-0 on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and R2R-CE Val-Unseen, as well as multiple real-world manipulation tasks. OmniBrain-0 combines strong cross-domain task performance with substantially lower inference and execution overhead than its closed-source teacher, demonstrating efficient transfer and consolidation of embodied capabilities into a compact unified agent.

title: How to Scrape Whatnot with Node.js: Seller Stats, Live Shows, Search, and a Viewer Tracker (2026)
description:
Whatnot is where a lot of trading cards, comics, Funko Pops, and sneakers get sold now, live, one auction at a time. If you sell there, or you're studying the market, you want numbers: which sellers move the most items, who is live right now, how many people are watching, and what a card goes for when it's listed.

The first thing most people search is "Whatnot API". There is one, but it probably isn't the one you want. So this post covers both: what the official Whatnot API gives you, and how to build a small Whatnot scraper in Node.js for the public data it doesn't cover.

The scraper is one file, no npm dependencies, Node 18+. It will:

  1. Discover seller handles from the sitemap Whatnot publishes in robots.txt
  2. Read a seller's profile: followers, items sold, rating, reviews, live status
  3. List a seller's live and scheduled shows, and their shop listings
  4. Run a search and read a category feed
  5. Read a single listing with price, condition, and seller
  6. Snapshot live viewers in a category every few minutes into a CSV

Everything below was run on October 28, 2026, and the output is real.

Before you start: Whatnot's Terms of Service prohibit scraping, crawling, and other automated access to the app. robots.txt allows the public pages used here, but robots rules and terms are different things. Treat this as a learning project or small-scale research, keep request rates very low, don't resell the data, and don't build profiles of individual buyers or sellers. If you're a seller who wants your own data, use the official API first.

Is there a Whatnot API?

Yes. Whatnot has an official Seller API (REST, https://api.whatnot.com/seller-api/rest/v2, docs at developers.whatnot.com). You create a personal access token in the developer dashboard and send it as Authorization: Bearer wn_pat_tk_.... It covers products, inventory, orders, shipments, your shows, and show analytics.

The catch is in the name. The Whatnot API is for your own store. It answers "what did I sell and what do I need to ship", not "how many followers does that seller have" or "who is live in Pokémon cards right now". There is no official public endpoint for other sellers, search, or category feeds.

So, a quick decision table:

You want Use
Your own orders, inventory, show analytics Official Seller API
Other sellers' public stats, live shows, search results, listing prices The public website, which is what this Whatnot scraper reads

How whatnot.com looks from a scraper's point of view

Three findings shaped the code.

1. robots.txt is friendly and points to sitemaps. It allows everything except account pages, the player, and a few others (/account/, /dashboard, /messages, /order/, /player, /video/, ...). It also lists seller-sitemap.txt, users-sitemap-index.xml, and listings-sitemap-index.xml. That's your discovery layer.

2. The data is already in the HTML. whatnot.com is a Next.js app with Apollo GraphQL. When the server renders a page, it embeds the GraphQL results it used in two places:

  • (window[Symbol.for("ApolloSSRDataTransport")] ??= []).push({...}) script tags. These hold the query results for feeds: search, category, a seller's shows, a seller's shop.
  • self.__next_f.push([1,"..."]) script tags. That's the React Server Components payload, and it carries the seller profile and the listing details.

So you don't need a headless browser, and you don't need to call the GraphQL endpoint yourself. The browser's GraphQL calls go to /services/graphql, which is protected by Kasada bot detection. Leave it alone. The HTML is enough.

3. Cloudflare sits in front, and it cares about honesty. This surprised me. From Node's built-in fetch, a request that pretends to be Chrome gets Cloudflare's "Just a moment..." challenge every time. A request with an honest, descriptive User-Agent gets a normal 200:

round  user-agent                status  bytes   challenge?
0      Chrome 130 string         403     5768    true
0      whatnot-research-script   200     830788  false
0      (none, Node default)      403     5533    true
0      curl/8.5.0                403     5533    true
1      Chrome 130 string         403     5768    true
1      whatnot-research-script   200     830827  false

My guess is that a Chrome User-Agent with a non-Chrome TLS fingerprint looks like a disguised bot, while a script that says it's a script looks like what it is. That might change, but "say who you are" is good practice anyway.

Step 1: A polite fetch helper

One request every 3 to 4 seconds, an honest User-Agent, 404 treated as "gone", and a hard back-off when Cloudflare shows up.

// whatnot.mjs - a small Whatnot scraper in Node.js (18+), no dependencies.
// Reads only public, robots-allowed pages: sitemaps, /user/, /tag/, /search, /listing/.
import fs from "node:fs";

const BASE = "https://www.whatnot.com";
// Say who you are. A fake Chrome UA from Node gets Cloudflare's challenge (see "Pitfalls").
const UA = process.env.WHATNOT_UA ?? "whatnot-research-script/1.0 (+mailto:you@example.com)";
const MIN_DELAY_MS = 3000; // one request every ~3 s is plenty for this kind of job

// ---------- Step 1: a polite fetch helper ----------

let lastRequest = 0;
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

export class BlockedError extends Error {}

export async function get(url, { tries = 3 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= tries; attempt++) {
    const wait = lastRequest + MIN_DELAY_MS + Math.random() * 1000 - Date.now();
    if (wait > 0) await sleep(wait);
    lastRequest = Date.now();

    const res = await fetch(url, {
      headers: { "user-agent": UA, "accept-language": "en-US,en;q=0.9", accept: "text/html,*/*" },
      redirect: "follow",
    });
    const body = await res.text();

    if (res.status === 404) return null;
    // Cloudflare's interstitial: 403 + "Just a moment..." (or a challenge platform script)
    if (res.status === 403 && /Just a moment|challenge-platform/.test(body)) {
      if (attempt === tries) throw new BlockedError(`Cloudflare challenge on ${url}`);
      await sleep(30_000 * attempt); // back off hard, don't hammer
      continue;
    }
    if (res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) {
      await sleep(5_000 * attempt);
      continue;
    }
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} on ${url}`);
    return body;
  }
  throw new Error(`gave up on ${url}`);
}

BlockedError matters. If you see a challenge after a long back-off, stop. Don't rotate User-Agents or proxies to get around it.

Step 2: Read the data the page already ships

Two small parsers. The Apollo blocks are JavaScript object literals, not strict JSON: they contain undefined, so we swap it for null before JSON.parse. The RSC payload is a series of JSON strings that we concatenate. Then we pull out typed objects by looking for {"__typename":"..." and slicing a balanced {...}.

// ---------- Step 2: get the data the page already ships ----------

// (a) Apollo SSR transport: the GraphQL results the server rendered with.
// They are JS object literals (they contain `undefined`), not strict JSON.
const APOLLO = '(window[Symbol.for("ApolloSSRDataTransport")] ??= []).push(';

export function apolloResults(html) {
  const out = [];
  let i = 0;
  while ((i = html.indexOf(APOLLO, i)) !== -1) {
    const start = i + APOLLO.length;
    const end = html.indexOf(")</script>", start);
    const chunk = JSON.parse(html.slice(start, end).replace(/:undefined\b/g, ":null"));
    for (const v of Object.values(chunk.rehydrate ?? {})) if (v?.data) out.push(v.data);
    for (const ev of chunk.events ?? []) if (ev.type === "next" && ev.value?.data) out.push(ev.value.data);
    i = end;
  }
  return out;
}

// (b) React Server Components payload: self.__next_f.push([1,"..."]) strings.
export function rscText(html) {
  const re = /self\.__next_f\.push\(\[1,("(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*")\]\)/g;
  let m, text = "";
  while ((m = re.exec(html))) text += JSON.parse(m[1]);
  return text;
}

// Pull one balanced {...} object out of a text blob, starting at `from`.
function sliceObject(text, from) {
  let depth = 0, inStr = false, esc = false;
  for (let i = from; i < text.length; i++) {
    const c = text[i];
    if (inStr) {
      if (esc) esc = false;
      else if (c === "\\") esc = true;
      else if (c === '"') inStr = false;
    } else if (c === '"') inStr = true;
    else if (c === "{") depth++;
    else if (c === "}" && --depth === 0) return text.slice(from, i + 1);
  }
  return null;
}

// Every object in the RSC text that starts with {"__typename":"<type>"
export function rscObjects(text, typename) {
  const needle = `{"__typename":"${typename}"`;
  const out = [];
  let i = 0;
  while ((i = text.indexOf(needle, i)) !== -1) {
    const raw = sliceObject(text, i);
    if (raw) { try { out.push(JSON.parse(raw)); } catch { /* skip partial chunks */ } }
    i += needle.length;
  }
  return out;
}

The brace slicer is a bit crude, but the payload is machine-generated JSON, so a string-aware depth counter is enough. If a slice fails to parse, we skip it.

Step 3: Find sellers from the sitemap

seller-sitemap.txt is a plain list of profile URLs. On October 28, 2026 it had 7,740 handles.

// ---------- Step 3: discover sellers from the sitemap robots.txt points to ----------

export async function sellerHandles() {
  const txt = await get(`${BASE}/seller-sitemap.txt`);
  return txt
    .split(/\r?\n/)
    .map((l) => l.trim().match(/\/user\/([^/?#]+)$/)?.[1])
    .filter(Boolean);
}

$ node whatnot.mjs sellers 5
{
  "count": 7740,
  "sample": ["001spades", "1099comics", "10k_sportscards", "112comics", "123readycomics"]
}

The sitemap is stale in places. In two random samples, 4 of 14 handles returned 404 (renamed or closed accounts), including 10k_sportscards from the sample above. That's normal. Treat 404 as data, not as an error.

Step 4: Seller profile and shows

A seller page renders whichever tab the seller picked as default. Some open on Shows, others on Shop, and the Apollo data changes with it (GetUserLiveStreams vs ProfileShop). Requesting /user/{handle}/shows forces the shows tab, so the data is always the same shape. The profile object (followers, sold count, rating) is in the RSC payload on every tab.

// ---------- Step 4: seller profile + shows from /user/{handle}/shows ----------

const money = (m) => (m ? { amount: m.amount / 100, currency: m.currency } : null); // amounts are in cents

function cleanShow(s) {
  return {
    id: s.id,
    title: s.title,
    status: s.status, // PLAYING = live now, CREATED = scheduled
    start_time: s.startTime ? new Date(s.startTime).toISOString() : null,
    active_viewers: s.activeViewers ?? null,
    bookmarks: s.totalWatchlistUsers ?? null,
    seller: s.user?.username ?? null,
    categories: (s.livestreamCategories ?? []).map((c) => c.label).join("|"),
    tags: (s.tags ?? []).map((t) => t.label).join("|"),
    url: `${BASE}/live/${s.id}`,
  };
}

export async function seller(handle) {
  // Plain /user/{handle} renders whichever tab the seller picked (shows or shop).
  // /shows forces the shows tab, so the Apollo data is always GetUserLiveStreams.
  const html = await get(`${BASE}/user/${encodeURIComponent(handle)}/shows`);
  if (!html) return null; // 404: renamed, banned, or deleted

  const user = rscObjects(rscText(html), "PublicUserNode").find(
    (u) => u.username?.toLowerCase() === handle.toLowerCase() && "followerCount" in u
  );
  if (!user) throw new Error(`no profile object on /user/${handle} (layout changed?)`);

  const streams = apolloResults(html).find((d) => d.getUser?.livestreams)?.getUser.livestreams;

  return {
    handle: user.username,
    id: Buffer.from(user.id, "base64").toString().split(":")[1] ?? user.id, // "PublicUserNode:190554"
    display_name: user.displayName?.trim() || null,
    bio: user.bio || null,
    followers: user.followerCount,
    following: user.followingCount,
    sold: user.soldCount, // null when the seller hides it / has none
    rating: user.sellerRating?.overall ?? null,
    reviews: user.sellerRating?.numReviews ?? 0,
    avg_ship_days: user.averageShipDays,
    is_live: user.isLive,
    verified: user.isVerifiedSeller,
    premier: !!user.premierShopStatus?.isPremierShop,
    shows_total: streams?.totalCount ?? null,
    shows: (streams?.edges ?? []).map((e) => cleanShow(e.node)), // live + scheduled, first 15
  };
}

Two things in there are easy to miss:

  • IDs are base64 Relay IDs. UHVibGljVXNlck5vZGU6MTkwNTU0 decodes to PublicUserNode:190554. Keep the numeric part. It doesn't change when a seller renames their account, and the handle does.
  • Money is in cents. {"amount": 5500, "currency": "USD"} is $55.00. There's also a localizedPrice converted to your currency based on your IP (I got VND from Vietnam). Always store price, never localizedPrice.

A seller who was live while I ran this:

$ node whatnot.mjs seller hititfromthepack
{
  "handle": "hititfromthepack",
  "id": "25944732",
  "display_name": "HitItFromThePack",
  "followers": 16358,
  "following": 128,

  "rating": 4.9,
  "reviews": 753,
  "avg_ship_days": 1,

    {
      "id": "359ac220-1a62-435d-9e2a-50c00ab85c4c",
      "title": "🇺🇸 MY BIGGEST $1 START STREAM EVER! $100K+ MID ERA",

PLAYING means live now, CREATED means scheduled. The seven shows were one live and six upcoming, so the profile shows live and scheduled streams, not the archive. bookmarks (totalWatchlistUsers) on a scheduled show is a nice early signal of how big that show will be.

And a random sample from the sitemap, via node whatnot.mjs sellers-csv 6:

handle,followers,sold,rating,reviews,avg_ship_days,is_live,premier,shows_total
sundazebest,7839,13691,4.9,2878,,false,false,0
comicselitelive,25574,91897,5,17060,0,true,false,51
king_espeo,197,117,5,43,,false,false,0
bfunko_collectibles,1262,414,4.8,149,,false,false,0

(The other two of the six were 404s.) sold is lifetime items sold, which is the most useful single number for sizing a seller. avg_ship_days is often null.

The seller's shop

Many sellers also keep buy-it-now and auction listings in a shop. /user/{handle}/shop ships the first 20 of them:

export async function shop(handle) {
  const html = await get(`${BASE}/user/${encodeURIComponent(handle)}/shop`);
  if (!html) return null;
  const feed = apolloResults(html).find((d) => d.getUser?.searchShop)?.getUser.searchShop;
  return flattenFeed(feed).listings; // first 20 listings
}

$ node whatnot.mjs shop bangarangcards
[
  { "title": "Typhoid Mary", "price": 5, "currency": "USD", "type": "BUY_IT_NOW", "status": "ACTIVE", ... },
  { "title": "Thena", "price": 15, "currency": "USD", "type": "BUY_IT_NOW", "status": "ACTIVE", ... },
  ...
]

Step 5: Search and category feeds

Search (/search?query=...) and category pages (/tag/{name}) both render a Feed. Its edges are a mix: FeedEntity wrappers around listings or livestreams, plus Section carousels. We flatten them and keep the three types we care about.

// ---------- Step 5: search and category feeds ----------

function cleanListing(l) {
  return {
    id: l.id,
    title: l.title,
    subtitle: l.subtitle ?? null,
    price: money(l.price)?.amount ?? null,
    currency: l.price?.currency ?? null,
    type: l.transactionType, // BUY_IT_NOW or AUCTION
    status: l.listingStatus ?? l.publicStatus,
    current_bid: money(l.currentBid)?.amount ?? null,
    bids: l.currentBidCount ?? null,
    quantity: l.quantity,
    seller: l.user?.username ?? null,
    url: `${BASE}/listing/${encodeURIComponent(l.id)}`,
  };
}

// Feeds mix listings, livestreams, users and "Section" carousels. Flatten them.
function flattenFeed(feed) {
  const shows = [], listings = [], users = [];
  const visit = (o) => {
    if (!o) return;
    if (o.__typename === "LiveStream") shows.push(cleanShow(o));
    else if (o.__typename === "ListingNode") listings.push(cleanListing(o));
    else if (o.__typename === "PublicUserNode") users.push({ handle: o.username, followers: o.followerCount, sold: o.soldCount });
  };
  for (const { node } of feed?.objects?.edges ?? []) {
    if (node.__typename === "FeedEntity") visit(node.object);
    else visit(node);
  }
  const dedupe = (arr) => [...new Map(arr.map((x) => [x.id ?? x.handle, x])).values()];
  return { title: feed?.title, hasNextPage: feed?.objects?.pageInfo?.hasNextPage ?? false,
    shows: dedupe(shows), listings: dedupe(listings), users: dedupe(users) };
}

export async function search(query) {
  const html = await get(`${BASE}/search?query=${encodeURIComponent(query)}&referringSource=typed`);
  const feed = apolloResults(html).find((d) => d.search?.objects)?.search;
  return flattenFeed(feed);
}

export async function category(tag) {
  const html = await get(`${BASE}/tag/${encodeURIComponent(tag)}`);
  if (!html) return null;
  const feed = apolloResults(html).find((d) => d.feed?.objects)?.feed;
  return flattenFeed(feed);
}
