$ node whatnot.mjs category pokemon_cards
# "Pokémon Cards": 24 shows, all PLAYING
{ "seller": "hititfromthepack", "active_viewers": 160, "bookmarks": 95, "title": "🇺🇸 MY BIGGEST $1 START STREAM EVER! ..." }
{ "seller": "koheitcg_jp", "active_viewers": 22, "tags": "Pokémon|Pokemon 30th Anniversary|$1 Starts|Shop from Japan|...", ... }

The limit: you only get the first page. Search gives about 18 to 24 items, and a category gives 24 shows. Later pages and the vertical filters (shows only, sellers only) are loaded by the browser through the Kasada-protected GraphQL endpoint. Adding &vertical=LIVESTREAM to the URL did nothing in my tests. For monitoring "what's big right now" the first page is fine. For a full catalog it isn't.

Also, the category feed is ranked, not sorted by viewers. Sort it yourself.

Step 6: A single listing

Listing pages carry the full ListingNode in the RSC payload, including description, created date, condition and other attributes. The node doesn't include its seller. The page passes the seller as a separate "seller":{...} prop, so we grab that too.

// ---------- Step 6: a single listing ----------

export async function listing(idOrUrl) {
  const id = decodeURIComponent(idOrUrl.split("/listing/").pop());
  const html = await get(`${BASE}/listing/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`);
  if (!html) return null;
  const text = rscText(html);
  const node = rscObjects(text, "ListingNode").find((l) => l.id === id);
  if (!node) return null;
  // The listing node itself has no user; the page passes the seller as a separate prop.
  const at = text.indexOf('"seller":{"__typename":"PublicUserNode"');
  const sellerNode = at === -1 ? null : JSON.parse(sliceObject(text, at + '"seller":'.length));
  const attrs = Object.fromEntries((node.listingAttributeValues ?? []).map((a) => [a.attribute.label, a.value]));
  return { ...cleanListing(node), seller: sellerNode?.username ?? null, description: node.description, created_at: node.createdAt,
    offers_allowed: node.transactionProps?.isOfferable ?? null, attributes: attrs };
}

$ node whatnot.mjs listing "https://www.whatnot.com/listing/TGlzdGluZ05vZGU6MjQ0ODA3NTg0MQ=="
{
  "id": "TGlzdGluZ05vZGU6MjQ0ODA3NTg0MQ==",
  "title": "Charizard Expedition Reverse Holo",
  "subtitle": "Moderately Played",
  "price": 175,
  "currency": "USD",
  "type": "BUY_IT_NOW",
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "quantity": 1,
  "seller": "bigmacspokeshack",
  "description": "Charizard Expedition Reverse Holo\nMP",
  "created_at": "Fri, 16 Oct 2026 20:25:26 GMT",
  "offers_allowed": true,
  "attributes": { "Condition": "Moderately Played" }
}

Listing IDs are base64 too (ListingNode:2448075841), and they can end in =. Encode them when you build URLs.

Step 7: A live-viewer tracker

Now the fun part. Live shopping is all about who's live and how many people are watching. Snapshot a category every few minutes and append each live show to a CSV:

// ---------- Step 7: live-viewer tracker ----------

export const csvCell = (v) => (v == null ? "" : /[",\n]/.test(String(v)) ? `"${String(v).replace(/"/g, '""')}"` : String(v));

export async function track(tag, { every = 10, times = 3, file = "live-snapshots.csv" } = {}) {
  const cols = ["snapshot_at", "tag", "show_id", "seller", "status", "active_viewers", "bookmarks", "start_time", "title"];
  if (!fs.existsSync(file)) fs.writeFileSync(file, cols.join(",") + "\n");
  for (let n = 1; n <= times; n++) {
    const at = new Date().toISOString();
    const feed = await category(tag);
    const live = (feed?.shows ?? []).filter((s) => s.status === "PLAYING");
    const rows = live.map((s) => [at, tag, s.id, s.seller, s.status, s.active_viewers, s.bookmarks, s.start_time, s.title]);
    fs.appendFileSync(file, rows.map((r) => r.map(csvCell).join(",")).join("\n") + (rows.length ? "\n" : ""));
    const viewers = live.reduce((a, s) => a + (s.active_viewers ?? 0), 0);
    console.error(`[${at}] ${tag}: ${live.length} live shows, ${viewers} viewers in the first feed page`);
    if (n < times) await sleep(every * 60_000);
  }
}

I ran it on Pokémon cards, every 2 minutes, 3 times:

$ node whatnot.mjs track pokemon_cards 2 3
[2026-10-28T04:12:14.735Z] pokemon_cards: 24 live shows, 6096 viewers in the first feed page
[2026-10-28T04:14:15.576Z] pokemon_cards: 24 live shows, 6150 viewers in the first feed page
[2026-10-28T04:16:16.457Z] pokemon_cards: 24 live shows, 7125 viewers in the first feed page

snapshot_at,tag,show_id,seller,status,active_viewers,bookmarks,start_time,title
2026-10-28T04:12:14.735Z,pokemon_cards,359ac220-...,hititfromthepack,PLAYING,155,95,2026-10-28T02:02:51.692Z,🇺🇸 MY BIGGEST $1 START ...
2026-10-28T04:12:14.735Z,pokemon_cards,729592e6-...,koheitcg_jp,PLAYING,24,21,2026-10-28T03:00:17.480Z,🇯🇵 Superbly Spectacular ...
2026-10-28T04:12:14.735Z,pokemon_cards,e3538101-...,clovrcards,PLAYING,208,152,2026-10-27T19:04:20.600Z,🇺🇸 🐉 EX EMERALD BOX ...

Grouping by seller across the three snapshots already tells a story:

spacenarwhalz      2043 → 1993 → 1963
novatcg            1075 → 1137 → 1252
saw_tcg             160 →  154 → 1096
shop_exp            531 →  551 →  529

A jump like saw_tcg's is exactly what you'd want an alert for. 27 different sellers showed up, and 22 of them were in all three snapshots. The other five moved in or out of the first page as the ranking shifted. That churn is a property of the feed, not of the shows, so don't read a missing row as "the show ended". To confirm that, check the seller's /shows page.

For a real tracker, run it from cron every 10 to 15 minutes, not every 2. That's 4 to 6 requests an hour per category, which is about as gentle as it gets.

Step 8: The CLI

A tiny command switch ties it together. Paste the blocks above into one whatnot.mjs (Node 18+, ES module, no dependencies), add this at the bottom, and run node whatnot.mjs for usage.

// ---------- CLI ----------

async function main() {
  const [cmd, ...args] = process.argv.slice(2);
  const print = (x) => console.log(JSON.stringify(x, null, 2));
  switch (cmd) {
    case "sellers": {
      const handles = await sellerHandles();
      print({ count: handles.length, sample: handles.slice(0, Number(args[0] ?? 10)) });
      break;
    }
    case "sellers-csv": {
      // Profile a random sample of sitemap sellers into sellers.csv
      const n = Number(args[0] ?? 10);
      const handles = (await sellerHandles()).sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5).slice(0, n);
      const cols = ["handle", "followers", "sold", "rating", "reviews", "avg_ship_days", "is_live", "premier", "shows_total"];
      const lines = [cols.join(",")];
      for (const h of handles) {
        const s = await seller(h).catch((e) => { if (e instanceof BlockedError) throw e; return null; });
        if (s) lines.push(cols.map((c) => csvCell(s[c])).join(","));
        console.error(`${h}: ${s ? `${s.followers} followers, ${s.sold ?? "?"} sold` : "skipped"}`);
      }
      fs.writeFileSync("sellers.csv", lines.join("\n") + "\n");
      break;
    }
    case "seller":
      for (const h of args) {
        try { print(await seller(h) ?? { handle: h, error: "not found" }); }
        catch (e) { print({ handle: h, error: e.message }); if (e instanceof BlockedError) return; }
      }
      break;
    case "shop": print(await shop(args[0])); break;
    case "search": print(await search(args.join(" "))); break;
    case "category": print(await category(args[0])); break;
    case "listing": print(await listing(args[0])); break;
    case "track": await track(args[0], { every: Number(args[1] ?? 10), times: Number(args[2] ?? 3) }); break;
    default:
      console.log("usage: node whatnot.mjs sellers [n] | sellers-csv [n] | seller <handle...> | shop <handle> | search <query> | category <tag> | listing <id|url> | track <tag> [everyMin] [times]");
  }
}

if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) main().catch((e) => { console.error(e.message); process.exit(1); });

Pitfalls, in one place

  • Terms of Service. Whatnot's terms prohibit automated access. robots.txt allowing a path doesn't change that. Keep it small, slow, and non-commercial, or use the official Seller API for your own data.
  • Cloudflare checks if your client is consistent. A fake browser UA from Node got challenged every time. An honest UA passed. If you get challenged anyway, back off and stop.
  • GraphQL is off-limits in practice. The browser's calls go through Kasada-protected /services/graphql, and introspection is disabled. Everything here comes from server-rendered HTML.
  • First page only. Search and category pages give roughly one page of results (about 24). No deep pagination without the browser's GraphQL calls.
  • Default tabs differ per seller. Use /user/{handle}/shows and /user/{handle}/shop explicitly.
  • Money is in cents, and localizedPrice follows your IP. Store price.amount / 100 with price.currency.
  • IDs are base64 Relay IDs. Decode user IDs and key on the number. Handles change.
  • Sitemaps are stale. Expect a share of 404s (4 of 14 in my samples).
  • Feeds are ranked and churn. Sort by viewers yourself, and don't infer "ended" from absence.
  • The markup will change. The parsers key on __typename and Apollo query results, which are more stable than CSS classes. If seller() throws "no profile object", look at the page again.

When DIY stops being worth it

The single-file scraper is fine for a few sellers and a category or two. It gets painful when you need page 2+ of search, a seller's full show history and reviews, or thousands of profiles a day without tripping Cloudflare.

For that I use ScrapeAtlas*, which has Whatnot endpoints with real cursor pagination. GET /v1/whatnot/search takes a query, a vertical (UNIVERSAL, LIVESTREAM, PRODUCT, USER, or CATEGORY), and a cursor, and returns 24 records per page. /v1/whatnot/profile takes a handle, user_id, or url, and there are /v1/whatnot/user/shows, /user/listings, /user/reviews, and /user/clips per seller, plus /v1/whatnot/category, /livestream, /livestream/listings, /listing, /product, and /categories. Auth is an x-api-key header, and failed requests don't cost credits.

If you only need what's on the first page, though, the DIY route above works fine.

Wrapping up

  • The official Whatnot API is a Seller API. Great for your own store, no help for market data.
  • The data is in the HTML. Apollo SSR blocks for feeds, the RSC payload for profiles and listings. No headless browser needed.
  • Be honest and slow. An honest User-Agent passed Cloudflare where a fake Chrome one didn't. Keep to one request every few seconds.
  • Know the limits. First page only, ranked feeds, prices in cents, base64 IDs, stale sitemaps.
  • Live viewers are the interesting metric. A tiny cron job gives you a category-level view of who's pulling a crowd.

What would you track on Whatnot: seller growth, prices for one card, or live viewers by category? Tell me in the comments.

*I build it.

title: FedSEAM: Federated Continual Learning of LLMs via Subspace Expert Agreement Merging
description:
arXiv:2610.33496v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks across several clients without sharing their data while retaining knowledge of earlier tasks. Sparse mixture-of-experts models support this setting by adapting selected parameters on a frozen backbone. However, clients learn different expert content as tasks evolve, making it difficult to share knowledge across clients without disrupting task-specific and client-specific specialization. Matching tile coordinates alone does not establish whether their learned content is compatible. We present FedSEAM, a federated continual learning framework that organizes task knowledge into sparse experts and selectively shares their content across tasks and clients. On each client, task-aware tile selection allocates capacity to a new task, while a subspace-based compatibility test determines which existing expert tiles to reuse and where to introduce fresh capacity. On the server, Subspace Expert Agreement Merging (SEAM) compares client updates as subspaces and moves each client towards consensus only along agreed-upon directions, leaving the rest of its update unchanged. We identify two remaining sources of forgetting, routing drift and merge erasure, and address them with three protections, one of which exactly preserves tile components in a selected prior-overlap subspace at every merge. We evaluate FedSEAM on TRACE using Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.2-3B, with component-wise ablations and studies of data size to assess its balance between learning new tasks and retaining prior knowledge.

title: BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render
description:
arXiv:2610.36371v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.

title: All-in-One: A Composable Attack on LLM Transformations
description:
arXiv:2610.33298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantization, pruning, and model merging are popular transformations applied to deployment-ready LLMs to improve efficiency and downstream performance. Recent work has shown that these transformations can introduce a security threat: an adversary can train a model that passes safety checks in its pre-transformed state, only turning malicious once it is transformed for deployment. However, prior attacks target one specific transformation (e.g., quantization) and generally rely on transformation-specific techniques, making them difficult to combine in practice. In this work, we introduce a simple, composable attack framework that targets multiple transformations simultaneously and triggers when any one of them is applied by a user. Our key insight is that the effect of each transformation can be approximated as a perturbation to the model weights, allowing us to jointly train the model with a benign loss on the original model and a malicious loss on each simulated transformed model. These perturbations are simple enough to simulate at every training iteration across diverse transformations, making them practically combinable within a single training objective, enabling a unified attack. Through extensive experiments across attack scenarios, model families, and a wide range of deployment-time model transformations, we show that our attack achieves high success rates. This demonstrates that model transformations may be utilized to trigger significantly different behavior from the original model and reinforces the associated security concerns by demonstrating that a single attack can jointly target diverse transformations.

title: 10 Production-Ready Micro-Interactions & Generative SVG Badges for Web3 Landings (Zero Deps)
description:
10 Production-Ready Micro-Interactions & Generative SVG Badges for Web3 Landings

Most modern SaaS and Web3 landing pages look identical: generic Tailwind blur gradients, uninspired hero sections, and stock component libraries. But high-converting pages stand out through tactile micro-interactions and crisp, vector-sharp generative assets.

In this guide, we dive into building high-fidelity interactive components using standard CSS variables, native DOM events, and standalone Python SVG generation — with zero heavyweight JavaScript framework dependencies.

1. The Physics-Based 3D Tilt Card (Roman Numeral Holler Card)

Rather than pulling a 50kb React spring animation library, modern browsers give us high-performance perspective transformations via CSS transform: perspective() rotateX() rotateY():

<div class="tilt-card" id="card">
  <div class="inner-glare"></div>
  <div class="card-content">
    <span class="badge">EDITION MMXXVI</span>
    <h3>Sovereign Node</h3>
    <p>Procedural cryptographic identity asset with dynamic ambient glare.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<style>
.tilt-card {
  width: 320px;
  height: 440px;
  background: linear-gradient(145deg, #18181b, #09090b);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1);
  border-radius: 20px;
  position: relative;
  transform-style: preserve-3d;
  transition: transform 0.1s ease-out;
  cursor: pointer;
}
.inner-glare {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  background: radial-gradient(circle at var(--mouse-x, 50%) var(--mouse-y, 50%), rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12), transparent 70%);
  pointer-events: none;
}
</style>

<script>
const card = document.getElementById('card');
card.addEventListener('mousemove', (e) => {
  const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();
  const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
  const y = e.clientY - rect.top;
  const cx = rect.width / 2;
  const cy = rect.height / 2;
  const rotX = ((y - cy) / cy) * -12;
  const rotY = ((x - cx) / cx) * 12;
  card.style.transform = `perspective(1000px) rotateX(${rotX}deg) rotateY(${rotY}deg) scale3d(1.02, 1.02, 1.02)`;
  card.style.setProperty('--mouse-x', `${(x / rect.width) * 100}%`);
  card.style.setProperty('--mouse-y', `${(y / rect.height) * 100}%`);
});
card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => {
  card.style.transform = 'perspective(1000px) rotateX(0deg) rotateY(0deg) scale3d(1, 1, 1)';
});
</script>

2. Procedural SVG Brandmark Generation in Python

Sharp vectors load instantly (0 HTTP network overhead when inlined) and look pristine on 4K Apple Retina screens. Here is how we generate customized geometric brandmarks on the fly:

import math

def generate_holler_badge(title: str, radius: int = 120) -> str:
    """Generates a concentric neo-brutalist SVG badge with mathematical precision."""
    cx, cy = 150, 150
    lines = []
    num_teeth = 24
    for i in range(num_teeth):
        angle = (2 * math.pi / num_teeth) * i
        x1 = cx + (radius - 12) * math.cos(angle)
        y1 = cy + (radius - 12) * math.sin(angle)
        x2 = cx + radius * math.cos(angle)
        y2 = cy + radius * math.sin(angle)
        lines.append(f'<line x1="{x1:.1f}" y1="{y1:.1f}" x2="{x2:.1f}" y2="{y2:.1f}" stroke="#10b981" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round" />')

    return f'''<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 300" width="300" height="300">
      <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#09090b" rx="24" />
      <circle cx="{cx}" cy="{cy}" r="{radius - 20}" fill="none" stroke="rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.2)" stroke-width="1" />
      {''.join(lines)}
      <text x="{cx}" y="{cy + 6}" font-family="monospace" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#f4f4f5" text-anchor="middle" letter-spacing="2">{title}</text>
    </svg>'''

# Example execution
svg_code = generate_holler_badge("VERIFIED_NODE")
with open("badge.svg", "w") as f:
    f.write(svg_code)

3. What Else is in the Production Kit?

We assembled a full library of 10 plug-and-play UI components built without framework bloat:

  1. Roman Numeral Holler Card: 3D tilt with metallic specular highlight.
  2. Neo-Brutalist Crypto Checkout Card: 1-click address copy, QR generator, network switcher.
  3. Animated Terminal Block: Typewriter command replay with copy button.
  4. Bento Spotlight Grid: Grid cards reacting to global cursor movement.
  5. Infinite Marquee Ticker: CSS hardware-accelerated continuous banner.
  6. Animated Radial Token Metric: SVG ring with live easing animations.
  7. Clean Accordion FAQ: Native <details> / <summary> with smooth height expansion.
  8. Toast Notification Engine: Micro-library for alerts under 2KB.
  9. Interactive Pricing Switcher: Monthly/Annual pricing calculator with animated toggle.
  10. Procedural SVG Generator CLI: Python script producing custom high-res assets in seconds.

title: Hierarchical Low-Rank Reparameterization for Parameter-Efficient
description:
arXiv:2610.37068v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods adapt large models by introducing a small number of trainable parameters. However, we find that these parameters still contain redundancy and can be further compressed while maintaining strong task performance. To this end, we propose a novel hierarchical low-rank reparameterization method. Its core idea is to reorganize the trainable parameters of PEFT methods into an approximately square matrix and then express it via a low-rank decomposition, which can be applied recursively. This forms a multi-level structure with factors compressed level by level, drastically reducing the number of trainable parameters. In our experiments, we combine this reparameterization with LoRA, DoRA, MoSA, and RaSA. We evaluate commonsense reasoning on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, with additional GSM8K math reasoning experiments on LLaMA-3.1-8B. Under comparable trainable-parameter budgets, our method combined with LoRA or DoRA achieves better performance. Furthermore,when the parameter count of the original methods is compressed by approximately an order of magnitude, our method can still maintain competitive task performance and even surpass the corresponding baselines in average accuracy across the eight commonsense reasoning benchmarks.

title: What Is Synthos Collective? A Plain-English Guide to the Layer 1
description:
By James Isham Williams, founder of Synthos Collective · October 28, 2026

TL;DR

Synthos Collective is an independent Layer 1 blockchain, written in Go, that has run on CometBFT consensus since October 22, 2026. Four validators with equal stake produce a block about every 12 seconds, and each block is final the moment it is committed. Two of those validators are rented servers; the other two are ordinary HP desktops in a home. The native coin is SYN, with a fixed supply of 100 billion. Synthos Collective also posts its block fingerprints to Base, so anyone can check its history against a second, independent chain.

The problem: validators live in a few data centers

A blockchain is only as independent as the machines that run it. Across the industry, a lot of validators sit with a small number of cloud and hosting companies, so one provider's outage or policy change can hit many of them at once.

Synthos Collective is built to test a different setup: validators that run on everyday hardware, next to rented servers, with no single company holding the majority. The node software needs no special rig, and a home validator connects out to the network rather than requiring open ports.

How the chain works

Synthos Collective splits the work in two. CometBFT, the consensus engine behind many Cosmos chains, orders and finalizes blocks; a Go application decides what each transaction does to balances and stakes.

  • Block time: about 12 seconds on average; when idle, the chain still makes a block at least every 10 seconds.
  • Finality: one block. Once committed, a block is never reversed.
  • Accounts: Ed25519 keys; an address is the first 20 bytes of the SHA-256 hash of the public key.
  • Joining as a validator: bond at least 10,000 SYN with a validator_bond transaction. Voting power equals the bond, and the validator set updates every 100 blocks.
  • Leaving: unbonded SYN unlocks after 86,400 blocks, about 12 days at the current pace.
  • Penalties: signing two different blocks at the same height costs 5% of the bond and permanently removes the validator.

The validator network today

Four validators secure Synthos Collective, each with 1,000,000 SYN bonded, so each holds 25% of the voting power.

Validator Machine Location Bond (SYN) Joined
hosteons-validator-1 Rented VPS Salt Lake City, US 1,000,000 Genesis, Oct 22, 2026
jim-pc-validator-1 Home desktop PC California, US 1,000,000 Genesis, Oct 22, 2026
hosteons-validator-ny-1 Rented VPS New York, US 1,000,000 Block 27,496
jim-tower-validator-4 Home HP tower California, US 1,000,000 Block 33,034

CometBFT needs more than two-thirds of the voting power to agree on every block. With four equal validators, any one of them can go offline and the other three, at 75%, keep the chain running. If two go down at the same time, block production pauses until one returns; no blocks are lost or reversed.

SYN tokenomics

SYN has a fixed supply of 100 billion, all created at genesis, and nearly half of it is earmarked for rewarding the people who run and use the network.

  • Founder vesting: 17B SYN unlocks in 10 equal yearly releases of 1.7B, each on May 29.
  • Founder launch allocation: 500M SYN at launch, for legal work, audits, infrastructure and validators.
  • Validator rewards (planned): a one-time 10,000 SYN activation reward per approved validator, then 5,000 SYN a month for uptime.
  • Staking: validators lock SYN as a bond; it stays the owner's and unlocks about 12 days after unbonding.

SYN is not listed or traded on any exchange today.

Live on Base: the SynthosAnchor contract

Synthos Collective records its block fingerprints on Base, Coinbase's Ethereum layer 2, through a small contract called SynthosAnchor. Each record stores a Synthos Collective block height, that block's hash and its state hash, so anyone can check the chain's history against a public ledger that Synthos Collective does not control.

  • Contract: 0xae4C167ff08d13CaC9b397D13c50904bb9c881a5 on Base mainnet
  • First record: Synthos Collective block 42,288, written in this transaction on October 28, 2026
  • Only one approved relayer can write, and heights must always go up, so old records can't be rewritten
  • A Synthos Collective server posts a new record automatically every hour

SYN itself is not on Base and is not traded on any exchange. The anchor proves history; it doesn't move tokens.

Honest status and what's next

Synthos Collective is live and producing blocks, but it is early. All four validators are run by the founder today, so the network is spread across machines and locations, not yet across independent operators.

Known limits right now:

  • Both home validators share one home internet connection, and both servers use the same hosting company. Either outage takes down two validators at once and pauses the chain until one is back.
  • Blocks are mostly empty; there is no outside transaction volume yet.
  • History from before the October 22 switch to CometBFT, more than 75,000 blocks from the chain's original engine, is kept on a single server.

Next up:

  1. Bring in outside node operators and validators.

title: How I Compress Website Images with Squoosh for Blazing-Fast Page Speeds
description:
Heavy, unoptimized images are one of the fastest ways to kill a website's load time and drag down your PageSpeed Insights scores. When you're building lightweight, single-file HTML templates, every asset needs to be lean.

Here is my go-to workflow for keeping images small without sacrificing visual quality:

The Squoosh Optimization Process

  1. Resolution Cap: I resize images down to a clean, crisp standard (typically 800x600 for optimal web display).
  2. Modern Formats: I convert and compress everything into AVIF and WebP formats. These formats offer incredible compression ratios compared to traditional JPEGs or PNGs.
  3. Quality Tuning: I dial in the compression settings on Squoosh.app to get file sizes down significantly while keeping details sharp.

By keeping image payloads minimal, every page loads instantly on mobile and desktop alike, keeping performance scores consistently in the 90s and 100s.

title: Spatial-Frequency Learning for Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy Image Enhancement
description:
arXiv:2610.36487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) enables the observation of atomic arrangements at sub-angstrom resolution and plays a key role in the discovery and characterization of advanced materials. Raw STEM images are often noisy and blurred due to multiple degradations. Although recent deep learning methods improve STEM images, their performance remains limited under severe degradations. In this work, we propose a spatial-frequency learning framework for STEM image enhancement. Specifically, we design a spatial-frequency fusion network that exploits periodic atomic arrangements in the frequency domain and restores local atomic details in the spatial domain. Spatial- and frequency-domain features are enhanced separately and then fused. We also present a STEM noise calibration method for synthesizing more realistic STEM images. The parameters of scan noise, pointwise noise, and background noise are estimated through statistical analysis and fitting of real STEM images. Using these calibrated parameters, we construct a diverse dataset containing a wider range of atomic arrangements, imaging modes, and degradations. Random masks combine different atomic arrangements to simulate interfaces between multiple materials. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art enhancement performance on synthetic datasets and real images of advanced materials while improving atomic localization accuracy.

title: SAGE: Saliency-Annealed Gated Encoder for Universal Vision Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.36719v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When adapting self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) to dense prediction, existing methods often treat the ViT as a passive feature extractor and may underuse the rich priors encoded in its representations, including saliency, global context, and high-frequency details. We propose SAGE (Saliency-Annealed Gated Encoder), an enhanced ViT-Adapter backbone that explicitly exploits these priors through three complementary innovations: (1) a saliency-guided architecture that extracts DINO-style class-token (CLS) saliency to guide feature gating and high-frequency enhancement, together with dynamic multi-layer aggregation and a local-detail branch; (2) an annealing-based training paradigm designed to improve convergence and feature quality during early training while reducing feature drift later in training; and (3) a two-stage, quality-aware training mechanism that smoothly transitions from focal loss to Varifocal Loss (VFL) within a single training run. Across the evaluated tasks (Fig.~\ref{fig:fig_com}), SAGE achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or competitive results on COCO (62.8 box AP and 55.3 mask AP), COCO keypoint estimation (78.5 AP), ADE20K (60.3 mIoU for semantic segmentation and 44.9 mask AP for instance segmentation), TinyImageNet classification (94.76\% Top-1 accuracy), and DIOR-R oriented object detection (78.8 AP$_{50}$). The same backbone is used across tasks, with task-specific decoders. To the best of our knowledge, SAGE is the first framework to achieve multi-task state-of-the-art results on Huawei Ascend NPUs. Code and pretrained models will be released after internal review.

title: The hard part of a no-backend collage tool wasn't the collage
description:
I built a small photo combiner that runs entirely in the browser — no upload, no server, no account. You drop in a few photos, pick a grid, drag to reposition, hit export. The collage logic took an afternoon. Keeping the exported PNG identical to what you saw on screen took the rest of the week.

Here's the thing nobody warns you about: a preview and an export are two different rendering engines, and they do not agree with each other by default.

Two engines, one layout

The preview is DOM. I lay the cells out with CSS Grid because the browser already does everything I want — 1fr columns, gap, object-fit: cover, border-radius. A few lines and it just works:

el.style.gridTemplateColumns = `repeat(${cols}, 1fr)`
box.style.gridColumnEnd = 'span ' + (cell.c || 1)
im.style.objectPosition = `${item.panX}% ${item.panY}%`

The export is Canvas. And Canvas gives you none of that. There is no object-fit, no gap, no 1fr. You get drawImage and a blank rectangle. Every bit of layout the browser did for free in the preview, you now recompute by hand so the pixels land in the same place.

So the real work is writing the Canvas version of CSS.

object-fit: cover, by hand

In CSS, object-fit: cover crops an image to fill a box without distortion. In Canvas you do it yourself by picking the right source rectangle out of the original image:

function coverRect(img, dw, dh, panX = 50, panY = 50) {
  const ir = img.naturalWidth / img.naturalHeight
  const dr = dw / dh
  let sw, sh
  if (ir > dr) {        // source is wider than the box: full height, crop sides
    sh = img.naturalHeight
    sw = sh * dr
  } else {              // full width, crop top/bottom
    sw = img.naturalWidth
    sh = sw / dr
  }
  const sx = (img.naturalWidth - sw) * (panX / 100)
  const sy = (img.naturalHeight - sh) * (panY / 100)
  return { sx, sy, sw, sh }
}

That panX / panY is the other half of it. In the preview, dragging an image inside its cell just changes object-position. In the export, the same percentage becomes an offset into the source rectangle. Same number, two completely different code paths — and if they drift, the exported photo is cropped differently from what the user framed. That bug is invisible until someone complains their cat's head got cut off.

The number that stops phones from crashing

Early on, exporting on a phone would sometimes produce a blank image or just kill the tab. Canvas has a maximum area — not width or height, total pixels — and mobile Safari's limit is lower than you'd guess. A 4x-scaled collage of big photos sails right past it and toBlob quietly hands you null.

So the export scale is capped against a pixel budget, not a dimension:

const MAX_AREA = 5e7 // 50 megapixels

function computeScale(w, h, format) {
  const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1
  if (format === 'png') {
    let r = dpr
    if (w * h * dpr * dpr > MAX_AREA) r = Math.sqrt(MAX_AREA / (w * h))
    return Math.min(r, 4)
  }
  return Math.min(dpr * 1.5, 3)
}

5e7 is a conservative ceiling that held up across the phones I tested. Render at device pixel ratio for sharpness, but the moment the canvas would exceed the budget, back off to whatever scale keeps it under. Better a slightly softer image than a blank one.

One listener set, not one per render

A smaller thing that bit me: dragging to reposition a photo needs mousemove/touchmove on window, not the element (your finger leaves the box). My first version attached those listeners inside the render function. Every re-render stacked another set. After a dozen edits the page had dozens of live listeners all firing.

The fix is boring and correct: register the move/up listeners once at module load, and keep a single active object describing whatever is currently being dragged. Render swaps the data, not the listeners.

Why no backend at all

I could have thrown this on a server and done the compositing with an image library. I didn't, and not only to save money. Photos are personal. "Combine your pictures" and "upload your pictures to my server" are very different promises, and the second one is a liability I don't want. Everything here — decode, draw, toBlob, download — happens in the tab. Close it and nothing of yours was ever anywhere else. URL.createObjectURL on the blob, click a hidden <a download>, revoke the URL a second later. No request leaves the machine.

It also turns out to be the simpler architecture once you accept the constraint. No uploads to rate-limit, no temp files to garbage-collect, no abuse surface. The whole thing is static files on a CDN.

If you want to see the end result it's at Photo Combiner — grid, long-image and side-by-side layouts, all client-side. Happy to answer anything about the Canvas side in the comments.

title: How we cut CDN metadata lookup latency by 91%
description:
Every request to Vercel passes through our CDN, which executes on average over 80 million routing instructions per second. Part of that work is looking up metadata to determine which paths exist and how to serve them. When that metadata isn’t cached, the CDN has to fetch it before it can serve the response.

We used to fetch and cache metadata one path at a time, retrieving only what each lookup needed. That seemed efficient at the time, but large deployments can contain hundreds of thousands of paths, each with its own cache entry. Every new deployment introduced fresh metadata, making cache misses a recurring cost for large sites that deployed frequently.

Fetching more metadata at once made these lookups faster. By grouping paths together, each fetch could populate the cache for many subsequent lookups. But fetching too much introduced its own costs. Through production experiments, we found a balance that cut P99 metadata lookup latency by 91% and made deployments faster along the way.

How the CDN finds the right route

The path in a request doesn’t always match the path of the content or function that serves it. Framework routing rules connect the two. A request for /blog/hello-world, for example, might resolve to the dynamic route /blog/[slug]. A request for that page’s React Server Component payload might resolve to /blog/[slug].rsc. As the CDN applies these rules, it may need to check several target paths to find the right response.

The framework describes those routes during a build. With framework-defined infrastructure, application code declares which outputs are static, which need Functions, and which responses can be cached or regenerated. Frameworks translate that intent into Build Output API outputs, and Vercel generates the routing metadata the CDN reads.

At request time, the CDN needs to determine which target paths exist and retrieve their metadata. The Bloom filters we added to global routing rule out paths that definitely don’t exist. Remaining paths need an exact metadata lookup.

Originally, we stored that metadata as a separate object per target path. The CDN fetched and cached each object independently. This worked well for smaller projects that deployed infrequently. But every new deployment created a fresh set of cache keys, so the first lookup for each path missed the cache.

Fetching metadata in groups

To reduce cache misses, we grouped metadata for many paths into files called shards. We bounded each shard’s size to control how much data a lookup had to fetch. Fetching a shard brought metadata for all of its paths into the cache, so later lookups for those paths could reuse it.

Each shard also included an index that let the CDN locate an individual path’s metadata without decoding, decompressing, or parsing the other entries. Each fetch warmed many paths, while each lookup still parsed only the record it needed.

Fetching more without parsing more

We built the shards using JSONL layouts already used for other large routing datasets at Vercel. JSONL stores one JSON value per line. We borrowed the sorted, alternating key-value records from Bulk Redirects and the directly addressable Base64 data structures we first built for our Bloom filters.

We kept the data layout separate from the lookup structures over it, so each workload can pick the properties it needs:

  • Inspectable, sorted key-value JSONL records with random access

  • Optional inline indexes for low-overhead binary search

  • Embedded Base64 data with offset-based decoding

  • Bounded shards that control transfer and cache costs

Each shard stores sorted target paths and their metadata as alternating JSONL records. An inline index records where each entry begins, so the routing process can jump directly to it. These positions are stored as fixed-width pointers. Each pointer is a whole number of six-bit Base64 characters, so any single pointer can be decoded in place without first parsing the index line as JSON or decoding the complete Base64 string.

As with Bulk Redirects, the first metadata fetch for a deployment already identifies which shard holds a given path, so selecting the shard adds no extra round trip.

Within that shard, the routing process uses the index pointers to binary-search the encoded paths. Finding a path takes O(log n) pointer reads and string comparisons. Once it finds a match, it parses the metadata value on the next line. The rest of the shard remains unparsed.

Finding the right shard size in production

We initially hoped the path metadata for most deployments would fit in a single shard. Because the index and binary search kept parsing cheap, we started with multi-megabyte shards.

Large shards only made sense if they stayed cached close to the request. Each routing process keeps a small least-recently-used (LRU) cache of recent shards in memory, in front of a larger cache shared by every process in the region. With only a few shards per deployment, we expected LRU hits most of the time, which would offset the cost of transferring larger shards.

In testing, the regional cache hit rate was high but the LRU hit rate was low, because requests were spread across many processes in each region. Transferring the multi-megabyte shards also cost more than we expected.

We settled on shards of about 200 KB, which kept the regional cache hit rate high and made LRU misses cheap to fill.

Production measurements showed lower average and P99 lookup latency:

Metadata lookup metric

Before: per-path metadata

After: indexed shards

Improvement

P99 latency

215.8 ms

19.1 ms

91% lower

Average latency

8.59 ms

1.81 ms

79% lower

Standard deviation

44.9 ms

19.0 ms

58% lower

Shrinking shards further wasn't worth the rollout

Putting fewer entries in each shard lowered transfer cost but raised the shard count. We also evaluated shrinking shards without increasing their number by encoding the same entries more compactly. We tested three approaches:

  • Front-coding the sorted paths so each stores only what differs from the last.

  • Splitting the shard into JSONL documents that deduplicate metadata.

  • Using a more compact custom serialization format.

Offline simulations measured both encoded size and lookup cost.

Each approach produced much smaller shards, but the simulations predicted only modest latency gains. We decided the extra encoding, compatibility, and rollout work wasn't worth it for this migration. When another workload makes more indexing or compression worth the effort, it will go into the shared library.

Changing routing safely

The CDN runs this lookup on requests to every deployment. If the sharded metadata disagreed with the per-path metadata, we would serve a stale route, a wrong status code, or a 404 for a path that exists.

We checked for that disagreement offline first, then in production. Offline, we built test deployments and ran a harness over them that looked up every path both ways and compared the answers.

In production, behind a feature flag, the routing system did both lookups on a random sample of requests while still serving the old result. It compared the new result against the old one in the background, and we watched for mismatches over several weeks without slowing production requests. We called this shadow mode.

Shadow mode found differences, and they were extremely rare. One was a bug in the old encoding, which packed paths into RFC 2047 encoded words to fit non-ASCII text into ASCII-only fields, and only showed up when an emoji was split across two words. The new format stores paths as plain UTF-8, so the bug can't happen there. Catching this edge case increased our confidence in the comparison, so we started letting the shards serve production traffic.

Faster builds

Once the shards were serving production, we went back to the build pipeline and removed the work they had made redundant:

  • Skipping the per-path metadata upload saves about 9.7 seconds.

  • Writing route group metadata into the manifest saves about 4.5 seconds.

  • Not uploading the files those two changes left empty saves about 2.4 seconds.

Together those save roughly 16.6 seconds. Across all deployments, the deploy step is about 10% faster, and for metadata-heavy deployments, where these steps dominate, we estimate closer to 25%.

Faster routing for your next deployment

Faster metadata lookups improved route resolution as a whole. For large sites, P99 route resolution is now roughly twice as fast. On our own marketing and docs sites, P99 metadata lookup latency fell from 203 ms to 31 ms. Median metadata lookup latency stayed around 0.7 ms.

The application’s Build Output API contract stayed the same. Frameworks still describe what the application needs, while Vercel improves how the CDN serves it.

Deployments built after July 17, 2026 already use the new metadata shards. For an older deployment, redeploy your project to pick up the faster lookups.

title: ETAMem: Decoupling and Aligning Heterogeneous Memory for Long-Term Conversational Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.37443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-term memory enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain coherent and personalized interactions across extended conversations. However, existing memory systems face two key challenges: (1) Information Entanglement, where heterogeneous information is mixed within coarse-grained memory units; and (2) Organizational Mismatch, where memory structures based primarily on semantic similarity may overlook other associations. To address these challenges, we propose ETAMem, a multi-view memory framework that decouples heterogeneous conversational information and aligns memory representations and organization with its distinct characteristics. Specifically, heterogeneous information parsing extracts atomic memory units and identifies affective information. View-specific memory structuring then organizes these units into three complementary hierarchical views: Event, Affect, and Time. ETAMem incrementally maintains memory structures with adaptively calibrated thresholds. For retrieval, entropy-based retrieval allocates query-specific budgets across views and performs hierarchical search within each view. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that ETAMem outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving relative accuracy improvements of 12.46% and 7.96%, respectively, while maintaining competitive token efficiency. Further analyses demonstrate the complementary benefits of different memory views.

title: Extracting invoice fields with validation: what auto-posts and what goes to a human
description:
Pulling an invoice number or a total out of text is the easy half of the job. The useful half is deciding, for every field of every document, whether it goes straight into the accounting system or lands on a person's desk. Here is how a small demo handles it. Everything below is test data from a public synthetic dataset, not a client result.

What the demo does

Input: the OCR text of an invoice. Output: invoice number, date, IBAN and gross total, each with a confidence. Fields with low confidence are routed to a human instead of being posted.

The data is mychen76/invoices-and-receipts_ocr_v1: OCR text plus ground-truth fields. The invoices are synthetic with a fixed layout, and only the invoice-type documents are used (484 of about 2,200; the rest are receipts with a different schema).

Candidates first, then a ranker

For each field the code generates candidates with patterns, then a small logistic regression picks the right one using context: the words around the candidate, its position, its format. This matters most for the total, because an invoice contains many amounts (net, tax, line items, gross) and "the biggest number" is not the answer.

Validation beats confidence for IBANs

For IBANs the demo does not trust a score at all. It validates the ISO 13616 checksum. If OCR confused one character (S for 5, O for 0, a dropped or doubled character) and exactly one repair makes the checksum pass, it applies the repair. If no unique valid value exists, the field goes to a human.

def iban_ok(s: str) -> bool:
    s = s.replace(" ", "").upper()
    rearranged = s[4:] + s[:4]
    digits = "".join(str(int(c, 36)) for c in rearranged)
    return int(digits) % 97 == 1

A checksum is a hard gate a model cannot talk its way past.

Results on 74 held-out documents (test data)

Field Docs scored Accuracy when automated Automated share
Invoice number 74 100% 97.3%
Invoice date 74 100% 100%
IBAN 56 100% 100%
Gross total 74 98.6% 100%

96.4% of clean documents were fully automated (all four fields), and 98.2% of those had every field correct. Thresholds were tuned on a validation split for a 98% target; the held-out set was used for reporting only.

Honest caveats

  • 74 documents with a fixed synthetic layout is a small, friendly test. Real, varied invoices will score lower, and a pilot starts by measuring on the client's own sample.
  • In 18 of the 74 documents the dataset's IBAN label itself fails the checksum while the OCR text passes it, so the label is corrupted. Those are excluded from the IBAN score and counted separately in results.json. Check your ground truth before blaming the model.
  • The input is OCR text. Turning scans and PDFs into that text is a separate, replaceable step.

Takeaways

  1. Decide per field what is allowed to auto-post, with a number as the bar.
  2. Use deterministic validation (checksums, date ranges, sum checks) wherever it exists.
  3. Route what you cannot validate to a human, and make that route cheap.
  4. Audit your labels before you measure.

title: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.36623v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.

title: Implicit Beliefs as Scalable Process Rewards for Strategic Persuasion
description:
arXiv:2610.33527v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) for multi-turn strategic persuasion faces two coupled obstacles: (i) realistic simulation of psychologically grounded persuadees, and (ii) dense, faithful supervision for credit assignment in strategic dialogues. Outcome-only rewards are sparse and uninformative about which conversational moves drove success, while LLM-judge process rewards are expensive and decoupled from the underlying interaction dynamics. We address both challenges with a unified framework. First, we introduce PersuArena, a persuasion simulation environment that produces realistic, non-monotonic trajectories. Second, building directly on this environment, we propose Process Rewards via Online Belief Elicitation for Relative Policy Optimization (Probe-RPO), an online RL framework that converts the persuadee's internal state into dense process rewards. At each turn, three introspective probes are read from the frozen persuadee's logits, yielding a multi-dimensional reward signal that is faithfully aligned with persuasion dynamics. With extensive experiments on PersuArena spanning healthcare, financial advising, workplace management, education, and personal relationships, we demonstrate that our Probe-RPO achieves the full acceptance rate of 52.5%, compared with the 35.8% for the strongest GRPO ablation and 25.8% for the best off-the-shelf LLM. We also conduct comprehensive analyses on the generalization across persuadee models and the persuasion dynamics across conversations. Our work offers a promising paradigm that can provide effective process supervision for strategic dialogue.

title: Why We Built Bundler on Native Shopify Functions (Not Theme Code Hacks)
description:
Why We Built Bundler on Native Shopify Functions (Not Theme Code Hacks)

A lot of bundle and discount apps on the Shopify App Store still calculate pricing client-side and inject it via JavaScript — which works until Shopify changes something about checkout, and then it quietly stops working. We built Bundler differently on purpose.

🩹 The Old Way: Client-Side Discount Injection

JavaScript-based discount apps calculate the bundle price in the browser and try to apply it before or during checkout — a pattern that's fragile by design, since it depends on checkout's DOM structure staying stable, which Shopify doesn't guarantee.

⚡ What Shopify Functions Actually Changes

Functions run server-side, compiled to WebAssembly, directly inside Shopify's checkout logic — not bolted on after the fact. The discount is calculated and applied as a native part of the order, which means it survives theme changes, checkout updates, and works identically across every sales channel, not just the storefront.

🛡️ What This Means for Merchants Day to Day

No "the discount stopped working after we updated our theme" support tickets, no checkout extension conflicts with other apps, and no risk of the discount silently failing to apply at checkout even though it showed correctly on the product page.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: Deterministic Safety: Bounding AI Agents with DMN Engines
description:
As Large Language Model (LLM) agents transition from passive informational assistants to active autonomous decision nodes in core banking architectures, financial institutions face a critical governance challenge: The Stochastic Vulnerability of Generative AI.

While autonomous agents excel at reasoning across unstructured trade documents, parsing customer dispute histories, and recommending exception overrides, their underlying execution model is inherently probabilistic. Prompt engineering, system instructions, and temperature tuning reduce—but never eliminate—the risk of model hallucination, parameter drift, or prompt injection attacks. In a Tier-1 banking environment, an unconstrained AI agent that recommends an invalid $500,000 credit line increase or waives a mandatory Anti-Money Laundering (AML) verification check creates immediate compliance and financial liability.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms eliminate non-deterministic operational risk through the Hybrid AI-DMN Safety Pattern. This pattern mandates that autonomous AI agents never possess direct execution authority over financial transactions. Instead, AI agents act strictly as Proposal Generators, whose outputs are intercepted, validated, and clamped by deterministic Decision Model and Notation (DMN 1.3) engines running on Flowable DMN before any state mutation can occur.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain Guardrail Mapping

In a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) topology, financial and operational risk parameters vary across service domains. The hybrid AI-DMN guardrail pattern assigns specific DMN policy enforcement mechanisms based on domain criticality.

BIAN Service Domain AI Agent Scope Proposed AI Output Deterministic DMN Guardrail Hit Policy Guardrail Action
Consumer Advice Product eligibility & rate matching Recommended APR & fee waiver Max fee waiver cap & APR floor table FIRST (F) Clamp / Hard Override
Credit Assessment Commercial credit exception scoring Proposed credit limit adjustment Debt-to-Income ($DTI$) hard cap & regulatory ceiling UNIQUE (U) Reject & Escalate to Human
Payment Execution FX surcharge exception handling Dynamic FX spread reduction Tiered currency spread floor matrix COLLECT (MIN) Enforce Minimum Spread
Fraud Evaluation False positive transaction triage Recommended hold release Historical transaction anomaly threshold ANY (A) Reject / Require Dual Sign-Off
Customer Onboarding Identity verification exception review Document validation pass/fail Regulatory KYC risk score matrix UNIQUE (U) Hard Compliance Rejection

The Hybrid AI-DMN Safety Architecture

The core tenet of Deterministic Safety is the separation of Probabilistic Suggestion from Deterministic Execution.

An AI agent analyzes complex inputs and constructs a structured proposal payload. This payload is passed into a stateless Flowable DMN Engine, which evaluates the proposal against versioned, business-approved decision tables.

                              HYBRID AI-DMN SAFETY TOPOLOGY

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | PROBABILISTIC LAYER (Non-Deterministic AI Agent)                                |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  Unstructured Data / Event ---> [ LLM Agent Reasoning Loop ]                    |
  +--------------------------------------------------|------------------------------+
                                                     |
                                            1. Generates Dynamic Proposal Payload
                                               (e.g., Proposed Limit: $75,000)
                                                     |
                                                     v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | DETERMINISTIC GUARDRAIL LAYER (Flowable DMN Engine)                             |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  |  | Flowable DMN Decision Table                                               |  |
  |  |                                                                           |  |
  |  |  Input: { ProposedLimit: $75,000, RiskTier: "TIER_2", MaxAllowed: $50,000 }|  |
  |  |  Evaluation: Rule Violated (ProposedLimit > MaxAllowed)                   |  |
  |  |  Output: { Status: "CLAMPED", FinalLimit: $50,000, Escalation: false }     |  |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  +--------------------------------------------------|------------------------------+
                                                     |
                                            2. Evaluates & Clamps Proposal
                                                     |
                                                     v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TRANSACTIONAL EXECUTION LAYER (Temporal Saga / Microservice)                    |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Execute Ledger Mutation with Guardrailed Payload: $50,000 ]                  |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Safety Execution Lifecycle

  1. Proposal Generation: The AI Agent receives an operational task, executes internal reasoning tools, and outputs a structured JSON proposal containing its recommended actions and confidence metrics.
  2. Deterministic Interception: A Spring Boot application service intercepts the AI proposal before invoking any transaction API or downstream Temporal Saga.
  3. DMN Guardrail Evaluation: The proposal parameters (along with verified customer facts retrieved directly from core databases) are injected into the Flowable DMN Engine.
  4. Enforcement Execution:
  5. PASSED: The proposed payload falls within legal policy parameters and proceeds to execution.
  6. CLAMPED: The proposal exceeds non-critical limits (e.g., requested fee discount is too high); the DMN engine automatically clamps the value to the maximum permissible threshold.
  7. REJECTED / ESCALATED: The proposal violates strict regulatory or risk boundaries; the execution path is halted, and control is routed to a human compliance officer.

Mathematical Reliability & Safety Probability

By introducing a deterministic DMN guardrail between the stochastic AI agent and the financial database, the composite system safety probability Psafe-execution​ moves from probabilistic uncertainty to absolute deterministic boundary control.

Let Pagent-valid​ be the probability that an LLM agent generates a correct, non-hallucinated proposal, and Pdmn-coverage​ be the coverage completeness of the DMN rule table. The overall safety probability of the system is defined as:

Psafe-execution​=Pagent-valid​+(1−Pagent-valid​)×Pdmn-guard-block​

Where Pdmn-guard-block​ is the probability that the DMN engine successfully catches and intercepts an out-of-bounds or hallucinated proposal:

Pdmn-guard-block​=1−Prule-omission​

Because DMN 1.3 tables are exhaustively verifiable for completeness and overlap using automated static analysis, Prule-omission​→0 , guaranteeing that even if Pagent-valid​ drops during model degradation, Psafe-execution​≈1.0 for all defined financial boundaries.

Technical Implementation: Flowable DMN Guardrail Integration

1. DMN 1.3 Decision Table Definition (ai-credit-override-guardrail.dmn)

The DMN table below evaluates an AI agent's proposed credit limit override for a commercial account. It enforces hard ceiling caps based on verified internal customer risk tiers and flags required human sign-offs.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<definitions xmlns="https://www.omg.org/spec/DMN/20191111/MODEL/"
             xmlns:flowable="http://flowable.org/dmn"
             id="definitions_ai_credit_guardrail"
             name="AI Credit Override Guardrail"
             namespace="http://xenon.banking/dmn/safety">

  <decision id="aiCreditOverrideGuardrail" name="AI Credit Limit Override Guardrail">
    <decisionTable id="decisionTable_ai_guardrail" hitPolicy="FIRST">

      <!-- Inputs from AI Proposal and Core DB -->
      <input id="input_1" label="Customer Risk Tier">
        <inputExpression id="inputExpression_1" typeRef="string">
          <text>customerRiskTier</text>
        </inputExpression>
      </input>

      <input id="input_2" label="AI Proposed Credit Limit">
        <inputExpression id="inputExpression_2" typeRef="number">
          <text>proposedLimit</text>
        </inputExpression>
      </input>

      <input id="input_3" label="AI Agent Confidence Score">
        <inputExpression id="inputExpression_3" typeRef="number">
          <text>agentConfidenceScore</text>
        </inputExpression>
      </input>

      <!-- Outputs -->
      <output id="output_1" label="Guardrail Decision" name="guardrailDecision" typeRef="string" />
      <output id="output_2" label="Sanitized Credit Limit" name="sanitizedLimit" typeRef="number" />
      <output id="output_3" label="Require Human Review" name="requireHumanReview" typeRef="boolean" />
      <output id="output_4" label="Policy Violation Reason" name="violationReason" typeRef="string" />

      <!-- Rule 1: Reject low-confidence AI proposals instantly -->
      <rule id="rule_1">
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_1_1"><text>-</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_2_1"><text>-</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_3_1"><text>< 0.85</text></inputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_1_1"><text>"REJECTED"</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_2_1"><text>0.00</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_3_1"><text>true</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_4_1"><text>"AI agent confidence score below threshold (0.85)."</text></outputEntry>
      </rule>

      <!-- Rule 2: High Risk Tier - Absolute Cap at $25,000. Clamp if exceeded. -->
      <rule id="rule_2">
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_1_2"><text>"HIGH_RISK"</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_2_2"><text>> 25000</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_3_2"><text>>= 0.85</text></inputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_1_2"><text>"CLAMPED"</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_2_2"><text>25000.00</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_3_2"><text>true</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_4_2"><text>"Proposed limit exceeded HIGH_RISK tier maximum cap ($25,000)."</text></outputEntry>
      </rule>

      <!-- Rule 3: Medium Risk Tier - Absolute Cap at $100,000. Clamp if exceeded. -->
      <rule id="rule_3">
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_1_3"><text>"MEDIUM_RISK"</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_2_3"><text>> 100000</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_3_3"><text>>= 0.85</text></inputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_1_3"><text>"CLAMPED"</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_2_3"><text>100000.00</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_3_3"><text>false</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_4_3"><text>"Proposed limit clamped to MEDIUM_RISK policy cap ($100,000)."</text></outputEntry>
      </rule>

      <!-- Rule 4: Standard Approval Pass-Through -->
      <rule id="rule_4">
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_1_4"><text>-</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_2_4"><text>-</text></inputEntry>
        <inputEntry id="inputEntry_3_4"><text>>= 0.85</text></inputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_1_4"><text>"PASSED"</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_2_4"><text>proposedLimit</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_3_4"><text>false</text></outputEntry>
        <outputEntry id="outputEntry_4_4"><text>"NONE"</text></outputEntry>
      </rule>

    </decisionTable>
  </decision>
</definitions>

2. Spring Boot Guardrail Interceptor Service (Java 21)

This application service receives the AI agent's raw recommendation, executes the Flowable DMN Engine synchronously, and enforces the resulting sanitized bounds.

package com.xenon.banking.ai.guardrail;

import org.flowable.dmn.api.DmnDecisionService;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public record AiProposalPayload(
        String customerId,
        String customerRiskTier,
        double proposedCreditLimit,
        double agentConfidenceScore,
        String agentReasoning
) {}

public record GuardrailedExecutionPayload(
        String customerId,
        String executionStatus, // "PASSED", "CLAMPED", "REJECTED"
        double finalApprovedLimit,
        boolean requiresHumanReview,
        String violationReason,
        String originalAgentReasoning
) {}

@Service
public class AiDecisionGuardrailService {

    private final DmnDecisionService dmnDecisionService;

    public AiDecisionGuardrailService(DmnDecisionService dmnDecisionService) {
        this.dmnDecisionService = dmnDecisionService;
    }

    public GuardrailedExecutionPayload sanitizeAgentProposal(AiProposalPayload proposal) {
        // 1. Prepare Fact Environment for DMN Engine
        Map<String, Object> inputVariables = new HashMap<>();
        inputVariables.put("customerRiskTier", proposal.customerRiskTier());
        inputVariables.put("proposedLimit", proposal.proposedCreditLimit());
        inputVariables.put("agentConfidenceScore", proposal.agentConfidenceScore());

        // 2. Execute Flowable DMN Decision Table synchronously
        Map<String, Object> dmnResult = dmnDecisionService.createExecutionBuilder()
                .decisionKey("aiCreditOverrideGuardrail")
                .variables(inputVariables)
                .executeWithSingleResult();

        if (dmnResult == null || dmnResult.isEmpty()) {
            // Safety Fail-Closed: If DMN execution fails, default to total rejection
            return new GuardrailedExecutionPayload(
                    proposal.customerId(),
                    "REJECTED",
                    0.00,
                    true,
                    "CRITICAL: DMN Guardrail engine failed to return execution result.",
                    proposal.agentReasoning()
            );
        }

        // 3. Extract Sanitized Output Parameters
        String guardrailDecision = (String) dmnResult.get("guardrailDecision");
        double sanitizedLimit = ((Number) dmnResult.get("sanitizedLimit")).doubleValue();
        boolean requireHumanReview = (Boolean) dmnResult.get("requireHumanReview");
        String violationReason = (String) dmnResult.get("violationReason");

        // 4. Construct Final Guardrailed Execution Context
        return new GuardrailedExecutionPayload(
                proposal.customerId(),
                guardrailDecision,
                sanitizedLimit,
                requireHumanReview,
                violationReason,
                proposal.agentReasoning()
        );
    }
}

Operational Guardrail Patterns: Clamping, Escalation, and Rejection

When an AI agent's proposal triggers a DMN rule violation, the system handles the exception deterministically based on three core architectural patterns:

                                GUARDRAIL EXCEPTION PATTERNS

                    +------------------------------------------+
                    | AI Agent Proposal Input Payload          |
                    +--------------------+---------------------+
                                         |
                                         v
                    +--------------------+---------------------+
                    | Flowable DMN Engine Evaluation           |
                    +----+---------------+---------------+-----+
                         |               |               |
        [ Outcome 1 ]    | [ Outcome 2 ] | [ Outcome 3 ] |
        Proposal Passed  | Clamped Limit | Policy Reject |
                         |               |               |
                         v               v               v
                +----------------+ +-----------+ +-----------------+
                | Direct Machine | | Execute   | | Suspend & Route |
                | Saga Execution | | Clamped   | | to Human User   |
                |                | | Value     | | Task (Flowable) |
                +----------------+ +-----------+ +-----------------+

1. The Clamping Pattern (Value Bounding)

If the AI agent suggests an action that is conceptually valid but numerically excessive (e.g., an dynamic FX rate discount of 1.5% when maximum policy allows 0.5%), the DMN engine mutates the execution variable to the maximum policy boundary (0.5%). The transaction proceeds without breaking operational velocity, while an audit event logs the clamping action.

2. The Human Escalation Pattern (Flowable BPMN Hand-off)

If the AI agent proposes an exception on an account flagged as HIGH_RISK, or if the agent's internal confidence score falls below policy threshold ($< 0.85$), the DMN engine sets requireHumanReview = true. The system suspends automatic processing and instantiates a native Flowable BPMN User Task, routing the AI proposal and DMN violation audit log to a senior human underwriter.

3. Hard Policy Rejection (Fail-Closed)

If an AI agent attempts an action that violates zero-tolerance regulatory rules (such as waiving a mandatory sanction screening step), the DMN engine returns a hard REJECTED status. The transaction halts instantly, preventing the downstream Temporal Saga from initializing.

Observability, Regulatory Lineage, and Auditability

Financial regulators (such as OCC, EBA, and MAS) require full explainability for every automated decision, especially when AI models are involved. Storing only the LLM's prompt and completion logs is insufficient because prompt completions do not prove that policy guardrails were enforced at runtime.

Enterprise Safety Audit Event Schema

For every AI proposal processed through the guardrail service, an immutable compliance audit record is written to the centralized log stream (Kafka / Elastic Search), binding the AI context to the DMN execution result:

{
  "eventId": "AUDIT-SAFE-2026-880192",
  "correlationId": "BIAN-CRED-2026-44012",
  "bianDomain": "CreditAssessment",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:01:00Z",
  "aiAgentMetadata": {
    "modelId": "xenon-risk-agent-v3",
    "promptHash": "a8f92b...3c11",
    "rawProposedLimit": 75000.00,
    "confidenceScore": 0.91,
    "agentReasoning": "Strong cash flow history over 12 months justifies limit increase."
  },
  "dmnGuardrailMetadata": {
    "decisionKey": "aiCreditOverrideGuardrail",
    "decisionTableVersion": "v2026.2.0",
    "evaluatedHitPolicy": "FIRST",
    "ruleMatched": "rule_2",
    "guardrailOutcome": "CLAMPED",
    "enforcedFinalLimit": 25000.00,
    "violationReason": "Proposed limit exceeded HIGH_RISK tier maximum cap ($25,000)."
  },
  "executionTrace": {
    "downstreamSagaTriggered": true,
    "sagaExecutionId": "SAGA-CREDIT-77019",
    "humanOverrideRequired": true
  }
}

Combining stochastic AI reasoning with deterministic Flowable DMN engines solves the core AI adoption dilemma in enterprise banking. By relegating Large Language Model agents to proposal generation and enforcing absolute financial and regulatory boundaries via DMN 1.3 decision tables, core banking platforms achieve advanced operational automation without compromising system safety, financial predictability, or regulatory compliance across BIAN service domains.

title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision-Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation
description:
arXiv:2610.35910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.
