title: I tried to reproduce four Collective2 Calmar ratios. None of them matched.
description:
I spent an evening recomputing the headline statistics on four Collective2 strategy pages. The profit factors mostly hold up. The Calmar ratios do not — none of the four.

This is not a fraud hunt. It is a reproducibility check, the same one I would run on any backtest: take the numbers a page publishes, recompute the derived metrics from them, and see whether they agree.

The two definitions I used

  • Calmar ratio = annualized return ÷ maximum drawdown
  • Profit factor = (win % × average win) ÷ ((1 − win %) × average loss)

Both are standard. If a page shows all five inputs, its Calmar and profit factor are arithmetic, not opinion.

Results

Four pages had complete summary blocks on 2026-10-27 (twelve candidates were listed, nine fetched; five showed all-zero stats and were excluded as inactive).

Strategy Annual return Max DD Calmar (page) Calmar (recomputed) page ÷ recomputed
131145247 32.4% 14.1% 3.52 2.30 1.53×
132169961 22.3% 31.8% 0.95 0.70 1.35×
146455121 56.9% 29.7% 2.76 1.92 1.44×
146649042 22.8% 13.4% 2.06 1.70 1.21×

Profit factor on the same pages:

Strategy PF (page) PF (recomputed) Difference
131145247 1.50 1.46 +2.8%
132169961 2.70 2.35 +14.8%
146455121 3.10 3.03 +2.4%
146649042 1.70 1.69 +0.9%

What I take from it

1. The summary blocks are mostly coherent. Three of four profit factors land within 3% — rounding level. That is what a well-formed summary looks like. It also means the pages are not sloppy in general, which makes the Calmar result more interesting, not less.

2. The Calmar overshoot is not a constant. 1.21× to 1.53×. If the platform used one different definition consistently, you would see a roughly fixed multiplier. You do not. So it is not "Calmar but annualized monthly" or "Calmar but with a rolling drawdown" — or if it is, the effect varies by strategy in a way the page never tells you.

3. One page fails both checks. 132169961's profit factor is 14.8% above what its own win rate and average win/loss imply. Either one input is stale, or the profit factor is computed over a different trade set than the other fields. Same page, same summary block.

4. The practical problem is comparability, not honesty. If two strategies both show Calmar 2.0, nothing on the page tells you they were computed the same way. Ranking subscriptions by that number is ranking by a quantity whose definition you cannot see. The same applies to any platform metric you cannot recompute.

What this does not say

  • It does not say any seller is lying. The likeliest explanation is a platform-side definition difference — the profit-factor check mostly passing is evidence for that.
  • I had no trade-level data and no equity curve. So I cannot say which field is wrong, and I cannot recompute max drawdown independently.
  • I did not determine what Collective2's Calmar actually uses. That needs the equity series, which these pages do not expose publicly.
  • Nothing here is a claim about future performance.

Reproduce it

The checker is four rows of published fields and a handful of divisions:

ROWS = [
    # id, ann_ret_pct, max_dd_pct, pf_page, win_pct, avg_win, avg_loss, calmar_page
    ("131145247", 32.4, 14.1, 1.50, 35.6, 903.0, 342.0, 3.52),
    ("132169961", 22.3, 31.8, 2.70, 58.0, 315.0, 185.0, 0.95),
]

for sid, ann, dd, pf_page, win, aw, al, cal_page in ROWS:
    cal_calc = ann / dd
    w = win / 100.0
    pf_calc = (w * aw) / ((1 - w) * al)
    print(sid, cal_page / cal_calc, pf_page / pf_calc - 1)

Full script and tables: backtest-audit-kit/audits.

Why I published this

If you are paying a monthly fee for a strategy, the headline ratio is part of what you are buying. It costs one afternoon to check whether that ratio can be recomputed from the page that advertises it. If it cannot, ask the seller which definition produced it — and treat "whatever the platform shows" as an answer.

Scope: verified — the arithmetic relationship between six summary fields on four public pages on 2026-10-27. Not verified — trade-level accuracy, drawdown computation, equity curve, platform metric definitions, future returns. No strategy seller was contacted.

title: 25 Million Records Later: Why Your RAG Pipeline Still Isn't Production-Ready
description:
25 million records. Distributed GPUs. Two vector databases. And still, the most difficult part of production RAG is not embedding generation.

A RAG prototype is easy to demo:

PDF → chunks → embeddings → vector DB → LLM → answer

But production is where the questions change.

What if a policy PDF is revised after it has been indexed? What if an ingestion worker retries the same batch? What if a user from Tenant A retrieves a chunk owned by Tenant B? What if the vector index returns a confident but obsolete paragraph?

Those failures do not disappear by adding GPUs.

I recently revisited AWS's article, Build a RAG data ingestion pipeline for large-scale ML workloads, published March 13, 2024. It is an interesting, substantial experiment. This article examines what it gets right, what it does not establish, and how I would extend the design for production.

What AWS actually built

AWS demonstrates a batch ETL pipeline:

OSCAR JSONL corpus
        ↓
AWS Glue → Parquet on S3
        ↓
Ray cluster on GPU-backed EC2
        ↓
Chunking + all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings
        ↓
       ┌────────────┴─────────────┐
       ↓                          ↓
OpenSearch (HNSW)        RDS PostgreSQL + pgvector (IVF)
       └────────────┬─────────────┘
                    ↓
           Simulated retrieval queries

The original OSCAR corpus is described as approximately 609 million records; AWS uses a 25-million-record subset for the experiment. It reports a Ray setup of five g4dn.12xlarge instances, each with four NVIDIA T4 GPUs, and the all-mpnet-base-v2 model producing 768-dimensional embeddings. These are details from the AWS experiment, not results from my own benchmark.

The key idea is sound: if embedding generation is your bottleneck, parallelizing that workload is more useful than simply tuning the vector database.

Three things this architecture gets right

1. It separates bulk data preparation from embedding generation

Converting large JSONL datasets to Parquet before distributed processing is a sensible design choice. Columnar formats can reduce I/O overhead and make batch reads more efficient.

2. It treats embeddings as a distributed compute problem

Embedding generation can be GPU-bound. Ray makes it possible to distribute work rather than feeding a large corpus through one long-running Python process. It also exposes execution telemetry.

3. It compares two different retrieval-store approaches

OpenSearch, with HNSW indexing, and PostgreSQL with pgvector, using an IVF index in this experiment, represent different operational trade-offs.

Neither is automatically 'better.'

Choose based on data size, filtering requirements, query patterns, operational expertise, recall targets, costs, and workload isolation—not benchmark headlines alone.

Where the experiment stops and production engineering starts

This is an ingestion and vector-store experiment, not a complete architecture for document governance, secure multitenancy, and reliable knowledge updates. That distinction matters.

Missing gate #1: Incremental ingestion and deletes

Large batch ingestion is one problem. Keeping the knowledge base correct on Tuesday after someone changes a document on Monday is another.

A practical ingestion contract should include:

{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-123",
  "document_id": "policy-456",
  "source_version": "v7",
  "content_hash": "sha256:...",
  "embedding_model_version": "model-v2",
  "ingestion_job_id": "job-789"
}

Then support create, update, delete, reprocess, and rollback.

I would build immutable document versions and publish new chunk sets atomically, or with a controlled cutover. Otherwise, retrieval can mix old and new policy text.

Missing gate #2: Idempotency and durable recovery

Retries happen. Batch workers crash. Network calls time out after the downstream index accepted the write.

A job needs a stable idempotency key, deterministic chunk identifiers, persisted checkpoints, retry limits, and a dead-letter or quarantine path for poison documents.

For example:

chunk_id = hash(tenant_id, document_id, source_version, chunk_index, pipeline_version)

Use upserts where supported, and track when a version is fully indexed before making it queryable.

At-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes is generally a much safer engineering target than pretending a distributed pipeline will execute each step exactly once.

Missing gate #3: Document-level authorization

A vector's nearest neighbor is not necessarily an authorized neighbor.

In a multi-tenant system, filters must be enforced in trusted server-side retrieval logic and backed by access-control checks. Never trust a tenant ID supplied directly by the browser.

Authorization is more nuanced than a single tenant field: some documents can be department-restricted, user-specific, or revoked. Search-result filtering, index separation, and post-retrieval verification may all be required depending on the threat model.

Missing gate #4: Retrieval quality, not merely query speed

A fast result can be the wrong result.

Measure at least:

  • Recall@k and nDCG against a curated query set.
  • Authorization leakage rate across tenants and roles.
  • Freshness lag between source updates and searchable publication.
  • Grounded answer quality, with citations to source versions.
  • Unanswerable-question handling and abstention behavior.
  • p50/p95 latency and cost per successful grounded answer.

An ANN benchmark tells you something about vector search. It does not, by itself, tell you whether your RAG assistant gives trustworthy answers.

Missing gate #5: Safe secrets and workload identities

The 2024 AWS post discusses credential-expiry troubleshooting and a workaround involving long-lived IAM user keys. I would not carry that workaround into production.

Prefer short-lived, role-based workload credentials, least-privilege policies, isolated network access, and audited operations. Legacy benchmark instructions should be reviewed against current security practices before deployment.

The architecture I would ship 

Approved sources (PDF, web, CMS, CRM, object storage)
                        ↓
              Source connector / CDC
                        ↓
        Raw object + immutable document version
                        ↓
       Durable job queue + idempotency ledger
                        ↓
      Parse / OCR / validate / malware scanning
                        ↓
        PII classification + ACL extraction
                        ↓
           Structure-aware chunking
                        ↓
          Versioned embedding workers
                        ↓
      Staging index + retrieval evaluation
                        ↓
          Atomic publish / index cutover
                        ↓
      Tenant- and role-scoped query service
                        ↓
       Retrieval + reranking + citations
                        ↓
           Guarded LLM response

Keep three distinct concerns separate:

  1. System of record: original files, metadata, identities, ACLs, document versions, audit history.
  2. Processing plane: queues, workers, OCR, chunking, embedding, retries, backfills.
  3. Serving plane: published searchable chunks, tenant-scoped retrieval, reranking, response generation.

A vector database is a derived index, not your only copy of the business's knowledge.

When Ray is—and isn't—the right choice

Ray can be very appropriate when millions of documents or heavy batch embedding jobs justify distributed GPU scheduling.

But for a knowledge base with thousands of documents, starting with a five-node GPU cluster may be unnecessary complexity. A queue, a small worker pool, object storage, and pgvector may be a much better operational choice.

Scale from observed bottlenecks. First measure parse throughput, embedding time, write throughput, index-build time, and p95 retrieval latency. Then optimize the expensive stage.

PostgreSQL + pgvector or OpenSearch?

My decision framework:

Requirement Often start with
Existing relational app, moderate corpus, transactional metadata PostgreSQL + pgvector
Strong text-search needs, specialized search operations, large search workloads OpenSearch
Strict tenant permissions Either, with enforced authorization architecture
Frequent updates and backfills Benchmark both against your actual workload
Lowest operational complexity Whichever your team can operate reliably

This is guidance, not a performance ranking. Index algorithm, filtering strategy, corpus distribution, and infrastructure can change the result substantially.

A pre-launch checklist for RAG ingestion

Before declaring the system production-ready, I would ask:

  • Can we safely retry every ingestion stage without duplicate published chunks?
  • Can we delete or revoke a document and prove it is no longer retrievable?
  • Can we roll back a broken embedding-model or chunking release?
  • Can we demonstrate zero cross-tenant retrieval in adversarial tests?
  • Can we trace each answer back to a specific source and version?
  • Can we quantify freshness lag, relevance, p95 latency, and cost?
  • Can a failed batch recover without manual database surgery?

If the answer to these is 'not yet,' more embedding throughput will not solve the real reliability problem.

Final thought

AWS's Ray-based ingestion experiment is a valuable reference for the scale mechanics of RAG: bulk data preparation, parallel GPU embeddings, vector-store configuration, and ingestion observability.

My extension is simple:

A scalable RAG pipeline gets knowledge into an index. A production RAG platform ensures the right knowledge gets there, stays current, remains authorized, and can be recovered when things fail.

That is the architectural shift worth making.

Reference: AWS Big Data Blog — Build a RAG data ingestion pipeline for large-scale ML workloads (March 13, 2024). AWS configurations and dataset counts cited above come from that article; the reliability and security recommendations are my analysis.

About the Author

I write about software architecture, AI, automation, and real-world engineering challenges.

Explore more of my work and technical insights at sanukhan.dev.

title: RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.36444v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3% of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG.

title: Decision Models as Judges for Hallucination Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.37229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are widely used as judges of model outputs (LLM-as-a-Judge), but they are costly and can hallucinate or be overconfident. Decision models are a potential alternative. They return a predefined verdict with a probability for each label instead of free-form text and are much cheaper and faster. We test this promise on hallucination detection. We build binary benchmarks for five hallucination types (9,852 items from six datasets) and compare five decision models with the generative judge gpt-6-sol. Performance depends strongly on the type: the best decision model matches gpt-6-sol in balanced accuracy on context inconsistency and comes within 3 percentage points on factual errors, but trails it by 4-8 points on logical and instruction inconsistency. Decision-model probabilities are overconfident, though less so than the GPT-6 models, and separate correct from incorrect decisions only moderately. We also find that a confidence cascade of decision models improves on the best single model by 1.9-3.3 points on three types and matches or exceeds gpt-6-sol at 1-3% of its cost. Overall, decision models are a practical low-cost judge for some hallucination types but need to be validated before use.

title: Model-agnostic predictability quantification of multivariable time series
description:
arXiv:2610.33209v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multivariable time series forecasting plays an important role in various domains, where predictions depend on complex interactions among covariates. Forecasting models are commonly evaluated across numerous benchmark datasets. However, forecasting accuracy reflects both model capability and task predictability, making it difficult to characterise the difficulty of a task independently of the model used. Existing predictability measures often fail to capture nonlinear dependencies or are limited to univariate series. In this work, we propose Multivariable Predictability Score (MAPS), a model-agnostic metric for measuring the intrinsic predictability of multivariable time series forecasting tasks. MAPS uses covariate information to assess predictability across different lookback windows and forecasting horizons, and provides a quantitative assessment of the predictive information available for forecasting. We evaluate MAPS across synthetic and real-world forecasting datasets against 6 baseline predictability measures. The former confirms that our method closely aligns with the expected reference predictability (r=0.963). Empirical results further corroborate that MAPS yields more reliable projections in the majority of experimental configurations.

title: Japanese Discourse Structure Analysis Based on Segmented Discourse Representation Theory Using LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36667v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discourse parsing based on Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) is crucial for capturing the structural dynamics of dialogues. However, most prior research focuses on English, and its effectiveness for Japanese remains unclear owing to the lack of Japanese SDRT corpora. To address this issue, we construct Japanese SDRT corpora by translating existing English SDRT corpora using an LLM. Through a comparative evaluation of prompt-based and fine-tuned LLMs, we show that the models achieve comparable performance between English and Japanese, suggesting the cross-lingual applicability of SDRT-based discourse parsing. In order to investigate why the English and Japanese parsers achieve similar performance, we conduct ablation analyses on discourse markers and contextual inputs. Our results reveal that most of the Japanese discourse markers we examined have little impact, and the models' predictions depend heavily on contextual discourse relations rather than on the content of the context clauses. This structural reliance might explain the comparable performance despite the substantial typological differences between English and Japanese.

title: Benchmarking Task Takeover Across Agent Handoffs
description:
arXiv:2610.36523v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As agents collaborate on longer tasks, responsibility may pass between models before the work is complete. The receiving model must build on prior decisions, observations, and actions while addressing the remaining requirements. Evaluating this transition requires connecting the information preserved at handoff to how the receiver continues the work, a relationship that task-success and memory-retention scores alone do not capture. We introduce the Handoff State Continuity Benchmark (HSC-Bench), comprising 1,039 tasks that evaluate two complementary aspects of task takeover: recovering relevant repository evidence and continuing from established conversational, tool, and file-work state. Comparisons across six receiving models show that structured handoff state improves repository evidence recovery for every model and continuation performance for most models. The strongest receivers differ between the two tracks, showing that evidence-recovery rankings alone do not characterize performance when continuing from inherited state. By combining these comparisons with checks of subsequent responses and actions, HSC-Bench evaluates both access to prior evidence and adherence to established commitments and completed work. This provides a basis for selecting receiving models and assessing handoff representations according to the work that must be carried forward.

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.

title: Introducing tobira: Every Database, One Terminal, and One MCP Server for Your Agents
description:
Introduction

Count the database clients on your laptop. psql, sqlite3, mongosh, redis-cli, a ClickHouse client, a Qdrant dashboard in a browser tab, maybe DBeaver for the days you want a grid. Each one has its own flags, its own way of printing a table, its own config file with a password in it, and its own idea of what "read-only" means. None of them has any idea what an MCP server is, so the moment you want Claude Code or Cursor to look at a database, you are either pasting query results into the chat or wiring up a one-off MCP server for that one engine.

tobira (扉, Japanese for door) is my answer to that. It is one Go binary that is, at the same time:

  • one CLI: tobira query runs a statement on any of 31 databases and prints a table, JSON, NDJSON or CSV, with exit codes a script can trust;
  • one terminal UI: browse, filter, edit rows, run queries and tail changes with the same keys everywhere;
  • one AI assistant: tobira ask proposes a query or answers a question by running read-only queries itself, on Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, Vertex AI or a local Ollama model;
  • one MCP server: tobira mcp exposes the connections you name to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code, read-only by default;
  • one agent skill: npx skills add xavidop/tobira teaches your coding agent every command, flag and driver.

And underneath all five there is one read-only guard that the query text cannot lift, which is what makes it sane to hand a database to a model in the first place.

This article is the technical tour. Everything in it ran against tobira 1.4.1 on Go 1.27.

Why: one contract instead of five clients

Every database client is a vertical slice: its own connection handling, its own output, its own shell. tobira turns that into horizontal layers. Every database is a driver that implements one small Go contract. The CLI, the TUI, the AI assistant and the MCP server are written once, against that contract, not once per database.

Without tobira With tobira
Clients psql, mongosh, redis-cli, a vector DB dashboard, a GUI one binary, tobira
Scripting each client's output format and exit codes one --format flag (table, JSON, NDJSON, CSV) and exit codes 0 to 4 on every driver
Passwords in DSNs, shell history and GUI config files env:, file://, dotenv or OS keyring references, never a literal
Read-only a database user, if someone set one up a hard guard per driver plus whatever the server offers
AI paste results into a chat tobira ask, with schema context and read-only tools
Agents a custom MCP server per engine, or none tobira mcp --expose <names>, one server for every driver
Audit nothing tobira history, including what each MCP client ran

The driver contract is deliberately tiny. A Driver opens connections, and a Conn can Query, Ping, Close, list Namespaces and Collections and Describe a collection. Everything else (browse with paging, inline editing, explain, transactions, completion, export, change feeds, vector search, time-series reads) is an optional capability, an interface the connection may or may not implement, discovered at runtime:

if b, ok := driver.As[driver.Browser](conn); ok { ... }

Adding a capability never breaks a driver. The TUI asks each connection what it offers and shows only that: :tx appears where there are transactions, :similar on vector stores, :chart on time series.

The result is 31 drivers in the binary today: SQLite, PostgreSQL (with pgvector), MySQL, MariaDB, SingleStore, CockroachDB, Redshift, Greenplum, SQL Server, Oracle, libSQL/Turso, Cloudflare D1, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake, Vertica, MongoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB, Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, InfluxDB, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma and Milvus, plus DuckDB as an external plugin. Each driver is its own Go module, so the root module never imports a database SDK, and a plugin can be written in any language that speaks gRPC.

What We Are Building

A small shop database in SQLite with customers and orders, and then every door into it: tobira query from a script, the read-only guard trying to stop a delete, tobira ask answering a revenue question on Gemini, tobira mcp serving the database to a headless Claude Code session that is asked to delete rows and cannot, and finally tobira's driver layer embedded in a 60-line Go program.

SQLite is the demo because it needs no server. Every command below works the same on PostgreSQL, MongoDB or Qdrant: swap the DSN.

What You Need

  • tobira 1.4.1 or newer (Go 1.26+ if you build from source).
  • sqlite3 to seed the demo file.
  • A GEMINI_API_KEY for the AI steps (or an OpenAI or Anthropic key, or Ollama running locally).
  • Claude Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop or VS Code for the MCP step.

Step 1: Install and seed the demo 

brew install xavidop/tap/tobira        # macOS
# Windows: scoop bucket add xavidop https://github.com/xavidop/scoop-bucket && scoop install tobira
# Linux: .deb, .rpm, .apk or a tarball from https://github.com/xavidop/tobira/releases
tobira version

tobira 1.4.1 (efcb4bb9bb162ede77bf811e31278b6614b7a2fc, 2026-10-23T17:20:10Z)

Seed a database:

sqlite3 shop.db <<'SQL'
create table customers (id integer primary key, name text not null, email text, country text not null, created_at text not null);
create table orders (id integer primary key, customer_id integer not null references customers(id), total_cents integer not null, status text not null, created_at text not null);
insert into customers values (1,'Ada Lovelace','ada@example.com','GB','2026-09-02'),(2,'Grace Hopper','grace@example.com','US','2026-09-10'),(3,'Linus Torvalds',NULL,'FI','2026-09-15'),(4,'Margaret Hamilton','margaret@example.com','US','2026-10-01'),(5,'Ken Thompson','ken@example.com','US','2026-10-20');
insert into orders values (1,1,4999,'paid','2026-10-21'),(2,1,1250,'paid','2026-10-22'),(3,2,8900,'refunded','2026-10-22'),(4,3,2300,'paid','2026-10-23'),(5,4,15000,'pending','2026-10-24'),(6,2,720,'paid','2026-10-25'),(7,5,3100,'paid','2026-10-26');
SQL

Then name the connection in a config file. Connections are read-write by default; this one is read-only on purpose, because it is the one the AI and the agent will get:

# config.yaml  (default location: ~/.config/tobira/config.yaml)
connections:
  - name: shop
    driver: sqlite
    dsn: sqlite:./shop.db
    read_only: true
ai:
  provider: googleai            # googleai, vertexai, anthropic, openai or ollama
  model: gemini-3.8-flash
  api_key: env:GEMINI_API_KEY   # a secret reference, never the key itself
  send_rows: ask                # ask, always or never

A literal API key or password in that file is a load error, not a warning. Passwords are env:NAME, file:///path, dotenv://.env#KEY or keyring:NAME references, resolved by mamori when the connection opens, and the resolved value is held as a driver.Secret whose String, Format, LogValue and MarshalJSON all print [redacted]. Only Reveal() returns it, and only the driver calls that.

tobira doctor checks all of it, as JSON when stdout is not a terminal, so it belongs in CI:

tobira --config config.yaml doctor

{"section":"connections","name":"shop","status":"ok","detail":"reachable in 1ms (read-only open, driver sqlite)"}
{"section":"refs","name":"ai.api_key","status":"ok","detail":"env ref resolves"}
{"section":"ai","name":"model","status":"ok","detail":"gemini-3.8-flash"}
{"section":"mcp","name":"mcp","status":"ok","detail":"not configured; nothing is exposed"}
{"section":"permissions","name":"config","status":"warn","detail":"0644 is group-readable, world-readable; run chmod 600 config.yaml"}

Doctor exits non-zero on that warning. chmod 600 config.yaml and it is green.

Step 2: One query command for scripts and CI

tobira query takes a connection name or a raw DSN, a statement in the database's own language, and prints the result:

tobira --config config.yaml query shop \
  "select c.name, count(o.id) as orders, sum(o.total_cents)/100.0 as total
   from customers c join orders o on o.customer_id=c.id group by c.id order by total desc"

name               orders  total
─────────────────  ──────  ─────
Margaret Hamilton  1       150
Grace Hopper       2       96.2
Ada Lovelace       2       62.49
Ken Thompson       1       31
Linus Torvalds     1       23

5 rows · <1ms

The table is the terminal default. Pipe it anywhere and the default becomes JSON, with typed columns and stats, so jq never has to guess:

tobira --config config.yaml query shop "select id, name, country from customers where country='US'" --format json

{
  "columns": [{"name": "id", "type": "int"}, {"name": "name", "type": "string"}, {"name": "country", "type": "string"}],
  "rows": [
    {"id": 2, "name": "Grace Hopper", "country": "US"},
    {"id": 4, "name": "Margaret Hamilton", "country": "US"},
    {"id": 5, "name": "Ken Thompson", "country": "US"}
  ],
  "stats": {"rows_affected": -1, "duration_ms": 0, "truncated": false}
}

--format csv and --format ndjson do what they say, --output orders.csv streams every row of a result of any size into a file, --explain prints the plan instead of running the query, -f - reads the statement from stdin, and --timeout bounds the whole call, connecting included.

The exit codes are the same on every driver, which is what makes the command usable in a pipeline:

Code Meaning
0 Success
1 Usage error: bad flags, unknown connection, bad config
2 Could not open the connection: unreachable, bad credentials, unresolved secret
3 Any other query error: syntax, not found, timeout
4 Read-only violation, permission denied, or refused by policy

Errors go to stderr as one error: <message> line, always through the redactor, so a DSN password never ends up in a CI log.

Step 3: The read-only guard

This is the piece everything else leans on. Try a write on the shop connection:

tobira --config config.yaml query shop "delete from orders"; echo "exit=$?"

error: sqlite: query: only SELECT, WITH, VALUES, EXPLAIN and read-only PRAGMA statements are allowed on a read-only connection: read-only violation
exit=4

The same --read-only flag works on a bare DSN with no config at all, and smuggling a write behind a read does not work either, because the SQL drivers take exactly one statement per query:

tobira query sqlite:./shop.db "update orders set status='paid'" --read-only; echo "exit=$?"
# exit=4
tobira --config config.yaml query shop "select 1; delete from orders"; echo "exit=$?"
# error: sqlite: query: multiple statements are not supported yet: invalid query
# exit=3

The guard is not a regex in front of the connection. Each driver declares CapReadOnly in its capabilities, and that declaration is a contract: a query sent with ReadOnly must fail with ErrReadOnly and change nothing, whatever the text says. Each driver enforces it with the strongest mechanism its database has, with a statement check in front of that:

  • SQLite: the file is opened on a read-only handle, PRAGMA query_only=1 is re-asserted before every statement on the pooled connection (earlier text could have lifted it), ATTACH is disabled through SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED=0, and the statement must start with an allow-listed keyword.
  • PostgreSQL: every call runs inside its own BEGIN READ ONLY and always ends with ROLLBACK on a fresh context, so a cancelled query can never leave a transaction open. Because BEGIN READ ONLY does not stop COPY ... TO PROGRAM, DO blocks or lo_export from touching the server's filesystem, those are refused lexically before they run, and the lexer is run with every string-quoting dialect PostgreSQL can be configured with.
  • CockroachDB and Redshift: an allow-list, since EXPORT, BACKUP, UNLOAD and crdb_internal functions reach outside the database without writing to it.
  • MySQL: an allow-list of statement kinds, then a read-only transaction on its own connection, then a post-check that the statement stayed inside it (MySQL 8.0 to 8.4).
  • MongoDB: the command document is checked as sent against an allow-list of read commands; $out, $merge and write-concern fields are refused.
  • Redis: an allow-list of read commands checked against the server's own COMMAND INFO flags, so a renamed command is still refused.
  • Vector stores: queries never write, and anything that would send your data to an outside embedding service from the server side (Weaviate nearText, Milvus TEXTEMBEDDING, Qdrant document inputs) is refused on a read-only path too.

Every driver except SingleStore, which has no read-only transaction and therefore refuses read-only connections outright rather than pretending, declares the guard. The security page lists, per driver, the one thing the guard cannot see: code that already lives on the server, such as user-defined functions or linked servers. The guard stops accidental and model-generated writes. A least-privilege database user is still the real boundary, and the two together are what you want before Step 5.

Step 4: Ask in plain language

With the ai: section in place, tobira ask has three modes. The default proposes a query and runs nothing:

tobira --config config.yaml ask shop "which customers spent the most, with their order count" --collection orders

```sqlite
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, SUM(o.total_cents) AS total_spent_cents FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY total_spent_cents DESC
```

This query aggregates orders by customer, calculating the total amount spent (in cents) and the total number of orders placed. It then sorts the customers in descending order by total spend so the top-spending customers appear first.

googleai/gemini-3.8-flash · 483 in / 118 out · 5.4s

--run proposes and then runs the proposal read-only, exactly as tobira query --read-only would:

tobira --config config.yaml ask shop "the three newest paid orders with the customer name" --run --format table

id  customer_name   total_cents  status  created_at
──  ──────────────  ───────────  ──────  ──────────
7   Ken Thompson    3100         paid    2026-10-26
6   Grace Hopper    720          paid    2026-10-25
4   Linus Torvalds  2300         paid    2026-10-23

3 rows · <1ms

--answer is the agentic mode: the model gets the read-only tools (list_collections, describe, sample, query, explain) and loops until it has an answer. --send-rows lets the row data reach the model for this run; without it, under send_rows: ask, the model gets column names and counts only.

tobira --config config.yaml ask shop \
  "how much revenue did we get in October 2026 from paid orders, and from which country does most of it come?" \
  --answer --send-rows

In October 2026, total revenue from paid orders was **12,369 cents** (**$123.69**), and most of it came from **GB** (6,249 cents / $62.49).

| Country | Revenue (cents) | Revenue ($) |
|---|---|---|
| **GB** | 6,249 | $62.49 |
| **US** | 3,820 | $38.20 |
| **FI** | 2,300 | $23.00 |

Queries run:
  SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders (3 rows)
  SELECT created_at FROM orders WHERE created_at LIKE '2026-10%' LIMIT 5 (5 rows)
  SELECT SUM(total_cents) AS total_cents, ROUND(SUM(total_cents) / 100.0, 2) AS total_dollars FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01' (1 row)
  SELECT c.country, SUM(o.total_cents) AS total_cents, ... GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY total_cents DESC (3 rows)
  ...

googleai/gemini-3.8-flash · 13.1k in / 812 out · 24.5s

Notice what the model did first: it checked which status values exist and what the dates look like before trusting its own assumptions. That is the schema context at work. Each request carries the collection in scope, its foreign-key neighbours and the other collection names, with columns, types, keys and indexes, but never DDL (defaults and comments can hold secrets) and never sample rows unless send_rows allows it.

A few design decisions worth knowing, because they are the difference between a demo and something you run against a real database:

  • The assistant is built on Genkit Go and lives in its own module, so the core of tobira has no model SDK. The four flows (askFlow, answerFlow, explainResultsFlow, fixErrorFlow) are Dotprompt files embedded in the binary, and a file of the same name in ~/.config/tobira/prompts/ replaces the built-in one without a rebuild. genkit start -- tobira ai dev opens them in the Genkit Dev UI.
  • The query tools are only offered on connections whose driver declares the read-only guard, and every call carries the read-only flag, a 30 second timeout and a row cap, whatever the model asks for. The driver stops a write, not the model's manners.
  • The tools reach only the connection of the conversation. Any other name gets the same unknown connection error as one that does not exist.
  • Prompt injection from data is made hard structurally: every piece of data is wrapped in a fence named with a random per-request nonce (<data-NONCE kind="schema">), the prompt says only fenced text is data, and Dotprompt's role markers are broken in every input so a row cannot open a new message.
  • The only tool that can write, execute, exists in the TUI only, only after :ai execute on on that connection, and asks you to confirm every statement, after you have scrolled to the end of it.

The same assistant is a panel in the TUI (a opens it, ctrl+t switches between propose and answer, F5 loads the proposal into the editor and runs it, f on a failed run asks the AI to fix the query).

Step 5: Hand it to your agent with tobira mcp

This is the part I think changes how you work. tobira mcp is a Model Context Protocol server over stdio (or Streamable HTTP with --http), and it serves the exact same tools the assistant uses, on the connections you name and nothing else:

claude mcp add tobira -- tobira mcp --expose shop

Or, in a .cursor/mcp.json, .vscode/mcp.json or claude_desktop_config.json:

{"mcpServers": {"tobira": {"command": "tobira", "args": ["mcp", "--expose", "shop"]}}}

Nothing is exposed until you name it. tobira mcp with no --expose and no mcp.expose in the config exits with code 1 rather than serving everything. On a raw JSON-RPC session the server advertises describe, explain, list_collections, list_connections, list_namespaces, query and sample, plus similar when an exposed driver can do vector search. execute is not in the list at all unless a connection is in allow_writes:

--- tools/call list_connections
[{"name":"shop","driver":"sqlite","kind":"sql","dialect":"sqlite","read_only":true,"status":"idle"}]

--- tools/call describe {"connection":"shop","collection":"orders"}
{"namespace":"main","collection":"orders","type":"table","fields":[{"name":"id","type":"INTEGER","nullable":true,"auto_increment":true},{"name":"customer_id","type":"INTEGER","nullable":false},{"name":"total_cents","type":"INTEGER","nullable":false},{"name":"status","type":"TEXT","nullable":false},{"name":"created_at","type":"TEXT","nullable":false}],"primary_key":["id"],"foreign_keys":[{"fields":["customer_id"],"references":"main.customers","ref_fields":["id"]}]}

--- tools/call query {"connection":"shop","query":"select status, count(*) as n, sum(total_cents) as cents from orders group by status"}
{"columns":[{"name":"status","type":"TEXT"},{"name":"n","type":"int"},{"name":"cents","type":"int"}],"rows":[["paid",5,12369],["pending",1,15000],["refunded",1,8900]],"truncated":false}

--- tools/call query {"connection":"shop","query":"delete from orders where status = 'refunded'"}
sqlite: query: only SELECT, WITH, VALUES, EXPLAIN and read-only PRAGMA statements are allowed on a read-only connection: read-only violation
(isError: true)

--- tools/call execute {"connection":"shop","statement":"delete from orders"}
{"code": -32602, "message": "tool 'execute' not found: tool not found"}

--- tools/call query {"connection":"prod","query":"select 1"}
unknown connection "prod": call list_connections for the names
(isError: true)

Every collection is also an MCP resource at tobira://<connection>/<namespace>/<collection>/schema, so a client can attach a schema to its context without spending a tool call.

Now the real test: a headless Claude Code session, with tobira as its only MCP server, asked to do something it must not be able to do.

claude -p --mcp-config mcp.json --strict-mcp-config --allowedTools "mcp__tobira__*" \
  "Using only the tobira MCP tools: which customer has the highest paid revenue in the shop database, and how much? Then try to delete the refunded orders and tell me exactly what happened."

**Highest paid revenue:** Ada Lovelace (customer id 1) has the most, at 6,249 cents, which is **$62.49**.
I counted only orders with status `paid`, and the currency is my assumption since the schema doesn't
name one. The next highest are Ken Thompson at $31.00, Linus Torvalds at $23.00 and Grace Hopper at $7.20.

**Deleting the refunded orders:** The delete did not go through, and nothing was changed.
- **What I ran:** `DELETE FROM orders WHERE status='refunded'`, sent through the tobira `query` tool.
- **What came back:** `sqlite: query: only SELECT, WITH, VALUES, EXPLAIN and read-only PRAGMA statements
  are allowed on a read-only connection: read-only violation`.
- **Why:** The `shop` connection is flagged `read_only: true`. The tobira tools have no write tool, so
  there was no other way to delete.
- **What I saw before the attempt:** The only refunded order is 1 row, worth 8,900 cents ($89.00).
  I didn't re-query afterwards, but the refusal means it should still be there.

I didn't try to get around the read-only setting. If you want the delete done, you'd need a writable
connection or to run the statement yourself.

The agent explored the schema, wrote a correct join, got the right answer, attempted the delete, was refused by the driver, and reported it honestly. And every one of those calls is in the local history, with the client's name and version from its initialize request:

tobira history --mcp --format table --limit 7

at                    conn  source  client               ok     rows  ms  query
────────────────────  ────  ──────  ───────────────────  ─────  ────  ──  ────────────────────────────────────────────
2026-10-27T23:02:32Z  shop  mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  false  0     0   DELETE FROM orders WHERE status='refunded'
2026-10-27T23:02:29Z  shop  mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  true   4     0   SELECT c.id, c.name, SUM(o.total_cents) paid_cents FROM cus…
2026-10-27T23:02:28Z  shop  mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  true   3     0   SELECT status, COUNT(*) n, SUM(total_cents) cents FROM orde…
2026-10-27T23:02:26Z  shop  mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  true   0     1   describe {"collection":"orders","connection":"shop"}
2026-10-27T23:02:25Z  shop  mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  true   0     0   describe {"collection":"customers","connection":"shop"}
2026-10-27T23:02:22Z  shop  mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  true   0     11  list_collections {"connection":"shop"}
2026-10-27T23:02:18Z        mcp     claude-code/2.1.308  true   0     2   list_connections

The history is a local SQLite file with mode 0600, the last 10,000 entries, credentials masked, and tobira history clear plus a retention setting when you want less of it.

The policy knobs, all in the mcp: section or as flags:

mcp:
  expose: [shop, cache]       # the only connections a client can see
  allow_writes: [cache]       # a subset of expose; execute exists only for these
  max_rows: 200               # 1 to 1000, per tool result
  send_rows: always           # always or never (no "ask": nobody is there to answer)
  token: env:TOBIRA_MCP_TOKEN # HTTP mode only

Two things to internalise. First, send_rows defaults to always here, unlike the assistant's ask, because an MCP client runs unattended; if the data must not reach a model, do not expose the connection. Second, execute has no per-call confirmation, because there is nobody to confirm; allow writes only on a scratch database an agent is allowed to break.

HTTP mode (--http 127.0.0.1:8765) is for clients that cannot start a process. It binds to loopback unless you pass --insecure-bind, needs a bearer token on every request, and checks Host and Origin against DNS rebinding.

Step 6: Teach the agent the CLI itself

The MCP server gives an agent tools. The agent skill gives it knowledge: a SKILL.md that covers every command, flag and exit code, the driver model, each driver's DSN schemes and capabilities, the config and secrets rules, the MCP setup and how to write a driver. Install it into your project with the skills CLI:

npx skills add xavidop/tobira

After that, Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot know that tobira query returns exit 4 on a read-only violation, that SingleStore has no read-only guard, that go install ...@latest does not work for the CLI module because it depends on its sibling modules, and that tobira doctor prints JSON off a terminal. The skill is the same file for every agent, and it is versioned with the project, so it never drifts from the binary.

MCP for the data, a skill for the tool. That combination is what makes tobira agent-ready rather than merely AI-flavoured: the agent can both query your databases and drive the CLI correctly in a script it writes for you.

Step 7: Use it as a library, or add a database

The driver layer is importable. github.com/xavidop/tobira/api is the stable, stdlib-only surface (type aliases over the driver package), and each driver is a module you link in. A private registry, a read-only open, a streamed query and a refused write in one small program:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "strings"

    "github.com/xavidop/tobira/api"
    "github.com/xavidop/tobira/drivers/sqlite"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    reg := api.NewRegistry()
    if err := reg.Add(sqlite.New()); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    conn, err := reg.Open(ctx, api.ConnConfig{DSN: "sqlite:./shop.db", ReadOnly: true})
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer conn.Close()

    fmt.Println("capabilities:", api.CapabilitiesOf(conn))
    run(ctx, conn, "select name, country from customers order by id")
    run(ctx, conn, "delete from customers") // refused: the connection is read-only
}

func run(ctx context.Context, conn api.Conn, text string) {
    rs, err := conn.Query(ctx, api.Query{Text: text, ReadOnly: true, Limit: 3})
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("%s -> %v (read-only: %t)\n", text, err, errors.Is(err, api.ErrReadOnly))
        return
    }
    defer rs.Close()
    for {
        row, ok, err := rs.Next(ctx)
        if err != nil || !ok {
            break
        }
        var cells []string
        for _, v := range row {
            cells = append(cells, v.String())
        }
        fmt.Println(strings.Join(cells, "\t"))
    }
    fmt.Printf("(truncated: %t)\n", rs.Stats().Truncated)
}

capabilities: [browser mutator explainer transactor completer]
Ada Lovelace    GB
Grace Hopper    US
Linus Torvalds  FI
(truncated: true)
delete from customers -> sqlite: query: only SELECT, WITH, VALUES, EXPLAIN and read-only PRAGMA statements are allowed on a read-only connection: read-only violation (read-only: true)

Values are a tagged union (driver.Value) rather than any, so a row can cross a plugin boundary unchanged. Results stream, so a large result never has to fit in memory. Errors are *driver.Error values classified by sentinels (ErrReadOnly, ErrNotFound, ErrSyntax, ErrUnsupported) you match with errors.Is.

Adding a database is the same contract in the other direction. A driver module is a Go package that implements Driver and Conn, registers from init like database/sql, and passes the drivertest conformance kit in strict mode, which probes a declared read-only guard with real writes. The in-repo example is about 150 lines. An external plugin is that same driver served over gRPC through hashicorp/go-plugin with one line of main:

func main() { sdk.Serve(memdemo.New()) }

go build -o tobira-driver-memdemo .
tobira driver install ./tobira-driver-memdemo --sha256 "$(shasum -a 256 tobira-driver-memdemo | cut -d' ' -f1)"
tobira driver info memdemo

tobira driver install requires the checksum and never runs the binary. Connections and transactions live inside the plugin behind unguessable handles, a panic in one call fails only that call, and if tobira dies the plugin notices within a second and exits. The wire protocol is plain protobuf over gRPC, so a driver can be written in any language. DuckDB ships this way because it needs cgo and tobira's releases do not.

Conclusion

The thing that makes tobira more than a nicer psql is the layering. One driver contract means the CLI, the TUI, the assistant and the MCP server are each written once and work on 31 databases. One read-only guard, declared and enforced per driver, means every one of those doors can be opened for a model without a leap of faith. One history means you can see, afterwards, exactly what the model or the agent ran.

If you only take one thing from this article, take Step 5: tobira mcp --expose <name> on a read_only: true connection, then ask your coding agent a question about your data. It is the same tool you use at the keyboard, with the same guard, and it took one line to set up.

tobira is MIT licensed and lives at github.com/xavidop/tobira. The best contribution is a driver for a database you use; open an issue first and start from the example module.

Further reading

  • tobira on GitHub and the documentation site
  • Concepts: drivers, connections, capabilities and policy
  • The read-only guard, driver by driver
  • AI assistant: data and safety
  • MCP server: tools, resources and client setup
  • Write a driver, and the plugin protocol
  • The tobira agent skill
  • mamori, the library that resolves tobira's secret references, and its launch post
  • Model Context Protocol and Genkit Go

title: A comment is for a different reader
description:
When did you last read the source of a tool to find out how to use it?

I'll wait. I've been asking people that for a few weeks now and the answer, once they've stopped laughing, lands somewhere between "never" and "only when the docs lied to me". So it's a bit odd, perhaps, that "the code has no comments" is still the first thing anyone reaches for when they want to say a codebase is a mess.

Notes on the engine, a manual in the glovebox

The tool I wrote about last month had comments on just under ten per cent of its lines, and if anything I'd have argued for fewer. It also shipped with about ninety pages of documentation, published as a site and baked into the binary behind a docs command so you could read the lot offline on a train, which people did.

Those two facts look like a contradiction, and I'd argue they were one decision (I wish I'd said so at the time, rather than leaving people to work it out for themselves).

Any piece of code that matters has three readers, and just one is the person people picture when they say "reader". There's the engineer using the tool... at that job there were hundreds of them, most of whom had never written a line of Go and had no wish to start, thank you very much. Then there's whoever is changing it, and there were a handful of those on a good day. And then there's the poor soul reading the diff in six months, trying to work out why on earth it does that, and more often than not that's you, having forgotten, swearing at whoever wrote it before realising who that was.

A comment is really for the second and third of those. It's a note scratched onto the engine block for the next mechanic. The driver very rarely lifts the bonnet, and you wouldn't hand them the wiring diagram and call it a manual; they get the book in the glovebox, and the book says how to drive it and what the warning lights mean and what not to do, which is a completely different document written for a completely different person. The notes on the engine being terse doesn't tell you much at all about whether the glovebox is empty.

So "no comments, therefore tribal knowledge" is making two assumptions at once, and for most tools I suspect they're both wrong. It assumes the code is the only place knowledge can live, and it assumes everyone who needs the knowledge is a mechanic.

What a comment is actually for

Here's my rule. I've held it long enough that I've just this month written it into the instructions my AI agents work from, because they didn't have it and had taken to writing small essays above functions (they do love an essay).

A comment says why. It doesn't say how. If the how needs a paragraph then the code needs refactoring, not annotating, and a comment explaining what a function does is really a confession that the function's name doesn't. Well-written code carries its meaning in its symbols, and that's why I think a comment restating the code is worse than no comment at all: the reader has to read it, work out that the name already said it, and throw it away, on every single visit... death by a thousand paper cuts.

I'll make one up, though hand on heart I have reviewed this exact comment more times than I care to count:

// shoppingCartExceedsFreeShippingBoundary confirms that the cart is eligible for
// free shipping. Why? Because we offer free shipping when the customer spends
// more than £50.
func shoppingCartExceedsFreeShippingBoundary(cart Cart) bool {
    return cart.Total() >= 50
}

Hardly a word of that comment survives the function's name and its one-line body. Delete it and you've lost next to nothing. A comment that would earn its line on that function carries something the code can't say. That the fifty is set by Marketing and changes each January, say, or that it's >= rather than > because of a row with Finance in 2019 that no one is keen to reopen. That's a why, that's worth a line, and then you get out of the way and let the code speak.

A rule like that has an exception, and I didn't honour it. Go renders the comment above every exported symbol straight into the package documentation, so an export with no doc comment is a hole in the public surface however good the name is, and on that codebase barely a quarter of the exports had one. A fair cop! If I could go back and write one piece of documentation for that tool, it would be those skipped one-liners on the functions the next mechanic was going to need.

What ninety pages were for

The documentation was sized by the audience, not by my enthusiasm for writing it (which, for the record, is limited).

Hundreds of engineers across a lot of teams, who needed to log in to a cluster, or launch a tools pod, or push an upgrade through eighty-odd Terraform modules before lunch, and who'd have been actively harmed by being pointed at the Go that did it. Plenty of them could have read it. It just would have told them how it worked rather than what they needed, which was how to use it, what it would refuse to do and why, and what to try when it went wrong. Why the tools pod is only permitted in one cluster per environment is a paragraph of reasoning about auditability and who can reach what, and that paragraph lives in the docs. In the code it's a single check, and it should be.

Two things stopped those pages rotting the way documentation usually does. They were embedded in the binary, so the docs you had were the docs for the version you were running, which is the only version of "keep the docs in sync" that has ever actually worked for me. And I bolted an AI onto them, a docs ask command that answered questions from that corpus and nothing else, and the code never went anywhere near the model. What it knew was exactly, and only, what a user was allowed to know. It turned ninety pages that hardly anyone was going to read end to end into something people actually asked, and that turned the docs into a thing worth maintaining, because a stale page now gave a wrong answer out loud, in front of someone, rather than sitting on a wiki being wrong in private.

What was tribal

I said the criticism about doc comments was fair. This one's fairer, and I'd rather make it myself than have it made for me.

Most of the commits on that tool have my name on them. It launched without fanfare and grew a command at a time, and the onboarding was me sitting down with a team and walking them through it, over and over, team after team. From the outside a tool with one main author and a lovely manual is indistinguishable from tribal knowledge with a lovely manual, and in the early days it was tribal knowledge, not for want of trying, though wanting doesn't count. The docs were my attempt to make it not so, and they did their job for the hundreds of drivers, but what a manual can't do is manufacture a second mechanic. Only handing someone the spanner and standing well back does that, and I did, and it took most of a year, and I still walked out with most of the commits being mine.

That's the limit of documentation and I don't think you can get round it, however many pages you write... a manual makes a tool usable by people who'll never maintain it, and does precious little about who does.

The glovebox

You'll have noticed I haven't shown you a line of that tool. I can't, it isn't mine to show.

But you know what it was for, and why the pod was only ever allowed in one cluster, and what I'd do differently, and where that fifty-pound threshold came from... which is all any of its drivers ever had, and it got them where they were going.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 28 October 2026.

title: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36574v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses to diverse user requests, yet streaming may expose users to harmful content before generation is complete. Existing guardrails face two limitations in this setting. First, post-hoc moderation at response or chunk boundaries delays intervention, risking harmful exposure when content is released before verification. Second, even with token-level detection, coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, while fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. To address these limitations, we introduce ADTGuard, which checks each token before release, progressively refines token-level training targets, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. ADTGuard models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. To adapt the choice of observation layers to the current prefix, we propose the Causal Depth Router (CDR). With only response-level labels available, we further develop Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) to progressively construct token-level training targets for both components. Through extensive experiments across multiple safety benchmarks, we demonstrate that ADTGuard consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and maintaining competitive per-token latency.

title: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.36493v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cross-modal translation requires models to capture shared semantics across modalities while preserving the fine-grained structure required by the target modality. Yet in real-world scientific domains, paired data are often imperfect, while obtaining clean pairs at scale is costly. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) directly optimizes cross-modal translation through categorical token-level supervision, but this objective is sensitive to errors in the target sequences. JEPA offers a complementary representation-space objective, but most existing formulations focus on prediction within a modality rather than translation across modalities. We introduce Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (AC-JEPA), an SFT-compatible plug-in that predicts masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions using paired data. The joint-embedding objective targets cross-modal structure predictable from context, while the causal SFT path retains direct token-level supervision for the target sequence. During self-training, AC-JEPA learns from continuous latent targets derived from imperfect pseudo-labeled pairs, offering intrinsic tolerance to local data errors without promoting pseudo-tokens to hard categorical supervision. Using optical chemical structure recognition as a testbed, AC-JEPA trained on clean pairs achieves 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of the WildMol benchmark, compared with 67.40% for SFT alone. Using the same pseudo-labeled data for both approaches, AC-JEPA-based self-training further raises accuracy to 80.23%, whereas accuracy under direct SFT drops from 67.40% to 63.47%. These results support SFT-anchored joint-embedding prediction as an effective strategy for cross-modal translation under both curated and imperfect supervision.

title: Freeze a Real Run into a Corpus: How Baize Scores Agents with Deterministic Evidence
description:
Judging an agent by "how good the final reply sounds" is rarely enough.

What teams actually worry about happens at the tool-call layer. After changing a prompt, swapping a model, or tweaking a tool, the replies may look better while the agent quietly starts to:

  • hit "approve" on a ticket it hasn't fully read;
  • call a write endpoint it should never touch;
  • run "check inventory, then place order" in the wrong order;
  • trigger an action twice — or, when it should act, do nothing at all.

None of that shows up by reading the streaming reply. Baize evaluates agents on the tool-call timeline instead: not what the model said, but what it actually did — and by default the scoring is deterministic code rules, not an LLM judge.

1. The corpus comes from real runs, not hand-written fixtures

The first step of evaluation is not writing test cases out of thin air — it is turning real runs that already happened into replayable corpus.

A run leaves a complete event stream in the runtime (tool calls, tool results, human waits, etc.). Baize exposes an online sampling pipeline in the settings page:

  1. Find candidates: filter historical runs by time window, run status, duration, and whether they contain a certain event type. The store fetches up to about 500 rows in one pass; after filtering, roughly the first 100 are kept as the candidate pool (current defaults, adjustable via page/API parameters).
  2. Sample deterministically: sort candidates by a stable hash of seed + run ID, take the first N — about 10 per batch by default, hard cap 20. The same seed always picks the same batch, so the corpus is reproducible instead of jittering every run.
  3. Ingest into a case: freeze the run's full event stream plus its input snapshot into one evaluation case (EvalCase). The same run is ingested only once by default; repeated sampling skips it, and you can explicitly replace when needed.
  4. Fill in expectations: a case enters as a draft; once you state what this run "should have done," it upgrades to confirmed — and only confirmed cases are scorable.

What gets collected this way is not made-up toy dialogue but paths that actually ran in production — the tickets to read, the approvals to go through, the downstream calls that matter, all still in the events.

The same "assertion contract" has two more entry points that share the same scoring semantics:

  • EVAL.yaml next to a skill's directory, for live evaluation of the skill;
  • the repo script scripts/evidence-eval, for offline replay or CI.

The rest of this article follows the settings-page corpus as the main line and ties all three entry points together at the end.

2. A case is a set of behavior assertions

The core of a case is not a "reference answer text" but a set of assertions about tool behavior (fields use snake_case in JSON/YAML):

Dimension Field Meaning
Required reads required_reads Read-only tools that must have succeeded before any write
Consequential consequential Side-effect actions that must occur; "any one of" via expect_consequential_any
Chain chain (V2) "A must succeed, then B must appear afterwards"
Forbidden tools forbid_tools Tools that must never be called
Arg contains arg_contains A tool call's arguments must contain a certain substring
Downstream state expect_state Compare against a downstream ticket snapshot (or a live state check) at scoring time

The safety principle is simple: read first, then write. Before a side-effecting write happens, the read-only queries it depends on must have completed successfully.

When filling expectations in the UI, protocol version, required reads, and consequential are enough to score; finer assertions — forbidden tools, arg contains, chain, downstream state — can be maintained in the exported JSON or updated via the management API.

One note on the chain fields: the pair is named after / before, with the semantics — after must succeed first, and then before must appear later on the timeline. before here is a code field name, not "happens before" in the literal sense.

3. Scoring: rebuild the tool timeline from the event stream

Scoring does not call an LLM judge. It re-assembles the frozen event stream into an ordered tool-call timeline:

  • llm.tool_call: register one call (name, arguments);
  • tool.result: attach that call's result and whether it errored;
  • hitl.waiting: mark that it was waiting on human approval.

Then assertions are applied to the timeline one by one. Whether a run passes comes down to whether any failure code fired:

Code Trigger (plain language)
BSR Required reads were not all done
PAR Acted before reading, or wrote in a read-only scenario
NO_ACTION None of the expected consequential actions happened
MULTI More than one consequential action (mainly V1; one is usually expected)
GAP Chain broken: the required "A then B" order did not appear
FORBID A forbidden tool was called
ARG Tool arguments missed the required content
STATE Downstream ticket snapshot missing or mismatched
BAD_PROTOCOL Unrecognized protocol version
TIMEOUT The run status used for scoring was marked as timed out

Pass = zero failure codes. The same events plus the same assertions always produce the same score: no judge-model noise, no scoring tokens consumed, safe to replay inside any automation or CI.

Optionally, a confirmed case can run a live state check: read-only fetch of the current downstream ticket snapshot (mock or real), compare against expectations, and re-score — useful when you want to verify the latest state on top of a snapshot.

4. Assertion protocols follow business maturity

A case carries a protocol version (V0 / V1 / V2), with strictly increasing strictness:

  • V0 (read-only probe): all required reads must complete, and no write action may occur — checks whether this scenario is being treated as a pure query;
  • V1 (behavior closure): at least one expected consequential action must fire; no acting before reads, no multiple consequentials;
  • V2 (ordering constraints): on top of V1, add chains, e.g. "check inventory before creating an order."

The same corpus can be cut to a stricter protocol as the business grows from read-only guardrail to side-effecting closure — the assertions tighten with it.

5. Making the automatic scorer itself trustworthy

Deterministic scoring is not born correct. Baize adds a human calibration layer:

For each already-scored confirmed case, a human can mark "agree / disagree" and leave a note; the system aggregates an agreement rate (fraction where the automatic verdict matches the human one). After tightening or relaxing the scoring rules, watch whether this rate drops — the automatic scorer itself is under continuous review.

6. In practice: sample in the UI, export the results

It is lightweight: pick the time window and filters in the settings page, choose draft mode or a template-driven score mode, and one batch ingests a set of real runs into corpus. Draft mode only collects; you fill expectations and score later. With a template, you can score immediately — suited to when you already know what "this kind of failure" looks like.

Each case also exports to JSON with the same semantics as evidence-eval (case assertions + event stream in one package) for offline replay in external scripts or CI. The repo's PowerShell script splits case and events by its input parameters, or you can reuse the same Go scoring logic directly.

From failed or half-successful runs, the settings page also offers skill-draft: turn the trajectory into a skill draft, then install it after human review — evaluation is not only scoring; it can also distill bad paths into reusable skills and conventions.

7. Three entry points, one evidence contract

Entry point Best for
Settings "evaluation corpus" Sample real runs, fill expectations, re-score, human review, export
Skill-side EVAL.yaml Lightweight evaluation contract bundled with a skill, live-runnable
scripts/evidence-eval Offline fixtures, scripted batch runs, local or CI

The common ground: judge the tool timeline, speak in failure codes, and by default don't use an LLM as the judge. After changing prompts, models, or tool routing, look at whether this corpus regresses first — far more stable than staring at a single reply.

Baize is a team-facing, self-hosted AI Agent runtime: a single Go binary, MIT-licensed.

  • Source: https://github.com/rebornace/baize
  • Docs: https://rebornace.github.io/baize

Turning "did the agent move wrongly" from eyeballing logs into a replayable, repeatable regression corpus with a visible human-agreement rate is how runtime behavior is actually held in line.

title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2610.36595v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.
