title: MLIPDiff: Guiding Denoising Diffusion Models for Structure-Based Drug Design via Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
description:
arXiv:2610.33315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models have become a dominant approach to structure-based drug design. However, because they are trained primarily to fit reference structures, they often place ligands in physically implausible poses that clash with the protein. We introduce MLIPDiff, an inference-time guidance method that can be applied to pretrained diffusion models for ligand generation. The method uses physics-informed guidance from UMA (Universal Models for Atoms), a machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP). The guidance combines four weighted energy terms (protein-ligand interaction, ligand strain, steric clash, and pocket anchoring) and uses the original model checkpoint without retraining. On CrossDocked2020, MLIPDiff completely eliminates protein-ligand collisions while preserving the ligand's local geometry, improving bond-length distributions and physical plausibility relative to the base model. Compared to models such as NucleusDiff that are specifically designed to reduce atomic clashes, MLIPDiff achieves clash-free structures without compromising local geometry. It maintains the base model's PoseBusters pass rate and attains the best median Vina Score, Vina Min, and Vina Dock, surpassing both the base model and NucleusDiff, with a median of 59.6\% of ligands per pocket binding more strongly than the reference. MLIPDiff thus addresses a limitation of prior methods by generating physically plausible structures with favorable predicted binding affinity using a single frozen model and no additional training.

title: HTTP QUERY Method Explained: RFC 10008, QUERY vs GET vs POST
description:
The HTTP QUERY method is a new request method, defined in RFC 10008 (June 2026), that sends a query in the request body and is both safe and idempotent. Think of it as GET with a body: you get POST's room for complex filters and GET's guarantees for caching and automatic retries.

Try Apidog today

If you've stuffed a 3 KB filter into a URL, or sent a read-only search as POST and watched your cache and retry logic ignore it, QUERY is the fix. This guide covers what the spec says, how QUERY compares to GET and POST, what supports it today, and how to test a QUERY endpoint with your coding agent.

What is the HTTP QUERY method?

QUERY is an HTTP method that asks the target resource to run the query described in the request content and return the result. The request body and its Content-Type define the query. The method is safe (the client expects no state change) and idempotent (repeating it has the same effect), so clients, proxies and caches can retry and cache it like GET.

The spec is RFC 10008, "The HTTP QUERY Method", a Proposed Standard published in June 2026 by Julian Reschke (greenbytes), James M. Snell (Cloudflare) and Mike Bishop (Akamai). IANA has added it to the HTTP Method Registry with "safe: yes, idempotent: yes", right next to the WebDAV-era SEARCH method it almost became.

A QUERY request looks like this:

QUERY /contacts HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept: application/json

select=surname,givenname,email&limit=10&match=%22email=*@example.*%22

The server answers with 200 OK and the result in the body.

Why GET and POST weren't enough

You had two options for a complex read before QUERY, and both leak.

GET puts everything in the URL. RFC 10008 lists four problems with that:

  1. Size limits are unknown ahead of time, because a request crosses many systems. RFC 9110 only recommends that senders and recipients support at least 8,000 octets.
  2. Encoding structured data into a valid URI is wasteful.
  3. URIs get logged and bookmarked far more often than request bodies, which is a privacy problem for sensitive filters.
  4. Every combination of query inputs becomes its own resource.

GET with a body isn't the answer either. RFC 9110 says content in a GET request has no defined semantics. Some servers read it, some drop it, and some proxies reject the request. You can't count on it across the path.

POST works, but it lies about intent. A POST search runs fine, yet nothing tells a client, cache, proxy or retry library that the operation is read-only. So caches skip it and clients won't retry it after a dropped connection. If you've had to bolt an idempotency key onto a pure read just to make retries safe, you've felt this.

QUERY keeps POST's body and adds GET's guarantees.

QUERY vs GET vs POST

Here's the comparison, based on Table 1 of RFC 10008:

Property GET QUERY POST
Safe Yes Yes Potentially no
Idempotent Yes Yes Potentially no
Request body No defined semantics Expected, defines the query Expected
URI for the query itself Yes, by definition Optional, via Location No
URI for the result Optional, via Content-Location Optional, via Content-Location Optional, via Content-Location
Cacheable Yes Yes, body is part of the cache key Only for later GET or HEAD
CORS preflight from browsers Not for simple requests Always Not for simple requests

The short version: use GET when the query fits comfortably in the URL, QUERY when it doesn't, and POST only when the request changes state. For a refresher on the classic methods, see our guides to HTTP methods and GET vs POST.

What RFC 10008 defines

Content-Type is mandatory

Servers MUST fail a QUERY whose Content-Type is missing or inconsistent with the body. The RFC recommends these status codes:

  • 400 Bad Request: no media type, or a type that doesn't match the content. Servers can't sniff the body and override it.
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type: the resource doesn't support that query format.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: the format is fine but the query can't run, such as SQL naming a table that doesn't exist.
  • 406 Not Acceptable: the client asked for a response type the resource can't produce.

Location and Content-Location

A server can return two optional headers that turn a QUERY into something you can GET later:

  • Content-Location points to the stored result of this specific run. It might be temporary.
  • Location points to the stored query itself. A GET on it reruns the query with fresh data, without resending the body.

The RFC suggests clients switch to GET on the Location URI for repeat requests, since GET caching is simpler. If you return either header for a query with sensitive data, the URI SHOULD NOT contain sensitive parts of the original body.

Caching

QUERY responses are cacheable. The cache key MUST include the request content and related metadata such as the media type. Caches MAY normalize the body first, for example by removing content encoding or normalizing JSON for a +json type, to get more hits. The spec warns that bad normalization can return the wrong response, so expect CDNs to be careful here.

Redirects

A 301, 302, 307 or 308 means "send the same QUERY to the new URI". Unlike POST, a QUERY must not be rewritten to GET on a 301 or 302. A 303 See Other means "fetch the result with a GET on this URI".

The Accept-Query header

Accept-Query is a new response header that advertises QUERY support and the query formats a resource accepts. It's a Structured Field list, so parse it as one:

Accept-Query: "application/jsonpath", application/sql;charset="UTF-8"

Clients can also discover support with OPTIONS and read the Allow header, or just send the QUERY and handle a 405 Method Not Allowed.

Which tools support QUERY today?

Support is uneven, so test your own stack. Here's what we confirmed on October 28, 2026:

Tool Result
Node.js 24 http server http.METHODS includes QUERY; a plain server received the method and body
Node.js 24 fetch Sent a QUERY with a JSON body
curl 8.7 curl -X QUERY with -d sent the method and body
Python 3.14 http.client Sent a QUERY with a body
OpenAPI 3.2 The Path Item Object has a query field for QUERY operations
Apidog CLI 2.2.12 The endpoint-create schema accepts "method": "query"

Here's the curl call we used against a local Node server:

curl -i -X QUERY http://localhost:3000/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"q":"running shoe","limit":2}'

The Fetch Standard only forbids a body on GET and HEAD, so browsers can send QUERY with a body. QUERY is not a CORS-safelisted method, though, so every cross-origin QUERY triggers a preflight. Your server must list QUERY in Access-Control-Allow-Methods.

The gaps are in the middle of the network: reverse proxies, API gateways, WAFs and CDNs that allowlist methods or don't key their cache on the body. Check each hop before you ship. The APIs You Won't Hate newsletter notes that many web frameworks already handle QUERY directly or through custom-method routing.

How to adopt QUERY without breaking clients

You don't have to rip out your POST search endpoints.

  1. Add QUERY alongside the POST route. Point both at the same handler. New clients use QUERY; old ones keep working.
  2. Advertise it. Return Accept-Query on the resource and include QUERY in Allow on OPTIONS and 405 responses.
  3. Enforce Content-Type. Return 400 or 415 as the RFC recommends, and 422 for queries that parse but can't run.
  4. Fall back on 405 or 501. Clients should retry the same body as POST when a hop rejects QUERY.
  5. Fix CORS. Add QUERY to Access-Control-Allow-Methods for browser clients.
  6. Decide on caching. Only enable shared caching where your cache keys on the body. Otherwise return a Location URI and let clients GET it.
  7. Document it. In OpenAPI 3.2, define the operation under query: on the path item: 
openapi: 3.2.0
paths:
  /products:
    query:
      summary: Search products
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductQuery'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Matching products

Short, simple filters can stay as query strings on GET. RFC 10008 itself says that if your query is that short, GET is probably the better choice.

Let your coding agent test a QUERY endpoint with Apidog CLI

A new method means checking the happy path, every error code and the fallback route. Hand that to Claude Code, Codex or Cursor and let it drive the Apidog CLI.

Install the CLI, log in, and add the Apidog skill to your agent:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Then give your agent one prompt:

In Apidog project <projectId>, add a QUERY /products endpoint that takes a
JSON body {q, limit}. Create test cases that assert 200 with an array for a
valid body, 415 for Content-Type text/plain, and 400 with no Content-Type.
Run them against the staging environment and summarize any failures.

The agent reads each schema, validates its payload and only then writes:

apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

The endpoint.json it writes sets "method": "query", which the CLI's endpoint-create schema lists alongside get, post and the WebDAV methods. Add --upload-report to see the run in the Apidog app. The same apidog run command with -r junit drops into CI; see how to run API tests in CI with apidog run and how to use the Apidog CLI in Claude Code. Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users.

FAQ

Is the HTTP QUERY method an official standard? Yes. RFC 10008 is a Standards Track, Proposed Standard RFC published in June 2026, and IANA lists QUERY in the HTTP Method Registry as safe and idempotent.

Is QUERY just GET with a body? Close, but it's better defined. RFC 9110 gives a GET body no semantics, so intermediaries can ignore or reject it. QUERY makes the body the query, requires a Content-Type, and folds the body into the cache key.

When should I use QUERY instead of POST? Use QUERY for any read-only search or filter that's too large or too sensitive for a URL. Keep POST for requests that create or change something.

Can browsers send QUERY requests? Yes, through fetch with a custom method. Cross-origin QUERY requests always need a CORS preflight, so your server must allow the method.

Are QUERY responses cached? They can be. Caches must include the request body and its metadata in the cache key. Many CDNs and proxies don't do that yet, so check yours or return a Location URI that clients can GET.

Does OpenAPI support QUERY? OpenAPI 3.2 adds a query field to the Path Item Object for QUERY operations, so you can document them without extensions.

title: Learning to Read Braille: Benchmarking and Improving Braille Recognition Capabilities of VLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.36195v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite rapid progress in visual understanding and document transcription, modern vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with a fundamental accessibility task: reading Braille from images. We introduce BrailleBench, a manually curated benchmark of 259 real-world Grade-1 and Grade-2 Braille images. We evaluate proprietary, open-weight, OCR-specialized, and tool-assisted multimodal systems and find that standalone general-purpose models perform poorly at directly transcribing Braille images, whereas tool-assisted systems perform much better. We design a synthetic Braille generation pipeline with diverse layouts and image perturbations. A 2B VLM model trained on our synthetic data reaches 87% exact match on Grade-1 and 61% on Grade-2 BrailleBench, outperforming standalone VLMs and achieving the highest Grade-2 exact match score among the evaluated systems. We further show that high accuracy on synthetic validation data does not guarantee high accuracy on real photographs in our experiments: models trained on prior synthetic data reach up to 96% on their synthetic validation set but at most 3.26% on Grade-1 BrailleBench. Our results identify an accessibility-relevant capability gap in multimodal systems and show that targeted synthetic supervision can improve real-world Braille transcription.

title: OpenAI API key exposed in the browser: NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_ and dangerouslyAllowBrowser
description:
The client said undefined, so the key got a prefix. Then the SDK refused to run in the browser, so it got a flag:

"use client";
const openai = new OpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENAI_API_KEY,
  dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true,
});

It works. And the OpenAI API key is now in plain text in a JavaScript file every visitor downloads. (A made-up example, but a very common one.)

Prefixes publish values

  • Next.js inlines NEXT_PUBLIC_ values "into any JavaScript sent to the browser".
  • Vite: "VITE_* variables should not contain sensitive information such as API keys."
  • Create React App: "Do not store any secrets (such as private API keys) in your React app!"

The OpenAI and Anthropic JS SDKs block browsers by default "to avoid exposing your secret API credentials". dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true switches that guard off.

Five ways AI keys reach the bundle

  1. A public prefix on the key (.env, CI, Dockerfile)
  2. Reading that variable in client code
  3. dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true
  4. A server-only key in a "use client" file (and the "fix" of adding a prefix)
  5. Vite define, webpack DefinePlugin, next.config env

Plus a key pasted into a component "just to test".

Fix: call the provider from a server route with a server-only variable, have the page call that route, and rotate any key that was ever deployed. Deleting it from the code is not enough: old builds and caches still have it. In a Vite app with no server, a small serverless or edge function does the same job.

Checked in VS Code

I built BrowserKey, a free VS Code extension that catches all of these for Next.js, Vite, CRA, Expo, Nuxt, Gatsby, SvelteKit and Astro, and for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, xAI, OpenRouter and more. Six rules, a Quick Fix to rename to a server-only variable, and an activity bar panel:

NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENAI_API_KEY in .env.local is bundled into the browser
new OpenAI({ dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true }) exposes the API key
hardcoded OpenAI key sk-proj-**** in browser code

Keys are always masked. No network, no telemetry, no child processes.

code --install-extension jaytankdev.browserkey

Source (MIT): github.com/jay-tank/browserkey

Full write-up (framework docs, the server route fix, all six rules, FAQ): OpenAI API key exposed in the browser

title: Multi-Label Agreement: A Flexible Framework for Inter-Annotator Reliability
description:
arXiv:2610.37292v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable evaluation of inter-annotator agreement (IAA) is important for assessing the consistency of annotation processes. While established IAA metrics such as Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa, and Krippendorff's alpha are commonly applied in single-label settings, multi-label tasks require additional decisions about how full label sets, joint selections, and joint omissions should be compared.
  In this work, we present Multi-Label Agreement (MLA), a flexible framework for evaluating agreement in multi-label annotation tasks. MLA preserves the full binary label vectors assigned to each item and uses average pairwise Hamming agreement, thereby accounting for both joint selections and joint omissions. Its pooled-marginal form is not a mathematically independent coefficient: it is a chance-disagreement-weighted average of label-wise Fleiss/Scott-type coefficients and is closely related to Krippendorff's alpha with normalized Hamming distance. The framework supports pooled-marginal, Gwet AC1, and fixed-baseline normalizations, yields item-level, label-level, and corpus-level results, and includes a conditional minimum-agreement diagnostic. Through a worked example and Monte Carlo simulations, we show how the resulting values depend on label prevalence, the declared label inventory, and the selected model of expected agreement. We also provide a Python implementation. MLA thus offers a transparent and interpretable framework for multi-label agreement analysis without claiming that one normalization is universally preferable.

title: React: estados de verificación que sí explican
description:
Un formulario de registro puede funcionar perfectamente y aun así dejar al usuario preguntándose qué pasó. Pulsa “Enviar”, el botón gira, llega un email y la pantalla sigue pareciendo congelada. En una interfaz que usa un generador de correo temporal para pruebas, este problema se ve rápido, pero también aparece en productos reales.

La solución no es añadir otro spinner. En mis revisiones de frontend, suele funcionar mejor modelar la verificación de email como un conjunto pequeño de estados, hacer que cada estado explique la siguiente acción y medir cuánto tiempo permanece visible. Así React, CSS y accesibilidad trabajan sobre la misma decisión de diseño.

El problema no es solo esperar

Una verificación tiene varios momentos distintos: el formulario se está enviando, el servidor aceptó la solicitud, el mensaje todavía no aparece, el usuario lo abrió, el enlace caducó o algo falló. Si todo se representa con loading: true, la interfaz pierde información.

También pierde información para lectores de pantalla. Un cambio visual en un icono no garantiza que el cambio sea anunciado. Y si el mensaje de éxito reemplaza el formulario sin mover el foco, una persona que navega con teclado puede quedar en un lugar inesperado.

Por eso conviene escribir primero el contrato de la interfaz:

  • idle: el formulario está listo para recibir datos.
  • sending: la acción está en curso y el botón no debe duplicarla.
  • waiting: la solicitud fue aceptada, pero el email aún no está confirmado.
  • verified: la dirección fue confirmada.
  • error: la persona tiene una acción clara para recuperarse.

Este enfoque se parece a revisar estados de espera más tranquilos en React, pero añade una distinción importante: esperar al servidor no es lo mismo que esperar al usuario.

Modela el flujo como estados visibles

Un estado útil no describe solo lo que hace el código. Describe lo que la persona puede entender. waiting debería decir que el email fue solicitado, cuánto puede tardar aproximadamente y qué hacer si no aparece. No hace falta prometer una cifra demasido exacta si la entrega depende de varios servicios.

En React, un componente sencillo puede centralizar esa comunicación:

const messages = {
  idle: "Introduce tu email para continuar.",
  sending: "Enviando el mensaje de verificación…",
  waiting: "Revisa tu bandeja. Puedes solicitar otro mensaje en un momento.",
  verified: "Email verificado. Ya puedes continuar.",
  error: "No pudimos enviar el mensaje. Inténtalo de nuevo."
};

function VerificationStatus({ state }) {
  const isBusy = state === "sending";

  return (
    <section aria-labelledby="verification-title">
      <h2 id="verification-title">Verificación de email</h2>
      <p role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
        {messages[state]}
      </p>
      <button type="submit" disabled={isBusy}>
        {isBusy ? "Enviando…" : "Enviar verificación"}
      </button>
    </section>
  );
}

El role="status" evita que el mensaje dependa de un cambio de color o de una animación. aria-atomic ayuda a anunciar el texto completo y no solo la palabra que cambió. En un formulario más complejo usaría un aria-describedby para asociar errores específicos con cada campo, pero la regla es la misma: cada salida importante debe tener una relación semántica.

CSS y accesibilidad que no compiten

Los estados pueden verse claramente sin convertir la pantalla en un semáforo. Un borde, un icono con texto y un espacio estable suelen ser suficientes:

.verification-status {
  min-height: 3rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  border-inline-start: 0.25rem solid currentColor;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    scroll-behavior: auto;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms;
    animation-duration: 0.01ms;
  }
}

Reservar una altura mínima reduce el salto visual cuando aparece el mensaje. Eso es un detalle pequeño, pero evita que el botón se mueva justo cuando alguien va a activarlo. El color puede reforzar el estado, pero nunca debe ser la única señal. Tambien conviene comprobar el contraste en el estado de error y en el foco visible.

En equipos que prueban muchos flujos aparece a veces la frase “temp org mail”. Puede servir como término de búsqueda interno para localizar fixtures, pero no debería convertirse en una etiqueta visible para el usuario: la interfaz debe hablar de verificación, no de cómo se creó el dato de prueba.

Cómo medir si la espera mejoró

No mediría solo el tiempo hasta que llega el email. Hay tres señales más útiles:

  1. Abandono durante waiting: cuántas personas vuelven atrás o cierran la pantalla.
  2. Reintentos: cuántas pulsan “enviar otra vez” antes de que expire el intervalo.
  3. Recuperación: cuántas completan el flujo después de un error o de una primera entrega lenta.

Un evento como verification_state_changed puede registrar el estado, el tiempo transcurrido y un identificador de ejecución no sensible. No guardaría la dirección completa en analítica si no es necesaria. Para revisar el flujo completo, es útil probar renovaciones de correo en un SaaS con un buzón aislado y casos de entrega lenta.

El rendimiento también cuenta. No hace falta montar un componente grande para cada mensaje ni recalcular toda la página al cambiar de estado. Mantén el estado cerca del formulario, evita efectos que hagan polling sin límite y cancela las solicitudes cuando el componente se desmonte. Así se reduce el trabajo innecesario y el error de actualizar una pantalla que ya no existe.

Checklist antes de enviarlo a producción

  • ¿Cada estado tiene una explicación en texto, no solo un icono?
  • ¿El mensaje cambia dentro de una región anunciable?
  • ¿El botón evita envíos dobles sin dejar al usuario sin salida?
  • ¿El foco queda en un lugar lógico después de verificar?
  • ¿El layout conserva su altura cuando aparece un error?
  • ¿La interfaz respeta prefers-reduced-motion?
  • ¿Las métricas distinguen entrega lenta, error y abandono?
  • ¿Las pruebas cubren un mensaje tardío, un enlace caducado y un reintento?

Una verificación de email es una conversación corta entre producto y usuario. Si React conoce los estados, CSS conserva el espacio y la capa accesible anuncia lo que ocurre, la espera deja de sentirse como un fallo. El resultado es más claro para la persona, más fácil de probar y practicamente más sencillo de mantener.

title: Augmentation-Guided Adversarial Training via Local Stability-Based Sample Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.33331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial training remains one of the most effective defenses against adversarial attacks, but its standard PGD-based training is computationally expensive because adversarial examples are generated for every training sample. Selective adversarial training reduces this cost by perturbing only a subset of samples. However, existing selective techniques typically rely on point-wise difficulty signals such as loss, entropy, margin, or gradients. We show that these point-wise criteria do not capture local instability in a sample's neighborhood. Motivated by this, we propose Augmentation-Guided Adversarial Training (AGAT), a selective adversarial training framework that uses augmentation-induced local variation to allocate samples with unstable neighborhoods for adversarial training. AGAT ranks samples using Augmentation-based Local Stability (ALS), a lightweight score that measures the normalized change in model logits between an input and its label-preserving augmented variant. Experiments across different architectures on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet-200 demonstrate that AGAT achieves comparable or higher robust accuracy while applying adversarial supervision to only 20-30% of the training samples in each minibatch. AGAT also requires less training time than all other adversarial training baselines in the computational cost evaluation.

title: One Durable Object per room: how Kadal Deck runs a live audience on Cloudflare
description:
The presenter view said "1 phone connected". The phone was in a pocket, screen off, and the presenter had already pressed Disconnect. Nothing changed.

That bug, and the Durable Objects behaviour behind it, is a good way into the live room in Kadal Deck, which we launched this week. A talk is one MDX file, and every published deck gets a room: the audience scans a QR code, with no app and no login, and their phones follow the slides, answer polls and quizzes, ask and upvote questions, and react. The presenter's phone can be the remote. It runs on Cloudflare Workers, with one Durable Object per room.

This post is about how we built that room, what we traded away, and what broke.

Why not just link to a polling app?

Most interactive talks use two products: the slides, and a separate audience tool. The speaker says "go to this other site and type code 4417", and the talk splits in two.

  • The audience leaves the talk to join a second thing, often behind a sign-up.
  • The second thing has no idea which slide is showing.
  • The speaker switches windows to show results, in front of everyone.
  • Afterwards, the questions and votes live in someone else's export.

We wanted the poll to be part of the slide: <Poll id="stack" question="What do you deploy on?" options={[...]} /> in the MDX, and the same connection that carries the slide position carries the vote. That means the room has to know the talk, not just the poll.

The shape of it

In short: one Worker on two hostnames. deck.kadal.cc serves the account and dashboard; decks.kadal.cc serves published decks and the APIs a deck calls. Phones and the presenter view open a WebSocket to /api/rooms/<id>/ws on decks.kadal.cc. The Worker checks who they are and forwards the upgrade to that deck's Durable Object (DeckRoom). The room writes its state to its own storage, and writes what should outlive the talk (sessions, questions, poll results) to D1. Published files sit in R2, addressed by SHA-256.

A few details matter here.

Two origins, one Worker. A published deck is somebody's HTML and JavaScript. It used to share an origin with the dashboard and the sign-in cookie. Now decks live on decks.kadal.cc, and the session cookie is __Host-kd_session, which is host-only, so the browser never sends it to the decks origin. A deck has no account authority at all. The presenter proves who they are with a short-lived ticket scoped to that one deck. The page keeps it in memory, and it usually arrives in the URL fragment, which never reaches a server log.

Rooms are named by deck id. When the host serves a published deck, it writes room: deck.id into the page's index.html. The Worker calls ROOMS.idFromName() with that id, so every phone in the world that opens that deck reaches the same object, wherever it runs.

Files are content-addressed. Publishing sends a manifest of path to SHA-256. The Worker answers with the hashes it doesn't have yet, the CLI uploads only those, and the Worker hashes each body again before writing it to R2 at blobs/<sha256>. Republishing after a one-line edit uploads a handful of files, not the whole build.

Why one Durable Object per room

A talk is small, busy, ordered state: one slide position, a few polls, a list of questions, a few hundred phones. A Durable Object gives us one single-threaded place for all of it. Two people upvoting the same question at the same moment can't race, because there is nothing to race against. No locks, no pub/sub layer, no "which server holds this talk" lookup.

The cost is a ceiling. One object handles one room, and we can't spread a room across machines. So we cap the audience by plan, and the room itself enforces it. The Worker passes the cap in a header: 25 viewers at once on Free, 100 on Starter, 500 on Pro, 1,000 on Team. The presenter always gets in.

The Worker, not the socket, decides who you are:

app.get("/api/rooms/:slug/ws", async (c) => {
  const slug = c.req.param("slug");
  if (!validSlug(slug)) return c.text("bad room", 400);
  const wantsPresenter = c.req.query("role") === "presenter";
  // … phone remotes take their own path (pairing, below)
  const presenter = wantsPresenter && (await isPresenter(c, slug));
  if (wantsPresenter && !presenter) return c.text("presenter passcode required", 401);
  if (!presenter) {
    const ok = await verifyTurnstile(c.env, c.req.query("t") ?? null, clientAddress(c));
    if (!ok) return c.text("verification required", 403);
  }
  const headers = new Headers(c.req.raw.headers);
  headers.set(ROLE_HEADER, presenter ? "presenter" : "viewer");
  headers.delete(DETAIL_HEADER); // the full snapshot is the Worker's to ask for
  headers.set(SLUG_HEADER, slug);
  const room = await publishedRoom(c.env, slug);
  if (room) headers.set(CAP_HEADER, String(room.audience));
  else headers.delete(CAP_HEADER);
  return c.env.ROOMS.get(c.env.ROOMS.idFromName(slug)).fetch(new Request(c.req.raw, { headers }));
});

Inside the room, the role is stored on the socket and a hello message can't change it. A viewer that sends a presenter-only message (nav, poll:open, session and 24 others) is ignored without a reply.

How state survives

The room uses WebSocket hibernation (ctx.acceptWebSocket), so an idle room is evicted from memory while its sockets stay open. When a message arrives, the runtime builds the object again and we reload. That splits the state in two.

Per-socket facts (viewer id, current slide, pace vote, raised hand, last ping) live in each socket's attachment via serializeAttachment, which survives hibernation. Room-wide state is one object in Durable Object storage, written at most every 250 ms:

private async load(): Promise<Persisted> {
  if (this.data) return this.data;
  const stored = await this.ctx.storage.get<Persisted>("room");
  // … the phone remote's pairing and the slug load here too
  this.data = stored ?? { state: structuredClone(EMPTY_ROOM), voters: {}, pollVotes: {}, /* … */ };
  // Presence is live, never restored.
  this.data.state.presence = { viewers: 0, presenter: false, bySlide: {}, /* … */ };
  this.data.state.pointer = null;
  return this.data;
}

private save() {
  if (this.saveTimer) return;
  this.saveTimer = setTimeout(() => {
    this.saveTimer = null;
    if (this.data) void this.ctx.storage.put("room", this.data);
  }, 250);
}

Presence is never stored, because it would be wrong the moment it was read back. It is recomputed from the attachments of the sockets that are still open, and it counts people, not sockets: one viewer id on a phone and a laptop is one person.

Two caveats we accept. A crash can lose up to 250 ms of changes. And the per-viewer rate-limit counters live in memory, so they reset when the room hibernates. That's fine, because a room only hibernates when nobody is sending anything.

A Durable Object has one alarm, and ours does three jobs: it drops sockets that have been silent for 90 seconds (clients ping every 25), it closes a quiz when its timer runs out, and during a session it writes a summary to D1 every minute.

Fanning out the presenter's position

When the presenter moves, the room stores the position, serialises the message once and sends the same string to every live socket except the sender:

private broadcast(m: ServerMessage, except?: WebSocket) {
  const s = JSON.stringify(m);
  for (const [ws, a] of this.live(except)) {
    if (a.pending) continue; // a phone remote that hasn't paired yet
    try {
      ws.send(s);
    } catch {
      /* closed */
    }
  }
}

The server doesn't track who is "following". Every viewer gets every nav, and the client decides. A viewer starts in step with the presenter. Any move of their own (a key, a swipe, the overview) stops following, and a pill offers to follow again. That keeps the room simple and lets people flip back to the slide with the code sample without fighting the presenter. The presenter still sees where people are, because presence includes a count per slide.

Polls without accounts

There are no audience accounts, so "one vote per person" means one vote per anonymous viewer id. The client makes a random id once and keeps it in localStorage (deck.viewer). The room keeps every answer by that id, so a reconnect restores your vote and a second vote moves it instead of adding one:

case "poll:vote": {
  const p = data.state.polls[m.id];
  if (!p || !p.open) return;
  const votes = (data.pollVotes[m.id] ??= {});
  // … "words" and "multi" polls elided
  const option = p.def.kind === "rating" ? ((m.rating ?? 0) | 0) - 1 : (m.option ?? -1) | 0;
  if (option < 0 || option >= p.counts.length) return;
  const previous = votes[a.viewer] as number | undefined;
  if (previous !== undefined) p.counts[previous] = Math.max(0, (p.counts[previous] ?? 0) - 1);
  else p.total++;
  p.counts[option] = (p.counts[option] ?? 0) + 1;
  votes[a.viewer] = option;
  this.patch({ polls: data.state.polls });
  return;
}

Question upvotes and quiz answers work the same way. To be honest about it: the id is the client's own word. This stops the common accidents (two tabs, a dropped connection, an eager double tap), not a determined script that opens fresh connections. Writing this post turned up a cheaper hole: a second hello on an open socket used to replace its viewer id, so one socket could vote again and again. Now the first hello names the connection for good, and repeats are rate-limited. What raises the cost of a script further is the audience cap, the rate limits below, and a Turnstile check the Worker can demand before a viewer's socket is accepted. We leave that one off, because joining a talk should take one scan and nothing else.

Limits

Every message passes three gates, in this order: presenter-only types from a viewer are dropped, a paired phone remote may only send command, and then a per-viewer, per-type counter over a fixed window:

const LIMITS: Record<string, { n: number; per: number }> = {
  react: { n: 8, per: 2000 },
  "qa:ask": { n: 1, per: 5000 },
  "qa:vote": { n: 10, per: 5000 },
  "poll:vote": { n: 6, per: 5000 },
  "quiz:answer": { n: 3, per: 5000 },
  pointer: { n: 120, per: 2000 },
  draw: { n: 60, per: 2000 },
  // …
};

Everything else is clamped: frames over 64,000 characters are ignored, questions are cut to 280 characters, the room keeps the newest 200 questions, a slide keeps 200 strokes of up to 2,000 points each, and a poll has at most 12 options. The writes to D1 for questions and votes are fire-and-forget. During the talk the room is the source of truth, and D1 is the record afterwards.

What went wrong

Closed sockets that stayed. Back to the phone in the pocket. The room counted every socket ctx.getWebSockets() returned. A socket the room has closed stays in that list until the other end answers the close, and a phone that has gone to sleep never answers. So "1 phone connected" stayed, and Disconnect closed a socket that kept counting. The fix: mark the socket gone in its attachment before closing it, and count only open sockets that aren't marked:

private live(except?: WebSocket): [WebSocket, Attachment][] {
  const out: [WebSocket, Attachment][] = [];
  for (const ws of this.ctx.getWebSockets()) {
    if (ws === except) continue;
    const state = (ws as { readyState?: number }).readyState;
    if (typeof state === "number" && state !== 1) continue;
    const a = this.att(ws);
    if (!a.gone) out.push([ws, a]);
  }
  return out;
}

We wrote scripts/remote-check.mjs to reproduce it over real WebSockets with a client that never answers the close. Before the fix it reported remotes=1 after Disconnect. After, 0.

A command that ran twice. In the same change we found that the phone's commands went to every presenter socket, including a leftover socket from a page that had never said hello. That window ran each command a second time. Routing now skips sockets that haven't introduced themselves.

The presenter who left. Viewers of our tour deck were offered "Follow the presenter" long after the presenter had gone. The room counted a presenter socket as present until the next sweep dropped it. Now a presenter counts only if it has pinged in the last 90 seconds. We also moved the alarm's rescheduling ahead of the quiz and session work, because a throw there could have stopped the sweeps for good.

The tab that wouldn't stop presenting. Even with that fix, a presenter view left open in a background tab kept presenting, because a hidden tab still pings (Chrome slows its timers to about once a minute, which is inside 90 seconds). The engine now steps a presenter view down to a viewer after 15 minutes hidden, unless a session is live or a phone remote is paired, since a phone may be driving that hidden window on purpose.

What's open and what's hosted

The engine, @kadal/deck, is AGPL-3.0 and on npm. It includes the room client and the protocol types. Import ClientMessage, ServerMessage and RoomState from @kadal/deck/protocol, and your server can't drift from the client. It also ships kadal-deck relay, a small relay so the phone remote works for a deck on a static host.

The room server itself, the DeckRoom class we've quoted here, is not in the engine repo yet. What is public is the protocol and the endpoints a host has to answer, written up in the self-hosting docs, so you can run your own room on whatever you like and point a deck at it with live.api.

Try it

The tour deck has a live room. Open it on a laptop and join from your phone: https://decks.kadal.cc/@kadal-hq/tour/

  • Engine: https://github.com/kadalcc/deck
  • Docs, including the room protocol and self-hosting: https://deck.kadal.cc/docs/

If you've handled closed-but-listed sockets on Durable Objects another way, we'd like to hear how.

title: GSM to Kilograms: Work Out Copier Paper Weight per Ream in Python
description:
Ordering paper for an office is easier when you know what a carton weighs before it arrives. The GSM printed on the ream (grams per square metre) is all you need to work it out.

The formula

weight of one sheet = GSM x sheet area (m²)

A4 is 210 x 297 mm, so one sheet is 0.21 x 0.297 = 0.06237 m². A3 is exactly twice that.

SIZES_M2 = {"A4": 0.210 * 0.297, "A3": 0.297 * 0.420}

def ream_kg(gsm, size="A4", sheets=500):
    return gsm * SIZES_M2[size] * sheets / 1000

for gsm in (70, 75, 80):
    print(gsm, "GSM A4 ream:", round(ream_kg(gsm), 2), "kg")

Output:

70 GSM A4 ream: 2.18 kg
75 GSM A4 ream: 2.34 kg
80 GSM A4 ream: 2.49 kg

An 80 GSM A3 ream comes to about 4.99 kg.

Cartons

Paper usually ships in cartons of 5 or 10 reams:

def carton_kg(gsm, reams, size="A4"):
    return ream_kg(gsm, size) * reams

print(round(carton_kg(80, 5), 1))   # 12.5
print(round(carton_kg(80, 10), 1))  # 24.9

That is paper only; the carton itself adds a little more.

How many reams a month? 

def reams_per_month(pages_per_day, working_days=26):
    return pages_per_day * working_days / 500

print(round(reams_per_month(400), 1))  # 20.8 -> order 21 reams

Picking a GSM

As a rough guide, 70 GSM is lighter and cheaper per sheet and works for internal drafts, while 80 GSM is stiffer and less see-through, so it suits double-sided printing and documents that go to customers. 75 GSM sits in between.

PackForge supplies A4, A3 and legal-size copier paper in 70, 75 and 80 GSM, by the ream of 500 sheets or in cartons of 5 or 10 reams: Printing and copier paper.

title: Why Positive Grid Profit Can Coexist With Negative Total P&L
description:
A grid-bot dashboard can show profitable completed cycles while the overall account is losing money. These figures describe different parts of the strategy. For anyone building a trading dashboard, preserving that distinction is an accounting requirement.

Separate completed cycles from open exposure

Grid profit summarizes completed buy/sell cycles according to the platform's reporting rules. Total P&L also depends on open positions and the costs assigned to the account. Read the venue's definitions before combining its fields: a fee already included in a reported profit must not be subtracted again.

Consider an explicitly hypothetical example:

Component Illustrative units
Completed-cycle profit +20
Open-position P&L -35
Additional costs not yet counted above -3
Total -18

The positive cycle result does not cover the open loss and remaining costs. This is an accounting illustration, not a backtest or a claim about a real bot.

Make the accounting boundary explicit in code

A small pure function can express the example, provided every input uses the same currency, time window and accounting boundary:

from decimal import Decimal

def illustrative_total(cycle_profit, open_pnl, extra_costs):
    # extra_costs is positive for costs, and excludes costs
    # already included in either of the first two inputs.
    return cycle_profit + open_pnl - extra_costs

result = illustrative_total(
    Decimal('20'), Decimal('-35'), Decimal('3')
)
# result == Decimal('-18')

This is not a universal exchange reconciliation function. Real adapters must separately handle deposits, withdrawals, realized position P&L, funding and the exact definition of each venue field. Decimal arithmetic avoids binary floating-point surprises, but it cannot fix incorrectly classified inputs.

Four questions for a dashboard

  1. Is the result live, backtested or simulated?
  2. What time window and starting capital does it cover?
  3. Which fees, funding and capital flows are included?
  4. Can another reader reproduce the inputs and assumptions?

For a platform-specific example of the distinction, see Bybit's Spot Grid Bot FAQ. Spot and futures accounting should not be treated as interchangeable.

Published by the Grid Bot Wars project, which explores grid mechanics, costs and risk. Educational material; no verified return or universal optimal strategy is claimed.

title: Frankly Speaking: The Company Election Integrity Keeps in Congressional Communication
description:
arXiv:2610.36187v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Election integrity is a shared commitment in American politics, but Democrats and Republicans in Congress increasingly mean different things by it. Analyzing 10,420 congressional e-newsletters sent from 2010 to 2025, we examine how the two parties invoke election terms such as ``integrity,'' ``security,'' and ``fraud.'' Using diachronic word embeddings, which track semantic change through how words are used in context, we measure how differently each party uses each term, how much each party shifts, and whether they share nearest semantic neighbors. We show that members of Congress do not need different words to tell different stories about elections. They need only place those same words in different company. Across nearly every term and year, the two parties surround election-integrity vocabulary with entirely different words. That divergence is easy to miss, because most election vocabulary is no more divergent than other words used at roughly the same frequency, and neither party's usage shifted more than the other's. Only a subset of terms grew more divergent, most notably ``certification,'' while ``rigged'' and ``stolen'' entered election discourse after 2020 and polarized there. By 2024, Democrats surround ``voter,'' ``election,'' and ``integrity'' with the language of access and administration. Republicans surround the same terms with ``citizenship verification,'' ``noncitizen voting,'' and ``border security.'' For one party, integrity means protecting eligible voters' ability to cast a ballot. For the other, it means protecting the electoral process from illegitimate ballots. Election officials, who must administer a single system under both definitions, inherit this tension.

title: Cross-Platform Development with React: Build for Web, iOS, and Android
description:
Building separate applications for the web, iOS, and Android can quickly become expensive. Each platform introduces its own development requirements, testing challenges, and maintenance costs, making it difficult for teams to deliver consistent experiences without duplicating significant amounts of work.

React offers a practical way to approach this problem through reusable components, declarative UI development, and a shared JavaScript ecosystem. By combining React for the web with React Native for mobile applications, teams can reuse business logic while adapting interfaces to the capabilities of each platform.

The key is understanding what should be shared and what should remain platform-specific. Cross-platform development is not about forcing every screen into identical code; it is about reducing duplication without compromising usability or maintainability.

Building a Shared Architecture with React and React Native

React and React Native share a component-based programming model, but they target different rendering environments. React typically renders interfaces using HTML elements in a browser, while React Native uses native platform components such as View, Text, and Pressable. React Native Web can also help teams reuse React Native components in web applications when the project architecture supports it.

A maintainable cross-platform application usually separates business logic, data access, validation, and domain models from presentation. For example, authentication rules, product filtering, currency formatting, and API communication can live in shared JavaScript modules. Web and mobile interfaces can then consume those modules while maintaining platform-appropriate navigation, accessibility, and interactions.

Consider an application that displays products from an API. The product service can fetch and normalize data once, while the web interface and mobile interface independently decide how to display loading indicators, errors, and product cards. This separation makes the codebase easier to test and allows platform teams to evolve their interfaces without duplicating core business rules.

The following runnable JavaScript example demonstrates this architecture without requiring a browser or React Native runtime. It simulates an API, validates product data, applies shared business logic, and renders platform-specific output as text in Node.js. The same service and domain functions could later be imported into actual React and React Native components.

const API_BASE_URL = "https://example.com/api";

// Simulate an API response so the example runs without credentials.
const mockProducts = [
  { id: 1, name: "Wireless Headphones", price: 79.99, stock: 12 },
  { id: 2, name: "Mechanical Keyboard", price: 129.5, stock: 0 },
  { id: 3, name: "USB-C Hub", price: 39.95, stock: 8 },
];

// Step 1: Define shared validation for data received from any API.
function validateProduct(product) {
  if (!product || typeof product !== "object") {
    throw new TypeError("Product must be an object");
  }

  if (!Number.isInteger(product.id) || product.id <= 0) {
    throw new TypeError("Product ID must be a positive integer");
  }

  if (typeof product.name !== "string" || !product.name.trim()) {
    throw new TypeError("Product name is required");
  }

  if (!Number.isFinite(product.price) || product.price < 0) {
    throw new TypeError("Product price must be a non-negative number");
  }

  if (!Number.isInteger(product.stock) || product.stock < 0) {
    throw new TypeError("Product stock must be a non-negative integer");
  }

  return { ...product, name: product.name.trim() };
}

// Step 2: Keep API access separate from UI components.
async function fetchProducts() {
  console.log("[API] Preparing product request...");
  console.log(`[API] Base URL: ${API_BASE_URL}`);

  // Replace this mock with fetch() when a real backend is available.
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
  const products = mockProducts.map(validateProduct);

  console.log(`[API] Received ${products.length} valid products.`);
  return products;
}

// Step 3: Share business rules across web and mobile applications.
function getAvailableProducts(products) {
  return products.filter((product) => product.stock > 0);
}

// Step 4: Share currency formatting across platforms.
function formatPrice(price, locale = "en-US", currency = "USD") {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, {
    style: "currency",
    currency,
  }).format(price);
}

// Step 5: Build a platform-independent product view model.
function createProductViewModel(product) {
  return {
    id: product.id,
    title: product.name,
    formattedPrice: formatPrice(product.price),
    availability: product.stock > 0 ? "In stock" : "Out of stock",
    canPurchase: product.stock > 0,
  };
}

// Step 6: Render output differently for each platform.
// Real applications would use React DOM or React Native components.
function renderWebProduct(product) {
  const status = product.canPurchase ? "Buy now" : "Unavailable";
  return `<article><h2>${product.title}</h2>` +
    `<p>${product.formattedPrice}</p>` +
    `<p>${product.availability}</p><button>${status}</button></article>`;
}

function renderMobileProduct(product) {
  const action = product.canPurchase ? "[ Buy now ]" : "[ Unavailable ]";
  return `📱 ${product.title}\n` +
    `   Price: ${product.formattedPrice}\n` +
    `   Status: ${product.availability}\n` +
    `   Action: ${action}`;
}

// Step 7: Run the shared workflow and display platform-specific results.
async function main() {
  try {
    console.log("\n=== Cross-Platform Product Demo ===");

    const products = await fetchProducts();
    const availableProducts = getAvailableProducts(products);

    console.log(`\n[Business] Available products: ${availableProducts.length}`);

    const viewModels = products.map(createProductViewModel);

    console.log("\n=== Web Presentation ===");
    viewModels.forEach((product) => {
      console.log(renderWebProduct(product));
    });

    console.log("\n=== Mobile Presentation ===");
    viewModels.forEach((product) => {
      console.log(renderMobileProduct(product));
      console.log("---");
    });

    console.log("\n[Done] Shared business logic completed successfully.");
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("[Error] Product workflow failed:", error.message);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

// Step 8: Start the application when this file is executed.
main();

Conclusion

Cross-platform development with React works best when teams treat code reuse as an architectural decision rather than a requirement to share everything. API services, validation, business rules, and data transformations are strong candidates for shared modules, while layouts, navigation, and platform-specific interactions may need separate implementations.

For production applications, organize shared logic into packages, use TypeScript to strengthen contracts, and test domain functions independently of the UI. Consider React Native Web when shared interface components are valuable, and introduce platform-specific files when native capabilities or user experience require them.

Start with one feature that has clear business rules and implement it across the platforms you support. Measure how much code is genuinely reusable, validate the experience on real devices, and refine the boundaries as the application grows. The goal is not maximum code sharing; it is delivering reliable experiences with less duplicated effort.

title: WithinVAE: Compact Visual Autoencoding with Self-Distilled Semantics
description:
arXiv:2610.36593v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual autoencoders must balance reconstruction fidelity, compactness, and semantic structure. Existing semantic tokenizers typically inherit semantics from pretrained recognition encoders, whose invariances can discard the appearance detail required for inversion. We show that this inheritance is unnecessary: semantic structure can be learned inside an autoencoder's own reconstructive representation. We introduce WithinVAE, a compact variational visual autoencoder with a sequential bottleneck, DINO/iBOT-style self-distillation from an exponential-moving-average copy of the autoencoder itself, and position-dependent token masking to achieve a 4-fold compression ratio, which is free of pretrained representation encoder or external semantic target. On ImageNet-1K at $256\times256$, WithinVAE improves all four reported reconstruction metrics over RPiAE including PSNR by 1.36 dB, while using half its latent scalar capacity. Under frozen evaluation, the same latents improve linear probing by 6.5 points over RPiAE and 5.1 points over our reconstruction-only baseline, attributing the semantic gains to self-distillation rather than architecture or external supervision. An auxiliary latent-to-latent model reproduces the ordered-compression trend, and a pixel-to-latent model transfers the objective to a pretrained generative space. These results separate the origin of semantic supervision from its use: a compact visual autoencoder can organize semantic structure without borrowing a recognition representation.

title: What Spexop UI Is Building — and What Exists Today
description:
Spexop UI is an early, free, local-first, open-source UI/UX desktop companion in development. I am sharing the direction and the current evidence separately so readers can tell what exists today from what we still intend to build.

The intended workflow

A developer keeps their existing strong coding agent in charge of planning, design decisions, risk, and oversight. User-configured free or low-cost LLM API workers are intended to take on bounded routine UI tasks. Spexop coordinates a small milestone, gates, and tasks in the background. It should verify each result with deterministic checks and a real browser when the task needs one, then show plain progress, blocked, and needs-user-action states.

The goal is to make small UI changes easier to delegate and inspect without losing the developer’s control of the project.

What we have actually checked

Current evidence is a private local coordination prototype that uses test doubles, plus a loopback browser status view. The prototype has technical tests and a real-browser observation of the local status flow. Those results support only that narrow prototype.

There is no packaged native desktop app, no verified live LLM API worker, and no external product acceptance yet. The Groq access path remains blocked by a provider-side 403 response. The public-source review is still open, so the current monorepo is not being presented as a public release. Earlier Theme, Foundation, Capture, and icon work are technical assets, not evidence that this new companion is ready to install.

Where to follow and contribute

The current product direction and status are on spexop.com. You can also follow the Spexop UI LinkedIn page.

I would value feedback on one question: what is the smallest UI task you would trust a bounded worker to do if a coding agent planned it and independent checks reported the result?

title: HTTP QUERY Metodu Nedir? RFC 10008, QUERY vs GET vs POST
description:
HTTP QUERY yöntemi, RFC 10008'de (Haziran 2026) tanımlanan, sorguyu istek gövdesinde gönderen ve hem güvenli hem de idempotent olan yeni bir istek yöntemidir. Onu gövdeli GET gibi düşünün: POST'un karmaşık filtreler için sunduğu alanı ve GET'in önbellekleme ile otomatik yeniden denemeler için sağladığı garantileri elde edersiniz.

Apidog'u bugün deneyin

URL'ye 3 KB'lık bir filtre tıkıştırdıysanız veya salt okunur bir aramayı POST olarak gönderip önbelleğinizin ve yeniden deneme mantığınızın bunu yok saydığını gördüyseniz, QUERY çözümdür. Bu kılavuz, spesifikasyonun ne söylediğini, QUERY'nin GET ve POST ile nasıl karşılaştırıldığını, bugün nelerin desteklediğini ve kodlama ajanınızla bir QUERY uç noktasını nasıl test edeceğinizi kapsar.

HTTP QUERY yöntemi nedir?

QUERY, hedef kaynaktan istek içeriğinde tanımlanan sorguyu çalıştırmasını ve sonucu döndürmesini isteyen bir HTTP yöntemidir. İstek gövdesi ve Content-Type sorguyu tanımlar. Yöntem güvenlidir (istemci durum değişikliği beklemez) ve idempotenttir (tekrarlanması aynı etkiyi yapar), böylece istemciler, proxy'ler ve önbellekler onu GET gibi yeniden deneyebilir ve önbelleğe alabilir.

Spesifikasyon, Julian Reschke (greenbytes), James M. Snell (Cloudflare) ve Mike Bishop (Akamai) tarafından Haziran 2026'da yayımlanan Önerilen Standart RFC 10008, "HTTP QUERY Yöntemi" belgesidir. IANA, onu HTTP Yöntem Kaydı'na "güvenli: evet, idempotent: evet" olarak ekledi; neredeyse olacağı WebDAV dönemi SEARCH yönteminin hemen yanına.

Bir QUERY isteği şöyle görünür:

QUERY /contacts HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept: application/json

select=surname,givenname,email&limit=10&match=%22email=*@example.*%22

Sunucu, 200 OK ve gövdede sonuçla yanıt verir.

GET ve POST neden yeterli değildi

QUERY'den önce karmaşık bir okuma için iki seçeneğiniz vardı ve ikisi de sızıntı yapar.

GET her şeyi URL'ye koyar. RFC 10008 bununla ilgili dört sorun sıralar:

  1. Boyut sınırları önceden bilinmez, çünkü bir istek birçok sistemden geçer. RFC 9110 yalnızca göndericilerin ve alıcıların en az 8.000 okteti desteklemesini önerir.
  2. Yapılandırılmış veriyi geçerli bir URI'ye kodlamak israftır.
  3. URI'ler, istek gövdelerinden çok daha sık günlüğe kaydedilir ve yer imlerine eklenir; bu da hassas filtreler için gizlilik sorunudur.
  4. Sorgu girdilerinin her kombinasyonu kendi kaynağı haline gelir.

Gövdeli GET de cevap değildir. RFC 9110, bir GET isteğindeki içeriğin tanımlı anlambilimi olmadığını söyler. Bazı sunucular onu okur, bazıları atar ve bazı proxy'ler isteği reddeder. Yol boyunca ona güvenemezsiniz.

POST çalışır, ancak niyet hakkında yalan söyler. Bir POST araması sorunsuz çalışır, yine de hiçbir şey bir istemciye, önbelleğe, proxy'ye veya yeniden deneme kitaplığına işlemin salt okunur olduğunu söylemez. Bu yüzden önbellekler onu atlar ve istemciler bağlantı düştükten sonra onu yeniden denemez. Yalnızca yeniden denemeleri güvenli hale getirmek için saf bir okumaya idempotency anahtarı eklemek zorunda kaldıysanız, bunu hissetmişsinizdir.

QUERY, POST'un gövdesini korur ve GET'in garantilerini ekler.

QUERY vs GET vs POST

İşte RFC 10008'in Tablo 1'ine dayanan karşılaştırma:

Özellik GET QUERY POST
Güvenli Evet Evet Potansiyel olarak hayır
Idempotent Evet Evet Potansiyel olarak hayır
İstek gövdesi Tanımlı anlambilim yok Beklenir, sorguyu tanımlar Beklenir
Sorgunun kendisi için URI Evet, tanım gereği İsteğe bağlı, Location ile Hayır
Sonuç için URI İsteğe bağlı, Content-Location ile İsteğe bağlı, Content-Location ile İsteğe bağlı, Content-Location ile
Önbelleğe alınabilir Evet Evet, gövde önbellek anahtarının parçasıdır Yalnızca sonraki GET veya HEAD için
Tarayıcılardan CORS preflight Basit istekler için değil Her zaman Basit istekler için değil

Kısa versiyon: sorgu URL'ye rahatça sığıyorsa GET, sığmıyorsa QUERY ve yalnızca istek durumu değiştiriyorsa POST kullanın. Klasik yöntemler hakkında bir hatırlatma için HTTP yöntemleri ve GET vs POST kılavuzlarımıza bakın.

RFC 10008 ne tanımlar

Content-Type zorunludur

Sunucular, Content-Type'ı eksik veya gövdeyle tutarsız olan bir QUERY'yi BAŞARISIZ bırakMALIDIR. RFC şu durum kodlarını önerir:

  • 400 Bad Request: medya türü yok veya içerikle eşleşmeyen bir tür var. Sunucular gövdeyi koklayıp bunu geçersiz kılamaz.
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type: kaynak bu sorgu biçimini desteklemiyor.
  • 422 Unprocessable Content: biçim uygun ancak sorgu çalıştırılamıyor; örneğin SQL, var olmayan bir tabloyu adlandırıyor.
  • 406 Not Acceptable: istemci, kaynağın üretemeyeceği bir yanıt türü istedi.

Location ve Content-Location

Bir sunucu, QUERY'yi daha sonra GET'leyebileceğiniz bir şeye dönüştüren iki isteğe bağlı başlık döndürebilir:

  • Content-Location, bu belirli çalıştırmanın saklanan sonucuna işaret eder. Geçici olabilir.
  • Location, saklanan sorgunun kendisine işaret eder. Bunun üzerinde bir GET, gövdeyi yeniden göndermeden sorguyu güncel verilerle yeniden çalıştırır.

RFC, GET önbelleklemesi daha basit olduğu için istemcilerin tekrarlanan isteklerde Location URI'si üzerinden GET'e geçmesini önerir. Hassas veri içeren bir sorgu için bu başlıklardan birini döndürürseniz, URI orijinal gövdenin hassas kısımlarını İÇERMEMELİDİR.

Önbellekleme

QUERY yanıtları önbelleğe alınabilir. Önbellek anahtarı, istek içeriğini ve medya türü gibi ilgili meta verileri İÇERMELİDİR. Önbellekler daha fazla isabet elde etmek için önce gövdeyi normalleştirebilir; örneğin içerik kodlamasını kaldırarak veya bir +json türü için JSON'u normalleştirerek. Spesifikasyon, kötü normalleştirmenin yanlış yanıt döndürebileceği konusunda uyarır, bu yüzden CDN'lerin burada dikkatli olmasını bekleyin.

Yönlendirmeler

301, 302, 307 veya 308, "aynı QUERY'yi yeni URI'ye gönder" anlamına gelir. POST'un aksine, bir QUERY 301 veya 302'de GET'e yeniden yazılmamalıdır. 303 See Other, "sonucu bu URI üzerinde bir GET ile al" anlamına gelir.

Accept-Query başlığı

Accept-Query, QUERY desteğini ve bir kaynağın kabul ettiği sorgu biçimlerini duyuran yeni bir yanıt başlığıdır. Bu bir Yapılandırılmış Alan listesidir, bu yüzden onu öyle ayrıştırın:

Accept-Query: "application/jsonpath", application/sql;charset="UTF-8"

İstemciler ayrıca OPTIONS ile desteği keşfedip Allow başlığını okuyabilir veya doğrudan QUERY gönderip bir 405 Method Not Allowed yanıtını işleyebilir.

Bugün hangi araçlar QUERY'yi destekliyor?

Destek dengesiz, bu yüzden kendi yığınınızı test edin. 28 Ekim 2026'da doğruladıklarımız şunlardır:

Araç Sonuç
Node.js 24 http sunucusu
curl 8.7 -d ile curl -X QUERY, yöntemi ve gövdeyi gönderdi
Python 3.14 http.client Gövdeli bir QUERY gönderdi
OpenAPI 3.2 Path Item Object, QUERY işlemleri için bir query alanına sahiptir
Apidog CLI 2.2.12 endpoint-create şeması "method": "query" değerini kabul eder

Yerel bir Node sunucusuna karşı kullandığımız curl çağrısı şöyledir:

curl -i -X QUERY http://localhost:3000/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"q":"running shoe","limit":2}'

Fetch Standard yalnızca GET ve HEAD'de gövdeyi yasaklar, bu yüzden tarayıcılar QUERY'yi gövdeli gönderebilir. Ancak QUERY, CORS-safelisted bir yöntem değildir, bu yüzden her çapraz kaynaklı QUERY bir preflight tetikler. Sunucunuz Access-Control-Allow-Methods içinde QUERY listelemelidir.

Boşluklar ağın ortasındadır: yöntemleri izin listesine alan veya önbelleğini gövdeye göre anahtarlamayan ters proxy'ler, API ağ geçitleri, WAF'ler ve CDN'ler. Yayına almadan önce her atlamayı kontrol edin. APIs You Won't Hate bülteni, birçok web çerçevesinin QUERY'yi doğrudan veya özel yöntem yönlendirmesiyle zaten işlediğini belirtiyor.

İstemcileri bozmadan QUERY'yi nasıl benimsersiniz

POST arama uç noktalarınızı söküp atmanız gerekmez.

  1. QUERY'yi POST rotasının yanına ekleyin. İkisini de aynı işleyiciye yönlendirin. Yeni istemciler QUERY kullanır; eskileri çalışmaya devam eder.
  2. Duyurun. Kaynakta Accept-Query döndürün ve OPTIONS ile 405 yanıtlarında Allow içine QUERY ekleyin.
  3. Content-Type'ı zorunlu kılın. RFC'nin önerdiği gibi 400 veya 415 döndürün ve ayrıştırılan ancak çalıştırılamayan sorgular için 422 döndürün.
  4. 405 veya 501'de geri düşün. Bir atlama QUERY'yi reddettiğinde istemciler aynı gövdeyi POST olarak yeniden denemelidir.
  5. CORS'u düzeltin. Tarayıcı istemcileri için Access-Control-Allow-Methods içine QUERY ekleyin.
  6. Önbellekleme konusunda karar verin. Paylaşımlı önbellekleme yalnızca önbelleğiniz gövdeye göre anahtarlıyorsa etkinleştirin. Aksi halde bir Location URI'si döndürün ve istemcilerin onu GET'lemesine izin verin.
  7. Belgeleyin. OpenAPI 3.2'de işlemi path item üzerindeki query: altında tanımlayın: 
openapi: 3.2.0
paths:
  /products:
    query:
      summary: Search products
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductQuery'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Matching products

Kısa, basit filtreler GET üzerinde sorgu dizileri olarak kalabilir. RFC 10008'in kendisi, sorgunuz bu kadar kısaysa GET'in muhtemelen daha iyi seçim olduğunu söyler.

Kodlama ajanınızın Apidog CLI ile bir QUERY uç noktasını test etmesine izin verin

Yeni bir yöntem, mutlu yolu, her hata kodunu ve geri dönüş rotasını kontrol etmek anlamına gelir. Bunu Claude Code, Codex veya Cursor'a verin ve Apidog CLI'yı kullanmasına izin verin.

CLI'yi kurun, oturum açın ve ajanınıza Apidog becerisini ekleyin:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Ardından ajanınıza bir istem verin:

In Apidog project <projectId>, add a QUERY /products endpoint that takes a
JSON body {q, limit}. Create test cases that assert 200 with an array for a
valid body, 415 for Content-Type text/plain, and 400 with no Content-Type.
Run them against the staging environment and summarize any failures.

Ajan her şemayı okur, yükünü doğrular ve ancak ondan sonra şunları yazar:

apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file endpoint.json
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json

Yazdığı endpoint.json, "method": "query" değerini ayarlar; CLI'nin endpoint-create şeması bunu get, post ve WebDAV yöntemleriyle birlikte listeler. Çalıştırmayı Apidog uygulamasında görmek için --upload-report ekleyin. -r junit ile aynı apidog run komutu CI'ya girer; apidog run ile CI'da API testleri nasıl çalıştırılır ve Apidog CLI, Claude Code'da nasıl kullanılır sayfalarına bakın. Apidog'un Ücretsiz planı 4 kullanıcıya kadar kapsar.

SSS

HTTP QUERY yöntemi resmi bir standart mı? Evet. RFC 10008, Haziran 2026'da yayımlanan bir Standards Track, Proposed Standard RFC'dir ve IANA, QUERY'yi HTTP Yöntem Kaydı'nda güvenli ve idempotent olarak listeler.

QUERY sadece gövdeli GET mi? Yakın, ancak daha iyi tanımlanmıştır. RFC 9110 bir GET gövdesine anlambilim vermez, bu yüzden aracılar onu yok sayabilir veya reddedebilir. QUERY, gövdeyi sorgu yapar, bir Content-Type gerektirir ve gövdeyi önbellek anahtarına dahil eder.

POST yerine ne zaman QUERY kullanmalıyım? Bir URL için çok büyük veya çok hassas olan her salt okunur arama veya filtre için QUERY kullanın. Bir şey oluşturan veya değiştiren istekler için POST'u saklayın.

Tarayıcılar QUERY istekleri gönderebilir mi? Evet, özel bir yöntemle fetch aracılığıyla. Çapraz kaynaklı QUERY istekleri her zaman bir CORS preflight gerektirir, bu yüzden sunucunuz yönteme izin vermelidir.

QUERY yanıtları önbelleğe alınır mı? Alınabilir. Önbellekler, istek gövdesini ve meta verilerini önbellek anahtarına dahil etmelidir. Birçok CDN ve proxy bunu henüz yapmıyor, bu yüzden kendinizinkini kontrol edin veya istemcilerin GET'leyebileceği bir Location URI'si döndürün.

OpenAPI QUERY'yi destekliyor mu? OpenAPI 3.2, QUERY işlemleri için Path Item Object'e bir query alanı ekler, böylece onları uzantı olmadan belgeleyebilirsiniz.

title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations
description:
arXiv:2610.36389v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems

title: Climate downscaling with likelihood functional flow matching
description:
arXiv:2610.33482v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decisions about heat, frost and flooding are made locally, yet reanalyses and climate models resolve tens of kilometres. Generative downscalers add kilometre-scale detail with uncertainty, but are tied to a grid, costly to sample and lack a tractable likelihood. Here we introduce CD-FFM, a functional flow-matching model that treats the high-resolution field as a continuous random field that one model can query at any location and resolution. Its velocity acts pointwise, so spatial variability comes from a noise prior fitted to the observed spectrum and every observation has an exact likelihood. Downscaling ERA5 to 1 km daily temperature over Fennoscandia, CD-FFM lowers the continuous ranked probability score by 27-31% against regression and 12-18% against a forty-times larger neural operator in each of three test years, and outperforms a CorrDiff-style diffusion model while sampling about fifty times faster. The same model transfers to precipitation and makes large kilometre-scale ensembles affordable.

title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.36308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
