title: Do We Need an LLM to Know Why Sources Conflict? Decision Models for Knowledge-Conflict Typing in RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.36915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When the sources retrieved for a query disagree, the right response depends on why they disagree: a question with several valid answers, a contested topic, stale information and a false source each call for different behaviour. Cattan et al. (2025) showed that telling a generator the conflict type improves its responses by about 24 points, but that predicting the type is hard even for frontier LLMs. We study whether typed decision models, which return probabilities over fixed options in a single forward pass instead of generating text, can do this classification fast and cheaply. Using the CONFLICTS benchmark and the original paper's prompt verbatim, we evaluate all 11 decision models served by one commercial inference gateway, from 7 providers, against Gemini models on identical inputs. Asked directly, the decision models reach 50.0--67.0% accuracy; 10 of the 11 match or exceed Gemini 2.5 Flash, the paper's model (61.3%), at 4--39x lower billed cost (2 were free) and 2.6--6.0x lower latency. The current Gemini 3.8 Flash (70.0%) is significantly more accurate than 8 of them, but sending each decision model's least confident quarter of queries to it gives a cascade statistically tied with it for 8 of the 11, at 25--37% of its cost. End to end, answers generated with the types of 10 of the 11 follow the expected behaviour as often as with the LLM's types. Decomposing the taxonomy into yes/no questions lowers accuracy for every model, and a repair fitted on one model does not transfer. Pre-specified diagnostics show that dates play no measurable role and that sensitivity to source order varies widely between models. Decision models detect a planted false source less reliably than the LLM as hard labels, but their probabilities still separate planted from clean sources. We release code, prompts and all model outputs at https://github.com/Parv17k/decision-models-conflict-typing.

title: Rust solved the compatibility trap with editions
description:
Delete a user from a stock SQLite database, forget to delete their posts, and nothing complains. Insert a new user afterward and, because SQLite recycles ROWIDs, that account can take the integer ID the deleted user held. The orphaned posts then join cleanly to the new account. The author's example runs it end to end: Bob writes "Hello, I am Bob" and deletes his account, Alice signs up and gets Bob's recycled ID, and a join across the users and posts tables returns "Alice | Hello, I am Bob." No error fires at any step.

The cause is the first of several SQLite defaults the author argues are simply wrong: foreign key constraints are ignored unless you enable them with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. As far as the author knows, SQLite is the only RDBMS that doesn't enforce them out of the box. With the pragma on, that stray DELETE fails with "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed (19)" instead of quietly corrupting the join.

Type affinity is the second. A column declared INTEGER isn't restricted to integers. SQLite stores a valid numeric string as a number and leaves anything else as-is, so an INTEGER column accepts the text 'Way too long, I mean come on' and keeps it verbatim. The author once cleaned up a project where code had written the strings '1' and '0' into a column meant to hold the integers 1 and 0. STRICT tables turn the mismatch into "cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column" at insert time, and the ANY type still covers a column that should genuinely hold any value. There is no pragma to make every table strict, so you tag each CREATE TABLE by hand.

Third is concurrency. SQLite allows many readers but one writer, and by default a second process reaching for the write lock gets an immediate SQLITE_BUSY instead of waiting. The author traces real-world bugs to this default, systems that would sometimes just crash, and wrote retry loops by hand to work around it. PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000 makes the writer wait up to five seconds for the lock first. Concurrent writers are never fast, but interactive cleanup with the sqlite3 tool or an occasional admin script shouldn't be able to crash the main process by colliding with it.

Fourth is performance, where the big one is that the write-ahead log is off by default. PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL gives a large write speed-up in most cases, and PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL cuts disk syncs further without risking corruption under WAL.

Each of these has a one-line fix, and the reason usually cited for why they stay wrong by default is backwards compatibility. Flip a default and you break software that quietly relied on the old behaviour, and you teach people to fear upgrading the library at all. The author draws the parallel to being afraid to upgrade Python because every upgrade breaks something. Not breaking your dependents is a real and uncommon virtue, which is also what keeps SQLite stuck. Until that changes, you apply it yourself: enable the settings with their pragmas and add STRICT to every table.

Rust's editions are the escape the author proposes. A single opt-in pragma would set a whole generation of defaults at once. The sketch is PRAGMA edition = 2026, standing in for foreign_keys = ON, busy_timeout = 5000, journal_mode = WAL, and synchronous = NORMAL, plus strict tables as the default. A database that never sets an edition keeps today's behaviour, so nothing breaks; new code opts into the sane set in one line.

The year in the name does real work. The author takes it straight from Rust editions and prefers it to a flat switch like JavaScript's "use strict" because sensible defaults shift over time. If Hctree's WAL2 reaches the main branch around 2034, PRAGMA edition = 2034 could set journal_mode = WAL2 while edition = 2026 stays on plain WAL. Each edition is a snapshot of what good defaults looked like that year, and code records which snapshot it was written against.

Making strict tables the default would cost one genuinely useful quirk, which the lobste.rs user 'zie' raised. Non-strict SQLite decides a column's affinity from substrings in the declared type: anything containing "INT" gets INTEGER affinity, "CHAR", "CLOB" or "TEXT" gets TEXT affinity, and so on. That lets you invent type names like DATETIME, KEY_VALUE_SET or COLOR and have a connector read them back to serialize and deserialize the column, or just use them as documentation. Strict tables drop that. The author's answer is type aliases, something like CREATE TYPE KEY_VALUE_SET = TEXT usable inside a strict table. As the lobste.rs user 'masklinn' pointed out, SQL 99 already specifies exactly this as CREATE DOMAIN, constraints included, so SQLite wouldn't have to invent anything, only implement the standard statement.

title: Tree Depth and Sample-Quality-Associated Features: Two Hidden Factors in Boruta Selection for RNA-Seq Data Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.33307v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Boruta is a widely used method for selecting gene panels from RNA sequencing data, and its most used implementation recommends Random Forest trees of depth 3 to 7, an untested setting. We tested whether this setting changes which genes are selected, using pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (10,469 tumors, 33 cancer types) and breast cancer PAM50 subtyping (981 tumors, 5 subtypes). A leakage-free protocol fitted every label-dependent step inside training folds, measured every effect against seed-to-seed variation, and held out a locked test set per task. In pan-cancer data, shallow trees changed the selection far more than a new seed did: the top-500 overlap with unlimited-depth selections was 0.37 at depth 5, against 0.84 to 0.93 between seeds at depth 5 or unlimited depth. Shallow trees confirmed 3.5 times fewer genes, missed markers of large classes and produced less accurate 50-gene panels (balanced accuracy 0.809 vs 0.889). The effect vanished once the cap reached about 60 to 75% of the depth that unrestricted trees grow to, set mainly by the number of classes, not sample size, and leaving depth uncapped cost no accuracy in either task. The effect replicated in a second cross-validation repeat and under permutation importance. About a third of pre-filtered candidates also tracked sample quality within class; a within-class filter removed them without loss of test accuracy (balanced accuracy 0.943 vs 0.942 with 1,000 genes). We recommend uncapped trees, or a cap chosen from the realized tree depth, and a within-class quality filter before Boruta.

title: Your WAV file says it's empty: keeping recordings readable when the process gets killed
description:
I found the bug through a test that transcribed nothing. A streaming speech-to-text harness read a recorded call, sent zero audio, and reported success. The WAV file was several megabytes, but Python's wave module said it had 0 frames. So did the media players.

Then I checked the rest of the recordings folder: 4 of 19 files looked the same. Every one of them came from a session that had ended with Ctrl+C instead of a clean stop. These were interview recordings people wanted to keep. The audio was all there; the files just said otherwise.

Why the file lies

A canonical PCM WAV file starts with a 44-byte header, and two of its fields are sizes:

  • bytes 4–7: RIFF chunk size, which is the file size minus 8;
  • bytes 40–43: data chunk size, the number of audio bytes that follow.

A streaming recorder doesn't know the final size when it starts. The usual approach writes the header with zeros, appends audio for the whole call, then seeks back and patches both sizes on close. If the process dies before close, the sizes stay zero. Readers that trust the header, which is most of them, see an empty file. Some APIs scan the raw data anyway and hide the problem, which is why it took a while to notice.

Fix 1: checkpoint the header while recording

The recorder in our Rust audio engine now patches the header periodically instead of only on close. A dedicated writer thread receives PCM chunks and writes them through a BufWriter. After every 5 seconds of audio (sample_rate × 2 bytes × 5), it checkpoints:

fn checkpoint(&mut self) -> Result<()> {
    self.writer.flush().context("failed to flush WAV audio")?;
    self.writer.seek(SeekFrom::Start(4))?;
    self.writer.write_all(&(self.data_len + WAV_HEADER_LEN - 8).to_le_bytes())?;
    self.writer.seek(SeekFrom::Start(40))?;
    self.writer.write_all(&self.data_len.to_le_bytes())?;
    self.writer.flush().context("failed to checkpoint WAV recording")?;
    self.writer.seek(SeekFrom::Start(u64::from(WAV_HEADER_LEN) + u64::from(self.data_len)))?;
    self.checkpoint_data_len = self.data_len;
    Ok(())
}

The order matters. Audio is flushed first, so the header never claims bytes that aren't on disk yet. Then both size fields are patched and flushed, and the writer seeks back to the end so the next chunk appends rather than overwrites. Closing the recorder is just one last checkpoint.

If the process is killed now, the header is at most one checkpoint behind. Players see a valid file that ends a few seconds early, and whatever audio reached the disk after the last checkpoint is still in the file for recovery (below).

Two guards came with it:

  • Size limit. WAV sizes are 32-bit. The writer uses checked arithmetic and refuses to grow past 4 GiB instead of wrapping the counter, which would produce a header that lies in a new way.
  • Backpressure. The capture side sends chunks over a bounded channel of 128. When it's full, for example when a reconnect releases a backlog of audio, the sender waits up to 100 ms before giving up. A momentary stall shouldn't end the recording for the rest of the call.

Testing a crash, for real

A unit test can't kill its own process, so the test spawns its own test binary as a child. The child runs an ignored helper test that writes 80,000 samples (5 seconds at 16 kHz) and then sleeps. The parent waits until the file is 160,044 bytes with a data size of 160,000 in the header, then kills the child:

let mut child = command.spawn().unwrap();
let ready = loop {
    if std::fs::read(&path).ok().is_some_and(|bytes| bytes.len() >= 160_044 &&
        u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[40..44].try_into().unwrap()) == 160_000) { break true; }
    if std::time::Instant::now() >= deadline { break false; }
    std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(20));
};
let _ = child.kill();

After the kill it reads the file again and checks the size and the header field. The test proves what users depend on: a hard kill leaves a file that standard readers open. On Windows the child gets the CREATE_NO_WINDOW flag so the test doesn't flash a console.

Fix 2: repair the files you already have

Old recordings still had zero-size headers, and even with checkpoints the last few seconds sit after the recorded size. The app has a "recover audio" action on a finished session. The Python side is careful in a few specific ways:

  1. Refuse anything unexpected. The file must be inside the recordings folder (no symlinks), start with RIFF/WAVEfmt, have data at offset 36, and be 16-bit mono PCM with a sane sample rate. Anything else is "not a recording of ours" and is left alone.
  2. Compute the real size from the file length, rounded down to whole samples: (size - 44) // alignment * alignment. A trailing half-sample from a write cut short gets trimmed and reported as such.
  3. Do nothing if the header is already right. Recovery runs repeatedly without side effects.
  4. Never edit in place. Copy the original to name.wav.before-recovery, adding a numeric suffix if one already exists. Write the patched header and the audio to a temporary file in the same folder, fsync, then os.replace it over the original. If the source changes size mid-copy, it raises instead of producing a half-file. 
patched = bytearray(header)
struct.pack_into("<I", patched, 4, data_size + 36)
struct.pack_into("<I", patched, 40, data_size)

os.replace is atomic on the same volume, so at every moment there's either the old file or the complete new one, plus the backup.

The endpoint also refuses to run while the session is still recording. Repairing a file that another process is appending to is a race you don't want.

What I'd tell myself earlier

  • If your format has sizes in the header, decide what a crash leaves behind before you ship. "We patch it on close" means "we lose it on crash".
  • Flush data before you update the header that describes it.
  • Test the crash with a real process kill, not with a mock.
  • Repair tools should be idempotent, keep a backup, and replace atomically. The user's only copy is in that file.

title: How to Connect HtmlSave with ChatGPT via MCP: Build and Host Websites Using AI
description:
Imagine prompting ChatGPT to design a website and watching it instantly write the code, organize the assets, and publish it live to the web with a public URL—all within seconds.

With Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, you can connect your HtmlSave account directly into ChatGPT as a custom tool. In this tutorial, we will walk you through setting up the HtmlSave MCP server in ChatGPT and using it to generate and host multi-file web applications automatically.

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have:

  1. An active account on HtmlSave.com (with API / MCP access enabled).
  2. A ChatGPT Plus/Team/Enterprise account supporting MCP plugins/integrations.

Step 1: Generate Your MCP Server URL on HtmlSave

HtmlSave provides an authenticated MCP server endpoint tied directly to your account.

  1. Go to htmlsave.com and log in.
  2. Click your Profile icon in the top navigation bar.
  3. Scroll down to the Advanced Settings section and open the API Token tab.
  4. Click + Generate API Token (or refresh if needed).
  5. Locate the MCP Server URL field at the bottom.
  6. Click the Copy button next to the MCP Server URL (it will look like https://mcp.htmlsave.com/?token=hs_tok_...).

Step 2: Add HtmlSave as a Custom MCP Server in ChatGPT

Now configure ChatGPT to communicate with your HtmlSave server endpoint.

  1. Open chatgpt.com.
  2. Click your profile name in the bottom-left corner and select Settings.
  3. In the sidebar, navigate to Integrations / Plugins.
  4. Click Browse directory in the top right corner.
  5. Click the Add dropdown menu in the upper-right corner and select Add custom MCP server.
  6. Fill in the server details:
    • Name: HTMLSave
    • Connection: Select Server URL and paste your copied MCP URL from Step 1.
    • Authentication: Select No authentication (your secret token is already embedded in the URL).
    • Check the box: "I understand and want to continue".
  7. Click Create as a plugin.
  8. In the confirmation dialog, click Connect HTMLSAVE. Once verified, a green banner confirming "HTMLSave is now connected" will appear.

Step 3: Prompt ChatGPT to Build and Deploy Your Website

Once connected, you can call HtmlSave directly in any conversation using @HTMLSave.

  1. Start a New Chat in ChatGPT.
  2. In the message box, mention the tool: @HTMLSave.
  3. Enter your prompt. For example:

Prompt:

@HTMLSave Can you create a simple site using Three.js CDN to create a beautiful clock widget with separate HTML, CSS, and JS files.

  1. When the permission prompt appears ("Allow ChatGPT to use HTMLSave?"), click Always allow.
  2. ChatGPT will process your request, generate your files (index.html, styles.css, app.js), deploy them via the MCP connection, and return:
    • A live link (e.g., https://yoursubdomain.htmlsave.net).
    • An overview of created files and features.

Step 4: Verify Your Live Site and Assets

  1. Test the Live URL: Click the link provided by ChatGPT in the response to view your interactive, fully functioning website running live on the internet.
  2. Inspect Files in HtmlSave:
    • Return to your HtmlSave Dashboard > Manage Sites.
    • Your newly created website will appear in your site list.
    • Click Update Site to view and edit individual assets (home page, styles.css, app.js, etc.), check view analytics, or adjust subdomain settings.

Summary

By bridging ChatGPT with HtmlSave via MCP, you transform ChatGPT from an AI that merely writes code into an autonomous agent capable of deploying production-ready landing pages, interactive widgets, and multi-file web apps on demand.

title: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging
description:
arXiv:2610.36379v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.

title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
description:
arXiv:2610.36150v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/

title: Task-Utility IQA: Rethinking Image Quality Assessment in Embodied Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.35905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.
